The name [of the work] is *Cintyācintyaviśvasādākhyam*.
I bow to that trunk of the elephant, the circle of union with Caṇḍikā, which with its pillar-like snout shatters the ornaments of the wild beasts. || 1 ||
Having prostrated before Sadāśiva, the omniscient Lord of the gods of gods,
Maheśa, having performed salutations and other marks of reverence, questioned him.
In the beginning, Śrīṇṭha, the lord of the mountain-born goddess, questioned Maheśvara;
he who is Brahmā, the Lord of Truth, the Lord of Gods, and the cause of the cause of Rudra.
Having bowed at his feet, he spoke thus to Ratnagarbha:
"The one who fulfills desires, the one born of yoga, the one to be meditated upon, the cause, and likewise the unconquered."
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabhedaka, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyaṃbhuva, and Anala.
Vīra and Raurava, as well as Makuṭa and Vimala; Candrajñāna and Bimba, and likewise Prodgīta and Lalita. (6)
The Siddha, Santāna, Śarvokta, and Pārameśvara, as well as the Kiraṇa and Vātula, [are the scriptures]. || 7 ||
That which was previously described as "Diti" is known to have innumerable subdivisions;
because of its vastness, O Lord, one should omit the details of that which has arisen from it.
O Ānandin, out of my particular affection for you, I have revealed this inconceivable work of eight thousand verses called the Viśvasādākhyam. (11)
Endowed with knowledge and joined with the practice of ritual action, each succeeding stage is superior to the last;
yet that which is beyond action and free from stain is devoid of both cause and example.
Therefore, O Nandin, understand this: it is the supreme, true path;
it is a synonym for right vision, the true path, and knowledge. (13)
Śrī Nandikeśvara said: O Lord, why would there be the path of the Sahas? How does the path of the Putras come to be?
By what means does the path of the Dāsas arise? O Blessed One, please tell this to me.
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the Sahamārga, which has the scope of twenty-five syllables;
it is liberated from meditation on form and joined with meditation on the formless. || 15 ||
That which is endowed with manifold means, free from manifold obstacles, and devoid of illusion, is known as the Sahaja-mārga (the Innate Path). || 16 ||
One's own nature, the path of the companion, and the synonyms for yoga—this is the path of the son and one's true essence; indeed, the Guru alone is the deity.
One should meditate with devotion upon one's own auspicious guru, the bestower of knowledge;
likewise, [one should seek] the knowledge proclaimed in all the Agamas, as well as all sovereign powers.
The attainment of the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) occurs entirely through the command of the Guru;
this is called the path of the son (putramārga), and likewise the path of the servant (dāsamārga) is spoken of.

Whether one has a shaven head, matted hair, or a topknot, provided one is engaged in the practice of subjugation (vaśya-sādhana), it should be understood that his garment is merely a loincloth; how then could there be an upper robe?
(5) Alms-food is for the sake of nourishing the body, and likewise the construction of temples;
monasteries and the like should be established by those committed to lifelong celibacy for the purpose of providing a dwelling. (21)
One should also diligently establish water-distribution stations, the acquisition of Śiva-scriptures, as well as tanks and water-lifting mechanisms for wells.
One should provide the construction of a garden, the gathering and binding of flowers, water for the purpose of bathing, and the cleansing of the body and so forth. (23)
Sprinkling and smearing, and so forth, constitute the path of the servant (dāsamārga);
immediately following that are the path of the true one (sanmārga), the path of the companion (sahamārga), and the path of the son (putramārga).
"O Blessed One, O Lord, tell me: how is the path of the servant (dāsamārga) distinguished?
The Lord said: It is the true path, the jewel of reality, indeed the sole leader of all principles. (25)
(6) Between the path of servitude and the path of the son, the path of the son is superior;
nevertheless, O God, the path of the son is primarily dependent upon the Guru. 26.
Therefore, the path of the son (putramārga) should be known as the best by its very nature;
among these four paths, it is to be followed by one who desires liberation.
Even if it is deficient by even one [limb], it breaks the ladder to liberation; having obtained fruits such as sovereign power and the like, one undergoes rebirth again. (28)

Then, having obtained the yoga of knowledge and the fourfold practice of ritual action, and having gone forth and manifested [the truth], he who is of the nature of liberation proceeds gradually. (29)
Through association, Śiva is to be known; thereafter comes affection.
[He bestows] grace upon his grandson, the servant-path that brings joy to Śiva. (30)
Therefore, O Sadānandin, with every effort this fourfold [teaching] should always be practiced for the sake of the cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (31)
O Nandikeśvara! This hand-held vessel, which resides in my own hand, has been given by you and me with special intent; it bestows all that is desired.

Thus ends the first chapter, "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the section on the inconceivable descent [of power] within the *Upabhedatantra*, which is known as the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*, in its *Kriyāpāda* (Action Section).
The Lord.
O Nandikeśvara, listen as I describe the characteristics of an Ācārya:
he is so called because he correctly practices knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct. || 1 ||
Therefore, he is indeed called the Ācārya for the sake of the welfare of all beings. Two types of Ācāryas are declared; the first should be one who is dispassionate.
The second would be the elemental (bhautika), while the first is specifically [the spiritual];
then follows the lifelong celibate student (ājanmabrahmacārī) and the ascetic (yati).
And thus, that which was stated regarding the first and the second [stages], as well as the second [set]— namely,
the householder and the forest-dweller— is declared to be fourfold.
Birth is indeed said to be of two kinds, known as initiation (dīkṣā) and procreation (prasava).
One who is established in the final stage (naiṣṭhika) and one who is not yet so established (anaiṣṭhika)—he should initiate householders in due order.
But the Bhautika should not perform initiation other than that of a householder. The Bhautika is joined with the Liṅga; for him, no [specific] caste exists. (6)
Because he lived together with his wife and because he bore her characteristics,
he was utterly devoid of any continuous stream of thought, being utterly deluded by worldly conventions.
O Nandikeśvara, one should initiate [disciples] solely on account of the distinction of caste!
Now listen, O observer of good vows, to the characteristics of these preceptors. || 8 ||
He was non-violent, truthful, supremely devoted to compassion for all living beings,
patient, tranquil in mind, and great in both restraint and favor.
Endowed with proper conduct, skillful, devoted to recitation and meditation, joined with the initiation of higher knowledge, and proficient in devotion to the Guru. || 10 ||
One who knows the four-limbed internal scripture consisting of knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct;
who is free from hypocrisy and deceit; and who has abandoned trivial activities. (11)
He who knows the virtues and faults of disciples, is wise, has conquered his senses, is completely free from attachment and aversion, and is endowed with the quality of compassion. || 12 ||
He is the upholder of the essence of knowledge among all commitments;
endowed with the three empowerments, he has reached the further shore of the three modes of movement.
Endowed with the threefold command and possessed of the threefold sound, he is united with the experience of Śiva; he is the one who cuts through doubt and is himself free from doubt.
He was a knower of mantras for subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, paralyzing, and eradication;
he was free from diseases such as leprosy and was supremely handsome. (15)
Free from pride, free from egoism, free from cruelty, and free from conceptual construction;
devoid of darkness, a knower of the scriptures, and a contemplator of the ultimate truth. (16)
One endowed with these characteristics is called an excellent preceptor (ācāryavara), especially if he is a householder provided with a lawful wife. || 17 ||
One who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics is called a material teacher (bhautikācārya).
Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the characteristics of the teacher, in the Kriyāpāda of the Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra, within the Upabhedatantra.
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods! For the sake of protecting the world, and especially for us, please describe the characteristics of one who is not an instructor of ritual action (karmānācārya).

The Lord said: "One who is devoid of the initiation of higher knowledge (vijñāna-dīkṣā), who is bereft of devotion to the guru, who transgresses the guru’s command, and who even contemplates the faults of the guru; || 2 ||"
He was covetous of his teacher's property and desired all possessions;
he was devoid of service to his teacher and was full of censure toward him. || 3 ||

One who acts against the wishes of the guru, one who shows disrespect to his elder brother, one whose eyes are moistened by anger and greed, one who is malicious, and one who adopts a hypocritical guise; || 4 ||
He was untruthful, greedy, a thief, crooked, foolish, and deceitful; he was fickle, a doer of evil, wicked, and engaged in base actions.
He is egoistic, ungrateful, and a defiler of the conduct of his commitments; being devoid of the yoga of knowledge, he is afflicted by diseases such as consumption and leprosy. (6)
The rogue, the one attached to sense-objects, the immoral, the deceitful, as well as the one who knows and the one who does not know, the arrogant, the glutton, and likewise the foul-mouthed. || 7 ||
One endowed with such qualities as these is indeed not worthy of worship on the surface of the earth;
one should not confer upon him the title of Ācārya nor perform his consecration.
If the consecration is performed through negligence, one shall incur fault.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of One Who is Not an Ācārya."
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of disciples; listen.
One who is endowed with non-violence and truthfulness, and is free from anger and greed— || 1 ||
Patient, possessed of a resolute mind, and free from all afflictions, [he should provide] a seat, a tooth-stick, and likewise water for washing the feet. || 2 ||
Then follows the stretching of the feet, bathing with ashes,
the massaging of the soles, as well as wrestling and debate.

Furthermore, one should not engage in leaning heavily against anything in the presence of a guru, nor should one indulge in excessive laughter, arrogance, playful gestures, or stretching out one's limbs.

He who does not place his hand upon the region of his hip in the presence of the Guru—whether during the exposition [of the teachings], the consecration, the mandala, or the gathering of disciples—[is at fault]. (5)
(15) If one is on the road, one should perform the guru’s command with a single morsel [of food]:
clapping the hands, dancing, singing verses, and sleeping. (6)
One should avoid the disheveling of matted hair in the presence of the guru;
likewise, one should not step into the shadow of the teacher's dwelling or the shadow of the teacher himself. || 7 ||
One should present [the gift] to the teacher with sweet speech;
however, if the teacher’s own teacher has been seen, one should likewise salute the preceptor.
Or, through initiation as the primary factor, or through affection, service, and respect,
one should bestow the status of seniority upon the virtuous by designating them as a guru.
In that regard, O Nandikeśvara, the eldest brother should be honored like a guru;
he should travel as one intent on avoiding reproach, even at night, through water, in fear, or on the road.
One should always adopt good conduct, grasping at virtues and not grasping at faults;
success lies in the accumulation of virtues, but there is no success in the collection of faults.
Listen to the superior quality that belongs to all disciples alike: devotion, faith, freedom from malice, and steadfastness in obeying the guru’s command. (12)
Faith, tranquility, forgiveness, truthfulness, as well as purity, sacred learning, and gratitude—if these twelve qualities exist in a disciple, [he is fit]. (13)
He is the foremost among disciples, yet these others are not his primary ones;
even if a disciple is endowed with devotion, the guru will not teach him if he does not [deserve it]. (14)
It is certain that the sin committed by the disciple's ignorance falls upon the teacher;
therefore, one should examine all qualities with every effort.

One should initiate [the disciple] when there is a preponderance of virtues over minor faults and at the proper time; specifically, at the end of a year of service, following the examination of his qualities and defects. (16)

Even if [the disciple] possesses superior qualities, the good disciple should perform the office of an ācārya for him through the initiations, purificatory rites (saṃskāras), and so forth; this [office] proceeds gradually until the limit of higher knowledge (vijñāna) is reached.
By the mere act of initiation, even a disciple becomes free from all defects;
yet, subsequently, defects may arise through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (18)
Having thus informed the Guru of all that [occurred] due to calamities and so forth,
as well as every fault, he should again pay obeisance to the supreme teacher.
And the preceptor shall subsequently proclaim the rule for atonement;
in the absence of the preceptor, it should be performed in the presence of the eldest [brother].
Through expiation one becomes pure; through purity, one attains liberation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the disciple, within the *Upabheda* known as the *Acintyaviśvasāda*.
(19) I shall here explain the secret extraction of mantras and so forth, which is the "Womb of Jewels" (*ratnagarbha*);
it is called the weapon that protects the world, beginning with the contemplation of the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).

The meaning of all mantras is that which is called Sādākhyā; it consists of the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the consciousness of Śiva. It is devoid of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, yet it is the sphere of mind, speech, and body.
It is immeasurable, peerless, free from conceptual proliferation, and beyond defining characteristics;
it is partless, the supreme reality, infinite, immovable, and eternal. (3)
Formless and changeless, consisting of mind and free from affliction,
it is without support, self-cognizable, the fundamental substratum, and higher than the highest.
This reality of Śiva is declared to be the culmination of all principles—unthinkable, immutable, subtle, and devoid of logical causes or illustrative examples. (5)
That body, which is the cause of persistence and origination, is of two kinds:
it is considered to be twofold, namely, the single intermediate [body] and the single collective [body]. (7)
There is no need for Sauvīrya in that task; there are only flesh, bones, and blood.
Its form is like a rainbow, a single embodiment of supreme power.
One who dwells in the center of the effortful joy, endowed with power, is equal to Brahmā by means of his own thumb; above that is the protector Śiva.
And that form should always be meditated upon when [the deity] possesses the nature of an Ārya;
for the sake of the accomplishment of practitioners, this supreme subtle form is [to be cultivated]. (10)
Three-eyed, four-armed, fierce, with the luster of a blue lotus petal,
with hair standing erect and tawny eyes, he is the supreme performer of universal protection. (11)
This form of the Guru, endowed with the nine rasas and slightly adorned with fangs,
should be known as the very form of Śiva for the devotees of Śiva.
For the sake of the accomplishment of practitioners, this supreme subtle form is declared to be the body of the Guru; here it is called the body of emanation.
The god is endowed with four colors, adorned with matted locks and a crown;
he has a single body, four faces, and is possessed of twelve eyes.
Four-faced, with four noses, four ears, and four petals; endowed with eight arms and joined with eight ornaments. || 15 ||
Red, black, white, and dark-blue are the colors starting from the east.
In the east, he holds a chisel and a trident; in the south, a sword and a serpent. (16)
The western [face] is gentle, endowed with a noose and a goad, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
it is the sky-clad Lord, equal [to the others], and possessed of four faces. (17)
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with divine garlands, his limbs were anointed with divine perfumes; he sat upon a seat facing in every direction.
The true path is called Śaiva; it is the mouth of Śiva. That which is named Sandhyā is declared to be the southern [face], and Pināka is the western.
The northern [face] is declared to belong to Viṣṇu, consisting of will, knowledge, action, and so forth;
from the grace of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, that which is called Sanmeṣa arises. (20)
Each one of the [faces] beginning with Īśāna in the east should be known as fivefold;
it is said to be endowed with five faces by means of will, knowledge, action, and so forth.
The powers of will, knowledge, and action arise together as the state known as Sādākhya.
Each one of the [faces] beginning with Īśāna in the east should be known as fivefold;
they are said to be endowed with five faces through [the powers of] will, knowledge, action, and so forth.
The power of will, knowledge, and action arises equally from that which is called Sādākhya.
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with every kind of garland. || 25 ||

In the right [hands], he holds a trident, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a vajra, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness; in the left, a noose, a goad, a serpent, a skull-topped staff, and the gesture of granting boons. (26)
The god was clad in celestial garments, possessed long arms, and had resplendent nails;
his limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garlands.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now proclaim the middle-level *tattvasiddhānta*, which provides the singular true path, along with the *arghya-mantra* in its various forms.
The sound, the primordial sound, the sound joined with the peaceful crown;
endowed with the syllables situated between *bha* and *ya*, and between *ha* and *ya*. (29)
The syllable of Varuṇa joined with fire (Ra), and Marut (Ya) endowed with the sixth vowel (Ū)—this ninefold mantra resides within all beings. (30)
(25) Having *ha* and *kṣma*, with the two final syllables *la* and *cu*, endowed with the causal seed-syllable (*sāyuka*),
preceded by the *praṇava*, and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*. || 31 ||
One should join the mantra consisting of the manifest and unmanifest, which is called Sādākhya and constitutes the body of the mantra, with Śiva during the time of worship and recitation. || 32 ||
One should perform the remaining rites as before, [visualizing him] with a black face and hair standing erect. || 33 ||
I shall describe the form of Manonmanī, endowed with four arms,
possessing three eyes, resembling the color of the dawn, and worthy of being meditated upon.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with a bodice of *kaulaka* cloth,
the goddess holds a lotus and a blue water-lily, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness.
She should be meditated upon on the left side of Sadāśiva by the best of practitioners, as before... [omitted] ...endowed with the letter Na. (36)
The supreme mantra associated with Bindu and Nāda belongs to the dispassionate;
however, dispassion (virāgitā) consists in the avoidance of passion and other such attachments directed toward Śiva. (37)
Therefore, one endowed with the knowledge of reality should always offer salutations.
They know the supreme seed-syllable of Viṣṇu to be pervaded by Nāda and Bindu;
because his essential nature is the bliss of Śiva, Viṣṇu is always to be worshipped by the wise. (39)
Because her form was divided by Viṣṇu, the power of Viṣṇu remains indivisible for the sake of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and liberation, and for the expansion of the Vedas and Āgamas. (40)
For the purpose of entering into all scriptures, for generating devotion,
and for the benefit of living beings, [I shall explain] the supreme truth known as Sādākhya. (41)
The God may have one face or many faces, two arms or many arms;
he assumes various forms and is endowed with various colors.
Hara, who is endowed with the meaning of various scriptures and devoted to various divine sports,
did not see Ananta seated there, nor the five gentle dancers.
The God of gods, adorned with serpents, is endowed with manifold forms;
he is joined with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon serving as his crest-ornament.
The omnipresent Lord, whose banner is the bull, is mounted upon a bull and accompanied by Bhavānī;
the sun and moon are his two eyes, and fire is his eye of flame.
The Great Goddess became the eye of the earth, while the Lord of the Thirty-three [Indra] became gold;
he produced the Sound (nāda) conjoined with Time (kāla), united with Fire and Wind. (46)
Joined with the sixth vowel and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, this single mantra of Maheśa is supreme and bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). (47)
O twice-born one, hear now of Vidyā Gaurī, who occupies the left lap of Maheśvara:
Bhavānī is of a dark complexion, possessing one face and two arms. (48)
Another woman had full breasts, a beautiful face, and plump thighs and hips;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every kind of ornament. || 49 ||
Slender-waisted, with a deep navel, bimba-red lips, and beautiful eyes—listen, O Nandin, without weariness, to the five Brahmans and the six limbs. 50.
The first is Sānta; the third is Sadyojāta; Vāmadeva is the fifth; Aghora is the seed-syllable numbered as Rudra (the eleventh); and Puruṣa is the twelfth. (51)
The thirteenth is Īśa; here it is called Pañcabrahma.
Together with the Brahma-saṃhitā and the scriptures, the Saṃhitā shall consist of the mantras.

All [the mantras] are joined with the bindu and nāda, their respective names in the dative case, followed by the word "namaḥ" and the appropriate number of mātrās; after this follows the meditation (dhyāna) on each of them. 53.
The stalk is white, golden, and likewise hanging with the luster of crystal; and those of the colors beginning with Sadyojāta have three eyes and four arms.

Likewise, those bearing the trident and the ṭaṅka, as well as those endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, are called Aghora and Raudra; the remaining ones are remembered as Saumya.
One should know the second [syllable] as the heart; the fourth shall be the head.
One should know the sixth syllable as the tuft (śikhā); the twelfth shall be the armor (kavaca). || 56 ||
The fourteenth is the eye (netra), and the sixteenth is said to be the weapon (astra).
The weapon is formed with the visarga, while the heart and the other [limbs] are formed with the anusvāra.
The classes [of mantras] end with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *huṃ phaṭ*;
those mantras are proclaimed as being joined with [the six limbs] beginning with the heart (*hṛt*) and ending with the weapon (*astra*). (58)
White, yellow, red, black, and resembling collyrium—these shall be the colors of the six limbs; they are three-eyed and four-armed.
Endowed with the boon of fearlessness, they hold axes and tridents;
likewise, [the colors] are red, white, golden, black, and saffron.
One should avoid [the images of] Aruṇa, Añjanaprakhya, and those with the colors of Vidhi, Īśa, and Krama, as well as the Kṣetreśas, Yakṣeśas, and Dvāreśas. || 61 ||
And [he should meditate on] all other gods situated upon their respective seats;
first, the state of the Praṇava, and immediately after that, within the heart.

The seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of the first letter of one's own name, followed by a salutation (namaskāra) and ending with "svāhā," should be used in all mantras, especially at the time of the fire-oblation (homa).
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the mantra for the offering (bali) to all beings, as well as their forms, faces, and all their colors thereafter. (64)
One should recite this mantra ending with *oṃ ā a huṃ phaṭ svāhā*;
beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), this mantra should be employed as "asugati. (65)
In all cases, the primary mantra (agramantra) is said to begin with the *praṇava* and end with *svāhā* for the heart; now hear the Pāśupata mantra. (66)
One should meditate on [the deity] with lightning-like luster, holding an axe,
a noose, and a trident in his left hands, as well as a rosary;
all [deities] should have three eyes and possess a hand granting boons.
This form of the Lord as Pāśupata is praiseworthy. || 67 ||
Having meditated thus with the mind, one who desires to speak should perform worship;
I shall proclaim its mantra—listen, O Nandikeśvara! (68)
The sixth [syllable] should be the second [vowel], conjoined with the fourth vowel;
it is further endowed with the subsequent [consonant] following the second [vowel], and accompanied by five vowels from the left. (69)
This Pāśupata weapon is conjoined with the Śikhā-mantra;
it consists of *huṃ phaṭ* followed by *kalaḥ*. At the end of *kala*, it is joined with the vowel *e* (the fourth vowel) and the letter *na*.
At the time of initiation, especially for the purpose of severing the bonds, the mantra of the deity Kṣurikākalavadeva is like pure crystal. (71)
O twice-born one, listen to the subtle form of the mantra known as Aghora:
it consists of the *nāda* joined with the *yānta*, preceded by the *praṇava*. (72)
O twice-born one, listen to this form which should be employed ending with the *visarga*:
it has the luster of a blazing lightning-fire, is encircled by serpents, possesses sharp fangs, three eyes, and holds a trident,
a noose, a bell, a sword, a shield, and a flaming great mace.

One should meditate with a disciplined mind upon him who holds the goad of desire and the no-fear mudrā in his right hand, and likewise the terrible weapon at his fierce-faced side, for the sake of universal peace.
In the pacification of foreign armies and during the outbreak of great diseases; (74)
During earthquakes, the conflagration of the quarters, destruction, and fierce winds—
likewise during such primordial times— in the presence of the mouth of Aghora.
Having performed one hundred and eight [recitations], everything is pacified. Now I shall proclaim to you the great mantra that pervades the sky. (76)
One should know the first to be the Praṇava; the second is the second [syllable];
the third is said to have three vowels, and the fourth shall have six vowels.
The fifth is that which would be the fourth [syllable], joined with the mantra Oṃ;
this is known as ending with the eighth. Then, after that, follows the seventh.
The eighth [consonant] joined with the end of the series [k], conjoined with the vowel 'a', joined with the end of the [dental] group [t], and adorned with the third vowel. (79)
The ninth is the letter *ya*, followed by the letter *e*; joined with these is the *praṇava* (OM), making ten.
O best of beings, listen as I describe its form in brief.
Three-faced and possessing seven tufts of peacock feathers, sometimes red and sometimes white— this form, which is beyond arising, is called space and has the nature of space. (81)
During an eclipse, at the equinoxes, and manifold times during the Vyatīpāta yoga;
at the time of a king’s consecration, at the commencement of war, and on one's own birthday. (82)
At the conclusion of a festival, at the end of a pilgrimage, or when afflicted by fever, Āryā, or other ailments,
the milk bath, the honey bath, and the great bath (mahāsnāna) are highly recommended.
By means of this mantra, one should cause Nandīśa, the Lord of the Immortals, to be fashioned;
misfortunes shall come to destruction, and one shall obtain the desired fruit. (84)
I shall now declare the six ancillary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in their proper order:
"Praśāntaṃ heti" is the heart; "Omnipervading One, salutation" (praṇavātman namaḥ) is the head. (85)
For Śiva, *jaṃ* is to be known as the *śikhā*; *sākāraṃ* (saḥ) is for Puruṣottama. *Phaṭkāraḥ* is the *astra* for Strī; *moṃ* is desired for the *netra*. (86)
One should apply everything from the heart-mantra up to the eye-mantra in the same manner; as is the case for *hṛ* and the others beginning with *yā*, so too is the passion (*rāga*) of the Vidyā.
Indeed, at the time of offering the sprouts during the preparation of Śambhu’s throne, one should recite three times the great mantra consisting of the principal seed-syllables: *Bhṛṃ Jña Ḍa Jñām*.
At that time, the wise one should employ one and three mantras;
the seed-syllable of Brahmā, joined with the bindu at the beginning and the end, is so remembered. (89)
The first seed-syllable is that of Vāyu; the second is Kāmarāja;
and the third is the syllable Sau, each joined with a bindu. (90)
That which begins with the *praṇava* and ends with the *visarga* is known as the *Sārasvata*.
[He who bears] three eyes, a crystal [rosary], a small bell, and a sacred thread—
The four arms are adorned with the splendor of the book of exposition. || 91 ||
I bow to this Vāṇī, who wears white garments, who holds garlands of white flowers,
and who is devoted to the lotus-throne of hymns of praise.
It should be joined with the syllable *yānta* repeated twice and endowed with the seed-syllable of Māyā. || 92 ||
The Śrī-bīja, joined with Bindu and Nāda, bestows all accomplishments;
likewise, that Durgā-bīja is conjoined with the fifth vowel. (93)
Endowed with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, it shall grant all desired objects.
She has one face, three eyes, the luster of a pomegranate, and four arms. (94)
The goddess holds a noose and a goad, her hands bestowing boons and fearlessness;
she is seated upon a lotus throne, gentle in appearance, and adorned with all ornaments. (95)
With a serene countenance and draped in red garments,
this Rudra-śakti is the Vidyā who, through her presence, bestows all accomplishments. (96)
This mantra—*hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*—is the rampart that becomes nectar;
because it is known as "the moon," *hrāṃ hrīṃ* is multiplied by the sun. (97)
The syllable *ga* belongs to Gaṇeśa, who wards off all obstacles;
we know the one with the curved trunk, we meditate upon the elephant-faced one. (98)
May that Dantin inspire us.
This [mantra] consists of the entire Kṣetrapāla ending with the final syllable, endowed with fourteen [vowels], joined with Bindu and Nāda, and completely free from all fear. (99)
O Nandin, for the benefit of all beings, the Ajapā [mantra] shall be explained;
it is auspicious, consisting of all knowledge, and present in all living beings and in all [mantras]. 100.
Free from the denoted and the denoter, and endowed with devotion to Śiva;
the first syllable is Vyoma (the letter *a*), joined with the Bindu-sandhi, followed by Bhṛgu (the letter *s*). (101)
Know that she who recites [the mantra] without effort is the personification of the Guru of all mantras;
she is the supreme reality without parts, transcending all other principles. 102.
Without beginning or end, empty, incomparable, and causeless; it cannot be grasped at its beginning, middle, or end, nor does it ever come to an end.
Neither existence transcending all cultivation, nor non-existence, nor both;
having realized that "it does not exist," one attains non-existence—this is the supreme nirvana within oneself. 104.
It is free from disease, devoid of limbs, all-pervading, and facing in every direction;
it is without end, without a master, and the cause of all causes. || 105 ||
Stainless, devoid of radiance, inactive, and independent;
[he is] Sadāśiva, Śiva, Śakti, Īśa, Rudra, and Janārdana. (106)
One should worship Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Soma, and likewise Sūrya, as well as the deity who consists of all the gods and the celestial Svagvī. 107.
Merely by hearing the mantra, while regarding the Guru as a deity and endowed with devotion and faith, one attains the perfection of the mantra. (108)
Having risen at the time of dawn, one should contemplate the form of the Guru;
thereafter, by his command, one may perform a thousand or even an infinite number of Guru-pūjās.
Six hundred [verses] are for Gaṇeśa, six thousand for Prajāpati,
six thousand indeed for Viṣṇu, and six thousand for the wielder of the Pināka bow.
There should be a thousand repetitions for Sādākhyā and a thousand for Ātman;
likewise, one should perform the continuous recitation of the mantra just once.
Knowledge, yoga, recitation (japa), and so forth are perfected through the mouth of the Guru;
thus, by means of this mere division, the recitation is performed day and night. (112)
In the forest, the fire of the forest tree protects its body from the roots upward;
yet it does not protect itself by means of that very [fire], nor does the fire protect its own roots and so forth. || 113 ||
The mantra, like a fire within oneself, burns away impurity along with its very root;
for it is like one desiring to cross a great river, or as if [crossing] otherwise. (114)

In that same way, those who possess the mantra of the Self cross over the ocean of nooses—whether they be celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers, or those who are united [in renunciation]. 115.
For one who contemplates the supreme syllable, being detached and supreme among those who enjoy sense objects,
is not tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, nor by merits such as [the performance of] sacrifices. (116)
Meditating with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose upon that which has the form of the supreme syllable,
the meditator— whether walking, standing, sitting, or even while sleeping— [remains absorbed].
Whether eating, drinking, chewing, or playing at all times; whether angry or peaceful, or wherever one may be situated— (118)
Whether pure or impure, the knower of yoga in all states produces that knowledge which is to be expressed; it cannot be otherwise, even by tens of millions of scriptures. (119)
Therefore, whatever is here that is extremely hidden or situated somewhere else, when the Guru is satisfied, all that—both the moving and the unmoving—is satisfied in this world. (120)
Then, the guru should satisfy the one who was arrogant while in the celestial chariot.
The guru is indeed the mother, the father, the brother, and one's kinsmen. (121)
There is no kinsman equal to the Guru; of this there is no doubt.
Having obtained the Guru’s compassion, one is impelled by the command of Śiva. (122)
And listen: liberation is attained without effort in this very life.
Therefore, for people, the rudrākṣa is the cause of devotion to Śiva. 123.
By this alone liberation shall be attained; there is no further rebirth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Acintyaviśvasādākhya.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the ritual implements,
as well as the characteristics of the fire-drill (araṇi), and the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva).

Next, the characteristics of the sacrificial fuel (samidh) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi), as well as the marks of the prokṣaṇī vessel and the characteristics of the ghee vessel, [are described]. || 2 ||
The characteristic mark of the *caru* vessel, the measurement of the oblations, the water for bathing, the support, and the characteristics of the flower vessel [are described]. (3)
The characteristics of the vessels for water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamana),
as well as the characteristics of the incense burner, the incense bell, the lamp vessel, and the mirror [are now described].
One should also observe the movement of the *nīrājana* lamp, the conch, the parasol,
and the fly-whisks, as well as the signs of grace from the *vardhanī* and the *śivakumbha*.
(45) The general mark of a jar and the characteristic of water-pots,
the mark of the lotus-eyed one and the characteristic of the staff; || 6 ||

The characteristics of the devotee’s treasury, the definition of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), likewise the definition of the purifier (pavitra), and the definition of the turban and the upper garment (uttarīya). || 7 ||

The characteristics of the rudrākṣa beads, as well as the characteristics of the rosary for recitation and so forth, the characteristics of the loincloth, and the characteristics of one who has a long beard; || 8 ||
The characteristics of a water-vessel, the characteristics of large bells, as well as the characteristics of a cooking pot and likewise the characteristics of a three-legged stand; || 9 ||
The characteristics of sacrificial ladles, the excellent characteristics of rows of lamps, the marks of the eight auspicious symbols, and the characteristics of ornaments; || 10 ||
(46) The characteristics of golden flowers, silk bands, and balls;
the characteristic of the yoga-band, and the characteristic of the [other] unequal [objects]. || 11 ||

Listen now in due order to the characteristics of the *nārā* and the *lakṣaṇa*, as well as the correct characteristics of the manuscript, the various divisions of measurement such as finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and their respective distinctions.
The length of the middle joint of the middle finger on the right hand of the preceptor is said here to be equal to one *mātrāṅgula*.
Having taken a blade of *pippila* grass or a *vāruṇa* reed from a well-kindled sacrificial fire,
it should be sixteen finger-breadths in length, with a width of eight finger-breadths.
Half of that is declared to be its thickness; one should place it upon the surface of the earth.
Its length is thirty-six finger-breadths, and its circumference is five units.
The churning [staff] should be made of *khadira* wood, perfectly round in every respect;
its length should be one *rañju* and a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and its curvature should be half of that. (16)
One should know that half of that [measurement] is the thickness for both sides;
the fist is exactly eight finger-breadths, and its circumference is about one *caṇa*.
Having placed it upon the churning apparatus and rotated it with a cowherd’s rope, the characteristics of the *araṇi* have been declared; now hear these characteristics of the *sruk*.
It does not shine with gold, nor even with copper, nor with Khadira, Karañja, or any of the four types of trees. (19)

It should be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood and endowed with all the proper characteristics. The circumference [of the neck] is eight fingers; the *kumbha* (the body) is sixteen fingers in height and two fingers in width; the *garbha* (the interior cavity) is made twenty-two fingers deep; and from that, the *gaṇḍikā* (the base or shoulder) follows.

The Vedic portions and the Vaidika parts are then doubled; the ear and the space above it are auspicious, and from that the face should be equal to the hoof; the pupil is made with three parts. || 20 ||

At the mouth, it is equal to the length of the *tāra*; at the ear, it is made with four [units]. Then the *vedikā* is adorned with a *tāra* and a double-pointed *bilā* at its tip; and by half of that, up to the end of the *ghāta*.
Therein, the first *gaṇḍikā* is made with four [units], while the others are reduced by half and half again.
When the staff has a moist portion at its base, it is called *sahita*; when it has no such portion, it is *nirnāhaka*. || 21 ||
On all sides, outside the *bala*, it should be half a finger-breadth;
outside that, the *vayava* should be one *yava* deep, and the outer fillet (*paṭṭikā*) should be half a *yava*.
Having dug from the base upwards toward the mouth for the measure of the little finger, thus the characteristic of the *sruc* has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the *sruva*.
Twelve finger-breadths in length and the girth of the little finger,
it should be made of flawless, supple leather, free from worm-holes or cavities.
The characteristics of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) have been declared; hereafter follows those of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
It is said that the enclosing sticks should be made of the very same wood as the fuel-sticks with which the oblation was offered. (25)
One span in length and the thickness of the middle finger is declared for the circumference;
now hear the characteristics of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
The width and height [of the face] should be twelve finger-breadths (ādityāṅgula), the lip is said to be one finger-breadth, and its shape is like that of the full moon. || 27 ||
The characteristic of the vessel for holding clarified butter (dhṛtapātra) is similar to that of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel;
its lip should be one finger-breadth wide and equal in height to the *caru* cooking pot. || 28 ||
The rim is said to be two finger-breadths wide, and the belly twelve finger-breadths;
the mark on the sacrificial vessel (carusthālī) may be made either of clay or of copper. (29)
Listen, O Nandikeśvara, to the materials for the oblation along with their proportions:
for one hundred oblations, there should be one *prastha* of clarified butter, and twice that amount of honey. (30)
In the case of an offering of sugarcane juice, however, it should be threefold, like that of honey.
[One should offer] sesame, mustard, mung beans, barley, black gram, and horse gram. (31)
Barley flour and rice, as well as half a *yuṣṭi* and half of that [half], are respectively the best, the middling, and the lowest; thereafter, it becomes inferior.
Rice, roots, cakes, śamī, bilva with dūrvā grass,
or the leaves of the netra or palāśa tree— these may be used, either individually or combined in pairs.
One should know that bathing water is of three kinds— superior, middling, and likewise inferior— and it is declared to be even the lowest.
Impurity firmly established in the heart, joined with the defects of bathing, like a stagnant pool, or water from a mountain spring situated on a path—such impurity remains present. (35)
Having especially avoided [the meat] of two-colored animals, even when combined with milk,
whether in a river, a pond, on a raft, in a dug-out pit, or even in a lake; (36)
The water of waterfalls and wells shall be very sweet;
bathing with eight droṇas of such water is said to be the most excellent.
Half of that is declared the middling [measure], and half of that is the smallest;
this is declared to be the water for bathing—now hear about its vessel.
Having taken one made of gold, silver, copper, brass, or even clay,
it should be endowed with the proper characteristics and fashioned into a square shape.
Filled with one drona of rice mixed with sesamum seeds and eight [other ingredients], this is declared to be the vessel for the bath; now follows the supreme procedure for the flower vessel.
It should be one cubit in width and twelve finger-breadths in height;
it may be made of bamboo, but it would be excellent if made of gold and other precious materials. (41)
Now listen to the characteristics of excellent vessels for water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth:
their height and likewise their width should be five finger-breadths.
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth [in height], and its thickness should be half of that;
the vessels for water for the feet, the respectful offering, and for sipping are said to be made of gold and other such materials.
The conch is said to be equal to silver; the vessel for perfumes should have the luster of the moon.
The vessels for incense and other offerings should have their mouths slightly curved like a bow.
The lid is shaped like a bud and provided with many perforations;
this is declared to be the incense vessel (dhūpapātra), and after that, the incense bell (dhūpaghaṇṭā).
The height should be four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula), and the width should be double that;
the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be half the height of the bell (ghaṇṭā), and the neck (gala) should be provided with an additional half-finger-breadth. (46)
On the tongue [there should be] a finger's breadth, and likewise a stalk on the head;
above that, a pedestal of one finger's breadth, and above that, it should possess the bull and the trident.
The ritual for the incense bell has been declared; the great bell, however, brings about prosperity.
It should indeed have nine additional [features], and immediately after that follows the lamp-stand.
Beginning from twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) up to the middle of the Nivṛtti [kalā],
one should declare the nine measurements ending at five-four (twenty) finger-breadths.
The width of the base (pāda) should be one-third [of the total], and the width of the face (vaktra) likewise;
in the middle of that, one should fashion a bud (mukula), provided with various staff-like projections (daṇḍikā).
The remainder should be fashioned by skillful means from gold or silver;
it may also be made of copper, brass, or even iron. (51)
The support for the lamp has thus been declared; now hear about the vessel for the oblation (havis).
It is said that it should be three times the quantity of rice that is available. || 52 ||
Just as the vessel for the oblation is prescribed according to the form of the *caru*-pot, half of that is designated as the vessel for the side-dish (*upadaṃśa*). || 53 ||

It may be made of copper, or of earth, or even of the three metals combined; its silver [portion] should be equal to the silver [of the image], and it should be provided with rings according to the prescribed rule.
The vessel for the oblation is thus described, as well as the characteristics of the *sthalikā*;
its width should be one *smṛtyaṅgula*, and one should increase it by half that measure.
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in width, made of gold, silver, or other materials;
half of that is to be known as the medium size, and half of that again becomes the smallest.
The characteristics of the bowl (sthalikā) have been declared; next, the characteristics of the three-legged stand (tripādī):
one should know its height to be three finger-breadths, and its width at the mouth to be half of that.
I shall describe the ankles, the two joints of the feet, and the two toes;
at the base, however, the supreme form is prescribed as being shaped like a shallow bowl.
The medium-sized [vessel] should be the measure of a *vasu*, while the smallest should be the measure of a *svara*;
it may be made of gold, silver, or even copper. (59)
Having fashioned today itself a tripod made of either bell-metal or brass, with a width of twelve finger-breadths according to the measure of the sun and a height of four finger-breadths; || 60 ||
Among those, the middle finger's length is prescribed; one should have it made of pure bell-metal.
This is declared to be the sacrificial vessel (balipātra); now the characteristics of the ladle (darvī) are stated. || 61 ||
The length of the finger of the God of Gods is one *aṅgula*, while its width is half an *aṅgula*; the width of the foot is half of that, and the middle channel (*madhyavāhala*) is half of that again.
It should be made of pure bronze and shaped like the hood of a serpent;
such should be the characteristic of the ladle. Now hear the rule for the usnīṣa.
The best [stūpa] should have eight cubits; the middling, seven cubits;
and the inferior is said to be six cubits, as is also recorded according to the portions of the elements (bhūtabhāga).
It should be well-whitened, fine, strong, and resemble the moon;
make it of dukūla, paṭṭa, devāṅga, or even cotton.
p.
57) For this is the characteristic of the *uṣṇīṣa*, which is the characteristic of the upper garment (*uttarīya*);
one should have it made, O Nandikeśvara, with a length of six *karas*. 66.
The first [yogapaṭṭikā] should be made of tiger skin; the second should be of black antelope skin;
the third should be made of thread—thus the yogapaṭṭikā is of three kinds.

One should make the width and height [of the base] one solar digit (twelve finger-breadths), and the lower part (the *avakam*) four digits; however, for the fivefold [measure], one should make it a fist (twenty-four finger-breadths).
This is declared to be the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana); then follows the procedure for the rosary of recitation (japamālā).
By means of beads made of crystal, gold, or silver, one shall properly attain liberation. 69.
With coral beads there is the attainment of wealth; with lotus seeds, the destruction of evil;
and furthermore, with those made of knots of *kuśa* grass, it leads to the eradication of sin. (70)
By means of lamps made of gold, one shall have sons; by conch shells, fame shall arise; through pearls, one attains prosperity; and through crystal, good fortune shall come to pass. (71)
Through all these Rudrākṣas, one attains the most excellent liberation;
the origin of the Rudrākṣa is from the water that brought joy to the eyes [of Śiva].
One face is Śiva himself; two faces are said to be Śakti;
three faces would be the Trimūrti; and four faces would be the Unborn (Aja). (73)
The one called Varada has five faces; that which has six faces is the form of Guha;
the Mothers have seven faces, while the Vidyeśas have eight faces.
The nine sacred sites beginning with the Gaṅgā constitute the "Nine-Faced" (Navavaktra) pilgrimage;
the merit from each site increases a hundredfold, starting from the Nine-Faced and ending at the Single-Faced (Ekavaktra).
(59) With those well-known finger-counting beads (*japamālā*), [the merit] is equal to one finger-breadth;
by means of lines, one should know it is eightfold, and with "son-lamps" (*putradīpa*), it becomes a hundredfold. || 76 ||
A thousand-fold [merit] is gained from conch-shells and gems,
ten thousand from coral, ten thousand from crystal, and a hundred thousand is said to be gained from pearls.

A hundred thousand recitations performed with lotus seeds is said to yield prosperity; however, when performed with golden beads, it is called "wealth," and with knots of kuśa grass or rudrākṣa beads, the merit becomes infinitely multiplied.
By twenty-five recitations one attains the accomplishment of liberation;
and by twenty-eight recitations, there is accomplishment that bestows wealth and grain.
The number of fortnights may also be the determining factor; death would occur in the eighth.
Bestowing wealth and bringing fame, the thirtieth [fortnight] increases victory. (80)
But by offering everything with devotion, it becomes inexhaustible and yields fruit;
such is the rule for the rosary and the characteristics of the place for recitation. (81)
Furthermore, it may be performed in a pure and delightful place or even in one's own home;
however, it yields a hundredfold merit in a cow-pen and a hundred-thousandfold merit by a river.
In the presence of the Lord, however, the recitation is said to be infinite;
likewise on the seashore, before the Goddess, on a mountain, and in temples. (83)
In all sacred hermitages, the recitation of mantras becomes ten million times more effective.
The thumb grants liberation, while the index finger destroys enemies. (84)

From the middle finger come enjoyment and liberation; the ring finger indeed brings prosperity; the little finger effects attraction and paralysis—such is the sequence of recitation using the fingers and so forth.
I shall describe the ritual for the auspicious pitcher; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
Its belly is declared to have a width of twenty finger-breadths.
Because it has flowed away from the three qualities (guṇas), it is designated as "I am not" (nāham).
At the throat, its height is half a finger-breadth and its width is one kauśika-finger. || 87 ||
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth [in thickness] and its projection three fingers; this is called the Śivakumbha, as well as the other jars for the neck. 88.
Half of that [measurement] should be for the *vardhanīs*, and half of that again for the *kalaśas*.
The *kuṇḍikā* is a limb of the *kalaśa*; the remainder should be fashioned according to one's ingenuity.
The ghaṭa and tāla and so forth have been fully described; now hear about the lambakūrca.
It is joined with twenty-six darbha grasses and measures twenty-six finger-breadths in length.
(62) That which has a hanging beard (*lambakūrca*) is declared to be the characteristic of the *pavitra*;
it should be provided with twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and a pair of excellent rings. 91.
One should make that [mark] with knots and apply it to Umā;
as for the mark of the mirror, its width shall be twelve finger-breadths.
One should fashion half of that [length] as the height of the base out of pure bell-metal;
thus is the mirror described—now hear the procedure for the row of lamps.
It should be made either of iron or of wood;
one should fashion it like a door at the entrance and like a light-emitting shape on the back.
The golden procedure for the garland of lamps is now described here;
having taken wood from a sacrificial tree, one should have it fashioned according to the prescribed characteristics. (95)
On both sides of the illustrious Goddess are a mirror and a full water-jar,
as well as a bull, a sea-monster, a svastika, and a pair of fish. (96)
Listen as I describe the auspicious vessel equipped with a palm-leaf fan;
listen also to its characteristic marks endowed with defining features, O Bhūtakara, as they were told to me there.

To the maker of the trident, one should give a *pippala* tree and a *vaṭa* tree endowed with those same qualities; the width and height of the archway (*toraṇa*) are prescribed as being equal to that. || 97 ||
The measurement for the archway has been stated; now hear the procedure for the golden flowers:
the smallest [size] shall be one unit, while the medium [size] shall be the middle finger-breadth.
One should increase the measure of the supreme quality by half the width;
the flower is shaped like a lotus, and its form is like that of the *karṇikāra*.
In the center of that, one should have it fashioned either joined with a leaf or alone;
thus there shall be a golden flower. Now hear the procedure for the gold plate (hemapaṭṭa). || 100 ||
Equal in length to the thickness of the linga, and one-fourth as wide—this is here described as the characteristic of the *paṭṭa*; now hear the characteristic of the *golaka*. (101)
The height of the linga from its base to its top should be two finger-breadths;
its circumference should be equal to that height, or perhaps slightly more by the measure of one *soma*.
It should be made of pure gold, or one may have it fashioned from silver;
I shall now describe the characteristics of the staff, which should be endowed with variegated markings.
It should be smooth, glossy, straight, free from blemishes, and without holes; or it may be devoid of mottled spots—this is said to be its characteristic. (104)
When the staff exceeds six finger-breadths [in length], the work of knotting is prescribed.
The space between two knots is called a *parvan*. || 105 ||
A staff with a single joint, such as the *pajṛkā* and others, brings happiness; a staff with two joints should be known as "demoniac" (*rākṣasī*), which feeds on flesh and blood. (106)
The *triparvā* is named *padminī*, which, like a lotus-lake (*padminī*), bestows happiness;
whereas the *kāminī* has passion as its joint and increases all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (107)

A joint of the sage (muni-parvan) causes the ruin of one's purpose; a joint of the image (mūrti-parvan) brings about destruction. Therefore, from this point upward, one should not perform [the installation]. 108.
If the lower part of the foot-measure (pādāṅgula) is used, it leads to the destruction of one's sons;
therefore, it should be done with the specific finger-measures (sidhyaṅgula), for three [other measures] do not grant success.
Success is achieved at four finger-breadths; the fifth brings death.
At six finger-breadths there is success in grain; the seventh brings its destruction. (110)

This [staff] is declared to be eight finger-breadths in length; one should not make it longer than that. The tail, however, should be twice the length of the base; such is the characteristic of the staff.
It is said that for the teacher (deśika) it extends to the top of the head; for the practitioner (sādhaka), however, it extends to the end of the resonance (nāda).
For the spiritual son (putra) it is between the eyebrows, while for those bound by the pledge (samayin) it is always at the tip of the nose.
One should cause the hand of lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and householders to hold it with the sky;
indeed, an excellent bamboo staff should always be carried.
Alternatively, one may form a cloth from ashes using cotton or even silk;
this cloth, intended for use, should be provided with a measure (prastha) of ashes.
Or it may be made even half of that size, O Nandikeśvara!
The base of the circle should be firm, smooth, well-threaded, and fixed upon a staff.
Alternatively, he who holds [the image] situated in the middle of a bamboo, with its form suspended from the armpit, or even on an inner garment, is always Śiva himself. (116)
One should always have it carved for the total removal of all sins;
know that it may be characterized as a loincloth (*kaupīna*) or as a hand (*hasta*). || 117 ||
Its length should be thus, and its width ten or eight finger-breadths;
such is the loincloth described, which should be made of cotton or similar materials. (118)
O Nandīśa, listen again as I describe the procedure for the book, which is joined with fifty threads and has a triple-stranded girdle hanging down. (119)

Starting from the *mānāṅgula* (measurement finger) and increasing by one finger-width at a time, one should proclaim the nine measurements ending with the *vedabhūtāṅgula* (four-finger measurement). || 120 ||
It should be made according to its own measurement by means of a net-pattern or similar design;
or it may be made of copper, provided with two perforations. (121)
The measure of the bowl is divided into four parts; that [measure] is further of three kinds.
Between the fourth and third parts is the middle, and there should be a hollow at the center.
Having divided the length into five parts, there should be a hollow in the middle; it should be fashioned according to the proper method using one-third of one part.
One should devoutly prepare a cord with the measurement of a barley grain;
likewise, one should fashion a pair of wooden boards adorned with the width of the [respective] colors, like leaves.
Thus should be the mark of the book; now, the characteristic of the iron arrow (nārāca) is as follows:
it is sixteen finger-breadths in width, with its middle fashioned like an ant.
(69) Thus, both joy and the characteristic of non-laziness would be present.
It must be performed with sharpness alone, being very firm and free from defects. || 126 ||
The measurement of the *nārāca* (the central axis) shall be equal on both sides;
I shall now describe the construction of the moving temple (*calaprāsādaka*), and thereafter the method for making the temple (*prāsādakaraṇa*). || 127 ||
The description of the temple has been obtained; it may be made of gold or silver, or even of copper, wood, or a clay bowl.
One should likewise cause [the mandala] to be made by means of the eye and the thread in this sequence; outside the ghee-line, it should expand according to the measurement in finger-breadths.
It should be circular on all sides or even square;
its height from the base of the liṅga should be double that of the inner sanctum.
One should make it very firm and with solid walls, endowed with all kinds of beauty;
or else, one may increase its length and height by even a single finger-breadth. (131)

One should have that made equal in size to the pedestal of the liṅga and endowed with the proper characteristics; beyond this, it must not be made larger. Now hear concerning the base (upāna) and other parts.
Dividing that height into eight parts, one part shall be the ground level;
the ground level consists of the base (adhiṣṭhāna), the pedestal (vasu), and the plinth (āra-sūrakam).
One who knows these names and their synonymous expressions is proclaimed to have mastered twice as much as a Sūtra, even if it be only half a quarter-verse. || 134 ||
The *prastāra* (base) is half a *caraṇa*, while the *gala* (neck) is said to be equal to that;
the *śikhara* (spire) has the length of a *caraṇa*, and its height is half of that.
When the measurement of the foundation is twelve parts, one should plant [the seed-syllables] with twelve members (*dvādaśāṅga*).
Birth should be performed with one part, and the world (*jagatī*) indeed arises with two. (136)
In the same way, one should not cause even a single tremor in the height of the *kumuda*;
the neck is said to be a portion of the wing (*pakṣāṃśa*), and the upper petal is then a single part (*aṃśaka*).
One should have the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) made with two parts of cane and bamboo;
this is declared to be the base (adhiṣṭhāna), and beyond that is the core of the pillar (pādagarbha).
One should have the altar (vedī) made with one-fourth of the length of the base; it may also be made with one-third, two-thirds, or even five parts. (139)
A structure consisting of a single pillar alone, devoid of a *tāṭikā* (pedestal) and other such parts, whether octagonal or hexagonal, is said to have a uniform form. || 140 ||
The upper opening should be fashioned; that which ends toward the north is praised.
One should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and [sprinkle] its heart-mantras in sequence. (141)
The moving pavilion should likewise possess the characteristics of a parasol;
the parasol is said to be of two kinds, measured by the palm (tāla) or by the cubit (hasta). || 142 ||
It has the appearance of the full moon, is endowed with a bud, joined with a stalk and stem, and is resplendent with strings of pearls. || 143 ||
This supreme white parasol is excellent, richly adorned with various colors;
this fly-whisk is made of white hair and decorated with clusters of jewels.
That stalk should be one cubit long and provided with two palm-trees;
however, one may have it made half of that length, or even half of that again.
That which has not been explicitly stated [regarding] the primary divisions and so forth should always and everywhere be understood by means of the secondary categories. 145½.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the section on the Instruments, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme rite of sowing sprouts;
at the beginning of all auspicious rites, one should perform the sowing of seeds.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the rite according to the rules either within seven days, or five days, or even three days, or else immediately, so that the sprout may arise.
The Moon is the lord of seeds; one should sow the crops at night. It should not be done even during the day; if it is done so, it brings destruction to the sower.
Whether made of gold, or silver, copper, or even clay,
the *pālikā* should have a width of nine [units] and its opening should be as large as possible. (4)
The *dharmāṅgula* shall be the medium [size], while the *rudrāṅgula* shall be the best;
the height should be equal to the width, and half of that should be the width of the base.
Half of that is the width of the *nāla*, which is perfectly circular throughout;
this is declared to be the *pādapaṭṭa*. Now the *prastara* is described.
Starting from that point above, the uppermost part should be one part;
then a lotus [pedestal] of one part, and the height of the *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be three parts.
It should be provided with one eye and be devoid of a mantra;
thus is the *prastara* described, and its neck should be well-proportioned.

The wise one should fashion [the image] with a large nose and so forth, a navel, and devoid of the directional forms (diśāmūrti) and the like; it should be made together with the star (satāra), according to the form of a bell.
Having divided the height of the stūpa into two parts, one part is for the lotus, and with the other, the bud-height;
it should be perfectly circular or square.
One-third of the nose's width is said to be the pair of petals [of the nostrils]; one-sixth of the face's width is designated as the lip. (11)
One should sprinkle it with the Puruṣa-sūkta; Brahmā is its presiding deity.
It should be situated in a pure and delightful place toward the northeast direction.
One should perform [the rite] outside, or likewise straighten the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
having adorned it with Darbha grass and flowers, or even on a protected heap of earth.
One should fashion a *pālikā* with nine, seven, or five [fingers' breadth];
having placed it upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (14)
One should fill those [holes] in sequence with the tips of *darbha* grass or even *kuśa* grass, ensuring they are without gaps or perforations, using either wood shavings, sand, or clay.
One should fill the small earthen vessels with these very mantras:
sesame seeds, mung beans, black gram, peas, mustard seeds, and bamboo shoots.
One should sow with rice, kuluttha beans, fresh seeds, water,
and milk from cows, while reciting the Kavaca mantra.
In the center of that, one should place a moon-pitcher and sprinkle it with the waters of the person to be consecrated;
likewise, one should worship that pitcher with the moon [as the deity] using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

O Nandikeśvara, at the time of initiation (dīkṣā), during the rites of installation (pratiṣṭhā), and on other auspicious occasions, as well as at the beginning of any undertaking, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇaka) for Śiva.
The seventh chapter: The Ritual for the Planting of the Sprout.
O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
O Maheśa, you ought to declare our resolve for initiation. || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
O Nandīśa, listen with a concentrated mind to all that is supreme. First, I shall describe the initiation consisting of ritual action (kriyāvatī-dīkṣā), which possesses true qualification.
The true nature of knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
thus initiation is fully described as that which bestows will and knowledge.
Among all gurus, the true teacher (sadguru) is considered the foremost, for she bestows the path of truth;
the true teacher is remembered as the cause of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (4)
Just as darkness perishes in the presence of the sun, one is liberated from all sins merely by the glance of the Guru. || 5 ||
Whatever the Guru touches with his hand or whatever one beholds with his eye—all that becomes auspicious through the grace of the god Śiva. (6)
One is not smeared by impurity, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
therefore, Śiva is called the Guru, and the Guru is Śakti, the Manonmanī.
Even one who has committed hundreds of thousands of initiations, if he has not obtained the knowledge of Śiva, should resort to the pilgrimage of knowledge (jñānayātrā). || 8 ||
Having obtained a teacher devoid of knowledge, how can liberation be attained? Just as one who has boarded a shattered ship does not reach the far shore in the ocean. (9)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in one who has reached the further shore of knowledge, just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower within the forest. 10.
Likewise, a disciple who is greedy for knowledge may go to another teacher;
having obtained that [new teacher], the disciple should dismiss him, for there is the certainty of falling downward.

Initiation by action (kriyādīkṣā) is fourfold: that which possesses seeds (sabījā), that which is devoid of seeds (bījavarjitā), that which is joined with office (adhikārasaṃyuktā), and another which is without office (niradhikāriṇī). || 12 ||
That [practice] involving seeds belongs to men who are joined with the conduct of the pledge (samaya);
however, that which is devoid of ritual procedure is prescribed for women, children, and those such as the *paṅka* [outcastes]. (18)
That which is fit for the practitioner-teacher (sādhakācārya) shall indeed possess authority;
specifically, such fitness exists particularly in regard to the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites. (14)
Or, with a mind free from seeds, one enters the authority of the eternal measure alone;
thus has this fourfold initiation of action been described by me.
Then, having examined the disciple who was endowed with devotion and desirous of meditating upon Śiva, and perceiving him to be pure, the Guru [acted] out of compassion.
The Guru, having performed his daily rites, should perform the work of initiation;
for in the Kali age, three types of persons are to be graced according to the scripture: those possessing realized knowledge, those seeking dissolution [into the divine], and others.
The third is the Sakala, and likewise the first is the Vimalamātṛka; then there is the one joined with impurity and karma (Malakarmasamāyukta), and the Pralayākala.
And for those who possess all [the powers], such as Nivṛtti and the others, there is an increase of the *kalās* from one stage to the next;
O Nandikeśvara, their initiation (*dīkṣā*) involving ritual action (*kriyāvatī*) is of two kinds. (19)
Initiation is both with support and without support; it is with support for everyone, but for others it is indeed without support—thus has initiation been described by me.
But that rite which is performed by Śambhu through his intense power, independently of a teacher, is proclaimed as "unsupported" (nirādhārā).
Having assumed the form of the Guru, Śambhu performs initiation through devotion according to the distinctions of mild, intense, and so forth; that is the *sāttvikī* initiation.
On Mount Mahendra and Mahāmeru, on Malaya and Pāriyātrika, on Vindhya and Mandara, as well as on Śrīgiri and the Himavat mountain.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, the Kālindī, the Narmadā, the Tuṅgabhadrakā,
the Sarasvatī, the Payasvinī, and on the banks of the Kāverī and the Kanyakā; (24)
Or likewise in meritorious sacred regions such as Vārāṇasī, or on the pure bank of a river flowing to the ocean, or at a great lake. (25)
Or always in a flower garden, or near a milky tree, or in a palace, or in a monastery, or always in the house of one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). || 26 ||
In a pure, delightful, and even location with a well-swept surface,
one who is dispassionate should have a pavilion constructed, provided with pillars that are free from flaws.
One should construct an altar specifically joined with sixteen pillars or twelve pillars, resembling the smooth surface of a mirror.
Alternatively, in a confined space, one should fashion it in a suitable form; its height should be one cubit (*hasta*) or even one forearm-span (*ratni*). (29)
Or one may construct it at the height of a palm-tree (tāla), provided with a secondary altar (upavedī);
its height should be four finger-breadths and its width two finger-breadths.
The height is proclaimed to be either three finger-breadths or two finger-breadths;
then the wise man should construct an altar measuring one cubit or two cubits.
The fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) should be made quadrangular by those who come before;
it should be endowed with a girdle (mekhalā) and a womb (yoni), provided with a navel (nābhi), and beautiful to behold. || 32 ||
Alternatively, one may prepare a circular pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with all the required characteristics;
it should be smeared with cow-dung and encircled by garlands of darbha grass.
Adorned with canopies and banners, decorated with strings of pearls,
and strewn with garlands of flowers, one should encircle it with a wave-patterned border.
One should wrap the pillars there and gradually expand the mandala;
the colors are white, red, dark blue, yellow, and black.

With devotion and faith, one should likewise [worship] with the five jewels beginning with pearls, with crystals, with those originating from the *jāti* species, with emeralds, and with *jāmbīka* stones. (36)
One who knows the ritual procedure should [prepare the ground] with five types of collyrium powders;
it should be white with rice flour and likewise red with brick-dust.
Or one may drink powdered green gram or vegetable powder, or even turmeric;
or again, black powder produced from husks and charcoal, or the five-fold powder.
White rice is said to be colored by mineral pigments;
this should be known as red-colored when combined with the essence of *munipatra*. (39)
That same [mixture] is *śyāma* when made with mung beans, or *kṛṣṇaka* when made with king-beans (*rājamāṣa*);
thus, with whatever materials are available, preceded by the lord of teachers (the preceptor).
One should mark the points with rice flour, fresh ginger, cotton, and thread;
starting from the east and ending at the west, one should mark thirty-three points in sequence.
Furthermore, the north-south thread shall be thirty-three [units] long;
it shall again consist of twenty thousand lines of squares.
There, in the center of that thirty-sixfold grid, one should fashion a lotus endowed with eight petals, radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
Of that [area], one-third of a part is indeed for the pericarp and the filaments;
the pericarp is with yellow color, and the filaments with red color. (44)
One should draw it in white color at both the base and the tip;
it should be joined with the seed-syllable of the pericarp and endowed with white and red.
One should draw the eight petals as well as the circle with white lines; that which follows it should be black, while the circle is traditionally recorded as being white.
In the east is the saffron Liṅga, in the south the black Liṅga,
in the north the golden Liṅga, and in the west the white Liṅga.
In the southeastern direction, it should be of that same color and adorned with a creeper;
in the southwestern direction, it has the appearance of a dark-green color, and in the northwestern direction, it is black-colored.
In the northeast, one should fashion a white creeper ending in a lotus;
as for the remainder, even if gathered in one place, one should likewise fashion minor lingas and svastikas. (49)
One should arrange all the other remaining colors according to the proper method; then, because it originates from the *liṅga*, it is proclaimed as the *maṇḍala*.
The preceptor, joined with the *tāra* (the syllable Om) and accompanied by water for the respectful offering (*arghya*) held in his hand,
shall perform the worship of the guardians of the door and then dispel the obstacle at the threshold (*dehalī*).
There, seated upon his own high throne, the Guru should place the weapon-mantra;
having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), he should then worship within the inner self.
Siddhārtha, rice, sesame, flowers, dūrvā grass, water with kuśa grass, milk-water, and barley are specifically prescribed. (53)

The purification of the ritual substances is prescribed by means of water worthy of offering (arghya); likewise, one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) and prepare one's own seat for the sake of one's own purification. (54)
The mantra, previously worshipped, is purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, indeed, the materials are scattered with parched grain, sandalwood, and ashes.
They should be pure, either with kuśa and dūrvā grass or simply with pure parched grain (lāja);
they should be joined with [mantras] consecrated by the Astra-mantra and likewise sprinkled with water from the Astra-mantra.
O Nandikeśvara, having fashioned these destroyers of obstacles, which possess the luster of various colors, are described as such, and resemble diverse weapons; || 57 ||
[He took] that which was fashioned with the thirty-six *darbha* mantras, honored by Hāla,
consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra of Śiva, and possessing the form of a flute-player’s staff.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Gods through the mind according to one's desire for creation,
and having placed the partless Śiva, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva. (59)
One should place a white turban on the head, consecrated with the root mantra;
the upper garment with the Gāyatrī, and the lower garment with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should adorn oneself with sandalwood mixed with camphor powder, as well as with saffron,
fragrant ashes, and ornaments.
The preceptor should especially adorn [the deity] with extremely pure silken garments and various ornaments and other such items.
One should draw a maṇḍala with one's own fragrant substances using the right hand;
having worshipped Īśa therein, one should fashion the Śiva-hand.
Having placed that [mantra] upon his own head with the Śiva-mantra, he, being most radiant,
should then contemplate himself as the agent, non-different from Īśa. (64)
Acting as a witness, he should observe the ritual acts within the mandala;
likewise, he protects the sacrifice in the water-pot and the fire-altar.
The Great Lord, having taken [the disciple] into himself as the supreme support within the five substrates, should especially effect the liberation from the flood of bonds for the disciple there.
One should likewise cultivate a firm disposition, thinking "I am he; I am indeed that very one.
Standing in the southwest with disciplined composure, one should be equipped with the sword of knowledge.
One should purify the sacrificial site with water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
well-endowed with the rites beginning with inspection (īkṣaṇa) up to the consecration at the crossroads.
O Lord, even the preceptor whose form is that of the Lord should perform purification especially;
therein, he should gather together the scattered *vikira* offerings and the bundles of *kuśa* grass. (69)
The master carries [the deity] with the *vardhanī* vessel and casts them onto his own seat;
in the eastern direction of the mandala, there is a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
It may be performed with *droṇas*, or half of that, or half of that again, or even with *vrīhi* rice;
half of a *vrīhi* is said to be a *taṇḍula*, and half of a *taṇḍula* is traditionally held to be a *tila*.
The measurement for one pitcher shall serve as the standard for increasing the size of the other pitchers;
they should be endowed with all auspicious characteristics and free from all defects.
The Śiva-kumbha may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
likewise, it may be a kumbha or simply a kalaśa.
(Aligned) with the three-fold arrangement according to the rule of the *yuktisūtra*, it is surrounded by the eye-marks of the twice-born;
it may be four cubits, three cubits, two cubits, or even one cubit in size. (74)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should fashion a raised rim in its center,
endowed with eight petals and radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
Provided with four legs and an external enclosure, one should place three *darbha* grasses in the east, north, and west, following the sequence starting from the east. (76)
