Sahadevī, ekapattrā, bhadra, vaikaṅkata, and viṣṇukrānti—these five are known as the "five medicinal herbs" (pañcauṣadha). || 77 ||
Excellent rice, kodrava, barley, nīvāra, and bamboo-seed—these are declared the five grains; one should offer these into the jars.
On a mountain, by a pond, in the ocean, at the peak of a bull, and in a sacred field— five types of earth should be taken from these places and deposited in sequence. (79)
Pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, topaz, diamonds, coral, sapphires, emeralds, and likewise emerald-green gems (marakata). || 80 ||
These nine gems are prescribed; one should place them within the Śiva-pitcher and others.
Having set down a golden pitcher, one should wrap it with new cloths.
Having placed a tuft of grass in all [the vessels], one should place a mango leaf in the mouth;
likewise, with citron fruits, they are auspicious in the eastern direction.
One should worship the Vasudevas and Lakṣmī at the southwest gate; in the west, one should worship Saṃmukhī with red offerings, filling the sacrificial hall.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon the pavilions in the form of jewels, one should worship them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should worship the imperishable Śiva on the northern side of the pavilion. (84)
Then, having placed before him a disciple who has bathed, is purified, is clothed in clean garments, is fasting, and is full of faith; || 85 ||
Absence of anger, devotion, trust, and likewise obedience to the teacher's command;
[but] one who acts with malice toward the teacher, malice toward Śiva, or malice toward the sacred observances (samaya). 86.

One who is uninitiated due to a lack of kinship, one who is ungrateful, one who lacks discernment, one who perceives only the faults of the guru, and one who does not perceive his own faults—(these should be avoided). || 87 ||
One should not perform these eight [acts], and an oath must be avoided;
having thus disciplined even such a disciple, the preceptor—
One should sprinkle [the image] with water from the conch-tirtha and gaze upon it with the divine vision;
having placed it upon a vajra-throne, it should be endowed with all ornaments. (89)
Here, the noose (pāśa) should be fashioned, ending with the letter *jīva* (ya), conjoined with fire (*ra*), joined with *piṅgalā* (the letter *la*), and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*. || 90 ||
The second [syllable] is the peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara) conjoined with Māyā and Anala;
[it is] Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ, situated in the midst of the fire-maṇḍala and filled with masses of blazing rays. || 91 ||
When the state of Kālaveṣṭaka is well-applied at the secret door, the mantra becomes like an eye, and the paralyzing of the fetters (pāśastobha) is prescribed. || 92 ||
Having recited the Kṣurikā-weapon mantra, the teacher, being well-conducted, serene in soul, single-minded, and composed, should effect the severing of the noose. (93)
Having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should sprinkle the body of the disciple;
thereafter, one should fasten the protection-thread (rakṣāsūtra) upon his right hand. || 94 ||
Having positioned the naiṣṭhika [seat] facing north in the kūṭikāsana posture,
one should place the bhautika [seat] facing east or even facing west.
One should prepare that [amulet] with rice grains and a protective thread with ashes;
having consecrated it and worshipped the Guru, [it should be tied] excluding the left thumb.
Having tripled that thread, one should bind it to the hand of the disciple;
by means of the Kavaca mantra, that knot shall be protected with sacred ash.

Having worshipped the causal deities beginning with Brahmā there with the Heart-mantra itself, one should worship them with the Īśa-mantra in the case of the Naiṣṭhika, and with the Puruṣa-mantras and others in the case of the Bhautika.
The sacred thread (upavīta) must be placed upon the brahmins and others in the proper order;
thereafter, the preceptor (deśika) should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship of the mandala. (99)
Facing north, one should worship Śiva in the center of the lotus;
having placed Īśāna there, one should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east.
One should install Aghora in the southern part, Vāmadeva in the north, and Sadyojāta in the western direction; thus one should place the five Brahmans in their proper sequence.
One should place Vahni (Fire) in the heart; the head on the southwestern petal;
the Śikhā is said to be in the northwest; and the Kavaca likewise in the northeast. (102)
One should especially perform the placement of the eyes (netranyāsa) on the front part of the pericarp;
one should worship the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), beginning with Ananta, in sequence in the [remaining] directions.
Dharmajñāna, Vairāgya, and likewise Aiśvarya,
along with the lords of the Aṅgavidyās, are situated in the middle of the southeast corner and the others. (104)
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this manner, one whose mind is serene should thereafter perform the worship of the water-pot (kumbha).
One should place the Vardhanī vessel in the northeast direction, seated upon a lion and having the form of a sword.
Thereafter, one should worship her with the Astra-mantra, seated upon a seat preceded by the Praṇava;
and [one should worship] those [deities] stationed in the directions beginning with Indra, radiant with their vehicles and weapons.
Having worshipped the ten [deities] ending with Viṣṇu with prostrations and their own names,
one should take up that *vardhanī* vessel, which is directed toward following the front of the water-jar (*kumbha*).
And one should whirl an unbroken stream of water clockwise for the purpose of purifying the sacrificial pavilion,
while reciting the root mantra.
(99) The best of preceptors should cause the world-protectors to hear the command of Śiva;
having placed them in the pitcher, he should worship them for the sake of the rite, O Nandikeśvara. (109)
Afterwards, one should worship one's own body as the Lord (Īśvara) within the pitcher (kumbha) while remaining in a steady posture;
having assigned the state of being intoxicated (śauṇḍya) and the path (adhvan), one should worship the weapon (astra) in the vardhanī vessel.
Oṃ, homage to the weapon for the terrifying [of enemies], huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ, homage to the weapon for the embodied form, huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ!
Oṃ klīṃ ślīṃ, homage to the Pāśupata weapon, huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ, homage to the head, huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ, homage to the crest-lock, huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ śrūṃ, homage to the armor, huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ...
To the one with three eyes, *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ huṃ*, to the weapon (*astra*), *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (p.
100) Resembling a thousand suns, with a sound like the clouds at the end of an eon.
Four-armed and four-faced, with three eyes in each face. || 111 ||
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, his face is ever blazing,
he holds a spear, a mallet, a trident, and fire in his hands, and he has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
One should perform the union of the yoni and the liṅga by means of the yonimudrā;
one should touch the water-pot (kumbha) with the thumb while reciting the heart-mantra, and the vardhanī vessel with the fist.

O Nandikeśvara, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should touch that which is grasped by the fist—resembling a blazing fire with its flames, and well-united with the earth and the upward breath (kṣamū). 114.
Having worshipped the sword of knowledge (jñānāsī) in the southwest, one should worship Śiva upon the water-jar (kumbha).
One should worship Īśāna at the Śiva-kumbha and Puruṣa in the eastern jar.
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship Aghora in the southern pitcher, Vāmadeva in the northern, and Sadyojāta in the western pitcher. (116)
Outside of that, one should again worship Narmadā in the eight jars;
having worshipped Kanyakā in the south and Samudrikā in the west.
One should place Gaṅgā in the northern pitcher, Yamunā in the southeastern pitcher, Sarasvatī in the southwestern pitcher, and Kāverī in the northwestern pitcher. 118.
In the northeast, one should worship the Tuṅgabhadrā in due order,
from the invocation up to the dismissal, using their respective names preceded by "oṃ hāṃ."
One should worship the Tīrthamātṛkās with mantras ending in *namaskāra*:
"Oṃ, just as the temple of the Blessed One's face was constructed with effort... (120)

O Lord of the World, one should worship Vaṇīya, who stands at the forefront of all sacrifices, as well as Vighneśa— who resides in the syllable Oṃ and possesses four arms— in the southwest (nairṛta). || 121 ||
Having worshipped Ṣaṇmukha in the northwest according to the proper sequence and as is fitting,
the preceptor [should do so] with water mixed with sandalwood within the prepared maṇḍala.
Having thus worshipped outside the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the prescribed rite, he, together with his wife,
should then worship its middle and its expanse from the mound.
Having obtained permission there, the preceptor should proceed with the serpent;
for the satisfaction of the mantras, the Guru should go to the side of the sacrificial pit.
Seated on a secluded seat, having placed all the fragrant substances, arka-water, sacrificial fuel, darbha grass, sesame seeds, and so forth on his left side.
The consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the fire, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) should be performed as before.
Then, the preceptor, having worshipped Śiva in the center of the upward-facing fire, [proceeds]. (126)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the sequence of emanation upon one's own body, the mandala, the Śiva-vessel, the fire, and the disciple, one should purify the paths (adhvan) according to the prescribed rule.
Listen to the characteristics of the flames, which are the tongues of the fire named Mukha;
having ascertained the mouth [of the fire] by the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the oblation (āhuti) should be offered with the heart.
In the west, for one devoid of disciple-consecration and for the daily fire-oblation;
in the north, for nourishment, good fortune, subjugation, attraction, and pacification.
Indeed, for the purification of the nooses, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed;
while the application of weapons, ointments, foot-pastes, and pills is intended for the attainment of one's desires.
And for the sake of inspiring the students, the Guru should perform worship at the eastern face;
subduing, driving away, and killing are to be performed at the southern [face]. (131)
The expiatory oblation for liberation there is offered into the upward-facing [flame];
these are Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā. (132)

The seven tongues are proclaimed to be exceedingly red and multiformed, following the sequence of the directions starting from the northeast (Aiśāna), east (Indra), southeast (Vahni), southwest (Nairṛtya), and west (Vāruṇī). || 133 ||
The four [channels] beginning with Hiraṇyā are situated in the six [petals], having red interiors;
Bahurūpā, situated in the center, flows toward the south and the north.
Hiraṇyā has the luster of molten gold; Kanakā has the form of a diamond; Raktā has a radiance equal to the dawn; Kṛṣṇā has the brilliance of a sapphire. || 135 ||
Suprabhā is like the luster of pearls; Ratiraktā is like pollen; Bahurūpā has a radiance equal to the autumnal moon and the moonstone. (136)
A specific tongue is prescribed for each according to the desired object: Hiraṇyā for attracting gold, Vaśyā for subjugation, and Kanakā for paralyzing.
Red [light] is for causing enmity and delusion toward enemies, while black is for killing; Suprabhā is for peace, merit, and so forth, and deep red occurs for driving away.
In each individual face, she possesses a form that bestows all desired objects;
this [form] is prescribed for the *hora* of the tongues in the face that grants one's specific wish. (139)
The first two months consist of the letters devoid of the *repha* (r), while the *repha* is situated with the sixth vowel;
joined with the moon (*i*), the bindu, and the crest (*śikhā*), these are the seed-syllables of the tongues in their proper sequence. 140.
In rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with honey, milk, sugarcane juice, and so forth;
in rites of sorcery (ābhicāra), however, it should especially be performed with blood on the auspicious day.
With bulbs, salt, buttermilk, mustard seeds, and oil, and with fuel-sticks of kāraskara, ādara, and jṛmbhī plants, [he performed the sacrifice] without mantras. || 142 ||
With camphor-water, for the sake of attaining the fruit of the Vidyādharas; otherwise, the best of practitioners should not perform the oblation. 143.
One who desires the accomplishment of a yakṣiṇī should offer kadamba buds;
for the attainment of universal sovereignty, one should offer lotuses; and for the acquisition of pearls and other riches, one should offer [lotuses]. (144)
One desiring health should offer dūrvā grass, and for the subjugation of all living beings, one with a concentrated mind should offer flowers that are pleasing to the heart. 145.
One should offer oblations with the fresh sprouts of mango trees, which are sweet and grown from cuttings; indeed, this immediately brings about the pacification of irregular fevers. (146)
When soaked with ghee and honey, this becomes the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra].
Its mantra is: *Amukasya jvaraṃ nāśaya jñaṃ sau vaṣaṭ*.
Furthermore, by means of Palāśa flowers, it produces poetic genius in an instant. (147)
His mantra is: "Vada vada vāgvādinīṃ svāhā.
One who desires rain, especially so, should worship Pracetas with water offerings. (148)
One should offer sesame seeds with the *vāmadeva* mantra;
one should always inundate the entire world as if with masses of clouds. 149.
One should cause [the bonds] to burst apart in an instant by means of an oblation of sesame seeds with the *pāśupatāṇu* mantra.
Its mantra is: *oṃ ślīṃ ślīṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ sphoṭaya sphoṭaya huṃphaṭ*.
And for the sake of pacifying the seven afflictions, one should perform the Rudra-śānti rite with sesame seeds and other materials.
One should especially offer the entire oblation to the practitioner;
furthermore, the primary procedure shall now be explained in sequence according to the previously stated rule. (151)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, and ten parts [of the remainder] consecrated with mantras,
one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order while reciting the root mantra preceded by the syllable *pluta*.
Thus, one should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity] in order to initiate the disciple;
or else, for the sake of all prosperity, one should perform the homa according to the specific place and time. (153)
To ward off ill omens and for the accomplishment of auspicious signs,
one should offer oblations two hundred times each with the root mantra.
(109) One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) once for all the mantras from Śiva down to the weapons (*astra*), ending with *svāhā*.
The "kindling" (*dīpana*) is performed with mantras enclosed by the *śikhā* mantra and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*. 155.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śivāya svāhā"—this is for the libation (tarpaṇa);
"Oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ," etc., is for the illumination (dīpana).
One should purify the vessel with the water of Śiva and envelop it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should bind [the thread] upon the sacrificial pit and mandala, having had it touched by Śrīkaṇṭha and the other [deities].

Having recited the mantra for the armor and the weapon two hundred times for each component, one should prepare a mandala with water and arrange the seat consisting of Dharma, Jñāna, and the other [Tathāgatas]. (157)
Having invoked the Form and the Lord of the Form, one should worship Śiva with meditated flowers;
thus the best of teachers should worship with flowers measuring finger-breadths in the vessel. (158)

The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) are [to be described] on a hearth purified by inspection and other rites, specifically on the western side, which is joined with the seed-syllable *huṃ*. || 159 ||
One should place the weapon-mantra upon her who is the Dharma and whose form is Dharma; having placed a pure vessel there, or a razor [vessel], with water. (160)
And for the sake of success, having performed the protection from fear, one should empower a cow-horn with the Astra-mantra and consecrate it with the Prasāda-mantra. || 161 ||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times over unhusked rice, water, milk, and clarified butter, the supreme preceptor should place these, combined with five handfuls, before the disciple. (162)
One should gradually increase the number of disciples by three;
the principal [offering] is performed with the fire-mantra, while the covering is done with the armor-mantra.
The Guru should first cook the sacrificial porridges (caru) facing east with the root mantra,
in the center of the hearth that has been well-cleansed by the Śivapādakadīpinī mantra.

Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter (*ājya*), and having muttered the mantra ending with "svāhā" and the word "svāhṛtām," the Guru, the cause of liberation, then performs the oblation and heats [the vessel]. || 165 ||
p.

111) Having specially placed the cooking pot upon a mandala of darbha grass beneath the hearth, over which the *astra* mantra has been recited, one should cover its opening all around with the *tāra* mantra. || 166 ||
Then one should perform scraping and anointing with the heart-mantra;
having received the cool sprinkling, it gradually becomes cool.

O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the fire-oblation with clarified butter in a well-kindled fire, preceded by the mantra and accompanied by the utterance of "vauṣaṭ" at the end, offering it repeatedly.
Once the clarified butter for the *saṃpāta* offering has been prepared and the seats for Dharma and the other deities have been arranged,
the Guru, having placed the *sruva* ladle to the west of the sacrificial pit and its mandala, [proceeds].
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter with the sruva-spoon accompanied by the Saṃhitā-mantras,
one should wipe the sruva-spoon in this manner and offer again with the Saṃhitā-mantras.
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) ending with the syllable *vaṣaṭ* and having offered it once, the preceptor,
for the sake of pacification, should lead it to the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) after it has been turned into nectar by means of the cow-mudrā. || 171 ||

One should divide the clarified butter (ājya) into three parts for the sake of the gods, the fire, and the guests; then one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) for the guardians of the directions, followed by the threefold offering of fuel-sticks and clarified butter.
The milk offered with the heart-mantra ending in "namaḥ" is not for the purpose of the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Having offered the weapon-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Then, either to the east of the sacrificial pit or to the east of the Śiva-pitcher, [he should perform the rite] for the Mothers, the Udbhagaṇas, and others, using their respective names followed by the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). 174.
O Nandikeśvara, the internal bali-offering shall also be accomplished;
having studied the Lord and attained the eye [of insight], one should meditate with single-minded devotion. (175)
(113) Having fully traversed all paths and endowed with the qualities of omniscience,
he is the presiding authority over the great sacrifice for the sake of accomplishing our sacrificial rite. 176.
One should contemplate, "I am Śiva," and emerge from the sacrificial pavilion;
then, one should offer white oblations with weapons upon the maṇḍala of the equalized atoms.
On a blade of darbha grass with its tip pointing eastward, which has arisen from the latent impressions of the vital breath (prāṇavāsanā),
one should face the east for the sake of enjoyment (bhukti) and face the north for the sake of liberation (mukti).
There, the preceptor should indeed cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow and water infused with *kuśa* grass;
afterwards, he should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) according to the sequence of the mantra-ritual procedure.
One should perform the bath in this manner and gaze with the vision of Śiva;
having raised the disciple from his seat, especially one who desires liberation. (180)
One should gaze with divine vision starting from the feet up to the crown of the head;
one who desires liberation should look from the crown of the head down to the feet. (181)
O Ānandikeśvara, reflecting upon the greatness of Śiva’s splendor,
that best of teachers was pleased by the granting of eyes.
Having sprinkled oneself with water from the Astra-mantra for the sake of success, the bath with ashes is prescribed for the purpose of destroying obstacles. (183)
The teacher should sever the flood of bonds with the sword of knowledge;
he should then touch [the body] from the head down to the feet, as well as both sides. (184)
For the purpose of destroying the noose and the sprout, one should especially perform a bath with sacred ash;
indeed, one should bathe [the deity] with the ashes of the weapon-mantra according to the method of emanation and reabsorption.
Having sprinkled [the deity] again with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should perform the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa*.
Reciting the weapon-mantra, one should purify the area above the navel using the tip of a *kuśa* blade.

In the event of obtaining [the thread] in three ways, the true Guru should obtain it for the destruction of sin with its roots using those [mantras], and for the destruction of the two kinds of bonds below the navel, he should obtain it with the Astra-mantra.
One should present the teaching, ending with Śiva, within the body of the disciple;
having honored the disciple with flowers, one should [apply] the eye [mantra] to the eyes with either the Netra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should wrap the face with a white cloth together with a fringe;
then, having placed a white-colored flower into the cupped hands of the disciple— || 189 ||
One desiring devotion should likewise cast [the flowers] into the joined palms;
then, taking both hands together, one should proceed in due order before the Preceptor.
One should lead him clockwise around the southern side of Śiva;
having placed him upon the seat of the *praṇava*, one should establish the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). || 191 ||
One should subsequently project oneself, characterized by the lotus feet of the Mūrti, into the heart-lotus of the disciple, and then purify the disciple’s body.

Then, having performed the withdrawal (saṃhāra) in this manner with great intensity, and having made the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the one of pure conduct, one should meditate on Śiva and worship him once again. || 193 ||
For the disciple facing the east, one should place the Śiva-hand upon his head with the Śiva-mantra, while reciting the Rudra-pada for the sake of the goal.
One should cause the disciple to cast a flower into the mandala, and afterwards, having removed the blindfold, one should look at the spot where his foot fell and give the disciple a name.
For all castes, the naming ceremony should end with the word *deva*; for those of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes, the name should end with the word *śiva*. (196)
Or he may be at the head of a group among other gods; he should behave toward others like a father.
Especially for one who is lifelong (naiṣṭhika), he should not take account of distinctions of caste.
The letter *a*, the letter *i*, the letter *u*, as well as *e* and *o*—this constitutes the five vowels. (198)
Longevity, health, and prosperity, as well as decline and even death—success shall come according to these respective numbers; therefore, one should not hesitate at all. (199)

Having ascertained the first syllable of the name of the disciple whose name was previously mentioned, one should cause him to receive one [syllable] from among those three, such as his lifespan and so forth.
One should avoid both those who cause destruction and those who cause death;
furthermore, the supreme guru may give names to his disciples according to his own will. (201)
Furthermore, one should cause the names of the devotees and the hosts to be given, and especially the name of the consort and the name of the Śakti.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍīla) and the Vardhanī vessel in the form of Śakti,
the Guru should cause prostrations to be made toward Vahni, Īśa, and the Guru himself.
Having seated the disciple, who is facing north, upon a seat to his own right side, [he should place it] in the disciple's right ear.
Taking up the root mantra, one should [place] Sadāśiva in the left ear, as well as Maheśa and Vimukha, which destroy all sins. (205)
(119) One should visualize Sadāśiva in the Suṣumnā at the central root, and Maheśa in the Piṅgalā, within the body of the disciple. || 206 ||
Then, having placed its root at the teacher’s shank according to the rite,
and having gone to the disciple’s heart, he should exhale it by means of the root mantra.
Having arrived at one's own heart-atom (hṛdayāṇu) by means of inhalation (pūraka),
it is said that the connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) occurs again through the fire of Śiva (śivāgni).
O Nandikeśvara, having offered oblations with the heart-mantra for the sake of [the deity's] presence during the triad,
and having offered one hundred oblations with the root-mantra, the hand of Śiva shall become firm.
The preceptor, having filled the two hands of the disciple with auspicious flowers and having gazed upon the Linga worshipped in the north, [should place] those very flowers [therein].
Having cast [the offerings] at the feet [of the teacher], one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
one should offer one's body, wealth, and life to the true gurus. (211)
The teacher should look upon his disciplined disciple with compassion and say:
"By the grace of my command, you must perform that triad. (212)
The Guru should say, "Perform acts of charity, religious duty,
and ascetic practice," as well as [instruct him on] the monastery, the tree, the lineage, and likewise the sphere of activity.
In this very manner, the true guru [should impart] the lineage, the pentad, the monastery, the Āmardaka tree, the banyan tree, and likewise the clan to the disciple.
That pure reality has been fully explained; it is called the domain of the disciple.
One should cause the disciples to hear the lineage known as that of Nandikeśa. 215.
The preceptor should sprinkle the water in the jar and other items with their respective mantras.
Having thus reflected, [ends] the eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Initiation into the Observance of Action," in the Viśvasādākhya.
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
O Lord of Gods, destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before you, O best among speakers, look upon me with compassion and tell me about the twilight worship (sandhyopāsti).
Īśvara said:
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the teacher, standing facing the north,
should contemplate the pair of lotus feet of the Guru within the *guru-maṇḍala*.
Having paid homage to the root mantra at the tip of his tongue, with a serene mind,
he should meditate on Śiva within the lotus of his heart like a steady, flickerless lamp. (3)
Having reflected upon the auspicious duties to be performed, being composed in mind,
he should rise, go outside, and carry a staff and a water-pot in his hands.

Having arrived at a suitable place, and having performed the necessary duties along with his disciples— such as carrying the staff and water-pot— in the proper sequence and according to the requirements of that location, [he settled there].
Near a temple, in a cow-pen, at a crossroads, in a place of ashes, in a beautiful garden, or near a sacred tree; || 6 ||
In a watery dwelling, a dwelling of birds, a dwelling of wild beasts, or in a cremation ground;
near another caste, on a bridge, or even upon an anthill—(7)
Even near a dwelling, and especially in a black field (kṛṣṇakṣetra),
on ground containing cow dung, stones, urine, or bones; (8)
One should not discharge feces or urine on a mountain;
furthermore, one should place the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) upon the shoulder or at the base of the ear.
Having wrapped his head there, he should not shave with his body straight;
rather, having placed a blade of grass upon the ground, he should look down from a distance of half a cubit.
Having placed the sun to his right, he should discharge urine and feces,
with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose and not looking toward the cardinal directions.
Spitting by the twice-born is not prescribed in that place;
nor is cleaning performed with anything other than water, cow dung, stones, or wood.
One should not [use] grass or clods of earth for that very purpose;
rather, holding the penis with the left hand, one should take pure clay with the right. (13)

One who desires [the fruits of the rite] should especially avoid all earth found in the middle of a village, at the foot of a tree, on a bridge, or originating from an anthill— these three types of earth being particularly forbidden.
Having approached the water’s edge, one should perform the ritual purification thoroughly;
then, with water reaching the waist, one should take earth equal in size to a *dhātrī* fruit once.
One application [of clay] to the penis, five to the anus, ten applications to the left hand,
seven applications to both hands, and one should cleanse both arms with water.
As long as there is the purification of existence, so long should one practice purification;
without the purification of existence, it is not declared to be perfect purity. (17)
Having entered the riverbank, one should cleanse one’s feet and hands;
having spent one watch (three hours), one should wash them with pure water. (18)
Placing the right foot on dry land, one should set the left foot in the water;
having formed the hand like a cow’s ear, one should drink water that has submerged a single māṣa bean.
One should drink water a second and a third time according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, the cleaning of the teeth is especially for human beings. (20)
The characteristics of a tooth-stick are that it should have an even cut, be firm, pure, thick with sap, without joints, and possess a thickness equal to that of the little finger. (21)
The staff for those committed to lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika) is eight finger-breadths long, while that for householders (bhautika) is ten finger-breadths;
it should be made from the wood of the śirīṣa, ciribilva, karañja, khadira, or arjuna trees.
(126) It has been declared that this [practice] belongs to the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika); it is prescribed for those who are materialists (bhautika).
[The teeth should be cleaned] with twigs produced from the mango, apāmārga, khadira, plakṣa, and campaka trees. || 23 ||
And with the leaves of the *jambū*, *kapittha*, and *mādhava* trees which heal wounds, as well as those arising from the coconut palm and the *aśoka*, which are purifying. (24)
The cleansing of the mouth is performed with thirty-two mouthfuls of water;
[the teeth are cleaned] with castor, drumstick, vetiver, bamboo, and the "piśāca-bhakṣaṇa" [roots].
One should not perform the cleaning of teeth with *chātrī*, *netrayavakṣīrī*, *nimba*, *kāśa*, *aṅgulīyaka*, *lūśāṅguli*, *tāpa*, or iron. (26)
On the new moon, the full moon, the sixth lunar day, as well as the ninth and tenth days,
and especially for one seeking liberation, the cleaning of the teeth with a twig must be performed daily.
(127) One should perform a bath in water, which is auspicious and removes all sins;
it serves for the purification of both the exterior and the interior, and is the cause for the yoga of worshiping Śivā. 28.
It is the preeminence of all conduct and the destroyer of all evil dreams;
it brings about the destruction of indolence and the like, as well as of the Haridras and the Śūdras. (29)
It bestows vigor and strength, stimulates the digestive fire, increases nourishment,
brings about prosperity, grants long life, and likewise bestows complete subjugation over all.
In a river, a pond, a large tank, or even a well—these are the four types [of bathing places].
One should not perform a bath in a well unless rivers and the other [suitable locations] are unavailable.

A gift at a stepped well is ten times more meritorious than one at a common well; at the bank of a pond, it is ten times more than at a stepped well; and at a river, it is ten times more than at a pond’s bank—its fruit is said to be infinite.
The middle [type of reservoir] is like the bank of a lake; furthermore, the smallest is like a pond (kuṇḍa), a water-fall (nipāta), or equal to bathing in a well (vāpī). || 33 ||
Whether it be small or large, whatever is situated near a temple of Śiva contains all sacred fords (tīrthas); by the power of Śiva, it is like the Gaṅgā. || 34 ||
Having dug eight finger-breadths below, one should take up that earth again with the Heart-mantra, and then, with that same mantra, [prepare] the painting surface.
Having placed it behind him, he should then approach the bank;
having deposited that clay with the *śiras* mantra, he should purify it with the *astra* mantra. (36)
Having raised the crest-lock (śikhā), one should divide it threefold with the crest-lock and the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then, having washed from the navel down to the feet, one should again [wash] in a secluded place with the crest-lock mantra.
Having taken up the weapon-mantra, blazing with its central portion, one should touch the feet, the head,
and all the limbs three times, and completely restrain all the sense organs. (38)
Submerged in water with both hands, having restrained his breath and being self-controlled,
he should then place his hand upon his heart, [visualizing] the weapon [mantra] equal to the fire of time (Kālāgni).
This is declared to be the water-bath; thereafter follows the pure bath (śuddhasnāna), having drawn [the waters] from great holy sites such as the Ganges by means of the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā).
Having invoked [the deity] within the heart with the mantra and using the bathing mudrā,
one should take water from the northern sacred site (tīrtha) of the heart or from other waters.
Facing north, having divided the palm of his left hand into three parts,
he places one part in the southern section, consecrated with the *astra-mantra*.
First, one should divide it sevenfold with the Astra-mantra, and then tenfold toward the north with the Śiva-mantra.
In this way, one should make three portions; then, having consecrated them with the Astra-mantra, one should take them up. (43)
One should sequentially cast [the offerings] in the ten directions with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*;
then, having taken up the Śiva-linga situated in the north, one should recite the mantra over it in sequence.
One should cast the thread into the midst of the water; this shall become the Śiva-tīrtha.
Having recited the mantra over one's limbs, one should smear the entire body with it using the Aṅgavidyā.
First, one should cast [the offerings] from the head down to the feet on the right;
then, one should recite the four [mantras], beginning with the heart, in sequence while in the midst of the water. (46)

Having closed the eyes and other senses with both hands, and having submerged himself in the water of the Śiva-tīrtha while meditating on Śiva in his heart, he should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta). || 47 ||
One should sprinkle [the disciple] with the two hands in the form of the moon and sun using the *kumbha-mudrā*;
and one should repeatedly offer oblations with the six limbs, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*. (48)
Having performed the recitation of the mantras with the practitioner's own mantras ten times over,
one should consecrate [the disciple] in due order, constantly visualizing the nectar-water.
For the sake of protecting oneself and for the pacification of all obstacles,
one should sprinkle water consecrated with the Astra-mantra all around.
Alternatively, even in the vicinity of a monastery, one should perform the ritual bath in a water-pot with water drawn from a well, using the previously mentioned rites and mantras. (51)
Bathing in a copper vessel yields a hundredfold more merit than in an earthen jar;
silver is a hundredfold more effective than copper, and gold is a hundredfold more effective than silver.

Whether he be a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), one who maintains the sacred fires, or a householder, it should be performed equally with the honors due to a universal monarch, using fragrant substances, myrobalan, and so forth. (53)
By whatever means possible, one should not omit the daily bath;
even for a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika), the saffron robe or at least a white one is prescribed.
The waistband for the loincloth should be one cubit or even two cubits long,
and twelve or ten finger-breadths in width.

Having especially bound this [mantra] of mastery as a binding-enclosure (veṣṭi), and having sipped water according to the rule, being pure and endowed with the three principles (tattvas), [he should proceed]. || 56 ||
With crows, vultures, and pigeons; with cocks, cranes, and lapwings; and with such men as donkeys, camels, and village pigs. || 57 ||
(133) Also by deer, rogues, and dogs, which are born as enemies to his body;
and by those who steal his teacher’s property, who are the destroyers of that very property. || 58 ||

Nor by those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), nor by the ungrateful, nor by those bearing other sectarian marks (anyaliṅgin), nor by anyone at all who has not been initiated; especially so when touched by them. || 59 ||

One who knows the mantras should perform a bath in water during the wind-constellation (pavana), likewise during the wind-constellation; however, he should not touch the area above the navel with his hands, except when in contact with something pure.
Thus has been described the bath with water; hereafter follows the bath with ashes, which is victorious, bestows prosperity, meritorious, and destroys all sins.
This is pleasing to us, to the Goddess, to Vighneśa and Guha, especially to the gods, and particularly to the Daityas. (62)
(134) After bathing in water, the sacred ash destroys the fivefold bonds.
Bathing in water was previously prescribed for the purpose of preparing for contact with the sacred ash.
The killing of a living being while it is still moist is established as leading to an increase in the merit of the ash-bath;
however, if devoid of the ash-bath, it brings about the state of being a slayer of living beings.
For a devotee who is devoid of the ash-bath never attains liberation anywhere;
therefore, the ash-bath is desired with every effort. (65)
The triple mark with ashes is the specific rite of bathing for a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika),
and especially for a householder (bhautika), the triple mark should be applied according to the rule while the ashes are still moist.
That ash is said to be of four kinds: the first is called the primary (kalpa), the second the secondary (anukalpa), and the third the subsidiary (upakalpaka).
The fourth [initiation] should be without ritual form (akalpa), and each preceding one is likewise superior.
Those who are elderly, diseased, or possessed of ill-omened marks should be excluded. (68)
And [one should avoid] a cow devoid of its calf, as well as one that is foolish and lacking in intelligence;
rather, one should choose a Kapila cow with auspicious marks, whether red, white, or predominantly white. (69)
One should hold the cow dung of these [plants] with both hands in a lotus leaf born from water, or likewise in a Palāśa leaf, while positioned in the air.
One should take cow dung from a cow-pen and hold it while reciting the *sadyojāta* mantra;
one should apply it above and below, and then release the middle portion again.
The knower of mantras should fashion it into the shape of a ball with the Vāmadeva mantra and other [mantras];
having dried it with the Aghora mantra, he should then burn it in a pure location.
A person should especially place [the medicine] in a new vessel along with camphor,
uśīra, hrībera, ketaka, and likewise campaka. (73)
Therefore, one should especially recite the mantra for subduing with the country-mantra;
O Nandikeśvara, listen now to the secondary alternative (anukalpa) as well.
Having taken dried cow dung from the forest, it should be prepared as previously described according to the ritual rules;
one should perform it by the method stated before, and thus it becomes the prepared ash.
Having reduced it to powder and collected it, make it into a ball with cow's urine;
burnt according to the previously mentioned procedure, it becomes the prepared ash.
Setting aside the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the purification of the ash alone as if it were a *piṇḍa*; this is designated as the "unconditional" (*akalpa*) method. (77)
Ash produced by others is worshipped as being beyond conceptualization (*akalpa*).
This fourfold classification has been declared to be the destroyer of all sins. (78)
Then, having collected the ashes from the ritual fire, one should perform the binding of the directions;
with the remainder, using the Brahma-mantra, one should dust the head and other limbs.
This is declared to be the "Kalpa-bath"; after this follows the "Śiva-bath," consecrated with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the Nivṛtti-mantras and others.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
Aghora on the throat, and Vāmadeva from the navel to the end of the feet.
The procedure for smearing with ashes begins from the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra;
one should smear both arms with Sadyojāta and the face with the root mantra.
p.
138) One should mix ashes with conch-water and the root-mantra;
thereafter, one should apply the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra), which consists of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. || 83 ||
One should apply [the mantras] either to the thirty-two positions, or to the sixteen positions, or likewise to the eight positions, or even to the five positions. (84)
On the head, on the forehead, and likewise on the two hands and the two eyes;
then on the nose, the mouth, and the throat, and after that on the two shoulders. (85)
On the upper arms, at the wrists, on the heart, on both sides, on the navel, on the two private parts, as well as on the thighs, the two buttocks, the two knees, and the two shins. (86)
Or else, on the two calves, one should place the two feet; this is the supreme thirty-two-fold station.
Then [one should place] the eight immortals, the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) together with the vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are remembered as the eight Vasus. (88)
The wise one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with the Vāma mantra;
with a concentrated mind, he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* at sixteen locations. (89)
On the head, the ears, the forehead, and the neck; on both shoulders, the elbows, and the wrists; and on the heart, the navel, and the sides. || 90 ||
And on the back, one should likewise recite the mantra for the foundation; there, one should worship the presiding deities:
Śiva-Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, and Vidyā.
The nine powers beginning with Vāmā, as well as the two Aśvins, are traditionally taught as the sixteen [deities] located in the two arms,
the heart, the navel, and the pair of thighs.
(140) At the two knees and the two feet, as well as the back, there are sixteen [points]. Listen now to those presiding deities in these locations according to their respective application. || 93 ||
Śiva, Skanda, the Moon and Sun, Vighneśa, and Viṣṇu,
as well as Śrī and Prajāpati, are located in the region of the heart and likewise in the navel.
The Nāgas and Nāga maidens, as well as both types of Ṛṣi maidens, are at his feet; the oceans and sacred fords (tīrthas) are on his back, and the weapons are also there.
Or one should meditate thus upon the sixteen; the eight locations are now described:
the head, the forehead, and then the two ears. (96)
The two shoulders, the heart, and the navel—this shall be the eighth;
Brahmā and the seven sages are proclaimed as the presiding deities. || 97 ||
Alternatively, they say that the head, the two arms, the heart, and the navel are these five locations, and the deities are the five forms (pañcamūrti). (98)
Upon seeing a sacrificial oblation in the presence of one's guru, a deity, fire, or sacred knowledge;
or upon seeing those guilty of mortal sins, or even a person who has committed ingratitude. (99)
On a path consisting of impure elements, dusting is not prescribed;
therefore, one should remain pure, seated upon a seat even in a purified place. 100.
Facing north, remaining silent, and meditating upon Śiva and the Guru,
one should ensure that not even a particle of ash as small as an atom falls upon the ground.
In that same way, one should diligently adopt the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes;
thus, being liberated from all sins and endowed with complete purity. || 102 ||
By the mere sight of him, one is liberated from all sins;
what need is there for much speaking here regarding the presence of the gaze of the Guru? (103)
Even all sins born of mind, speech, and body, without exception, perish effortlessly merely by wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). 104.
For one who is devoid of the wearing of the ashes, even if intent upon various forms of knowledge, there is neither yoga nor meditative absorption, nor sacrifice, nor even charity. (105)
Therefore, with every effort, bathing with ashes is supreme;
sprinkling with water using a hand touched by ashes is the highest [form of purification]. 106.
Upon touching one who has not been initiated by a twice-born, an ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) is prescribed;
thereafter, having discarded the loincloth (kaupīna), one should remain equipped with the palm-gesture (tālamudrā).
Having covered his private parts with another cloth, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Then follows the Māhendra bath, together with the rays of the sun. (108)
With arms raised, meditating on Śiva, one who has taken seven steps and is skilled in devotion to the Guru should proceed while reciting the mantra of Īśa.
I declare that the Vāyavya bath consists of the dust raised from the hooves of cows;
or else, one may perform it while reciting the Puruṣa-sūkta or the Kavaca-mantra for a distance of seven steps.
Furthermore, the mantra-bath is performed with the mantras beginning with *jaleṣvadyaiḥ*;
one should perform it mentally with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), accompanied by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). || 111 ||
For thus the mental bath is prescribed in all cases;
now, O Nandikeśvara, listen as I describe the procedure for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having washed one's feet and purified the hands with water,
the hand should be joined in the kukkuṭāsana posture and formed like a cow’s ear (gokarṇa). 113.
With his hands placed between the knees and free from foam or bubbles,
he should take up water reaching the level of the beans with the hollow of his left hand.
Having first performed the purification of the mantras with water from the *brāhmatīrtha* located at the base of the thumb, one should contemplate the Self as consisting of knowledge and Śiva. 115.
Having first uttered the syllable *Tāraṃ* (Om), [one says] "O Svadhā, you who reside within my self, *Āhāṃ*";
O Nandikeśvara, through this first drinking, complete purification occurs.
The purification of the thirty-one principles begins with the Earth and extends up to Māyā;
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should recite: "Hrīṃ, by you, by the principle, Svadhā. (117)
Thus, by the second drink, the purification of the *yatatva* occurs;
this triad of principles is proclaimed as the pure *vidyeśa*, *sāda*, and *ākhyā*. (118)
Having uttered that ending with the syllable *oṃ*, namely "hrīṃ śivāya svadhātmane," the purification of the principle of Power (*śakti-tattva*) is performed again by the third draught. (119)
Thus, by means of sipping water (ācamana), there is the purification of the thirty-five principles.
Having wiped the lower lip twice, one should place [the mantra] ending with "namaḥ" above the heart.

Then, using the base of the right thumb, one should leave aside the middle, the index, and the little fingers; with the remaining three [fingers] placed together, one should touch those two [shoulders].
By pressing the thumb and forefinger together and sequentially touching the vital breaths (prāṇas),
and by drinking water three times, one will become dear to the Three Principles (tritatva).
In the same way, it is dear even to those who recite the sacred traditions (āmnāya), the devotees of Śiva,
because of the wiping of the lower lip with the Atharva, Sāman, and Yajus [Vedas]. (123)
Especially for one who is a devotee of Śiva, this act dear to him—performed with the three middle fingers—is the cleansing from top to bottom according to the Ṛgveda. (124)
The propitiation of the lords of the Gaṇas for the practitioners occurs through the root mantra;
one should touch both the feet and the head with water while reciting the root mantra.
And one is always dear to the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and the hosts (gaṇas).
Likewise, with the tips of the thumb and the ring finger, [one should touch] the pair of eyes. 126.
Joined with the *tāra* (oṃ) seed-syllable, it is dear to the Sun and the Moon;
likewise, the *pṛthvī* (la) seed-syllable and the *dhruva* (praṇava) are joined with the index finger and the thumb.
(147) Joining the ring finger, this is the unsurpassed *prīti* [mudrā] of emanation;
it consists of the seed-syllable of space (*vyoma*) and the *dhruva*, joined with the little finger. (128)
When Jelenā touches the ears, there shall then be joy in the quarters;
she is joined with Tāra and possesses a form four finger-breadths in height. (129)
Indeed, the five [limbs] beginning with the navel become pleasing to Viṣṇu;
one should do so while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) with the palm of the right hand alone. || 130 ||
By the mere touch upon the heart, the fire quickly rejoices;
having uttered the Śiva-mantra with the five fingers [of the hand]. (131)
Merely by touching the topknot, there shall then be the pleasure of Śiva;
even at the time of sneezing or spitting, one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Alternatively, one should touch the right ear with the right hand;
endowed with purity of intention, one should sip water twice for the sake of purification. (133)
Then, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, there should be three rounds of prāṇāyāma;
likewise, having mentally withdrawn the mantras, one should perform them three times.
Having sipped water again according to the rule and performed the salutation to the ears, one should,
with a single-pointed mind and a tranquil soul, perform the ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs.
Oṃ hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ. Having thus recited this mantra, one should purify the left hand; likewise, with the right hand, one should purify the right [hand], and with the left hand, the left. 134.
O Nandikeśvara, having recited that [mantra] once for purification:
*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ*. One should contemplate the two hands, endowed with the splendor of the weapon-mantra (*astra-tejas*), as far as the wrists. (137)
Having formed a hollow cavity with both hands, with the two thumbs between the middle fingers,
one should meditate upon the supreme circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala) in the form of nectar. (138)

Oṃ hauṃ! With the six [syllables] of Śakti, one should perform the immersion of those two hands; having visualized the letter Va within their cavity, one should likewise place the seat of Śiva in its center. 139.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva.
Having meditated upon the subtle form, one should thereafter recite the mantra:
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
In this manner, O Nandikeśvara, one should install the form of Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva.
Thus one should then contemplate the god Sadāśiva as all-pervading.
Afterward, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the assignment of limbs) is performed, extending from the little finger to the thumb.
(150) *Oṃ hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; thus on the little finger. *Oṃ hāṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; thus on the ring finger.
Oṃ hrīṃ śikhāya vauṣaṇnamaḥ. Thus on the middle finger.
Oṃ hauṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṇnamaḥ. Thus on the index finger.
Oṃ hāṃ astrāya phaṭ; thus [one recites] over the thumb.
Thereafter, one should effect the supreme identification (paramīkāya) by means of the root mantra.
Having veiled the body hairs, one should again [establish] the seat of Śiva at the navel.
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva"—thus established throughout the universe, the attainment of Sadāśiva extends from the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). 143.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva. (p. 151) One should then place the heart-mantra on the heart and the head-mantra on the head. || 144 ||
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] upon the crest-lock, the *tanutra* [armor] in the middle of the body, the *netra* [eye] in the eyes, and likewise the *hasta* [hand] in the two hands; 145.
With the *coṭikā-mudrā*, perform the binding of the ten directions;
having consecrated [the deity] with the root mantra, then follow the sequence of the *mahāmudrā*.
One should touch [the disciple] from the feet up to the head with both hands using the mantra ending in "śā vauṣaṭ. || 147 ||
Having purified the water by means of gazing and other rites, one should draw the sacred ford (tīrtha) onto the forehead with the Aṅkuśa mudrā, [reciting]: "Oṃ hāṃ, to the heart, vauṣaṭ. (148)

Having uttered the *tatpuruṣa* mantra ending with "namaḥ," one should cast [the offering] into the midst of the water with the *bhava-mudrā*, accompanied by the root mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). || 149 ||
Having consecrated it with the armor-mantra (*tanutra*), one should cause the two ears to be pierced;
one should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) to ward off the multitude of obstacles. || 150 ||

Oṃ hrauṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hṝṃ hraiṃ—by these [mantras], there should be three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). Then one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again, according to the prescribed procedure as stated. || 151 ||
For the destruction of the defect of initiation in people who are devoid of initiation, [the rite] beginning from sunrise and lasting for five nāḍīs [should be performed]. 152.
Then, [perform the offering] with the Dhenu-mudrā:
Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ hāṃ, namaḥ to the heart (hṛdaya).
Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the head. Oṃ hṛṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ hauṃ kavacāya hūṃ vauṣaṭ | Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ | One should perform the consecration of the head with these mantras using the water-pot mudrā.
Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor.
One should perform the enveloping of the body with water consisting of nectar. || 153 ||
At that time, during the morning twilight (prātassandhyā), one should meditate upon Brāhmī within the lotus of the heart,
wearing red garlands and garments, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, four-faced and four-armed,
she stands in the midst of a swan and a lotus, gazing upon the eight substances.
The supreme maiden, wearing the sacred thread, resplendent with a garland of lotuses,
and clearly holding a deer and a rosary in her two arms.
Likewise, with her two left hands she holds a staff and a water-pot;
she is radiant with triple lines of ash and adorned with all ornaments. (157)
Upon a red maṇḍala extending for hundreds of millions of yojanas,
one should visualize the Goddess firmly established in its center, the witness of all ritual actions. (158)

At midday, one should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇavī [form], who is white, radiant with white [garments], seated in the midst of Garuḍa and a lotus, possessing one face and in the full bloom of youth. || 159 ||
She wore a garland of forest flowers as a sacred thread, possessed firm and well-knit breasts, had lips like the *bimba* fruit, a beautiful face, a pair of eyes, and was adorned with earrings.
Holding a conch in her left hand and a discus in her right, she holds a mace and the gesture of fearlessness, with her head marked by the triple-ash line (tripuṇḍra). || 161 ||
Adorned with every ornament, she is the witness of all deeds,
upon a white mandala extending two hundred koṭis of yojanas.

There, at the time of evening, those who have attained the perfection of Śiva [should worship] the Goddess Raudrī, who is situated in the center, the essence, the one who effects stability, and who has the luster of a blue lotus. (163)
Her matted hair is adorned with the moon and the lord of elephants; her youth has slightly faded;
she stands in the midst of a bull and a lotus; she has one face and three eyes. || 164 ||
She wears a black antelope skin as an upper garment, is adorned with all ornaments, possesses every auspicious mark, and performs the process of withdrawal. || 165 ||

The Goddess, who bears the triple-ash mark and the trident with the *akṣamālā* in her right [hands], and the *śakti* and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her left, is the witness in all ritual actions. (166)
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon her situated in the center of the Bindu-maṇḍala, within that which is three hundred million yojanas wide and half-submerged.
One should then meditate upon the sky illuminated by their radiance;
this is the supreme and ultimate twilight, especially at midnight. (168)
Through the nature of Śiva and Śakti, she has attained oneness in unity;
she is subtle like a lotus fiber, red, white, and other colors as well. (169)
The fourth is the partless eternal [state], which is perceived as black;
for one who is devoted solely to the awakening of Śiva, that indeed becomes the supreme twilight (sandhyā). || 170 ||
The *brāhma* tīrtha is at the base of the thumb; that of Prajāpati is below the little finger;
the *paitra* is at the base of the index finger; and the *daivata* tīrtha is at the tip of the hand. (171)
The deity Āditya is on the palm of the right hand, or [the deity] Vāruṇa on the left hand;
the *ārṣatīrtha* is specifically at all the joints of one's own fingers.
But at the entry into the wrist-joint (maṇibandha), O Nandikeśvara, there is the Bhūtatīrtha and then the group of eight; below the Brāhmatīrtha is the Tīrtha of the Directions. 173.
Afterwards, one should sprinkle that water with mantras whose essence is Śiva;
having recited the Heart-mantra three times while holding the two hands below in a restrained position.
One should bind the *kuśa* grass with the right hand while holding it with the left;
having consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra, it should be covered with the armor mantra (*kavaca*).

Having performed protection with the weapon-mantra and having consecrated the bamboo seal with nectar, one should pour water beneath it, using the water that has dripped down from that [seal]. || 176 ||
One should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) upon the head with the six-limbed mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
then, having taken that remaining water along with sesame seeds in the left hand... (177)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, and having offered water for libation (arghya) to Śiva in the center of the solar disc, one should then mentally recite the Gāyatrī. || 178 ||
Sprinkled during the morning twilight, it should be offered at midday;
having been raised in the evening and given the arghya offering, one should sit before the Three-eyed Goddess.
Seated upon a lotus, white in color, with a serene body and a pure smile; she has one face, gracious eyes, and is established on a lotus throne. || 180 ||
She is adorned with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon serving as her crest;
she is radiant with triple lines of sacred ash and wears a white sacrificial thread.
The supreme goddess has four arms and four faces; she holds a rosary and is endowed with the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness, bestowing the fruits of the four Vedas. || 182 ||
One should mentally meditate upon the Gāyatrī, which cuts asunder all sins:
*Oṃ tanmaheśāya vidmahe vāgviśuddhāya dhīmahi*.
May that Śiva impel us;
thus, endowed with devotion, one should recite the Śivagāyatrī at the three junctions of the day. || 183 ||
"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā! Arghya to Śiva!
Having thus recited the mantra and offered the arghya, one should perform the immediate dismissal (visarjana).
Having circumambulated three times, the wise practitioner should recite the root mantra. (184)
Furthermore, for the purpose of illuminating the mantras, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa):
Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā | Oṃ hṛdayāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ śirase svāhā | Oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai svāhā |
Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya svāhā | Oṃ hauṃ netratrayāya svāhā | (p. 160) Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya svāhā |
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Sadāśiva; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vāgvādinī; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī.
O Nandikeśvara, one should thus offer libations to the Sādhyas and the deities of the mantras. 185.
And with these mantras, one should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, using their respective names:
*oṃ hāṃ aindryai svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ āgneyyai svāhā*;
*oṃ hāṃ dakṣiṇāyai svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ nairṛtyai svāhā*.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vāruṇī! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vāyavī!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Uttarā! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Aiśānī!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Antarikṣa!
In this manner, one should cause satisfaction for the ten directions and also provide the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Ādityas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Vasus!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Sādhyas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Maruts!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Bhṛgus! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Aṅgirases!
One should satisfy [these] deities, beginning with the Ādityas and ending with the Aṅgirases, using the *devatīrtha*.
There, wearing the sacred thread around his neck, he should perform the libations for the sages in the proper sequence.
With the middle of the *kuśa* grass, [one should touch] all those fingers and all the joints:
*oṃ hāṃ atraye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vasiṣṭhāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ hāṃ pulastyāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kratave namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhāradvāja. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viśvāmitra. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pracetas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sanātana.
The sages beginning with Atri and ending with Pracetas were born from the lineage of the gods. || 188 ||
The libation for human beings is performed from the base of the little fingers with the following mantras:
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanaka. Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanandana.
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanātana. Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanatkumāra.
Oṃ hāṃ kapilāya vaṣaṭ | Oṃ hāṃ ṛbhave vaṣaṭ | [These are for] the seven sages, beginning with Ṛbhu and Sanaka, in their respective order. || 189 ||
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with cooked rice as before:
"Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā); Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Rudra.
One should offer libations to the ten Caṇḍas, beginning with Śiva and ending with Caṇḍa. || 190 ||
One should satisfy the spirits with *hastamālya* along with rice grains:
*Oṃ hāṃ ākāśabhūtebhyo vauṣaṭ*. (p. 163)
Perform the libation for the elements, beginning with space and ending with earth.
Having placed the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder, one should perform the libation at the base of the index finger with the tips of *kuśa* grass together with sesame seeds. 192.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Kavyavāhana! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Anala!
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Soma! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Yama! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Aryaman! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Agniṣvātta!
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Ājyapa; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Somapa.
One should proceed with the offerings to the ancestors (pitṛs), beginning with Kavyavāha and ending with Somapa.

Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the fathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the great-grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the grandfather of my mother. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the great-grandfather of my mother.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all grandfathers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all kinsmen.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the teachers!
Then [the offering is made] to the human ancestors, beginning with the father and ending with the teacher. || 193 ||
And for the Mothers, the Grahas, and likewise the Rākṣasas,
one should perform the libation ending with "svadhā," exactly according to the prescribed rule.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the Mothers. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the Planets. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the Rākṣasas.
Oṃ hāṃ huṃ astrāya phaṭ—thus one should cast [the water] onto the bank.
Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ—thus [one should worship]. (p. 165)
One should dissolve all the sacred fords (tīrthas) into the heart by means of the Haṃsāraya-mudrā;
there, the right and left [channels] are equal, and immediately thereafter, one should recite another mantra.

Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa), one should immediately thereafter perform the ritual placement on the body (deha-nyāsa) for children, the simple-minded, the elderly, women, the sick, those who enjoy worldly pleasures, and kings. 196.
Having contracted [the visualization] through the mouth of the Guru, one should perform the libations and other rites. || 196½ ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, concerning the ritual for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), within the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is inconceivable.
Listen, I shall describe in detail the offering of water (arghya) and the worship of the Sun.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, one should begin the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya). (1)
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body from the heart to the weapon-mantra;
then, having meditated upon oneself as the sun, one should prepare the vessel for the arghya offering.
Having sat upon a seat facing the east, one should draw a circular mandala;
or else, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) on a pure spot of ground, one should do so with one's own hand.
One should smear the solar mandala with cow dung and water;
there, one should sprinkle it with water infused with red sandalwood while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having filled a copper vessel with water, [one should offer] red sandalwood,
rice, red flowers, kuśa grass, darbha grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and grains.
One should place a drop in the form of nectar upon the forehead-square;
having worshipped the Sun with the [five] limbs, one should perform the veiling with the armor-mantra.
Having performed protection with the Astra-mantra, he should kneel upon the ground;
then, with his gaze fixed upon the circle of ritual substances, he should extract what has become stuck there.
The practitioner should offer water for worship (arghya) to the Sun with the root mantra:
Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Sūrya. Oṃ Haṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to the form Khaṣolka.
Having recited the mantra for Mūrtimūrtīśvara, one should offer water for the arghya.
Having commenced the worship of the deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should reverently worship the circle of gurus correctly upon the crest-lock.
Having meditated upon the Sun-god, radiant with his limbs and attendants, within the heart,
one should worship the Sun within the conceptualized external image, as well as within the Moon. (10)
One should worship Daṇḍin and Piṅgala as gatekeepers:
Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Gurus.
One should invoke Gaṇeśāna in the northeast and the Guru in the southeast. || 11 ||
Having thus recited the mantra for Prabhūtāsana in the center of the white pedestal:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Prabhūtāsana.
In the southeastern direction, at the limit, and in the corners, respectively. || 12 ||
Then, having propitiated Vimalāsana, [one attains] the bliss known as the Supreme (Parama).
Oṃ hāṃ aṃ, obeisance to Vimalā; oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Ārādhya.
Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Paramasukha.
Having visualized above them a white, radiant pericarp,
[one should place] Oṃ Aṃ to Padmā.
[He gave] Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Rucā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and likewise Vimalā.
Amoghā and Vidyutā are likewise; in their midst is Sārvatomukhī.
One should worship the nine Śaktis in sequence, starting from the east to the northeast, and including the center.
Oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to Dīptā. Oṃ rīṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣmā.
Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Rucā. Oṃ rūṃ, obeisance to Bhadrā.
Oṃ raiṃ, obeisance to Vibhūti. Oṃ raiṃ, obeisance to Vimalā.
Oṃ rauṃ, homage to Amalā. Oṃ rauṃ, homage to Vidyutā.
Oṃ rīṃ, homage to Sarvatomukhī.
Facing all directions and situated everywhere, they should gaze upon it from all sides;
having recognized the sun-seat above, one should worship its weapon-mantra.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to the seat of the sun.
Grown upon a white lotus, auspicious and resembling a flower of illusion,
it is situated within a circle of exceedingly radiant, blazing red light.
Resembling many lamps, adorned with a crown of jewels,
clad in red garments, and anointed with red sandalwood paste.
With two white lotuses held at the base of his arms, adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, his auspicious fingers are joined in ritual gestures (mudrās). || 19 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord Bhāskara in embodied form— having one face, large eyes, and two arms, endowed with a thousand rays. (20)
Oṃ aṃ, salutation to Khaṣolkā, the Sun, the Embodiment.
Then, having filled the hollow of the hands with the palms joined and drawing [the breath] toward the forehead,
one should perform the installation with the pervasive root mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hauṃ sauṃ, salutation to Sūrya.
Then, one should meditate upon the invocation, the bringing near, the destruction [of obstacles], the veiling, and the installation of the forms by means of the mudrā.
For the sake of pleasing the King of Planets, one should display the Bindu-mudrā;
for that very mudrā is prescribed here as the Muditā-tri-mudrā.
Furthermore, one should perform the inconceivable sakalīkaraṇa of even the unity;
then, with Khaṣolkin, one should perform that [rite] and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).

Then the best of practitioners should present the head-offering, water for the feet, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and sacrificial food (caru), as well as the Pināka weapon, the leaf-seal, and the gesture (mudrā). || 26 ||
Their limbs are gentle in form, two-armed, and radiant;
with hands granting boons and holding lotuses, they resemble the pomegranate flower in hue.
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon the forms of Bhāskara’s body as having hair like blazing fire, two eyes, and being intensely agitated. 28.
Endowed with devotion, one should meditate upon the form of the Sun, whose face is formidable with fangs and who is supreme in threatening away the hosts of obstacles. (29)
Oṃ saṃ, homage to the heart. Oṃ aṃ, homage to the sun as the head.
Having properly worshipped at the ends of the Agni and Īśa petals,
the practitioner should worship the Śikhā and Varma in the direction of Nairṛti and the region of Vāyu respectively.
Oṃ raṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ. Salutation to Jvālinī, the crest-lock (śikhā).
Bhuṃ, salutation to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two eyes (netra).
Oṃ, salutation to the weapon; one should worship Bhadrākṣī in the north.
And one should display the heart-mantra and the others, as well as the ears and the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā). || 31 ||
With the *trāsanī* mudrā for the weapon and the *yonimudrā* for the two goddesses,
one should place Goddess Uṣā on the right side and Pratyuṣā on the left flank.
She has two arms and two eyes, possesses a face like a lotus,
is adorned with all ornaments, and is endowed with all auspicious marks. (33)
The best of practitioners, having [invoked] both of them, should worship them:
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the goddess Uṣā; Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Pratyuṣā. 34.
On the eastern petal, [one should worship] Soma with the mantra ending in "namaḥ"; then Budha in the southern vessel with the mantra ending in "namo budhāya. (35)
On the tip of the western petal as well: *Bṛṃ*, obeisance to Bṛhaspati;

she is the increaser of nourishment (*puṣṭivardhanakarī*). Therefore, in my worship on the days beginning with Sunday, the offering (*arghya*) and worship of the Sun-god must be performed for the sake of [attaining] success; [this is] always in the center.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of the Sun, within the *Viśvasādākhya* [treatise] on the inconceivable.

175) Now, listen in due order to that which is characterized as the *saṃskāradīkṣā*: the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the mandala, the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and the worship of the *liṅga*. || 1 ||
Just as the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā) and the consecration with the water-pot (kalaśābhiṣecana) are performed,
one should worship the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) on the outside and perform the remainder as previously described.
If one has previously performed the dialogue as instructed by the disciple with faith, and always maintains freedom from anger, devotion, trust, and obedience to the command of Śarva; (3)
Endowed with the fourfold [union] and free from all afflictions,
yet one who has committed acts of treachery against the Guru, treachery against Śiva, or treachery against the sacred commitments (samaya).
For one who is uninitiated, there is attachment to kin, ingratitude, lack of discernment, the perception of faults in the guru, and a failure to perceive one's own faults. (5)
A disciple devoid of these eight qualities is worthy of purification;
however, one should initiate again at the proper time a disciple who possesses the opposite qualities. (6)

Later, during the consecration of the ritual refinements (*saṃskāradīkṣā*), the excellent preceptor, having performed everything from the mandala up to the worship of the fire, will become a disciple (*antevāsin*).
One should present the disciple, who has been purified by bathing and other rites, on the left side,
within the fire of Maheśa and in the center of the heart-lotus.
One should invoke the two Śivas in union with the nectar from the heart;
having satisfied them, one should perform worship as the means for their presence.
One should offer five oblations with the mantra at the heart;
thereafter, one should strike the disciple's heart with a flower using the Astra-mantra.
One should meditate upon the light of consciousness (caitanya) as having the form of an internal flame;
having entered therein, one proceeds through the wheels by means of the application of the syllable *hūṃ*. (11)
Having drawn [the consciousness] in with the *saṃhāramudrā* and through inhalation (*pūraka*), one should place it in the heart.
"Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self. Although Śiva has been attained, the consciousness of the disciple remains within his mouth.
Having honored both its defects and virtues, everything is seen within the fire;
when the fire is blazing and free of smoke, the oblation grants the accomplishment of all aims.
If the fire is not blazing but is accompanied by smoke, the desired result of the oblation is not accomplished.
[A favorable fire] has a clockwise flame, is glossy, fragrant, and endowed with brilliance. (14)
Resembling the sound of a mṛdaṅga drum and accompanied by the roar of thunderclouds,
it is radiant, well-proportioned, white and red, and bestows auspiciousness. (15)
It possesses the luster of a flame, is joined with a crest, and is accompanied by sparks and ashes;
it is like a fish, has the sound of a child's cry, and resembles the voice of an owl.
Endowed with such vowels and so forth, the Hotṛ priest should bring about his own time;
he should then examine the signs of the disciple's sins by means of the fire.
The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a father, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the ungrateful, the reviler of the gods, and likewise the reviler of the wise; || 18 ||
A thief of knowledge, a usurper of land, one who associates with such people, and a reviler of the guru—
among these great sinners, there shall then be the stench of excrement.
In the case of one who has killed a fetus, leprosy and fire afflict them; in the case of killing a woman, they wander again.
In the case of one who has cut off a child's hair, the fire clearly bursts forth in an instant. (20)

O disciple, even during the performance of the fire-oblation, if the fire flickers and lacks luster due to the destruction of an embryo, one should clearly recognize that great impurity through these characteristics of the sacred fire.
One should burn away [impurities] by means of the *pāpabhakṣaṇa* oblation with this concluding mantra:
*oṃ khaḍgahasta! pāpakaluṣa bṛhanmayūkha phaṭ phaṭ pāpabhakṣaṇāya svāhā*. This is the *pāpabhakṣaṇa* mantra.
Having recited it twice for the destruction of sins, one should likewise meditate upon the portion belonging to Rudra.

For the purification through feeding the twice-born, for the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna), for the rite to ensure a male child (puṃsavana), for the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and for the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa). || 23 ||
One should offer oblations with the root mantra and the five Brahma-mantras one hundred times each during the rite of delivery,
as well as during the first feeding of solid food and the tonsure ceremony.

O Nandikeśvara! [One should perform this] at the initiation, the instruction of vows, the Godāna ceremony, the rite of ritual bathing, marriage, the life of a forest-dweller, and the state of a mendicant. (25)
One should perform a fire-oblation for each of the five parts with the root mantra;
for those established in the four stages of life (āśramas), the rite shall be according to the rules of their respective stage.
One should perform the consecration ceremony at that time, and from then on, one should not have it performed again—
especially regarding the states of being a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic.
The best of preceptors should perform the oblation with the root mantra as before;
this is the extraction of the power whose bonds have become loosened. (28)

The conception (garbhādhāna) regarding the Self’s status as the son of Rudra is thus described; likewise, the manifestation of qualities such as sovereignty constitutes the rite of male-conception (puṃsavana). (29)
Knowledge through the discernment of the illusory self is the "increase of the parting line" (*sīmantavardhana*);
the acceptance of real and unreal entities, beginning with Śiva, constitutes "birth" (*janana*). (30)
Awakening is that by which one attains the fitness for Śiva-hood through the state of being Śiva;
indeed, the entry into Śiva-hood is called "emergence. (31)
The consumption of this food is said to be supreme bliss;
that which is the excellence of Śiva’s grace occurs through the nature of the crest-jewel (cūḍā).
Bound by the thread of the knowledge of Nirvāṇa and supported by the life-force, the restraint of the senses is known as the instruction in the vows. || 33 ||
