Renouncing rebirth is proclaimed as the "gift of the cow" (godāna);
being free from attachment toward all things is said to be the "bath" (snāna).
The union with infinite power is proclaimed as marriage;
the separation from infinite power is held to be the state of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha). (35)
When it is demonstrated that the state of a seeker (yatitva) consists solely in the true being of Śiva,
one should discard the topknot, the external sacred thread, and so forth, for his sake.
One should perform all these [rites] during every initiation or at [the time of] Nirvāṇa and so forth;
for forty purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are proclaimed as the essential core.
Then,
having assumed the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should withdraw that [mantra] which resembles Tāraka into the lotus-heart of the Guru.
Having established [the elements] as appropriate, one should perform the ritual of retention (kumbhana) with the root mantra;
one should effect the state of essential identity (samarasībhāva) of Śiva and Śivā with the root mantra. || 39 ||
By abandoning the causal principles beginning with Brahmā through the sequential practice of exhalation (recaka),
and by means of the yoga of true being, one leads the self to the state of Śiva through the yoga of true being. (40)
Having taken that [mantra] through its emergence and enclosing it within the heart with the mantra,
one should [place it] by means of exhalation alone into the lotus-heart of the disciple.
Having become composed in mind, one should cast it upon that pericarp;
and having worshipped the auspicious fire, one should worship it with the *arbha* mantra.
Having caused [the disciple] to perform prostrations and likewise having made him bow down, the most excellent Guru should cause the disciple to hear all the pledges (samaya). 43.
One should not revile the causal deity, nor likewise the censure of knowledge, nor the practitioner, nor one advanced in knowledge, nor an elder endowed with devotion. (44)
One must not step over the shadow of the elder preceptor’s *liṅga*;
one must not consume the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*); and one must not revile the devotees of Śiva. (45)
One should not step over it, nor should one give it away—especially not to one who has been initiated.
Those seeking their livelihood must indeed perform the worship of Śiva, the fire, and the Guru.
Faith, devotion, trust, and likewise the observance of the guru’s command—this fourfold set must be practiced in due order with regular discipline. (47)

Betrayal of the guru, betrayal of Śiva, and likewise betrayal of the sacred pledge (samaya); being a kinsman to one who is uninitiated; ingratitude; and lack of discernment—(these are the causes of downfall). 48.
Beholding the faults of the teacher while failing to behold one's own faults—these [characteristics] especially belong to these twenty-seven types of śrāvakas. (49)
p.
185) Nineteen [rites] are to be performed, and the group of eight [rites] beginning with "it is to be done" [is also required].
As before, there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (caru). || 50 ||
From this point forward, one should primarily perform acts such as devotion to Śiva;
all these nourishors of the limbs of the vow, and that which is appropriate for them and so forth, [should be practiced]. 51.
Having consecrated the staff of devotion, the loincloth, and likewise the water-pot with the five Brahma-mantras and their ancillaries, as prescribed; 52.
Having placed [the materials] in a vessel, accompanied by the Saṃhitā mantras ending with "svāhā," and having obtained the command of Śiva, the Guru shall impart these vows to the qualified disciple.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, endowed with devotion and firm in his vows,
he should take that Lord into his heart and bear him there, accompanied by his disciple.
The initiation by refinement (saṃskāradīkṣā) is superior to the [initiation by] rule (samaya); it is especially fit for the fire-sacrifice (homa) according to the tradition (āgama).
The disciple, endowed with constant wisdom,
should likewise perform the worship of the liṅga.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the initiation through action, within the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is inconceivable.
I shall describe the meritorious daily worship, which bestows auspiciousness, destroys sin, grants yoga and knowledge, bestows liberation, and increases devotion. (1)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit equal to the worship of Śiva.
The worship of Śiva is twofold: for one’s own sake and for the sake of others. (2)
That fruit, having regard for one's own interest, is attained for the sake of oneself;
but the fruit of worship, being common, one should dedicate to all beings. (3)
That is declared to be for the sake of others, yet it is the fruit for oneself of all [beings].
All principles (tattva) and so forth are to be known as the cause of all causes.
The supreme light in the form of Śiva is designated as the *liṅga*; its radiance is called *śakti*, which is indeed the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), just like a base. (5)
Because it is the characteristic mark of the origin of everything, it is called the *liṅga* first;
because everything dissolves into it, it is called the *liṅga* due to its nature as a place of dissolution.
All this, whether moving or unmoving, consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti;
just as the branches of a tree are satisfied by the offering of water at the root of the tree.
(188) Therefore, the gods and all embodied beings are satisfied by the worship of the *liṅga*.
Now listen further to the specific details regarding the *caraliṅga* for one's own sake.
It is of three kinds: born of stone, born of metal, and born of gems.
That which is born of stone is of a single variety, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The [image] born of jewels shall be of eight varieties, and likewise that born of metals;
[the jewels are] ruby, coral, lapis lazuli, and crystal. (10)
Vajra, emerald, sapphire, and ruby are born of jewels;
the māṇikya is known to bestow prosperity, while coral brings about subjugation. (11)
Lapis lazuli leads to the attainment of sons; crystal bestows all success;
the diamond (vajra) causes the destruction of enemies; and emerald increases prosperity.
A blue [stone] bestows wealth and grain, while a topaz (puṣparāga) grants enjoyment.
Thus has that which is born of gems been described; now that which is born of metals is further explained. (13)
Gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, and brass; iron, lead, tin, and whatever is born of metal. (14)
A golden vessel is known to bestow prosperity, a silver one grants royal success, a copper one bestows sons, and a bell-metal one is indeed inauspicious. (15)
Lead causes expulsion and is an excellent poison; iron is the cause of victory;
tin removes disease, and all three increase longevity. (16)
Thus has that which is born of metal been described; now that which is born of stone is further explained:
it is that which arises at sacred fords such as the Narmadā and at confluences of rivers.
That liṅga which is called Bāṇa is for the worship of those committed to lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika);
the Saliṅga, when joined with a pedestal (piṇḍikā), bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (18)
Therefore, both the householder and likewise the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) [should perform] purification,
sipping water, and bathing according to the previously stated rules.
Having washed one's feet, one should enter the place of worship,
facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat.
Whether for the sake of others and oneself, or specifically for one's own self,
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, one should arrange the materials for worship.
Having offered the *praṇava-arghya* and performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the worship of the door;
the worship of the eastern door bestows prosperity and grants knowledge. (22)
Victory, fame, and good fortune [are attained through the eastern gate], while the southern [gate] likewise bestows strength;
this worship of the western door brings about dispassion and spiritual power.
For devotion and liberation, worship at all doors is common;
however, a northern door should not be made, and thus an eastern door is prescribed.
Having recited the syllable Oṃ ten times, one should prepare the arghya offering;
having sprinkled [the area] with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the gatekeepers.
Having worshipped the bull at the entrance: *oṃ hāṃ vṛṣabhāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ astrāya namaḥ* |
Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the southern [direction] of the Ūrdhvodumbaraka [mandala];
he is red in color, four-armed, and equipped with a ṭaṅka and a goad.
In the [right] hand, [he holds] a rosary, his own tusk, and a citron; in the [left] hand, [he holds] a lotus. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati.
And one should worship Sarasvatī on the upper-northern portion of the door.
[One should meditate upon] the goddess Sarasvatī, white as the moon and jasmine, with four hands and well-adorned;
[invoking her with] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. Between those two [goddesses], one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, golden-hued and adorned. (28)
She was consecrated by streams of nectar from the *śṛṅgāra* vessel held in the trunk of an elephant;
she had four arms, three eyes, and was adorned with all ornaments. (29)
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahālakṣmī.
Red in color, with three eyes, matted hair, four arms, and a large belly;
he likewise holds a mallet, a raised index finger, a trident, and a rosary.
And likewise [one should worship] Nandin, who holds [a staff], with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin.
[One should visualize] Śivā, who resembles pure crystal, has two eyes, and two arms. (31)
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all fragrances,
she is mounted upon the seat of a sea-monster (makara), holding a vessel of nectar and a blue lotus.
One should worship Gaṅgā, who holds the object in the form of water, with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ Gaṅgāyai namaḥ," and likewise worship Gaṅgā and Nandin on the southern branch.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with four arms and three eyes,
[he holds] a mallet, a trident, the gesture of emptiness (śūnyamudrā), and a skull-cup.
One should meditate upon him wearing a serpent as a sacred thread and having two severed feet, and one should recite the mantra:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. (35)
Yamunā is dark-complexioned, two-armed, and three-eyed;
she is endowed with a jar filled with nectar and blue lotuses. (36)
To the north of the branch, [one should worship] Kūrmavāhā, who has gracious eyes, who is a mass of merit, and who is dear to Śiva: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yamunā. (37)
One should worship each [rite] in sequence from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the lamp (dīpa), using the thumb and ring finger with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva" (śivāya namaḥ).
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) upon the three eyes, one should cast away the divine obstacles;
and having abandoned the divine obstacles, one should do so again with the nārāca-mudrā.
"Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ! By joining the index finger and the thumb [in this mudrā], O Nandikeśvara, the obstacles in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) are dispelled. (40)
By striking the ground three times with the outer heel, obstacles situated on the earth are destroyed;
by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, the removal of obstacles shall occur. (41)
The branch serving as the threshold for the sake of others should be at the front of the southern direction;
then, one should enter the temple again with only the right foot.

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with "oṃ hāṃ astrāya phaṭ" upon the mouth and the two arms, [one should visualize the deity] with four faces and four arms, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire. || 43 ||
Holding a spear, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons with his right and left hands;
endowed with a crown of matted hair, with the moon as his crest upon his head. (44)
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati). Thus also is the worship of the deity of the site performed in the middle of the threshold. (45)
Inside the door, on the right side, let them perform your worship [to the deity who is] red in color, four-armed, three-eyed, and moon-crested. (46)
Salutation to the leader of the Gaṇas, who is adorned with a crown of matted locks, endowed with the *namaskāra* mudrā,
and holding both an axe and a deer.
He held a cane in one hand at the base of his arm and a small dagger at his hip;
he was adorned with all ornaments, and his body was smeared with ashes.
He wore a sacred thread made of rudrākṣa beads, was clad in a white sacrificial thread,
and likewise bore a long necklace and a hand-garland of rudrākṣa beads.
Having uttered "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ca Sa," [one should say] "Salutation to Nandikeśvara.
Having thus worshipped Nandin, one should worship Yaśodevī on the left.
She is dark-complexioned, with gracious eyes, two-armed, and the leader of the Gaṇas;
she is adorned with all ornaments and beautiful with every auspicious mark. (51)
Then one should worship her holding a blue lotus in her right hand, having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ" and "Salutation to Yaśodēvī. (52)
Having thus worshipped her with devotion for the sake of the perfect attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should then worship the seat of one's own Guru with devotion in the northeast.
Oṃ hāṃ guṃ, one should indeed offer salutation to the seat of the Guru;
then, by means of the sequence of the five purifications, one should worship the imperishable Śiva.
Having first performed the purification of oneself, one should next perform the purification of the place;
the third is the purification of the ritual materials, and the fourth is the purification of the mantra.
The fifth is the purification of the *liṅga*; thus has the sequence of purifications been declared.
Having recited the root mantra three times with the *saṃhāramudrā* [56].
Then, one should touch [the body] with both hands from the crown of the head down to the feet, reciting: "Oṃ Hiṃ, obeisance to the Sadyojāta form. (57)
"Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret one"—thus also [it is said].
Having first uttered "Oṃ huṃ," [one offers] to Aghora and to the heart. (58)
After "namaskāraṃ namaḥ," [one says] "oṃ hentaṭpuruṣaṃ tathā vaktrāya namaḥ";
at the end, [one says] "oṃ homīśānamūrtaye. (59)
One should perform the salutation (namaskāra), placing [the mantras] in sequence from the little finger to the thumb:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, the form of the feet. "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the form of Īśāna.
Then one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga): Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart. || 60 ||
Oṃ hīṃ haṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ hoṃ, then for the crest-lock (śikhā), uttering it with "vaṣaṭ" at the end; then Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca). || 61 ||
Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
One should perform the worship upon the fingers and place [the mantras] at their tips.
One should especially encircle [the body] with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and the two hands;
having recited the root mantra, one should perform the rites beginning with the head, accompanied by the water-offering (arghya) and other elements.
One should visualize the Mahāmudrā and contemplate the mandala of the Guru at the tip of the crest-lock,
twelve finger-breadths [above the head], endowed with a thousand petals. (64)
Resembling ten million suns, as cool as ten million moons,
its form is pure consciousness-power alone, radiant with the pericarp of stars.

One should place that supreme form consisting of thirty-eight *kalās*, radiant with filaments, enriched with the seed-syllable of the five syllables, [and assign] its *Tatpuruṣa* face upon the mouth. (66)
One should assign Aghora to the heart and Vāma to the secret place;
one should place Sadyojāta on the two feet, and the sequence beginning with the crown (makuṭa) should be assigned accordingly.
Having placed the heart-mantra upon the heart, one should place the head-mantra upon the head;
having placed the crest-mantra upon the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
One should place the *netra* mantra at the region of the eyes and the *astra* mantra in the directions in due order.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* on the head, one should place the syllable *ā* at the heart. (69)
O Nandikeśvara, one should place the syllable *sūṃ* at the region of the throat;
then, one should place Śrīkaṇṭha in sequence, from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*.
Then, ending with Śrīkaṇṭha, there are Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Adhiśa, Bhogabhujiṣya, Āra, Bhūti, Atithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara. (71)
Jhaṣeśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūra, and Mahāsena are the personified forms of the vowels.
Then Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Pañcāntaka, Śivottama, Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekadru, and Caturānana. || 73 ||
Ajeśa, Sarvaperīśa, Lāṅgalin, Dāruka,
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Āṣāḍha, and Daṇḍin. (74)
Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, Śikhin, Calaraṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mahākāla, and Tānin; || 75 ||
Bhujaṅgeśa, Oṇinākīśa, Khaṭvāṅgabhīti, Baka, Śvetābhrakūla, Kūlī, and Saṃvartaka are remembered as forms of Śiva. || 76 ||
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and the third, Śālmalī; likewise Lohā, Alohā, Āvartulā, and Dīrghakoṇā. (77)
Sudīrghamukhī, Gaurī, and the ninth, Dīrghajihvikā;
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśinī, Mukhī, and Vikṛtapūrvikā. || 78 ||
Together with the splendor of the *Sajvālikī* [mantra], the primary Vidyās are the powers of the vowels (*svaraśakti*).
Likewise, Mahākālī and Sarasvatī are endowed with all supernatural attainments (*sarvasiddhi*). (79)
Gaurī, Tryailokyavidyā, and likewise Mantrātmaśaktikā; Bhūtamātā, Vidyate, Lambodarī, and Nāgarī—these eight are present. (80)
Khecarī, Mañjarī, Virūpī, Viriṇī, Kodarī, Pūtanā, Bhadrā, and Kālī—these indeed are the Yoginīs. || 81 ||
Śaṅkhinī, Garjanī, Kālarātri, and Kubjinī;
likewise Kapardinī, Bhadrājayā, and Sumukheśvarī. (82)
Revatī, Māyavī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vāyavī; another, Rakṣovadhāriṇī, as well as she who is Gayā. (83)
Lakṣmī, Vyāpinī, Mārī, and Mā—these are the Tāṇḍava powers;
together with these powers, one should install the syllables in their proper sequence. (84)
Having placed the syllable *a* on the crown of the head and the syllable *ā* on the face,
one should place the syllable *i* in the right eye and the syllable *ī* in the left eye.
The letter *u* is in the right ear, the letter *ū* in the left ear;
the letter *ṛ* is in the right nostril, and the letter *ṝ* in the left nostril.
The letter *ḷ* on the right cheek, the letter *ḹ* on the left cheek, the letter *e* on the upper lip, and then the letter *ai* on the lower lip. (87)
The letter *o* is on the upper lip and teeth; the letter *au* is on the lower teeth;
the letter *aṃ* is at the root of the palate, and the letter *aḥ* is in the middle of the palate. || 88 ||
In this manner, according to the sequence of the ritual procedure, one should place the sixteen vowels;
the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left hand. (89)
The *ṭa*-group is on the right side, the *ta*-group on the left side; the *pa*-group is in the region of the back, while the letter *ha* is situated below the navel.
Having placed the syllable *ma* at the navel, one should place the seven [syllables] beginning with *ya* above it;
[these correspond to] skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
Having placed the syllable *eka* in the heart and the syllable *la* in the region of the anus,
and having placed the syllable *kṣa* in the private parts, one is endowed with the mantra of placement (*nyāsa*).
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī.
Oṃ āṃ, obeisance to Ananta and Bindujā.
Oṃ jaṃ, homage to Sūkṣmā Śālī.
Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Trimūrti Lolākṣī.
Oṃ uṃ, obeisance to Amareśvara and Vartulā.
Oṃ ūṃ, salutation to Aghīśa and Dīrghakoṇā.
Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Sthāṇu and Dīrghajihvikā.
Oṃ Ḷṃ, homage to Hāra and Kuṇḍodarī.
Oṃ Ṛṃ, homage to Bhārabhūti, the one with a long face.
Oṃ Ṛṃ, salutation to the Overlord and to Gomukhī.
Oṃ eṃ, obeisance to Nyaruṇḍaśā, who has hair standing erect.
Oṃ aiṃ, salutation to Bhautika, the one with a distorted face.
Oṃ oṃ, homage to Sadyojāta and Jvālāmukhī!
Oṃ auṃ, salutation to Anugraheśa and Ulkāmukhī.
Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Akrūra, the foremost of the illustrious ones.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to Mahāsena, the foremost of those possessing vidyā.
Oṃ, homage to Krodhīśa and Mahākālī.
Oṃ Khaṃ! Homage to Caṇḍīśa and Sarasvatī.
Oṃ Gaṃ, homage to Pañcāntā for the sake of all accomplishments and activities.
Oṃ Ghaṃ, homage to Śivottama, the Vidyā of the three worlds.
Oṃ ṅaṃ, homage to Ekarudra, the power of the mantra.
Oṃ Caṃ, obeisance to the Tortoise and to Śakti.
Salutation to Ekanetra, the mere element of existence.
Salutation to the four-faced one and to the pot-bellied goddess.
Jhaṃ, obeisance to Ajeśa and Drāviṇī.
Homage to the city Sarvā.
Ṭaṃ, salutation to Someśvara and Khecarī.
Ṭhaṃ, salutation to Mañjarī, the wife of Lāṅgalin.
Ḍam, salutation to Dārukā and Rūpiṇī.
Ḍhaṃ, obeisance to Ardhanārīśvara and to Vīriṇī.
Salutation to the beloved of Umā; salutation to Kākodaryā.
Homage to that Āṣāḍhā, the purifier.
Salutation to Daṇḍin and to Bhadrakālī.
p.
209) Salutation to the Yoginī Damatrī.
Salutation to Dhammīnāyā Śaṅkhinī.
Salutation to the pregnant ewe; salutation!
Salutation to Pām, the red one, the Night of Doom.
Obeisance to Phamśikhinī and Kubjinī.
Bam! Salutation to Kapardinī, the one with matted hair.
Bhaṃ, salutation to Dviraṇḍa-Vajrā.
Salutation to me, Mahākāla, and to Jayā.
Salutation to Yam, the self of the skin, the sovereign goddess facing Bali.
Salutation to Revatī, the mistress of serpents, whose essence is blood.
Salutation to the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose nature is the path and the flesh, and salutation to Mādhavī.
Vam, salutation to the one whose self is fat, the wielder of the sword, belonging to Varuṇa.
Śam! Homage to the white-souled one with matted hair, belonging to the Vāyu [direction].
Oṃ, salutation to the white one who is the essence of the marrow and who bears the destruction of demons.
Salutation to Sahajā, who is of white nature and possesses a frown, O Bhrukuṭīśa.
Oṃ hrauṃ haṃ, obeisance to Bakulin, the self of vital breath, for Lakṣmī.
Salutation to Śiva, the pervasive one, whose nature is power, and to Vyāpinī.
Salutation to Kṣamā, to Saṃvartakā, and to Māyā.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ—having pronounced these separately—I bow to Īśāna, the head.
To Tatpuruṣa, the face; to Aghora, the heart; or [to Vāmadeva, the secret place]. || 93 ||
One should assign Vāmadeva to the secret part and Sadyojāta to the form;
[one should also assign] the Tāra (Om), the seed-syllable, and the Śakti, beginning with the mantra and ending with the syllable *tamaḥ*.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ, homage to Īśāna, the head.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ, homage to Vāmadeva, the secret one.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the placement of the heart and the six limbs;
one should place the [five kalās] beginning with Śāntyatītā on the head and so forth, down to the feet, in due order.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās:
five kalās of Īśāna and four kalās of Puruṣa.
The eight digits (kalās) of Aghora, the thirteen of Vāmadeva, and the eight digits of Sadyojāta are to be known; one should install them in sequence, beginning with the crown (makuṭa). 97.
Īśāna, Īśvara, Brahmā, Śiva, and Sadāśiva; Tatpuruṣa, Mahādeva—may that Rudra inspire us. (98)
Aghora, and then Aghora, and likewise Ghora;
then Ghoratara, and also Sarva from all sides. (99)
And salutations to you who are present in all; Rudra is said to consist of eight parts (kalās):
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, and likewise Kalavikaraṇa.
Balavikaraṇa, Balapramathana, Sarvabhūtadamana, as well as Mana and Unmana—these are remembered as the kalās of Vāmadeva. 101.
Sadyojāta and Sadyas, Bhava and Udbhava, as well as Anādibhava, and Bhavaskambhavadudbhava. || 102 ||
The thirty-eight digits (kalās) have been declared; now the power of the digits (kalāśakti) is described:
Śaśinī, Aṅgagā, Ceṣā, Marīci, and likewise Jvālinī. || 103 ||
One should place these five kalās upon the five pentads of roots:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. (104)

Thus, the fourfold power (śakti) has been described in its upward-facing aspect: darkness (tamas), hunger (doha), sleep (akṣayā-nidrā), contentment (dhṛti), forbearance (kṣānti), mindfulness (smṛti), and patience (kṣamā). 105.
In Aghora there are eight powers, and likewise they are spoken of in Vāmadeva:
Rajas, Pakṣāpati, Pālyā, Kāmā, Syandamanī, and Kriyā. (106)
Tṛṣṇā, Mohakṣudhā, Cintā, Mohinī, and Bhramaṇī—these are proclaimed as the thirteen powers (kalā-śaktis) of Vāmadeva. (107)
O Nandikeśvara, Siddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, Prajā, and Sadyas—these are declared to be the eight Kalā-śaktis. 108.

The five digits (kalās) of Īśāna are located in the pentad beginning with the upward-facing head; [the digit] Śaktyatītā is in the upward face, while those arising from Puruṣa are in the [faces] starting from the east. (109)
In this manner, one should place [the mantras] joined with the Śaktis upon the four faces:
in the heart of Aghora, in the right ear, and likewise in the left hand.
At the navel, the belly, the back, and likewise the chest;
Vāmadeva at the private parts, and likewise on the two testicles.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the two thighs, the two knees, the pair of shanks, as well as on the buttocks, the skin, the region of the waist, and the two sides. 112.
One should place Sadyojāta on the pair of feet, and likewise on the pair of hands,
as well as on the nose, the region of the head, and the pair of arms.
"Om Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ śaśinyai namaḥ"— thus [one should worship] on the upper head.
"Oṃ, the Lord of all beings; salutation to Gadā"—thus on the eastern head.
Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of Brahmā, the overlord of Brahmā, the bestower of desired boons; thus [one should worship] on the right head.
Oṃ śivo me astu marīcyai namaḥ—thus on the northern head. Sadāśivoṃ jvālinyai namaḥ—thus on the western head.
Oṃ, homage to Śāntyatītā; thus, homage to the upward-facing one.
Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe śāntyai namaḥ—thus on the eastern face.
"Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation to Vidyā"—thus [he recites] at the southern face.
"May Rudra grant us firm standing; salutation!"—thus on the northern face.
"Pracodayāt, salutation to Nivṛtti"—thus [he should worship] at the western face.
"Oghorebhyaḥ-tamaṃ laye namaḥ. Thus, [one should offer salutation] in the heart.
Then, [the mantra] "Obeisance to Ghorebhyaḥ Mohāyai" is at the throat.
Salutation to Aghorā on the right shoulder;
salutation to Aghoratarā and Nidrā on the left shoulder.
Salutation to Sarvatassavardhṛti at the navel.
Salutation to all for patience in the belly; salutation be to you at the union of Rudra on the back; salutation to the forms for destruction on the chest. Thus are the eight Aghora-kalās.

Salutation to Vāmadeva, salutation to Kalā, at the secret place (guhya). And salutation to Jyeṣṭha, salutation to Yakṣa, at the liṅga. Salutation to Rudra, salutation to Rati, on the right thigh. Salutation to Kāla, salutation to Pālī, salutation, on the left thigh. Salutation to Kalavikaraṇa, salutation to Vikaraṇā.
Salutation to Saṃyaminī on the left knee; salutation to Balakriyā on the right shank.
Salutation to Vikaraṇā; salutation to Sraṇā and Kāmā on the left calf.

Salutation to Balamohanā on the right hip; salutation to Pramathanā and salutation to Kṣudhā on the left hip; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanā on the right knee; salutation to Citā on the waist; salutation to Mohinī on the right side; salutation to Unmattā and salutation to Bhrāmiṇī.
On the left side: the thirteen digits (kalās) of Vāmadeva.
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation for the sake of accomplishment on the right foot.
Salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Ṛddhi on the left foot.
p.
218) "To Bhavī, salutation! on the right hand; "To Abhavī, salutation to Alakṣmī! on the left hand.

"Salutation to Anādibhava, salutation to Medhā on the nose; serve me, salutation to Kānti on the forehead; be present, salutation to Svadhā on the right arm; arise, salutation to Prajā on the left arm"—thus are the eight Sadyojāta-kalās.
One should perform the ritual placement of the parts (kalānyāsa) by means of the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
using either the seed-mantras alone or the mantras for the faces and other limbs of the deity.
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the root mantra upon the eyes and the chest of the deity.
Thus concludes the procedure for placement (nyāsavidhi).
Then one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), preceded by meditation and worship. || 115 ||

One should worship Śiva in the heart-lotus with flowers and other offerings, along with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth; that lotus has arisen from the root-tuber (*kanda*) at its navel and is endowed with eight petals. (116)
Endowed with the pericarp and filaments, situated at the side of the Suṣumnā, the seat (āsana) extends from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the earth element. || 117 ||

O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Śivāsana and the Mūrti, as well as the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the mantras, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of oblations (bali). || 118 ||
One should worship with substances such as perfumes and incense, especially while endowed with devotion toward the true nature of Sadāśiva. (119)

Through the gateway of the piṅgalā-nāḍī, one should worship the Śiva-fire that has arisen within oneself in the navel-pit (nābhikuṇḍa), offering oblations there in due order, as in a sacrificial rite.

O Nandikeśvara, having drawn [the breath] through the iḍā [nāḍī] by means of the filling [breath] (pūraka), and with the nectar of the auspicious atoms (śivāṇu), one should perform [this rite] using the very nectar of the dvādaśānta. (121)
One should always meditate upon the stainless Maheśvara, who resembles the autumnal moon, whose form is a drop (bindu), and who resides in the center of the forehead. 122.
The sequence for the purification of oneself has been taught; now listen to the purification of the place.
One should sprinkle it with the water of the general *arghya* while reciting the *astra-mantra*. (123)
Having performed the placement of the three eyes at the root, one should gaze with a divine vision;
thereafter, one should purify the vessel and the various substances therein.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or pure crystal and conch-shell; it may be fashioned from the leaves of the Palāśa or lotus, or made of wood or clay. || 125 ||
Or whatever else, such as a mechanical device and so forth, has been mentioned as being used for the worship of Śiva:
having washed it with water empowered by the *astra* mantra, place it afterwards face-down upon a hide. (126)
One should purify the yawning and the eyes with the heart [mantra], and fill them with water in the form of nectar flowing from the *bindu*. || 127 ||
Uśīra and sandalwood are for the water for washing the feet; thereafter is the water for sipping, combined with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, jasmine, and camphor.
These seven—betel nut, incense, milk, tips of kuśa grass, flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains—are for the water for sipping and the sacrificial altar. || 129 ||
Sesame seeds and white mustard seeds constitute the excellent middle eightfold offering;
one should fill [the vessel] with pure scented water while reciting the heart mantra. || 130 ||
The general *arghya* should be prepared as appropriate, along with bathing water scented with sandalwood,
agallochum, camphor, nutmeg, saffron, and cinnamon leaves. (131)
Uśīra and water likewise constitute the eight-fold fragrance for the worship of Śiva;
having filled [the vessel] with the six-limbed [mantra] starting from the heart, and having thus completed the filling, one should consecrate it with mantras.
Having performed the protection with the weapon-mantra, one should cover [the vessel] with the armor-mantra;
then, one should place a flower in the vessel and purify it with the dhenu-mudrā.
[One should offer] white arka, tulasī, niguṇḍī, bhadrakāsumana, dūrvā, mango, bilva, jambūka, munipatra, and kapittha. (134)
The mātuluṅga, the vakula, the karṇikāra, the āmalakī, the saptacchada, the priyaṅgu, the lavaṅga, and the nāgakesara. (135)
Aṅkola, bhujapatra, kadamba, bakapuṣpaka, kirañca, araṇḍaka, guñjā, dīrghavṛtta, and campaka. (136)
The Punnāga, Devadāru, Bilva, Dhūrdhūra, Tamāla, Agnimantha, Pāṭala, and likewise Varukā. || 137 ||
And Brahmakī, Parikrūra, Sabhātā, Ākulī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Krīṇī, Hādānavī, and likewise Sumukhī. || 138 ||
Sugandhī, muṇḍīsūryā, and likewise pādaparṇī;
devatālī, mallī, and likewise kaṅkirāta. || 139 ||
That which is *sācikaravīra* and likewise *nandyāvarta*, *hrībera* and *granthiparṇī*, and also *mahāpadma*. || 140 ||
The lotus, the mālatī, the kalhāra, the droṇapuṣpaka,
and the vyāghrāta flower— with the fine leaves and blossoms of these— (141).
The Nandyāvartī is prescribed for sunrise, the Karavīra at midday,
the Mallikā in the evening, and the Mālatī also at midnight.
One should worship with those flowers that are appropriate for that particular time;
[one should avoid] buds, fallen flowers, withered ones, those already smelled, or those defiled by insects. (143)
Nor should one worship a lotus that has been touched by a limb or one that has been stale;
among all lotus flowers, this blue lotus (nīlotpala) is supreme.
Devotion toward even a thousand blue lotuses is exceedingly supreme;
yet if that devotion is joined with faith, the fruit is even greater than that. (145)
Endowed with these—devotion, faith, and firm conviction—one should remain equanimous; with a single-minded focus and well-restrained, one should offer worship even to those who are censured. (146)
For in this way, the supreme triad of worship is indeed accomplished immediately;
even in the absence of flowers, there may be leaves, and in the absence of leaves, there may be fruit.
In the absence of fruit, one should worship with three types of substances such as rice and so forth;
one should sprinkle the articles of worship, the flowers, and other offerings with the water of the *arghya* offering.
One should look with the divine eye after reciting [the mantra] while observing the weapon-gaze;
this is declared to be the purification of substances. Now, the purification of mantras is described. (149)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, and then the Bindu and Nāda, one should recite the entire mantra in their midst, ending with a salutation (namaskāra). || 150 ||
And at the end of that, the purification of the mantra joined with the *kalā*s is proclaimed.
The Sun receives worship during the day, and likewise the Moon at night. (151)
Having first performed the worship of the twilight (sandhyā) again and again,
and having obtained the means for the disappearance of the moon and sun from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform the worship.
One should worship oneself with a flower and with water for the arghya offering;
and having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should especially employ it for the purpose of bathing.
One should prepare it either on the eastern side of the liṅga or in the northeast;
then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should fashion a square mandala.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring two cubits or one cubit, strewn with darbha grass and divided into five squares; in the center, one should worship the station of Śiva.
Having worshipped Sadāśiva in the east and the Vidyā-tattva in the south, one should worship the Puruṣa-tattva in the north and the Kāla-tattva in the west. (156)
Having thus worshipped in sequence, one should place the vessels upon them:
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of time (kālatattva).
Well-established and peaceful, with a form of radiant splendor, just so. || 159 ||
One should worship these five forms: Rakṣā, Udaya, Amṛta, Rūpa, and Pañca.
In the center is Kṣīrakuḍumba; to the east is Prastha, followed by Dadhi. (158)

Ghee together with a single *kuḍumba* measure should be placed in the southern [vessel], while in the northern [vessel] there should be a *prastha* of cow urine and cow dung brought from a cow-pen. || 159 ||
In the west, there should then be a vessel joined with water and having five compartments; one should fill the vessel in the northeast with pure water mixed with *kuśa* grass. (160)
One should prepare [the seat] joined with thirty-six blades of darbha grass, or twenty-five, or twelve, or five, or even with three. || 161 ||
There, the tuft (kūrca) should be circumambulated clockwise, consisting of nothing but long ashes;
its tips should be above the knot and exactly four finger-breadths in length.
Or, for a specific duration of time, one should recite the Kūrca mantra over Kuśa grass and Kuśa water,
and the Īśāna mantra over a vessel of milk, reciting each in sequence for a fixed number of times.
O Nandikeśvara, one should first worship the person twice;
then, with the Ghoramantra, one should offer a vessel of clarified butter three times on the right side.
Then, one should perform [the placement] four times with the Vāmadeva mantra in the north;
subsequently, one should place [it] five times in the western part with the Sadyojāta mantra. (165)
One should consecrate the water with kusa grass using the six-heart mantra itself;
one should then place the curd and other ingredients into the central vessel using the root mantra.
This is declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and now the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are described.
The pañcagavya should be placed in front, and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared as before.
Milk should be placed in the center, curd in the east, and ghee in the south;
honey should be combined in the north, and sugar should be in the west.
The offering of abundant water, as well as the placement of mantras and so forth, is as before;
this is declared to be the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta), which constitutes the ritual bathing of Śiva. || 169 ||
In the southeast or the southwest, seated comfortably, one should worship Śiva;
having brought the Lord of Gods face-to-face, one performs the ritual services during the worship. (170)
Having mentally consecrated the entire collection of offerings for worship with the heart-mantra and having veiled them with the armor-mantra, one should display the cow-mudrā.
Having offered a flower upon the seat and performed the lustration ceremony (īrājana) therein,
as well as during the waving of incense (uddhūlana), the vehicle, and even at the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana),
one should always remain silent, bound by the necessary vows and garments.
And for his own sake, he should especially have mats and other such items prepared;
having caused the great bells to be sounded, he should observe the characteristic signs for the removal of obstacles.
Having performed the worship specifically accompanied by the *pūrvakāla* [ritual], one should worship the *liṅga* with the *Gāyatrī* and then worship it with the five *Brahmans*. (175)
With that [water] from the *sadyojāta* [mantra], he should cast away the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) from the *liṅga*;
then, joined together, grasping a flower with the little finger and the ring finger—176.
At the time of discarding the floral remains (nirmālya), one should place that flower upon his head;
however, one must never leave the top of the liṅga devoid of flowers.
One should offer the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) to the fierce [deity] with the *aiśa* [mantra] and the *hṛdaya* [mantra];
and having repeatedly washed the condensed *liṅga* with the *astra* [mantra], [one should proceed]. || 178 ||
The yogi, moreover, should especially contemplate it in nine ways;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb.
The wise practitioner performs the placement of mantras on the heart and other parts;
having set aside the tortoise-mudrā (kūrmamudrā), he should employ the great mudrā (mahāmudrā). 180.
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra on both hands;
this weapon of Śiva, numbering in the millions upon millions, serves for protection and the warding off of obstacles.
One should cast [the mantra] into the quarters and intermediate directions preceded by three claps of the hands,
forming a rampart surrounded on the outside by a fence made of the armor-mantra itself.
One should indeed contemplate everywhere by means of the net of the upward and downward powers;
one should display the Mahāmudrā from the head down to the feet.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by the syllable Om,
one should fill [the lungs] with sixteen measures through the left [nostril] using the syllable A.
Then, one should retain [the breath] for sixty-four mātrās with the syllable *U*;
it should be exhaled specifically for thirty-two mātrās with the syllable *Ma*. (185)
The withdrawal [mudrā] begins with the little finger and the thumb, preceded by the Sadyojāta [face];
having placed [the hands] on the eyes and the palms, the weapon [mudrā] is formed with the index fingers. 186.
If the placement [of mantras] is described as extending from the feet up to the head, it begins with the big toe and ends with the little toe;
this is the emanation sequence starting from the northeast.
One should likewise join the middle fingers, the ring fingers, and the little fingers;
however, one should not join the three [fingers] nor the crest-lock, following the sequence of the head, heart, and so forth.
One should place the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, in their proper sequence;
having placed Īśāna on the head, [one should place the others accordingly]. || 189 ||
Having thus clearly visualized the lotus, one should worship within it in due order:
first that which is higher than the highest (parātparatara), then immediately after that which is higher than the high (parātparam). (190)
One should meditate on one's own guru in this manner in the center of the lotus;
if he is devoid of the yoga of knowledge, one should meditate on him in the form of a lamp.
In the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, like the sun, moon, fire, and śakti;
thus, above the four disks, by means of the saṃhāra-mudrā.
(Deha * * * * * * * * * * * * * * having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ," [one should say] "Salutation to the Self" as well:
"Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self.")
And above that, having established the Śakti by means of the dvādaśānta, one should perform purification elsewhere.
The elements beginning with earth are joined with the seed-syllable of the letter *ma*;
the deity of the seed-syllable of Indra is the heart of the Sadyojāta mantra, [conjoined] with the Nivṛtti-kalā.
One should become the Lord of the Maṇḍala through the mouth of Brahmā, recollecting the interval between the feet while first uttering the syllable Om. * * * * * * * * ||
The syllable HĀṂ, when repeated five times, shall be the cutter. || 195 ||
oṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||
Having thus visualized the mandala of the earth, one should likewise visualize the mandala of water.
The deity of the seed-syllable of Varuṇa is liquid in form, enriched with the letter *va*,
joined with the second [letter] of the lotus [series], and endowed with the abode of the head. || 197 ||
Viṣṇu, the presiding lord of the maṇḍala, is endowed with the power of *pratiṣṭhā*;
having thus clearly contemplated him as consisting of water, while first uttering the *praṇava* (Om), [one should proceed].

O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon the form of the Bimba, which is endowed with the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), possesses the syllable *hrīṃ*, and has Rudra as its presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). 199.
From the throat down to the ground, in the six points [of the body],
it is joined with the syllable *yuṃ*.
The presiding deity of the seed-syllable is Vāyu, conjoined with the digit of Peace (śānti). || 200 ||
The armor is joined with the Puruṣa;
there, Maheśa is proclaimed as the sound.
Having first recited the syllable *oṃ*, one should likewise recite *haiṃ*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *kakakāḥ*. || 201 ||
Oṃ hyaiṃ hyaiṃ huṃ phaṭ; this is performed. It is supreme.
From the region of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), it resembles pure crystal. || 202 ||
The seed-syllable *bindu* with its mark closed, as well as the syllable *huṃ*, is produced from sound; this is declared to be the god Sadāśiva. (203)
The Astra-mantra and the Īśāna-mantra are: Oṃ Jaṃ Huṃ Phaṭ; then again, [the arrangement] of these is as follows:
Sadāśiva is situated above them, and Bindunātha is above that.
The Power (Śakti) is established within the Sound (Nāda), and within the Power is the Supreme Śiva;
Śiva is Brahman, the supreme abode, the eternal Supreme Self. || 205 ||
That reality is subtle, the supreme lord, the locus of power, and stainless; it is unmanifest, both manifest and unmanifest, expressible and inexpressible, and beyond comparison. (206)
Therefore, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord with a disciplined mind;
through the path of the Guru’s grace, everything is always accomplished.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, the salutation to the Guru is supreme. Then, one should dry up the earth through the aperture of the vital breath (mārutarandhra). 208.
Furthermore, with the very mantra of the earth, one should offer the entire description of qualities and so forth to Brahmā, or the sphere of water to Viṣṇu.
Having purified that image with fire, one should offer all those qualities and so forth of the fire-image to Rudra; then one should purify the fire with water.
One should offer the wind, along with its qualities such as form and so forth, to the Lord;
having purified the wind within the earth, [one offers] the ether together with its qualities such as sound. (211)
One should offer that to Sadāśiva and purify it with a divine disposition;
or else, while recollecting one's own body as the banyan tree and so forth. (212)
With its roots above and branches below, and the process of withering and so forth as before,
one should contemplate a hollow within the body between the two big toes.
One should contemplate the pervasive Śakti within and outside the cavities in succession;
then, one should purify [it] by means of the kumbhaka breath-retention joined with the syllable *hyaiṃ* and the *śānti*.
Then, from "hyaiḥ hyaiḥ śāntikalāyai huṃ phaṭ," the mantra arises;
one should then again contemplate the cavity with the syllable "hrāṃ" and the seed-syllable of fire.
Endowed with the *vidyā-kalā*, resembling the blazing fire of time:
Oṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ, homage to the *vidyā-kalā*.
Then, with the syllable *huṃ phaṭ*, one should contemplate all of that within the heart. || 216 ||
One should also meditate upon all that [universe] within the ocean of milk by means of the wind;
this should be performed through the practice called *recaka*, transcending the form of the sky.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kalā beyond peace (śāntyatītakalā). Huṃ phaṭ is performed.
By a single utterance, it should be made into the form of space through concentration (dhāraṇā). || 218 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate on [the deity] resembling pure crystal;
one should contemplate the solar stream [issuing] from the head, which is adorned with Ananta, Padma, and the others. (219)
Having uttered the mantra in that [place], "Oṃ Hauṃ, to Śakti, Vauṣaṭ," [it extends] up to the Brahma-randhra, reaching the limit of the Śāntyatīta-kalā. || 220 ||
(241) This should be performed with a single recitation, up to the limit of the Śāntikalā;
one should then bathe the liṅga for the sake of purification using only the water of the general arghya.
The purification of the *liṅga* has been described in sequence; now the fivefold purification is stated here.
In this way, the substance residing in the self is the *mantra-liṅga* within the purifications. (222)
Having performed the worship according to the word of the Lord, one should worship Gajānana on a copper pedestal in the southwest (nairṛtya) direction. || 223 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the lineage of gurus in the northeast;
one should perform the entire ritual, beginning with the invocation, using the respective mantra for each. || 224 ||
To the south is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and to the north is Naṭeśvara;
in the center (the Brāhma direction) is Viriñca, in the west (Vāruṇī) is [Varuṇa], and in the southeast (Āgneyī) is Mahiṣāntakī.
In the northwestern direction, one should worship the son of Gaṅgā (Gaṇeśa) with a concentrated mind, having first uttered the Praṇava: "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. (226)
The cause of the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of all mantras;
the support of all and that which is supported—the most wonderful mantra of the Guru. (227)
Combined with the seed-syllable *huṃ*, [one recites]: *āṃ hāṃ guṃ*—homage to the Gurus.
Having uttered *oṃ hāṃ hīṃ*, [one says]: homage to Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 228 ||
One should recite the mantra ending with "namas," beginning with "Oṃ hāṃ maheśvarāya."
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Maheśvara; Oṃ hāṃ, one should recite the mantra ending with "obeisance to Brahmeśvara. || 229 ||
Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Brahmeśvara.
Oṃ hāṃ, having uttered the syllable *huṃ*, [followed by] "obeisance to Durgā" (*namonta*):
Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, obeisance to Durgā.
Oṃ hāṃ, having addressed Skanda, it is declared that [the mantra] ends with a salutation. || 230 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, concerning the procedure for the internal sacrifice and other rites, in the Śivakāṇḍa of the Pūjārṇava, which is to be cultivated with equanimity.
O Nandikeśvara, one should especially worship the seat;
first, having meditated upon Kūrmaśiva, whose form is that of Mūlaprakṛti.
Subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest,
this all-pervading Lord consists of whatever splendor belongs to the moon, the sun, and fire.
One should never meditate upon [the deity] with colors such as white, red, and so forth;
there is no fixed rule regarding specific [colors], nor regarding the elements or the qualities (guṇas).
Pervading everything both internally and externally, she is established everywhere;
she is to be perceived through the guru’s mouth as having a nature that is self-evident. (4)
Equal in both masculine and neuter genders, she is distinguished as Vinītmā;
she is called Pradhāna and Kūrma, and Śakti is a synonym for her.
One should worship that stone, which is circular in shape, with fragrant substances and other offerings;
first, having uttered the *tāra* (Om), one should recite "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kūrma" (*namo'ntakam*).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kūrma.
One should contemplate the Śakti, who is seated upon the tortoise-posture (kūrmāsana) and whose form is the foundational support (ādhāra);
she has the luster of a sprout from the lotus of the tortoise and a radiant form consisting of the nature of sound (nāda).
Oṃ hāṃ; first one should utter this, and afterwards say "namaḥ ādhāraśaktaye" (salutation to the Support-Power).
[He is] resembling the autumnal moon, with a luster like that of a lotus stalk. || 8 ||
Thus, [one should worship] the form of the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), endowed with the seat named Ananta; then, after that, the salutation "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda" is proclaimed.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nāla.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mukula.
One should worship both the stalk and the bud with the name-mantra;
the sprout has the luster of coral and the bimba fruit, while it possesses the brilliance of silver.
The stalk, known as the bulb, is like lapis lazuli and reddish-brown;
the tips of the petals are conch-white in color, and the lower petals are said to be red.
The filaments in the center should be slightly red and yellow;
in their midst, the wise one should conceive of the pericarp, which has the luster of gold.
One should visualize nine seed-syllables of golden luster in the center of that.
Listen with a concentrated mind as I describe the seat called Ananta. (13)
Dharma is the bull-like form, knowledge has the nature of a lion;
dispassion is the yellow elephant, and health is the white elephant. || 14 ||
Now hear concerning the infinite throne-legs and the side-poles:
one should conceive of them as unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty. (15)
One should arrange them all, resembling sapphire, starting from the east;
first, the serpent kings Ananta and Vāsuki.
Then Takṣaka, Kārkoṭa, and after that the one named Padma;
Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Gulika is remembered as the ninth. || 17 ||
(247) Each of the eight Vidyeśvaras assumes a form like that of a serpent, beginning from the tail with five hoods, then three, and finally one. 18.
Endowed with the form of a man, he shone within the womb; he had a beautiful face, was adorned with earrings, and was decorated with all kinds of ornaments. || 19 ||
Furthermore, on the upper part of the hood, one should visualize him with two arms, wearing silken garments,
his hands granting boons and fearlessness, possessing excellent conduct, and being most excellent.
One should visualize Ananta and the other [serpents], beginning with Gulika, in all directions around [the deity];
each is endowed with a single hood and has his palms joined in reverence.
Having beheld that preeminent and peerless lord of the nāgas, they should worship him by first uttering "Oṃ Hāṃ" followed by his name-mantra. || 22 ||
(248) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Naga King! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ananta! And so forth.
O Nandikeśvara, having fashioned an eight-petaled full-blown lotus for the god Ananta, one should place it upon the region of the head of the lord of the nāgas.
The Anantāsana has been described; beyond that is the Yogāsana.
The fourfold [set] consists of the Unmanifest (avyakta), Niyati, Kāla, and Kalā. (24)
One should place the circle in the great directions; Keśava is at the middle foot.
He is unmanifest, possessing the luster of all his own [emanations], a yogi with the radiance of black collyrium.
Kāla has the luster of a pomegranate flower, and Kalā has the brilliance of split collyrium;
having uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ" and likewise their own respective names, one should worship them.
In the center, however, one should worship Keśava, who resembles a dark blue cloud,
has four arms and three eyes, and is endowed with the conch, the discus, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
One should visualize him granting boons with his right hand, adorned with all ornaments,
and with a lotus flower facing upwards and downwards upon his head. (28)
Having first uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ," [one says] "salutation to the heart of the lower petals";
likewise, having uttered [the mantra] above, ending with "namas," [it is offered] to the yogic seat (yogapīṭhaka).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one who holds the umbrella above. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the yoga-pīṭha.
This supreme eight-cornered [diagram] is declared to be the yogic seat (yogāsana). 30.
Now I shall describe the lion-throne; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
Having worshipped the upper cover, one should install the ten seed-syllables in their proper sequence.
The syllable *oṃ* is the first seed-syllable, the letter *ā* is the second,
the letter *ī* is the third, and the letter *ū* is the fourth.
Vyokāra is declared as the fifth, and vyāṃkāra as the sixth;
vyāpi is declared as the seventh, joined with two syllables. (33)
The eighth is declared to be the syllable *naikāra*, and *hokāra* is the seed-syllable for each [of the others].
This is declared to be the ten-fold seed-mantra; one should install them starting from the east and ending with the northeast.
Oṃ hāṃ oṃ, homage! Oṃ hāṃ āṃ, homage!
Oṃ hāṃ īṃ namaḥ. Oṃ hāṃ ūṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ hāṃ vyoṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ vyāṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Pervasive One! Oṃ hāṃ neṃ, homage!
Oṃ hāṃ oṃ, obeisance!
[I bow to] those who, in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, and in the form of lions,
are each surrounded by retinues of ten million times ten million.
(251) With complexions shining like bumblebees, resembling pearls from Kāñcī and Kashmir,
with faces made terrifying by fangs, possessing three eyes, and of fearsome form; || 36 ||
One should worship in sequence with the names beginning with Kṛtayuga, ending with "namaḥ," such as:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṛtayuga," and so forth.
Then follows the square seat known as Siṃha and the Lotus seat (Padmāsana). (37)
First, he attained a white lotus with eight petals and filaments that had not yet emerged from its stalk;
then one with sixty-four filaments that shone like gold.
It is conjoined with the fifty seed-syllables and endowed with the nine powers:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Kalavikariṇī. (39)
Likewise Balavikariṇī, and likewise Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī—these are the internal powers (antaśaktayaḥ). || 40 ||
All of them were like ten million suns, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon;
they possessed four arms and three eyes, and held chowries in their hands. (41)
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, their lotus-hands resting upon Śivā,
one should place them on the tips of the filaments from the eastern petal to the northeast petal.
One should worship Manonmanī, white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, located upon the pericarp;
having first uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ," one should address her with her own respective names, ending each with "namas. (43)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikariṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikariṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī. Thus, [these are placed] upon the pericarp.
One should likewise arrange the three mandalas for these [deities] one above the other in sequence:
the mandala of Śiva-Sūrya, which resembles ten million suns. (44)
And [he saw] Āditya and Brahmā, whose essential nature is the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), having five faces, four arms, and three eyes in each face. || 45 ||
Salutations to the God who possesses the luster of molten gold, adorned with all ornaments,
accompanied by Rudra, and the cause of the cause of creation.
Having first uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ," [one says] "Salutation to the Solar Maṇḍala (sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ)";
then, having again spoken up to the end of the maṇḍala, [one says] "Salutation to Brahmā, the presiding deity (adhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ). || 47 ||
Salutation to the solar disc.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. In this same sequence, [one should worship] Viṣṇu and Soma, the leader of the lunar disc.
In the same way, the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) and Rudra are likewise joined with the mantra in that very place. (48)
One should clearly visualize Brahmā upon the crown of the head and the lunar disc,
endowed with the radiance of ten million moons and as cool as ten million moons.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the solar disc.
In its center is the primordial Viṣṇu, resembling a dark blue cloud, with all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with every ornament. (50)
Having one face and two eyes, adorned with earrings,
four-armed, holding a conch and a discus, and accompanied by a gesture of salutation.
[He saw] Viṣṇu, wearing yellow garments, the cause of the cause of maintenance, endowed with a crown and diadem, whose essential nature is the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). || 52 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala;
one should well-place [this mantra] upon the head of Viṣṇu, who is at the end of the southeast [direction]. (53)
One should visualize the fire of Śiva there, resembling an infinite conflagration.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the circle of fire.
[One should meditate on] Rudra, possessing the luster of the color of rubies, with one face and three eyes. (54)
Four-armed, with matted locks adorned by a crescent moon and flowers, his entire body smeared with ashes and resplendent with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). || 55 ||
[One should worship] the God accompanied by Umā and Rudra, the cause of the cause of dissolution:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala. Furthermore, [one should worship] the presiding lords of the three principles (tattvas), endowed with all the vidyās. || 56 ||
Adorned with all ornaments, one should place them individually in sequence;
this is declared to be the Pure Seat (vimalāsana), endowed with the three images.
Afterwards, there is the supreme maṇḍala of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), consisting entirely of light,
filled with thousands of petals, and resembling the moon or cow’s milk.
It is conjoined with Gaurī and Gāyatrī, consisting of will, knowledge, and action;
it pervades the principles from Earth up to Śuddhavidyā, and its locus is the mind.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva, the circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power of will (icchāśakti). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power of action (kriyāśakti).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti). Oṃ hāṃ, may we know Ambikā; may we meditate upon her of great austerity; may Gaurī inspire us.
In the four directions beginning with the north, one should worship Gaurī conjoined with the Gāyatrī mantra;
having worshipped the threefold self, one should [worship] the form of the Praṇava in the center.
Within that seed of grace is this supreme seat of Śiva;
in its center, one should meditate upon the Lord of the gods, the Supreme Lord.
In the form of Sadāśiva, resembling pure crystal,
he possesses five faces, and each face has three eyes.
He is endowed with a crown of matted locks and possesses ten arms;
in his right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In his left hands, he holds a noose, a serpent, a goad, a bell, and fire;
he is auspicious, possessing all limbs complete, and wearing divine garments.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, adorned with celestial flowers,
endowed with all ornaments, and crowned with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel. (65)
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, youthful, wearing a lotus garland, possessed of a serene countenance, tranquil, and the cause of all things. (66)
One should contemplate the God of gods seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana);
having thus deposited Sadāśiva, who is within the range of the power of the [deity's] form.
Having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ," ending with "namas" to the form of Śiva—
[that is,] "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva"—
by means of this very mantra, [one should worship] the Lord who consists of consciousness and bliss. (68)
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, who is the stainless goal of the true path,
and having abandoned the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, one should lead the mantra to the abode of Śiva.
The seed and root of the five Brahmans and the six limbs is the source of great prosperity; joined with its bindu and nāda, it is Śiva, the supreme cause. (70)
Having meditated on the shimmering light of the moon in the center of the forehead,
one should visualize a handful of flowers and cause it to enter into the image of the deity.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should worship with the mudrā;
or else, [one should worship] the Lord of the subtle form, the principle of the elements (bhūtatattva) together with the bindu.
Having meditated upon the Śaiva power (śakti), one should worship and encircle the liṅga;
one should utter the mantra ending with "Oṃ hāṃ auṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (vidyādeha). || 73 ||

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the one whose body is knowledge (vidyādeha). One should worship that primary form, which pervades the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by the power of Sadāśiva, as well as its length, which is equal to that of the liṅga. || 74 ||
Īśānā is the end of Śāntyatītā; Puruṣa has the face of Śānti; Aghora is the heart of Vidyā; and Vāma is the secret of the eye. (75)
He whose body hair causes the worlds, from the knees and feet up to the realm of Brahmā, to cease their movement instantly; the God who is difficult to sustain, yet supremely radiant. (76)
It consists of the elements such as skin, bone, marrow, and semen;
it arises from the three eyes of vision, action, and will, and from the digit of the moon of knowledge. (77)
The upper face, in particular, resembles pure crystal;
the Aghora face is like a man, the color of saffron, and radiant as a bumblebee.
Vāmadeva is proclaimed to resemble the hibiscus flower;
his right face is like a conch shell, a kunda flower, the moon, or cow’s milk. (79)
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship him thus, endowed with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Listen as the nature of the sequence beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) is now described. (80)
The respectful facing toward [the deity] who is all-pervading and exceedingly humble is called "invocation" (āvāhana), by means of delimiting the form. 81.
The heart, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
[therein reside] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 82 ||
Having abandoned the five causes and being composed in meditation,
[one perceives] the Supreme Lord, the Pervasive One, who is the twelve-fold Unmanī-śakti.
Having understood [the self] as consisting of light and mantra, and having drawn the *bindu* from the forehead,
one should sequentially place it upon the two hands joined with flowers and upon the heart-mantra.
(264) It is beneficial to perform the invocation starting from the heart up to the forehead and ending at the crown of the head;
while the two hands are joined in *añjali*, [the fingers] should be placed upon the root joints of the little fingers. (85)
With the two thumbs joined at their tips, this mudrā becomes the invocation (āvāhanī).
This is declared to be the invocation; immediately after that follows the installation (sthāpana).
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva.
With devotion, one should establish [the deity] there; being steady in some form [of the deity], that which is offered without interruption is proclaimed as [the proper offering]. 87.
In that same manner, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord with his face turned downwards, his fists bound in the *sthāpanī* posture, displaying his respective hand-gestures (*mudrās*). 88.
Having spoken of the act of bringing [the deity] near, for the purpose of perceiving the limitation by the form,
the mudrā with the two thumbs joined and well-supported is the "invocator" (saṃnidhāpinī).

But at the completion of the ritual action, when the presence [of the deity] has ceased due to the exhaustion [of the offerings], that cessation should be understood; and it is the same for the bridegroom as well. (90)
When the two thumbs are thus joined and hidden, it becomes the "restrainer of reality" (tattvanirodhanī);
it is called "the harsh one" (niṣṭhurā) in the Śiva-āgamas such as the Kāmika.
For that which is the very nature of the bliss of awakening and consists of all bliss,
its concealment occurs when it does not manifest among those who are unworthy.
Having placed [the hands] with the palms facing downward upon the head, one should then join the two hands in a handful of flowers;
then, by bringing them down to touch the feet, this becomes the *avakuṇṭhanī* mudrā.
Whatever rite is performed with a mudrā, its fruit shall be inexhaustible;
O Nandikeśvara, one should display the Liṅga-mudrā and the Namaḥ-mudrā.
With the thumb raised up in the middle, this is here called the *liṅgamuṣṭi* (the fist of the linga).
Having formed the *añjali* (palms joined) with both hands, one places it at the heart. (95)
She is called Namomudrā; one should display the Yonimudrā by coiling the two ring fingers and [placing] the two index fingers upon the two middle fingers. (96)
Having extended the two hands so they are joined together at the tips of the little fingers and with a space between the middle fingers,
one should display this Yoni-mudrā upon the pedestal of the Liṅga.
Then, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of integration) with six mantras at once;
the supreme amṛtīkaraṇa (the rite of immortalization) consists of the union of the limbs with their respective names.
One should form the *saṃpuṭa* (cavity) mudrā with both hands, with the fingers interlaced;
[the two] index fingers [should touch] the two middle fingers, and the two little fingers [the two] ring fingers. 99.
Having bound this Dhenumudrā, one likewise performs the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
Then, having uttered [the mantra] as prescribed, it becomes shaped like a cow's udder.
O Nandikeśvara, even the God of gods should be meditated upon with his own limbs made beautiful and invincible by the blazing rays of the sun. 101.
Having placed the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) in the heart, [one attains] the eightfold sovereignty beginning with knowledge (vidyā);
that which is the state of Śiva, not dependent on anything else, is situated above the crest-lock (śikhā). 102.
It is declared to be indivisible, excluding the splendor of the God of gods;
it is always and everywhere eternally established and continuously present at all times. (103)
That which is the vision that prevents the non-distinction of the self should be known as the eye of Śiva, the Lord of Gods. (104)
(268) It is said that this weapon of the Lord of Gods wards off floods of obstacles with its fire of unbearable prowess; it is impenetrable by gods and dānavas alike. 105.
Now listen to the mudrās for the placement of the mantras of the heart and other limbs:
having placed the tips of the *jyeṣṭhā* (thumbs) between the middle and ring fingers.
Having formed fists with the other two hands, one should place them at the heart;
this shall be the mudrā called Hṛdayā, with the thumbs joined within the fists.
Placing the hand upon the head, this is declared to be the Śiromudrā.
One should place the fist, with the thumb raised, behind the head.
This is the Śikhāmudrā; it is formed by placing the hands in the shape of a peak, having made fists with the hands and then extending the thumbs and index fingers. 109.
Having led it upward from there to the head, one should place it on the heart from both sides;
this is considered the Bhavaka-vaktra-mudrā, which effects protection against all [dangers]. (110)
Having joined the little finger and the thumb, slightly bending the index fingers and the ring fingers, the middle fingers are drawn together; this is called the *netrākhyā* [mudrā]. (111)
One should release [the fingers] outward from both sides with the index finger and the thumb;
this is the *choṭikā* mudrā of the weapon (*astra*), which removes all calamities.
In front of the deity, one should form a bud-like gesture with both hands at the crown of the head;
thereafter, one should release that mudrā so that it hangs down as far as the soles of the feet.
One should perform it again as before; that is known as Mahāmudrā.
Having performed the Prabhākaravatī rite and having delighted the immutable Śiva.
One should always offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the lotus-feet of the serene [deity] with the heart-mantra:
*oṃ hāṃ oṃ pādyaṃ śivāya namaḥ*.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into their mouths at the end of the word "svadhā" for those facing east and the other directions. || 115 ||
And furthermore: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, svadhā to Śiva, the mind.
One should present the arghya to Śiva, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta. (116)
One should offer, in sequence, the *arghya* ending with "svāhā" for Śiva, saying: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāyārghyaṃ svāhā*;
likewise, one should offer fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). || 117 ||
One should worship with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and by means of the name of the substance;
likewise, one should offer perfume on the forehead, flowers on the head, and incense as well. (118)
One part of agarwood should be taken, and the resin (niryāsa) should be double that amount; sandalwood is said to be double [the resin], combined with a small amount of camphor. (119)
One should fumigate this, which is soaked in honey, with the incense called *śītāra*;
one should present a lamp at the region of the eyes, and on the sides and behind. (120)

"Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ! [This is] for Śiva, [the offering of] fragrance," and so forth. One should also perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the root mantra. || 121 ||
One should perform the ceremonial bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) using the installation mantras in due order;
furthermore, one should offer incense and lamps at every interval.
One should offer the presentation of water, flowers, and likewise the arghya;
and having rubbed the seat and the deity with fragrant rice-flour paste.

Having repeatedly rubbed [the body] with bilva leaves and other such foliage, especially while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca) ending with "namaḥ," the cleansing (nirmārjana) should then take place.
Oṃ haiṃ, homage to the armor!
Oṃ hāṃ, "O Śiva, arise"— with these words, one should request Śiva for the ritual bathing.
Having honored him as he rises, [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva. || 125 ||
Immediately after, one should not bathe in water that is merely lukewarm;
thereafter, the great bath (mahāsnāna) should be performed with fragrant substances such as āmalaka and the like.
Thereafter, one hundred and eight ladles of fragrant water should be offered in succession; thus one should perform the consecration.
One may offer a bath for one's own sake even with water from the left hand;
one should then dismiss the flower previously placed there by means of the arghya offering.
One should pour a *gaṇḍūka* [of water] with the root mantra, and again an *āḍhaka*.
Water should be offered upon the top of the *liṅga*, and the remainder should be poured onto the altar (*vedi*).
On special days and at the proper time, one should perform the ritual bath and the consecration ceremony using as much water as has been prepared. (130)
If these are unavailable, one should bathe [the image] with pure water, such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth;
immediately thereafter, one should wipe it dry with a fine, clean cloth.
One should smear the body of the deity with fragrant substances— saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood— finely ground and mixed with cool water.
The rite should be performed with the root mantra; one should place a flower upon the head, bind the downward-facing mudrā, and should not rotate the hand upward.
Always placing flowers upon the top of the linga so that it is never empty,
the wise man should offer clothing, ornaments, flowers, incense, and lamps.
One should perform all of that with the root mantra, especially the rite of the weapon (*astra*);
having worshipped the flower with the head-mantra (*śiras*), one should strike it with the bell-mantra (*ghaṇṭā*). || 135 ||
One should perform the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) with the Heart mantra ending in "svadhā.
One should worship Īśāna in the center of the pericarp and Tatpuruṣa in the east.
One should worship Aghora in the south and Vāmadeva in the north;
one should worship Sadyojāta in the western region—thus one worships the five Brahmans. (137)
Having performed the *ārātrika* rite, which wards off the flood of obstructing spirits, [he offers] sacred ash, a mirror, an umbrella, a chowrie, and a palm-leaf fan. (138)
Having gratified the Lord of Gods with these, along with sprouts of kuśa and dūrvā grass,
one should especially place *lakṣmī* flowers upon his head at that time.
On the night [of the festival], one should especially perform the *ārātrika* ceremony according to the prescribed rites;
one should also perform the *nīrājana* rite, or else use a new vessel. (140)
Having taken up five vessels together with lamp-stands,
he should light lamps everywhere using flour-cakes that have been thoroughly heated.
Having placed [the object] upon the mechanical device, one should gaze at it with the divine vision;
sprinkling with the Astra-mantra is prescribed, and then sprinkling with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Perform the striking and likewise the weapon-mantra in this manner as a consecration,
together with the fire residing in the navel and the fire of the inhalation (pūraka).
Having joined [the breath] and led it out by means of exhalation (recaka) alone, one should immediately consecrate it with mantras;
then, having cast it into the orb of fire, one should either cast it outside or into the arati lamp.
Having offered three drops of *arghya* for the purpose of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) at each lamp, one should likewise display the lamp-mudrā. || 145 ||
Having bound that [mudrā] with all the fingers, one should place it in the interval in succession;
showing the left thumb for the purpose of restraint by means of the non-flaming [fingers].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth three times with the heart-mantra,
one should [perform this] near the head of the deity in the sequence of high and low.
O Nandikeśvara, one joined with devotion should rotate [the flowers] with the Netra-mantra;
then, one should sprinkle fragrant white flowers with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Having consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra, one should cleanse [the disciple] with ashes using the Astra-mantra;
then, having placed the remaining ashes into a lamp, one should collect them for him there.
One should place [the seed-syllables] in sequence upon the foreheads with the heart-mantra itself;
they should be placed on the heart, the regions of the arms, and in the northeastern corner. (150)
One should offer that [offering] specifically upon the two scents, as the Goddess is established separately;
one should perform all those rites, such as the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā) and so forth, in sequence as before.
Then, the rite of lustration (nīrājana) for Vināyaka and Skanda should be performed;
all those vessels should be cast outside upon the pedestal.
Then, having prostrated and received the command of the God, one should worship Gaurī;
[one should also worship] the four [deities] of Agni, Īśa, Yama, and Vāyu in the cardinal directions in due order.
O Nandīśa, the heart-mantra is like the moon; the head-mantra resembles gold;
the crest-mantra has the luster of a hibiscus flower; and the armor-mantra is like a bumblebee.
One should worship the eye consisting of all splendor within the pericarp [of the lotus],
[visualizing the deity] as being seated upon a lotus throne and wearing a crown of matted locks. (155)
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
they stand facing Śiva, holding a spear, a trident, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
O Nandikeśvara, one should utter the four-faced [mantra] with its own mantras;
