it is a most fierce weapon with fangs at that moment, resembling a thunderbolt. (157)
One should worship the remover of obstacles in the four directions, beginning with the east;
having worshipped him with his respective mantra, one should offer water for the feet and other offerings with the heart-mantra.
Incense, lamps, food offerings, water for rinsing the mouth, hand-cleansing water, betel-leaf, mouth-perfume, and a mirror. (159)
The preceptor should offer [the remainder] to his retinue with the Śiva-mantra; therefore, he should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the God of gods as before. (160)
One should wash [the grains] with pure, white, unbroken rice grains;
then, one should prepare them so they are well-cooked and fragrant according to the prescribed rite.
One should place [the offerings] in vessels made of gold and other materials, or in small bowls;
immediately thereafter, one should place them in dishes of clarified butter-rice and ghee-rice.
One should surround that abundant [offering] on all sides with various kinds of fruits—both ripe and unripe—as well as soups, cakes, side dishes, and so forth. || 163 ||
It is endowed with forms such as a wheel, spokes, petals, and rows of steps,
and is joined with vessels containing milk, curd, clarified butter, and well-cooked food.

One should arrange white fruits and the like, as well as mung beans and so forth, according to one's means, along with various kinds of pure food combined with ghee, curd, and other ingredients. (165)
Such is the offering described; in its absence, it should be a mental visualization.
One should especially prepare what is pleasing to Him and particularly pure. (166)
Having purified it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should release it with the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā);
one should perform the rite of armor (kavacīkaraṇa) and offer it with the heart-mantra (hṛd-mantra). || 167 ||
One should cause [the offering] to be given with a flower placed upon the middle, ring, and thumb fingers;
and then, in an instant, one should strike the bell with the Astra mantra.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented for the limbs and the retinue;
and water should be offered from the vessel like the moon, along with marrow.
One should prepare drinking water that is very sweet and cool, combined with a small amount of sandalwood and contained in a new clay pot. (170)
One should cause the offering to be presented with the heart-mantra using a cup;
there, one should cause the bali-offering to be presented to the retinue beginning with Śiva.
Then, at the conclusion of the offering, the water for sipping (ācamana) should be presented to the deity;
furthermore, sandalwood paste should be offered for the purpose of wiping the hands.
Having offered the floral remains (nirmālya) to Caṇḍadeva with a concentrated mind,
one should subsequently sprinkle them with the Astra-mantra and present betel leaves and other offerings.
A bright betel leaf, excellent areca nuts, combined with oil and camphor—this is celebrated as *tāmbūla*. (174)
One should cause camphor, cloves, and nutmeg to be offered as mouth-perfume;
thereafter, one should cause a bright mirror to be offered with the root mantra. || 175 ||
One should cause the purifying substance, accompanied by unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and especially by *dūrvā* grass,
to be offered after consecrating it by reciting the root mantra three times according to the three principles (*tatvatraya*).
One who seeks liberation [should worship] the principles of Śiva, whereas one who seeks enjoyment does the opposite;
[the latter should worship] daily that which is produced by the activities of speech, mind, and body. (177)
In the sense of the wind element (*pavana-dhātu*), it means "prior" (*pūrva*) and also "protecting" (*pālana*);
because it performs purification (*śuddhi*) and protection (*rakṣā*), it is celebrated as "pure" (*pavitra*). || 178 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should strike the Supreme Lord who is pleased by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, the gods, and various others of diverse kinds.
Afterwards, one should recite the root mantra while holding a rosary;
one should place a flower in the left hand with the right hand. (180)
Having placed his right hand upon [the disciple], he should especially perform the recitation (japa);
for disciples, this mental [recitation] is first and foremost the most excellent of the excellent. || 181 ||
That which is spoken aloud is said to be the lowest; the whispered [recitation] is called the middle.
Therefore, having abandoned speaking aloud, one should recite with the mind or in a whisper. 182.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times—neither too quickly nor too slowly—it should be consecrated with the heart-mantra and enveloped by the armor-mantra. (183)
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra and the mudrā known as Udbhava,
one should then cause the recitation of the limbs of Śiva, consisting of ten parts, to be performed.
O most secret of secrets, you who are to be guarded; accept this recitation performed by us.
May accomplishment be mine through your grace, while you remain present. (185)
Having recited this mantra, one should place [the flower] in the left hand of the deity of enjoyment (bhogadeva) using the water of the arghya-offering consecrated with the root mantra.
The *arghya* water, which was prepared for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), should be placed on the southern side;
having returned from there and offered it, one should then make the formal request (*vijñāpana*). || 187 ||
To the left of the deity, an area smeared with cow dung should be prepared;
outside, rice grains mixed with dūrvā grass and flowers should be arranged.
In the morning, at midday, and also in the evening, there should be an offering of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having placed the *liṅga* upon a base made of a copper vessel, the preceptor [proceeds]. (189)
One should indeed prepare the seat preceded by *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
"Obeisance to the form of the Pāśupata weapon"—thus one becomes the embodiment of the seat. (190)
Oṃ glāṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ; obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon. Oṃ śrīṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ; obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon. || 191 ||

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other limbs with the weapon-mantra while remaining composed, [he recites]: "Oṃ bhoṃ to the heart, huṃ phaṭ; oṃ śrīṃ to the head, ending with huṃ phaṭ. (192)
Oṃ śrīṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ; oṃ huṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ [ending with] -ka; oṃ huṃ netrābhyāṃ huṃ phaṭ; thus, oṃ haṃ phaṭ [ending with] -antāya huṃ phaṭ [ending with] -ka. || 193 ||
Having thus recited the six limbs, one should worship each one in succession;
then, one may worship a single food-liṅga, or five, or ten.
O Nandikeśvara! One should place [the items] there in the vessels and worship them;
the pair of sandals along with the weapons, such as the thunderbolt (vajra), and so forth. (195)
Having worshipped the Bull with the syllable Om, together with the Savitrī mantra and the Sātvika hymns,
and having adorned him with all ornaments, [one should worship] with songs, dances, and instrumental music.
Following the clockwise sequence, one should cast the garland of daily festivals;
having entered the interior of the temple, one should unite these with a concentrated mind. (197)
Having removed all [impurities] such as the *annaliṅga* and others from within that [liṅga],
one should propitiate the Blessed Lord with the pure *tāṇḍava* dance alone.
There, in front of the deity, again in the dance pavilion,
which has been smeared with cow dung and provided with a seat for the *praṇava*, || 199 ||
Having meditated upon the form with the *praṇava* mantra while remaining composed,
one should then invoke and worship Nandideva. (200)
Having worshipped it with its own name, one becomes pure through the tāṇḍava dance;
[one should likewise worship] a woman endowed with beauty and youth, well-bathed, and adorned with all ornaments. (201)
Having summoned that daughter of Rudra, he sprinkled her with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
gave her preeminent ashes and a garland, and performed the supreme Tāṇḍava dance.
One should perform the Śuddhatāṇḍava according to the path described by Bharata, [dedicating it] to Brahmā, Keśava, Rudra, and Īśvara. (203)
In the morning, at midday, in the evening, and especially at midnight,
one should perform the worship of the deities with their respective names for the sake of protection.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Śivakāṇḍa of the Pūjārṇava within the Cintyaviśvasādākhya.
(288) I shall now describe the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), preceded by the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The abode of the fire is of two kinds: either a pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*). || 1 ||
It may be square, a womb-shape (yoni), a half-moon, a triangle, circular, hexagonal, or it may be an eight-sided lotus. || 2 ||
The characteristics of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) from the east up to the northeast shall now be described;
furthermore, the characteristics of the eight fire-pits are being stated here.
First, one should lay down the eastern line; then another to the south and north;
and finally the western line, extending as far as the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O Rudra, by means of the cord, establish the square limit at the cardinal directions;
for the origin of all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) is within the square.
Outside of the square, one should place five parts on the Soma side;
by means of the north-south thread, it shall be provided with four corners.

That which extends from the southeast (āgneya) to the northeast (īśa) is known as the four-footed [line]. At that time, one should lay down the end of the thread extending from the southeast to the northeast.
Starting from the Agni-sūtra of Indra, one should lead it to the end of the Yama-sūtra;
indeed, that which resembles the shape of a half-moon is likewise [drawn] in the Nairṛta direction.
Having led that [line] to the western direction (Vāruṇī) and having placed it in the north (Soma) with its portion,
one should lead it from the tip of that [western line] to the end of the eastern line (Aindra), forming the shape of a triangle.
The removal of the outer and middle lines constitutes the supreme illumination; in a field divided into parts according to devotion, the wise man should discard the divisions made by those parts.
With that measurement, one should rotate an arc from the middle of it;
having divided the field into five parts on both sides as well. (11)
One should place each part there on the exterior of the mental thread;
then, having formed two fish-marks either in the southwest or the northwest.
By applying this method of measuring with three sides, a triangle clearly comes into being;
one should take half of the pit's circumference and project half of the area.
But having divided the excess into two parts, one should discard one part on the outside;
with that measurement, one should fashion the excellent circular pit (kuṇḍa).
Having divided the field into sixteen parts, one should place two portions on the outside; and according to the measurement of the width, there should be two pairs in the middle of each side.
One-sixth part of the sixfold sūtra is the sixth portion, which is the most excellent;
one-tenth [of that] is outside the field, and one part should be laid out further outside.
By that measurement, one should perform the circumambulation;
one should make a pericarp in the center and act as if it were a circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should lay out a field divided into twenty-four parts and set aside one part on the exterior;
with that same part, one should construct a square on all sides.
Outside of that, one should mark [the lines] with half the length of the corner of the square;
and at each corner, one should specifically take hold of the points to be grasped.
From the desire for the Sūtrapāda, the unsurpassed measurement of the elephant [is established];
such is the form of the *kuṇḍa*, and such is that of the *mekhalā*.

One should design the central section as being endowed with three girdles, measuring four and three [units] according to the sacred tradition, and having a height equal to the aggregate of the causal factors.
One should dig a pit similar to [the shape of] Vyāsa, free from depressions and elevations;
one should place the yoni upon the girdle like an aśvattha leaf.
The width and length should be five finger-breadths (bhūtāṅgula), the height seven finger-breadths;
such is the excellent characteristic of the yoni.
Its height should be one *aṅgula*, while its width should be a *bhūtāṅgula*;
one should fashion it in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of a lotus or a square.
The lotus-base should not be made [too large];
the lip should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and the outer neck should likewise be two finger-breadths. || 25 ||
One should have it constructed with bricks baked in lime or even with clay;
this is said to protect the four [classes] and increase the enjoyment of the universe. (26)
Health is indeed fulfilled, and this [rite] shall be capable of accomplishing all;
the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) brings prosperity, nourishment, and increases victory. (27)
An eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) bestows debt and likewise fear upon enemies;
for a homa of fifty [oblations], the handful [of fuel] should consist of *cannavāra* wood.
For a thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit should be one cubit; for ten thousand, two cubits is beneficial;
for a hundred thousand oblations, it should be four cubits; and for two hundred thousand, it should be six cubits.
Its height should be measured by a *guṇāṅgula* and be free from depressions or elevations;
it may be two *aṅgulas* or even one *aṅgula*, made with compacted rice grains.
Three lines should be drawn with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise for the northern half.
[These represent] Brahmā, Vaivasvata, Soma, Rudra, Śakra, and Keśava. (31)
The presiding deities of those [lines] directed toward the east, the southeast, and the north have been proclaimed;
at the time of worship outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the sage should also offer [libations] into the arghya vessel.
One should look upon the remaining materials of the oblation with the Śivadṛṣṭi;
then, sitting facing north, one should place its navel in front.
If the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is lacking, the attainment of the fire does not occur;
[therefore, one must perform] inspection, sprinkling, digging, and likewise pouring water.
If the pounding, sweeping, construction, plastering, as well as the cleansing of the cow-pen, have already been performed previously; || 35 ||
Furthermore, one should perform the inspection, the sprinkling, and the striking with *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra*, followed by the sprinkling with the *varma-mantra*, in due order. (36)
With the sword [is performed] the digging, the extraction, the filling, and the leveling;
with the armor [is performed] the sprinkling, and with the arrow-mantra, the pounding.

One should perform the sprinkling and the smearing, and worship with the Heart-mantra; with the Armor-mantra, one should place the foot of Akṣapāda, and the central pressing-stone should be done with the Heart-mantra.

In the midst of that, [he saw] the Goddess, well-established, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, who had bathed after her menses, possessed large eyes, and was adorned with perfumes, garlands, and unguents. (39)
Having thus meditated upon the great goddess Vāgīśvarī, who is endowed with all auspicious marks and has reached the age of sixteen, the wise practitioner [should proceed]. (40)
Having likewise installed the five-faced god Sādākhya, who possesses a universal form, and the god Vāgīśvara with the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu), [one should perform the ritual]. (41)
The preceptor should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by means of their respective names the fire produced from a sun-crystal or indeed that produced from a forest-dweller (araṇi).
One should bring it by a good path to a sacred field or to the house of a Vedic scholar;
having placed it in an earthen vessel or a copper vessel, one should do so with the heart-mantra.
Having assigned [the portion] to Agni, the Hotṛ, one should worship him especially;
having offered the portion of raw flesh as before, one should purify [him] through the rites of inspection and so forth.
Having equated the three fires—the expansive [fire] of the bindu and the terrestrial fire—one should place the consciousness of fire, which resembles the flame of a lamp. (45)
(297) Reciting the mantra ending with "namas," namely *oṃ hrīṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ*,
one should expel [the consciousness] outward through the path of the piṅgalā nāḍī by means of exhalation (*recaka*). || 46 ||
Having cast it again into the blazing fire while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantras,
one should worship [the deities] in sequence from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, ending with the word "namaḥ".
Having rendered [the substance] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* and performed protection with the *astramantra*,
the preceptor should lift it up with his hand while performing the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) for self-protection.
Having circled three times above the sacrificial pit while recollecting the seed-syllable of Śiva,
one should kneel upon the ground within the womb of Vāgīśī.
One should visualize it being cast forth by the god Vāgīśvara;
in both cases, however, one should cast the union toward the heart.
Then, having risen from the fire of the womb, there is a gathering at the region of the navel;
putting on another garment, one performs purification and sipping water with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (51)
O Nandikeśvara, for the protection of the fire within the lotus-hand of Vāgīśvarī,
one should bind it with a darbha cord for the sake of its preservation.
Furthermore, for the sake of conception, one should worship the Fire with the Sadyojāta mantra;
being composed, one should offer three oblations with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
In the third month, the *puṃsavana* rite should be performed under the asterisms of Puṣya or Śravaṇa;
one should offer water drops from the head while reciting the *Vāmadeva* hymn.
In the sixth month, he should likewise perform the parting of the hair (sīmanta) with the Aghora mantra;
he should offer oblations three times each, and for the topknot, he should do so with the Śikhā mantra itself.
The determination of the faces and limbs must be performed, as well as the opening of the faces and the expiation;
by means of the *varman* and the *puruṣa* alone, the rite together with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) is accomplished. (56)
Having kindled the fire, one should perform a bath with the *garbha* and other mantras to remove the impurities of the womb;
then, one should cause the ornaments of gold and so forth to be offered to the Goddess with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
And for the sake of purification over the fire of birth-impurity (sūtakāgni), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
having struck the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the sprinkling of the fire with the Varma-mantra.
One should skillfully place the girdles along the path from east to north;
having strewn [the ground] with the Astra-mantra, one should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) upon it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
To remove saliva from the mouth, one should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire;
specifically, those at the beginning and end should be sprinkled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and especially so with a sword.
One should worship Caturmukha, Śaṅkara, and thereafter Śārṅgin,
starting from the east and ending with the north, using the *hṛdaya* mantra for the seats. (61)
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship Śakra and the other world-protectors standing facing the fire, as well as the deity seated upon the pedestal, using the heart-mantra alone.
Having quickly warded off the host of Vasus, he will protect the boy;
let him proclaim this command of Śiva to those guardians of the quarters.
Having likewise taken up the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva), both possessing their characteristic marks and facing upwards,
he should strike them downwards in sequence— at the root, the tip, and the middle.
Having touched the root with the root, one should touch the tip with the tip;
having wiped the middle with the middle, one should cleanse [the vessel] in sequence with three blades of *darbha* grass.

Having placed two blades of *darbha* grass upon a spot touched by *darbha* grass, one should establish these two [blades], worshipped with flowers and other offerings, on the right side of oneself. (66)
Having worshipped the auspicious Ātmavidyā with the mantra ending in "namaḥ," one should worship in due order;
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship Śakti in the *sruk* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* ladle.
Having taken up the ladle and the clarified butter purified by means of inspection and other rites, and having heated it over the fire with the Astra-mantra, one should contemplate "Svadhā. || 68 ||
Having circumambulated the pit, one should place [the vessel] in the fire-corner;
then, having taken up the ghee consisting of Viṣṇu, one should deposit it starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
Having lifted the sacrificial ladle (ājya) with the tip of a blade of darbha grass,
one should offer a drop to Mukunda at the end of his own portion with the syllable *ṇun*, and place it in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having meditated upon the form of Rudra, one should contemplate it while endowed with devotion,
using two blades of *darbha* grass the length of a span, held between the tips of the thumb and the ring finger. (71)
With the Astra-mantra, the ghee facing the fire shall leap up;
with the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should direct it toward oneself, from which it shall flow back down.

For the sake of purification, one should cast [the ashes] into the ash with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the weapon-mantra ending in "namas. Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite with another *darbha* blade, the procedure is complete.
Having recited the mantra for burning and cast the tips of the *darbha* grasses into the fire, being composed,
he places into the fire the burnt *kuśa* blades, each measuring a span (*prādeśa*).
One should perform the oblation for both sides, offering the three items—clarified butter, fuel, and so forth—in sequence;
taking the clarified butter with the sruva-spoon from three portions, one should offer it into the fire.

(303) One should sequentially pour the remaining clarified butter into the fire in its respective portion with the word "svā" [and "svāhā"], reciting the mantra ending in "svāhā": *oṃ hām agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*. (76)
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! || 77 ||
For the purpose of opening the eyes, one who is intent upon the three eyes of the Fire-god should offer the fourth oblation with the sruva-ladle filled with clarified butter.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! Having consecrated [the offering] with the six-limbed mantra, one should cause it to be restrained by means of the Dhenu-mudrā. || 79 ||
One should protect the clarified butter by enveloping it with the Kavaca mantra and again with the Heti mantra;
by casting the seed-syllable of ghee along with the Hṛdaya mantra, there occurs another purification of the clarified butter.
The continuous stream of clarified butter poured as an oblation is said to be the sole instrument for [the purification of] the mouth.
[One should worship] Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna. (81)

One should perform the oblation with one's own respective mantra, beginning and ending with the Praṇava, the fire-syllable (agnibīja), and the Jaya-mantras; or, by means of a single oblation of clarified butter (ājya), this may constitute the "sprinkling" (abhighāra).
And one should perform the union of the faces by means of the mantra and the yoga of the mantra,
following the sequence from Īśāna down to the end, accompanied by the five Brahmans.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Aghora; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Tatpuruṣa. || 84 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Īśāna; oṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva;
oṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Aghora; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Aghora and Tatpuruṣa.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Puruṣa and Īśāna.
This is the offering of the heart-mantras from Pāvaka to Vāyu.
From the southwest to the northeast, with an unbroken stream of clarified butter. || 86 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform [the oblation] with the *sruva* spoon up to the end of the clarified butter (*ājya*) all at once, saying:
"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. (87)
One should not place a single face upon one's own preferred faces;
otherwise, remembering the desired face according to the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*, [one should proceed accordingly]. 88.
For the other faces, this same single procedure should apply;
and when the Īśāna-fire is complete, one should offer three oblations with the weapon-mantra.
Established within the body of Śiva, the wise one should perform [the rite];
he should then give a single name to his own Śiva-fire in the sacrificial fire.
(306) O Nandikeśvara, the form of fire is threefold: Vaidika, Miśraka, and likewise Miśravaidika; such is its essential nature. 91.
He has one face and two mouths, joined with various pairs;
he has six eyes, is endowed with a girdle, and is possessed of three feet.
He is considered to have four horns, two heads, and matted hair;
he wears the sacred thread, observes silence, and is endowed with seven hands.
Endowed with seven tongues and mounted upon a bull as his vehicle,
[the god] possesses tongues that are golden, yellow, red, and black on the right side.
She is intensely radiant, red in color, and possesses many forms;
thus is the tongue described in the Vedic tradition, whose vehicle is a ram.
O Nandīśa, listen afterwards to the true description of the Śaiva fire:
it is red, endowed with five faces, and resplendent with seven tongues of flame. (96)
Ten-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments, clothed in red garments, and seated upon a lotus. (97)
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), endowed with ten weapons;
then Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and thereafter Atiraktā. 98.
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, and another, Hiraṇmayī—these three are situated at the upward-facing [mouth], while the remaining ones are situated in the directions starting from the east. || 99 ||
The meditation on the Śiva-fire has been taught; the fire is proclaimed to be threefold.
Having understood the eyes, ears, and other [senses] as the fire, one should then perform the oblation (homa). 100.
(308) From an oblation in the ear, there is indeed disease; in the eye, the affliction of the eye;
in the nose, mental suffering; and in the hair, the arising of poverty. 101.
Because it bestows the accomplishment of desired food upon the body, one should therefore perform the oblation (homa) on the tongues;
bondage occurs at the region of the ears, while the nose has the nature of form.
Thus, the blazing eye and the ash are considered to be the head of Agni;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) precisely where the tongues of flame are ablaze.
The mouth is situated in the middle of the pit, and within that is the tongue;
it is provided with three enclosures above and joined with sacrificial fuel.
The Vedic fire is thus designated, while the mixed fire possesses the nature of both;
it is proclaimed in this scripture as having three or four enclosing sticks (paridhis). || 105 ||
Having worshipped the two parents of Fire while endowed with [the mantra of] the Heart,
he should then dismiss Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśa. (106)
Likewise, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is offered from the center with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
or, for the pleasure of Agni, it may be offered from the front with the *tilaka* ending in *svāhā*.
Having offered five oblations in sequence into the center of the fire-place:
"Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Agni! Oṃ, the divine splendor belongs to Agni. (108)
Because it is the supreme purifier.
"Therefore, having established him within the lotus of your heart, I shall fashion him.
Having thus requested the command of Śiva, [he meditated upon] Śiva together with his limbs and sub-limbs.
The sage should worship the seat in his own heart as before;
then, he should perform the invocation again in the lotus of the fire-heart and [worship] the head.
One should worship the imperishable Śiva with everything beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
One should perform the union of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) between oneself and the two Śivas [Śiva and Śivā] within the sacrificial fire.
One should perform the oblation ten times the portion of the *śakti* with the root mantra;
the oblation is said to consist of clarified butter, milk, and honey, measured by the *karṣa*.

The consumption of curd is said to grant nourishment; furthermore, a handful (prasṛti) of milk-rice (pāyasa) is beneficial, as is a mere handful (muṣṭi-mātraka) of parched grain (lāja) among edible foods.

Fruits [should be offered] according to their own natural size; roots, three finger-breadths; leaves and flowers, according to their own measure; and [other items] should be equal in size to the little finger.
The fuel-sticks should have their bark intact, and the wick should be eight fingers long;
likewise, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and yakṣakardama [are used]. || 115 ||
One should offer all types of musk as a measure-giver for all arts; guggulu resin is established as the eighth part of the primary ingredients. (116)
O Nandikeśvara, the measure of the sacrificial substances has indeed been declared;
one should perform the oblation while standing upon the pedestal using the five Brahma-seeds.
Endowed with devotion, the practitioner should perform oblations with the mantra to be accomplished;
then he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) using a sruva ladle filled with clarified butter.
Having slowly placed the *sruva* with the left hand so that its opening faces downward,
one should then place a flower on the tip of the *sruc* with the left hand.
Then, holding those two with the right hand using the *kambusannidhi* mudrā, remaining alert with the upper body erect, with feet level, and standing facing [the deity]. || 120 ||
Having placed the root of that [mantra] at the navel, free from inhalation and exhalation,
and fixing one's gaze on the tip of the sacrificial ladle (sruk), [one should contemplate it] as the cause of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others. (121)
Having emitted [the breath] through the path of the suṣumnā nāḍī while remaining composed, and having raised the blue [element] from those two toward the vicinity of the left hand. 122.
Having placed [the vessel] and become free from sloth, one should recite the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, while muttering the eternal [mantra], O Ānandikeśvara. (123)
One should offer oblations into the fire using only barley as the sacrificial material;
one should also provide water for rinsing the mouth, sandalwood paste, betel leaves, and other such items.
But in the absence of substances such as clarified butter, one should offer sesame seeds or likewise rice;
or, according to what is available, having offered with these according to one's capacity day by day—125.
One should not, out of devotion, pay homage by taking hold of the *sabhūti* [ashes];
afterwards, having worshipped the fire with the *śaṅkara* weapon while it is afflicted by the *astra-mantra*. (126)
Then, having withdrawn all the mantras along with their respective deities by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā],
he should say "forgive this" with reverence, endowed with that state of being.

Then, with the *pūraka* breath-retention, he should, with faith and using the heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*), [invite] those beginning with Brahmā— those infinite ones, as well as Indra, Agni, and the guardians of the quarters— into the lotus of his heart.
O Lord of the God of Gods, one should fumigate it with incense and other substances;
then, taking all [the materials] with their tips pointing eastward, one should fashion a pair of earrings.
In the rite of causing [the fire] to flow, one should cast the internal and external oblation into the pit;
having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, one should cast the oblation during the first part of the night.
One should offer the bali to the Mothers in the south; it should be for the Gaṇas in the west.
It should be for the Yakṣas in the northern part, and for the Planets in the northeast. (131)

Likewise, [the offering] for the Asuras is in the south-east; for Agni, in the south-west; for the Rākṣasas, in the south; for the Nāgas, in the direction of the wind (north-west); and for the Nakṣatras, in the center. || 132 ||
One should also offer the bali-oblation in the northeast or in the center of the zodiac signs;
likewise, the Praṇava is in the southeast, and the Viśvedevas are in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should offer the bali to Kṣetrapāla with his name-mantras:
"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Mothers! || 134 ||
Oṃ hāṃ to the Gaṇas, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Yakṣas, svāhā!
To the Hṛdas, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to the Asuras, svāhā! || 135 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the rākṣasas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the nāgas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the constellations! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the zodiac signs! || 136 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Kṣetrapāla!
One should worship [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna, each by their own name. And one should worship Brahmā, intended for the upper direction, in the innermost circle.
Then, designating the portion for the fluids (rasa), one should worship Viṣṇu in the southwest;
designating the middle portion, however, one should cast the bali-offering to the Kṣetrapāla in the center.
One should also offer an oblation of food for the crows and others, or cast an oblation in the cardinal and intermediate directions:
"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Indra! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni! (140)
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Yama! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Nirṛti!
Those Rudras who perform the deeds of Rudra and dwell in the abode of Rudra... || 141 ||
Some were gentle, and some dwelt in gentle places;
there were Mothers with the forms of Rudras at the sides of the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Likewise, others who have become obstacles and dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may they all, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering.
"May they always grant me success; may they protect me perpetually from all fears.
Having thus presented the offering, the devotee should bow down. (144)
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, and having bowed down and made a request with devotion:
"O Blessed One, [accept] my worship and all the ritual acts such as the fire-oblation (homa). (145)
One should perform the fire-oblation with the root mantra, saying, "Accept yourself as well. Then, having worshipped the imperishable Śiva in the eight directions, [one should proceed]. (146)
Whatever I have done out of delusion, whether deficient or excessive, may all that become complete through your grace, O Lord. (147)
O Nandikeśvara, having first made supplication according to the path previously described, one should then perform the worship of whichever deity is intended at the conclusion of the ritual.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
And in the portion of the gods, one should resort to that worship for Caṇḍa;
having stationed the obstacle residing in that place with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), [one should perform it]. (1)
Having cast it away, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa for that which is internal to Caṇḍeśa;
having cast it away, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa of the *nirmālya* with the roots of the *gāṅga* plant.

Having uttered the first two [syllables] followed by *pāśupatāstrāya phaṭ*, one should purify both hands with the Astra-mantra; thereafter follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship (*arcana*).
Oṃ, to the first and foremost Pāśupata weapon, huṃ phaṭ! Homage to Sanātanī!
One should worship this Mūrtīśvara as well by his own respective name. || 4 ||
"Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍamūrti; with the mantra 'Huṃ phaṭ svāhā' to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, one should then invoke Caṇḍa, the destroyer of great sins. (5)
Oṃ dhvani caṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, [one should perform this] for all six limbs in every respect. (6)
"Oṃ, salutation to the heart for the sake of presiding over all yogas; likewise, 'Oṃ, salutation to the head for the sake of the Supreme Lord. (7)
First, "Salutation to the one whose form is light, to the tuft (śikhā)"; and after that, "Salutation to the protector, to the armor (kavaca)."
Vauṣaṭ to Caṇḍanetra; the Vardhanī mantra is as before:
Oṃ, salutation to the heart of the one presiding over all yogas. || 9 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the supreme lord, the foot; salutation to the head.
Vauṣaṭ to the flame-form, the crest-lock. Oṃ, salutation to the protector, the armor. 10.
Oṃ, vaṣaṭ, obeisance to Caṇḍanetra; Oṃ, phaṭ, to the first Pāśupata weapon.
Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, one should first perform the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) rite. (11)

O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the sequence beginning with the heart; [one should place] the form produced from the syllable *kaṃ*, the fire, and the vowels, which has the luster of a lamp.
She is endowed with four faces and twelve eyes;
her matted hair is ablaze and adorned with the crescent moon, and she shines with armlets and bracelets.
She holds a trident and a water-pot in her left hands, while in her right she holds a small axe and a rosary;
she is adorned with serpent-bracelets and wears a sacred thread made of a snake.
One should visualize her with a face made terrible by fangs, exceedingly red, seated upon a white lotus throne, and the destroyer of the fear of her devotees. 15.
Having meditated, one should perform recitation with its root mantra according to one's capacity;
and having performed the recitation for the limbs and the ten [repetitions], O Nandikeśvara. (16)
Having consecrated [the disciple] with the root mantra, one should gradually cause him to undergo initiation;
[one should offer] cows, land, gold, garments, various kinds of gems, and ornaments.
Having set aside the remainder and the floral remains (nirmālya), one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa specifically with the mantra preceded by the sound "dhvani" and ending in "svāhā. || 18 ||
Liquids to be licked, foods to be sucked, meals, drinks, and the like, as well as betel, garlands, and ointments—these remains of offerings are given to you by the command of Śiva. (19)
O Caṇḍa, by your command I have performed the entire ritual section;
whatever was done deficiently or redundantly through delusion, may that become complete for me. (20)
Having thus informed Caṇḍeśa and offered the *arghya* with the mantra,
one should dismiss the *mūrti* with the *saṃhāriṇī* mantra while holding a flower. (21)
With the root mantra and through inhalation (pūraka), one should worship the mantras within oneself;
then, for Caṇḍa, [one offers] his floral remains (nirmālya) and the collection of obstructing spirits and the like.
The fresh sprouts of prosperity are always unfit to be touched by the Gaṇas as they are the remains of the offering (nirmālya);
one should abandon that nirmālya instantly, being intent upon fierce meditation.
Having washed one's feet and hands, one should then smear the ground with cow dung;
having removed the remains of previous offerings (nirmālya), one should sprinkle the place with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Rising from that place, one should wash one's feet and head;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly according to the rules, one should duly touch the sacred ashes.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of the mantra, one should manifest the portion of Śiva;
then, commencing with the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhi), one should practice according to the prescribed sequence. (26)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍa, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*.
Now the sādhana of Ardhanārīśvara himself shall be described;
he is beyond the supreme principle known as Asaṃjñaka, more subtle and infinite.
It is the nature of the Bindu and Nāda, the form of the Jyotirliṅga,
the radiant energy consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which is the reality that is the cause of creation.
O Nandikeśvara, the form assumed as Ardhanārīśvara is considered Ardhanārīśvara because it is the singular form of the union of Śiva and Śakti. || 3 ||
O Lord of the World, for the purification of both male and female, the first form became the nature of Sadāśiva; and Īśa [became] Aiśī Manonmanī. (4)

The worship of the Liṅga was explained previously; now [I shall describe] the Ardhanārīśvara form, as well as the Śiva-form and the Raudra-form, which bestow the perfection of the Command and are auspicious.
The true form and the "ever-woman" (sadānārī)—both of these grant liberation;
they perform the fierce task of the Command for the sake of power and for the purpose of pacification.
Therefore, the Lord indeed [manifests] as both the fierce and the gentle, and as the supreme Ardhanārīśvara; he is the Guru, the sky, and the cause, for he, the Master, causes fear to dissolve.
Because Śiva, the supreme cause, is called Rudra, [one should sit] on a soft seat, comfortably seated, with a one-pointed mind and a serene intellect. || 8 ||
One should perform worship of the Guru and worship Ardhanārīśvara;
the right side is white and the left side is dark—such is this form. (9)
They should be known as seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with two eyes and a slight excess [of height];
the eye on the forehead of the deity is incomparable, being but half an eye.
It should be ten cubits in length and resemble two crowns;
one should place six mudrās on the side of the deity and five mudrās on the left.
He is endowed with the five mudrās and adorned with a garland of heads;
he has a peacock feather on his ear and a piece of flesh on his left shoulder.
Hara holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, and a garland of bones;
he should firmly hold one hand, which is for making offerings, upon the support of all.
With both hands raised, he should hold even the elephant-hide;
having meditated thus, he should especially worship with perfumes and flowers. (14)
Having increased [the visualization] either upon a linga, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even on a cloth, or in a painting,
or by means of one's own voice, one should meditate and worship in due order.
Oṃ aiṃ glauṃ hreṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hrauṃ hlauṃ aghorebhyaḥ hrauṃ hlauṃ proṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gleṃ kṣmāṃ (66).
Having recited this mantra, one always obtains the command of Śiva. || 16 ||
One should worship with water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings, using the root mantra.
The fire sacrifice (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and likewise the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka) should be consecrated with a rosary of fifty-three seed-syllables (bījas). || 18 ||
With the seven primordial seeds and the five Brahmans and six limbs:
*oṃ heṃ hauṃ kṣauṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ īśānāya namaḥ* || 19 ||
And thus there would be the five Brahmans; thereafter follows the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), beginning with:
"Oṃ aiṃ hlauṃ praṃ prīṃ preṃ hreṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth.
Thus, the ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed; the worship and adoration are as before.
At the conclusion of the worship, however, the practitioner should again perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in due order.
Having always performed the recitation of mantras and constant meditation, which are themselves beyond conceptual construction,
one attains the ritual manual, the power of attraction, the agitation of the city [of the body], and the ultimate refuge.
The past and the future, as well as the present;
likewise, the relinquishing of the stages, their entry, sovereignty, and the increase of wisdom. || 23 ||
He ordains kings who are absorbed in illusion, as well as gods, Garuḍas, Kinnaras,
Dānavas, Asuras, Yakṣas, and Kiṃkaras. (24)
She shall obtain all-knowledge and achieve victory over all the immortals;
and the Goddess, always identical in form with the God, will be proclaimed by the God. (25)
For subjugation, attraction, and protection, he is two-armed, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
for rites such as merit and pacification, he is four-armed and golden-hued.
The fruit [is held] as the trident, the bestower of fearlessness, and likewise the bestower of boons;
for the rites of paralyzing and deluding, the Lord is like turmeric in color.
The four-armed one with noble limbs was previously described as being at the beginning of the urine [mantra];
for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the black, long-armed, and terrifying form is prescribed.
Then one should meditate upon him as holding a trident, a skull, a chisel, a khaṭvāṅga, a shield, a sword, and a noose. (29)
In the western quarter (Vāruṇa), [the deity] has the luster of smoke-colored ash, possesses sixteen ashes,
and holds in his upper arms a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting fearlessness, and a skull-cup.
He possesses the remaining twelve tridents and is endowed with a most terrible fear;
yet through his knowledge, he is the Lord who shines with a white complexion and a serene countenance.
Holding a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting fearlessness, and likewise the boon-granting gesture with his four arms— he, the husband of Umā, is indeed to be meditated upon.
One who is fully engaged in yoga and meditation regarding past and future effects perceives everything that exists as the visible world during the fleeting moments of the senses. (33)
And everything seen in a dream should be examined for its effects;
even while seated in the cock-posture, one should observe [the signs] very slowly. (34)
By repeatedly bending down according to the sequence of the fingers of the hand,
even one joined with the yoga of the elephant (vāraṇa-yoga) shall attain the power of traveling through the sky.

O Nandikeśvara, when one has not been explicitly instructed regarding any ritual act, one should inform the Guru; having received his command, one should perform the worship according to the prescribed path.
Seated comfortably in a field of merit, one should firmly retain this mantra;
by its recitation, success is swiftly attained, followed at the conclusion of the recitation by fire-oblations and libations. (37)
The consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed ten times [the number of recitations], and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) likewise ten times;
this should be done while endowed with devotion, trust, non-malice, faith, and tranquility. || 38 ||
The practitioner should observe these ten [rules]: obedience to the guru’s command, knowledge of truth, equanimity toward afflictions, and the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya). (39)
The complete Vidyā has been declared; now the Ardha-vidyā is described: [the mantra] for Tryambaka is human, and that which follows it is for Umā. (40)
This is indeed said to be the perishable, consisting of twelve syllables:
"Oṃ" for Tryambaka, and immediately thereafter "Umāyai. (41)
It is said that this consists of twelve syllables:
"Oṃ mānuṣaṃ tryambakāya umāyai kṣam" (Om, human [obeisance] to Tryambaka and Umā, kṣam). || 42 ||
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, the practitioner shall accomplish all the aforementioned tasks by means of this alone. || 43 ||
On a Monday, one should bind with a protection mantra at the root of an ant-hill where an *aṅkoṭa* tree has grown and which has been struck by weapons like thunderbolts. (44)
With the mantra "Stay, stay! addressed to the one of great strength and great merit, ending with the salutation "To Vīrya, to Śiva," [he should perform the rite]. (45)
"Oṃ, stay, stay! Homage to the one of great strength, of great heroism, and to Śiva!
Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed] afterwards on a Tuesday.
Facing northward, the practitioner, having taken the matted locks,
should grind the paste mixed with turmeric and yellow pigment in the prescribed order.
Having purified and clarified it with the juice of *naktagalika*,
the wise man should place it in a clean vessel in a spot that is sheltered from the rain and the sun.
Having recited the root mantra one thousand times with flowers and other offerings,
[one should purify] those joined with great sins and others who have committed offenses against Śiva. (49)
Practitioners should avoid acts of treachery against gurus, kingdoms, or villages;
they should bow at the feet of the guru and always seek his grace.
Anointing himself with ashes while engaged in recitation and meditation, he destroys those [obstacles], as well as gain and loss, pleasure and pain, and even great fear. (51)
Even if one encounters an army, the destruction of a city, fire, or any other such calamity—among all these, not even a single one will bring about success; indeed, there is no success at all.
Having performed three claps of the hands, one should immerse oneself in the water;
having cast off the garments on one bank, one should clothe oneself with others on the other.
One should not look behind or to the side, nor should one resort to other sects; [one should attend] with a respectful demeanor, using fragrant *āmalaka* and other such items. (54)
Then, having attained the Śiva-śakti and the consecration by the nectar-mantra,
he is endowed with the sixteen kalās mentioned as belonging to Bhairava.
Having recited the mantra, one should perform the consecration with jars of nectar; then, endowed with devotion, one should proceed to one's own ritual duties, clothing, and so forth.
Even upon seeing an ill omen, one should perform bathing, recitation, and so forth;
having cultivated the realization "I am Śiva," one should then perform an ablution with ghee and milk.
But having eaten food that is contemptible, such as being infested with flies and the like, and likewise upon seeing [such food], one becomes raw in the wings of one's caste. (58)

If, during the impurity caused by food, injury, the three-fold movement, or the extinguishing of the lamp and so forth, [the deity] is seen to have arisen, one should rise, sip water for purification, and remain with a serene mind. (59)
And with a concentrated mind, they should recite the Amṛtākṣara mantra according to their ability;
if free from ill omens, they should perform the rite after having offered the oblations equally.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and other rites, one should recite the syllable of nectar (amṛta).
For one lying in a pure place, everything is revealed in a dream.
Having reported the dream in its entirety to the guru, one should perform the ritual action;
for his command ensures that all undertakings attain their portion of success.
Though known as the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, it is endowed with many methods through its single syllable;
[the letters] "repha" (ra), the right arm (da), and "śveta" (śva) follow immediately thereafter. (63)
Mahākāla, Vahni, Māruta, and Marussara;
Aṃ, Īśānta—in this sequence, Jyotsnā is the supreme single-syllable Piṇḍa. (64)
It bestows enjoyment and liberation, and is dear to the God of gods.
With the syllable *kṣauṃ* and *ūṃ*, the heart is formed by the letter *ra*; the letter *a* becomes the head. (65)
With the syllable *ṣa*, the topknot (*śikhā*) is formed; with the syllable *ma*, the successive [limbs] follow;
the eye is formed by the fire-syllable (*va*), and the weapon (*astra*) arises from the syllable *ya*.
He saw Hara, who is both a fierce beast and the moon-crested one, who wears a crown of matted locks,
who possesses half of his body with two eyes, and who is the Lord devoted to the amorous play of women.
I bow to Śivā, whose hair is adorned with garlands of blue lotuses and mālatī flowers,
who possesses a single eye, whose inner being is tranquil, and who increases her love for her husband.
Adorned with ear-ornaments and wearing earrings, with a *tāṭaṅka* on the left ear,
having a dark throat and a beautiful nose— this was the wonderful appearance of the couple. (69)
In her left [hand] she holds gold, jewels, and so forth, while in her right she holds a tortoise;
in her left sprout-like hand, joined with the future state of existence, she holds a blue lotus.
His two hands are joined with a skull and a trident, and he wears bracelets of serpents; his pair of right arms is adorned with ornaments of jewels, gold, and other precious materials.
Her left side has one arm and one full, beautiful breast;
she wears a snake as a sacred thread and a necklace, while her right side is smeared with ashes.
The left side [of the image] is adorned with a hero’s necklace shimmering with pearls, and is anointed with saffron, sandalwood, camphor, agallochum, and musk. (73)
It was adorned with a sacrificial portion consisting of a tiger and a garland made of white water-lilies, and it was girdled by Vāsuki, who shone upon a tiger skin spread above. (74)
The right [hand] of the God of gods is adorned with variegated silken garments and enriched by a girdle of jeweled strings; and the left [hand] is the supporter of the world. (75)
The right foot of the Primordial God was adorned with an anklet and a hero’s bracelet, resplendent with a great lotus and joined by jeweled foot-ornaments.
The left [hand] was dyed with lac and adorned with small tinkling bells;
it was praised by gods and asuras and invoked day and night by the Vedas.

Having thus meditated upon the Lord Ardhanārīśvara, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, endowed with devotion toward the Guru.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part [of the total], and likewise the consecration (abhiṣeka);
thereafter, one should offer ten thousand oblations (homa) with sesame seeds and rice grains.
Endowed with devotion toward the Guru, one should prepare a seat arising from the six [ingredients] beginning with Ananta, mixed with honey, milk, ghee, and parched grain flour.
Having invoked [the deity] upon that [liṅga], one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
O Nandikeśvara, the rites beginning with invocation and ending with the dismissal (sadya) are to be performed as previously described.
The enclosure of the limbs should be worshipped, and thereafter the eight-syllable mantra;
one should worship with devotion using flowers according to the names of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti). 82.
Raṃ, obeisance to the self of the sun; kañja, obeisance to the self of the fire; raṃ, obeisance to the self of the pond; yaṃ, obeisance to the self of space. || 83 ||
Aṃ, obeisance to the Self (Ātman). Uṃ, obeisance to the Moon-Self (Somātman).
This is declared as the second enclosure; and [one should worship] Vṛṣa on the eastern petal of the directions. (84)
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship [the deity] in the south-eastern quarter;
having worshipped Nandin in the south, one should likewise worship Gaṇeśa in the south-west.
To the west, however, Guha should be especially placed;
and to the north and northeast of this deity, Kṣetrapālaka should be situated. || 86 ||
One should worship them in sequence with their respective seed-syllables ending in *namaḥ*;
one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the quarters in the fifth enclosure.

One should offer twelve thousand oblations into a well-kindled fire with wood produced from the *chinnodbhava* tree, measured in standard finger-breadths (*jāty-aṅgula*), and consecrated by boiling in milk.
For as many times as one should offer oblations,
for that many times may the two Supreme Lords, moistened by the fire of the jar of nectar, be eternally gratified. (89)
When the sādhana has been thus accomplished, one should thereafter speak again to the preceptor;
or the consecration may be performed by the gurus at the time of the sādhana.
Thereafter, one becomes capable of accomplishing every desired task in an instant—whether it be long life, health, sovereignty, the perfection of speech, or victory. (91)
It brings about subjugation, attraction, paralysis, delusion, and likewise expulsion;
it effects even the killing of those belonging to Indra’s host and removes the mantras of others.
How can there be certainty regarding his power to pacify malevolent magic and ward off all planetary influences for that one who is devoted to the Guru? 93.
One should apply the letter *ha* and the letter *sa* in the place of the letter *ra*;
the practitioner should recite this nine-syllable aggregate at the beginning of giving and other such acts. (94)
By ten thousand recitations alone, there shall be paralysis (stobha), as well as the subjugation (vaśya) and so forth;
if it is preceded by the syllable *sa*, it brings about pacification (śānti), nourishment (pauṣṭika), and increase (vardhana).
Having meditated upon this lunar orb—pure white, consisting of nine syllables, and situated in the midst of the sixteen vowels—above the maṇḍala of the Guru; 96.
One should consecrate that Guru with streams of water from its sūtra, and one should contemplate one’s own body as being honored by the stream of nectar from his lotus feet. 97.
It destroys untimely death, poison, headaches, fever, and the like;
for one possessed by a planetary spirit, [it is applied] upon the head within an enclosure of a circle of fire. 98.

In the center, one should contemplate the *manusvara*, and in reverse order, the *rasasvara*; likewise, one should contemplate the group of six beginning with the *repha* in the corners, starting from the eastern corner. (99)
Having placed the name of the person to be accomplished in the middle of that [syllable], one should meditate upon it as being like a blazing fire,
beginning with the letter *ra* and ending with the left ear (the letter *u*), resembling the fire of time (*kālānala*).
One should visualize [the deity] burning at the crown of the head for a moment, resembling the sound of a thunderbolt;
it is red for the rites of subjugation and attraction, and for paralyzing, agitating, and so forth. 101.
Nandikeśvara should contemplate [the syllables] beginning with 'a' and ending with 'suvarṇa';
it is smoke-colored for crushing, driving away, and for paralyzing those who cause harm to the kingdom.
And for the purpose of immobilization, the thread is said to be yellow in color, like a lute and so forth;
likewise, the seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja) and others are prescribed for those who desire liberation from beginningless time.
In the eyes, in the ears, likewise in the throat and the belly,
and in the vital points as well as in the head, [one should contemplate] that which resides in the center of the wind-maṇḍala. (104)
O Nandikeśvara, one should then visualize the three [deities] beginning with Śiva as having a black appearance;
by mere meditation, each respective limb that has been consumed perishes.
Having accomplished this afterwards, one is subsequently liberated;
one should then visualize the flow [of breath] as having entered the earth-mandala within the throat-pipe.
A white eye, ten thousand times the size of a stream of rice-balls, when meditated upon, removes all affliction;
one should contemplate this meditation on the eyes and so forth upon all the limbs.

The pacification of various diseases and other afflictions, the increase of mutual affection, and the performance of rites for subjugation and attraction—through these, one who lacks virtues becomes possessed of them. (108)
Therefore, the Guru should perform the drawing [of the disciple] and the worship of the sacrificial pit according to the path;
then, he should bind him within the center of the lotus-heart of the one to be accomplished (sādhya). (109)
Having formed that [syllable] upon its head with the letter *repha* (Ṛ) using the five-syllable mantra itself,
one should meditate on a moon-disk composed of nectar above it.
Having endowed him with a divine state by means of the seed-syllable of Vāyu,
both he and she will certainly be drawn forth, and everything will arrive.
All of them perform all his tasks;
[this occurs] within the *piṇḍa* mantra, in the middle of the letter *repha*, joined with the name of the practitioner.
O Nandikeśvara, one should draw the figure called Sādhaka in the eastern part;
then, having formed a circle of fire, one should place a hexagon outside of it.
One should enter the letter *ra* of that very corner, which has the brilliance of a blazing fire,
by means of the vowels in reverse order, following the proper sequence. (114)

Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, and having performed the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇas), one should bury it even in a collection of earth; this is the supreme method of drawing [the site].
Having divided into three parts an effigy made of rice flour mixed with honey, milk, and ghee, one should offer it as an oblation for the successful accomplishment of virtuous deeds.
For those desiring subjugation (*vaśya*), it should be performed in three ways according to the specific eye-mantra.
The seed-syllable (*piṇḍākṣara*) shall be the letter *A*, with the name placed in the middle. (117)
Having smeared [the ground] with *ūrdhvagarepha*, one should especially write the name of the disease;
it should then be surrounded by the syllable *ṭha*, and outside of that, there should be a *bhūpura* (fortress).
And in that corner, one should write the syllable *ṭha* on betel leaves;
thereafter, by performing meritorious recitation (*japa*), his disease shall perish. (119)
One should bind the ears of the person to be accomplished with the two preceding letters, *ra* and *ka*;
then, with the letters *ṣa* and *va*, one should likewise bind the pair of breasts. (120)
Having encircled it with the left and right sides, immediately thereafter,
one should offer many pairs together with the letter *ra*, the seed-syllable of wind.
One should bind the mouth and the navel with the very sound that is the limb of the syllable Oṃ;
having placed it in the region of the Bindu-pakṣa, one becomes Śiva, whose form is like a long crescent moon.
Having formed the *makara* mudrā with one another, they should play like a ball;
this is the *vaśistobha* on the ground, and the *stobhaka* on the surface of the poison.
The best of practitioners should write the seed-syllable, which is the pinnacle of all things, enclosed within a triangle, using the essence of the life-force of the *bindu*. (124)
Having established the fire there and worshipped it again according to the prescribed rite,
he should place the finger-ring made of metal into a copper vessel.
Having offered oblations with clarified butter, one should deposit the remnants upon the ring;
within the triangular casket, [one should place] the entire seed-syllable.
The best of men should scrape [the ground] with the intense sap of the Bandhūka flower;
having established the fire there and worshipped it again according to the rite. || 127 ||
Having placed the triloha ring in a copper vessel and offered oblations with clarified butter, one should pour the remnants of the offering (saṃpāta) over the ring.
Having prepared a hundredfold increase [of the mantra], one should place it upon a ring;
by inserting the finger of the person to be acted upon, it bestows the attainment of the desired fruit. (129)
O Nandikeśvara, by merely performing the vajra-consecration with those mantras, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus, with a six-cornered [figure] in its pericarp. (130)
In the center is a triangle; in its middle is the seed-syllable (piṇḍa) with the target (sādhya) in the center.
In the hexagon are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and again in the petals starting from the east [the same]. || 131 ||
Starting from the letter *ra* and so forth, one should write the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence;
having written them along with their vowels, there should be three circles on the outside.
One should place the sixteen vowels joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
outside of that, one should place the consonants from *ka* to *ma*, consisting of twenty-five letters.
Or else, one should write the eight [syllables] ending in *ha* on the outer circle;
having drawn a *bhūpura* (fortress-city) outside that, one should place the syllable *ha* in its corners. (134)
Having placed a full water-pot in the center of that [mandala] and invoked the deity,
one should worship with the eight fragrant substances and all kinds of flowers, endowed with devotion.
Then one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), which is supreme and provides all protection.
One should write the seed-syllable ending in the letter *i*, encircled by the sixteen vowels.
In the center of that, surrounded by two fire-houses (triangles) inscribed with the name of the person to be accomplished,
one should write the letter *ra* within the letter *na*, possessing the brilliance of a blazing fire.
Outside of that, one should place the seed-syllable Bhaṇu and the letters from Ka to Ja;
in the middle of that, and again outside of it, one should place a pair of earth-maṇḍalas.
O Nandikeśvara, having written that *saṃvartaka* [mantra] in the corners,
one should duly worship this wheel with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the proper sequence. (139)
The wearing of this yantra destroys the fears of planets, poison, and other calamities.
One should draw a Cintāmaṇi gem in the center of a pair of other discs.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the center, and the six syllables beginning with *agni* in the corners;
then, one should write the letters *vai* and *ka* and *u* and *kā* respectively in the corners and on the sides in due order. 141.
Outside that, one should draw the orb of the sun, and in its center, the Praṇava;
then, having again duly drawn two pairs of outer walls (bhūpuras) outside that.
One should draw [the design] in sequence upon that vessel with lac and gorocana;
having worshipped and honored it with flowers and other offerings, one should wear the supreme yantra.
It bestows long life, brings about nourishment, and increases prosperity;
it destroys defects such as slander and the like, and promotes subjugation and gentleness. (144)
This supreme protection, situated in the midst of the *rakṣā*, removes thieves, serpents, great beasts of prey, spirits, and epilepsy, and brings about all forms of protection. (145)
One should write the central syllable in the middle of the pair of fire-mandalas;
having written the root mantra, one should clearly erase it on the outside.
It was surrounded on all sides by flames of fire and poisonous trees, and covered with branches reaching upward; having recited [the mantra], he [performed] * * * * *. 147.
Tigers, thieves, boars, and hosts of enemies who act like boars; || 148 ||
They do not approach even the vicinity of the supreme protector of the world;
thus [is] the first *sadya* and so forth... (149)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of Ardhanārīśvara, in the Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra.
For the sake of protecting the world, for [its] instruction, and for the fulfillment of the gods' prayers, [he appeared] in the form of an elephant-faced Asura. || 1 ||
For the destruction of Vighnarāja and for his own manifestation, Śaṅkara himself, assuming the form of an elephant together with the Goddess, [appeared]. || 2 ||
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, [one should place them] again on the eight petals starting from the east.
One should place the sixteen [syllables] joined with the pair of deities on the inner base;
one should also place the five letters of the *ka*-group in the middle of the eastern petal. (4)
The *ca*-group should be in the southeast, the *ṭha*-group in the south;
the *ta*-group should be in the southwest, and one should place the *pa*-group in the west.
Oṃ śrīṃ glīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ klīṃ gaiṃ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ glauṃ goṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. || 6 ||
Oṃ Gaṃ Gaḥ, Phaṭ for the weapon. Thus the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) have been proclaimed.
Within the center of the pericarp is a hexagon, and in its center is a triangle. || 7 ||
Having meditated upon this form of the Yoni, one should contemplate the nine Śaktis on the petals:
Tīvrā, Jvālinī, [Kandā...].
And having spoken the state of all-pervading power, the hymn to the Lotus-Seated One was recited. (9)
One should place [the deities] in order upon the petals from the east to the northeast;
having thus assigned the eight Śaktis, the ninth is the bestower of desired fruits.
Having invoked the God seated in the midst of the lotus-throne, endowed with all perfections, one should recite the words of Sarvaśrī, which destroy all obstacles.
One should contemplate an island of jewels at the beginning and middle of the sugarcane field,
filled with wish-fulfilling trees such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta, while remaining composed in mind.
It was endowed with fruits of every season that bestowed desired fruits,
and it was pleasantly cool in all four directions, possessed of moonlight and gentle sunlight.
By the wind from Mount Malaya, which carries sprays of water droplets and roars with a harsh sound,
[the fire] was fanned.
It is always attended by sprouts of vajra-coral and jewels. || 14 ||
[He is adorned] with flowers endowed with all fragrances and accompanied by fruits;
[he holds] a great branch of ten million times ten million,
as well as a mace (raṅgadā) and immediately after that, a sugarcane bow.
Likewise, the trident and the discus are positioned on all sides in sequence;
on the left are the lotus, the noose, and the incomparable red water-lily.
A pair of anklets, spotless like Indra [the sky], a golden pitcher filled with jewels and surrounded by wealth. || 17 ||
Holding that [lotus] with his hand, he was of incomparable saffron hue,
adorned with a crown and tiara, and resplendent with three eyes.
[He saw him] surrounded by [the Śūrpaṇakhās],
casting [them aside], intoxicated with pride, and adorned with all ornaments.
[He saw her] reclining on his left thigh, she who is the cause of the cause of the world.
She was golden-hued, possessed of beautiful hips, endowed with all auspicious marks, her forehead shaped like a half-moon and adorned by the moon. || 20 ||
The goddess has three eyes and four arms, adorned with all ornaments;
she embraces the Lord of Gods with her right hand, overflowing with love. (21)
Holding a noose in her left hand and intoxicated with passion,
she [embraced] the god, whose chest was pressed firmly between her breasts, with her left arm.
And the Sādhikā repeatedly [embraces] with the tip of her lotus-hand that mass of jewels which is always perfectly clinging and overflowing with the nectar of bliss. (23)
The best of practitioners should meditate upon the Lord of the gods of gods as he rains;
having worshipped the Supreme Being with all the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana), [he should proceed]. (24)
In that same manner, one who is endowed with devotion and firm in his vows should worship the Goddess;
[he should worship] outside the triangle, on the six corners, and between the tips of the two deities.
And at the root of the *bilva* tree, one should worship Viṣṇu and Śrī, who is beautiful in every limb,
four-armed, large-eyed, and holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

Having meditated upon me, resplendent with the noose and goad, as holding in my left hand a lotus, and likewise holding an axe, a trident, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and being dissolved within him— 28.
To the east, at the foot of a *pippala* tree, [he should be depicted] with desire and likewise delight,
holding a sugarcane bow and flower-arrows, and likewise granting fearlessness and boons. (29)
One should meditate upon his goddess with her two hands holding red lotuses;
and to the north, one should meditate upon Bhūmidevī and Viṣṇu in the form of Varāha.
Holding a mace, a discus, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons with his four arms,
he [is accompanied by] his goddess, as well as Śukra, who was born from the tip of his throat.
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon her at the root of a Priyaṅgu tree— blazing with light, possessing a complexion ending in [the color] white, and adorned with all ornaments.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear about the second enclosure:
within the hexagon are the six Vighnas, the bestowers of all desired objects. (33)
And [he saw] Āmoda at the foremost part, and Pramoda within Sumukhī;
and Gaṇapa, resembling a jewel, endowed with the face of an elephant. (34)

The second enclosure is said to consist of the Śaṅkha treasure, which has the luster of a pearl, and the Padma treasure, which resembles a gem; and the third [enclosure] is joined with the [six] limbs.
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the fifth [deity] with the four and three world-protectors by their respective names, along with perfumes and other offerings.
Forty thousand, then four hundred thousand, and further four thousand; this is the sequence of the number of recitations as it has been declared. (37)
And one should satisfy forty [deities] with [offerings];
at the end of the recitation, one should perform oblations with the eight substances in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the recitation]. || 38 ||
Pṛthuka, modakas, parched grain (lāja), sugarcane, sesame,
flour (saktu), coconut, and the plantain fruit— these constitute the eightfold offering. (39)
With these substances, one should offer oblations day after day, endowed with devotion; and one should be consecrated by the Guru with the four kinds of jars.
Likewise, having prepared a four-petalled lotus with its root-mantra,
one should place bilva from a milk-tree, as well as vaṭa and pippala.
Having taken the *phalinī* plant and with their inexhaustible waters,
one should properly worship the water-pots and duly honor the six Gaṇeśas.

Having placed the seed-syllable of nectar (amṛtabīja), one should recite it one hundred and forty times; then the Guru, preceded by an act of grace, should consecrate the disciple with the sprinkling [of water]. 43.
Having worshipped with golden flowers, golden sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*),
golden rings, variegated garments, and grains of rice; || 44 ||
The disciple, endowed with devotion to the guru, should also offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
he should present it to the preceptor in accordance with his means. (45)
Afterwards, the practitioner should also perform all the ritual duties,
having offered oblations with the eight substances until each respective substance is exhausted.
One should offer twenty thousand oblations with honey for the attainment of gold;
likewise, one should offer with cow’s milk for the perfection of knowledge, and with cow’s ghee for the sake of prosperity.
One should offer sugar with parched grains for fame; one should offer curd for the attainment of all goals;
through food there shall be an abundance of food; and with sesame seeds, for the prosperity of one's literary works.
Having taken safflower together with rice grains, as well as garments,
and having collected earth from a desired sacred field mixed with milk, (one should proceed). (49)
One should perform oblations for the sake of attaining a sacred field (kṣetra) and especially for the attainment of a kingdom,
using the earth from the city festivals of a rival kṣatriya.
One should perform the oblation together with the eight substances and the like, along with milk;
the attainment of sovereignty will be accomplished before long—of this there is no doubt. || 51 ||
One desiring a maiden should offer oblations daily with shining flowers born of rice;
and one desiring a husband should offer oblations with the finest twigs of the *chinnodbhava* plant.
Anointed with the three sweets (stri-madhura), she obtains a boon in an instant;
likewise, for the increase of kingdoms, [one should worship] with lotuses or even with *ta-ka* fruits.

With white water-lilies, the minister should likewise offer oblations to the elder brothers with the best fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* and other trees; and for the horses, he should offer oblations of salt and *vetasa* wood. (54)
O Nandikeśvara, even for those of the lowest castes, one should offer oblations with the flowers of the Pāribhadra tree mixed with the three sweets.
O son, through the offering of *pāṭala* flowers one attains success for the sake of the kingdom and the pacification of enemies;
and by the oblation of *dūrvā* stalks, one shall always possess long life. (56)
The destruction of forgetfulness and other such ailments occurs through oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks;
likewise, by means of fuel-sticks grown from cuttings, combined with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Endowed with devotion toward the Guru, one should daily recite this mantra four times; it destroys poisons such as kālakūṭa and bestows all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis).
At the end of the body, he attains liberation right there; of this there is no doubt. (58½)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of Mahāgaṇapati, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Listen to the ritual procedure for the mantra-worship of Vighneśa, who bestows grace swiftly, grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and wards off all obstacles. || 1 ||
Then, in sequence, there is the Pañcārdhaka, the Ardhacandra, and the Saṃpatta;
these are joined with the Sūkṣma, likewise the Anāstra, and endowed with the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ). || 2 ||
Lohita joined with Vahni, Bhṛgu accompanied by Pāśa, Atri joined with the long [vowel], Śikhā, Vāyu, and ending with Namaḥ. || 3 ||
One should worship the deity, who resides within the nine powers such as Tīvrā and is endowed with the six limbs through the root seed-syllable joined with the long vowels and so forth, in the lotus.
As before, one should properly worship Vighna with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
He has a red body, is endowed with passion, and is adorned with a red garland. (5)
He has a noose, a goad, and a tusk, is joined by a *kalpa*-tree creeper,
possesses three eyes, and at the tip of his trunk holds a citron fruit.

Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun, endowed with a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and having the form of a religious student (brahmacārin). || 7 ||
Outside that, at the base of the petals, one should worship the eight root-deities:
Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and Ananta.
The bestower of boons, the elephant-faced one, and likewise the single-tusked one—
these are declared as Lambodara, each joined with its own seed-syllable according to its respective name.
Gaṃ, obeisance to Vighna; Gaṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka; Gaṃ, obeisance to Vīra; Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Śūra. || 10 ||
Gaṃ, obeisance to the Giver of Boons; Gaṃ, obeisance to the Elephant-faced One; Gaṃ, obeisance to the Single-tusked One; Gaṃ, obeisance to the Large-bellied One. || 11 ||
