One should worship the deity in sequence: first with this [mantra], then with the Mothers, then with the Limbs (Aṅgas), and the fourth with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). || 12 ||
One should perform oblations with clarified butter, milk-rice, and sugar,
especially for the sake of prosperity, fame, and the attainment of all perfections.
One may bring the world under control immediately by means of ghee alone;
one should likewise burn coconut with its husk and kernel in succession.
One should offer oblations one by one daily for forty days;
thus, the desired object is attained, and one should perform the fire sacrifice with the eight substances. (15)
Through the oblation of the eight substances, all perfections arise.
At the end of the day, both the householder and the lifelong celibate should perform the libation.
For the householder, there is the journey of worldly life; for the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), however, there is absolute liberation.
Specifically, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs after forty days.
From the mandala and from Savitṛ, there shall be a silver staircase;
having come by that path to the water, one obtains whatever is desired by them.
Vighna is gratified by libations poured upon his head again and again;
worship and fire-offerings should be performed for him just as they are for Mahāgaṇapati.
O Nandikeśvara, listen: I shall later describe that very deity who is honored in all scriptures and who destroys all obstacles. (20)
Endowed with the previously mentioned bathing rites, possessing the aforementioned qualities, pure, adhering to his own proper conduct, observing the vow, and free from greed; || 21 ||
Endowed with verbal silence, one should accomplish the rites for the lords of obstacles;
having first uttered the supreme *tāra*, thereafter [one should utter] the five-ending [mantra]. (22)
"Endowed with the Bindu, endowed with the Gaṇas, and also [ending] with 'pataye namaḥ'—Oṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ.
For both libation (tarpaṇa) and oblation (huta), one should utter the mantra ending in Svāhā. (23)
And with one's own long-conjoined seed-syllables, as before, the six-limbed rite [is performed]:
*oṃ hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. || 24 ||
Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca).
Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya). Oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon (astra). || 25 ||
Having thus worshipped the six limbs, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and body:
[He resides] upon an island of gold and jewels in the midst of the ocean of sugarcane juice.
It was endowed with wish-fulfilling trees, possessed of divine flower-creepers, furnished with celestial trees and creepers, and frequented by divine Māras. || 27 ||
It was filled with swans, cuckoos, bees, parrots, and peacocks, and was endowed with the fruits of all seasons, as well as with jackfruit and sandalwood trees.
It was joined with mangoes, rose-apples, wood-apples, auspicious plantains, pomegranates, and betel-nut trees, as well as various coconuts, sugarcanes, and citrons. || 29 ||
(371) In that place, frequented by divine and other trees as a result of former merits,
there stands in the center a Pārijāta tree endowed with various jewels. (30)
It was joined with many branches, endowed with fruits and flowers,
possessed of flawless sprouts, and as cool as moonlight.
One should visualize Ananta and the others, as well as Śiva and the rest, being bathed in its center, joined with the rays of the morning sun and endowed with every splendor.
In the center of that, one should worship the Mātṛkā-lotus according to the previous sequence;
it is endowed with many branches and provided with fruits and flowers.
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the powers of Intense (Tīvra) and the others;
and in the center of that, within a triangle, one should meditate upon Him.
One should worship Vighnanāyaka upon the lotus on the head of the elephant while he is playing;
one should perform the worship in the same sequence as before, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the food offering (naivedya). || 35 ||
Modaka, coconut, parched rice flour with sesame seeds, sugarcane, flattened rice, and plantain fruit, in that order. (36)

Having offered oblations with these eight substances on the first lunar day (pratipad) and so forth, or beginning from the fourth day, properly on an auspicious weekday and on a favorable day; || 37 ||
One should worship that Vighnarāja, the Lord of the Gaṇas, with its tip;
and Gaṇeśa in the southwest, and Gaṇanāyaka in the northwest. (38)
And at the base of the outer petals, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence;
in the center of the eight petals, however, are Vakratuṇḍa and Ekavaktraka.
One should worship Mahodara, Gajāsyaka, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, and Dhūmravarṇa immediately thereafter. (40)
Thereafter, one should worship the Mothers in the fourth enclosure in their proper order;
outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors at the ends of the petals with their respective names.
Endowed with devotion, one should worship [the deity] with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namas*.
First, there is a divine throne made of jewels, consisting of seven layers.
The second should be of golden color, the third should be made of silver;
the fourth should be of śāla-copper, and the fifth should be of crystal. || 43 ||
The sixth is said to be made of lead, and outside that is an iron rampart;
thus, one should visualize it surrounded on the outside by seven walls.
And at the eastern gate, the two treasures Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi are situated;
Śaṅkha has the luster of the color of a conch or the moon, while [Padma] should resemble one joined with a lotus. (45)
Both have large bellies and short arms, and both carry a conch and a lotus;
such is the form of the twelve Gaṇapas and likewise of the Aṅgas.
Red in color, with the faces of elephants, and equipped with nooses, goads, and lotuses—one should meditate thus and worship; the number of recitations and so forth will now be described.
Forty thousand repetitions constitute four hundred thousand;
the libation (tarpaṇa) is one-tenth of that, as are the rites of consecration (abhiṣeka) and the fire-oblation (āhuti). 48.
Having offered ghee, fuel-sticks, and food— specifically these eight substances—
and having recited the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, one should then recite the root mantra in due order.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should silently consume this.
Having become intent upon the person to be accomplished, they will be brought under control within seven nights. (50)
By performing oblations of *gaḍūcī* combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*) into the fire, the destruction of all complications and the destruction of fever are brought about. (51)

With sesame seeds and rice grains, it increases prosperity and brings about subjugation; for one desiring a daughter, it is likewise accomplished with parched grain, three peacock feathers, and sugarcane.
One who desires a boon should likewise offer oblations for seven nights;
the practitioner should offer coconuts on the fourth lunar day.
By the power of his royal glory, his prosperity increases day by day in due course;
and he shall accomplish every undertaking with oblations poured with clarified butter. (54)
At midnight, an oblation should be performed with salt mixed with curd;
likewise, through rites such as summoning (ākarṣaṇa), the fruit of the conversation [is attained]. (55)
Through oblation with palāśa flowers accompanied by three peacock feathers, one attains perfection in poetic composition and becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
With bilva leaves grown from well-watered plants, with those originating from golden flowers, and with blue lotuses, bandhujīvas, nandyāvartas, and campakas; || 57 ||
By means of oblations of *pāṭala*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *punnāga*, and the three sweets,
one becomes glorious like Indra, skilled in devotion to the Guru.
By offering oblations of sugar and parched grain, one becomes radiant like the sun;
having visualized oneself [as the deity], the wise practitioner should offer the sacrifice properly.
One should bind the water of the heart-lotus, endowed with the vital breath (jīva), within the state of equanimity;
having bound all that with the "remover of falling" (pātighna), one should [bind] the throat with its stalk (puṣkara). (60)
Having placed the sun upon his head, one should visualize him being urged from all sides by the Gaṇapas with blows of their palms on his back and flanks.
Through practice for seven nights, there shall be the grinding away of all sins.
Likewise, the seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja) conjoined with its own seed-syllable and endowed with the Anusvāra [should be used]. (62)
The syllable *glauṃ*, joined with the fierce moon (*caṇḍacandra*), serves for paralyzing (*stambhana*).
With turmeric, one should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the center of a vessel's opening. (63)
Immediately thereafter, having drawn a dark-blue [form] surrounded by a middle [enclosure],
one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) according to the sequence that will be described.
The breath of that person is here; his life-force is established here. All his sense-faculties, as well as the actions of his speech, mind, and body [are here]. (65)
"May the vital breaths (prāṇas) come here; svāhā"—thus the mantra should end.
Then the Guru should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) for the disciple according to the system of Śakra. (66)
In this very sequence, one should establish the vital breaths of the sādhya,
having worshipped with yellow flowers while reciting the root mantra.
Having performed one thousand recitations,
one should bury it in a four-cornered spot within a shallow earthen bowl, especially at midnight.
Having meditated on the object to be accomplished as facing downwards, and oneself as the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnanāyaka),
[one effects] the paralyzing of an elephant's trunk, its movement, and even its wrath.
One should avoid discouraging enthusiasm and the loss of Dharma;
one should write down the names of the practitioner and the object of practice using the female seed-syllable (yoṣā-bīja).
Having likewise recited the mantra enclosed between two bricks three thousand times as before, one should bury them on the path of the army.
In this way, there shall be the stabilization of the army; one should worship with these eight substances.
One should always give these substances to children with devotion.
One should write the name of the enemy upon the image using the juice of its leaves;
when accomplished through nine thousand recitations, it is effective on the path of the enemy.
One should bury the pillars for the installation as before during the worship of the obstacles (vighnas),
[casting out] the most sinful, the obstructer of dharma, the slanderer, and likewise the breaker.
One who steals the property of the gods and one who steals the property of the guru should be expelled from one's own country; the means for doing so is stated here. (75)
Having taken charcoal from a cremation ground and pulverizing that seed of the tree of the destruction of asceticism, one should write the mantra enclosed within it.
One should cast the powder of elephant, horse, and lion into the house of an enemy;
by contact with even a mere portion of that powder, he shall flee from one country to another.
Having taken a bone from a cremation ground, measuring the length of the desired finger-breadths,
one should recite [the mantra] over it one thousand times and bury it for the purpose of inciting hatred in an enemy.
This indeed shall be the eradication of one who is devoted to sinful deeds:
having taken the dwelling of a neem tree inhabited by crows and burning it on a Tuesday. (79)
Having cremated that [effigy] on a funeral pyre in a cemetery using fire produced from that very place,
one should write the name of the enemy in the middle of it, enclosed within the mantra. (80)
Having recited it three thousand times, one should cast it upon his head;
having moved from one country to another, he will certainly become miserable. (81)
One who is possessed of evil thoughts, cruel, untrained, and purposeless—listen now as I describe how such a person should be offered into the fire according to the prescribed method. (82)
Having written that name and syllable in the center of the *karmapaṭa*, and having placed it upon a palm leaf and within a doll immediately thereafter; || 83 ||
Having made that entire mass into a ball with beeswax at midnight,
one should [anoint it] with pungent oil and clarified butter in a cremation ground upon dry dūrvā grass.
One should burn those respective [substances] with sacrificial fuel (samidh) through the practice for seven nights;
thereby, there will be delusion for him, and especially forgetfulness. (85)
This is the duty regarding the Dharma, and one should cause the penance to be performed;
one should write the name of the person to be purified (*sādhya*) in sequence upon birch bark.
Having taken clay from the hand of a potter, one should fashion it into a form;
having placed [the substance] inside its belly, one should smear it with the oil of *bhṛṅgī*.
Having stirred it with that very water, one should smear [the object] for unsurpassed subjugation;
likewise, [one may use] the añjalikarī, the aindravallī, the lakṣmī, and the bhadrikā.
Having extracted the Viṣṇukrāntī, the Vārāhī, the Bhṛṅgī-ādi-devikā, and the Sahā, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times for each.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should wear it, for it brings all things under control. Although each has been explained there, listen now to the conjunction of them all. (90)
The añjali is said to have ten parts; the indrikā has twelve parts; the latā has eight parts; lakṣmī has eight parts; the drumāṅga has nine parts; and the sarvabhadrikā [has ten parts]. 91.
Viṣṇukrānti is said to be one part, Manasa sixteen parts, Musalī one-sixteenth part, and Mayūra two parts; for the rite of subjugation (vaśya), Dūrvā is especially recommended.
The Goddess, however, consists of the enumeration of qualities; she should always be one part.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each [deity] immediately thereafter— || 93 ||
Having combined and ground all these together, one should add curd and dry ingredients;
then, having formed them into pills and recited the mantra a thousand times with devotion, [one should consume them].
Having fully worshipped Gaṇanātha, there should be the application of a tilaka;
this, when combined with ashes, is supreme for bringing all under one's control. (95)
Indeed, that which has been prescribed for the worship of Mahāgaṇapati—namely, the destruction of all evils and the increase of wealth and grain—is truly appropriate here as well. (96)
Having been described by way of the means of accomplishment, Gaṇanātha especially becomes directly perceptible quickly through the practice of the fourfold repetition. || 97 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of Kṣipragaṇādhipa, within the Inconceivable Viśvasādākhya [Tantra].
But listen, O Nandikeśvara, to [the description of] the supreme Śivā, the Great Goddess Vāgīśvarī, who is the embodiment of knowledge and transcends all illusions.
First, the vase is proclaimed; immediately after that, those same two syllables, then the long vowel, then water, and again the end of the five. (2)

Devoid of the vowel *svara*, joined with the long [vowel], followed by *toya* (water), then two *yānt* [consonants] joined with the subtle [vowel], ending with *svāhā*; this is the ten-syllabled mantra. (3)
Immediately after that, I shall describe the [mantra] endowed with its birth and its six limbs:
that which consists of the four middle vowels from among the six vowels at the beginning and the end.
Having abandoned this neuter [syllable], one should serve that which belongs to your kind;
namely, the ka-group, the ca-group, the ṭa-group, and the ta-group. || 5 ||
The pavarga [consonants] beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'kṣa' should follow in sequence;
likewise, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) beginning with the heart constitute the six-limbed ritual.

The pair of vowels is encapsulated by the consonants from *ka* to *ya* according to their respective order; one should know that the first is the letter *a*, and the *ka*-group is accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*). (7)
The syllable *Aṃ* followed by *Namaḥ* constitutes this Heart-mantra;
likewise, the guttural class (*ka-varga*) and the others should be enclosed between vowels. (8)
Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the heart; iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ raṃ, svāhā to the head. || 9 ||
uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā). eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, hūṃ to the armor (kavaca). || 10 ||
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ phaṭ to the weapon. || 11 ||
Having spoken thus, one should place the six limbs and the syllables of the root mantra:
the letter *va* should be at the end of the twelve (the *dvādaśānta*), and one should place the deity in the two ears. (12)
O Nandikeśvara, one should place two sets of ten syllables on the eyes, likewise two *vādi* syllables on the nostrils, and the syllable *nikāra* in the middle of the mouth.
When the *liṅga* has been placed, one should perform the *vyāvīkaraṇa* with the *svāhā* mantra;
endowed with the previously mentioned qualities and possessed of the practitioner's enthusiasm. (14)
Having performed the daily observances consisting of purification, ritual sipping of water, bathing, and the performance of the twilight prayers,
he should be endowed with devotion to his guru.
Having performed the purification of the place, the body, and immediately thereafter the purification of the vessel,
as well as the purification of the substances and the mantras, one should remain endowed with the proper disposition.
With very white lotuses, *nandyāvarta* flowers, and *jāti* blossoms,
as well as with fragrant flowers, sandalwood, and moon-like [white] blooms. (17)
With kāleyaka, puras, saffron, and monkey flesh, combined with yellow pigment (rocanā) and fragrant juices, [one should bathe] with cool waters. || 18 ||
One should likewise offer water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), incense, and a lamp;
as well as food offerings, betel leaf, and mouth-freshener.
Having meditated upon this fivefold seat, beginning with Ananta and ending with the lotus of Mātṛkā, specifically within the pericarp (karṇikā), [one should proceed].
And in the middle of that [lotus] is Vidyeśvarī; above that is a white lotus;
on its filaments is Kāmarāja, and Vāgbhava is in its center.
And in the center of that [mandala], one should visualize Vāgīśī, who dwells within the fivefold reality;
she resembles pure crystal, sits in a state of ease, and possesses a radiant smile. (22)
Richly adorned with the beauty of a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
she has four arms, three eyes, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
He holds a book with his left hand and a pen with his right;
he holds a rosary of pure crystal in his left hand and a bell in his [other] hand.
She was graceful, with a radiant countenance, speaking as sweetly as a parrot or a peacock, and adorned with beautiful earrings, armlets, and ornaments of pearls. (25)
She is constantly bathed in the nectar-essence of the moon, ever affectionate toward her devotees,
and possesses rounded, full, and elevated breasts well-anointed with every kind of fragrance.
Adorned with a white garland and beautified by white garments,
she possesses a pair of firm breasts and broad hips— she is Śivā. (27)
Having thus meditated upon the Mother of the World, the mother of those who have received initiation,
one should worship her in due order like Śiva, beginning with the invocation.
And one should satisfy the entire world, consecrated by the respective yoga-mantras,
in front of the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyeśvarī) and within the eight petals.
O Nandikeśvara, as before, [one should worship] Yoga, Satya, Vimalā, and likewise Pūrṇā, as well as Smṛti, Medhā, and Prajñā.
And outside of that, one should worship the six limbs: the heart on the fire-petal, and the crest-lock (śikhā) on the northwest petal. || 31 ||
In the northeast, one should place the armor (kavaca), and again in the east, the eye (netra); then,
in the middle of the petal on the left side, one should worship the King of Mantras.
Gentle, white-complexioned, and lotus-eyed goddesses, accompanied by the Rudras and uttering "namas"—these are the Śakvarīs in number. (33)

On the tips of the petals, one should worship the Mothers, and outside of that, the World-Protectors; having worshipped them by their respective names, one should contemplate their respective forms. (34)
Having recited the mantra one million times, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that number;
likewise, one who is endowed with devotion should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) and the fire-oblation (huta). || 35 ||
One should offer oblations with white lotuses moistened with milk, up to ten thousand times;
they should be white, auspicious, cool, and sprinkled with the three sweets.

Having bathed in the morning and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should, in due order, perform the ritual assignments (nyāsa) and other rites, using fuel-sticks of *palāśa* or *gaḍūcī* mixed with clarified butter. (37)
Having gazed with divine vision at pure water in a pure vessel and having recited the root mantra one thousand times, he should drink that water. || 38 ||
Within a year, she became a poetess, composing in the sequence of prose and verse;
she remained within the solar disc, situated in water reaching as far as her heart.
Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī in the center of that solar disc,
one should constantly recite [the mantra] three thousand times until the completion of the mandala.
One's poetic composition shall become abundant, endowed with the ornament of *jāti*.
One should perform the oblation (*homa*) with well-formed leaves produced from the three sweets, honey, and *bilva* fruit. (41)
Fortune, the grace of poetic talent, and the power to subjugate the world arise [for one who performs this].
With palms joined in reverence, one should offer oblations of kindled fuel mixed with the three sweets. (42)
Great power of poetic composition arises for him;
one should cook [the medicine] well with the milk of a Brahmin cow, mixed with ghee. (43)
Having chanted [the mantra] three thousand times daily at dawn, one should apply it;
by a measure of only three karṣas, poetic skill shall arise from the circle.
And Viśvauṣadha, Suśveṣā, combined with the two Jananīs, Saindhava, Ajamoda, Vācā, and these Pippalīs; || 46 ||
Having powdered yaṣṭi and jīraka in equal parts,
the wise one should saturate it many times with the juice of brāhmī.
Having mixed it with ghee and *śīdhu* liquor, one should recite [the mantra] three thousand times in succession;
by practicing this for half a month, one should consume half a *mātrā*. (47)
By the recitation of these, poetic talent certainly arises even for the mute;
therefore, the accomplishment of poetry belongs to the practitioner without a doubt. 48.
The decoction of fifty medicinal herbs should be collected in a jar;
having chanted [the mantra] one thousand times at the beginning of each day, one should do so daily for one month. (49)
By means of the sprinkling with that water, intelligence, prosperity, fame, poetic talent, renown, subjugation, and wealth are successively accomplished.
A woman who is barren, consecrated by that water, shall obtain a virtuous son;
likewise, she obtains the fifty medicinal herbs beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
Sacred sandalwood, likewise red sandalwood, agallochum, and moon-fragrance (karpūra), as well as uśīra, kuṣṭha, and saffron. || 52 ||
Takkoḷaja, jātī, māṃsī, mura, and likewise cora;
then gandha, rocanā, patra, and thereafter pippalī. || 53 ||
Bilva, guha, red grass, clove, kumbhivardhanī, udumbara, kāmarīkā, and likewise vārāmajja; || 54 ||
A white conch-shell flower together with the mayūraśikhā plant, lac, agni-mantha, siṃhī, as well as kuśa and darbha grass; || 55 ||
The black conch-flower, the banyan tree, the bandhūka, the bṛhatī, the pāṭalī, the citrā, the tulasī, and likewise the kiṇika; || 56 ||
These forty [plants] have been declared immediately following the ten flowers: Indravallī, Bhṛṅgī, Viṣṇukrānti, and Sūkarī. (57)
Furthermore, on an auspicious day and a favorable weekday, one should worship Kṛtāñjali, Dūrvā, Śrīdevī, Sabhā, Lakṣmī, and Sadābhadra.
Then, having taken fifty sin-destroying medicinal herbs,
one should prepare pills from them, especially those placed within ashes.
Spirits, ghosts, and demons, as well as thieves, tigers, and the like,
when the root mantra is properly recited and worn, grant all accomplishments.
And having prepared the oil of *jyotiṣmatī* with the root-mantra, one should consume it daily in the prescribed sequence; after six months, one will become a lord of speech.
Though impure by birth, he was born into the Śaiva fold; having conquered his senses through austerity, he was devoted to daily bathing, a true devotee, and free from finding fault with others. (62)
Endowed with the qualities previously mentioned, compassionate, and the best of practitioners,
he indeed possesses the power to expound upon scriptures that have not even been studied.
But for those who worship the radiant Vāgīśī, the bestower of boons, with these four qualities,
she will surely come into their presence and grant their desired object.
By reciting this constantly one hundred and eight times, one shall attain the state of absolute liberation.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*.
Nandikeśvara.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the helpless, O Supreme Sovereign, be gracious so that I may perform worship to this form of yours. || 1 ||
"O Lord, tell me the path of worship for human devotees as well.
Īśvara said:
"Listen to that [teaching] which is the very womb of jewels and is solely devoted to devotion and knowledge."
Atri, Kṣaṇā, Kālakaṇṭhā, Kāyugrī, and Ikṣarohi— these five,
situated in the center of the Tuṣita heaven, [salute] the one who dwells at the root of the banyan tree.
Salutations to Rudra, the source of bliss, who is solely devoted to meditation;
this thirty-six-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the power of liberation (tāra-śakti). || 4 ||
The six-limbed [mantra] is considered to consist of Tāra, Śakti, and so forth, together with the heart and other limbs in sequence;
likewise, [the mantras] are six, two, eight, eight, five, and three respectively.
The six limbs are designated by means of the syllables of the root mantra.
Having thus performed the placement of the six limbs, one should place [the mantras] upon the fingers beginning with the thumb (jyeṣṭha).
Two [syllables] on the ears and two on the pair of breasts; two on the heart and two on the navel;
two on the hips and one on the secret place; and four on each of the feet.
With the remaining two [groups], one should sequentially perform the placement that pervades all limbs;
one should then perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa'.
One should place the primordial phoneme (praṇava), which is the root of the instruction on sound;
and one should place the fortieth letter, which is adorned by the nine groups [of consonants].
Two groups of vowels have been declared: the first consists of five and the latter of four;
there should be seven groups of consonants, containing seven, six, and five syllables respectively.
(400) Another [type] is illuminated by the three aims of life (*trivarga*); their origin is now described.
It arises from the application of a single *mātrā* to the ear, the palm, the lip, and the fingernail. (11)

The vowels *a*, *i*, and *u* are *savarṇa* (homogeneous); the first class [of consonants] consists of itself [plus its nasal]. Through conjunction with the letter *t*, the vowel *e* arises; however, with the following [vowel], it becomes *ai*.
And here, if the group [of consonants] ends with *m*, it is produced from the throat;
however, that which consists of a single *mātrā* is produced from the mouth being slightly opened, accompanied by the sound of breath. (13)

Another letter is born, the letter *ha*, the best of consonants; it arises from the six [phonemes] starting with *tā* (the palatals), and is the collection of the two [letters] *ka* and *va* at the end.
The second letter of the dental class (*da*) is indeed supreme;
it possesses the qualities of being an external contact (*sparśa*), a commonality of externality, resonance, depth, and lightness. (15)
The five groups [of consonants] indeed reside in the throat, palate, teeth, and lips;
these are the five groups recognized in the well-known script. (16)
The final [consonants] are said to be produced by two, two, four, and three [organs] respectively;
among them, the two [sibilants śa and ṣa] are produced at the palate and the head, while the letter *ha* joined with *uṣma* (the sibilants) is produced with the mouth wide open. || 17 ||
The sequence of the written letters begins with *śa-ṣa-sa* and the nine groups [of consonants];
the supreme speech, originating from the *mūlādhāra*, is endowed with the measure of a thread (*sūtramātrā*). (18)
Above that, at the region of the navel, she is Paśyantī and consists of half a mora;
having emerged from the heart, she herself is called Madhyamā, consisting of three-quarters [of a mora].
That very [speech], endowed with a single measure (mātrā) and consisting of distinct syllables, is Vaikharī;
it occurs even within the mouth through the conjunctions and perceptions arising from the eight locations [of articulation]. || 20 ||
At the time of origination, Vaikharī comes first; then Madhyamā at the meeting with audible sound;
Paśyantī occurs at partial contact; but Parā follows upon direct experience. (21)
"Origination and dissolution have been mentioned; therein, origination is now described:
the vowels, the consonants, and the letters arise in sequence from the sky, the wind, the moon, and the earth. (22)
Thus, by means of the venerable Bhūtayama, there would be the script of the elements (bhūtalipi).
Those phonemes produced from the collection [of sounds], beginning with space (ākāśa) and ending with earth (pṛthivī), [are as follows]: || 23 ||
The possessor of Śiva-śakti should grasp all the scripts from beginning to end;
this process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) is said to consist of the nature of Śakti and Śiva.
In this very way, the script also proceeds here step by step in successive order.
In the sequential order, [the letters] end with *kha* and so on, increasing; in the reverse orders, they are born from *a* and end with *kha*.
These are said to end in *visarga*, while in the reverse order they have *bindu* at their head. (26)
The visarga is the seed-syllable of Śakti, while the bindu is remembered as consisting of Śiva.
The vowels of worldly existence reside in the nine supports (ādhāras), beginning with *ha* and ending with *pa*.
Having placed the letter *ha* on the crown of the head, one should place the letter *ya* on the forehead;
likewise, the letter *ra* on the right side of the head and the letter *va* on the left.
The letter *la* is in the western part; the letter *pa* is at the tip of the thumb;
the letter *ka* is at the base of the arm, and the letter *kha* is at the end of the elbow. || 29 ||
The letter *sa* is at the base of the fingers, *ga* at the wrist;
the *ka*-group is on the left hand, and the *ṭa*-group is on the right foot.
The *tavarga* [consonants] are on the left foot, the letter *pa* on the left side,
the letter *pha* at the region of the navel, and the letter *va* on the side of the back. (31)
One should place the letter *sa* in the secret region and the letter *ṣa* in the middle of the fire;
having placed the letter *sa* in the heart, such is the sequence of the Bhūtalipi.
O Nandikeśvara, having thus performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this sequence, one should worship that divine [mantra], which removes all sins and increases all knowledge.
Pure in conduct, clean, bathed, a pure devotee of Śiva with his senses subdued,
he was diligent in the practice of the ash-bath and wore a sacred thread made of Rudrākṣa beads.
Then, endowed with purity from bathing and seated upon a seat,
one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and thereafter the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in due order.

Then, having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), thereafter one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa); having assigned Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, one should again perform the ritual placement of the Mātṛkās.

Śrī Nandikeśvara said: O incomparable Lord of the World, O Leader who is the cause of liberation, out of compassion for your devotees, please describe the initiation that brings about the extinction of the bonds.
Īśvara said:
One should first construct a pavilion adorned with ornaments,
[to be used] for seven nights, five nights, three days, or even immediately.
Prior to the initiation (dīkṣā), the offering of the sacrificial cake (kurārpaṇa) should be performed simultaneously;
having smeared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the altar (vedi), and all other areas with cow dung.
O Nandikeśvara, the worship of the Liṅga and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) are as described previously;
likewise, the altar for the Maṇḍala is according to the characteristics already mentioned.
One should properly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the substances and deities as before;
then, one should lay down thirty-three lines with the cord, equal in length from east to north.
In the center, one should draw a very beautiful lotus consisting of sixty-four squares,
provided with eight petals, using the tips of the lines.
That which is to be known as black is remembered as being circular;
that which is outside it is also circular, and that which is outside of that is called white. (43)
Having spread out all the colored powders (varṇas) evenly, one who is most skilled in ritual procedures should arrange the remainder according to logic; outside of that, he should fashion a square.
One should worship Īśāna in the center of the pericarp, Puruṣa in the eastern face as before, Aghora in the southern face, and Vāmadeva in the northern face. (45)
One should worship the five Brahmans at the western face immediately;
having worshipped the Heart in the southeast, one should worship the Head in the northeast. (46)
Having worshipped the *śikhā* in the southwest, one should worship the *kavaca* in the northwest;
having placed the *netra* in front, specifically upon the filaments (*kesara*).
Having assigned the weapon-mantra (astra) to Īśāna, one should perform the remaining rites as before;
likewise, for disciples undergoing the initiation of consecration (saṃskāra-dīkṣā), the eightfold [rite] is excluded.

It has been stated that nineteen [rites] are to be performed, augmented by the six virtues; the performer, endowed with Brahmanic qualities, should be free from pride regarding his status as a twice-born and so forth. (49)
One who is devoid of the status of being a son of Rudra is unfit for spiritual practice;
if one is devoid of these qualities, one is unfit even for Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, having performed the consecration of refinement (saṃskāradīkṣā), one should practice for liberation;
having worshipped the Śiva-fire as before, one should commence the rite of initiation (dīkṣākārya). || 51 ||
Initiation (dīkṣā), however, is indeed the severing of bonds; its function is thus fierce.
For all fierce rites, the "kindling" (dīpana) of the mantras must be performed at the beginning.

In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśyaka), and pacification (śānti), one should employ mantras ending with "vaṣaṭ," accompanied by "vauṣaṭ" and "vaṣaṭ," and situated above the seed-syllable of nectar (sudhābīja).
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with mantras everywhere, beginning with the Nādika;
the Śikhā-mantra is declared to be the root-mantra of the syllable Huṃ.
Fire alone is declared to be the crest-lock (śikhā); here, that which is cherished by the holders of the scriptures is not even found within the Mātṛkā, yet it is written above it.
Having extracted each one individually, or [having extracted them] one by one in that sequence.
First, having uttered the *tāra* (om), and immediately after that the *śikhā*, then the root mantra, and again accompanied by the *śikhā*. (57)
Having uttered the end [of the mantra] as "huṃ phaṭ," this is the illumination (dīpana) of the root mantra;
first uttering "oṃ haṃ phaṭ" and immediately thereafter the syllable "huṃ. (58)
The heart and the mind are the illuminators of the crest-heart (*śikhā-hṛdaya*).

Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ; likewise, the syllable *huṃ* is the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā-bīja*) immediately following. Immediately thereafter, that same [mantra] should be used as before, ending with the "End-maker" (*antaka*).
Oṃ iṃ huṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the illumination of the eyes; likewise, [the syllable] hauṃ is enclosed within [the two]. (60)

Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for illuminating the weapon (astra), which serves as a consecration placed within the middle [of the syllables]. Just as before, the illumination of the mantras is performed by means of the crest-syllable (śikhā). || 61 ||
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ! Having thus kindled the disciple with the root-mantras and their limbs, and having worshipped the disciple who stands in the space to his right, the preceptor— (62)
The thread fashioned by a maiden, tripled and then folded three times,
sprinkled with the Astra-mantra and protected by the Varma-mantra, should be wound around the pit while reciting the root mantra.

One should join the thread, which has been infused with the Suṣumṇā and purified by the root-mantra, to that disciple; one should bind it with the Śikhā-mantra so that it hangs down from the big toe of the foot.
One who desires liberation should bind [the thread] from the big toe up to the tip of the head;
for a man, on the left side, and for a woman, on the right side.
One should not place the thread upon him for the purpose of sustaining those who are to be withdrawn, even though the Śakti has been worshipped at his base with the Śakti-mantra. (66)
Having grasped the Suṣumnā with the root mantra upon the external thread,
and having placed it there, one should meditate upon it, worship it with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), and envelop it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
This should be kept in close proximity, especially to the heart; for a woman as well, one should act in this very same way everywhere with due propriety.

The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of mantras, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and the path of kalās—these six paths should be deposited in their proper sequence. 69.
The heart-mantra for the primary [mantras] begins with *tāraṃ* (Oṃ), ends with the dative case, and concludes with *namaḥ*:
*oṃ hāṃ tantrādhvane namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ padādhvane namaḥ*. || 70 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of mantras (mantrādhvan).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the self of worlds (bhuvanātman). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of kalās (kalādhvan). || 71 ||
Having projected the sixfold path according to the Sūtra and being united with the state of Śiva,
one should sprinkle the water that has been received with the palm of the hand toward the disciple.
With that mantra and a flower, one should strike the disciple’s heart;
with the *huṃ* syllable and the exhaling breath (*recaka*), one should place it within the disciple’s heart. (73)
In the midst of the *ajapā*, effect the separation of the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of the weapon-mantra *huṃ phaṭ*;
then, likewise, one should further delimit it with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ svāhā*. || 74 ||
In this manner, one should contemplate consciousness as indistinct by means of the power (śakti);
then, when it has become the thread of the channels (nāḍī), one should join it with the power of reabsorption (saṃhāriṇī).
Having recited "Oṃ jaṃ, homage to the self," the self shall become pervasive throughout the thread.
Having protected [the body] with the Kavaca mantra, one should likewise [protect] the heart with the Hṛdaya mantra; thus is the triad. || 76 ||
O Nandikeśvara, for the purpose of bringing the Self into proximity, one should perform that [rite] after having projected the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) and beholding the Śāntyatīta [level]. 77.
Having meditated upon it as if it were the mantra itself, one should contemplate it within the thread of the channels.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta).
With this very mantra, one should recite [it] in sequence for the purpose of vision. 79.
In the same way, there is likewise the weapon (astra) and the word (pada), consisting of sixteen syllables;
within this [word] are eight worlds, a seed-syllable (bīja), and a channel (nāḍī)—these two pairs.
Having thus internalized the object, the quality, and the cause, which is Sadāśiva,
one should strike [the breath] within the Śāntyatītā kalā that has been drawn in. (81)
Oṃ hauṃ, for the binding of the kalā of Śāntyatīta, huṃ phaṭ! Having grasped it with the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], he deposits it upon his own head.
One should offer three oblations for the purpose of bringing about proximity;
[these consist of] two principles, two syllables, and the pair of seed-syllables, channels, and birds.
The two qualities (guṇas), the two mantras, and likewise the Lord as the cause situated in the lotus—these are declared to be the twelve steps (padāni) and the seventeen worlds (bhuvanāni). || 84 ||
Likewise, having remembered a single object that is exceedingly supreme for tranquility in the middle of the *kṛṣṇā* [line], one should strike it as before. (85)
Having joined [the deity] with the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], one should fix it upon the *mukhīsūtra*.
With the seed-syllable *oṃ haiṃ haiṃ*, one should offer three oblations for the sake of invoking the presence (*sānnidhya*). (86)
The principles (tattvas) of the sevenfold knowledge are twenty-one;
there is one mantra of six syllables, and the twenty-fifth is a single [unit].
The three qualities and the single object are the cause therein;
having internalized them within the tongue that is intensely red, one should again proceed by way of the upward sequence.
In the seed-syllable, at the pair of channels and planets as before, Nandikeśvara— having taken [the thread], struck it, and purified it— should worship with Sthāṇu on the heart-thread.
Having uttered the mantra *hrūṃ hrūṃ*, one should offer three oblations for the purpose of invoking the presence (*sannidhāna*);
[these consist of] twenty-four principles (*tattva*) and twenty-five phonemes (*varṇa*).
The pair of seed-syllables, channels, and birds, thirty-two feet,
the four worlds, sixty, and the fourfold qualities. (91)
Having meditated upon the three mantras as a single object, the unshakable cause, and the middle foundation, beginning with the white, peaceful, and primordial [syllables]. 92.
One should perform the oblation for proximity as prescribed in the Ānābhi-sūtra; one should worship "hrīṃ loka" one hundred and eight times over twenty-one locations.
The seed-syllables, the channels, and the vital breaths; likewise for both types of sense organs, as well as their phonemes, principles (tattvas), and objects—these indeed [are to be known]. 94.
The fourfold mantra is proclaimed as being likewise in Nivṛtti;
one should imagine it in the center of the yellow-colored tongue and strike it. 95.
Having taken up the portion ending with the foot [of the mantra] and joined it to the thread, one should worship it;
for the purpose of bringing the Tantra into presence, one should offer three oblations.
Having thus taken up the *kalāsūtra*, one should join the bodies of the disciples;
however, in the case of a *sabīja* initiation, [one should release them] from the bond of the conduct of the *samaya*.
Furthermore, bondage is distinct from the merit that initiates the body, from the fruit of mantra-attainment, and even from the merit directed toward a desired object. (98)
The thread situated in the midst of the digits (kalās) is the earth-consciousness that is unobstructed;
by this very sequence, one should perform the satiation (tarpaṇa) and the kindling (dīpana). 99.
For the sake of satisfaction, there should be three oblations with each respective mantra;
likewise, for the purpose of kindling, one should offer oblations with the arrow-mantra (śarānu), ending with *huṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ śāntyatītakalāpāya svāhā. Thus, for each respective libation: pāśāya huṃ phaṭ. This is the triad of oblations. || 101 ||
For the sake of realizing pervasion (vyāpti), that thread [should be placed] in the five locations of the digits;
having cleansed it with saffron and clarified butter, one should worship Śiva along with his limbs there.

Having pierced the fetters in due order with the *kalā*-mantras ending in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, and having entered [the state] at the end with a salutation, "O Bond, become [the bond] of the planets! (103).
"Oṃ huṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ huṃ, I seize the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*);
I bind it," and so forth—with these mantras, the seizing and binding of the *kalās* are performed. (104)
One should contemplate, with respect to each flower, the uncoiling of the noose and other implements, their seizing, binding, and likewise the cessation of all activity. (105)

Having taught that thread, one should place it upon the shoulder of the disciple; then, for the destruction of [obstacles] such as the two-fold recitation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra. || 106 ||
The solar weapon (sūryāstra) should be placed around the edge of the vessel for the person; immediately after that, one should place the heart-weapon (hṛdayāstra) using the *saṃpuṭa* method. 107.
Having taken the *praṇava-arghya* from the sacrificial hall,
the preceptor should go outside and then construct three mandalas in sequence.
He should cause the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), the householders (bhautika), those with gentle faces, and those with faces like Indra’s—
to drink three handfuls of water in succession as his disciples under his control.
O Nandikeśvara, one should first perform the rite with the five products of the cow using the hand together with kuśa grass, and one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) at every interval.
In the second [case], the sacrificial pap (caruka) is prescribed, provided with three mouthfuls;
or it may measure eight mouthfuls, being devoid of sight and touch. (111)

With *palāśa* leaves, for the sake of liberation, upon the surface of the boat that carries worldly goals, the best of teachers should cause the disciple to partake of the total consumption [of the offering] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (112)
Afterwards, the ritual sipping (ācamana) should be performed again with pure water;
then, having offered a tooth-stick purified by the heart-mantra and cleansed by the eye-mantra.
One should subsequently purify it with water and cast the washed [substance] face upwards;
knowing that everything is purified without smoke, this is the supreme method of falling (pāta).
To prevent inauspiciousness, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *hetimantra*;
otherwise, for the sake of liberation from defects, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations.
O Nandikeśvara, for the sake of [their] satisfaction, one should perform all rites with devotion using the root mantra after offering them to the Lord of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍileśa). (116)
Upon the completion of that worship, one should also perform the worship of Caṇḍeśa;
having purified the remains of the offering (nirmālya), one should smear the ground with cow dung.
Having purified the ground with the root mantra, one should offer the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (caru) into the fire;
then, having worshipped the guardians of the quarters and the ritual jars, one should seal them.
That which constitutes the external protection should be released as the Gaṇapālakas;
one should offer the bali to the Lokapālas in brief, according to the proper sequence.
Having bathed either in the Āgneya or Vāruṇa [tirthas], one should enter the Gālaya;
there, one should place the lifelong practitioners (naiṣṭhikas) upon a bed of ashes, with their heads toward the south, starting from the heart.
(422) He placed all the elemental beings upon beds of *darbha* grass, previously protected by their original weapons, with their topknots tied up, and again guarded by Heti.
And there the Guru should impart the mantra for the Lord of Dreams:
*Oṃ hili hili śūlapāṇaye svāhā*; and that also [belongs to] the western [direction]. (122)
Oṃ hili hili pāṇaye svāhā | Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva! To Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul. || 123 ||
Salutation to Śambhu, the auspicious one, the Lord of the universe and of dreams;
Oṃ hili hili, salutation to the trident-bearer Nigini. || 124 ||
Having thus instructed the disciples in the mantra, the Guru should then have them lie down;
having gone outside and consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Just as he has seen the dream, the Guru should question the disciples thus:
[Did you see] a pleasure-house, a banner, an umbrella, an elephant, or a preeminent bull? (126)
Milk, meat, honey, as well as liquor, wine, and water; likewise, ascending onto a group [of people], and white garlands and ointments. || 127 ||
A brightly burning lamp and fire, Brahmā who has mastered the Vedas, a bride adorned with beautiful garlands, or even a courtesan possessing the auspicious marks of all her limbs.
Beholding one's parents, or the supreme sight of one's guru, and dreaming of ornaments such as gems, gold, and rings, are excellent dreams. (129)
Scorching by the orbs of the sun and other celestial bodies, falling into a blind well, anointing with oil, smearing with soot, and likewise the cutting off of limbs; || 130 ||
The sight of a widow, being veiled in new garments, and also a set of nine new earthen vessels, along with goats, buffaloes, and other such animals [are auspicious]. (131)
Also the crushing and the blackening, the appearance of the sun at midnight, the sight of serpents, and likewise such things as these which cause affliction. (132)
The sight of crows, vultures, donkeys, and the like brings inauspiciousness; however, an expiation must be performed according to the specific nature of each such vision.
Having performed the daily and occasional rites, he should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
having sipped water according to the rules, being pure, wearing a turban, and adorned with ornaments. (134)
The teacher should project the previously mentioned path to be purified onto himself,
and he should contemplate, O Nandikeśvara, the radiant Hand of Śiva.
Having visualized Śiva within the pitcher, endowed with all ornaments,
and having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the directions with a concentrated mind, (verse 136).
One should worship the imperishable Śiva either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or within a mandala;
thereafter, one should worship the fire until the mirror is reached as before.
Thereafter, for the pacification of bad dreams, one should offer oblations with the portion of the root mantra;
having offered the syllable *huṃ* enclosed within [the mantra], this is the "kindling" (*dīpana*) of the mantra. (138)
Between the pitcher and the mandala, the inner oblation (antarbali) is performed;
and having obtained permission for the entry of the disciples, one should go outside.

As before, at the edge of the mandala, one should then perform the oblation of the meeting-point (*saṃpātahoma*), which consists of the channels (*nāḍī*) and has the form of the limbs of the sacrificial victim (*arha*). 140.
One should offer three oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity;
then, having worshipped the Guru, who effects the severance of bonds, upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should know that there are one hundred and eight worlds; indeed, seven [of them] are as follows:
Kapāla, Jaladeha, Vajradeha, and Pramardana. (142)
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, Tridaśādhipa, Agnī, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, and Hari. || 143 ||

Jvalana (the Blazing One), Dahana (the Consumer), Babhru (the Tawny One), Bhasmānta (He whose end is ashes), Kṣayāntaka (the Destroyer of Destruction), Kālamṛtyuhara (the Remover of Death at its appointed time), Dhātā (the Sustainer), Vidhātā (the Ordainer), and he who is designated as the Kartṛ (the Doer). || 144 ||
He is Time, both Dharma and Adharma; the uniter and the disuniter;
the Lord of the South, the slayer, the killer, with a cruel gaze and terrifying appearance. (145)
Ūrdhvaśepha, Virūpākṣa, and Tralohitadantavān;
Mahābala and Mahābāhu—these ten are the venerated rākṣasas. (146)
Vala and Atibala, the mighty one with noose in hand, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka. || 147 ||
Baddhavāsya, Bhīma—these ten are impelled by Śani:
Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, Kṣayāntaka, [Kṣaya, Antaka,] and [the remaining two]. || 148 ||
He has five intestines, five tufts of hair, and matted locks; he is borne by clouds, is the Lord of Night, handsome, fortunate, gentle-bodied, and wears matted hair. || 149 ||
Lakṣmīdhara, Hara, Kāmī, Prasanna, and Prakāśita;
Vidyādhara, Jñānadhara, Sarvajña, and Vedapāraga. || 150 ||
Mātṛvṛtta, Piṅgākṣa, Bhūtabāla, Balipriya,
and Sarvavidyāvidhātā— these ten are the makers of happiness and suffering. (151)
Annabālaka, Dhīmān, Pātālā, as well as Vṛkṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Dhīra, Grasna, and Sarvatomukha. || 152 ||
Lohita and Phaṇīndra—these ten are resorted to by the Rudras;
they are the venerable lords, the chiefs of the Gaṇas, and are saluted by the thirty gods.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nāga, Lipsu, Vicakṣaṇa, Vīrabhadra, Kālāgnirudra, and Hāṭaka. (154)
Kūṣmāṇḍaka, Sāmya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Sītama, and Rudra—these they call the Rudras, who reside within the shell. || 155 ||
p.
429) These very names of the [eight] directions are the supreme among these worlds;
indeed, they stand forth in sequence as the twenty-eight steps of the Brahmin. (156)

Existence, the source of existence, the *haṃsa*, the bestower of happiness upon all beings, the maker of all things present, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—[He is] the inauspicious [destroyer]. (157)
O witness, witness who was present from before! O winged one, winged one!
O knowledge, knowledge! O sound, sound! O subtle, subtle Śiva, Śarva! 158.
Oṃ namaḥ śiva oṃ namaḥ śivāya namo namaḥ.
Thus, there are nineteen word-mantras (padamantra) beyond this. 159.
Immediately, the four eyes situated in the heart arise in succession;
the two syllables "ha" and "sa" are thus proclaimed. (160)
The two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, have been declared;
and the two winds, Prāṇa and Apāna, are likewise proclaimed in their respective order. (161)
The two sense organs are the nose and, following that, the generative organ; these are called the "fivefold group" (viṣṭi) and "fear. Thus, the five qualities are described. 162.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, in this order; thereafter, the earthly mandala is considered yellow and square. (163)
Marked by Indra, it is extensive and consists of one hundred crores;
within the Kalā-tattva there is cessation (nivṛtti), and there are also fourteen yonis.
Among animals, there are five types; among humans, one; and the state of divinity is eightfold.
There are also domestic animals, wild beasts, all kinds of winged creatures, and reptiles. (165)
Including the immobile, these five are wombs that have become like the sun;
one is human, while the other belongs to the divine womb—listen to that. (166)
The Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas, as well as those known as the Indras and the Brāhmyas—these are the eight sources of the deities. (167)
The earth-element is the locus for the eight [qualities], being the substratum of the letter 'a';
it is their foundation, and it is the cause for both experience and the intellect. || 168 ||
Brahmā, however, should remember the waking state as the pervasive cessation;
having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ," he should again withdraw the kalās.
One should utter the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and ending in *namaḥ*:
*oṃ hāṃ svāhāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ*. (170)
Having done this, one should then cast the noose into the center of the sacrificial pit [kuṇḍa],
reciting: *oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśāya namaḥ* || 171 ||

Having caused [the fire] to emerge by means of this very mantra and the *udbhava-mudrā*, one should establish it in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and offer the *arghya* with the word "namas" at the end [of the mantra]. (172)
Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *nivṛtti*-kalā.
With this very mantra, ending with *svāhā*, one should offer three oblations. (173)
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the kalā of nivṛtti. Likewise, one should perform the invocation of presence and the libation again with three [mantras]. || 174 ||
Then, having invoked Brahmā and Nivṛtti, one should worship them with:
"Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the Nivṛtti-kalā. (175)
For a Brāhmaṇa, the seating and the libation should be performed with the mantra alone;
furthermore, the recitation should be done with that same mantra ending in "svāhā. || 176 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā; O Brahmā, you have authority here.
Oṃ, Brahmā, by your authority, I initiate this seeker of liberation. || 177 ||
"You must act with favor; thus one should inform the officiant.
Then, one should invoke the goddess Vāgīśvarī, who is red in color. (178)
Endowed with a spirit of devotion, one should worship and satisfy the Goddess, who consists of will, knowledge, and action, and who unifies the sixfold path. 179.
Likewise, [one should worship] the god Vāgīśvara, who is skilled at agitating the womb, with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Self. (180)
Having struck the heart of the disciple especially with a flower,
[one perceives] his embodiment of consciousness, resembling quivering sparks of fire. (181)

Having placed [the deity] within the heart and established it in cessation (nivṛtti), one should sever the bonds with the Jyeṣṭhā [mudrā], using the mantra ending in "oṃ hāṃ hāṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ" and "oṃ svāhā. || 182 ||
Having drawn [the deity] forth with the *pūraṇa* hook and the *mudrā*, while endowed with meditative visualization, one should grasp it with the *ātman-mantra* and clearly unite it with oneself. 183.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self.
One should contemplate the union of Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī. 184.

One should make consciousness endowed with the state of being by means of the absolute alone, having led it through the sequential abandonment of the causal principles beginning with Brahmā to the abode of Śiva. (185)
Having taken her for the purpose of conception simultaneously into all wombs, [he entered] the noble limbs of Vāgīśvarī, who possesses the nature of all wombs. (186)
First, Vāgīśī [places] that element joined with her essence within the navel-cord;
afterwards, it enters the womb of Vāgīśvarī through the left side, known as *bhava*.
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon that which is projected by the mudrā and the vehicle;
endowed with devotion, one should worship with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self. || 188 ||
With this very mantra, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed five times;
for the sake of purification from all wombs, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the heart-mantra.
While he is departing for the sake of protecting the fetus and so forth, as well as for the *puṃsavana* rite,
one should then perform the *añjana* (anointing) upon his head simultaneously with [the other rites].
One should specifically perform the rite of empowerment with the *śikhā* mantra;
likewise, one should protect all parts with the *varman* mantra, as well as the sense objects and the self with the [root] mantra. (191)
One should contemplate non-duality, which is of the nature of delusion, and dissolution therein;
with the root mantra, one should offer five oblations for each of the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna). || 192 ||

One should offer one hundred oblations with the Heart mantra using the "half-pentad nose" (ardhapañcakanāsā) for the purpose of severing the bonds and for the obscuration of the power of impurity (malaśakti). || 193 ||
One should offer five oblations each with the Astra-mantra ending in *svāhā*;
likewise, one should recite the Astra-mantra seven times over the fetter (*pāśa*) situated within the beginning and end of the impurities (*mala*).
One should perform the severing of what is to be done according to the Kalā-śāstra, as follows: "Oṃ hūṃ, to the noose of the kalā of Nivṛtti, hūṃ phaṭ! Na! (195)
Having cut the Vimalavat-sūtra and coiled it into a circle, the true Guru,
having placed it in a ladle filled with clarified butter, should offer it into the fire.
Having reduced [the bonds] to ashes with the *kalāstra* mantra, one should offer five oblations in sequence for the purpose of removing the nooses and the goad: "Oṃ aṃ astrāya phaṭ. (197)

Oṃ aṃ astrāya phaṭ. With this weapon-mantra (astra), one should offer an oblation as an expiation. Therein, having invoked Brahmā, one should worship him and likewise satisfy him with libations. || 198 ||
Having first uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ" and likewise "Śabdabrahman," one should offer three oblations, saying, "O Brahman, accept the parrot. (199)
Oṃ hāṃ, accept sound and touch, O white Brahmā, svāhā!
Having gratified [the deity] with this mantra, one should especially offer a prayer.
(438) "I must once again effect the reconnection of Daṇḍin, the Brāhmaṇa who remains bound by the noose, so that the command of Śiva may be fulfilled. || 201 ||
Having released Brahmā there, [he should do so] slowly through the right channel by means of breath retention (kumbhaka),
his own mantra, and the withdrawal mudrā.
And especially one's own self, O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon it as being like a portion of Rāhu released from an eclipse, by means of the five-limbed bindu-bimba.
Having taken [the water], one should join it with the thread for the sake of emergence through the *recaka* breath;
having meditated upon the water in the *arghya* vessel as consisting of nectar and being incomparable. (204)
Having worshipped correctly with drops, one should cast [them] upon the head of the disciple;
then, having dismissed those two parents, one should do so with the weapon-mantra (śarāṇu) ending in vauṣaṭ.
Then, for the sake of completing the ritual injunctions, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation);
for this is the purification of *nivṛtti*, after which one should commence *pratiṣṭhā* in due order. (206)
The union of the two principles, characterized by purity and impurity, occurs through barley-grains;
and by the application of short and long [vowels], one attains the conjunction (*saṃhitā*) of the eater and the eaten. (207)
Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hrīṃ! Water, fire, air, ether, the elements, the senses, and the intellect; the three qualities and the ego—these constitute the twenty-four principles. 208.
For one established in the foundation, one should indeed contemplate these principles (tattvas), which consist of exactly twenty-five syllables ending with the letter *kha*. (209)
And fifty-six worlds, along with as many Rudras;
likewise Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara.
Āṣāḍha, likewise Daṇḍin, Bhārabhūti as the eighth,
Lakulīśa, Hariścandra, and Śrīśaila shall be the tenth. (211)
Alpīyo'mṛtakeśa is for Mahākāla as the middle [category];
Kedāra and Bhairava are the second [category]... [omitted].
Then Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhala, and likewise Nakhalam; Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and the one known as Bhīma. (213)
Vaiśrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu; || 214 ||
Artha, Sarvajña, Bhāsura immediately after him, Subāhu in the form of mantra, Viśāla, and likewise Jaṭila. || 215 ||
Then there shall be Raudra, Piṅgalākṣa, and Kāladaṃṣṭrin;
likewise Bindura, Ghora, Prājāpatya, and Hutāśana. || 216 ||
Kāmarūpī, as well as Kālakaṇṭha, Bhayānaka, Pataṅga, Piṅgala, Hara, and the one named Vidhātṛ; || 217 ||
Then, for the sake of liberation from worldly existence, one should invoke and worship Śaṅkukarṇa, Bhavānīśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha together with Candramauli.

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā"—thus the words ending with that have been declared in sequence; now hear the [subsequent] words: "Pervasive, O pervasive one! Form and formless! First, O first! Splendor, O splendor! (219)
O Light of lights, you who are formless, without fire, without smoke, without ashes, and without beginning;
Nā Nā Nā Nā Dhū Dhū Dhū Dhū Oṃ Bhūḥ Oṃ Bhuvaḥ Oṃ Suvaḥ. || 220 ||
O you who are without end, yet the source of the end; O Śiva, Supreme Self, Supreme Lord of Lords;
O Mahādeva, Lord of True Being; O Mahātejas, Sovereign of Yoga! || 221 ||
"Muñca muñca prathama prathama śarva śarva"—these are the thirty-two words. The seed-syllable is "reca," and this mantra belongs to Vāmadeva; it is the Śiva-śikhā-nāḍī. || 222 ||
When the tongue is joined with the wind within the channel of the Suṣumnā, which is equal to the concentration of the elephant, then that becomes the sense organ. || 223 ||
Taste is its object; color, touch, sound, and taste are its qualities.
Its mandala is like a half-moon joined with a lotus, and it belongs to Varuṇa.
Viṣṇu is said to be the cause when established in the state of dream;
one should meditate upon the entire world as named Bhuvana, situated within the Bhuvā. || 225 ||
Having entered by means of his own mantra, he should separate [the soul] from the body using the thread;
having uttered "Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ," he should likewise perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and the recitation of the narrative (kathā). || 226 ||
This mantra, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, is uttered for the *pāśa* [of the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā]:
*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ pratiṣṭhākalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ*. (227)

With this very [mantra] ending in *svāhā*, by means of the completion [of the ritual], and with the mudrā called the Hook (*aṅkuśa*), one should likewise attract [the deity] using [the mantra] joined with the seed-syllable and ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ hrūṃ hrāṃ, [to] the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* aspect, huṃ phaṭ! O Nandikeśvara, having taken that thread from those two as before, [recite]:
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* aspect. || 230 ||
Having grasped [the breath] with this very mantra by means of the *bhāvamudrā*,
one should specifically perform the *recaka* (exhalation) and likewise cause the *kuṃbhaka* (retention) to take place.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.
Having caused [the disciple] to inhale with this very mantra, one should visualize [him]. || 232 ||
With exactly three oblations ending in "svāhā," the Guru should effect the visualization;
he should likewise perform the oblation for the presence (sannidhāna) as before.
The heart-mantra ending with "namaḥ" should be for Viṣṇu in the center:
*oṃ hrāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having invoked and worshipped Viṣṇu with this very mantra... [234]
"Oṃ Viṣṇu! In this office of yours, I initiate this seeker of liberation;
you must be favorable. Thus one should inform Viṣṇu. (235)
Having invoked and worshipped Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśa, one should perform the ritual worship;
then, with a flower held in the right hand, one should strike the disciple on the chest. (236)
Having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ," joined with the sixteen vowels of the sky,
and having uttered [the mantra] ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one should enter preceded by the mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ!
With this very mantra, the Guru should divide the self;
[he should sever] that which is bound by the fetters with the weapon [mantra] and the Jyeṣṭhā-aṅkuśa mudrā. || 238 ||
Especially with the mantra beginning with *tārā* and ending in *huṃ phaṭ*—
namely, *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ*— and with the previously mentioned mantra ending clearly in *svāhā*.
Having drawn [the soul] into oneself and joined it, one should say "Obeisance to the non-dual self," and:
"Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the self. Then, having extracted the union of the parents by means of this *udbhava* mudrā: || 240 ||
p.
446) One should direct it by means of the *iḍā* right into the womb of the Goddess at its tip;
likewise for the arising of the limbs, and likewise for birth by means of the five-headed [breath]. || 241 ||

For the sake of authority and yoga, [the teacher performs] with the *śikhā* and *kavaca* mantras; with the weapon-mantra against the noose of saṃsāra, and with the *śiva* mantra for the disciples' stream [of initiation].
Having summoned him there, one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* as before in that pure place;
immediately thereafter, the severing of the bonds (*pāśaviśleṣaṇa*) should also be performed by means of the *śiras* mantra.
O Nandikeśvara, for the sake of expiation,
one should offer oblations a hundred times after having divided [the object] into five parts with a weapon that obscures the power of impurity.
One should especially offer five oblations for the severing of bonds;
having empowered [the weapon] seven times with the Astra-mantra, one should then cut [the bonds] with the Astra-mantra.
Having uttered [the mantra] preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and joined with the seed-syllable of the *kalā*,
one should again utter *haḥ* for the sake of the bond (*pāśa*) of the *kalā* and for its stabilization (*pratiṣṭhā*). || 246 ||
Endowed with the proper disposition, one should perform [the rite] with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*:
*oṃ hāṃ pratiṣṭhākalāya pāśāya haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. (247)
Having wiped it clean and made it circular with the weapon-mantra as before, and having offered clarified butter as before, the oblation shall be performed with the *kalāstra* mantra. (248)
Then, for the sake of averting the noose and the goad, one should offer oblations with the five-weapon mantra;
one should also offer eight oblations for the sake of averting the need for expiation.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ.
Having invoked Viṣṇu and worshipped him, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
O Nandikeśvara, everything such as the qualification (adhikāra) and so forth is to be done exactly as described for all [other deities]. 250.
Oṃ hāṃ Viṣṇo, [accept] the essence and the semen immediately thereafter;
having uttered the mantra ending with svāhā, it shall then be thus. (251)
Oṃ hāṃ, O Viṣṇu, accept the innumerable [offerings], svāhā!
O Hari, for that bound soul (paśu) whose fetters have been entirely consumed by you— || 252 ||
"One should not remain as a hostage; rather, one should cause the command of Śiva to be heard.
Then, having dismissed Viṣṇu, one should purify the self of Rudra.
Then, having made it abide within oneself by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, like the half-disk of the moon released from Rāhu, one should [emerge] by means of the *udbhavamudrā*.

Having joined [the threads] and placed them upon the cord, when one has previously offered a drop of water and dismissed the two ancestors, one should worship [the fire] with flowers and other offerings. || 255 ||
One should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of stabilization and purification,
together with the previously mentioned *kalā*, for the purpose of accomplishing the reconnection of the *vidyā*. (256)
O Nandikeśvara, all [the rites] beginning with the *tattvaparṇa* are as before;
[one should perform them] with the mantra *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hāṃ* during the *sandhāna*, and [establish] passion (*rāga*) by means of *śuddhavidyā*. (257)
Niyati, Kalā, Kīla, Māyā, and Śuddhavidyā—these shall be the seven principles (tattvas) in their respective order. || 258 ||
The letters ra, la, pa, śa, ṣa, and sa are declared to be the sixfold vidyā;
it is proclaimed to consist of twenty-one words, beginning with Tārā, O Nandikeśvara. (259)
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the source of Śarva, to Śiva; to the one whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, and whose heart is Aghora. || 260 ||
Salutations again and again to Vāmadeva, the secret one, whose form is Sadyojāta;
to the protector of that which is more secret than the secret, who is imperishable and the foremost of all yogas. (261)
O Omniscient One, Lord of all sciences, whose form is light, Supreme Lord!
O Supreme Lord, conscious and unconscious, sky and non-sky, [the Lord] of the Rudras. 262.
Now the essential nature of the worlds is described:
first, there is Vāmadeva, from whom all those various existences arise. (263)
The Lord Vajradeha is the Sustainer, possessing the radiant splendor of sequential strides;
he is named Ardha, the Tranquil One, and is designated as the Supreme Immutable (Paramākṣara). || 264 ||
And Diva, Sudiva, Babhru, Akṣaya, Śambhu, Adṛṣṭarūpadhāraṇa, and likewise Rūpavivardhana; || 265 ||
Homage, homage! Mahāvīrya and Citrāṅga immediately after him;
these should be known as Kalyāṇas, numbering twenty-five. (266)
The mantra, Ghorāhara, the two channels, and likewise those two [elements]; the worship, Hastijihvā, Vyāna, the two Nāgas, and the two Maruts. (267)
Form is thus the object, as are the feet, the eyes, and the sense organ;
sound, touch, and form—these alone are remembered as the three qualities. || 268 ||
Or the state may be deep sleep (suṣupti), and the deity Rudra is the cause;
one should then contemplate the world and so forth when [the breath] has reached the top of Vidyā. || 269 ||
There, by means of the vidyā, there shall be beating, piercing, entry, and binding; indeed, the drawing forth of the grahas occurs at the region of the heart. || 270 ||
Having ascended [the fire] and gathered it within himself, he should employ it in the *kalā-kuṇḍa*.
Having invoked Rudra, the cause, and having informed the disciple who is endowed with devotion, [he should proceed]. (271)
One should perform the sowing [of the seed] upon the heart of the parents and strike the disciple's chest;
one should then separate the consciousness from it there by means of the mantra, as before. || 272 ||
Having drawn [the breath] according to the previously stated method and having taken it, one should unite it with the self;
one should join it with Bharga through the *iḍā* channel, having grasped it in twelve parts.
Then one should perform the arising of the body, as well as the presiding over the birth, enjoyment, cessation, the stream, and the purification of the principles (tattvas). || 274 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should worship and satisfy [the deity] there for the sake of liberation and expiation from impure actions and the like, indeed with a hundred oblations.
O Nandikeśvara, the severing of the bonds is also performed by Heti;
likewise, it occurs during the concealment of the Root Power (mūlaśakti), as well as its cutting and crushing. (276)
Likewise, for the purpose of avoiding the need for expiation in cases of rounding [the body], burning, or the loss of a finger, there is the invocation of Rudra.
Then he should perform all that worship as before;
he should assign the form, the knot, and the ankle to Rudra. (278)
Oṃ hāṃ! O Rudra, accept the white form and fragrance; svāhā!
Having proclaimed the command of Śiva and having dismissed Rudra, the causal agent, [he proceeds]. || 279 ||
Likewise, I initiate Rudra, who desires liberation, into this office;
you must act with favor, and your request shall be made with devotion. (280)
"One should not remain for the sake of bondage; rather, one should contemplate the command of Śiva. Having established the Self within the self, one should then apply the fetter there. (281)
Having placed the half-moon on his head, he should then dismiss the two parents;
and having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) especially according to the prescribed rule.
And the wise one should perform all acts, such as striking and so forth, according to the prescribed rule;
for this is indeed the seed-syllable of the Vidyās, especially by means of the letter *ra*.
Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hāṃ, for the noose of the power of knowledge, huṃ phaṭ!
By this very mantra, the purification of the speech of knowledge [is performed]. (284)
Having joined the Knowledge-mantra (vidyā) with the Peace-mantra (śānti), one should cause the rite to increase;
then, one should contemplate these two as gradually dissolving into the Peace-mantra.
One should meditate there upon both Īśvara and the one called Sādhā;
their wings and colors are declared to be those of Bhuvanādhipa and Rudra.
They were renowned by their own names and possessed the aforementioned numbers:
Prabhava, Kṣamaya, Kṣudra, Vimala, and Śiva. (287)
Ghana, Nirañjana, Oṃkāra, Suśiva, Dīptā, Kāraṇa, and also Tridaśeśvara. (288)
Tridaśa, Kāla, Sūkṣma, Ambuja, Īśvara, and these eighteen Rudras are the lords of the world of Śānti. || 289 ||
And these are declared to be, in order, the lords of the worlds;
furthermore, in the case of the specific words, it should then begin with the Praṇava (Om).
Oṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, whose form is the sky, who pervades all;
to Śiva, the infinite, the protectorless, and the non-dependent. || 291 ||
To the eternal and everlasting one, established upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), the perpetual yogi whose sustenance is meditation... || 292 ||
When it has been spoken thus, there is then pervasion beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava).
The two mantras for the armor (kavaca) are [the seed-syllables] consisting of the nasal drop (bindu) and the letter ya.
The two channels Pūṣyā and Yaśasvinī are likewise pure; immediately following are the two winds, Kūrma and Kṛkara, as well as Tvarāga and Indriya. (294)
The contact with sense objects would thus be the prevention of contact with the qualities;
the Lord, however, is said to be the hand, while the fourth is below.
Having meditated upon all things, beginning with the worlds, as situated within tranquility, one should perform the striking, piercing, entering, and joining, just as before. (296)
The drawing forth and the grasping [of the deity] are performed according to the manual for pacification;
having planted it within oneself and grasped it, one should employ the *kalā* in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
"O Lord, I initiate you, who desire liberation, into this office.
You must be favorable toward my request and so forth. (298)
The father should perform the invocation and the striking of the disciple, and he himself should properly unite his own self within his very self according to the prescribed rule. (299)
The oblation is performed with the heart; it serves for the generation of the body. The head serves for the sake of the five people, and the tuft (śikhā) constitutes the authority. || 300 ||
Enrichment occurs through the armor-mantra alone, and withdrawal through the weapon-mantra;
