for the accomplishment of the streams [of the channels], it should be performed with the root-mantra, and for their perfection, with the heart-mantra of the principles (tattva). || 301 ||
O Nandikeśvara, all the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) should be performed as before;
furthermore, the severing of the fetters (pāśaviśleṣaṇa) should then be accomplished by means of the armor-mantra (tanutra).
Having performed the expiation by offering a hundred oblations for the suppression of the power of impurity (mala-śakti),
one should likewise offer five oblations with the *hetimantra* for the purpose of severing the bonds (*pāśa*).
Having recited the Astra-mantra in every way, one should cut [the thread] with the Kartari-weapon;
likewise, within the interval of the Śānti-kalā, one should enclose it with the Bīja-mantra.
The mantra is proclaimed in sequence, ending with *huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ* for the noose:
*hauṃ hauṃ śāntikalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ*. || 305 ||
Having rolled everything together into a ball with the *pāśāstra* as before,
and having placed it in a *sruva* ladle filled with clarified butter, an oblation (*huta*) should be performed with the *kalāstra*. (306)
To eliminate the nooses and hooks, one should offer oblations five times with the weapon-mantra;
furthermore, one should offer eight oblations for the sake of averting the need for expiation.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ!
Having invoked the Lord into the heart, there should be worship and libation;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the white rite for him according to the prescribed rule. (308)
Oṃ hāṃ! O Īśvara, understand this; with two *huṃ*s, take [this] white [substance], svāhā!
O Īśvara, by you, the bonds of this child have been completely burnt away without remainder. (309)
For the purpose of leading [the soul], one should perform the rite and cause the command of Śiva to be heard;
there, one should dismiss the Lord and enjoin the self of Rudra.
Then, like the lunar orb swallowed by Rāhu at its fifty-fold [fullness],
one should conceive of the disciple within oneself and unite him with that according to the ritual rule. (311)
One should unite the disciple with the state; one should unite him with the Bhava-mudrā.
With the root mantra, one should place a drop of nectar upon the head of the disciple.

O Nandikeśvara, having dismissed the parents of the fire after they have been well-honored with flowers and other offerings, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rite.
Even in the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the procedure for the *vidyā* and so forth is as before;
the only distinction would be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) for the sake of purifying the *kalās*.
For the purification of the junction between Śāntyā and Śāntyatītā,
one should perform there, as before, the sequence beginning with the colors and so forth.
Having uttered *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*, this occurs during the conjunction (*sandhāna*).
When the principles (*tattva*) of Śakti and Śiva are mentioned, the eight worlds (*bhuvana*) are said to be proclaimed. (316)
Dīpika, Raucika, Mocaka, and Aurdhvagāmika;
Vyomarūpa, Anādi, and likewise Anāśrita as the eighth.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, [Śānti], and Śāntyatītā in the heart; together with Ilīkā and Rodhikā, these seven are remembered as the fifteen. (318)

The syllable *tāra* (om) and likewise the two *aiśāna* [mantras] constitute the mantra; the letters are sixteen, beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*, together with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the *nāda* and *hakāra*.
Kūhū is at the end of the nāḍī, and immediately after that is Śaṅkhinī;
likewise, Devadatta and Āñjana are further below in eightfold [succession]. 320.

(462) Even in the case of the sense-faculties—the tactile organ, the ear, and so forth—it would be by means of their objects alone; furthermore, sound as a quality would transcend [the senses], and there would be a fourth [element] and so on. || 321 ||
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva as the cause— the pentad beginning with Tattva—
situated within the Śāntyatīta-kalā, one should perform the striking and other rites.
Having struck with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and having pierced the noose of the *kalā*,
one should enter [the disciple] with the mantra ending in *namaḥ* and join him here with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having formed the *śikhā* and *hṛdaya* mantras in a joined (*saṃpuṭa*) manner, ending with *svāhā*, one should draw forth the consciousness by means of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā and inhalation (*pūraka*), and then distribute it.
One should request that [the mantra], joined with the weapon (astra) and the noose (pāśa), with devotion;
then perform the worship, the invocation (āvāhana), the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors, and the presence (sannidhi). || 325 ||
One should strike the chest of the child with the seed-syllable of the Self enclosed within the heart-mantra:
*oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ*. Then, by means of this very mantra, one should separate the consciousness.
With the Astra-mantra joined with the Pāśa, and with the Jyeṣṭhā-mantra accompanied by the Sṛṇi-mudrā—

[reciting] "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ"— one should, with a focused mind, perform the visualization of drawing [the deity] forth using the Svāhā-mantra encapsulated within the heart-seed syllable (hṛdbīja). || 327 ||
Having taken that [offering] with the word "namaḥ" at its end, one should apply it to one's own self:
*oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ ātmane namaḥ*. By means of the *udbhava-mudrā*, the union of the parents should be manifested. || 328 ||
One should unite [the breath] with the womb of the Goddess by means of exhalation through the iḍā;
by the previously mentioned procedure, the entire sequence beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) shall take place.
O Nandikeśvara, immediately thereafter, for the purpose of severing the bonds and for expiation, one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra.

p. 464) For the concealment of the power of impurity (mala-śakti) and likewise for the severance of the bonds (pāśa), one should offer five oblations for each [of these], with the mantra as before. || 331 ||
Immediately after reciting the mantra seven times according to the scripture, one should sever the bond with:
*oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ* (332).

Having reflected and rolled [the thread] into a circle, one should worship it as before with the *pāśa* weapon-mantra; then, having meditated on the full [thread], one should perform the oblation with the *kalā* weapon-mantra.
One should offer five oblations for the purpose of nullifying the noose and the goad;
and one should offer eight oblations for the cessation of transgressions.
One should always perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for this deity in the heart as before,
and furthermore, one should exercise authority according to the previously stated rule.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva; O Bindu, white one, accept [this offering], svāhā!
For Śiva, whose bonds have been entirely consumed, there is always Sadāśiva. (336)
"You must not remain for the sake of bondage; rather, you should cause [the disciple] to hear the command of Śiva.
Having said this, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and dismiss Sadāśiva with the root mantra.
Then, having offered himself as an oblation, he should unite the Guru within himself by means of the Raudrī-saṃhāra-mudrā, appearing like the autumn moon.

One should place [the deity] residing within the body of Śiva by lifting it up with the *udbhava-mudrā*; then, with the head and neck straightened, one should perform the utterance of the *nāda*. 339.
One should offer water for the sipping and other rites, beginning with a drop of water from the head;
having worshipped the two parents with devotion, one should dismiss them immediately thereafter.
"O my two parents, since you were interrupted by me during the initiation of a disciple,
please forgive me out of compassion and go to your own abode. (341)
With a pair of scissors consecrated by the *śikhā-mantra*, which is the very embodiment of the *rodha-mantra*,
he should cut four finger-breadths of the disciple's topknot using the *śiva-astra* mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ, for the crest [of the deity], hūṃ phaṭ.
The washing of the sacrificial ladle and spoon, the bathing of the disciple, and the sipping of water (ācamana) are performed by the Guru. || 343 ||
There, endowed with devotion born of inner feeling, one should perform the rite especially;
having struck [the object] with the Astra-mantra, one should instill consciousness.
O Nandikeśvara, having distinguished, drawn forth, and gathered [the breath] as before from the dvādaśānta, one should join it to the lotus of one's own heart.
O Nandikeśvara, having specifically joined [the ladle] to the lotus of the heart,
one should fill the *sruva* with clarified butter and offer the *sruva* in sequence ten times. (346)
Having performed [the rite] according to the path prescribed for daily practice with the mudrā resembling a conch shell,
one should extend the head and neck while accompanied by the utterance of the *nāda*.
The gaze fixed in meditation, the head tranquil, and again endowed with the primordial state (purābhāva);
from the mandala, the jar, and the fire, the head [emerges] from that very source, undisturbed.
Having brought the sixfold vehicle, the sacrificial ladle here is the life-channel;
having known the destruction of the moon and sun, that then occurs at the equinox.
Having meditated upon that which is endowed with seven divisions, one should gradually utter the Nāda;
first is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), then the contemplation of its true nature.

That which is uttered through the unstruck sequence (*anāhata-krama*) is the distinguished one known as mantra; it is the resonance (*nāda*) situated within the interior of the *brahman-āḍī*, and it is the fourth state (*turīya*). (351)
And by the abandonment of the causal factors, the seventh equinox occurs;
at that moment, one should attain peace and desire dissolution.
Having reached the family of Suṣumnā, one should proceed upward even within the sound (nāda);
that movement is attained through instruction regarding the sphere of Śakti. || 353 ||

The seat (āsana) of the universal vital breath (sarvaprāṇa), which extends to the limit of power and is devoid of mental constructs (māna), is the sixth equinox (viṣuva); likewise, the seventh is that which has transcended [it]. || 354 ||
One should separate [the breath] from that [state] during the equinox (viṣuva) within the perception of reality;
having meditated upon inhalation and retention, one should indeed take hold of the mouth with care.
One should gradually extract the root and quickly train in the dissolution of the mind; liberation arises from the dissolution of the mind—this is the certainty of the scripture. (356)
In this awakening of the living being within the six paths, within the syllable *ha* which blazes like lightning,
one should extend it from the navel for a span’s length, with the *ha* situated all around.
Above that, the letter *ma* is the heart, measuring four finger-breadths;
then, extending eight finger-breadths to the end of the ears, the letter *u* is said to be Viṣṇu.
One should contemplate the syllable *mukāra*, whose deity is Rudra, extending from the tip of the tongue to four finger-breadths;
and one should contemplate the *sādākhya* [syllable], which is in the form of sound (*nāda*), extending to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). || 359 ||
One should gradually release the Śakti situated in the center of that Brahma-randhra;
in that moment, a divine sensation like the touch of an ant arises therein.
Having experienced all that in an instant at the *dvādaśānta*,
one [reaches] that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), stainless, pure, and free from both the signified and the signifier. (361)
One should contemplate that which consists of eternal bliss, which is subtle, devoid of existence and non-existence, the absolute oneness, a mass of consciousness, peaceful, and auspicious. || 362 ||
One should visualize the disciple’s self dissolving right there;
one should also offer a stream of clarified butter into the supreme Śiva, even at the edge of the flame.
Then, for the sake of stabilizing the state of union (sāyujya), one should offer oblations with the root mantra;
having uttered it ending with "vauṣaṭ," one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rule.

"Hauṃ Vauṣaṭ. The mantra for the feet of the qualities (guṇapāda), joined with the letter *tā* and the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), ending in "svāhā," should be: "Become omniscient like the Self. || 365 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, may the self become omniscient; svāhā!
Oṃ hauṃ, may the self become one whose power is never lost; svāhā! || 366 ||
Oṃ haḥ! O Self, arise from infinite power, svāhā!
Having thus grasped the Self endowed with six qualities from the supreme syllable (paramākṣara), [one should proceed]. || 367 ||

Endowed with the nature of the ritual procedure, one should join [the mantra] within the body of the disciple for the sake of pacifying the exhaustion produced by the descent of the intense power (tīvra-śakti).
The Guru should sprinkle drops of the nectar-like water from the *arghya* vessel upon the head of the disciple,
and he should then consecrate all the vessels, beginning with the *śivakumbha*, in their proper sequence.
Having placed that [maṇḍala] upon the maṇḍala on the right side of the Lord (Īśvara),
one should visualize it facing north upon his head, while the other is on the south.
And this [disciple] has been favored by you; having assumed a physical form, you shall be his preceptor before the divine Fire. Increase the devotion of the Lord. (371)
Having thus informed the deity and having himself prostrated, the Guru should respectfully invoke the auspiciousness of Śiva, saying, "May you be invited to the highest welfare."
Endowed with devotion, one should offer black flowers to the God and consecrate him with the waters from the Īśī-kumbha and other jars.
One should also withdraw the worship performed in the mandalas and other such rites into that very [reality];
and all initiation as well as knowledge arises through the grace of Śarva.
Therefore, with every effort, service to the Guru is supreme;
furthermore, that service should be performed continuously and with devotion. (375)
Thereafter, there should be the receiving of the Guru’s grace and supreme service;
the disciple, illuminated by the lamp of Nirvāṇa, becomes fit for union with the Guru. (376)
He possesses the qualification for the worship of the Linga for the sake of others; furthermore, no impurity arising from death or birth exists for him. (377)
For one who is material, purification is especially granted by mere bathing.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Ritual for the Initiation into the Extinction of Karma, within the Acintyaviśvasādākhya [Tantra].
In the prescription for atonement, however, re-initiation is ordained;
for that reason, one who is devoid of the previously mentioned qualities [is also eligible]. (1)
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing those qualities, one should perform the reverent worship of the Three Principles (tritatva).
For the sake of success in such matters as these, one should initiate [the disciple] according to the sequence of the Three Principles.
(474) O Nandikeśvara, listen now to the initiation by action (*karmadīkṣā*) concerning the three principles (*tritatva*).
One should perform everything, beginning with the worship of the *liṅga*, as previously described, starting from the front.
Then, having worshipped Śiva everywhere— in the mandala, in the water-jar, in one's own internal fire, and in the disciple— according to the previously stated procedure.
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) and other rites in their proper sequence, beginning with primordial ignorance (ādyavidyā) and ending with action (kriyā);
furthermore, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the mouth of Agni and the kindling (dīpana) of the mantras.
One should perform the ritual as before, followed by the suspension of the thread;
having worshipped the Śakti on the head of the disciple, one should take it up with the mudrā.
One should join [the mantra] "I bow to Śakti" to that thread in sequence; having concealed it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should perform the libation and other rites as before.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) as before;
then, one should sprinkle the disciple’s head with the water from the general arghya vessel.
Then, having struck the disciple’s heart with a flower according to the rite,
and having entered by means of the mantra, the loosening of the bonds occurs.
One should perform the attraction according to the prescribed rite and join the Śakti with the thread;
having first uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ," one should say "Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Self. (10)
Thereafter, one should perform the arrangement of the forms and worship them in the sequence beginning with invocation;
having performed the libation for the mantras, one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva.

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva. Having struck [the thread] with the mantra ending in *haṃ phaṭ*, and having encased it with the *śikhā* mantra, one should place it upon the head-thread with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*. || 12 ||
Oṃ hāṃ ātmane huṃ phaṇnamaḥ.
Having worshipped the Śiva-tattva, one should encircle it with the armor-mantra (varman).
Having performed the satiation of the mantras, one should contemplate the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).

Having struck [the thread] with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*— namely, *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ huṃ phaṭ*— and having encased it with the *śikhā* mantra, one should place it upon the head-thread (*śiras-sūtra*) with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*. || 14 ||
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the self, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having worshipped the Śiva-tattva, one should encircle it with the armor-mantra (varma).
The libation and the worship should also be performed according to the previously prescribed rite. (15)
The Guru should then draw the Vidyā-tattva in the center and worship it with:
*oṃ hrīṃ vidyātatvāya namaḥ*.
Then one should perform the worship with flower-strikes and other rites as previously described. || 16 ||
One should contemplate the reality of the self; having uttered the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ" joined with the reality of the self and ending with "namaḥ," the Guru should perform worship as before. || 17 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
One should perform everything, beginning with the striking [of the bell], according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Furthermore, for the satisfaction of the mantras, one should offer three oblations (āhuti).
One should illuminate the bonds beginning with the Śiva-tattva, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*;
then, between the Anāhata and Ājñā wheels, one should apply a thread with saffron water.
Thereafter, one should cause the illumination; this shall be the sequence for the mantras.
For the Śiva-tattva, "huṃ phaṭ" shall be the illumination. (p. 478) || 20 ||
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, for the principle of Śiva, hūṃ phaṭ!
In that sūtra, however, having worshipped Śiva, immediately thereafter follows the severing of the bonds;
the seizing and binding of those [bonds] is performed with the seed-syllable encapsulated by the heart-mantra. (21)
One should then place that thread upon the left shoulder of the disciple;
subsequently, one should perform the oblation with the six limbs and complete the rite with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) using the root mantra.
One should place the *saṃpāta*— the honored thread together with the mantras—
within a casket made of two noble vessels near the *śivakumbha*, for the sake of protection.
As before, on the fifth day, one should likewise place the portion of the sacrificial pap (caru),
as well as the offering (bali) and the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha), at night, according to the previous procedure.
The teacher, having consumed the sacrificial porridge (caruka), performs the offering as before;
this they call "consecration" (adhivāsana), and he should likewise recollect the rite of initiation (dīkṣā). || 25 ||
Having slept during the Brāhma-muhūrta, he should perform the two-fold rite;
then, having led the disciple to the side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should proceed in due order.

Having performed the joining of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna), he should then tie the thread of continuity (santāna-sūtraka) upon the crest-lock (śikhā) of the disciple, so that it hangs down from the head.
Having seated [the disciple] upon the seat, one should contemplate the reality of the Self (ātmatattva);
and one should contemplate that which is encompassed by the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) by means of the pervasive [mantra]. || 28 ||
One should perform the striking as before, pervading from the heart to the end of the disciple;
having seized the consciousness of the disciple, one should cast it into the midst of the fire.
(480) All the offerings for libation up to the end of the worship should be performed as before with the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, having invoked Brahmā, one should worship him and cause [him] to hear [the scripture]. || 30 ||
Having struck the disciple on the chest with a flower as before,
he who possesses the wind of the true path should cause [the deity] to enter his own self.
Furthermore, one should gradually unite the consciousness of the disciple within oneself,
beginning from the edge of the Guru-maṇḍala and employing the Udbhava-mudrā.
O Nandikeśvara, having performed worship and libation according to the rules of consecration, one should join [the breath] into the central channel within the womb of Vāgīśī.
For the destruction of birth and enjoyment, for the purification of the streams [of the senses],
and for the expiation of mantras, māyā, and so forth, one should worship Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas).

Then, for the sake of severing the bond of concealment consisting of impurity and karma, one should subsequently perform oblations with the Astra-mantra; thereafter, [one should act] with the Astra-mantra recited seven times. (35)
Then, having determined the true nature of what is to be done, one should cut it with the weapon;
having reflected upon it and made it circular, one should hold it on the tip of the sacrificial ladle in due order.
Oṃ hāṃ, for the principle of the self (ātmatattva), huṃ phaṭ.
With this, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the removal of the noose and the goad;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, the expiation follows immediately thereafter.
Afterwards, one should gradually offer dry [food], especially to Brahmā:
"Oṃ hāṃ! O Brahmā, [I offer] smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. (38)
Having informed [the deity] with the mantra "O Śuklabrahmāṇa, svāhā," he should dismiss [the deity] in due order.
Then, as before, the preceptor should take the consciousness of the disciple into himself. (39)
And after that, O Nandikeśvara, one should join it with the Mukhasūtra;
then, one should pour the water for the arghya offering onto the head of the disciple who has been well-prepared.
Then, for the sake of purifying the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
With the purified principle of the Self, one should bind the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).

Oṃ hāṃ; one should utter the mantra consisting of the principle of the self (ātmatattva) and the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), followed by the principle of the supreme (paramatattva), ending with the dative case and the word "namaḥ. (42)
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two principles of the Self (ātmatattva) and Knowledge (vidyātattva).
[This applies] to both the pure and the impure through the application of short and long vowels.
Having thus uttered the mantra, one should contemplate the reality of the Vidyā.
One should contemplate the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), ending with the light and the *la* and *ṭa* groups of consonants for the child [initiate].
Having performed the pervasive six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga-vyāpaka*), one should perform the striking with flowers and other substances. (44)
Then, having invoked Viṣṇu as before and worshipped him according to the ritual rules,
he should strike the face-thread and collect the consciousness of the disciple.
Having performed [the rites] as before, the Guru, [starting] from the entry,
should unite [the disciple] with his own self and lead him to the End of the Twelve.
Having brought [the deity] from that location, one should place it within the womb of Vāgīśa;
then, one should offer oblations to the Lord of Origination, Enjoyment, and Withdrawal.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the fire with the Śiva-mantra as before,
the concealment of the root-power (mūlaśakti) shall occur by means of the Heti-mantra as previously described.
Having recited the Astra-mantra seven times, the Guru should then perform the cutting;
having wiped it and rolled it into a ball, he should offer it as an oblation as before. (49)
The expiation must be performed according to the rite with the Astra-mantra:
"Oṃ Hāṃ! Having conceived Viṣṇu as the form of intellect and ego. (50)
"Accept the white [oblation], svāhā!"—this shall be the libation for Viṣṇu.
"Oṃ hāṃ! O Viṣṇu, who are the form of intellect and ego, accept the white [oblation], svāhā! || 51 ||
Having informed Viṣṇu for the sake of protection, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) should take place,
having repeatedly withdrawn the consciousness specifically into one's own self.
O Nandikeśvara, one should apply the ointment in the middle of the thread on the head;
then, one should sprinkle drops of the nectar-water of the *arghya* upon the disciple’s head. (53)

One should perform a striking with a flower, having invoked [the deity] there with reverence; then, having cast [the offering] into the fire and worshipped, one should satisfy [the deity] in due order. (54)
Having meditated upon Śiva, one should thereafter perform the worship and the libation;
having addressed that Rudra, one should initiate him at his feet.
When [the disciple] is to be graced, the Guru should inform Rudra;
then, having taken the consciousness of the disciple and entered within, the Guru— || 56 ||
Having established [the deity] within one's own self, one should worship it as residing in the maṇḍala of the Guru;
then, taking that [deity] through the process of emergence, one should place it within the stalk of the womb of Vāgīśī.

One should again apply [the mantras] in sequence and perform three oblations generated from the root mantra; one should not perform the limb-mantras, but rather begin the fire-oblation with the weapon-mantra (hetimantra).
For the purpose of concealing [the soul] from the fetters and especially for their purification,
there is the burning of the fetters through their severance, and the expiation (prāyaścitta) is as before. (59)
Having performed the worship of Rudra, there is the offering of the white [substance] to him:
"Oṃ hāṃ, O Rudra, the mind is of the nature of the Bindu and likewise white. (60)
"Take [it], svāhā"—this is the mantra uttered for the purpose of concealing the bonds and especially for their purification. (61)
The cutting of the nooses, their burning, and the expiation are as before;
having performed the worship of Rudra, one should offer him the white [garment]. (62)
"Oṃ hāṃ Rudra, you whose nature is the drop of the mind (manobindu), who are white—accept [this]! This is the mantra uttered, ending with "svāhā. (63)
Oṃ hāṃ Rudra, take this mind-drop, white in color; svāhā!
Having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rite, one should then dismiss him.
O Brahmin, having attentively established consciousness in the disciple for a moment, [he should proceed].
Having purified it with the *recaka* breath, one should apply it to the thread on the head;
one should then place drops resembling nectar upon the disciple’s crown.
Then, for the sake of purifying the Śiva-tattva,
one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra "Oṃ huṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ," which has been recited over the eyes.
One should cut off the topknot as before with a knife or a weapon;
having placed it upon cow-dung, one should set it in a ladle filled with clarified butter.
One should offer that crest-lock into the fire according to the ritual injunctions and wash it with the *sūkta*;
then the preceptor, endowed with devotion, should bathe with sacred ashes.
One should bathe the disciple with waters according to the sequence of the prescribed ritual.
Furthermore, within that [disciple], one should [infuse] the consciousness of the child, extending for a yojana.
Having joined the sacrificial ladle and spoon according to the rule upon the head of the image,
while reciting the mantras for the renunciation of Brahmā and the other causal deities.

One who possesses the ego-sense "I am Śiva" should discharge the stream of clarified butter into the supreme Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, and should thus unite the disciple's self with Him. 71.
Devotion, tranquility, faith, and likewise the observance of the guru’s command;
endowed with these and free from all afflictions—[he is] "calasmatha. || 72 ||
Betrayal of the guru, betrayal of Śiva, and betrayal of the *samaya*; befriending one who is uninitiated, ingratitude, and lack of discernment. (73)
Looking for the faults of others and constantly looking for one's own faults— one who is devoid of these eight qualities [but] observes the commands of the guru and so forth. (74)
Endowed with all the previously mentioned qualities, free from worldly conduct, possessed of the virtues prescribed in the Agamas, and devoted to the meditation upon the Guru. || 75 ||
Having spoken these and other such words to him, one should consecrate him outside;
thus, at the conclusion of the section on the three principles (tritatva), one should perform all that has been prescribed.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, concerning the ritual procedure for the three principles, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall describe the supreme practice for accomplishing the mantra, which grants all siddhis;
O Nandikeśvara, I shall then describe the maṇḍala, the mantra, and the meditation.
Having washed his hands and feet, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as prescribed by the rules.
Taking a beautiful seat, he should purify it with the Astra-mantra.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and worship the deities of the nyāsa;
one should worship the lotus above the head and worship the circle of gurus (gurumaṇḍala).
Then, with the preceptor as the principal, one should have him meditate upon the three principles (tritatva).
I shall now proclaim this mantra, the sole leader of all mantras.
The sound (nāda) conjoined with the syllable Om (praṇava) and endowed with the Time-spirit (kāla), ending with "namaḥ" for Śiva, the glorious Lord of Śivā, in the ocean of qualities. || 5 ||
It is proclaimed that one should recite the mantra; furthermore, one should arrange a wheel. One should place two *praṇavas* at the front and the back of the practitioner.
Outside of that, one should arrange the number of Gaṇas all around;
having drawn a circle outside of that, one should place a trident in each cardinal direction.
Outside of that, one should write at the four corners of the four triangles:
Stambhinī, Mohinī, Jambhinī, and likewise Haṃsinī.
And there are four [mantras] for the Śaktis according to the sequence of the Mātṛkās:
"To Stambhinī, svāhā! To Mohinī, svāhā! (9).
"Hastine hastinī svāhā. Having uttered these mantras, one should perform worship in the four directions. || 10 ||
All of them, possessing swords and shields, of terrifying form and great strength, performed meditation in particular according to the sequence of circumambulation. || 11 ||
In the center of this wheel, one should meditate there on the three forms; likewise, one should meditate on Rudra at the *mūlādhāra* and Brahmā in the heart as well. (12)
One should likewise contemplate Viṣṇu between the eyebrows; thus one should visualize Rudra in these three places—[as] the pervasive Lord, resembling fire, with one face and three eyes.
Endowed with four arms, joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding an axe and a deer, and adorned with all ornaments. (14)
One should meditate upon Brahmā in the heart—wearing a crown of matted hair, accompanied by his consort Adhīśvarī and the Śakti, golden-hued, and four-armed. (15)
Endowed with four faces, each possessing three eyes, and holding a rosary and a water-pot in his two hands. (16)
To the north and to the south [of him], one should worship Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī, who are seated and endowed with power, according to the prescribed rite. (17)
One should place Viṣṇu between the eyebrows— dark-complexioned, three-eyed,
endowed with four arms, and equipped with the conch and the discus.
Hari is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing a crown and a diadem, and clothed in yellow garments.
Having meditated thus, the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should specially arrange [the deity] well-established within the triangle above the pericarp, accompanied by devotion. (20)
Having meditated thus, the constant yogi should perform worship according to the prescribed rite;
at the conclusion of the worship, however, he should, in accordance with the rule, contemplate the supreme light.
Starting from the *mūlādhāra* and extending as far as Śiva, one should contemplate;
having established [the self] in the abode of Śiva, the wise one should contemplate the nectar (*amṛta*). (22)
Afterwards, the yogi should go to the station of Viṣṇu, and from there to the station of Brahmā;
he should enter the station of Rudra, contemplating it with particular care.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship the Three Principles (tritatva) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
likewise, all food, whether solid or soft, especially at the place of Rudra.
One should cause [the disciple] to perform true meditation, true recitation, and devotion to the Guru;
thereby, by warding off the noose and the goad, one attains the perfection of the Command (ājñāsiddhi).
And because of the prevention of birth from the three causes through meditative absorption, one should therefore always cultivate the three principles with every effort. (26)
Having attained the knowledge of yoga, it shall lead to liberation in due course. || 26 1/2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter [on the Meditation on the Three Principles] in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
(495) Initiation into the principles (tattvas) is said to be specifically [performed] according to the rule;
it is likewise prescribed for disciples who possess ordinary qualities. || 1 ||
Especially for a husband and a disciple who are endowed with supreme virtues, there is the initiation of action (kriyādīkṣā) based on a single principle; that indeed is the liberation from bonds.
Or, O Nandikeśvara, one may perform all the initiations;
even when they serve the purpose of expiation, the worship of the Preceptor is supreme.
At that time, the pavilion, the mandala, the ritual jar, and the worship of the linga were prescribed;
likewise, the fire-ritual, the offering of arghya, and the illumination of the mantras.
The preceptor, endowed with the proper disposition, should perform the ritual as before;
and as before, he should perform the binding of the thread upon the head of the disciple.
One should sequentially arrange the single principle (tattva) beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva;
one should place [the deity] at the top of the Śiva-tattva, either red or the color of a newborn infant.
O Nandikeśvara, all [rites] beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) are as before;
having performed the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), one should worship Śiva in the fire.
The offering of all white substances should be performed with the Śiva-mantra;
one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra, containing the [syllable] *prātaḥ* within it.
Thus, for the sake of attaining union with Śiva,
one should perform oblations with the hundred-root mantra for the destruction of the fetters, so that they may be extinguished and rendered stable [in their cessation].
The inspection of the mandala, as well as the name, conduct, and so forth, are as before;
one should offer one's body, wealth, and life to the true gurus. (10)
By whatever means possible, the supreme satisfaction of the Guru [must be achieved];
one who has thus completed the initiation through ritual action is the most excellent in qualities. (11)
He alone is qualified for the initiation into yoga, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Section on Yoga Initiation," within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall proclaim the initiation of yoga; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
Regarding the etymological meaning of the root *yuji* as "to join," it refers to that which joins the individual soul (*jīva*) with Śiva.
Union is said to be *saṃśleṣa*, clearly the "path together" (*sahamārga*);
it is the state of non-existence and decay, which brings about the existence of true knowledge.
The union with the principle of Śiva (śivatatva) is called the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā).
[It does not depend on] the mandala, the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, the water-pot, the worship of the deity, and so forth.
Endowed with the previously mentioned qualities, it was characterized by self-restraints and observances; it had attained an extreme state of detachment and was free from greed. (4)
O Nandikeśvara, one should initiate an excellent disciple endowed with such qualities as these;
[the procedure for] the lamp of the mantra, his satisfaction, and so forth, is as previously described.
The preceptor should perform that entire fire-ritual according to the previously stated procedure,
and he should worship Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśa as before.
With a flower upon the disciple’s chest, one should perform the piercing and so forth as before;
one should carry out the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) according to the previous procedure.
Then, one should also contemplate the ten channels within the body of the disciple;
they are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and likewise Suṣumnā.
Gandhārī, Saptajihvā, Pūṣā, Yaśasvinī,
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth. (9)
And the fourteen vital airs, beginning with Prāṇa, are fully present;
Prāṇa is the first wind, followed by Apāna and Vyāna. (10)
Udāna, Samāna, Nāga, Kurma, and Kṛkara as the seventh, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya are thus proclaimed. || 11 ||
Vaivanta, Mukhyaka, Antaryāmin, and Prapañcaka—
thus these fourteen winds, beginning with Prāṇa, have been described.
In all those channels, the vital airs also circulate;
however, there should be a stabilization of the channels and the vital airs each in their own respective locations. (13)
By means of the *praṇava* and the *śakti*, through the recitation (*japa*) of the hundred seeds (*bīja*) and other rites,
one should establish [the deity], worship it, meditate upon it, and contemplate its form as Śiva. (14)
Among the channels, there are three principal ones: Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā;
and among these as well, the preeminence of Suṣumṇā is proclaimed.
In the center of that is the Brahma-nāḍī, the supreme abode of Śiva and Śakti,
extending from the Mūlādhāra up to the Brahmarandhra.
And its stationary state is to be known as characterized by nine stages:
the anus, the space between the anus and the penis, and immediately thereafter, the dissolved root. (17)
Then [one should touch] the heart, followed by the root of the ear;
then the root of the palate, and immediately after that, the middle of the two arms. || 18 ||
The forehead and the *brahmarandhra* are declared to be the nine foundations (*ādhāras*).
The *mūlādhāra* has four petals, and above that there is one with six petals. (19)
Then, from that [place], the eight-petaled [lotus] is called Anāhata;
the throat is said to be the twelfth, and the root of the palate is the sixteenth.
Likewise, one should sequentially meditate upon the forehead and the space between the eyebrows as the immediate abode of Śiva,
consisting of three hundred and sixty divisions according to the distinctions of the phonemes.
Having the luster of gold and the luster of crystal, immediately thereafter the form of fire,
resembling the newly risen sun and like blazing radiance.
Afterwards, one should contemplate that which consists entirely of splendor and is beyond the reach of mind and speech;
within these locations, one should conceive of Brahmā and the other causal deities.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are,
in the supreme Śiva, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti). 24.
One should contemplate the locations of the orbs of fire, sun, and moon right there:
the circle of fire at the navel and the circle of the sun at the heart.
Between the two bows, the lunar disc is said to be located;
in the power of action (kriyā-śakti) there is the point (bindu), and in the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) there is the resonance (nāda).
In the power of will (icchā-śakti), Kalā is said to reside; therein is the supreme nectar (paramāmṛta).
Above that, in the station of Śiva, is the most excellent nectar of bliss (ānandāmṛta).
Having meditated thus, the preceptor should visualize the nine mantras within that [space],
and then sprinkle the body of the disciple with the arghya water.
Just as the fire situated within the hearth is ignited by the wind,
so too should one utter the respective mantra while stationed at the locus of the *ādhāra*. (29)

At the *mūlādhāra*, one should recite the *tāra* (om), the *marāla* (ha), and the union of *śakti* and *śambhu* (hrīṃ) nine times in sequence, using the tips of nine blades of *darbha* grass as the points of focus.
Endowed with the bindu, nāda, and kalā, reaching as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the supreme teacher should cause the light, resembling a lotus fiber, to ascend. 31.
One should visualize the form of the mantra as having the appearance of a blazing lamp-flame, flashing like lightning back and forth, situated upon a thread and above another thread. (32)
This is the Mūlādhāra; immediately following it is the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Having recited the Śivatantra, one should worship the God of gods.
At the root of the ear, one should place the power of action (kriyāśakti) and Bhṛgu, followed by the vowel joined with the letter *ma*;
then two crescent moons (*candrakhaṇḍa*) constitute the illumination of the mantra's recitation. (34)
The element joined with the *bindu* and *krośa* with the earthly [element], and having conjoined *mahāmāyā*, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) are thus proclaimed. (35)
The best of teachers should visualize [the deity] resembling Indra, Agni, and Sūrya;
starting from that, he should visualize the space up to the middle of the pair of bows.
One should meditate upon the sun, which resembles fire in appearance, within the disc of gnosis;
and from that disc of gnosis, one should thereafter [meditate upon] the lunar orb.
First, O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon fire, the sun, and the moon as the supreme light;
one should meditate on the seed-syllable of Śiva in the place of Śiva.

Having meditated thus, having performed worship, and having worshipped [the deity] within oneself and in the disciple, one should perform the laying out of the lines according to the prescribed ritual. (39)
One should visualize the crest-lamp and the measurement of the threads,
extending from the chin to the heart, from the heart to the navel, and reaching the region of Viṣṇu.
One should likewise lay down five threads reaching to the *mūlādhāra*;
thus, the fivefold thread is provided with the crest-lock of the disciple. (41)
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose constitute the pentad;
speech, hands, feet, anus, and the generative organ constitute the other pentad. (42)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell constitute the pentad; speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure constitute the [other] pentad. (43)
One should place the twenty principles (tattvas) upon the line of the face;
on the line of the heart, one should place the triad of mind, intellect, and ego. (44)
The mind, passion, and illusion are on the thread of the navel;
knowledge, necessity, and time are on the thread of the eternal foundation.
One should meditate in sequence upon Śuddhamāyā and Śuddhakalā as the twelfth;
specifically, one should perform sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and striking (tāḍana) with the weapon (hetin).
And having entered [the body] by means of the yoga of exhalation (recaka) conjoined with the syllable *huṃ*, the separation of his consciousness from the *ajapā* [mantra] occurs as before. (47)
One should apply [the mantra] to the thread and to the mouth with the *saṃhāramudrā*.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to one's own self. || 48 ||

One should perform the pervasive protection (*vyāpaka-rakṣaṇa*), as well as the presence-oblation (*sannidhānāhuti*), the withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), the gazing (*ālokana*), and the worship (*pūjana*) just as before. (49)

In this way, one should apply [this method] to other sūtras and to the stages of the channels (nāḍībhūmi). Having drawn forth the consciousness of the disciple, one should unite it with one's own self alone. (50)
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon the conjunction of the *piṇḍas* as before;
one should perform the sacraments beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) according to the previous ritual procedure. (51)
Then, having dismissed both Vāgīśī and likewise Vāgīśa, and having invoked Vimalāsana and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite; || 52 ||
To that Śukla [mantra], one should impart [the teaching] up to the bliss of the ears and other senses;
one should utter the Tāra, the Śakti, the Upaga, and the singular Bliss of Brahman.
Then one should worship the Reality (tattva), the "I-am-that" (so'ham), and the head in succession:
*oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ brahmaṇe śrotraṃ so'haṃ svāhā* || 54 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, the tongue, so'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, the nose, so'haṃ svāhā! || 55 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā in speech, so'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā in the hand, so'haṃ svāhā! || 56 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, the feet, so'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, the anus, so'haṃ svāhā! || 57 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, the organ of procreation, so'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, sound, so'haṃ svāhā! || 58 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, touch, so 'ham, svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, form, so 'ham, svāhā! || 59 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, [I offer] taste, so'haṃ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, [I offer] fragrance, so'haṃ svāhā! || 60 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, speech to Brahmā, so'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, grasping by Brahmā, so'haṃ svāhā! || 61 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, [I offer] movement; so 'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, [I offer] emission; so 'haṃ svāhā! || 62 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Brahmā, bliss, so 'haṃ, svāhā!
With these twenty mantras, the offering of pure Brahman is presented. (63)
"O Brahmin child, whose bonds have been completely burnt away, svāhā!
You must not remain subject to bondage again; thus one should cause him to hear the command of Śiva. (64)
Having taken the mouth-thread and coiled it as before,
one should place it upon the ladle filled with clarified butter and perform the oblation with the Astra-mantra.
When [the breath] is situated in the pitcher (kumbha) and flows through the right channel (savyanāḍī), one should then dismiss Brahmā;
having established him in the mūlādhāra, O Nandikeśvara, one should worship him. 66.
"O Viṣṇu, by your authority I initiate this seeker of liberation;
you must be favorable," thus one should inform Viṣṇu. (67)
Then one should perform the Viṣṇu-śukla rite for the mind, intellect, and ego;
having worshipped the mantra and the Tāra (Om) and recited it twice, one should then offer the oblation.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Viṣṇu, the mind, I am that, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Viṣṇu, the intellect, I am that, svāhā! || 69 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, [I offer] the ego-sense to Viṣṇu; so 'haṃ svāhā!
Having thus given this to the disciple, one should then dismiss Govinda.
Having invoked [the deity] into the substratum, one should establish it and then dismiss it in due order;
having brought the thread from within the heart and made it circular as before, [one should proceed].
Having offered a ladle filled with clarified butter, one should perform the oblation with the *heti-mantra*.
[The deity] is auspicious, resembling the moon freed from its five stains and two parts.
One should meditate upon this even while sleeping, but during deep sleep one should apply it;
one should worship the consciousness with the thread of the navel and with water worthy of honor.
The entire sequence beginning with the striking and ending with the consecration (saṃskāra) is as before;
having invoked and worshipped Rudra, who is endowed with stability and other qualities. || 74 ||
"Since the noose of Rudra has been completely burnt away by you, you must not remain for the sake of binding him again; thus, let him hear the command of Śiva. (75)

For Rudra, as before, one should apply the *chalka* with devotion; one should likewise cause the mind, passion (*rāga*), illusion (*māyā*), and limited agency (*kalā*) to be bestowed upon that very [deity]. (76)
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Rudra, [I offer] the mind, so 'ham svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Rudra, [I offer] passion, so 'ham svāhā! || 77 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Rudra, [I offer] Māyā; so 'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Rudra, [I offer] Kāla; so 'haṃ svāhā! || 78 ||
With these mantras, one should cause the white [substance] to be offered while endowed with devotion;
one should then install that Rudra in the region of the Maṇipūraka in due order. (79)

Having invoked the subtle [deity] during deep sleep— one who has a dark spot, is diminished by three parts, and possesses a luster like the orb of the moon— one should worship with the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu).
"Since the bonds of this young creature have been completely burnt away by you, you must not remain to bind him again; rather, you should cause him to hear the command of Śiva. || 81 ||
Furthermore, O Nandikeśvara, one should cause a white [garment] to be given to Īśvara;
and one should offer Vidyā, Niyati, and Kāla with the mantra-encasement as before.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Īśvara, [I offer] Vidyā; so 'haṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Īśvara, [I offer] Niyati; so 'haṃ svāhā! || 83 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Īśvara, kālaṃ sohaṃ svāhā.
Endowed with devotion, one should perform the offering of white substances with these [mantras]. || 84 ||
Therefore, having invoked the Lord, one should establish him in the lotus of the heart;
then, endowed with devotion and with senses subdued, one should worship him according to the prescribed rite.
Having taken up the thread located at the consecrated site and extracted it as before,
one should place it into the fire filled with clarified butter and blood, and perform the oblation with the Astra-mantra.
One should perform the ritual of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) beginning with the noose, the goad, and the withdrawal;
[the altar] should be circular, square, or crescent-shaped like the moon.
The fourth [state] is that which resounds, leading beyond to the form of the Self;
the procedure for striking and so forth, up to the final consecration, is as before. || 88 ||
Having invoked that Sadāśiva, one should worship him with devotion;
being composed, one should offer pure Māyā, the pure Kalā, and the white [substance]. (89)
Having joined it with the root mantra and the previous mantras, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa):
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ hauṃ, to Sadāśiva, [I offer] pure Māyā; so 'haṃ svāhā. || 90 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ hauṃ, to Sadāśiva, [I offer] the pure digit; so 'ham svāhā.
O Nandikeśvara, in this manner the offering of the white [substance] should be performed. 91.
"Once the bonds of the Lord and of the child have been completely burnt away by you, you must not remain for the sake of binding them again; thus, let him hear the command of Śiva. (92)
Within the purified body, one should perform the installation and worship of that supreme reality called Sādākhya, endowed with devotion. || 93 ||
Having placed [the vessel] and taken up the thread, having coiled it as before, one should offer oblations into the tip of the ladle filled with ghee by means of the heart-mantra. (94)
Furthermore, one should meditate upon consciousness as being free from all blemishes, possessing a splendor equal to the king of autumn, and consisting of a mass of pure radiance.
Having taken [the syllable] from the *haṃsa* mantra, one should join it with the *praṇava*;
from the *praṇava*, one should join it to the seed-syllable of Śakti, and from that, one should join it to the root-mantra.
Having recited this mantra—*oṃ haṃsaḥ oṃ hrīṃ hainyāya haum*—one should apply it at the *mūlādhāra*. || 97 ||
In this [state] which is a mass of consciousness, stainless, peaceful, eternal, and devoid of everything, one should unite even the pure self and contemplate it as Śiva. 98.
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending to the end of the *dvādaśānta*,
one should contemplate [the deity] in the form of the ninefold self (*navātmarūpaka*) and utter the mantra joined with the *nāda*. (99)
[He should recite] the Nāda [mantra] together with Bhṛgu, followed immediately by Saṃvartaka;
then Mahendra joined with Kāla, and Vāruṇa conjoined with Vahni. 100.
Endowed with the sixth vowel *marut* (u) and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, one should join this nine-syllable cluster (*piṇḍa*) with the consonants (*hal*) and vowels (*mātrā*). 101.
With this very mantra, one should touch well with the tip of a blade of darbha grass;
beginning from the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate the procedure up to the *dvādaśānta*.
One should visualize that disciple as a calf, [and] as the body of the disciple;
having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should indeed perform the rites of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the rest. || 103 ||
Having performed the external consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the Guru should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Having worshipped him again with perfumes and other offerings, he should perform the remaining rites as previously described. (104)
Furthermore, the knower of the ritual procedure should give the yoga-band with the Kavaca mantra;
in the initiation into Yoga through knowledge, there is no requirement for preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Therefore, one should abandon [worldly] yoga and worship the feet of the Guru with offerings of golden flowers and golden sacred threads.
With crowns, rings, and all kinds of ornaments, with heaps of various jewels, and with inlaid gems upon the ground; || 107 ||
One should devotedly offer [these] along with garments and so forth to the Guru;
for he who is endowed with the initiation of yoga is Śiva himself manifest upon the earth. (108)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, [Yogadīkṣā], in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
519) For the benefit of yogins, the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) is here described.
From the bulb (kanda) below the navel, [channels] extend horizontally and upwards with their openings facing those directions. (1)
The body of all embodied beings measures ninety-six finger-breadths in length. O God, [he who] practices [this]... he alone shall be a Śiva-yogin, saluted by the thirty gods. (2)
By means of the fire residing within the body and that which is attained through the practice of yoga,
the yogi indeed resolves the accumulation of worlds through the practice of yoga.
The space between the anus and the genitals is the mandala of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni);
it is triangular and radiant in form, especially for human beings.
For animals, it should be square; for birds, indeed circular;
for reptiles, it should be elongated; and for quadrupeds, it should be in the form of a heart.
For animals and for those born from eggs, it is established in the middle of the bulb (kanda);
and for humans, it is located nine finger-breadths from the bulb by name.
In that very place, all the channels and the fourteen principal ones seem to descend into the region of the navel, which is endowed with twelve spokes.
Enveloped by impurity, māyā, and the rest, the individual soul (jīva) revolves in this wheel;
accompanied by the instruments of waking and the other states, the soul experiences the upper and lower realms.
Just as a spider constantly wanders around its web,
so too do the individual soul and the vital breath move about daily with great vigor.
The Self (Ātman) is mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), while Kuṇḍalinī is situated below;
the Suṣumnā, the most excellent channel, is located in the middle of the kanda.
The neck of the lute is the bow-staff, and the string extends to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
In its center is the channel of Brahmā (brahmanāḍī), the Suṣumṇā, which possesses a variegated form.
The unmanifest [nāḍī] should be known as the right [channel] of that [suṣumṇā], while the right [channel] belongs to it on the left;
Suṣumṇā is described as being threefold: white, red, and black. || 12 ||
The *iḍā* has the luster of a conch or a jasmine flower, while the *piṅgalā* has the appearance of sunlight;
both surround the *nābhicakra* (navel-center) and are joined with the *prāṇa* wind.
Indu moves in the iḍā, while Bhāskara moves in the piṅgalā;
the Moon is said to be tāmasa, and the Sun is called rājasa.
And in the middle is the Sāttvika nāḍī, endowed with the three qualities (guṇas);
it is Sarasvatī, white in color, resembling a white lotus. 15.
Yaśasvinī, Himendvābhā, Citrā, Viśvodarā, and Śubhā. || 16 ||
Kuhū, Āñjanābhā, Śaṅkhinī, Payasvinī, Payovarṇā, Alambuṣā, and Pītavarṇikā. || 17 ||
The Āgandhārī [nāḍī] should be like the neck of a peacock in color;
the Iḍā is nectar, while the Piṅgalā is poison and resembles the exterior of night. (18)
Sarasvatī and Kuhū are situated at the sides of Suṣumnā;
and Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are on the front and back of Iḍā.
Piṅgalā and the illustrious Pūṣā are situated on the eastern back;
likewise, Pūṣā and Sarasvatī are on the two sides of Payasvinī.
p.
523) ...are to be meditated upon? On both sides [are] Gāndhārī and Payasvinī;
Alambuṣā, O Nandīśa, is situated below the middle of the throat. || 21 ||
To the east of the Suṣumnā are the Piṅgalā and the Kuhū;
they are to be known as extending from below to above, [the former] being the Vāraṇā and [the latter] the Milinī.
His [channel] Yaśasvinī goes as far as the tip of the big toe and is indeed stable;
there, Piṅgalā goes to the end of the left nostril and moves upwards.
Piṅgalā is merged into the back; Pūṣā resides in the right eye;
likewise, Payasvinī and Nandin should be situated within the left ear.
The abiding of Sarasvatī is proclaimed to be here at the tip of the tongue;
then Śaṅkhinī, having ascended, becomes the range of perception as far as the end of the throat.
Standing behind the iḍā, Gāndhārī resides in the left eye;
and the iḍā itself is situated on the left side, reaching to the end of the left nostril. (26)
The one reaching to the tip of the big toe is indeed Hastijihvā on the left;
the one named Vighnodayā resides in the belly, performing the fulfillment of the form.
The Alambuṣā is situated below the base of the Vāyu;
from these very channels, there are seventy-two thousand [others]. (28)
There, a network of channels (nāḍīs) arose like the withered leaves of an ashvattha tree;
within those fourteen channels, there are likewise fourteen vital airs (vāyus).
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 30 ||
The primary [vital breath], the one characterized by detachment, and likewise the inner controller (antaryāmī)— thus these fourteen winds beginning with prāṇa have been described. (31)
Therefore, the vital airs (vāyu) indeed circulate everywhere within the channels (nāḍīs).
Among these, five are primary; of those two, [the first] is prāṇa and apāna.
And this vital breath (prāṇa) is the chief of all the winds within living beings;
it resides at the base of the two nostrils, its function being inhalation and exhalation. (33)
The vital breath (prāṇa) moves from the center of the heart to the center of the navel;
therefore, the primacy of prāṇa exists, as does the functioning of apāna.
It carries all food, drink, and so forth downward for embodied beings; by that very process, the excrement, urine, and sense organs become devoid of essence.
The Vyāna wind causes the intense bending of the limbs; the Udāna wind causes the mouth and eyes to tremble as well as the lower lip. (36)
The Samāna wind, established by its very enumeration throughout all the limbs, produces intense piercing pain in the vital points (marmas) of the entire body. (37)
Pervading all the flavors that have been drunk and eaten along with the digestive fire,
it moves through the midst of the seventy-two thousand channels.
Likewise, the movement of the *samāna* wind carries [the breath] through the limbs;
it performs the function of exhaling for the *nāga* wind and the opening and closing of the eyes for the *kūrma* wind. (39)
Kṛkara is indeed hunger, and Devadatta is yawning;
Dhanañjaya is accompanied by sound, and he does not leave one who is devoid of breath. (40)
Mukhya is joined with the mind (manas), Vairambha is joined with the intellect (buddhi),
Antaryāmin is characterized by ego (ahaṃkāra), and Prapañca is joined with consciousness (citta). || 41 ||
The vital breath (prāṇa), resembling lapis lazuli, always blazes like fire;
it divides the water and food situated within the stomach together with the digestive fire.
Having placed water before the fire, one should place food and so forth upon that water;
beneath it is the apāna wind, resembling an indragopaka insect.
Having kindled the fire right there, he should slowly inhale it with the downward-moving breath (apāna);
[he should then consume] food accompanied by very hot water and mixed with various side dishes.
Then, the impurities of the receptacle become liquid and undergo digestion;
sweat and urine go outwards, and in due course, they become rasa and vīrya.
From the essence (rasa), blood is produced; from blood, flesh arises;
from flesh, fat is derived; and from fat, sinews and bone are formed. (46)
From the bone comes marrow, and that marrow, together with its vital essence (ojas), becomes feces; thus, in this sequence, it is called the sevenfold constituent (dhātu). // 47 //
In Vyāna, which has a brilliance equal to lightning and fire, one should contemplate Udāna;
and Udāna has a radiance equal to the fire resembling the filaments of a lotus.
White in appearance like cow's milk, he is equanimous and devoted to sprinkling;
resembling the safflower, he brings about the fear of hiccups. (49)
That tortoise is yellow in color and causes dullness, horripilation, and trembling;
the *kṛkara* is black in color and causes the knitting of the eyebrows. (50)
Agnivarṇa is Devadatta, who performs tasks such as the *tandrī* and *kumbha* rites;
Śveta is declared to be Dhanañjaya, devoted to the maintenance of the body. (51)
In this way, when there is both the intention and the distribution [of the food],
then the Bhoja becomes free from the defects of the Sūta and others, as well as devoid of defects in the food itself.
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all, the attainment of Śiva shall occur in due course;
restraint (yama) has been declared to be tenfold, and likewise, observance (niyama) is now being described.
Purity, austerity, contentment, study of the scriptures, worship of the Lord, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings—these are auspicious. (54)
Through the sacred bathing places (tīrtha) of Varuṇa and Agni, purification of the body becomes certain;
now, the purification of action is described as occurring simply by avoiding [unrighteous acts]. (55)
Through truthful speech, there shall be purity for the sake of the complete purification of initiation (dīkṣā).
Purity is said to be sixfold, as is austerity such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances. (56)
Austerity is the tormenting [of the body] for the sake of one's goal and the purification of the senses;
through practices such as the *kṛcchra*, it is the exhaustion of bodily defects and the drying up of the causes [of rebirth]. (57)
The drying up of enjoyments that ought not to be indulged in, and the abandonment of pride and envy—this is declared to be the form of austerity, the supreme means for accomplishing yoga. 58.
One should be satisfied with meager gain; contentment should be as it was before. One who seeks fulfillment through everything always encounters suffering. (59)
The study of the Śaiva Āgamas, the recitation of the Purāṇas associated with them, and the observation of places suitable for one's own spiritual practice. (60)
Constant practice and the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya) are proclaimed as such;
by this alone, O Nandikeśvara, the [divine] form becomes manifest. (51)
All that worship beginning with the adoration of the *liṅga* has been previously described;
it should be performed by one endowed with devotion to his own guru, in accordance with the requirements of place and time. (62)
Together with non-contentious people who are worthy [of company] and endowed with faith, one should listen to the established doctrine;
indeed, this constitutes listening to the established doctrine. (63)

Joined with the sovereignty of the Guru yet devoid of one's own [limited] sovereignty, the command of the Guru is like the clay in the potter’s hand; it is so called because of its being maintained through the Guru’s authority. (64)
For this essential nature of his is capable of being the cause of both curse and favor;
however, the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures regarding whatever action may be contemptible [is as follows]. (65)
The splendor that exists therein is declared to be the Śaiva *hrī*;
and by means of the mantras taught by the Guru in the *Dīkṣottara*, (66)
[He saw him] endowed with devotion, faith, and spiritual delusion, performing the service of obeying the guru’s commands and so forth,
accompanied by his wife, disciples, and others, and filled with compassion.

Having made the measure neither deficient nor excessive, avoiding the *klīla* [recitation], the *sūtra*, and so forth, one should bring about the destruction of the moon and sun through recitation that is spoken aloud, whispered, or mental. 68.
That which is whispered is superior to the spoken, and the mental is superior to the whispered;
having thus received [the instruction] from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform the recitation—such is the recitation.
The fire-ritual (agnikārya) has been declared as the oblation (huta); thus the performance of the sacrifice (hutakriyā) is explained.
The observances (niyama) are said to be tenfold, and with the restraints (yama) and so forth, they total twenty.
If the yoga is deficient by these twenty [degrees], it will cause evil.
If one should perform a gift out of delusion, the disciple will incur sin. (71)
Therefore, with every effort, the Guru should bestow [this] upon a worthy disciple:
the Padma, the Svastika, the Gomukha, and likewise the Viśada.
Sūkṣma, Ekapāda, Kukkuṭa, Vīra, Padmāsana, Kha, Puṣṭa, Kūrma, and Vimala. || 73 ||
Daṇḍa, Caṇḍa, Gokarṇa, and thereafter Siddhāsana;
Vṛtti, Kaṭika, Gajāsya, and Mayūraka. (74)
Twenty postures have been proclaimed; listen now to each one in sequence.
O Nandīśa, having placed the auspicious soles of the feet one above the other— (75)
This is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is the supreme and most honored of all postures;
it consists of placing the two auspicious soles of the feet in the space between the knees and the thighs. (76)
As before, one should keep the body straight; the *svastika* posture is most auspicious in every respect. One should join the right ankle behind the left side [of the hip]. (77)
Likewise on the right and similarly on the left, one should join the cow-faced [hands] (gomukha) with the feet above the head and at the sides of the ears.
With both hands, one should strike the ground between the arms;
this is declared to be the *viṃśadanta* [mudrā], and immediately after that is the *sūcī*.
With both hands, the right one should be placed upon the ground;
the body and both feet should also be bent, and the face should be directed upward toward the body.
Standing like a needle is extremely fierce; it is indeed well-known as "the needle" (sūcī).
For the purpose of traveling through the sky, one should gradually become like a cock. (81)
One should place one foot on the ground and the other foot upon the hip;
then, having placed the left hand upon the sole of that [right] foot, [one should likewise place] the right [hand]. 82.
Raising the fingers upward while covering [the body] and standing on one leg—this is the supreme posture, to be accomplished through most intense austerity. (83)
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should draw both hands up to the elbows between the thighs; this, O dear one, is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana). || 84 ||
Placing one foot upon the thigh and the other foot on the ground, through the union of the knees and elbows, this is called the vīrāsana posture. (85)
This [posture] serves for the purpose of exposition and brings about the understanding of the meaning of all scriptures;
furthermore, the two [hands] are placed at the sides of the sacrificial vessel, while the [other two hands] are at the ankles of the bull.
Having placed the sides of the feet upon the hands with a firm binding, this becomes the Bhadrāsana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons. (87)
Having joined the two soles of the feet together, they should again spread out within;
the pair of hands is positioned on the back and sides, with the feet turned downwards.

With the face turned toward the back and the nails facing backward, primarily obstructing the flow of breath, one should place the feet like a lotus and hold them between the thighs with both hands. (88)
Having cast [the breath] into those two, one should bind it at the throat as before;
this is the arrest of the vital breaths and the great kindling of the fire of the body. (90)
Having performed a salutation with palms joined, as if a child within the womb, it is recommended for the gradual drawing forth of the waters; this shall be the kindling of the root-fire. (91)
This is declared to be the piṇḍāsana; immediately after that is the gokarṇa.
Having placed both knees on either side of the pair of feet [on the ground], [one assumes the gokarṇa posture]. 92.
Placing both hands on the ground with the right one uppermost,
standing with the body perfectly erect, this is Gokarṇa, the binding of the vital air.
Having placed his hands upon his knees and extended his fingers,
with mouth agape, he should gaze fiercely with eyes fixed intently on the tip of his nose.
It pacifies heat, wind, and other ailments, and extinguishes forest fires;
having joined the two feet together and placed them upon that back, [one should remain]. (95)
Sitting with the body straight, one should place the feet upon the hands;
one should perform the drawing up of the *apāna*, which is the supreme means for increasing the bodily fire.
Having collapsed one arm onto the surface of the earth, he then immediately extended his breast with his hand. (97)
Having taken hold of the teacher's hand, one should extend the knee and the foot;
looking at the big toe of the foot is called the "elephant-bowing" (gajāvanamita) posture.
Then there shall be the pacification of the winds in the back and the sides;
it is renowned as increasing longevity and stopping diarrhea. (99)
Firmly pressing the ground with the palms of both hands, one should place the pair of elbows at another spot on the ground. (100)
With the head and feet raised high, remaining in the sky like a staff—
this is the Peacock Posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins. 101.
All diseases perish, as do poisons and their objects;
they say that the limbs attain their proper sequence and movement becomes always swift. (102)
Twenty postures have been proclaimed, of which the comfortable seated posture (sthitasukhāsana) is the best.
Next, I shall describe breath control (prāṇāyāma), preceded by the purification of the channels (nāḍīśuddhi) and other preliminaries.
It is the most excellent remover of all sins, the warder-off of all diseases, the constant manifestation of Śiva, and the cause of absolute liberation (kaivalya) attained through gradual stages. 104.

By means of this [prāṇāyāma], all that pertains to the water element—which requires time, exertion, and effort to accomplish, such as visiting sacred fords like the Gaṅgā—is achieved through prāṇāyāma alone. || 105 ||
Without that, going elsewhere may occur for one who is devoid of fortune;
therefore, with every effort, the Guru should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma). (106)
In a place that is silent and devoid of people, located elsewhere than at the ocean, free from cold and heat, and shunned by those who commit great sins; || 107 ||
It was free from bedbugs, female ants, and the like, as well as mosquitoes and other such insects;
at that time, there were no ungrateful people, nor those prone to anger, nor those who transgressed the commands of their gurus.
One should not practice yoga in the dwelling of outcastes;
rather, having risen in the morning, being self-controlled, and having performed purification and ritual sipping of water (ācamana). || 109 ||
The Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and likewise the Mānasa—each of these is a manifold bath, especially for yogins. (110)
Now, there is one method of mantra-bath that cuts away all sins;
the first type has already been described in this manner, and another is now being stated. (111)
That bathing with the water from the feet of the Guru becomes the Vāruṇa bath;
the Āgneya bath is performed with ashes for protection, and the Vāyavya bath is the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The nectar of the Mahendra-bath is the mental vision of Yoga;
it is accomplished by means of cloth, antelope skin, kuśa grass, and an earthen seat. || 113 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the lotus of the Guru above the head;
then, one should worship Vighneśvara on the southeast petal of its pericarp.
Facing either east or north, with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose and remaining seated in his body, he should keep his neck, head, and torso straight, and not let his teeth touch one another.
With one's gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should behold the lunar disc situated there,
containing a drop in its center and endowed with flowing nectar. (116)
Being well-composed, one should gaze right there with both eyes;
having recollected the seed-syllable of fire within the left nostril. (117)
The wise practitioner should properly fill [the body] with air from the big toe up to the head; he should fill it through the left nostril just as before.
One should practice in this very manner with the right hand alone;
thus, by counting five, six, or seven [repetitions], it becomes inferior, middling, or superior.
One should practice this constantly for half [the duration] or even half of that;
such a perfected prāṇāyāma is called the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana). || 120 ||
At the three junctions of the day, there is indeed an upward increase of fire from the belly; this, conjoined with the body, is the tongue that manifests the *nāda*. (121)
O Vatsara, the complete accomplishment of the sāsamarta occurs after four months;
one should continue the practice as long as these signs are not yet perceived.
This purification of the channels has been described immediately following the breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
using either the Prāsāda mantra or likewise the Praṇava.
When one has ascended to breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and is reciting the syllable-less mantra within the heart, one should not perceive any characteristic there; it always abides in all things.
First, the wise one should fill the rising [breath] for sixteen mātrās;
the retention (kumbhaka) should last sixty-four mātrās, and thus it becomes the full vessel (pūrṇakumbha).
Then, one should exhale the upward-moving breath with thirty-two *mātrās*; indeed, one should constantly practice sixteen such breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*). (126)
The superior, the middling, and likewise the inferior;
the inferior consists of twelve *udghātas*, while the middling consists of twenty-four. || 127 ||
They say that the supreme characteristic of this training consists of thirty-six [units]:
twelve breath-retentions (dhāraṇā) constitute one regulation of breath (āyāma), and twelve such retentions constitute one meditation (dhyāna). 128.
Meditation up to twelve [breaths] is designated as samādhi;
having completely abandoned exhalation (recaka), one should place inhalation (pūraka) into retention (kumbhaka).
If one is unable to perform the inhalation and exhalation repeatedly, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) in due order:
namely, trembling, whirling, and likewise whirling and leaping.
One attains stability of the body and shall attain stability of the vital breath;
one attains stability of the mind and shall attain purity of the mind. || 131 ||
Then, having drawn in the compressed air through the tip of the nose, one should exhale it by means of yoga, repeatedly drawing it in again and again whenever one becomes fatigued. (132)
By the practice of three upward thrusts, the obstructions at the anus are destroyed;
having made the region of the three places either thick or [well-defined], the concentrated yogi [proceeds]. (133)
With the head directed toward the lower region, one should expel the anal polyps,
as well as the terrible tumors arising from the genitals and those located throughout the entire body.
Through the practice of retaining [the breath] in all its parts, one who knows how to withdraw and apply it should,
having resorted to yogic sleep, sleep upon the written [scripture] regarding both the seen and the unseen.
Whatever one whose self is disciplined perceives, all that becomes his,
even in a dream, by the power of yogic sleep for one who is joined in yoga. (136)
Whether requested by someone else or acting on his own initiative, one who is endowed with the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) should perform this rite; this which I have spoken is the truth. (137)
One should properly perform each [practice] connected to the objects of the mind;
one should practice this constantly at the sixteen twilights for the duration of a single month. (138)
He shall be liberated from the sin of killing an embryo, there is no doubt;
he purifies even the sin committed in another birth within six months. 139.
Through a year of constant practice, the knowledge of Śiva is held in the palm of one's hand;
and from the continuous practice of yoga, there arises the complete restraint of the vital breaths.
By that, the destruction of the mind occurs; liberation is held in his hand. The internal drawing-in of the vital air must be preceded by that [external practice]. (141)
