O Nandin, that becomes the exhaling breath (recaka); indeed, in this very sequence, perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and bliss follow immediately thereafter. (142)
Therefore, that which is clear and supreme becomes certainly the highest;
through the dissolution of the vital breath, even one's intellect becomes clear and one attains happiness in an instant.
One should arise from the destruction of the vital breaths along with the seat itself,
from the midst of that which has the form of inhalation and exhalation and the form of the *haṃsa*.
By bringing the central seed-syllable [to the point of dissolution], one becomes composed of the bliss of Śiva;
indeed, through the absorption of the vital breath (prāṇa) during the retention of breath (kumbhaka), it does not arise again. || 145 ||
The filling of the breath and likewise its exhalation—
having released both of these in yoga, the retention of the breath is supreme. (146)
Prāṇāyāma consists of exhaling everything, filling [the breath], and subsequently performing the retention of breath (kumbhaka). || 147 ||
One should practice *kumbhaka* daily, either with [recitation] or alone;
one should practice the "with" (*sahita*) variety until the perfection of the "alone" (*kevala*) is attained. (148)
When, through practice, the kumbhaka (retention) is perfected— devoid of both exhalation and inhalation—
there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain.
The perfection of his mind-swiftness is not matched by even the playful hair on his head; neither old age nor paternal grief is seen in him, nor is the Vaijayantī garland ever absent.
Accompanied by the *kumbhaka* [retention of breath], one brings about the production of sound;
[this is] the vitalization of the breath...
This is the means for conquering the vital breaths, which wards off all death. || 151 ||
Having filled the abdomen with air, one should perform the retention of the vital breath (prāṇadhāraṇā) at the tip of the nose, in the center of the navel, or on the two big toes. 152.
Freed from all diseases and with a pure mind, one may live;
the means for conquering the vital breath (pavana) is the gazing at the tip of the nose.
The wind situated in the center of the navel, at the tip of the nose, and in the center of the navel—the wind situated in the center of the navel indeed leads to the destruction of disease. (154)
And by fixing the mind on the two thumbs, there arises supreme lightness of the body;
one is slowly suspended by the wind through the very cavity of the bird’s beak. 155.
Fatigue, burning sensations, and the like would not occur, and his body would become firm.
At the time of Agastya’s rising, however, [one should recite] from between the two "royal teeth" (the upper and lower incisors). || 156 ||
The Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) performs the inhalation of air for two seasons;
by means of those two seasons, diseases undoubtedly go to their destruction. || 157 ||
Having brought [the breath] to the root of the tongue, by obstructing its base, the yogi who drinks the nectar attains all perfections. (153)
Having brought consciousness into the center of the two bows,
one should [meditate] upon that supreme [state], which removes all diseases through the drinking of nectar.
Or, having drawn the wind through the two channels into the navel and the stomach, by holding it for the duration of one ghaṭikā, [the result is attained] after only one month. || 160 ||
With firm limbs and a purified self, he too is liberated from diseases;
for one month, during the three junctions of the day, he should drink the vital air (māruta) with his tongue. (161)

Furthermore, for one who [visualizes] the deity composed of nectar at the navel and also on both its sides, there arise abdominal tumors, stones, splenic disorders, and other such ailments, as well as various afflictions of the limbs. (162)
Whatever diseases exist within the belly, they all go to destruction;
poison, fever, and even death—all these go to destruction. (163)
The hand becomes like a pair of tongs and the eye becomes like that of Garuḍa;
all this indeed results from practice and is truly the victory over the vital air (vāyu). 164.
Seated in the svastika posture with a concentrated mind, having brought the senses under control and withdrawn them from their objects. (165)
With the neck uplifted, one should perform breath control while continuously drawing up the anus;
having once expelled everything, one should slowly follow the path of the *kampuli*. (166)
One should contract that [mantra] of the speaker as before with the *praṇava*,
and one should bind it with the two hands as the fire of the cause, like finger-rings.
One should hold it covered until the conclusion of the gift; and especially on the crown of the head, the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyamana) is supreme. 168.
The movement of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) occurs within the Suṣumnā at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
by that means, the resonance (nāda) arises, pure and stainless like crystal.
The splendor of this sound exists from the base up to the head like the neck of a lute;
at first there is the sound of a conch, and in the middle, the continuous sound of thunderclouds.
Afterwards, when the wind has entered the aperture of space, one becomes the best among the gods;
when the wind has entered the lunar aperture and abides in eternal consciousness. (171)
Constantly joined with bliss, by that means the wind (vital breath) becomes conquered;
one devoted to prāṇāyāma becomes pure, free from both exhalation and inhalation. || 172 ||
Pressing with the left ankle the two veins of the scrotum, one should place the right [foot] on top of them all.
O Nandin, between the shanks and thighs, the messenger [of breath] should be without gaps;
from both eyes it reaches the left ankle, situated above the axle.
One should utter the full resonance (nāda) with the mantra preceded by the Praṇava. 175.
This [practice] on a seat is especially equal to the lamp-in-the-hand [posture];
it brings about lightness of the body and increases the digestive fire. (176)
Then, having perceived the signs, one should restrain the vital breath (māruta) within the center of the Suṣumnā channel; thereafter, the mind indeed attains dissolution.
Therefore, at that time, one should observe moderation in eating in the midst of the flow of the channels;
by this very means, through the gradual retention of the vital winds, one becomes established in the middle state.
The awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs through the fire joined with the vital wind (pavana);
having fallen from her own place, she extends the body of the serpent-king.
The wheel at the base of the navel suddenly awakens, and the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) proceeds to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) via the Suṣumṇā. || 180 ||
Within that interval, having uttered the *tāra* with the mind, one should fix [the breath];
then one should fix it on the region of the heart, again on the ear, on the *bhrama*, and on the wind. || 181 ||
O Nandikeśvara, having gradually drawn that fire of life (prāṇāgni) from there along with the mind, one should hold it by uttering [the mantra] all at once.
There, in that sky filled with Maruts, he was endowed with all limbs;
having cultivated his self-nature there, he appeared in the firmament like the orb of the sun.
Having formed the resolve for the upward departure (*utkrānti*), one should practice the yoga correctly;
with the long *prāsāda* [mantra], one should utter it at the tip of the nose. (184)

Having become composed in mind, the knower of yoga should mentally project [the breath] through the aperture of Brahmā at the crown of the head; he should utter the Praṇavas while the great vital breath is in the middle channel.
Having united one's own self with Śiva— who transcends the body, who is the life-force of the universe, and who consists of eternal bliss— there is no further rebirth. (186)
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) at various times, especially at specific intervals;
for there is nothing equal to breath control for the pacification of all sins. 187.
This offering which belongs to him should enunciate the withdrawal [of the senses];
it is the forceful drawing back from objects such as sound and the rest. (188)
When that very [mind] is withdrawn from those [objects], he is then liberated;
he perceives everything as suitable and all that as being within himself in due order. (189)
Furthermore, withdrawal (pratyāhāra) as well as the performance of daily rites (nityakarman)—that which one perceives within oneself alone constitutes their true practice. || 190 ||
(557) And that would constitute withdrawal (pratyāhāra) even without the mind directed toward external objects;
among the fourfold yogas, Śivayoga is the most preeminent. || 191 ||
The withdrawal from each respective stage among the eighteen stages of action is pratyāhāra; thus, it is said to be fourfold.
Now hear, in due order, the locations of the eighteen vital points (marmas):
having extended the two big toes, the second [pair] would be the two ankles. (193)
The third [should be placed] in the middle of the shanks; the fourth is based on the *cintya* [lotus]; the fifth is the pair of knees; and after that, the pair of thighs. (194)
The seventh is the root of the thighs, the eighth is the root of the feet;
the ninth is the mūlādhāra, and beyond that is the adhiṣṭhāna.
The eleventh is [the letter] *ya*, while the twelfth would be [the letter] *ra*.
The thirteenth is purity (*viśuddhi*), and the fourteenth is the root of the palate (*tālumūla*). (196)
The sixteenth [vowel] is in the eyes, and the [consonants] are in the middle;
the forehead is known as the seventeenth, and the head as the eighteenth. (197)
Now hear in order the locations for these eighteen vital points (marmans):
four [fingers] and a half, and the measure of two thumbs. 198.
In the same way, the middle of the shank should be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure;
the base of the position of the lower part of the shank is traditionally recorded as eleven finger-breadths (rudrāṅgula).
The measurement from the two joined fingers [of the hand] to the knees is likewise;
then, O Nandin, the distance from the middle of the thighs to the base of the Guru is nine finger-breadths.
The middle *mūlādhāra* is said to be two and a half finger-breadths in extent.
Above that, one should know the region of the penis to be two and a half finger-breadths;
from the penis to the navel, it is again ten and a half finger-breadths. || 202 ||
O Nandikeśvara, from the navel to the middle of the heart is fourteen finger-breadths;
from that middle to the end of the throat-pit is six finger-breadths.
The root of the tongue is four finger-breadths above the throat;
the base of the nose is likewise four finger-breadths from the root of the tongue. || 204 ||
The location of the eye, measured from its base, shall be half a finger-breadth;
the middle of the two bows (the eyebrows) shall be seven finger-breadths, in that sequence.
O Nandikeśvara, above that, the forehead should be three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula);
from the forehead to the brahmarandhra, it is likewise said to be three finger-breadths.
In these locations, one should practice the movement of the vital air with the mind;
withdrawing it from each location to the next, one should practice this daily.
Diseases go to destruction and yogis attain union.
O Nandikeśvara, listen as I speak again of pratyāhāra.
Holding the breath through the nose by means of the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, one should retain the wind from the big toe up to the crown of the head like a full jar.
Having drawn [the breath] from the aperture of space (vyomarandhra), one should lead it down as far as the forehead;
and from the forehead, O Nandikeśvara, one should restrain it between the two eyebrows.
One should likewise obstruct [the breath] at each of the ten locations starting from this point; one should also obstruct it at the feet, extending as far as the big toes. (211)
Drawing [the senses] from their respective locations, one should hold them with perfect concentration;
thus does this wise person perform pratyāhāra. || 212 ||
One may burn [the world] until the moon and stars perish; one lives once the noose and the goad are removed.
Having filled the wind through the two channels (nāḍīs) on both sides of Kuṇḍalinī— || 213 ||
The practitioner of sacrifice who should hold [the breath] simultaneously is liberated from saṃsāra;
O Nandikeśvara, one should hold it after filling it within the heart.
One should indeed reveal to him the true nature of supreme bliss; what more need be said? At that very moment, his disease shall go to destruction.
Having drawn in the breath through both nostrils and filled it so that it resides in the abdomen,
[one should draw it] from the middle of the bow of the eyebrows and immediately after the pair of breasts. (216)
Having raised and sustained it, the yogi gradually attains the supreme state;
having raised the vital breath (prāṇamāruta) of his own self as far as the midpoint between the eyebrows.
O Ānandikeśvara, one should perform this according to the prescribed rule until the mind indeed attains dissolution within the aperture of the Suṣumṇā.
The conjunction with the locus of knowledge is called its retention (*dhāraṇā*).
It is of five kinds; now, listen to them. (219)
The stabilization of the mind within oneself, characterized by qualities such as restraint (yama) and the rest,
is likewise declared to be "dhāraṇā" when it is firmly established in the region of the navel.
In the center of the space of the heart, one should visualize the bearer of the external space;
or else, the earth-element situated from the feet up to the knees. (221)
The water element is established from the knees down to the anus;
starting from the location of the anus up to the heart, it is joined with fire.
Beginning from the Unstruck (anāhata) and extending to the middle of the two bows, it is declared to be the principle of air (vāyutatva); above that, up to the end, is space (ambaram).
Likewise, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) occurs in sequence through the causes, the sins, the five groups of digits, and especially through the paths. || 224 ||
One should clearly visualize the Brahma-nāḍī from the feet up to the crown of the head as being yellow,
white, red, and like a vajra.
Resembling pure crystal, located separately in five places,
it is a mass of radiance, the nature of consciousness, and the pentad of causes. (226)
Having meditated in this manner, the yogi should gradually withdraw [the breath] from place to place;
he should hold it for five *ghaṭikās* in sequence at the station of Brahmā.
Having taken that accumulation of fire, one should withdraw it into the station of Viṣṇu;
and in the station of Viṣṇu, for five *ghaṭikās* at a time, separately.
Having drawn [the breath] up as far as Sadāśiva, one should join it at the station of knowledge (jñānasthāna).
And if it should be otherwise, then it must be performed in another location.
For one who loves their son, milk flows; at the end of suffering, there is the shedding of tears.
But when the host of senses flows for the sake of desire and wealth, the bliss of knowledge arises. || 230 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should not meditate on anything above nor on anything else; for *dhyai* and *cintā* denote the root meaning of "unwavering knowledge. (231)
But when the flesh is cast into the target, especially along with the path [of the breath], there arise sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—the six objects of the senses. (232)
One should perceive the dwelling in its own place, the equal release of wealth, death, the state of an immortal body, and the excellent star of the Guru’s splendor. (233)
Having abandoned the pairs of opposites, one who exerts every effort for six months shall subsequently attain bliss and master the Vedas and the Shastras. (234)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, concerning the procedure for the eightfold yoga, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall here declare the divine *rasāyana*, well-expounded in this tantra,
for the benefit of yogins and especially for those possessed of knowledge. (1)
For it has been said, "He is indeed essence (rasa)"; therefore, he is called Śiva. The virility of Maheśa, who possesses eight forms, is declared to be rasa. || 2 ||
One who constantly practices this vigor, endowed with devotion, becomes as powerful as Śiva and is worthy of worship by those residing in the world of Śiva and other realms. || 3 ||
The sight of the king of elixirs yields that fruit over seven lifetimes;
the sin committed during seven births is certainly destroyed by the mere sight of it.
By touching [it], O Nandin, one destroys even the sin of killing a cow; of this there is no doubt.
Even those who have committed sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, the murder of women, or the slaughter of children [are purified].
By the consumption of the ash of mercury, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
But the sick man remains sick and does not become a knower, according to the entire teaching of Kālapāda. (6)
Planets bestow desired results only when they are in their own country and time;
however, in another country or at another time, those very same planets become causes of undesirable results. (7)
In the Vaināśika yoga, in the asterism of death, in the eight-and-a-half asterisms,
in his own natal asterism, and especially at the beginning of the Vipat period and so forth— || 8 ||
In the eighth sign from that very [ascendant], the actions such as death are measured by the constellations Yama, Āśleṣā, Agni, Śraviṣṭhā, Vāruṇa, and Maghā. (9)
One should avoid Jyeṣṭhā and the three Pūrva-nakṣatras in rites for prosperity; likewise, Saturday and Tuesday should be avoided.
(568) For an enemy, the performance of delusion and other [sorcery] would be a praiseworthy evil deed;
for those who revile the triad beginning with Śiva, this is the supreme means of accomplishment.
By this very procedure, vomiting shall then occur;
on the desired day, one should perform all auspicious rites for the performer. (12)
For stealing gold, one should give double [the amount] for the sake of Śiva;
by reciting the Aghora mantra nine hundred thousand times, one shall attain purification.
Those men who do not rejoice in the worship of Śiva’s peak, who do not bow even upon seeing it, and who do not praise it with heedfulness; || 19 ||
Those who do not perform ritual service in the presence of Śiva, the fire, or the Guru,
even if they are devoted to and attached to devotion for Śiva, are indeed the most sinful of men.
When the reviling of Śiva is completed, that indeed shall be the expiation. Those who, having honored the knowledge of Śiva, study it and write it down... (21)
Even one who hears or reads the lineage of gurus and disciples, or even sells it for profit, or is devoted to other forms of knowledge; || 22 ||

Even if one possesses the capacity, if one places [the teaching] in an unsuitable location, does not study it, and instead engages in other chatter while neglecting the discourse on the knowledge of Śiva, [one fails]. 23.
Even after performing worship, one should indeed disparage it by remaining silent; for everything is equal to the sleep of knowledge, and thus purification is prescribed.
Without having performed worship of the Guru, one studies the knowledge of Śiva;
likewise, [one must possess] service, devotion, faith, and the avoidance of hypocrisy. (25)
One who neglects out of greed would abandon a kinsman, a beloved person, or even one who has gone to another land, as well as one who is being oppressed by enemies. (26)
By insulting his wife, his son, or his friend;
by insulting his elder brother; and by defiling the sister of one's maternal uncle. (27)
O Nandikeśvara, it has been declared that all acts such as disparaging one's own lineage, criticizing the meaning of words, or mutual reviling are equal to the reviling of one's guru. (28)
One should perform this perpetual rite for one's father, mother, and others, as well as the single offering of wealth,
in the auspicious directions with an inconceivable number of knots.
One may have little intelligence yet be wise; one may have little vigor yet possess great strength. || 30 ||
p.
571) For one whose intellect is highly developed in alchemy (*rasāyana*) as well as in the *rasa* [tattva], there will indeed be the attainment of everything; of this there is no doubt. (31)
For those whose intellect has perished, the knowledge of tastes is difficult to attain;
therefore, those fools who claim that truth is known through direct perception [are mistaken]. (32)
Merely by being honored by him, it becomes equal to the worship of the Liṅga;
all diseases shall perish when the mercury is exalted through devotion.
Alternatively, if a man should always consume it combined with ashes,
he too enjoys the three worlds and becomes undecaying and immortal.
When the ash of the deceased has been consumed according to this procedure, such a result as this arises for that practitioner. (35)
It destroys wind, bile, phlegm, and the like; of this there is no doubt. It cures the pain of abdominal tumors (gulma) and subdues the influence of malevolent planets and spirits. (36)
It cures deafness as well as discharges, and removes the pain of toothaches; it also cures blindness, film over the eye, cataracts, most terrible diseases, and fistula-in-ano.
There are eighty-four types of piercing pain (śūla), eighteen types of head ailments,
one hundred and eight types of fever, and likewise eighteen types of spider-bites (lūtā).
The most terrible diseases of blood and bile (raktapitta) go to destruction without a doubt;
as do epilepsy, the grahas, and those grahas who are yakṣas and rākṣasas. (39)
Eighty-eight thousand beings who seize [the body] turn back upon eating the ashes of one who has cast them off; thus are the *grahas*.
By means of a single fruit, the ash of a woman may belong to yogins;
a man who has indigestion should consume that which accomplishes the unrefined [state]. (41)
That man of wicked conduct is a slayer of a Brahmin, a great traitor, and a suicide;
for thousands of crores of kalpas, and even for hundreds of crores of kalpas [he remains there].
In that terrible Raurava hell, and also in the most dreadful Suduḥsvara hell,
he drank [blood] and his own flesh was eaten by him as he was tormented by hunger.

Therefore, with every effort, one should not consume the "child-born" (bālasūta). Mercury (pārada) is of two kinds: that which possesses seed (sabīja) and that which is devoid of seed (bījahīna). || 44 ||
Devoid of refinement and seedless, it is not joined with [anything];
yet, when possessed of seed and accompanied by the consumption of mindfulness, it is joined with gold, jewels, and very sharp [iron].
The Lord himself is the direct bestower of curses and favors;
by him who has consumed the three fruits, a man becomes capable of assuming any form at will. (46)
The sweat produced from its limbs indeed penetrates the eight metals;
then one should consume all that divine gold, which has thus become pure.
One attains the power of assuming any form at will and takes on the nature of elephants and other such beings;
whatever state one desires is achieved when the golden ash is consumed.
There is one subtle defect when the birth of a child is consumed [by a spirit]: when the twenty-first day has arrived, the child becomes intensely copper-eyed. (49)
One may agitate a thousand passionate women within a single day;
O Nandīśa, the essence lies in the bodily movement during union with a woman.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not indulge in the service of women;
rather, one should always properly consume mercury-ash (rasabhasma), increasing the dose further and further. || 51 ||
And one attains the great siddhi; there is no need for deliberation here.
A worldly person, for the sake of destroying sins, should consume it very little by very little. (52)
For the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) who practices the path taught by Viṣṇu, there is no doubt that he attains the eight perfections beginning with atomization (aṇimā) in due course. || 53 ||
Even one who is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) especially attains the perfection of concentration (dhāraṇā) and yoga;
however, having released [the time for] that, he should especially consume mercury (pārada), the Guru.
Therefore, every light action is to be performed; indeed, consumption [of these] is an elixir.

The light of the sun’s rays is clearly present during the portion of the night; since these times of day are characterized by the perception of twilight light, this [practice] is not to be abandoned by us. || 55 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, concerning the procedure for the elixir, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.

576) Now I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the six supports (ādhāra). It is taught that the supported (ādheya) is of six kinds; such is the definition of support and supported. || 1 ||
They say the anus is the Ādhāra; the Svādhiṣṭhāna is the secret place (guhya);
the Maṇipūra is at the navel, and the heart is the Anāhata.
Purity is in the region of the throat, while the Command (ājñā) is indeed between the eyebrows;
this is declared to be the support of the lotus, and that which is supported is the six-syllable mantra.
The knower of yoga should contemplate the impurity located at the region known as the *mūlādhāra*, the knot of the *ma* syllable,
situated between the anus and the genitals; he should meditate upon the fourteen letters ending with the letter *sa*.
The *haṃsa*, the *tāra*, and the *śakti*— supreme and resembling the sound of a conch—
followed by the humming of a bee, which is the very nature of the *parāśakti*. (6)
It is called the foundational lotus; thus it is the secret abode of Śiva.
Its seed-syllable is the letter of space (Ha), radiant with a brilliance like that of the sun.
Above that is the Svādhiṣṭhāna, a radiant six-petaled lotus,
endowed with strength and splendor, possessing the luster of clear water.
Exalted in its color, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
it ends with the letter *ḍha* and consists of a flood of ten syllables possessing the splendor of the rising sun.
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon the lotus called Maṇipūra, which has ten petals, is brilliantly radiant,
and is conjoined with the seed-syllable of Krodhīśa.
Above that, one should visualize a lotus with twelve petals in the very center,
[adorned] with the multitude of twelve syllables ending in *kaṭha*, which possess the radiance of a thousand rays.
The resonance (nāda) is held to be the support known as the Unstruck (anāhata);
that seed-syllable, conjoined with the seed of Indra, has the luster of yellow orpiment.
It is conjoined with the sixteenth vowel, united with that which is called Viśuddha,
resembling pure crystal, and joined with the seed-syllable of the letter *ṭha*.
And in the lotus called Ājñā, between the eyebrows, there is a two-petaled water-lily,
joined with the letter *akṣa* (kṣa) and brilliantly illuminated by the letter *repha* (ra).
One should meditate upon that which is joined with the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, and endowed with Śakti;
it is united with the junctions of the six paths and is the activator of all awakening. || 15 ||
(579) Endowed with the nectar-like essence of knowledge, this supreme means for attaining liberation is proclaimed as having six supports; it is obtained through the mouth of the Guru. 16.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, concerning the procedure for the six supports, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall describe the ritual of the nine supports; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
The first is declared to be the *ādhāra* (the foundation), and the second is the *svādhiṣṭhāna* (the self-abiding).
The third is Maṇipūra, while the fourth is the heart;
one should contemplate the fifth, called Viśuddhi, at the root of the throat. (2)
The lotus of action is at the root of the palate; it is supreme, joined with the divine tip.
The staff of the self strikes the middle; this is the seventh, the reflection of knowledge.
The forehead is declared to be the eighth, which is endowed with the lunar disks;
above that, O Nandikeśvara, is the ninth, the Brahma-randhra.

Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending up to the *viśuddhi*, as before, the triad of spheres consisting of the powers of action (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and will (*icchā*) is likewise [to be visualized]. (5)
Each [petal] has sixteen petals, each possesses the sixteen vowels, joined with the bindu, nāda, and kalā; this is the accumulation of the nectar of supreme bliss.
Above that, however, is the supreme location of the head, consisting entirely of splendor;
there, too, shall be a petal with three hundred and sixty segments.
Having the form of a downward-facing bud, with four petals hanging down,
it is the Great Lotus of the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti), difficult to attain even for the gods.
Having meditated thus, the yogi gradually attains liberation;
[he becomes] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (9)
Knowing this, the yogi is always the very embodiment of Śiva.
Now listen to [the description of] Kuṇḍalinī, from the Ādhāra up to the Pradhāna. || 10 ||
Thus, she who consists of all powers is firmly established in the beginning, middle, and end;
if she, residing within the awn of the wild rice grain, were sown, she would take the form of a serpent.
When consciousness is joined with Śiva, who is higher than the highest,
she is the supreme power who distinguishes and awakens all the supports without exception.
She is the stream of the nectar of natural outflow, whose very nature is her own power;
she pierces the three mandalas and is triple-circular like the syllable TĀRA. 13.
Having meditated thus, the yogi, ever intent upon it, [should contemplate] the nine supports;
thereafter, that goddess Kuṇḍalinī, showering nectar, [unites with] Śiva. (14)
Nourishing everywhere and bestowing both spiritual accomplishments and liberation,
the goddess Mūlakuṇḍalinī beheld the mantras and seed-syllables.
One should drink the memory of those various forms conjoined with the excrement of wine;
thus is Kuṇḍalī described, which is exceedingly profound and of great excellence.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, concerning the ritual of the Kuṇḍalinī of the Nine Supports, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Nandikeśvara said:
O Lord, first [tell me] the origin of all the imperishable syllables (akṣara);
from the Imperishable (Akṣara) everything is born, due to the absence of the state of being perishable (kṣara). || 1 ||
p.
583) For this very reason, according to the sequence of phoneme-compression (pratyāhāra), the syllables from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa* arise from the letters of the Mātṛkā. || 2 ||
From the supreme space within the heart-lotus of Sādākhya, the time-unit (tuṭi) arises from the Supreme Nāda as a resonant vibration.
Endowed with ten *tuṭis*, the *bindu* becomes superior to the *nāda*;
and by being joined with that time, the *bindu* arises from the supreme *bindu*.
The seed-syllable arises from the Bindu, and therein especially;
yet, in the state of childhood of the seed-syllable, Parāvāṇī is fully manifested.
When she has reached youth, her form is indeed doubled;
when one perceives her splendor as tripled, she becomes a woman of middle youth.

Having attained the form of *vaikharī* speech and being endowed with a single measure (*mātrā*), this syllable is called by the name [of the letter], possessing both long and short durations through its *kalā*s.
It is said that [the vowel] is pervaded by the three forms; it is called "long" when it has two forms.
Through the divisions of will, knowledge, and action, that bindu becomes threefold.
The letter *a* arises from the *kriyā-bindu*, and it is the most excellent of all;
the letter *ā*, which has the nature of stability, arises from the *jñāna-bindu*.
The form arising from the *icchābindu* is the means for attaining liberation;
through the union of the letters *a* and *u*, the supreme golden syllable *oṃ* is produced. (10)
When the syllable *tāra* (OM) is joined with the letter *ma*, thus arising,
and conjoined with these three syllables, it becomes the sound of the Brahman.
Just as the emergence [of fire] occurs through churning within the midst of the letters at the beginning,
so too does the production of nectar arise solely from churning in one place.
Rava, dhvani, anusvāra, and visarga—these five phonemes are praised, arising in sequence from the letter 'a'. (13)
The three syllables beginning with Oṃ are indeed produced from the letter U;
likewise, the letters from Ka to Bha are truly born from the letter Ma.
The four castes originate from the sound of the letter *ya*, and likewise, all [consonants] from *śa* to *bha* arise from the resonance. (15)
Because there is no distinction between the two *lalas*, and also due to the union of the two eyes, the arising of the two *lalas* was already explained previously. (16)
(586) Through the pervasive extension of the God of gods, the pervasion of the phonemes is proclaimed;
furthermore, the origin of all phonemes is held to proceed from the form of the Praṇava.
The three principles (tritatva), the three worlds (triloka), and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are of the nature of the Praṇava;
they consist of the letters from 'A' to 'KṢa', each distinct from the others.
The specific [forms] are considered to consist of vehicles, seats, forms, and so forth; their colors, according to the elements, are transparent, reddish, white, and yellow. (19)
The bodies, beginning with the short and long ones, armored and weapon-bearing, remain even now;
they end with the comets, their colors being equal to coral.
With Vaiḍūrya, Puṣya, Vajrendra, Nīla, Gomedaka, and Gāruḍa [gems],
he has eight eyes and arms, and his body extends for four hundred thousand yojanas.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, his garments fragrant with sandalwood;
possessing a majestic luster that draws all beings, he is profound and armed with bracelets.
Akāra has the color of a stone from Vṛttāsana and rides upon a tortoise;
he is seated on a discus, resembles a wheel, is adorned with pearls, and holds a chisel.
Two-faced, one hundred thousand leagues in extent, his form is borne by goats;
he is four-armed, three-eyed, a Kṣatriya, and yet neuter.
This [letter] 'I' (ikāra) is extensive in its expanse, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli;
it moves slowly near a lotus, is sweet, and holds a pair of lotuses.
It is like the day, possesses fragrance, and has a swan as its vehicle. (26)
And [he saw] Klastrāsana, two-armed, with a trident in his hand and a harsh voice;
having drawn forth the scent of saffron-robes, his body was adorned. (27)
The triangular seat brings about the destruction of pride; it is bound with deerskin.
The square seat is sweet; it holds the noose and the vajra of Kapila.
He has golden ornaments, matted hair, and two thighs that are slightly bent;
he has four arms and three eyes, and wears a pearl necklace and a sacred thread.
He has a serene gaze, is auspicious, and is dear to the heart with his crown of matted hair;
he holds a sword and a discus, and possesses a sweet, peacock-feathered [ornament].
Ten yojanas in height, his mount is named Cakravāka;
he has three seats, is dark-colored, possesses two arms, and holds a trident and a vajra.
The essence of passion is the letter *e*;
its taste is sweet; it resembles molten gold; and its fragrance is *trivṛt*. (32)
He is all-pervading, omnipotent, the one to be worshipped by all, and born from the lotus; he is the creator of all, the sustainer of all, and the author of the scriptures for all the deities.
The transformer of all forms, the wise one, difficult to perceive,
with arms facing in every direction like the syllable Om, he whose vehicle is the bull.
Seated in the *vṛtta* posture, with four arms and a yellow speech, they are exceedingly powerful;
holding a vajra and a noose, they possess a sweet saffron hue and the fragrance of flowers. (35)
He is the abode, the sweat, the impurity, the bearer of the trident and the mace, the terrible and difficult to cross,
the destroyer of bonds, the one of beautiful form, and the one whose vehicle is the sword.
Clad in yellow garlands, perfumes, and ointments, with a steady gait and beautiful eyes,
he wears a crown of matted hair, carries a trident and a mace, and has the thunderbolt as his weapon. (37)
A man who is a divine ornament, a universal monarch, a preeminent kṣatriya,
measuring one thousand [in extent], possessing six corners and six lakhs of gardens.
The letter Ka, joined with the flower of Bhajavāhanastambhana, is declared to have Indra as its presiding deity; it is the supreme among syllables. (39)
The Vyāla-brāhmaṇa, who is considered to have thirty crores [of attendants], has another presiding deity;
he is equipped with spears and javelins, and is adorned with auspicious garlands and unguents.
The letter *kha* is golden, known as the sky-goer (*khagama*), and is said to be ash;
it is a masculine vowel, the sound of a conch, incense, and speech, white-robed, and of serene intellect. (41)
Adorned with pearl ornaments, two-armed, and holding a fruit and a lotus,
he is seated upon a lotus throne, borne by a virtuous swan, and possesses a serene intellect. (42)
In the tenth position from Mālya is the letter Na, whose presiding deity is Yakṣa;
it is like Vyāsa, characterized by darkness, devoid of power, and possessing a broken, raspy sound. || 43 ||
Kaṭhoragandha, Kṣāra, Raudradṛṣṭi, Napuṃsaka, Uṣṭra, Oṣṭa, Aṣṭaka, Mathapīṭha, Vidvān, Dhūmra, and Mahābala. || 44 ||
Śūrpāsa, Kākavāha, and Durgandhasvarasaṃśraya. || 45 ||
Yama, the neuter, the spear, the javelin, and the battle-axe;
he who bears these, as well as the thousand-rayed sun, the fire, and the earth. 46.
He has four arms and bears matted locks, a crown, a garland, a conch, and a lotus. || 47 ||
He possesses the gait of Yama and the Asuras, is marked by both male and female characteristics, yet has a beloved form;
he is a thousand crores in extent and is adorned with jewel ornaments.

The twice-born one is the day of the sun during the month of Nṛpla, possesses a great fragrance and voice, bears a spear and a thunderbolt, is adorned with pearls, and has Varuṇa as his presiding deity. || 49 ||
Puṣpāda, Amṛtagandha, Sāhasra, Vāruṇa, Jaṭī, Makuṭī, Jakāra, and likewise Dhukāra. (50)
He was borne by crows, black in color, a performer of evil deeds, and impotent; he held a chisel, was cruel, terrible, and moved with a roar that reached for a yojana. || 51 ||
(593) Sarvaraudra is the destroyer of Śiva; Aryaman has swift hands for us.
Sanātana is the essence of nectar, Kāla is [the one who] ... he is the two-armed person. || 52 ||
Madana, Varṇa, Vajradhṛk, and Vajravarṇadhṛk;
Vyāla, Upavītī, Candra, and Daivakāṣṭhu are proclaimed [as the names]. (53)
Gajavāha, Dhanuṣpīṭha, Śaṅkhacakranibha, Mṛta, Vajrapadmāyudha, Jambūdvīpamāna, and Surakṣita.
Saṃka possesses a sweet fragrance; Kovera is stationed on the lip;
Kaustubha is a man with a ram as his vehicle who bears a very sweet scent. || 55 ||

He is beloved by the Vidyādharas, fierce, possessing power equal to the fire of cosmic destruction (Kālāgni), the subduer of the senses, sweet-smelling, and known as [the one whose name ends in] -ka. || 56 ||
He has the body of a *bhiṇḍipāla* (javelin), possesses a vajra, and wields the supreme weapon of fear;
he is a thousand *yojanas* in extent, whose abode is truth, and who is the presiding deity. || 57 ||
Wearing a crown of matted hair and holding two types of shields,
that man was ten thousand yojanas in height, and another was half of that, and yet another half of that again.
He has four arms, holds a hammer and an axle, possesses ten million sacrifices, and has a wolf as his vehicle.
He is adorned with divine ornaments, is fragrant, is the source of wealth, and is the deity of the letter *ṛ*.
He is fierce, pungent, sweet, and savory; he is the six-faced one himself. (60)
Holding a ṭaṅka, a goad, a bow, a staff, a noose, a trident, and a musuṇḍi, and bearing a tomara, the southern [face] is accompanied by grace. 61.
One who has such a love for the burden of the far-reaching [path], he is that one:
neuter, black in color, with an upward-pointing heart and a cruel mount. || 62 ||
He has a cruel sound, the scent of raw meat, and wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) all over.
He is a man who rides upon a dove, and he has a noseless face.
He is twenty-four [finger-breadths] in height, is fierce, and carries a water-pot (*ghaṭī*) and a *muṣuṇḍī* weapon.
Rudra is with Sitapavara, and Nairṛta is Dhūrārthin and Dhūr. || 65 ||
The neuter [gender] has a height and breadth of one hundred [units], possesses two arms, has the voice of a crow, wears black garments, has a variegated face, and has disheveled hair. (66)
Clad in an upper garment of tiger skin, wielding a plough, and performing fierce deeds;
known as Madhu, Guggulu, and Taila, he is a man who is harsh in speech. (67)
The letter 'ma' is declared to have a wicked appearance; its presiding deity is Yama.
It possesses ten rays, is radiant, and holds a lotus of honeyed knowledge.
He possesses all weapons, has four arms, and has Garuḍa as his vehicle;
he is adorned with a forgotten sword-sheath sixty million fathoms in length.
He who is worshipped with oblations of clarified butter as if by serpents, who is the pervasive one adored by the gods and others,
the man who is perfected, possessing the luster of lightning, is Gāruḍa, seated upon a lotus.

The man named Ugraprabha, who had ten crores as his circumference, was a giver of desired boons; he possessed ten times ten times eight times ten million faults, yet he was a tortoise-like one who was sweet in his speech.
With the sacred thread suspended over the right shoulder (muktopavītī), bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
seated upon Gaṇeśa, and possessing the fragrance of flowers— this is declared to be the letter *va*. (72)
The Kaṭaka, Niprayola, Lakṣa, Viṣṭhura, Tvara, Umābheda, Dhūma, Ūrdhvavaktra, and Napuṃsaka [are the types of mountains]. || 73 ||
The letter Bha has Raudra as its presiding deity and Nairṛta as its overlord;
it is compassionate in nature, a source of joy, the Supreme Person, and seated upon a lotus. 74.
May there be infinite compassion for all kalpas by the divine power;
may the snake, the earth, the asuras, the illustrious one, the swift one, the intoxicant, the sorrowful one, and the twice-born be [favorable]. (75)
The letter *va* represents conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth, while *gha* represents a horse; this [syllable] is neuter.
The letter *dha* has the color of *dūrvā* grass and is declared to have Yama as its presiding deity.
The letter *ra* (repha), which has twelve suns as its nature, measures ten million, is neuter,
resides in the triangle, belongs to the fire element, and has a buffalo for its vehicle. (77)
The King (Pārthiva) has a mace in his hand and possesses the power to paralyze women and to make them yellow;
he is white with red spots, possesses the female gender, and has a fish as his vehicle.
Varuṇa is the letter *Vā*, who brings about subjugation (*vaśya*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and the production of stable colors.
He is remembered as having ten arms and being very tall, even five thousand [yojanas] in height;
he is feminine in gender, sweet-voiced, the sun, and has four arms.
Wearing red garments, he is the beloved of the forest. || 81 ||

Clad in red garments, seated upon a lotus throne, and holding a conch and a discus in his hands—this is the primary ritual procedure for subjugation and attraction; through it, one bestows a peaceful gaze. (82)
The male [deity] has the luster of a peacock's neck; he is the slayer of enemies and holds a noose and a vajra.
From Lakṣāyatas come Kaṣkabhas, who are born from the seat of Kūrmavāha; they resemble the stalks of a lotus bud and possess the fragrance of musk. 84.
Then there was a man with red lips and eight arms, bearing a conch and a mace as weapons;
he was a hundred thousand cubits tall, broad-chested, and adorned with ornaments of lapis lazuli.
He is Kauberī and Madhura, and he wears a crown of matted locks;
he is Śveta and Śvetāṅkuśa, the all-pervading, and the neuter.
(600) Possessing all weapons, the creator of all, with a gentle fragrance and slow-moving;
he has Śrī as his presiding deity, knows the proper time for women, is all-knowing, and the letter *śa* is everywhere. 87.
He is masculine in form, yellow in color, and extensive in measure; he sits upon a square throne, is adorned with all ornaments and garlands, and has an elephant as his vehicle. || 88 ||
Bearing the thunderbolt, conch, discus, mace, noose, and *muṣuṇḍi* weapon,
he is honored by the earth as he strides past the *laṣṭya*, Garuḍa, and Gandharva in succession.
The peak-syllable is the letter *kṣa*, the seed-mantra which is neuter;
it possesses the forms of leaves, fragrance, and taste, along with vehicles and weapons.
The nature of the moth species and that which is taught as distinct from the state [of bondage]—these too, through the dissolution of their conjunction, attain the vehicle of the soul. || 91 ||
O Goddess, may the discordance of the forms of the deities be stilled by your illusion,
just as a charioteer crosses over a multitude of enemies by leaping across their union.
Redness also arises from the combination of lac, resin, and *sakṣu* juice;
furthermore, other colors are produced by the specific application of various pigments according to their respective capacities. || 93 ||
However, by means of the differentiation of qualities such as *kalā* and so forth, a single mantra alone may bring about both prosperity and misfortune for oneself or for another. (94)
In creation, maintenance, and the fierce [aspect], as well as in liberation through knowledge, the sixteen vowels are the causes;
they are gentle, especially in the six-syllable mantra.
And Hāsva is indeed the form of the Sun; from that [source] come these syllables:
the letter Kṣa, the letter Va, the letter Ṭha, and the fourth, Ka. (96)
From the atom smaller than the smallest, and from the dust finer than dust, the world of moving and unmoving beings has been obtained;
yet even from the atom smaller than the smallest, there is no [substance] finer than the sun's rays.
Its long vowels are Sūryā; [then] the syllables *uṃ*, *gu*, *daṃ*, *ca*, *ra*, *dīn* are called the forest-syllables (*vanyākṣara*). (p. 602)
Ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, and the vowels beginning with 'a' up to 'lā' are indeed the internal [vowels] starting from 'ma'. || 98 ||
The letters of the fire-mantra are *va*, *ta*, and *ra*; the seed-syllable of the moon is *ha*.
This tri-syllabic form represents the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
The locations of the digits (kalās) beginning with Earth shall be described starting from the Mūlādhāra;
they are Sṛṣṭi, Rūḍhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, and likewise Svadhā.
Dhṛti and Ṛddhi are proclaimed as those born from the stage of Kalā;
[the others are] Sthirā, Vyapālinī, Śānti, Aiśvarī, Mamakā, and Rati. (101)
O Kṛṣṇa, Prīti is mental, while Dīrghā has ten arts;
Madhyā is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī) and deluding (mohanī), and Candrākṣī is wrathful out of fear. || 102 ||
Yellow, white, reddish, and black—these four arise from the wind. || 103 ||
Indrikā, Vikramā, Mohinī, Recikā, the other [Māyā], Mṛtajñānā, Vyāpinī, Sthiti, Vyomarūpā, and Sadyānandā—these are the sixteen Nara-s. (104)
Tapanī, Tāpanī, Dhūmrā, Marīcī, Jaḍinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 105 ||
Beginning with Ka and ending with Ṣa, twelve [vowels] are proclaimed;
they are the giver of immortality to the dead, the nourisher, the bestower of prosperity, and they move as Smṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Agni, Prīti, Śāradā, Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kāmadā, Aśvinī, Asvarā—these are the digits (kalās). 107.
Sajīvanī, Svadhāpāpaharṣiṇī, Kledinī, Sudhā, Ajarī, Amarī, Ghorā, Gambhīrā, and likewise Varṣaṇī. (108)
Āhlādinī, Anandā, Klinnā, Saubhāgyavardhanī, Subhagā, Surūpī, and the sixteenth [digit], Kalāśakti. 109.
Ānandinī, Mahānandī, Prīti, Divyā, Kāminī, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Sṛti, and likewise Janarañjinī. || 110 ||
Medhā, Kāmā, Sthirā, Sṛṣṭi, Subhagā, Pālinī, and Parā—these are celebrated as the sixteen Kalās, which bestow supreme bliss. 111.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, concerning the procedure for the arising of the syllables, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Concentration will be described as subtle, free from all dualities;
knowledge itself is concentration, and when that is purified, it is so designated. (1)
The waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states, along with their mutual connection and impermanence—
all these are brought within the fourth state (turiya), which is indeed the eternal nature of the Self.
The states of waking and so forth are to be known as twofold, pertaining to worldly existence and liberation;
that which is with the path is to be known as the middle way, while the path of worldly existence is now described.
According to each respective karma, that old age becomes downward-facing;
it should be known as "awakening" (jāgram) at the mouth, and from that, it brings about the end of sleep.
Beginning from the heart and extending down to the navel is the state of deep sleep (suṣupta);
below that is the fourth state (turya), and beyond that is the subtle body (liṅgaka).
p. 606) Thus, the locus of waking and so forth is said here to be the initiator.
During the time of waking, it pervades the skin; likewise, in dream, it is the mouth. (6)
In deep sleep, it pervades the flesh; in the fourth state (turiya), it resides in the fat.
That which is beyond that is proclaimed as the pervasion of the individual soul (jīva) that has transcended those states.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the group of five vital breaths;
and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. (8)
Speech, feet, hands, anus, and the genitals as the fifth;
these constitute the pentad of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing bliss.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna;
nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 10 ||

The mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta), as well as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña); passion (rāga), illusion (māyā), limited agency (kalā), ignorance (avidyā), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla). || 11 ||
Sound and the rest, the skin and the rest, the nose and the rest, and the mind and the rest— up to the end of desire and so forth, these thirty-one [elements] exist in the dream state.

By those very same perceptions, one withdraws into the state of dreaming; while awake, there is the enjoyment of objects, yet that which is like a dream does not exist in the state beyond [waking]. (13)
Just as fire arises from the conjunction of iron and fire, and fire consumes the iron,
so too does consciousness consume the instruments and other factors of the sacrifice.
O Nandikeśvara, the vital breaths and so forth, as well as the mind, speech, and the rest— these eighteen indeed persist during deep sleep.
The Self, the vital breaths, and knowledge—these are proclaimed as the fourth state (turīya).
But that which is solely pure consciousness is the Great Exaltation. 16.
However, I shall speak that which is most secret; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
For even Prakṛti increases excessively when one eats more than what is necessary for one's own self. (17)
That state which consists of natural activities is called *agra*;
it is the action of the self without the instruments of the body. (18)

Mental activity exists solely as a dream within the absence of objective states; it is naturally established in the Self, yet this [state] is led away by exhaustion through attachment to objects. (19)
O Nandikeśvara, the mind and its functions are motionless in deep sleep;
salutations to that which is devoid of activity, where the coming and going of mental ignorance ceases.
Of the eighteen [factors], eight are non-visible; of the [remaining] ten, eight are both visible and invisible. (21)
The Great Lord, whose nature is knowledge, is himself the supreme light that is to be realized;
he is the gross, the subtle, the very subtle, as well as that which transcends all functions and is most proximate.
The gross is known as the waking state; the subtle is said here to be the dreaming state;
the very subtle would be deep sleep, and the fourth is the subtlest of all. (23)
Beyond that is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); thus it is remembered as being fivefold:
dream, deep sleep, [the waking state], and indeed that which is superior to those.
The waking state is perceived by the yogi through the gradual stages; having seen the activity of the waking state, it is stilled by means of pratyāhāra (withdrawal).

Through *dhāraṇā* one should conquer the dream state; through *nādānusandhāna*, the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*); through *samādhi*, that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*); and the fourth state (*turīya*) through Śiva. (26)
In the five states beginning with waking, that which was past exists in the form of knowledge;
through the instruction of the true guru, it is revealed—of this there is no doubt. (27)
Having understood this specifically, the wise one should practice meditative absorption (samādhi).
That which is to be known as "form is empty" is designated as samādhi. (28)
Having established the mind in purity, which is indeed the very characteristic of Śiva, one should constantly practice the yoga of Śiva, which is the bliss of Śiva-yoga. (29)
But that blissful yoga is established within the body;
because a living being tastes bliss, he therefore desires bliss.
Its own nature is green, empty, and illuminated by radiance;
it is devoid of cognition and the like, and is the destruction of the intellect, mind, and ego. || 31 ||
Having meditated with a mind free from darkness, contemplating the dissolution of those very desires,
there is the destruction of sin and supreme liberation, which is the destruction of saṃsāra.
That which is devoid of thought is indeed the liberation of the self;
there is no doubt that liberation is contained within bliss for him alone. (33)

When "Nandanandaka" is uttered, it is the embodiment of the knowledge of the three worlds; I shall now describe that yoga which is formless, yet whose very form is yoga, and which is beyond all forms.
She should begin with the vision of her own linga, characterized by touch. || 35 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, [concerning] the procedure for samādhi, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme king of meditative absorptions (*samādhirāja*),
either at the time of twilight or at any other time, preceded by the ritual of twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*). (1)
If, at the time for the worship of the Liṅga, one performs the worship of the Liṅga, and afterwards practices yoga, then at that [yogic] time, one should practice yoga alone. || 2 ||

For one who renounces, every moment may be [an occasion for death]; it is the destruction of the moon and the sun. However, in the vicinity of a Guru or near a true yogi, [death is auspicious]. || 3 ||
Or he should always wander accompanied by a disciple endowed with the six virtues,
or together with one who seeks spiritual lineage and is devoted to the worship of the Liṅga.
When the yogi established in samādhi performs more than the prescribed rite,
his companion should also perform the worship of the liṅga for that yogi.
Purity and sipping water (ācamana) are the first; the second is the seat;
and the third is standing while facing north. (6)
The fourth is bathing with ashes; the fifth is the ash of mercury (rasabhasmaka);
the sixth consists of ornaments such as the sacred thread and others made from rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
The seventh is meditation on the guru; the eighth is the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana);
the ninth is indeed cremation (dāhana); and the tenth is likewise immersion (plāvana). || 8 ||
The eleventh is breath control (prāṇāyāma), and the twelfth is renunciation (sannyāsa);
furthermore, O Nandīśa, there is the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) preceded by the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
The thirteenth is the Suṣumnā situated within the channels, and the fourteenth is the Mūlādhāra; the fifteenth is the Brahmanāḍī. || 10 ||
The heart [mantra] consists of nineteen syllables; the purification (viśuddhi) becomes twenty. || 11 ||
And the thirty-first is the ground; beyond this is the teaching on gnosis.
The three are the image, and the twenty-fourth shall be Śiva.
The fifteenth is the Sthāṇuliṅga; immediately after that is Samādhi.
Ānanda consists of twenty-seven [parts]; now hear again its divisions. (13)
But without what was previously mentioned, they would not exist; therefore, listen now to the "Womb of Jewels" (Ratnagarbha).
One should diligently contemplate the one named Śiva in the form of the Guru. || 14 ||
Indeed, he makes his form and the color of his form infinite;
he who bears radiance destroys all defects.
One should perform the meditation on the mantra, becoming oneself the very body of Sadāśiva;
whatever form consists of Śiva, that the disciple, being composed, should meditate upon. (16)
That which is called Śiva, appearing in the form of the Guru, should be known as the most excellent of all;
having meditated thus, the practitioner of yoga remains concentrated with an unwavering mind. (17)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti;
Śāntyatītā, as well as Kriyā-śakti and Jñāna-śakti. || 18 ||

One should meditate upon the power of will (icchā-śakti), the supreme power (parā-śakti), and the ninefold auspicious state; one should first contemplate the primordial principle as previously described, and afterwards contemplate these [powers].
The ten kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi reside in the earth; those beginning with Sthira are the ten belonging to Varuṇa;
and the ten fire-kalās are known as Tāmasī, Mohanī, and so forth.

In the heart, one should likewise contemplate the four [realms] beginning with Pāda and extending downward from Bhava; and following those, the twelve [hells] beginning with Raurava and the narratives beginning with Tāpanīya. (21)
O Nandikeśvara, one should contemplate the sky-element (vyomakalā) beginning with Śuddhikā in a pure location; there, one should indeed meditate upon the nine [syllables] beginning with the Name.
One should contemplate the sixteen vowels beginning with *jīva* (a) by means of the station of the *bindu*;
or, in the station of the unborn (*ajā*), one should remember the sixteen digits (*kalā*) conjoined with the wind (*vāyu*).
One should sequentially invoke Ānanda, Mohānandinī, and the others;
then, in the place of the Moon, there are sixteen [energies] beginning with Mṛtā, Nāda, Pūṣā, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the ninefold group beginning with *prīti* in the middle of each [of those];
and at the *mūlādhāra*, one should meditate on the *santā* group and above that, the sixfold group of children (*bāla-ṣaṭka*).
The syllable *sa* with the vowel *pha* (sapha) is the twelfth, ending in *kāla*.
From the letter *a* up to *kṣa*, it is as before in the region beginning with *kānta*. (26)
One should also visualize the two syllables *bha* and *kṣa* at the root of the palate;
the vowels are in that very place, while the sixteenth vowel is in the lunar orb between the eyebrows.
Right here, one should contemplate the Brahmarandhra, which transcends speech and mind;
they know that the Guha is said to be at the Mūlādhāra, and it is the supreme object to be established there.
Having meditated upon the Prāsāda mantra joined with the Haṃsa-mantra and endowed with the Śakti-bīja, one should contemplate it immediately above that.
One should place the Praṇava at the seat (the base), the Cintāmaṇi at the navel,
the Mṛtyuñjaya at the heart, and the Śivayantra in the Viśuddhi [cakra].
One should meditate on the form of the Triple Brahman in the locations beginning with Kāla;
above that, one should meditate on the seed-syllable of Śiva and then the seed-syllable of Śakti. || 31 ||
Śiva is not devoid of Śakti;
one should meditate upon that which is described as the abode and which consists of the form of light. (32)
Or, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the stainless Śiva-yogin should meditate;
thus has the means of accomplishment been declared, and now the locus of knowledge is likewise described.
They do not know the region of gnosis, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
therefore, one should settle the mind within one's own eye.
Having established [the mind] there, one should then remain with a single-pointed mind and a serene intellect, as long as the light remains in the ether through diligent effort. (35)
Having thus emerged, the elemental self (bhūtātman) remains above the body and beholds the entire world situated above its own body. (36)
There, indeed, one beholds the seven worlds with the eye of yoga;
moreover, the moist liṅga at Jñānadeśa is celebrated as Sthāṇuliṅga. || 37 ||
Beginning from the mūlādhāra and extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
it is expert in bestowing the splendor of all splendors.
The knowledge of the thirty-six principles is itself the first among all principles;
it is peaceful, free from affliction, and indeed of the nature of the individual soul (jīva).
It is a mass of consciousness, all-pervading, subtle, blissful, immovable, and eternal. (40)
He who has eyes everywhere, faces on all sides, eyes in every direction, and arms on every side;
he whose compassion extends to all.
He is all people, all actions, the supreme, the highest, and auspiciousness itself. || 41 ||
One should meditate upon the supreme yoga as a light resembling a spider’s thread;
Kuṇḍalinī is the support of the world, whose nature is the vastness of names.
Having the form of light, endowed with the power of impulsion,
thin like the awn of a wild grain (*nīvāra*), and likewise tawny in appearance,
they pierce the lotuses that serve as their respective supports and proceed to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having thus awakened Lambā, Añjā, and Mukulā with the stream of nectar, worship Śiva there, who is drawing [them] forth; [this is the practice] of the *lī*s. 45.
One should meditate on her flooding [the body] sequentially from above and below;
thus, one should gradually offer the lotus of the fourth state and consciousness right there. (46)
Having thus abandoned everything up to the state of meditative absorption (samādhi), one should contemplate right there;
that subtle absorption, consisting of the support and the supported, will now be explained. (47)
When a sunbeam has traveled for some time, a speck of dust is seen within it;
they declare that to be the ultimate measurement of atoms. (48)
Then, one should contemplate each individual aggregate of the measure of all forms within that very [object]. (49)
One should lead [the breath] to dissolution in the locus of knowledge of Śiva;
when it is without support, the splendor of Śiva is seen therein. (50)
p.
622) With the eyes opened at the root [of the nose] in the center of that image of Śiva, one becomes single-pointed in due order; thus, the light of Śiva is perceived. (51)
In the unstruck (anāhata), the mind is established simultaneously;
that splendor of Śiva, which is beyond and devoid of beginning and end, shines forth.
One should utter the *prasāda* syllable, accompanied by the fivefold sound (*pañcanāda*), in successive order;
it should be meditated upon as the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), wherein the state beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītā*) shines forth.
In the case of those who break [the rules], there is a whirlpool with six enemies of the wheel;
likewise, for those who are well-disposed toward the wise, there is a great rising of food when they are released from the gross [bonds].

This [consciousness], gradually established through the charming and progressively lengthening sounds such as *cāpala*, is directed toward another object; yet, upon the dissolution of that [object], it merges into Śiva.
When the union of the two [lights] is cultivated through the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) at the junction of the heart and the *dvādaśānta*, one enjoys all-bliss (*sarvānandatva*). (56)

Whether in the substrate (ādhāra) or in the power (śakti), because of the dissolution of the mind through the grace of the teacher, there is the supreme state upon the pacification of the trembling and other disturbances caused by the poison of the power (śakti). || 57 ||
Having filled the breath from the head down to the base of the navel, and having meditated upon Brahman at the point of dissolution,
one becomes Śiva through the yoga of the door-panels.

One should meditate upon the subtle power (śakti), which is both sequential and non-sequential, whose form is light from the very root up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and ending in supreme peace; thus there shall be the arising of Śiva.
Having pierced the lotus of awakening, the three sheaths, and the power (śakti) of those who lack earrings and the eight Yakṣas, one becomes supreme in the void above that.
Having withdrawn his gaze into the great expanse of the sky, which is like the moon, the sun, fire, and water, the one-pointed yogi shall himself behold the void. (61)
When the sap of the mind is bound firmly by the slight meditation on non-separation from Śiva,
and the vital breath is cast into the *kumbhaka* and other [breath-control] states, one should produce that gold which is Śiva.
Having attained the power of invisibility, one may wander upon the earth;
O Nandikeśvara, such a yogin shall always abide in bliss.
The eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), will certainly be attained; there is no doubt.
These include traveling through the sky and other such prosperities of all-encompassing knowledge.
One moves through all worlds as if looking at a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand;
indeed, through the vision of yoga, one perceives the entirety of the moving and the unmoving.
The joy born of the vision of yogins is certainly unequalled.
O Nandikeśvara, listen as I describe the characteristics of that bliss. (66)
Bliss is said to be twofold: the lower and the higher.
The lower is said to be threefold, designated as delusion, life-force, and perception. (67)
And the world is said to be the delusion of bliss in divine power; likewise, the delusion born of attachment to the acquisition of sons, grandsons, and so forth, is the bliss of the stars. 68.
That which is produced by food, drink, and so forth, and is designated as the bliss of life, is called worldly bliss (laukikānanda), extending up to the bliss designated as fame and the like. (69)
This entire [universe], which for all beings exists as the bliss of delusion, is indeed of the nature of that Cause; it is the beloved limb, endowed with all characteristics.
The supreme [power] consists of sixteen parts, the middling of twenty-four, and the inferior is known to consist of thirty; this is called the definition of power (*śakti*). || 71 ||
Complete in all its limbs, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
possessed of every beauty, it causes instantaneous piercing.
He has obtained the root of the bliss of delusion as well as life and the rest;
the attainment of supreme bliss is said to be his very perfection (siddhi).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—each of these is to be known as fivefold; this is called the pentad of sound. (74)
The secret speech of loved ones becomes a refuge for union, as does the hearing of the ritual procedures for the Gandharva marriage, which arises from that [union]. (75)
Measured and generating passion, it would consist of the essence of self-praise;
for in this way, there are five sounds and five touches. (76)
The touch of a beloved, likewise the touch of a son, the embrace of a friend, and the pleasant sensation of the wind; 77.
At his will, he likewise experiences the touch of cold and heat as the fifth, and the sight of the beloved—thus beholding his beloved naked. (78)
The sight of dancing and so forth, the sight of gold and such, and the sight of various wonders—these are declared to be the fivefold objects of touch. (79)
Eating is fivefold: solid food, that which is to be chewed, that which is to be licked, that which is to be drunk, and that which is to be sucked;
thus there are five tastes arising at their respective times. (80)
The scent of rut, the supreme fragrance of sandalwood and the like, and the inhalation of the nectar-like scent of flowers— these are called the fivefold sense of smell. (81)
Passion increases in fools, while the wise abandon passion;
one who is endowed with the right means is seen playing even with a serpent. (82)
Endowed with the yoga of knowledge, one is seen playing with a serpent;
the five senses are the reality joined with the yoga of knowledge. (83)
The twenty-fifth bliss would arise from the supreme bliss;
thus, by means of the intellect, the supreme bliss of one's own bliss-lord is now described.
That supreme bliss is threefold, consisting of reverence born from the yoga of knowledge;
these three constitute supreme bliss and become the cause of liberation. || 85 ||
(629) Furthermore, there is the hearing of the limbs of the traditional scriptures, as well as devotion to the praise of the guru,
the hearing of words pleasing to the guru, and likewise hundreds of instructions. || 86 ||
Thus, the group of five joined together produces the bliss born of hearing;
likewise, there is the touching of the *liṅga* and the touching of the sacred ash (*bhūti*) and so forth. (87)
Touching the lotus feet of the guru, as well as touching the guru’s body and the place where knowledge was imparted—this is declared to be the fivefold touch (sparśapañcaka). || 88 ||
The vision of the Śiva-liṅga, the vision of the Śiva-sacrifice and so forth, and the world of the yogic vision and so on—this is the arising of the fivefold form. (89)
The food and other offerings from the grace of the Guru, the water from the lotus feet of the Guru,
and the tasting of the nectar-essence of Yoga— these are said to be the threefold rasa.
The fragrance arising from yoga is a divine scent, incomparable,
[surpassing] that of all the gods, including Brahmā and Indra, even through tens of millions of births. (91)
The divine, ineffable bliss of awakening that grants liberation has never been obtained by anyone;
O Primordial One, abiding from the beginning, you have never given anything to anyone at any time. (92)
Through the remembrance of that mother’s sport, the supreme bliss is born;
thus should the "higher than the highest" be known, as well as the avoidance and the eating [of the sacrificial substance]. (93)
These indeed consist of the gross and the subtle, as well as the extremely subtle;
it is more secret than the secret, transcending the highest, and devoid of both the grasped and the grasper. (94)
Free from passion and dispassion, devoid of duality and non-duality;
liberated from the conceivable and the inconceivable, and free from the expressed and the expresser.
Thus, Ānanda, when these two are attained, liberation itself is certain; through the mouth of the Guru, that perfection is achieved, and bliss is indeed beyond doubt. (96)
The yogi should cultivate bliss, which eradicates all afflictions.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the King of Samādhis, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Listen now to this supreme state of the yogas, which is indeed without support.
The worship of the ten [deities], the assembly hall, and so forth, should be performed as previously described. || 1 ||
There is indeed a distinction regarding the twilight (sandhyā): the supreme twilight is ever-arisen;
the morning twilight is Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā would be the midday.
At midnight, during the pure western twilight, [one should meditate] through the Suṣumṇā;
it is auspicious, consisting of lotus fibers, and possesses the splendor of the twelve-fold sun.
One should meditate on the nature of the self through its form as being of a tawny (piṅgalā) color;
one should then meditate on Śivā, resembling the tip of that [light], within the Suṣumnā.
And with the syllable *ukāra*, one should meditate upon that Vidyā as the essence within the range of meditation,
at the time of sunset, in the eye, possessing a radiance equal to a sesame seed and fire.
One should contemplate the supreme Śakti, resembling a lotus fiber, as a light cooler than ten million moons, by means of the syllable *ma*, which is called Śiva.
At midnight, one should meditate upon the goddess Svarā-sandhyā within the Suṣumnā;
she consists of all splendor and destroys both the moon and the sun.
One should worship the supreme goddess Sandhyā, who resides in the center of the Bindu;
one should place the letter *A* at the root-support and the letter *U* above it.
Above that, [is] the letter *ma* with a bindu upon it;
above the bindu is nāda, and above nāda is the syllable ŚAKRIḌAI.
Thus, according to his capacity, the yogin should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana);
then, having emitted twenty [breaths], he should contemplate the aspects of bliss (ānanda).
One should cast away the mind, the intellect, and the ego within that [state] under the guidance of the teacher;
one should also cast away passion, illusion, and the kalās within the fourth state.
One should emit [the energies] from Vidyā up to Śuddhakālī until they reach the end of Turyā;
and through the dissolution of the mind, one attains supreme liberation.
He should meditate upon the nature of the absolute Self as being of the form of pure knowledge.

Having spoken of the supreme reality that transcends knowledge, which is all-pervading and faces every direction, as well as the state of Śiva, one should thus contemplate "May there be well-being. (14)
There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti;
having meditated thus, the great yogi attains unbroken, supreme prosperity. (15)
The meditator, the object of meditation, and the water become Śiva, the supreme state;
freed from all taints, that alone remains as the absolute.
That supreme Śiva, whose form is stainless, shines forth as such;
all cognition comes to him, and that [cognition] serves as the fourth state (turiya). || 17 ||
The knowledge that "I am indeed [this]"—which conforms to the principles of pure reality and so forth—is like a kingdom of the mind or a former form reflected in a stainless, clear mirror. (18)
When one who is facing inward sits down and meditates, he then becomes self-controlled;
[this state] is free from the duality of jars, all-pervading, and extends to the limit of consciousness. (19)
One who does not perceive this [reality] abiding within one's own body cannot be happy;
yet, perceiving this form of theirs as being the entire universe, one becomes identical with the All.
Even a child possesses the cognition that "this is to be grasped" and "this is the grasper";
yet the yogi, perceiving the identity between the two, attains fullness. (21)
Reflecting upon this as "I" and visualizing the throbbing mandala with one-pointed concentration, Śiva, the soul of all, meditates upon it as if it were his own body. (22)
Simultaneously reflecting upon space, the body—both external and internal—as consisting of consciousness, or even the entire universe, the yogi becomes Śiva in that very moment. (23)

Having placed this "wheel of differentiation" (bhedayantra) in the center, with its great splendor both within and without, one should contemplate the form of consciousness as superior in every respect, devoid of the luster of duality.
Even though she has emerged from within the Veda and exists outside it, and even though she is like a courtesan,
she remains as one who reflects upon herself, thinking, "I am the unfolding of the mind."

When the manifestation consisting of consciousness arises through the gateway of her organ of speech, and when one reflects upon the universe as being dissolved within the *suhitti*, one becomes Śiva. (26)

"Or, because of the commonality of specific qualities, the procedure for the green [substance] does not depart; yet it would be different in his body. Having thus reflected, he performed the dissolution (*yolaya*).
In that which is all-pervasive, without beginning, eternal, void, and devoid of limits—
in the lower wheel and externally— the Supreme One ascends.
The yogi, established in form, should look beyond yoga;
with a mind free of support, he shall quickly become Śiva through the power of consciousness. (29)

When all seeing and acting have come to rest in the unconditioned nature of consciousness, what can those devoid of yoga see, or what can that formless [reality] do? Or rather, they are destroyed [in their capacity to act]. 30.
By practicing this supportless yoga, one shall attain Śiva;
there is no yoga equal to this, O Nandikeśvara. (31)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the supportless yoga, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall proclaim the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā), which brings liberation for the virtuous along with its cause—
that reality which is pure, pervasive, enlightening, and free from delusion.
(638) Furthermore, that which is endowed with the previous initiation is the most excellent for disciples;
it is merely the dissolution of the body, wherein there is no dissolution of the vital breath at all. || 2 ||
In this way, the Guru, through his own devotion, should perform the initiation of knowledge;
it is threefold, consisting of the individual (āṇava), that which arises from power (śākta), and that which belongs to Śambhu (śāmbhava). || 3 ||
The Śāmbhava initiation is performed by you for Śakti,
while the Āṇava initiation is performed by others, according to the distinctions of dull, intense, and so forth.
O Nandikeśvara, having constructed a variegated pavilion and a mandala and so forth according to the previous [instructions], specifically using the aforementioned materials; || 5 ||
Especially at midnight, one should offer— excluding the formal acceptance (adhivāsana)—
fragrant unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, and sacrificial oblation (caru).
Endowed with all substances and accompanied by the incalculable [mantras],
he should then perform the purification of the substances according to the previously stated procedure. (7)
One should complete the mandala by cutting [the lines], especially at midnight;
and [one should honor] the disciple with fragrant flowers, incense, ornaments, and so forth.
When the mind of Śiva has been attained, as well as the darkness of the path of time,
the teacher should enter the science of the elements by means of the jewel of the Tāra.
Then, having established the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) through the constant union of Śiva and Śakti,
the leader of the true path should recite the mantra of Śiva and that of Śakti.
Having realized this knowledge, one should maintain steadfastness until its conclusion;
having recited [the mantra], one attains supreme bliss, the essence of the Guru’s supreme knowledge.
p.
640) Through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one should place therein whatever has arisen within the mouth of the disciple;
and that which has been brought forth right there, full of flavor, should be made the object of the disciple's perception. 12.
The temple should be consecrated with the Śiva-mantra, and the Vāgīśakti-mantra should also be employed;
