having first mastered these two, one should cause the construction to be performed by means of these mantras.
From that which is well-perceived, knowledge arises; this is the second face of the Lord.
Released from the nectar-essence of yoga, it is the mandala accompanied by the mudrā.
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, and play according to one's own will proceed;
there is constant bliss in the body, and likewise neither hunger nor sleep. (15)
One may perform dance, laughter, and knowledge, and run about according to one's own will;
[this is] endowed with seven steps and the excellence of the qualities of those steps.
The first is said to consist of the three qualities (triguṇa); the second, the five objects;
the third, the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā); and the fourth, the eight accomplishments (siddhi). || 17 ||
The second is the island (dvīpa), the third the condition (pratyaya), the fourth the five, and the fifth the sixth; the sixth would be the ten fruits.
The seventh should be known as bliss (ānanda), and the eighth as accomplishment (siddhi) through final reflection. || 18 ||
The individual (āṇava) [means] trembling and so forth; power (śakti), however, is said to be the dyad.
The mental state (citta) devoid of afflictions and the like is considered the Śāmbhava, which possesses the three qualities (triguṇa). || 19 ||
One should personally offer these: a mirage, smoke, a firebrand, and likewise a retrograde movement; all of this constitutes the five lamps of the region.
The power of transformation, the recollection of former abodes, and the divine eye and ear—these are the five supernormal knowledges (abhijñās). || 21 ||
One's own support and accomplishment are established through the form of knowledge;
likewise, even seedless methods [serve as] a weapon against poison. (22)
The kindling of the fire, as well as the mastery of the channel of the wind, and likewise the union with the bindu, the nāda, and the stainless body. (23)
The appearance of smoke and light occurs spontaneously as the activity of death;
thus, listen to the eighteen-fold power which indeed possesses ten conditions. (24)
Mental anxieties, requisites, inclination toward liberation, accumulation, birth, power, the mind of the Dharma amidst suffering, and the fruit of austerity. || 25 ||

And that state, consisting of greatness and so forth, which is to be accomplished, one indeed attains correctly and in due order; they know these to be the qualities resulting from instruction, such as knowledge and the severing of bonds. (26)
The innate [nature] transcends speech and mind; it is unbroken and of great exaltation.
It consists of all accomplishments and is the singular leader of the three worlds as a whole. (27)
And the yogic accomplishment of the disciple shall become more intense than the most intense;
likewise, there is destiny even in the blinding of calamity, as well as the possession of the qualities of the creative arts.
Through the piercing (*vedha*) of the Vidyādhara, there is destruction by means of *nāśamāra*;
this peaceful method (*śāntopāya*) has been proclaimed, and therein the Śāmbhava [state] exists. (29)
And when the two-footed staff called Sādākhya is blinded, the girdle of muñja grass shines forth;
this piercing from the level of Śuddhavidyā is said to be the Śāmbhava [piercing]. (30)
The disciple's devotion is demonstrated in such a manner;
one should recognize this [state], beginning with the removal of obstacles (āvaraṇa), through these signs of conviction.
Having known [the disciple's fitness] and observed him with compassion, Śiva should cause the hand to be placed [upon him];
afterwards, he should cause him to perform prostration and bestow upon him a name. || 32 ||
The Guru should distribute the alms-bowl, staff, seat, and so forth, as previously described;
whether the fire-rite has been performed or not, it shall be as if the fire-rite were performed.
One should offer one's body, wealth, and life to the guru;
indeed, even one's very body and life, following the permission of the guru. (34)
Then, always endowed with devotion, one should know this through direct experience and offer all of one's wealth to that guru. (35)
Then, having surrendered all his own autonomy through mind,
speech, and action, the wise disciple should act solely for the sake of the guru.
Then, O Nandikeśvara, having performed the consecration as before,
[one should worship] the earth with fragrances, perfumes, and so forth, as well as with pure garments and the like. (37)
The Guru should further adorn the disciple and have him fashion the image;
O Nandikeśvara, he should then dismiss the deity from the sacrifice.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the initiation of knowledge, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall declare the determination of the principles (tattvas); listen, O Nandikeśvara! I shall speak of the principle known as Rasa (Taste) together with its designations. || 1 ||
Because of its purity, it is designated as "Śiva," and because of its supremacy, it is called "the Supreme.
It is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) due to being full of knowledge, and it is "one" (*eka*) due to the perfection of its likeness. || 2 ||
Because its essential nature is the bliss of happiness, that enemy is designated as "consciousness" (citsaṃjñā). || 3 ||
O Nandikeśvara, he is the supreme cause for the origin of the world of moving and non-moving beings; therefore, he is designated as the sole seed of the universe.
But consciousness, according to each being's own respective karma, having brought about the ripening of karma—the sense of "I" and experiences such as pleasure and pain—[remains]. (5)
Because it bestows favor upon all, it is known as "the Favor of All";
because it is free from ignorance and is absolute liberation, it is the bestower of Nirvāṇa.

His nature consists of knowledge and action; because he relies upon the powers of knowledge and will, and because he protects by delivering those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, he is the Lord (pati).
Through the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, one becomes Śiva whose body is composed of mantra;
[these are] those known as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), preservation (*pālana*), concealment (*tirodhāna*), and grace (*anugraha*). (8)
Because it is the intrinsic nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), it is designated as the "five-whole" (*pañcakṛtsna*).
Thus, in this primary enumeration, those digits (*kalā*) have been proclaimed. (9)
Indeed, Śakti is for the sake of bestowing grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious;
she is inseparable from Him, like a flame from the fire that consumes the oblation.
Furthermore, the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti is indeed a case of mutual dependence;
for the knowledge of both the conscious and the unconscious belongs to those who assume forms according to their own will. (11)
The supreme bindu, the supreme śakti, māyā, amāyā, kuṇḍalī, the space of the sacrificial post (yūpavyoma), and likewise icchā—these are synonyms for Him. || 12 ||
(648) Will, knowledge, and action indeed always abide in Śiva;
for the sake of objects corresponding to Śiva’s own will, the primary one possesses the power of knowledge and will. (13)
They each perform their respective functions for the sake of constant grace;
they are the power of knowledge and the power of action, which is the manifestation of the All.
The principle known as Sadāśiva is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala);
it is characterized by the predominance of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and the subsiding of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). || 15 ||
In that state, as it expands forth to consume [objects], this becomes what is called Īśvara;
there, the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is diminished while the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is predominant. (16)
Then the arising of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) occurred from the Womb of Knowledge (jñānagarbha);
from the Bindu, the Kalās were born, which sustain all principles. || 17 ||
p.
649) And the two, Nadya and Odbindu, have come into being resting upon Sādākhya;
for they are devoid of connection with the *kalās* of the five pure principles (*tatvas*). || 18 ||
There is no increase or decrease beyond the Śiva-tattva; this is certain.
In reality, the supreme truth of the Śiva-tattva has been declared here.
The possession of infinite mental power belongs to Śiva alone and is innate to his very nature,
just as flame is to fire and moonlight is to the cold-rayed moon.
"By the power of Bhava, may I indeed become the body of this Śiva;
for Śiva, endowed with Śakti, exists for the liberation of the living being from birth. (21)
The cause of liberation for perfected beings, whose entities are free from beginningless impurity, likewise becomes the benefactor of all, even of the insentient multitude. 22.
Śiva’s form is indeed identical to the form of Śiva;
there is equality everywhere, both in the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala). (23)
That is declared to be *sāyujya* (union), while *sārūpya* (likeness) is equality with liberation.
*Sārūpya* is likeness of form, due to assuming a body according to one's own will. (24)
The attainment of Śiva’s world and so forth is called *sālokya*, which is one form of liberation;
this fourfold [attainment], along with *śaktisāyujya*, constitutes the highest state. (25)
For one who desires the attainment of the supreme state,
especially because of his residual impurities, there remains the station of a Vidyeśvara.
Through the ripening of latent impressions (vāsanā) and through initiation (dīkṣā), one may attain the Supreme;
yet because karma is beginningless, it must be experienced for the sake of liberation.
p.
651) For the sake of experience, Śambhu has fashioned the instrument, the deity, and the entire world in every respect; he has also fashioned the instrument for experience through his power. || 28 ||
Māyā, accompanied by the beginningless power (śakti), is subtle and all-pervading;
though without beginning or end and indeed one, it is the material cause (upādānakāraṇa). || 29 ||
Having agitated Māyā—the mother of all births, the producer of delusion—by means of his own powers and through the influence of karma, Śambhu [acted]. || 30 ||

For the sake of providing objects of experience for the person (puruṣa), Śiva, through His power (śakti) and especially by means of the instruments (karaṇa), bestows the body, the senses, and so forth.
In her who is the form of infinite power, Māyā arises at that time;
she then becomes threefold in form as the past, the present, and the future.
When the impurities had ripened, it was the time for the manifestation of the accumulated [karma]; and once again, O deities, he brought forth Māyā and Niyati. (33)
Assuming the form of Niyama, she did not create anything that was barren or incomplete;
she herself, as Māyā, again produced the Kalās in due order.
Having merged the weapon-mantra (astra), the individual soul (māṇava), and the gross (sthūla) into one,
and having established them in the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), one should manifest the power of agency (kartṛ-śakti).

The meaning of the root *kam* is the bondage of desire for the sake of the bodies of the selves; this state of being subject to time is proclaimed for the sake of the enjoyment of those bound like frogs. (36)
And having concealed the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), there is the manifestation of the power of agency (kartṛ-śakti);
it is called impure (aśuddhā) and limited (alpikā), O Nandikeśvara, and it belongs to the departed (pareta). 37.
This very *kalā*, together with *niyati* and *kāla*, [proceeds] again from *māyā* up to *niyati* by means of its own respective functions and activities. (38)
The three, who are experts in creation and the other cosmic functions, perform their work in unison;
through a portion [of their power], they have become endowed with the creative capacity of the Puruṣas.
It likewise becomes the objects such as sound and the instruments [of perception], endowed with the three qualities (guṇas) in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion. (40)
Then that knowledge becomes the intellect (buddhi), which is the object of experience for the self;
and when there is indeed the cognition of grasping, it pertains to objects such as sound and the rest. (41)
This very [state] is called the cause of manifestation (abhikāraṇa); the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva) becomes twofold, just as curd arises from the contact of milk with a fermenting agent.
When, having churned the milk, the state of duality arises,
then true knowledge itself becomes the intellect (*buddhi*), and likewise the instrument (*karaṇa*). (43)
Indeed, at the time of re-creation, Śiva alone expands;
for at the end of the dissolution, that which exists is endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
Everything has been relinquished by me; that is proclaimed as Reality (tattva).
In that regard, the stainless self is indeed the cause of bondage and birth. (45)
Through the destruction of both impurities and their latent impressions (vāsanā), liberation occurs without a doubt;
and the destruction of those impurities certainly comes about through initiation (dīkṣā).
Forty sacramental rites (saṃskāra) are to be performed even by Brahmins and others;
after that, O Aṅga, follows the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
The *puṃsavana*, the *sīmanta*, and thereafter the *viṣṇubali*; likewise the *jātakarma*, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and the first outing (*niṣkrama*). (48)
The first feeding of solid food, the reunion with beloved ones, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the ritual release [of the fires], and the rites for the five states and for unification. (49)
The Pārāyaṇa, the gift of a cow, and likewise the bath and proper conduct—this is declared to be the eighteenfold purification of the body. (50)

The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, likewise the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to Brahman—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices. || 51 ||
The Sthālīpāka, the Āgrayaṇa, the Śrauta, the Smārta, the Paitṛka, and the Paitṛmāsa—these seven are the Pākayajñas. (52)
The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), likewise the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, and immediately after that, the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*). (53)
The Nirūḍhapaśubandha, the Sautrāmaṇi, and my Rathas;
these seven are called the Haviryajñas, as well as the Soma-saṃsthas. || 54 ||
The Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśaka, the Vājapeya, the Atirātras, and the Aptoryāma as the seventh; these are the [sacrifices] at the Agniṣṭoma. || 55 ||
Indeed, there are forty established traditions that are very dear to the Vedic sequence;
even for one who has performed [the rites] according to the stated path, liberation is attained through initiation alone.
There is no sacred ford equal to initiation; there is no austerity equal to initiation;
there is no Nīla equal to initiation; there is no wealth equal to initiation. || 57 ||
There is no dharma equal to initiation; there is no quality equal to initiation. There is no knowledge equal to initiation; there is no mindfulness equal to initiation. (58)
There is no greater good than initiation; there is no lineage equal to initiation.
Likewise, initiation brings about the destruction of latent impressions, as well as knowledge and ritual action.

The practice of conduct (*caryācaryā*) consists of four parts; through the increase of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it certainly brings about the ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). One should also render the water-element (*vāruṇa*) barren.
The intellect, consisting of merit and demerit, as well as the latent impressions born of karma, are undoubtedly destroyed solely through the worship of the Śiva-liṅga. (61)
Likewise, according to the doctrine of the five winds, there is that which arises from the movement of latent impressions (vāsanā),
as well as joy, destruction, and the remainder resulting from the dissolution of the mind.
And in the Jñāna [Tantra], the Tāla is joined with four [beats] even in the illusory [rite]. || 63 ||
It goes to destruction gradually; listen, O Nandikeśvara, as I describe it.
Through hearing from Śivā, the knowledge of Śiva becomes firmly established.
Furthermore, through constant experience, as well as through seeing and hearing, even the forgetfulness that has been produced goes to its destruction; of this there is no doubt. (65)
Due to the inherent nature of the time of creation, of the Goddess, and of Kandarpa; because of the steadfastness of the best of Puruṣas; and because of their reliance upon noble women—66.

A Brahmin who possesses only his birth, and one who stands in the condition of a Caṇḍāla, are equal in status once they possess the birth of initiation—the birth of Śiva; no other distinction of birth exists.
Initiation proceeds precisely from the order of emanation; thus, the Father is devoid of initiation.
Likewise, Śivā is declared to be the Mother of the world and of all individual souls. (68)
Because of the length of time, his father, mother, and grandfather [have passed away]. || 69 ||
Sons, friends, wives, brothers, maternal uncles, and uterine siblings—these are the first [group], followed by a third and a fourth group, each numbering in the thousands. (70)
Since they themselves have become fathers and so forth, there is no fixed sequence for each;
likewise, all living beings are originally one and the same.
Because of the association of karmas, [the notion of] fathers and so forth exists in every respect as a debt;
therefore, there is no such thing as desire, reflection, and so on, in the means for attaining true knowledge.

O Nandikeśvara, from the cessation [of the rite] down to the ground, the consecration (adhivāsana) takes place there in the morning; for at the end, the body is indeed [purified] by that splendor. 73.
Pervading the activities of mind, speech, and body, it indeed performs its function through the seven or six latent impressions (vāsanās); otherwise, it performs the function of reality (tattva).
And for one who has entered the path of the knowledge of Śiva in particular, there is no longer any duty whatsoever to be performed regarding actions associated with latent impressions (vāsanā). 75.
If there is still the presence of attachment to latent impressions (vāsanārāga), one is not a knower of reality;
therefore, the teacher, having realized the knowledge of reality that illuminates the truth, [should act accordingly]. 76.
That very [reality] is the embodiment of the knowledge of truth, from which all outflows have been liberated.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the Determination of Truth, in the Acintyaviśvasādākhya.
I shall speak; listen, O Nandīśa, to the supreme procedure of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*):
the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), and the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) as the third. (1)
The path of action (kriyādhvan), the path of convention (samayādhvan), and the path of the parts (kalādhvan) constitute the sixth;
by these six paths, all that is moving and unmoving is indeed pervaded everywhere.
Having spoken thus for the sake of establishing the path, I created this world,
which extends from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to the hundred Rudras and is renowned as the Egg of Brahmā (Brahmāṇḍa).
Dust is dispersed by the rays of the sun made manifest by all its flames;
it is in this context that the atom is described here as being devoid of spatial division.
Then, at each successive stage of eightfold increase, one should grasp a hair;
likewise, two lice make a nit, eight nits make a barley-corn, and eight barley-corns make a finger-breadth (aṅgula).
Twelve *aṅgulas* constitute one *tāla*; the space between two *tālas* is likewise extended. Two *tālas* are declared to be one *kara*, and two of those [make] one *dhanus*. (6)
Two bow-lengths are said to be one *dhanurdaṇḍa*, and two thousand of those make one *krośa*.
Three *krośas* constitute a *gavyūti*, and two of those would be a *yojana*. (7)
One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand; a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, and likewise a hundred million, O Ape. || 8 ||
Immediately after that, the place called Nyarbuda is described;
then Padma, Mahāpadma, and immediately after that, Śaṅkha.
Mahāśaṅkha, Vṛtta, Mahāvṛtta immediately following,
Samudra preceded by Mahat, and the one called Samudraka immediately following.
Nikharva, guru, and immediately thereafter mahāvāyu; ākāśa and mahākāśa—thus it becomes limited. || 11 ||
The measurement increases tenfold from place to place;
specifically, the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa is considered to be [composed of] hundreds of millions of yojanas.
Above that, for exactly that same distance, is the Fire of Kāla (Time) made of gold; it possesses the fierce heat of the world-process and a brilliance like ten million suns. || 13 ||
Surrounded by many Rudras, he is called Kālāgnirudra;
in that splendor, all the paths of existence are stretched out.
Fear arose, impelled by the power of the Lord's withdrawal;
from his own nature, ten crores of flames burst forth. || 15 ||

(664) This world of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), which is most terrible and consists of as many thousands of yojanas as there are units in the number of smoke (dhūma), extends for sixteen crores of yojanas.
Then there are thirty-three crores of ten-lakṣas of *puṭas*;
this indeed is the world of Kālāgni, and above that are the hells.
Within it, thirty-two million places of torment have indeed been fashioned for wicked-souled sinners.
I shall now declare their names; listen, O Nandikeśvara:
Raurava, Tamas, Śīta, Uṣṇa, and Bhāvaka.
The eighth thread is said to be the time of the lotus-born [Brahmā] born of heat;
these are the well-known hells—now hear of their presiding lords.
The Sūtra, the Kālakhaṇḍa, the Kṣmādhāra, the Ambarīṣaka,
the Taptāṅgāra, the Mahīnāha, and the Saṃtāpa are thus proclaimed. (21)
There were eight women who followed the words of the great-sounding Bhavatrāma; having applied a lac-dye ointment, they sat upon high seats with their thighs covered.
He is proclaimed as the king who creates for those afflicted by thirst and hunger the two mountains, the śalmalī tree, and the fire. || 23 ||
The pillar of gain, as well as excrement and urine, and the river Vaitaraṇī;
Tāmisra and Āyatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava. (24)
O Rājarājeśvarī, [there are] Mahāpāśa, Anu, and Vīci;
this [number] is the count of the hells together with the Puṭas, measured in yojanas. || 25 ||
p.
666) There are two crores [of yojanas], and then another crore;
beyond that, there is the Kūrma-egg, which is the earth consisting of sixty-two segments. || 26 ||
By means of the previously mentioned practice of yoga, one should join the heart and half of the iron [element] from that cloth made of gold.
The lord of the hells, known as Kūṣmāṇḍa, who has traversed a thousand yojanas, possesses a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon. || 28 ||
Round-eyed, with a wrathful face, possessing many fangs and being most terrible,
he held a battle-axe and was likewise attended by spirits (bhūtas).
Thereafter, O Nandin, I shall proclaim the seven netherworlds (pātāla);
indeed, the seven families are said to extend as far as the end of the netherworlds.
Nāgas and rākṣasas, as well as deities and apsarases,
seated upon Mahātala, sport with unrestrained joy. (31)
The height is nine hundred thousand [yojanas], and the interval is said to be one hundred thousand;
the measurement of the netherworlds (pātālas) is likewise seventy hundred thousand.
In the east were the Daityas Śaṅku, Śiśu, Prahlāda, Śiśupālaka, Karkāntuka, Hiraṇyākṣa, Bṛhadgarbha, and likewise Bali. || 33 ||
The sons of Kadrū were Kuṭilaka, Vāsuki, [Bhoga], Kārkoṭaka, Vālāṅga, and Durdarśa. || 34 ||
Vikṛta, Lohitākṣa, the one called Yama, Vikaṭānana, Karāla, Bhīmanirhrāda, and Piṅgala—these were the Rākṣasas. (35)
Above them is the sovereign of Pātāla in its entirety;
beyond that is the golden Pātāla, measuring ten lakhs [of yojanas]. (36)
Above that is the city of the Great Lord known as Hāṭaka, the lord of the gods,
which is surrounded by ten million [attendants] and endowed with various transformations.
Because all of that is gold (hāṭaka), it is indeed called Hāṭakeśvara;
above that, nine lakhs [of yojanas] are proclaimed to be within.
The height of the world is prescribed as ten lakhs [yojanas];
beyond that, the earth extends for a hundred crores, providing refuge for various classes of beings.
Adorned with the circles of mountains, islands, rivers, and oceans,
[the earth consists of] Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śārṅga, Gomeda, and Puṣkara.

The continents are twice as large [as the preceding one], surrounded by the oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk; these are the Salt Ocean, the Ocean of Milk, the Ocean of Clarified Butter, the Sugarcane Ocean, and the Ocean of Honey-water. (41)
The seven oceans are proclaimed as follows: they are known as Svādūdaka (Sweet-water), Kṣīroda (Milk-ocean), and so on;
Kṣīroda is two hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent, and each subsequent one is twice as large as the preceding.
The ground consists of gold produced by karma, as does the Lokāloka mountain; beyond that is the Garbhoda ocean and the shell, which constitutes the surface of the world.
O Nandikeśvara, the earth should always be understood by the Bhāgavatas as being adorned with variegated mountains, rivers, islands, forests, and oceans. 44.
The navel of the earth is that region known as Jambū; it is circular and measures one hundred thousand yojanas, surrounded by the Ocean of Milk which is of equal extent.
In its center stands the golden mountain, the king of kings;
Meru, whose splendor eclipses the light of the sun, is inhabited by the gods. (46)
It extends sixteen thousand [yojanas] from the surface of the earth;
it is known to be one hundred thousand [yojanas] at its base and sixteen [thousand] at its root.
Within its three intervals between the spokes, at the four points where they are bound, there are rims shaped like mountain ridges that have emerged with great brilliance.
The first [period] consists of eleven thousand years, and the subsequent ones decrease by one thousand each;
at the end of that [cycle], there is the Naimittika dissolution, which takes place when the world-protectors (lokapālas) withdraw [to their abodes].
Indra’s [palace] named Cakrapāṭa, radiant with the splendor of all jewels,
is situated below that, where Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Maruts all reside.
Upon its eight peaks, the eight [deities] beginning with Indra are stationed in the eastern and other directions; their names contain that [syllable] *bha* as their core. (51)
Amarāvatī, the golden city, possesses the radiance of many jewels, its interior sky resplendent, and is filled with Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Garuḍas.
The city of Tejovatī, belonging to the Āgneya region, is filled with light and surrounded by golden ramparts and gate-towers made mostly of red and yellow jewels.
The city of Saṃyaminī, belonging to Death, is enclosed by an iron wall;
it is surrounded by the noose of Time, ancestral diseases, and hosts of spirits and ghosts.
In the southwest is the city Kṛṣṇā, surrounded by cruel Daityas,
and endowed with the luster of sapphire, great sapphire, and blue gems.
To the west is the city of Varuṇa, also called Śuddhavatī,
which is filled with arches and banners fashioned from pure crystal. (56)
In ancient times, the city of Gandhavatī belonged to Gaddhabāhu; it was filled with fish resembling pure clouds and with fierce, single-flaming sea-monsters (makaras).
Adorned with white banners that had been washed clean, the army stood ready;
that city, meanwhile, shone on all sides in succession with masses of radiance.
The city of Soma is truly constructed of pearls and crystal;
it is named Mahodayā, and is especially frequented by yakṣas and gandharvas.
With its sword-like trees and [other features], it shines, praised by hosts of gods and adorned with cities that possess the luster of mountains. (60)
In the northeast is the city Sākṣā, surrounded by Yaśovatī;
it is joined by many Rudras and resplendent with various jewels. (61)
It was endowed with flowers of all seasons, frequented by divine beings,
filled with various birds, and adorned with diverse trees.
Created by Brahmā for the prosperity of those who follow the wheel of the world-protectors, these [paths] leading to heaven have been proclaimed by those whose nature is directed toward heaven. (63)
The city of Brahmā is directly named Manovatī;
it is fourteen thousand yojanas in extent.
And in the midst of the world-protectors, surrounded by gods in the center of Meru, she makes the sky laugh with the rays of the sun as they are driven forth. (65)
(674) Rivaling the Sāvitrī [mantra], she dwells among those who desire heaven and the like;
upon her, the gods and the highly exalted sages meditate. 66.
The great mistress of yogis, together with the Skandas, the Vaitas, and the Vasus, [resides] on the fifth direction of Meru; there the peak of Vaikuṇṭha is located.
Adorned with every ornament and attended by supernatural powers and accomplishments,
its width and height are exactly fourteen thousand [yojanas].
It has the luster of all kinds of jewels, with walls and gateways as bright as individual suns;
there Viṣṇu dwells together with the hosts of all the gods.
Dwelling thus for the sake of protecting the world of mortals,
they likewise perform the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe in due order, day by day.
On the eastern side of that mountain, there is a peak resembling the sun;
they call it Yakta-jyotiṣka, and it is dear to Paśupati. (71)
On his banner, however, were stationed the great lords Skanda, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and others, adorned with gold and various jewels.
On the summit is the abode of the God of gods, the enemy of Tripura;
endowed with such characteristics, Parvateśvara shines forth. (73)
O Nandikeśvara, that which is renowned as Kailāsa is indeed not the Self;
it is joined by hosts numbering ten million Ārdrās and by the supreme gods beginning with Brahmā. (74)
Thus, below Mount Meru there are other mountains situated in the various directions;
listen now to the nine islands and the regions (varṣas) adjacent to them that exist here.
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat, the best of mountains, are to the south of Meru; Nīla, Śveta, and Bhṛṅgin are to the south [of those]. (76)
The intermediate oceans, extending two thousand [yojanas] in width and ten in height, stretch eastward; they are joined by mountain ranges and number one hundred crores.
Then, with half that measure, the Viṣkambha mountains Mālyavat and Gandhamādana extend to the south and north of Meru, reaching as far east and west as those [preceding] mountains.
To the east of Mālyavān is the region Bhadrāśva, crowded with excellent people;
to the west of Gandhamādana is Ketumāla, abounding in lotuses.
To the south of Niṣadha and from Hemakūṭa lies the region known by the name Kimpuruṣa; it is red in color, extending as far as the Himavat mountain.
From that mountain, Hiraṇyaśveta,
which is the source of joy for all beings, the region to the north of its peaks is called Kuruvarṣa. (81)
And due to ill omens, Brahmā, desiring the stability of Meru,
established these very firm mountains there in the form of buttresses.
Those [mountains] are five hundred thousand [yojanas] high; among them, Mandara is to the east, resembling a sacrificial altar and the color of turmeric powder, while Gandhamādana is to the south.
Nīlagiri is indeed in the west, and Supārśva is in the north; Aruṇa is in the east.
They are each one thousand yojanas in height, and upon them stand the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas).
The Kambajā, Abjā, Aśvatthā, Vyagrodhā, and Uttarāntikā rivers arise from the juice of the jambū fruit and flow as far as Mount Meru. (85)
p.
678) Having turned the earth itself into gold by means of this very source of excellence, all birds, beasts, monkeys, and the like drank it. (86)
And those beings who were golden in that land became known by the word "ungrateful" (kṛtaghna);
however, on the island [of Jambudvīpa], they became [known as] Jāmbū... || 87 ||
Just as Prabhāvatī described it, this Jambūdvīpa extends from there;
at the foot of the supporting mountain in the east lies the Caitraratha forest.
There is a lake named Aruṇodaka, adorned with golden lotuses; to the south is the river Nimnagā, [and] the Gandharvas... [89]
There is that Nandana grove, and there the lake known as Mānasa; and at the root of the Pula mountain is the Vaibhrāja forest, surrounded by the Sitoda lake.
The lotuses, radiant with the brilliance of the sun, should be used for the service of the God alone;
those who possess fortitude and pure hearts [should remain] at his side.
The Saugandhika lotus is always consumed by the Cinnas and the Pitṛs;
thirteen thousand [of them] subsist on the juice of the Jambū fruit. 92.
Above the world of Meru are the people known as Satvaśikhāvṛtas;
the people there are of fiery nature, possessing divine physical forms, happy, and powerful.
They have the luster of the moon’s orb and sit upon blue lotuses; they are accompanied by auspicious horses.
The lifespan of those who perform sacrifices at birth is ten thousand years;
and for those who eat the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree, their lifespan is thirty thousand years.

The people possess a knowledge of the pairs, the primordial source, and the radiance of flowers; they are characterized by the union of the thousand upward-pointing beings within a single direction. (96)
Candrabhadra, Ākarādhipa, Candrarakta, Amburuha, and Ailāvṛta are the lords of the [nine] regions. || 97 ||
At that time, who indeed was present to provide food consisting of fruits and roots, as well as clothing? (98)
And twelve thousand middling golden fruits of the *lāṅgula* tree, which are like the constant fruit for the people who hate Indra, were carried away by the horse. 99.
For a person who eats the fruit of the banyan tree for thousands of years, there remains [only] a speck of dark dust on its tip. 100.
On the mountain Niṣadha, people possess a lifespan of ten thousand years and have the luster of silver;
on Mount Meru, they are golden-hued, and on Plakṣa, their sustenance consists of food and they remain for ten thousand years. (101)
Thus, are these [ages] such as Kṛta and the rest merely years?
Indeed, there is a distinction of states within those nine-year periods, beginning with Kṛta and so forth.
It was nine thousand yojanas in width and extended as far as the edge of the ocean;
it was crowded with various inhabited lands and filled with the fears of old age and disease.
People who subsist on food grown through agriculture experience slight happiness amidst great suffering;
their lifespan of a hundred years and their very constitution are determined again by the influence of the four ages (yugas). 104.
Thus, without merit (*guṇa*), there is no acquisition of the fruits of good or evil deeds;
therefore, among all the worlds beginning with Bhūr, this [earth] is the land of results and the land of action.
The land renowned as Karmabhūmi, and likewise the heavenly realm (svargabhūmi) above;
having obtained the fruit of enjoying the earth there, one attains Śiva through diligent effort. (106)
In that regard, Bhāratavarṣa is divided into nine parts;
listen, O Nandikeśvara, to those beginning with Indradvīpa.
Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Vāruṇa. || 108 ||
The ninth is called Kumārikā; it is frequented by various trees and creepers and is filled with diverse species, as described in the section known as Bhakta.
It is endowed with the four castes and filled with the four stages of life;
furthermore, five hundred rivers and streams are to be known there.
(683) Endowed with millions of holy fords, auspicious, and the source of great merit,
there is the great peak of Kailāsa on the northern side of the Himavat. || 111 ||
On the Silver Mountain (Raupyādri), however, Śiva is well-served by goddesses, sages, and perfected beings;
he is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with divine trees. || 112 ||
The gods and the Sādhyas dwell there eternally, and their presence is also found upon the mountain;
the sixty-eight great sacred fields, beginning with Vāraṇāsī, are purifying.
The six islands, beginning with Aṅga-dvīpa, are situated within the ocean as visible objects;
[therein are] Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śaktimān, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges; they are auspicious, resembling gold, and joined with the boundary mountains of the continents. || 115 ||
Endowed with various wonders, they sport with the lords of the *rākṣasas*.
Listen now to that which is known as Jambūdvīpa, surrounded by the salt ocean. (116)
And the twelve mountains beginning with Lakṣādyam, which are perfectly pure and have Vimalodadhi as their abode, are likewise well-known in the salt ocean (Lavaṇodadhi). || 117 ||
Vṛṣabha, Dundubhi, Parvata, Cakra, Maināka, and likewise Balāka on the south. || 118 ||
Between those two is the depth of the ocean and the mouth of the submarine fire (Baḍavāmukha);
Varāha and Somaketu are in the western direction, at Nandana.
Beyond that are Kaṃsacandra and Droṇa situated on the north; this is called the Salt Ocean. Now hear about Śākadvīpa.
In Śākadvīpa, indeed, Śeṣa is below; [the others are] Vapuṣmat and Kuśadvīpaka.
Jyotiṣmat is in Krauñcadvīpa, and likewise Śālmali and Ucimān.
By Gomeda, the lords of the five islands are said to have been proclaimed;
seven sons were born to each, divided into groups of seven. (122)
The region from the mountains to the ocean is proclaimed to be divided into seven parts;
and it is there, on the island named Puṣkara, that the one of great strength dwells.
Those two sons are thus described; they are celebrated there as the two continents.
[There is] the mountain named Mānasottara, which is circular in shape. || 124 ||
The time for the inhabitants of Śākadvīpa and other islands is like that of the Kṛta and other ages;
the extent of Meru and the rest has the luster of vermilion, and there are five oceans.
The numbers beginning with seven hundred thousand have indeed been proclaimed in brief.
Beyond that is the great land of Hema, which has an extent of one hundred million [yojanas]. (126)
It is proclaimed on all sides that for the sake of the gods' sport, there exists the mountain known as Lokāloka, which is circular in form. || 127 ||
It begins at a thousand yojanas and rises to a height of one hundred thousand yojanas;
the world-protectors (lokapālas) reside there, surrounded by Siddhas and gods.
Beyond that, the sun is difficult for the virtuous to behold, and thereafter lies darkness;
the ocean-king Garbhodadhi surrounds the Lokāloka mountain.

Encompassing the ocean of the womb (garbhodadhi) is known as the earthly covering (pārthivāvaraṇa); and encompassing that earthly [covering] is the one extending ten million [yojanas], which is called "I" (Aham). 130.
Mahāmeru is recorded as being fifty koṭis from Kaṭarāha;
its measurement should be known as equal in all ten directions, at ten koṭis [each]. (131)
The terrestrial world (Bhūrloka) has thus been described; now hear concerning Bhuvarloka.
The world of the Sun is established at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas.
The Viśvedevas are two, the Vasus are eight, and likewise the Rudras are eleven;
they say the Ādityas are twelve, and thus there are thirty-three deities.
They too dwell there eternally due to their service to the Lord;
by circumambulating Meru, it is known as the Bhuvarloka.
And above that, at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas], the world of the Moon (Candraloka) is established;
at a distance of only fifty thousand [yojanas] from the Moon, the circle of the constellations (Nakṣatramaṇḍala) is situated.
At two hundred thousand [yojanas] one should know Mercury; at two hundred thousand, Venus is recorded;
at two hundred thousand, Mars; and at two hundred thousand, Jupiter. (136)
The rising of the sun is said to occur at two hundred thousand [yojanas], while its setting occurs at one hundred thousand yojanas.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu— 137.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis);
and above them, at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas, Dhruva is said to be situated.
Indeed, everything above the planets up to Dhruva is exactly one hundred and fifty lakṣas;
from the surface of the earth to the end of Dhruva, it is likewise one hundred and fifty lakṣas.
Above that, Maharloka is considered to be twenty million yojanas;
Janaloka is proclaimed to be eight million five hundred thousand [yojanas]. (140)
The Tapoloka is situated above [the Janaloka], measuring eighty million [yojanas] from top to bottom;
likewise, it is recorded as being twelve and fifty million [yojanas] in extent. (141)
It is said that she who supports the cosmic egg extends for a hundred million yojanas;
she is the Buddha named Kapālīśa, whose body is adamantine and who is the crusher of all. 142.
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa—endowed with sovereign power, they overcame the strength of Indra. || 143 ||
The great Rudras, highly honored by the command of Vahni, roam about; in the southwest (Nirṛti) are the Māṇavas, Krodhahan, Trasta, and Avilohita. 144.
He whose liṅga is erect, who has three eyes, who possesses fangs, and from whom the fruit of his name arises;
he who is of great strength, great arms, a comet, and endowed with excellent tusks.
Having overcome the power of Nirṛti, the great Rudras, endowed with sovereign power and honored by the Lord of Rākṣasas, roam about. (146)
Balas and Atibalas, the mighty Pāśahasta, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka. || 147 ||
And Meghanāda and Sunāda—these ten are stationed in the west;
having overcome the power of Varuṇa, they are endowed with the energy of mastery (prabhu-śakti). || 148 ||
The great gods, honored by Varuṇa, roam about;
[the wind] is swift, light, possessing the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, and terrifying. (149)
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana—endowed with sovereign power, they have overcome the purifying force. || 150 ||
The great gods, honored by Vāyurāja, roam about;
and there is the omniscient Vidyādhara, the bearer of knowledge who has reached the further shore of the Vedas. (151)
Sureśvara, Sarveśa, Bhūtapāla, Balipriya, Sukhada, and Duṣkṛta—these ten are [the forms] in brief. || 152 ||
Having overcome the power of Īśāna and being endowed with sovereign power,
the great gods, well-honored by Īśāna, move about.
Viṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Antaka, Īśa, Svakhimāśana, Bhūtara, Kumbhara, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭraka. || 154 ||
Even in the lower region, having overcome the power of Viṣṇu,
the great gods remain well-established and wander about, being highly honored by Īśāna.
Śambhu, Vibhu, Guṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, Tridaśakādita, Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabholipsu, and Vicakṣaṇa. (156)
The gods, Vīrabhadra and others, are proclaimed as the ten Nandins;
moreover, they have ascended even above Brahmā by means of their sovereign powers.
The great gods wander about, well-honored by Brahmā;
and it has been said that you shall attain the knowledge of the reality of the earth—now listen. (158)
Above the Brahmāṇḍa is the principle called Water (Toya), ten times its size in extent;
it is the abode of Rudra, known as Vipada and Vimukta, and possesses great power. || 159 ||
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇurudraka—
these indeed constitute the eight purifiers (pavitrāṣṭaka) situated within the enclosure of space (vyomāvaraṇa).
In the middle of that, one should [worship] the eight *ahaṃkāras* and the *prakṛti* with ten-fold [offerings],
as well as Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mokkoṭa, and Muṇḍakeśvara. (161)
One should know this group of eight locations—Kālāñcana, Śaṅkukaṇṭha, Sthūlaśa, and Sthaleśata—as beginning from the east and ending with the northeast (Īśāna). 162.
The white is declared to be the Guhyāṣṭaka; the red shall be the most secret (Guhyatama). The black is the Guhyādguhyāṣṭaka, and the smoky-colored (dhūmra) is also pure (pavitra).
The eightfold station is said to resemble pure crystal;
thus the five groups of eight have been proclaimed, though they are merely mental constructs for those on the earthly path.
It is by himself, among the other five disputants, that he [establishes] the world as having the form of a Plakṣa tree, governed by the lords of the worlds. (165)
Thus the place of enjoyment for Śrīkaṇṭhanātha has been proclaimed.
Above this, there is the intellect (buddhi), which is enveloped by ten qualities. (166)
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājeśvara, and Brāhmya are remembered as the eight divine wombs (devayoni). || 16 ||
Know this to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), which rests upon the veil of the intellect;
all the aforementioned stations are endowed with every form of sovereignty.
But above the veil of qualities (guṇāvaraṇa), ten qualities of the intellect (buddhi) are recorded:
Akṛta, Kṛta, Bhairava, and Brāhma. || 169 ||
The Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Auma, and the Śrīkaṇṭha—
thus the group of eight in the south has been described as resting upon the Guṇāvaraṇa.
The yogins who are devoted to the Lords of Yoga and apply themselves to yoga with single-minded intent proceed in due order to their divine abodes. (171)
Above this, however, stands the Aripata mountain, surrounded tenfold by Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, Sthāṇu, and Rudraka.
Thus, the eight purifiers (pavitrāṣṭaka) are indeed situated within the enclosure of space (vyomāvaraṇa):
Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, and Sūra. (173)
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and the Īśvaras together with Śiva—thus is the group of eight Mahādevas situated within the unmanifest enclosure (avyaktāvaraṇa). || 174 ||
The Unmanifest, Prakṛti, and Pradhāna are spoken of here;
as well as Rudra, Piṅga, Gaṇeśāna, and those headed by Bhuvaneśa. (175)
Those gods are the size of a thumb; from the thumb they are known as Śiva.
They are completely free from desire and anger, and possess the nature of the Supreme Lord. (176)
In that very place, persons should be known as relying on the veil called passion; they consist indeed of the sixfold sheaths of the elements, the objects, and the senses. 177.
The intellect, the mind, the ego, and especially the three qualities—endowed with these, the Puruṣa is established in the principle of passion (rāga-tattva). || 178 ||
Above that is the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva), which is a hundred times greater than Rāga;
then there are Vāmadeva, Bhīma, Ugra, and likewise Bhava. (179)
Śarva, Īśāna, Vīra, Īśvara, Pracaṇḍadhṛk, Umābhartṛ, Giriśa, and Ananta. (180)
The principle of Kalā (kalātattva) exists above [that], and the principle of Vidyā is even higher than that. || 181 ||
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Raudra, Kāla, and likewise Kala;
Kalavikaraṇa, Balavikaraṇa, and Balapramathana. || 182 ||
Sarvabhūtadamana and Manonmana—these ten Rudras are indeed situated there, and they are remembered as the lords of the physical forms (vigraheśas). || 183 ||
Beyond this is the principle called Niyati, which possesses a hundred times the qualities of Kalā.
[Its presiding deities] are Ucchuṣma, Ambara, Caṇḍa, Mātaṅga, and Ghorarūpaka. (184)

Those who practice the conduct of the Yāmodyaṣaṇḍha [deities] remain for a period a hundred times longer than that, established in the principle of Time (kālatattva) through their withdrawal. || 185 ||
Hālāhala, Kroḍa, and the third named Vāḍava; Sthūlarudra, Paṭarudra, Rudra, and Gurvalaya. (186)
These six are considered to be predominantly established within the principle of Time (kāla-tattva).
And the principle of Māyā is said here to possess a hundred times the power of Kāla. (187)
There are two *saṃpuṭas*, twelve months, and eleven Rudras situated there;
below is the *saṃpuṭa* of Vidyā, and above is the ancient *saṃpuṭa* of Drava.
Aharīśa, as well as Adhyakṣa, and likewise Hariprabhu is remembered;
Daśośāna, and likewise Prabala, and Gopati as well. || 189 ||
Furthermore, those residing within the Māyā-enclosure are proclaimed to be six:
Kṣemīśa, Brahmadhāmīśa, and likewise the Vidyeśas.
Viśveśvara, Śiva, and Ananta— these six alone are proclaimed as the Rudras who reside within the enclosure of the upper Māyā. (191)
And in their midst, the Blessed One Ananteśa, the Lord of the World,
having first brought them into being, acts according to his own will as the Sovereign.
From Māyā down to the earth, those Rudras who are stationed in succession enjoy the objects of experience right there, with their souls full of joy. (193)
Resorting to its mouth, one should take refuge in the Śiva-tattva.
The characteristic [of the path] up to Māyā has been declared; now hear the characteristic above that. (194)
Above Māyā, however, the Ātman exists, increased a hundredfold;
that pure Ātman is designated by the groups beginning with Kratu. (195)
This should be known as the seed of the world, for the sake of manifesting Śiva;
likewise, the person (puruṣa) is essentially free from the five categories of objects. || 196 ||
The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is declared to be that which is free from the light of Śiva;
by the will of Śiva, it becomes the individual soul (jīva) extending from Māyā down to the earth.

This reality of the Self (ātmatattva) has been declared; now hear the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva). The reality of knowledge is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than the reality of the Self. (198)
The principle of Īśvara stands above, situated at the summit of all principles;
there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti. (199)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space, as well as ego, intellect, and the unmanifest—this is the group [of principles]. (200)
p.

701) Following that, within that [Prakṛti], there is the principle of Rāga (Attachment), as well as the ten and five faculties (the eleven senses), Vidyā (Knowledge), Kalā (Limited Agency), Niyati (Necessity), and immediately thereafter the principle of Kāla (Time). || 201 ||
Above the principle of Māyā is the principle of Kāla;
above that is Śuddhavidyā, and above that is the principle of Īśvara, which is mixed with other principles.
Sādākhya, Bindu, and Nāda; beyond that is the Śakti-tattva;
and the supreme Śiva-tattva is proclaimed as the thirty-sixth and most excellent principle. (203)
The thirty-six principles indeed arise from the Śiva-principle;
these principles that have been mentioned are established within the five principles.
The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is to be known as the earth; water extends up to the limit of Prakṛti;
fire likewise extends up to the limit of Vidya; and Vāyu is joined with the principle of Īśvara. (205)
p.
702) For these [principles], their state of existence is indeed the principle of space (vyomatattva), extending up to the power of space (vyomaśakti).
Nivṛtti is to be known as earth, and Pratiṣṭhā shall be water. || 206 ||
The splendor of knowledge (vidyā-tejas) is likewise specified as being joined [to it];
the past (atītā), peace (śānti), and space (vyoman)—these five digits (kalās) are established. || 207 ||
Arising from the power of will (icchā-śakti), they are the sustainers of all beings;
beginning with the element of earth and ending with the principle of self (ātma-tattva), the principle of self is thus proclaimed. (208)
From the principle of Vidyā up to Śakti is declared to be the principle of Vidyā;
above that is the principle of Śiva—thus the three principles have been declared.
From earth up to Māyā, that which ends with Māyā is declared to be the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva).
The Self alone is the principle of the Self (ātma-tattva); therefore, it is the Lord of all principles.
From the principle of *vidyā* up to the end of the *śivatattva*, the *śivatattva* is the supreme beyond the supreme.
It exists in three ways: as *prakṛti*, as *puruṣa*, and as *īśvara*. (211)
Māyā is said to be *prakṛti*, while the Self is the *puruṣa*;
all that, beginning with the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*), is the supreme principle belonging to the Lord.
Among those, starting from the center, it is proclaimed that there are half as many principles (tattvas) as Rudras;
in your fivefold path (adhvan), there is a conjunction with the five kalās.

The three paths have been declared and described as the path of the arts (kalādhvā) and so forth; within this very [path], the letters (varṇa) of the elements are traditionally known as *la*, *va*, and *ra*.
The letter *la* should be known as earth; the letter *va* is said to be water.
The letter *ra* is indeed conjoined with fire, and the letter *ya* is air itself. (215)
The letter *ha* is the color of space; thus there are five syllables.
Together with the *kalā* of the syllables, the path of syllables (*varṇādhvan*) arises through meditation. (216)
The origin of the path of words arises from phonemes; now hear the path of words in due order.
Śarva, the source of the manifestation of all states of being, bestows happiness upon all creatures. (217)
The sole instrument for accomplishing all that is to be achieved, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; he who stood there before being praised; the witness of witnesses; Ṛtu, Ṛtu. || 218 ||
Pataṅga, pataṅga; piṅga, piṅga; jñāna, jñāna; śabda, śabda; sūkṣma, sūkṣma; Śiva, Śiva; Oṃ namaḥ; obeisance again and again to Śiva. || 219 ||
And one should speak thus for cessation, but not with the twenty-eight [syllables]:
"Pervasive, pervasive! Formless, formless! First, first! || 220 ||
p. 705) Tejas-tejas | Jyotis-jyotis | Rūpa | Artha | Asmabhavam anāde | Nā nā nā nā | Dhū dhū | Oṃ bhūḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ || 221 ||
Without end, without end; born from the end. Śiva, Śiva!
Supreme Self, Maheśvara, Maheśvara! Mahādeva, Maheśvara! || 222 ||
O you of great splendor! To the Lord of Yoga, release, release! O foremost one, foremost one! Śiva, Śarva! 223.
It is endowed with thirty-two words, and the installation [of the mantra] is especially significant:
"Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the source of all, whose head is Īśāna. (224)
Obeisance again and again to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, who is Vāmadeva, who is Guhya, and whose form is Sadyojāta. || 225 ||
p.
706) To the protector of the most secret of secrets, the undying one—these twenty-one words of the Vidyā have indeed been declared therein. (226)
Oṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, whose form is the sky, who pervades all;
Oṃ, to Śiva, the infinite, the lordless, the non-dependent. || 227 ||
And to him who is established upon the seat of yoga in the hall, the eternal yogin who subsists on a diet of meat, || 228 ||
Thus, the group of twelve has been proclaimed specifically as the yoga of Peace (Śānti).
The single word "Oṃ" is eternal, the state belonging to the digit beyond Peace (Śāntyatīta).
The path of words (padādhvan) consisting of ninety-four [syllables] is contained within the Ratnagarbha;
therein, the path from Īśāna to Śiva will be explained.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, together with Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—these are declared to be the five faces;
they are considered the supreme Brahmā of the Lotus. (231)
One should recite each mantra individually, beginning with Śāntyatītā and ending with Pṛthvī;
likewise, the heart, the head, the crest, and the armor.
And right there, the three eyes and the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) come into being;
the eye is to be known as beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Śiva, beyond Śānti.
The root mantra is declared to be Śiva, joined with the supreme path of mantras (mantrādhvan). Therein, the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, will be described.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti—these are declared to be the five kalās, which are further known as the kalās of the five Brahmans. || 235 ||
The five kalās of Īśāna have been declared; furthermore, his son [possesses] them again.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti—these are proclaimed as the four digits (kalās) of Puruṣa. || 237 ||
Tamas, Moha, Akṣaya, Niṣṭhā, Mṛtyu, Māyāmayā, and Jarā as the eighth—these are known as the powers (vidyās) of Aghora. || 238 ||
Lākṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, Rakṣā, Rudrakā, Kapālinī, Kalakāmavikaraṇā, Svayamī, and Parikriyā. (239)
Vikaraṇā, Kāryā, Bhrāmaṇī, and Mohinī—these, along with the Vāmadeva-kalās, are declared to be the thirteen. (240)
Vṛddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svara, and Dhṛti—these eight are the kalās of Sadyojāta; thus thirty-eight [kalās] have been declared. (241)
Thus, having been liberated from the path of the arts (kalādhvan) as well, one attains the determination of the six paths;
and by means of these six paths, one enters indeed into supreme Śiva on this way.
Thus, for one whose cognition of the six paths is such, that becomes the destroyer of the bonds (*pāśahā*).
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, "The Determination of the Six Paths," within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim initiation (dīkṣā) conjoined with specialized knowledge,
because it is preceded by specific knowledge, because of its manifold nature, and because of its unfolding.
That is declared to be the initiation of consciousness (vijñāna-dīkṣā), the most excellent among all initiations;
it is for one initiated even if devoid of mantra, devoid of ritual action, or devoid of meditation.
Because it is established as being complete, initiation is indeed purifying; for through that initiation, one's state of Śiva-hood is attained and all doubt is destroyed. (3)
Because it possesses such a distinguished nature, it is celebrated as "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Merely by the sight of the Guru, one becomes endowed with extreme devotion. || 4 ||
With his body bristling with horripilation and eyes filled with tears of joy, he was at all times longing to hear [it] and always intent upon hearing it. || 5 ||
Always intent on serving the guru, free from greed,
and devoted to carrying out his commands— whether it be happiness or even suffering.
And there is a lack of independence in that body, like clay for a potter;
this is true whether it falls into the ocean or even into the Ganges.

If, even when falling upon tigers, snakes, and the like, one follows the command without hesitation, and if it has been resolved by him that "all my possessions have been cast into the ocean," [then he is liberated]. (8)
One must always be exceedingly proficient in that task;
indeed, having cast away wealth and the like upon the ground, one should seek the path of knowledge.
If his mind is set upon completely renouncing mother, father, son, brothers, and wife,
then he is one who delights in renunciation.
Having accepted everything that was spoken by the Guru,
one should never, in such matters as these, fail to carry them out until the initiation is complete.

The Guru, who is perfected and the leader on the true path, should out of compassion initiate with the initiation of higher knowledge (vijñānadīkṣā) the disciple who has already been joined with the previously mentioned initiations. || 12 ||
(712) Through initiation by means of mere mental activity, [initiation] occurs in due order;
that initiation may indeed be known as the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā) and the initiation of higher realization (vijñānadīkṣā). || 13 ||
In a beautiful and auspicious place, at a delightful time, and during pleasant circumstances—when both [the teacher and the student] experience an equal state of happiness. (14)
At that very moment, that initiation which destroys the entire cycle of worldly existence occurred;
and he, established in the five supports, became firmly situated within the body of the Guru.
And within the maṇḍala of the path of the Guru is the supreme maṇḍala of the Guru;
it consists of all witnesses and is Śiva, the ultimate cause. (16)
Thereafter, by the grace of the Guru, the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and so forth is performed as before;
indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside upon the palm of the Guru’s hand. (17)
The Brāhma [tīrtha] is indeed at the base of the thumb; that of the gods and of the mantras is at the tips of the fingers;
and that which arises from the joints of the finger-phalanges is to be resorted to by the divine sages (devarṣis). 18.
The sacred bathing place at the base of the little finger belongs to humans and sages;
that at the base of the hand is said to be the sacred bathing place of the spirits.
The Pitṛ-tīrtha is situated between the index finger and the thumb;
one should visualize that seven tīrthas exist within that hand.
Having meditated upon the sacred fords as being of the nature of the *bindu*, the wise one [should perform the rite] with his right hand, pervaded by the Śiva-mantra. (21)
The Guru should contemplate the left [side] as pervaded by the Śakti-mantra;
he should likewise cause the disciple to be honored with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having seated him on a comfortable seat, with his mind fixed upon that [object] within the field of vision, the disciple should become such; immediately thereafter, he becomes a guru. (23)
Then one should contemplate the fire of Śiva arising from the sacrificial pit of the fire at the Mūlādhāra,
as well as the clarified butter in the path of the Ājñā and the nectar situated within the lunar orb.

And having established the fire in the ladle (sruva) within the auspicious mandala, the preceptor [prepares] the mind as the sacrificial ladle (sruc), the intellect as the dipping-spoon (sruva), and the ritual portions (kalās) as the fuel-sticks (samidh). || 25 ||
Having raised the vine-like arms upward with the root-kuṇḍalinī,
one should likewise contemplate iḍā and piṅgalā as the moon and the sun.
Having performed the purification of the clarified butter (ājya) by means of the thread of the nature of sound (nāda),
and because the fire was already established previously, he likewise performed it without the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) rite.

Having recited the *tāra* (oṃ), the *śakya* (śakyamuni), and at the end Śiva, as well as the other [mantra] enclosed between them, the mantra ending with *puṣpa* (namo) shall be thus; these are the unsurpassed oblations of knowledge (*jñānāhuti*). || 28 ||
Oṃ haṃ saṃ seṃ, I am the Sun; to Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa, so haṃ hauṃ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ oṃ! || 29 ||
One should offer oblations in the *mūlādhāra* by means of the path of the *piṅgalā* nāḍī:
*oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ oṃ hāṃ īśvaramayaḥ sohaṃ hauṃ svāhā*. || 30 ||
Thereafter, one should offer oblations through the iḍā and perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) at the mūlādhāra with:
oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ sūryasomāgnissohaṃ hauṃ svāhā. || 31 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ huṃ aghorassohaṃ huṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ tatpuruṣābhyāṃ sohaṃ svāhā || 32 ||
oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ hiṃ vāmadevassohaṃ hauṃ svāhā | oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ aghoravāmadevābhyāṃ sauṃ hauṃ svāhā || 33 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ saṃ, to Sadyojāta, sohaṃ sauṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Śāntikalā, sohaṃ hauṃ svāhā! || 34 ||
Oṃ hrīḥ haṃsaḥ | Svāhā to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. || 35 ||
Having unified [the elements] with such mantras as these, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa):
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsassohaṃ hauṃ svāhā. || 36 ||
With this very mantra, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) until the point of satisfaction;
O Nandikeśvara, one should offer oblations with the limb-mantra for one-tenth of that amount.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to the Nivṛtti-kalā, so'haṃ haiṃ svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ so'haṃ haiṃ svāhā! To the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, so'haṃ hauṃ svāhā! || 38 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to the Vidyā-kalā, so'haṃ hauṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to the Śānti-kalā, so'haṃ hauṃ svāhā! || 39 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the fire sacrifice with the seed-syllables of Vāgīśvarī: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ śāntyatītakalāyai sohaṃ hauṃ svāhā*. 40.
Then, with the *prāsāda* mantra, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti*;
having drawn forth the consciousness of the disciple, one should unite it with the *mūlādhāra*.
Having drawn [the water] from that place, one should again offer the arghya with the Brahmamantra.
And in the center of the Guru-maṇḍala, [one should offer it] with the mantra "Sadānandāmṛtojjvale."
Having united the disciple’s self with [the deity] and bestowed the true path in due order,
he should meditate upon this form of Śiva and again join it to the root. || 43 ||

One should offer oblations with the names of Śiva, beginning from the netherworld (tala) up to the end of all worlds; likewise, the thirty-one principles (tattvas) beginning from Māyā down to the earth (bhūmi).
One should perform the oblation for each individual letter, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', and all of that in reverse order. || 45 ||
The ninety-four-word mantra, beginning with *bhava* and ending with *praṇava*, is as follows:
*oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ bhavassohaṃ hauṃ svāhā*. || 46 ||
"Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ bhavodbhavassa haṃ hauṃ svāhā"— with such a mantra as this, the preceptor should perform the oblation mentally.
O Nandikeśvara, one should offer the oblations of the kalās, such as Nivṛtti and the rest;
one should offer the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) with Śiva himself, being permeated by Śiva.
The Guru himself, whose form blazes with the bliss of compassion, should perceive the disciple’s body as consisting of Śiva and Śakti and behold it as the three eyes. (49)
It is for the purpose of the constant Śiva-sacrifice, known as the Ajapā mantra; it brings about the cessation of the moon and sun and constantly increases yoga. 50.
Know that whether waking or sleeping, standing or moving about,
the Śiva-sacrifice remains perpetually present at every moment.
Having taken the consciousness of the disciple and joined it in the midst of the circle of gurus, one should contemplate both Śiva and the disciple as merged therein.
Having joined [the deity] to the body of the disciple, one should meditate upon the form of Śiva,
specifically the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), beginning from the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama). (53)
The leader of the true path should cause everything to dissolve into "Śiva," which is devoid of both the signified and the signifier, and beyond the reach of mind and speech. (54)
It is immeasurable, without beginning, free from conceptual proliferation, and without defining characteristics;
it is empty of beginning and end, absolute, nameless, and infinite.

Having thus meditated upon that which is higher than the highest, beyond the measure of death, and devoid of both duality and non-duality, the great knower embraced his disciple with intense affection.
If one places it upon the head and remembers it at any time with an unimpaired body, bliss arises for him right there; of this there is no doubt. (57)
Trembling, perspiration, and horripilation arise there, as does the dawning of all-encompassing knowledge;
and right there, one becomes distinguished, possessing the very form of Śiva. (58)
Having placed a garland of flowers upon his own head right there, the bestower of the true path should perform the consecration with both hands. (59)
"If one is devoid of the initiation of consciousness (*vijñāna-dīkṣā*), how can there be liberation? How can there be Śiva?
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, concerning the procedure for the initiation of consciousness, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
O Nandikeśvara, listen to the reality of the self and the *samaya*, which is Śiva—higher than the highest, subtle, immeasurable, and unsurpassed. || 1 ||

In the beginning, there was a twofold ignorance according to the distinction of its functions: one characterized by the supreme transcendence, and the other, through sin, that which perceives the Aśvattha tree. (2)
Knowledge that reveals Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna;
whereas the knowledge concerning Caidya is the lower (apara) cognition, which reveals the meaning of the fetters of the bound soul (paśu).
Nandikeśvara said: What are the systems such as those of the Buddhists, and how do their respective divisions arise?
Tell me, how are their various principles characterized by both non-confusion and confusion?
"O Blessed One, why should a discourse on false origins be told to me?
[The systems of] the Buddhists, the Ārhatas, the Pāñcarātras, and the Śaivas— [5]"
The commitment (samaya) shall be fourfold; its respective divisions will now be explained:
the Śāpaka, the Mahāyāna, and then the Pratyekanāyaka.
Having analyzed the Vaibhāṣika [system], which ends with that [treatise] as a distinction of bondage,
there is likewise the Lokāyata and that which follows the Mahāyāna. (7)
In the Mahāyāna, the prima facie position would be that of the Lokāyata; in that regard, the Pratyekabuddhas are devoid of the words of the Sautrāntikas.
From that, one becomes a Yogācāra; from that, one may fall away from the Tantra.
The Vaibhāṣika position is twofold, and likewise for each Śrāvaka.
And therein, the Mahāyāna is traditionally held to be of two supreme kinds:
the Supreme Vehicle (Paramayāna) and the Everlasting Vehicle (Aśaśvatayāna), as well as the Excellent Mantra Vehicle (Sumantrayāna).
The Sautrāntika is cited as having the reality of the method of others;
through the two-fold yoga residing in mantra, there is both movement and non-movement.
That [emptiness] is twofold: with form and without form; likewise, those who follow it are called Mādhyamikas, and from that [arises] the non-dual Madhyama. (12)
For all those disputants are proclaimed to be established in the Dharma; one should know that they abide within the divisions of Buddhism, and now the great division is described. (13)
The *laśrāvana* is stainless and without blemish; it is threefold.
One should establish the fourfold stage of life (*āśrama*) by means of these three groups of three.
The householder, the mendicant, likewise the student, and the forest-dweller—these are declared to be the stages of life (āśramas). || 15 ||
The Vaiṣṇava tradition is said to be threefold; its divisions are now described:
the Pañcarātra, the Bhāgavata, and likewise that which is approved by the Vaikhānasas. (16)
Thus, threefold [inquiry] has been proclaimed: Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, and Ātmavāda, respectively. (17)
And the division of those Vedic [traditions] is declared; that which is called Vāma is now described.
Vāma is said to be threefold: Anādi, Pūrva, and Paścima. (18)
The Great Vow (mahāvrata) is of four kinds;
beyond that, there would be the Kālāmukha, the Kāpāla, and likewise the Pāśupata.
Śaivism is said to be fourfold, while the Siddhānta is of two kinds:
namely, Karmānta and Jñānānta; Jñāna is remembered as the supreme, being situated above them.
Caryā and Kriyāyoga shall be the means for accomplishing ritual actions;
then knowledge, joined with Caryā, Kriyā, and Yoga, shall also come to be.
Śakti, Śiva, Sādākhya, Mantra, and that which consists of Pradhāna; and the state of having all impurities exhausted—liberation is said to reside in that very [state]. (22)
In this way, there would be a karmic obscuration; however, above that, it is free from obscuration:
the Bindu, the Nāda, the Śakti, the Para, and the Parātpara.
The limit of attaining Brahman is indeed the bliss of the bliss of the Self;
thus, the Śaiva division is likewise the highest, being entirely free from obscuration.
Since these [offerings] constitute a single oblation, their commingling does not constitute a fault;
however, there is a specific distinction regarding such cases—listen now to that distinction.
The universal form of Śiva is indeed the very body of Śiva;
it is the supreme state, free from passion and worthy of the Arhats, which has been forgotten since the unmanifest.
The attainment of the bliss of sovereignty, distinguished by the Pañcarātra and other systems,
is to be known as Śaiva, which is higher than the highest and the sole leader of all principles. (27)
It should be known as consisting of all mantras and as being composed of all deities;
it arises from the knowledge of the true path through austerities performed in previous births. (28)
One should not transgress the command of the Guru through the actions of mind, speech, or body;
for by such transgression, one goes to hell and likewise becomes a thief of knowledge.
Therefore, one should not transgress the command of the guru with any effort whatsoever;
for one who is devoted to the propitiation of the guru, the knowledge of the agent becomes manifest. (30)
It is designated as "tattva" (reality) because it consists of seven [elements] and because it arises from them;
its perfection belongs to one endowed with a body, and indeed, it persists even at the end of that body.
One endowed with a body may attain knowledge, but perfection is devoid of the body. Through various means, there is only the further increase of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (32)
O Nandikeśvara, Śiva must perform what is necessary;
I shall declare the designation for one who is established in the Śaiva Siddhānta—listen to that.
The monastery, the tree, the lineage, and likewise the sphere of activity—these five objects of worship, along with the karmic obscurations, are included in the *Yuktaka*. (34)
Mukhānanda, Maṭha, Darśana, Vāsana, as well as Pañcatattva, Guhā, Vṛkṣa, and Vanam; || 35 ||
It consists of the lineage, the sphere, the continuum, and the twelve cognitions;
thus it is the practice of cognition, and its name is not distinct [from that]. (36)
The face of Īśāna is also declared here as the divine Śiva;
the monastery is renowned as Brahmā, and the path of truth shall be the philosophical system (darśana). (37)
They speak of the triad beginning with Jñāna, as well as Āvāsa and Parvata; likewise, the incomparable one called Mano-bhaṅga, Siddhi-mantra, and Guhā. (38)

The world has become a forest to be consumed by fire; the ear is the state of pure Sugata, while the object of perception is the auspicious mantra; thus, the mental continuum shall become identical with that. || 39 ||
Having recognized these and other such [states], one should awaken the supreme son to the highest all-knowing wisdom through this very investigation. (40)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the *samaya*, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
730) Now I shall explain in detail how to protect the *Ratnagarbha* [mantra], as well as the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the four classes beginning with the Brahmins and for the six [castes]. (1)
The status of being a teacher (ācārya) is prescribed for these ten classes;
they shall determine the local customs, the consensus of the people, and the distinctions between castes.
Out of respect for the purifying seat of others according to their birth and conduct,
one should not perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) for those of the ten classes who have not received initiation.
Even if the ritual for the Śiva-fire is not prescribed specifically for the Vaiṣṇava,
nevertheless, it must be performed by the ascetic, especially according to the Śaiva path.
Indeed, there is a certain distinction among the various classes of teachers (ācāryas), as well as among the ascetics (yatis)—
specifically between the paramahaṃsa-yatis and those who have renounced through austerity (tapassannyāsins).
In these two [mantras], their application in fire-rituals is not prescribed;
likewise, their consecration is prescribed without a *homa* offering. (6)
Endowed with the previously mentioned qualities, possessed of prior initiation,
joined with the knowledge of what has been heard, and endowed with the virtues of an ācārya.
The most excellent preceptor should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) directed toward him;
all [the deities] are to be worshipped as complete [as before], and the pavilion and other elements are to be arranged as previously described.
Upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), there should be jars; in the lowest [arrangement], one should place the Śiva-jar and, to its left, the Vardhanī jar, joined with the Śakti.
One should place [the vessels] upon eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāna) on the outside of that [mandala],
either with fifty medicinal herbs or with ten flowers.
Sahadevī, ekapatrā, bhadra, vaikaṅkata,
and viṣṇukrānti— these five constitute the "five medicinal herbs" (pañcauṣadha). || 11 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, hrībera, and māsī, along with saffron, uśīra, kanda, and the four spices (caturjāti). || 12 ||
Filled with the five precious medicinal herbs and mixed with grains of śāli rice,
they were completely filled with pure water and adorned with mango sprouts.
Among them are the oceans of salt water, milk, curd, and clarified butter;
and the seas produced from the essence of sugarcane juice, pure water, and [other] waters.
Having worshipped them in sequence on the exterior, one should also worship the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras):
Śikhaṇḍin in the east, and Śrīkaṇṭha in the corner.
Trimūrti is in the southern part, and Ekarudra is also in the south; Ekanetra is in the western quarter, and Sūkṣmadaṃṣṭra should be placed there. (16)
One should place the formless [deity] in the northeast, and [the other forms] at the beginning, middle, and end;
one should place the ocean of Śiva in the center and the ocean of Śakti in the *vardhanī* vessel.
One should worship everything, beginning with Nivṛtti and the other Kalās, as well as the five Kumbhas, like Śiva himself, using the eight utterances of the root mantra.
Alternatively, there may be an ablution with a single such pitcher;
however, in the case of five pitchers, one should place two Vidyeśvaras in each pitcher.
One should likewise place two oceans;
in the center, one should place the Śiva-pitcher and similarly the Śiva-ocean.
Beside that, one should also place the *vardhanī* vessel together with the ocean of power (*śakti*).
And on the northern side of the pavilion, there should be an excellent bathing pavilion. (21)
Having constructed an altar eight finger-breadths high with two cubits on each side,
and having placed a seat made of śrīparṇa wood or similar materials upon it, one should fix the mind on the worship.
Having seated the disciple facing the east and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
one should worship him with rice from a potter's kiln, clay, ashes, dūrvā grass, and balls of cow dung.
Then, one should perform churning with the waters of *siddhārtha* and *ghṛta*,
following the sequence of the Ocean of Milk, using the mantras of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) in the heart.
One should consecrate the disciple with the protective mantras (kavaca-mantras) and armor-mantras;
having wrapped him in a pure cloth, one should seat him to the right of Śiva.
On the seat previously described, one should again perform the ritual for the disciple as before;
[offering] the turban, the crown, the parasol, and indeed the white fly-whisks. (26)
In that case of division, however, one should give to the preeminent lifelong teacher a chariot,
horses, elephants, vehicles, and so forth, as well as a pair of scissors, a knife, and a water-pot.
In this manner, one should likewise cause the other suitable items for both to be given,
such as a rosary, kusha grass, a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle, a book, and so forth.
I, who have reached the further shore of the true path, should offer five oblations for the sake of satisfying the network of mantras at the arising of the auspicious consecration. (29)
Likewise, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and establish [the deity] to one's own right;
one should listen to the knowledge of Śiva and cause it to be heard as requested.
