One should complete the initiation for a disciple endowed with the previously mentioned qualities;
one should perform a small amount of recitation and offer a small oblation into the fire.
In that [state], there should be only slight meditation, slight recitation of mantras, and study of the Āgamas toward the Guru; everywhere indeed, one should become pure. (32)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the Ratnagarbha-vidhi, within the Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra.
O Nandikeśvara, I shall describe the consecration for practitioners,
as well as the pavilion and other structures, the worship, and the fire-ritual, just as before.
O Nandikeśvara, having brought together the triad of kalās beginning with nivṛtti and ending with vidyā, as well as śānta and samanta, one should purify them.
Then, having meditated upon Sadāśiva with the root mantra and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
one should perform a hundred [recitations] and effect such a quality eightfold.

Atomicity (aṇimā), levity (laghimā), and attainment (prāpti), as well as irresistible will (prākāmya), magnanimity (mahimā), lordship (īśitva), and mastery according to one's desire (vaśitva)—[these are the eight siddhis]. || 4 ||
And because of mastery over desires and wisdom, there are these eight sovereign powers (aiśvaryas): Oṃ hāṃ! May the power of atomization (aṇimā-śakti) come into being, svāhā! || 5 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, O Self, may attainment be yours, svāhā!
In this manner, one should join [the mantra] ending in the dative case with the word "svāhā."
Having performed the application as before, one should offer oblations with the word "svāhā" joined [to the mantra];
having performed the application as before, together with the five jars.
Having meditated upon the *kutaṣañca* together with the mantra and its associated components,
one should offer oblations in sequence one hundred and eight times using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). || 8 ||
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the consecration with the fifth vessel, the *śāntikumbha*;
one should then perform the consecration with the jars representing the oceans of the eastern and other directions.
Seated upon a throne facing north, one should consecrate the practitioner with the thought that it is a shower of nectar, using the mudrā arising from the exhalation (recaka). || 10 ||
Having performed one hundred oblations with the mantra of the deity to be accomplished, he should perform the consecration with those seven [substances];
furthermore, having seated his beloved, who is fully manifest (sakalī), on the right side of Śambhu.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform for him, as before, the rite of the uṣṇīṣa and also the kartarī; and in that very place, one should cause the empowerment (adhikāra) to be bestowed.
Then the preceptor, having uttered the *sādhya-mantra* together with the *satāra*, should,
by means of the *recaka* breath, place [the mantra] into the joined palms [of the disciple] along with flowers and other offerings. (13)
Having been addressed as "Great Favor," one should place her, radiant as the autumnal moon,
within the heart-lotus by means of the *pūraka* breath, for the sake of the practitioner.
Having withdrawn the mantras to be accomplished into the fire, endowed with the meditative state (bhāva),
one should worship the lotus of the Mātṛkās within the mandala and other [sites] on the right.
O Nandikeśvara, having obtained the permission of the Guru, one should worship the mantras of the object of accomplishment in their midst, and then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in due order.
In an auspicious time when the ascendant is favorable,
the practitioner of mantra should perform the "sealing" (saṃrodhana) for the sake of attaining the supernatural powers such as aṇimā and others, using either ghee or milk.
The true guru should then commence a fire sacrifice (homa) of either one thousand or one hundred oblations,
following the lineage succession beginning with the venerable Triṇayana. (18)
By the instruction of the true guru, everything is accomplished instantly.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the ritual for the initiation of the practitioner, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall specifically describe the consecration by means of the weapon-mantra (astra) for kings,
men, and women such as those who are barren.
This auspicious [practice] bestows immediate peace upon those afflicted by great calamities;
it grants the attainment of fortune, prosperity, victory, desired dharmas, and other perfections. (2)
Oṃ śrīṃ; having first uttered [this], phaṃ granthiṃ huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ śrīṃ ślīṃ śirase haṃphaṇṇamaḥ || 3 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; oṃ huṃ netrebhyo huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Having recited the mantra once, the Guru should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body. (4)
One should perform the placement of the five [limbs] beginning with the limbs, starting with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should then recite the weapon mantra (*astra*).
In either a square mandala or one adorned with a lotus,
[one should visualize] the Lord of Gods seated upon the Tara-throne, endowed with ten arms.
Possessing five faces and endowed with ten ears,
he has three eyes for each face and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
With fangs formidable and extremely fierce, emitting a great roar and possessing immense strength,
he was licking with his tongues and possessed the splendor of ten million suns.
Thus, one should worship the Supreme Lord, who is seated in the midst of the *aṇimā* [powers], as the Pāśupata weapon that destroys the multitude of obstacles. (9)
Success is certain for one who recites the mantra ten thousand times;
or rather, listen now to how the task is accomplished by mere recitation alone. (10)
In rites such as killing and the like, [the practice] is devoid of bindu and nāda;
however, for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation, there is complete success when it is endowed with bindu and nāda.
One should place the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) for the fire-pit, the syllable *śrī* for Kedāra,
the syllable *pa* in the southwestern quarter, and the syllable *śrī* in the region of the wind (northwest).

Having thus deposited the syllable *huṃ* in the eyes of the deity and the syllable *phaṭ* on the lunar and directional petals, and having performed worship according to the rule, one should prescribe the fire-oblation (*homa*).

When the fire has been consecrated there, the Navātman [mantra] is then used for the offerings; the performance of the *homa* for the King of Mantras should indeed be done with the three sweets (*madhutraya*). (14)
There, one should diligently perform one hundred and eight oblations according to the prescribed ritual,
beginning first with the filling of the water-pot.
O Nandikeśvara, having worshipped the seat of the Praṇava as before,
one should worship the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) with the mantra consisting of one hundred and eight syllables.
As before, one should bathe the disciple on the head with the water-pot itself,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, musical instruments, and hymns of auspicious proclamation.

Having placed many disciples, clothing, and so forth, as well as ornaments of gold, gems, and the like before the Guru, one should offer them for his pleasure and for the sake of spiritual accomplishment. 18.
Thus, the empowerment of the weapon (astrābhiṣeka) also destroys the flood of great sins. || 18½ ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the weapon-mantra, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall describe the nectar-consecration (amṛtābhiṣeka); listen, O Nandikeśvara!
It bestows joy when performed and wards off all diseases.
It is the conqueror of untimely death, bestowing the siddhi of freedom from old age and immortality;
it is a wheel consisting of a flood of nectar, bringing forth intense bliss in its entirety.
By means of this, the preceptor Candraśekhara, endowed with the consecration,
[bestows] the wheel-mantra, meditation, the means of accomplishment, and the consecration.
I shall now describe the application and all its various divisions:
one should draw an eight-petaled wheel upon a surface such as a cloth or a leaf.
One should write with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, and saffron, combined with snow-water and liquid substances. (5)
A golden brush should be fashioned by way of the path of nectar;
and upon that, a pair of lotuses together with a pericarp of the lotus should be made.
The great mantra is a flood of nectar, joined with many syllables,
and indeed endowed with a single extraction, like another wish-fulfilling gem.
Immediately above that is the syllable *ṭha* joined with a bindu;
then the syllable *sa* and the syllable *ja*, at the end of which is conjoined with the letter *ra*.
The Śiva-mantra, the bindu, and likewise the nāda—
this is the great mantra-piṇḍa, which should reside in the center of the pericarp.
The form of the moon is also mobile and endowed with four faces. || 10 ||
The seed-syllable of Sadāśiva, joined with the fire of Ajeśa, combined with Śakti in its center, and conjoined with the Likuca fruit. || 11 ||
The seed-syllable (piṇḍa) joined with eight seeds, endowed with bindu and nāda:
Hrīṃ Phaṃ Hauṃ.
One should specifically place the sixteen digits (kalās) outside the enclosure (dalabāhya). || 12 ||
Some [place] the second lotus petal; some [place] the third petal;
the third [is placed] on the third, and the fourth on the row of petals.
One should write the Varuṇa seed-syllable ending in *m* in the fifth square;
having placed the *dānta* (the letter *t*) in the sixth, one should place the Śiva seed-syllable in the seventh.
Having placed the *bindu* of the *kalā*, the wise one should then sequentially place the syllables situated outside it, joined with the sixteen vowels. (15)
But listen now, Nandikeśvara, to another, the middle wheel.
One should draw a sevenfold wheel endowed with sixteen spokes;
as before, one should place the great mantra in the form of a seed-syllable (piṇḍa) in the center of the pedestal.

One should place the syllable *ca* (caturthī) in the sixteen external vessels; then, one should place the syllable *ja* outside of that, and further outside of that, one should place the syllable *va* (vāruṇa).
Outside that, he should place the syllable *sa* within a circle; outside that, the seed-syllable of Soma (*soṃ*);
and previously, he should place the *śaktis* along with the *dharmas* and *jñānas*.
On the northern side of the deity, the wise one should have a mandala prepared,
having smeared it with cow dung so that it resembles the surface of a mirror. (20)
One should sprinkle the pavilion and other areas with fragrant sandalwood water;
being pure, clad in white linen, and with one's body smeared with ashes. (21)
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, he was adorned with white flowers,
endowed with incomparable pearls, and wore a white sacred thread.
As before, in the center of the altar, one should draw the previously mentioned wheel using white flour mixed with camphor and cold water.
Having prepared a seat with a ritual grass mat (kūrcaka) and having performed the three types of ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence,
the wise practitioner should contemplate himself and Śiva as being non-dual.

Having meditated upon one's own auspicious Guru-bhakti as consisting of that very image, and having visualized the Guru above it, [one should bathe him] with the nectar-water flowing from his limbs. (25)
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon oneself being sprinkled [with water];
then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the recitation of the mantra together with its form (sārūpya). || 26 ||
One should satisfy this [deity] with water mixed with fragrances, using white and blue flowers, as well as white rice grains—one-eighth part of which [should be used]. (27)
One should worship Śiva, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, with clarified butter, milk-rice (pāyasa), and jasmine flowers; and one should offer the supreme milk-rice as a sacrificial gift.

Thus, this supreme mantra, which brings about all accomplishments when properly recited, should be used by one desiring long life; furthermore, one should worship Skanda and the others three times on the scale.
Having gathered apāmārga plants along with the previously mentioned [substances], ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa),
one should offer them into the fire; this destroys untimely death.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations three times a day for a thousand repetitions each day, using fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood mixed with the three sweets.
In this manner for the first month, and subsequently for each following month, it should be performed for three days; thus, the full moon day (paurṇamī) and so forth shall be reached.
The embodied one shall live for a hundred years and, at the end of the body, go to Śiva;
this is achieved even by using twenty-one days of Gaḍūcī with white rice.
One should offer oblations with white sesame seeds according to the previously mentioned number for the sake of health;
likewise, one desiring rain, having bathed in the morning on the eastern day, should remain composed.
Having prostrated before the lotus-feet of the Guru and having received his permission,
he should again worship Vighneśvara and the other deities as before. (35)
"For the sake of protecting the worlds, I shall bring about rain";
having thus resolved in his mind, he should feed those who are devotees of Śiva. (36)
As before, the practitioner should create a charming ornamentation for the mandala and so forth; in its center, he should construct an altar measuring one cubit.
Its height and its dimensions should likewise be measured; in the center of that, one should place a lotus made of four *droṇas* of rice grains, complete with eight petals and leaves.
One should place a jar filled with water, together with sprouts, a lid, and two pieces of fine silk, into the eastern pitcher containing a *droṇa* measure of water.
Silver, combined with fragrant substances and joined with roots,
encircled by pearls and strewn with flowers that serve as its ornament; || 40 ||
In the center of that, one should worship Śivacandra with the piṇḍa-mantra;
immediately thereafter, one should worship him with white, fragrant flowers.
O Nandikeśvara, one should offer the sacrificial food (naivedya) consisting solely of milk-rice (pāyasa);
having meditated upon Agni and Candramas, one should [offer] excellent fuel-sticks of Vetasa wood.
One should offer a thousand oblations, mixed with the three sweets, in successive order;
even at the end of twenty-seven days, a great rain will occur.
If there is obstruction caused by other such views, it should be removed with salt;
however, for the purpose of subjugation, one should use honey, clarified butter, and jasmine flowers.
Having become one who accomplishes the object of attainment through milk-rice offerings on a bright full-moon day,
one should then recite the root mantra followed by the name of the object of attainment. (45)
Ending with "vaśam ānaya" and joined with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* mantra),
one should offer oblations a thousand times, or perhaps one hundred and eight times.
Within twenty-one days, while another person is engaged in mental recitation,
[the practitioner] cuts [the bonds], beginning from the right foot and ending with the left foot.
Then, one should perform oblations with honey and clarified butter using the root mantra for twenty-one days; having done so, one should perform the concluding rites, such as the *pūrṇāhuti*.
At midnight, one should certainly perform the summoning of that [target];
or else, one should offer oblations with rice-powder (siktha) for the purpose of drawing forth the actual form of the sādhya.
One may perform the heating with beeswax or by means of a lamp;
this is declared to be the method of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), or it may also be done with clay from a potter’s wheel. (50)
The wise one should perform the oblation as before; this is the supreme method of attraction.
For the pacification of fever, burning sensations, and so forth, it should proceed through the sequence of the wheels as previously described.
One should cause an auspicious image to be drawn and presented as an offering, and have it given to the Moon,
together with ashes from the eastern direction and so forth, along with clarified butter and milk-rice (pāyasa).
And one should offer oblations, one thousand for each [deity];
by this alone, within seven days, there is the pacification of fever, burning sensations, and other ailments. (53)
The Śrīcakra should be worshipped as before, also with the five limbs of the Bilva;
one should offer oblations seven thousand times for great prosperity.
O Nandikeśvara, one should obtain Śivacandra and worship him;
those who are called Mahāgaṇapatis should also perform the rite of piercing (tīhaṇa). || 55 ||
As before, the wise one should fashion a Śivacandra at its tip and perform three thousand oblations with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having informed the god of his desire, he should worship Vighna and Durgā;
in that very abode, there is a well whose water is like the nectar of the ocean.
And having summoned him who was dejected and devoted to mantra and meditation,
he [revealed] his own abode of nectar, the crushing [of poison] which destroys venom.
[One should place the seed-syllables] on the thumbs, the soles of the feet, the joints, the knees, the private parts, the navel, the chest, the breasts, the throat,
the nose, the eyes, the ears, the eyebrows, the cheeks, the crown of the head, and the top of the head. || 59 ||
In men, it revolves by means of the right [hand] alone;
[it causes] despondency and that which is bitten by poison, as well as the previously mentioned wheel. (60)
Having visualized above his head the sprinkling of streams of nectar with twelve niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again; || 61 ||

Then, O Nandikeśvara, having constructed a lotus with half of that measure or even half of that again, the preceptor [should perform] all the rites regarding the water within the pavilion as previously described.
The wise one should have an altar prepared measuring four cubits;
having drawn the previously mentioned [design] in due order, he should worship it endowed with devotion. (63)
In the center of that [space] is an amṛta-pitcher, and in the center of that is a lotus;
one should fill the pitcher in the four corners with auspicious, fragrant waters.
Having realized that this [water], endowed with the nine jewels and joined with mango sprouts,
is of the nature of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), one should know the water situated within it. (65)
Having meditated on it as having the form of nectar, one should worship the moon of Śiva in its center with white flowers and the powers of the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites.
One should also encircle that charming [mandala] with two white oblations,
accompanied by the resonance of the Vedas and endowed with the sound of hymns of praise.
One should consecrate that disciple with all auspicious sounds;
endowed with devotion to the guru, one should worship him in due order as if he were Śiva himself. 68.
Furthermore, one should give gold, jewels, and other such wealth to the guru according to the order of one's means; and with devotion, one should prostrate before him like a staff.
Thereafter, however, one should worship the devotees of Śiva in the same sequence as before. || 69½ ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the consecration with nectar, in the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is beyond thought.
Now I shall specifically describe the nine auspicious types of food:
that obtained through continuous fasting, alms, and likewise what is unasked for.
"Nakta" indeed refers to eating at night; it is of four kinds.
The first is the consumption of food, drink, and so forth, while the crow is still eating. (2)
Furthermore, at other times, one should neither eat nor drink, nor even release [food];
that which is endowed with these characteristics is considered by the virtuous to be a fast.
The *mādhūkarī* form of alms consists of avoiding all but one house;
the *ayācita* form consists of receiving what is offered without being asked, with due respect and honor. || 4 ||
From food and so forth up to the ground, whatever alms may be obtained unasked; having made a request for something else, one consumes one's own property. (5)
There, he also practiced two things acquired through righteous means:
the worship of Śiva’s Liṅga and the like, as well as the performance of the three daily prayers (trisaṃdhyāvandana) without being asked.
Having performed the fire-ritual, one should thereafter partake of various kinds of food;
this is called "that specific meal," which destroys all sins.
Eating by day is not [true] eating; eating at night is called *nakta*.
O Nandikeśvara, that alms-food is indeed superior because it is a fast with lamps (*dīpavāsa*).
Among alms and other forms of food, that which is unasked for is best; among those unasked for, the fast is supreme.
The offering to the deities is performed in the forenoon, while the abundant meal for oneself is at midday.

In the afternoon it belongs to the ancestors (pitaras); at twilight, it belongs to the Guhyakas and others. Having bypassed all these times, there is the practice of eating at night (naktabhojana). || 10 ||
Therefore, having set aside the rules for alms-gathering from all kinds of food and eatables, that lord of sages [partook]; now hear of the three types of meals.
In a secluded dining hall thoroughly purified with cow dung and other substances, having brought food that is pure and free from insects and the like; (12)
Then one should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra ending with "vauṣaṭ" there;
and seven times, one should sprinkle it with drops of water using *darbha* grass.
Having removed all the top layer [of the earth] for the sake of the triad beginning with Śiva,
one should prepare half of the remainder for the hearth-offering (cullī-homa) according to the prescribed rule.
Having made the *vardhanī* pure white according to the previous yoga,
one should [perform] it with a fire that is not too intense, or with the wind through the *recaka* breath. (15)
Having taken up the fire-seed (raṃ) in its sequential order through the locations beginning with 'ka',
and having uttered "śivāni svāhā," one should perform the oblation into the fire on the hearth.
One should recite the mantra thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūrya. Thus: Oṃ hāṃ. Oṃ hāṃ. || 17 ||
Salutation to all the gods! Thus: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 18 ||
Having worshipped [the deities] in sequence from Agni up to Sūrya,
one should offer oblations ending with "svāhā," ask for forgiveness, and then dismiss them.
p. 762) Therein: *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ* on the right arm, beginning with the shoulder; *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ* on the left arm; *oṃ sara-* || 20 ||
The self-transformation: for the sake of the journey toward Kāñjina and others, for the sake of Jaṃ, Jalāya, Śruta, and Varuṇa, [I offer] homage. Om. || 21 ||
In the water vessels: *Oṃ hāṃ viśvarājāya namaḥ*. Thus.
*Namaḥ* to the one impelled by the planetary deities and the goddesses. *Oṃ saṃmārjanam*. || 22 ||
"Obeisance to Kāma, the flower-armed one. [Touch] the head. "Oṃ.
Obeisance to Skanda, the lord of the grahas. Thus, below the central pillar. 23.
Having thus offered the *vāstubali*, there should be the washing of the hands;
both the householder (*bhautika*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) should offer the oblation by means of that [same] procedure. (24)
Having become equanimous, perfectly composed, and pure, one should then enter into meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Right there, one should offer an oblation (bali) to all the deities and to the solitary ones (ekāḥ). || 25 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the goddess Gṛhopakaraṇā, the vehicle.
In this manner, or specifically for the preceptor, it should be performed there. || 26 ||
[He was surrounded] by those endowed with devotion to Śiva, possessed of good conduct,
auspicious, pure Śaivas, established on the true path, devoted to austerity, and most steadfast.
Seated in a single row with those of similar caste who are gathered together and seated nearby, one should eat silently, with a focused mind and pure. (28)
In vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, well-purified, [should sit] the Guru, the practitioner (sādhaka), the sons, and those following the order of initiates (samayin). 29.
The leaf of the lotus, the palāśa, as well as the kadalī and the panasa; the leaf of the mango, the coconut, and likewise the madhūka. (30)
Furthermore, any other pure and blameless leaf that is free from mantras may be used;
or else, [the vessel] should be purified seven times with ashes in a bronze vessel or on a leaf.
And when the arm has been consecrated with the mantra, then there shall be purification of the bowl by means of [powders] derived from the bhallātaka,
plakṣa, aśvattha, and arka trees, prepared at the feet [of the deity] and so forth.
Nor should one eat from leaves of the castor plant (eraṇḍa), the water-lily (alābu), or beautiful arka leaves, nor from other vessels that are foul-smelling or otherwise forbidden. || 33 ||
Especially for one who is materialistic, a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood or a lotus leaf is unsuitable for food; if one eats from such a vessel, it is indeed a transgression.
Even for a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), eating from his vessel destroys sin;
furthermore, bathing with ashes shall serve as the protection of the [sacred] lines. || 35 ||
Raising his knee high, remaining silent and seated in the vīrāsana posture,
he should touch the vessel with his left hand or otherwise touch it.
One should offer oblations consisting of ghee into the fire of the stomach, which has been purified by the *pūrṇāhuti* mantra, consecrated with faith, and kindled with the *astra-mantra*. (37)
Having performed the *āpośana* rite again and being joined with the *praṇava* and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should offer five oblations ending with *svāhā*, O Nandikeśvara. (38)
To Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—svāhā for the secondary vital breaths (*upaprāṇa*). || 39 ||

Having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) according to the rule with the mantra "Oṃ, svāhā to the out-breath," and having eaten, one should rinse [the mouth] with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are the covering of immortality. || 40 ||
"Having taken a handful with the hand wetted, one should sip water"—this is one part;
however, one should fill [the vessel] by means of the *graha* itself. || 41 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should fill one part with water;
one should fill another part for the purpose of circulating the vital breath (prāṇa). || 42 ||
One should avoid the śigru, onion, garlic, betel nut, honey, meat, the sound of cawing, food given by hand, and salt. (43)
Of foods, however, that which is free from salt [is recommended]; likewise the udumbara, the alābu, the śārṅga-wood, and the kumārikā. 44.
Sauvīra that has stood overnight, as well as side-dishes that have stood overnight,
eggplant, kākuja, mushrooms, and likewise the *bimbaka* fruit. (45)
One should especially avoid vaśañcikā, ādraṃ, marīṣa, and all types of sprouts; these should be particularly excluded even when used as side dishes with food.
One should not eat with the head held too high, nor should one eat from a broken vessel;
likewise, one should not yawn or chatter while eating. (47)
Even after washing one's hands, one should not drink the water remaining on them; nor should one drink with the mouth, nor with the hand, nor with a distracted mind. (48)
Having removed ants, flies, and the like, as well as dirt from nails and hair, and having discarded any other impure substances or remnants of mantras, one should wash the hands.
O Nandikeśvara, one should also apply ashes for the sake of purification;
one may eat the remainder at the end of the meal with water that has the nature of nectar. (50)
Having said, "I have covered [my mouth]," and having washed both hands,
one should sprinkle the right big toe with water from the [other] thumb.
With that very same food, prepared with a mind intent on liberation, he should feed the guests as they arrive, according to what is available, even while wandering.
Indeed, on the big toe of the right foot resides the Self, which is higher than the highest of the worlds; therefore, consecrate it there with the Abhijyeṣṭhā [mantra].
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa as before for the sake of pacifying the fault of consumption,
one should bind [the thread] up to the tip of the nose with the mudrā called Ghātinī.
The rule for alms-gathering, specifically the supreme *mādhūkaraka* method,
is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the enhancer of ascetic merit. (55)
Starting from the barber's house, then in the houses of those of lower castes below him, or in the house of outcasts, or even in the house of one who has betrayed his guru; || 56 ||
One should never seek alms in a house where Śiva is reviled, nor in a house where knowledge is reviled, nor even in a house where liquor is drunk. (57)
A wise man should not go about seeking alms even at the houses of Śeṣikas;
just as a bee, even while taking honey, does not harm the flower.
In that same manner, being patient, he should receive alms from the master of the house;
he should practice the *mādhūkarī* mode of begging and avoid food from a single source. (59)
Even in the house of the ignorant, the pure *mādhūkarī* [alms-gathering] is likewise [permissible];
however, one should not eat food from a single source, even if it comes from the family of Bṛhaspati. (60)
Furthermore, begging for alms causes harm due to the obstruction of prayers and other duties;
nor should one beg from the leaves of the Palāśa, Kadali, Āmra, or Panasa trees. || 61 ||
Whatever vessel is used for the purpose of eating is indeed a bowl;
likewise, in its absence, a gourd-shell or even a begging-bowl may serve as such.

For one desiring liberation, however, [he should perform] the excellent *bheruṇḍa* [mantra], consecrated with the *bahurūpa* [mantra], the washing of the feet, and the veiling with the *kuṇḍala* [mantra]. || 63 ||
The bath with pure ashes, adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), is for the seeker of liberation;
if he desires food, he should wear white garments. (64)
Having put on the loincloth and the upper garment, he should perform his duties;
silent and firm in his vow, he should meditatively contemplate Śiva and the secret [deity] with devotion. (65)
Having received permission there, holding a staff consecrated with mantras and carrying an umbrella, he should go from house to house for the sake of alms.
One should avoid spitting on the path, as well as offering [impurities] upon that path;
one should also abandon reviling and [the path] crowded with carvīs and the like.
Having formed the resolve, "Give alms," with his gaze fixed on the tips of his big toes,
he should wait for that duration of time which it takes for two young calves to move away.
The sage attains conception there and may then go elsewhere;
even while returning from his journey, he is not summoned there again.
The sage should take back that which has been brought by the sacrificer and others;
he should not take it with his hand, nor with speech, nor with a bronze vessel. (70)

A woman from Malaya, one who has testicles, one who is pregnant, one who is diseased, one who is suffering, one who is weeping, and so forth—one should stroke with the hand [the area] beginning with these. 71.
Having visualized the world as beautiful and his own hermitage likewise, he should go there with the alms-bowl full to its brim and with no lack of mantras. || 72 ||
Then the mendicant, having placed his alms-bowl in a clean spot,
washed his feet and dusted his entire body.
Having sipped water according to the rule and honored [the vessel] with water for the feet, one should worship it with the Astra-mantra;
then, having sprinkled it with the nectar of the moon, one should perform the ritual with the Dhenu-mudrā.
One should divide [the portion] into three parts; one part indeed for the deity and likewise for the preceptor, and taking the third part for one's own meal. (75)
One should take food as before, and thereafter engage in the study of sacred texts;
then one should perform the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) in due order, just as previously described.
On a pure spot of ground covered with grass or on a deer skin—or, in the absence of a tiger skin—there should be a spread for the ritual covering. || 77 ||
Having placed his body with mantras and having lain down in yogic sleep,
he caused the moon and sun, conjoined with Śiva, to perish along with Ajapā.
Having performed worship even at the time of sleep, the yogi should always go to rest;
for the wise, that [time] is especially the fourth state (turya) and the twilight (sandhyā).
Between the east and the west, there are ten nāḍīs during the night;
this is declared to be the time for sleep, after which one should perform [the rites] as previously described. (80)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, [the section on] the rules for eating, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall describe in detail the worship of devotees,
which grants liberation to those seeking liberation and bestows wealth upon those seeking wealth.
It grants victory to those seeking victory, bestows sons upon those desiring sons,
destroys the diseases of the sick, and grants devotion to one devoid of devotion.
It bestows knowledge upon ignorance and is the supreme bestower of all powers;
the worship of Śiva is twofold, consisting of the immobile and the mobile. (3)
O Nandikeśvara, there the worship of the *liṅga* and other [emblems], as well as the worship of the retinue, takes place;
even at the time of worship, there is the presence [of the deity] within the immobile splendor of Śiva.
And Śiva maintains his presence at all times within that which is mobile.
By the measurement of the mobile, the immobile becomes fruitless;
however, among the castes, one who is fit for initiation—and especially one who has been initiated—is [qualified]. (6)
There is always a specific distinction of caste for those who have been initiated;
having entered a body born from the womb of Vāgīśvarī, he becomes a son of Śiva.
Because he has established the state of being her offspring, he is called a Śaiva;
and because of the destruction of the three impurities (mala) as well as through the discernment of consciousness (vijñāna-kalana).
Supremacy belongs to him; he alone would be distinguished above all others, whose mind is dissolved in Śiva—[even] while remembering his birth and other such things. (9)
Indeed, he who perceives a stone-like notion regarding the Śiva-liṅga is a sinner;
knowledge, dispassion, and devotion are the marks of one who has been initiated.
O Nandikeśvara, listen also to what was previously taught regarding the differences in names and so forth here, according to one's former births, and the ritual that must be performed therein.
Then, silver, copper, lead, and likewise iron—these are produced by means of piercing (vedha) using pills and other such substances; one should understand them accordingly.

The prior form, the cognition, the characteristic mark, and the distinction of names—all these, upon the establishment of its being gold, attain the status of a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). || 13 ||

Therefore, O Nandikeśvara, listen: for those who have been initiated, there is no distinction of caste among devotees, from Brahmins down to Śūdras; rather, it is devotion that constitutes the excellence of a worthy recipient. 14.
The first is one who has not been initiated; the second is one who has been initiated;
the third should be one who studies the Vedas; and the fourth is one who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī). || 15 ||
In that very context, the fifth is proclaimed as those who perform sacrifices and the like;
the sixth would be the performer of long sacrificial sessions (satrayājī), and the seventh is remembered as the Vedāntin. || 16 ||
Each succeeding one among these is superior by thousands of qualities;
the foremost knower of Vedānta is the best of ten million and is dear to Me.
Among species of flowers, there is none equal to its petals;
likewise, among those who have received initiation, there is none equal to it in the world. (18)
As is Śiva, so is the devotee; as is the devotee, so is Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, one should provide food for those who have been initiated. (19)
Because it is the means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation, this supreme cause is dear to me;
it should be located in a pure, delightful, and most excellent place adorned with ornaments.
Seeking liberation, he should constantly bring together twenty-five pure Śaivas who are endowed with devotion, treating them as his own gurus.
Having diligently brought all things—seats, water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, bathing garments and the like, as well as food, drink, and so forth—all of which must be pure. (22)
One should feed them according to the prescribed rite and in due order, ensuring they do not mingle with one another;
one may feed them day by day, month by month, or even year by year.
O Nandikeśvara, one should also perform worship according to one's means;
there is no doubt that liberation arises from that very act, as it is known as grace (prasāda). || 24 ||
Whenever one who is devoted performs worship even for thirty devotees, Śrī herself becomes truly great; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
For the complete accomplishment of one's desired object, it should be twenty-seven days;
for the sake of nourishment, it is twenty-eight days; the worship of devotees is supreme. (26)
In victory there are thirty, and in the destruction of enemies sixteen;
furthermore, one hundred and eight [recitations] shall bring about all-pervading peace.
O Nandikeśvara, I shall now describe how every affliction caused by spirits, diseases, and so forth, goes to peace in that person's home through the performance of worship with offerings. 28.
In a previous birth, he was a killer of Brahmins and a consumer of liquor and meat in that very place.
All our happiness is for others, while theirs is for achieving other ends. (29)
Furthermore, by exposing the faults of others, one's own prosperity is diminished;
therefore, the gift of gold is prescribed for those who are gurus and great devotees of Maheśvara.
In that same manner, he should likewise attain one additional quarter through knowledge;
he should daily worship the Liṅga with the Śrīrudras and the Pāvamānī verses.
The mind of the Guru becomes scorched by all [afflictions] and possessed of heat;
[he attains] auspiciousness through waters cooled by sandalwood, uśīra, and camphor. 32.
Having properly installed the Goddess as well, one should worship her especially;
a peace-offering (śāntihoma) must be performed, along with twenty-eight feedings.
Having worshipped the devotees of Śiva, one should also perform the worship of the Guru;
on that day, there shall be peace for one who is endowed with devotion and faith. (34)
For that man who, out of delusion, causes pain to his gurus and others, there shall be a cold fever as well as terrifying leprosy. 35.
For the pacification of diseases arising from various ailments such as abdominal enlargement, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and foot diseases—[the following is prescribed]. || 36 ||
Having first performed the consecration, one should carry out the peace-offering (śāntihoma);
there shall be a meal for twenty-eight devotees, including all its constituent parts.
In the case of leprosy, one should give a gift of silver; for fistula-in-ano, a gift of jewels;
and for diseases of the feet, one should cause shoes and a vehicle to be given.
The giving of wealth by one's foot is especially praised,
as is providing poison to one who trusts, or the eating of what is forbidden to eat. (34)
From eating unwholesome food and from the theft of divine property, there arises for that person a dependence on others and the affliction of hunger. (35)
Even one who eats much becomes [purified] by eating those things that are not to be eaten;
furthermore, it shall be as if he has fed fifty-eight devotees.
Through the worship of Śiva, the fire-sacrifice for peace, and likewise the worship of the Guru, as well as by the gift of seven niṣkas of gold, they attain peace. (37)
A man should extract the eyes of living beings who are devoid of knowledge;
and he should look upon the wives of others with passion only for the sake of purification.
One who bears false witness or commits treachery against his guru is born with a disease of the eyes.
Having performed the Mahābhiṣeka consecration and having fashioned a Śivaliṅga... (39)
Having commenced the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform the oblation with the Netra-mantra;
and endowed with devotion and faith, one should present the sacrificial gift to the deity. (40)
A meal for fifty-eight people is prescribed;
according to one's ability, one should cause milk-rice (pāyasa) to be given, which bestows heaven.
It is certain that diseases of the eyes and other ailments will surely afflict the eyes;
moreover, those who constantly steal food will always suffer from indigestion.
Having performed the great consecration of the Lord and the propitiatory fire-offering,
one attains peace by feeding twenty-eight devotees.
From approaching another's wife, from sexual intercourse with animals,
and likewise from union with a maiden or a widow; (784) 44.

Recalling the violation of the preceptor’s bed, as well as urinary disorders and the like, and likewise [the sins] of animals, those who have violated their vows, and those who consume sugar or honey [inappropriately]. (45)
When affliction by diseases such as these occurs,
one should then perform the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) of the Lord with devotion and a concentrated mind.
The wise one should perform the fire-oblation with the Aghora weapon mantra;
having worshipped thirty portions, O Nandikeśvara, he should offer them as oblations.
Mercury ash (rasabhasma) should be consumed day after day for the pacification of the noose;
yet the lowest of men might, out of delusion, approach his sister or his mother. (48)
One will suffer from diabetes; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
One should perform the worship of Śiva and offer oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra. (49)
Having recited [the mantra] in its non-terrible form (aghorarūpa), one should afterwards feed the devotees;
there, the feeding of twelve or a hundred devotees should take place. (50)
And worship of the guru must be performed; it bestows peace and long life.
[One should avoid] the command of a guru who is averse, or that which is unjust or deceitful toward others. 51.
If one performs the cutting [of a tree] or utters a falsehood regarding a person, or speaks of something that has a beginning,
diseases will certainly arise in his mouth.
For its pacification, one should worship Śiva with various wish-fulfilling gems;
one shall attain peace through fire-offerings and by providing food for the devotees.
The pacification of the devotees through feeding is said to be eighty-fourfold;
likewise, the head of auspicious awakening arises simply from hearing of the faults of the Guru. (54)
Because of the perception of impurity, one who is sattvic [should not listen] to what is unfit to be heard;
if he engages in pricking the ears, disease and wind arise. (55)
His peace, as well as worship and devotion toward the Liṅga, should be constant;
and one should offer oblations to the Lord with various hymns and with the Aghora weapon-mantra.
Peace is desired through feeding twenty-eight people;
furthermore, one should indeed give them clothing, grain, and books. (57)

But by stealing the ointments and such belonging to one's guru, deities, and others, or by stealing woolen blankets and the like, and especially by the misappropriation of ritual fees (karma-deya), [one incurs great sin]. || 58 ||
By killing deer, boars, antelopes, or horses that serve as guards, leprosy arises; of this there is no doubt. (59)
Its pacification is achieved by worshipping Śiva, the supreme cause,
with an āḍhaka of ghee as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other offerings.
The consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed, and one should offer oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
furthermore, twenty-eight meals should be provided to the devotees day after day.
The ash of mercury (rasabhasma) should be especially consumed for the pacification of disease;
however, it destroys the guru’s splendor and utterly ruins one's auspicious fortune.
The practice of harming living beings and so forth, the obstruction of what others desire, and likewise the treatment of diseases arising from anger, greed, and delusion. (63)

Compassion for the suffering of others arises from the ill-omened signs such as sores and the like; there, affliction by dog-bites, leprosy, and other diseases occurs, and for that, an expiation must be performed. (64)
Having performed the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa);
then, one should offer oblations with the Gāyatrī and the Ghorāstra mantra.
And the feeding of devotees during the period of sixty-four [days] is prescribed;
it is certain that afflictions such as white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha) will be pacified. || 66 ||
He provides food for eighty-six devotees and,
being compassionate toward those who revile him, bestows the prosperity of cities, sons, and other riches.
And in that very state, there is envy upon seeing the worship of others;
such [envy] does not exist for one who has attained the secret of another through mutual [realization]. 68.
Because of such faults as these, [the defect] arises for you... and so forth.
Therefore, having worshipped the Supreme Lord, one should likewise worship Vāgīśī. (69)
For the sake of pacification, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) one thousand and eight times with both the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra and the Vāgīśī mantra.
There shall be food for eighty-six devotees day after day;
as long as [the Lord] remains in the state of awakening, so long shall there be the provision of food.
One should offer the oblation and other rites to the Guru, as well as an ablution with honey;
by that, everything pertaining to Śiva certainly attains pacification. 72.
One who steals the property of the gods and one who destroys the property of the guru—
these two [suffer] past fear [as a result] of their actions.
One who is devoid of that which is primary should depart; one should dismiss him by means of growth.
For one who is devoid of contact with the ashes, he who causes an obstacle to the gift brings about a hindrance. (74)
Great afflictions such as poverty arise; of this there is no doubt—even for one devoted to the worship of Śiva, the neglect of the worship of a devotee of Śiva [brings such results]. (75)
There is also the worship of Vināyaka, his mantra, and the fire-oblation (homa) performed therein;
through the giving of thirty portions of food and the subsequent eating, there is indeed peace.

Therefore, O Pārvatī, one who is devoid of discernment regards other gods as equal [to me], and views both the Guru and myself with a sense of mere equality, lacking any recognition of our venerable status.
One who possesses a mind afflicted by defects such as physical marks becomes epileptic;
likewise, there is poverty, lack of food, and especially the absence of honor. (78)
Having performed the concluding fire-oblation for the Guru, one should then perform the *ātrahoma* (the fire-oblation for the [deceased] soul).
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora-Astra mantra.
One should cause all things, such as gold and jewels, to be given to the preceptor;
[this cures] cold fever, abdominal disease, and eruptions on the hands and feet.
For its pacification, Śiva should be worshipped with the Aghora mantra a thousand times;
through this oblation, as well as by feeding the devotees, they attain peace.
There are thirty [verses], as well as the worship of the guru, especially for the sake of pacification;
likewise, one who is impure should not touch the Āgamas and other scriptures.
Placing his foot upon the mortar and other such objects out of delusion, he falls;
then the powerful Graha named Mahāntihva seizes him. (83)
O you who possess the awakening of the image, for the sake of his peace, recognize him as the one who performs the work at his feet;
there is also long sighing, trembling, and even horripilation. (84)
Furthermore, his inability to walk becomes certain;
as before, one should perform the worship of the *liṅga* and offer oblations (*homa*) with the *aghora* mantra. (85)
One should also provide twenty-eight meals for the devotees;
having consumed the mercury-ash (rasabhasma), it quickly bestows peace. (86)
Having dug into the back of a hole in the wall of an anthill, one is harmed by snakes and the like;
the planet Vāsava seizes that pride, and a great fever takes hold of him. (87)
Abuse, delusion, insanity, and abdominal disease will indeed occur;
having performed worship as before, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Aghora mantra.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should offer thirty portions of food;
likewise, one should perform the worship of the Guru with garments, gold, and other such offerings. (89)
Speaking of the faults of one's mother, father, teacher, or kinsman; and entering a house by means of committing acts of violence. (90)
Its symptoms are fever, cough, labored breathing, aching in all the limbs, itching, a distaste for food and drink, and a disorientation of movement. (91)
For the pacification of that disease, the worship of Śiva is prescribed;
one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghorāstra mantra.
One should also feed thirty devotees of Śiva there for the sake of pacification,
even for one who delights in censuring his guru or delights in censuring Śiva.
Even for anyone who is devoted to disparaging knowledge, [this occurs] repeatedly over a long period of time due to wind (vāta) and likewise due to bile (pitta). (94)
However, he himself will suffer affliction from disease for a long time;
having worshipped Śiva as before, one should perform the fire-oblation with the Aghora weapon mantra. (95)
One should worship the devotees of Śiva numbering eight thousand;
for those numbering thirty and so forth, O Nandikeśvara, the seat [is established] through their very pacification.
By that, they attain peace through the worship of the Guru and so forth, as previously described.
Through the descent of peace upon these [deities], all disease is dissolved by its division. (97)
At the time of departure (utkrānti), there is attainment through all three [means] alone, and no perception of fault;
however, at other times, for all [practitioners], it results from the disparagement of the triad beginning with Śiva. || 98 ||
Faults indeed arise [from this]; therefore, one should utterly abandon such faults.
Having consumed food for the sake of the three [deities] beginning with Śiva, one later grieves. (99)
Indeed, the desire to take back [what was given] is seized by the grasp of truth and peace;
likewise, it brings about the disease of swelling, blindness, and leprosy. 100.
And from the drinking of milk by a suckling infant, [an offense arises];
having worshipped the Śivaliṅga, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma). || 101 ||
By feeding twenty-eight people, one attains peace; [specifically] by feeding deities, gurus, brahmins, and ascetics. (102)
If, at a time of calamity or even when it has arrived of its own accord, or during a period of pacification, [the debt] is given, then there shall be the seizing of the ears and oppression. 103.
He suffers from various kinds of hiccups and deafness.
For his pacification, one should worship Śiva; he shall become free from disease and attain peace as before. (104)
By worshipping thirty devotees of Śiva, there shall be peace for him;
however, due to the specific influence of Garbhayā, there will certainly be an obstruction of feces and urine, as well as vomiting, and indeed the seizure of wealth. 106.
For its pacification, one should worship Śiva and perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma);
indeed, by feeding thirty people, there is certainly peace.
In the case of approaching another's wife, there arises the affliction of *grahaṇī* (chronic diarrhea) like that of a crow's chick, and one also becomes a eunuch. || 108 ||
For its pacification, one should worship Śiva and perform oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
furthermore, mercury-ash should be consumed for the purification of all sins. (109)
On one's birth star, or at an auspicious time, and especially under a meritorious constellation,
one should then feed thirty devotees of Śiva for the sake of peace.
Having understood the specific nature of the disease, the Guru should effect its pacification;
if the patient is poor, he should perform the recitation of mantras for the purification of his sins.
Even through the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and the salutation of devotees,
and especially by means of mercury-ash (rasabhasma), disease indeed goes to its destruction.
If one who possesses wealth should observe the gravity or lightness of a disease, he should perform rites of pacification for as long as the illness persists. || 113 ||
(798) Indeed, for the sake of one's own self, everything must be accomplished through the acquisition of wealth;
and in the matter of accomplishing all goals, O Nandikeśvara, [one must rely] upon human beings. 114.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform rites for peace;
for through the worship of the Liṅga and the performance of peaceful rites, devotees attain [their goal]. || 115 ||
In this world he attains peace, and hereafter he shall attain the state of Rudra;
by drinking milk, bile and the affliction of hunger are removed. (116)
In the same way, peace and the ultimate goal are attained by devotees through eating [this food]. || 116½ ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the worship of devotees, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.

O Nandikeśvara, for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goals, one should also perform [the rite] with the fivefold honey (*pañcamadhura*): milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice. (1)
Having installed the God of gods, especially upon the altar, with the five products of the cow and other substances that produce fruit; || 2 ||
Having bathed [the image] gradually with pastes of āmalaka and other substances, as well as with fragrant waters, one should wipe it dry with a clean cloth.
Having smeared [the image] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and the eight fragrances,
one should adorn the immutable Śiva with all kinds of garments and ornaments.
O Nandikeśvara, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth;
one should offer a row of lamps and an ārati accompanied by *indravartī*.
p.
800) Or else, there may be an oblation of five colors, or even pure milk-rice (pāyasa), combined with various side-dishes and accompanied by various fruits. || 6 ||
Then, at the conclusion of that, one should cause betel-leaf and mouth-perfume to be given,
prepared with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, nut-grass, camphor, and coloring.
This mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) should be prepared by adding pieces of myrrh (madviṣat).
Having prostrated and made a formal request to those who have attained knowledge, one should resort to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and sesame seeds, he should conclude with the full mantra.
Having prayed to the Karma-deva for his desires, he should bow down once more.
One should perform it starting from a single time up to the end of seven days;
or even double, triple, or four or five times [that]. (11)
The number [of recitations] is said to be six or seven times [the usual], or until the rite is accomplished;
and the special worship has been described as previously stated. || 12 ||

The occasional rite (naimittika) should be performed even at the conclusion of the obligatory rite (nitya), provided there is no contradiction; however, when the occasional rite occurs while the obligatory rite is still in progress, [the latter must be completed first]. || 13 ||
Having completed [the daily rites] when the time has arrived, one should perform the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) duties;
even if the twilight occurs at the later part of the day, it should be performed if the earlier part still exists.
One should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) at its proper time, especially without hesitation;
indeed, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) in a short amount of time during the latter part of the day.
In this Tantra, one should perform the pervasive practice in both cases;
the food offering (naivedya) may consist of milk-rice (pāyasa) or even parched grain (paryuṣita). || 16 ||

Having performed the obligatory rite at its proper time, one should then perform the occasional rite; for if the occasional rite is a major one, it should indeed be commenced at its own specific time.
Having completed the remaining rites up to the end of the first enclosure (āvaraṇa) at the time of twilight, one should then,
in due order, place the deity within the white water-pot (kalaśa) using the Vedic mantras.
When two signs occur simultaneously regarding the attainment [of a goal] such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, one should perform the lighter [rite];
if that [lighter rite] is similar [to the other], then the practice according to one's desire is prescribed.
Time is also said to be of two kinds in the ritual rules:
the Great Time (*mahākāla*), consisting of eclipses and so forth, and the Small Time (*svalpakāla*), which is the fierce [moment]. (p. 803)
While the sun was being seized and the moon was being released.
Now, if [the victim] has been bitten at the time of *ekāla*,
at the equinox (*viṣuva*), or at the midday period, one should perform the ritual bathing and other rites.
One should likewise perform it at the beginning of Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Taurus;
for half a watch, one, two watches, or even for a single ghaṭikā.
First, [the fee] is omitted in rites such as the ritual bathing;
afterwards, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Furthermore, the materials used for the sacrifice, such as gold, clothing, and so forth, should be given to the preceptor; one should not put them to any other use. || 25 ||

The materials remaining from the sacrifice, the ornaments of the pavilion, the cloth, the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the water-pot (*kumbha*), and that which bestows a single [portion]— [these are for the teacher]. (26)
The archway, the two ladles (sruk and sruva), the eight auspicious items, the nine gems, the sacrificial oblation (caru), the food offering (naivedya), and whatever remains of the pavilion; || 27 ||
The bed, incense, a lamp, and whatever else is required for the bath should be given to the preceptor, who is the leader of the family on the true path. (28)
The teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā) is considered to be ten niṣkas or more;
for others, it is reduced by eight niṣkas, then by half of that, and then by half again.
In the sequence of the Minor [Tantras], there are nine kinds of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the best of meditations;
however, in the Nitya [Tantra], one should cultivate devotion and likewise the burning away of the sheath of the mind.
On a Friday coinciding with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and the Śravaṇa asterism, it bestows longevity; on a Sunday falling on the second lunar day, it likewise grants long life. (31)
On Thursday, one seeking merit should perform the fifth [rite] under Mṛgaśīrṣa;
and on the seventh day, O Nandikeśvara, it should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
To destroy disease, it should be performed on a Tuesday or even on a Sunday,
during the third birth-asterism (janmatraya), the asterism of calamity (vipadṛkṣa), the pratyara, or likewise the sixth.
One should worship the Guru according to the prescribed rite on the eighth lunar day, which is of the Vaināśika type;
likewise, on that same asterism, one should perform the sixteen-fold worship for the destruction of enemies and the increase of virtues.
Thus, O Nandikeśvara, this special worship (viśeṣapūjā) must indeed be performed.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the section on the procedure for special worship, in the Acintyaviśvasādākhyam.
Now I shall describe again in detail the Śivarātri vow,
which bestows the bliss of Śiva and is the most excellent among all vows. (1)
For the sake of accomplishing her desires, the Goddess previously performed this rite;
even the harassment by the servants of Yama, the King of Death, does not increase.
One who follows this vow, however, does not see hell,
especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha.
That night is indeed Śivarātri, which brings all merit and auspiciousness;
on the previous day, having performed a thorough bath, completed the prescribed rites, and being pure—
And afterwards, O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the Śivaliṅga at night; having performed the recitation of the infinite Śiva, this should be done.
Having performed the fivefold purification according to the ritual, the supreme practitioner, being fully composed, should place a small seat there. (6)
Having worshipped that Śiva with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and so forth, and having brought him into presence,
one should then rub his left side with fragrant unguents and a paste made from flour.
One should consecrate [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to their respective formulas;
then, one should perform the purification with the five sacred threads (pavitra) in sequence using the five limbs.
Having repeatedly rubbed the Lord of the Gods with ground flour,
and likewise with full amounts of ground flour and thickened colored powders (rajas).
One should purify it with cleaned cloth and water, and subsequently consecrate it with coconut water alone. || 10 ||
Having wiped the liṅga together with its pedestal using a clean cloth,
the one who knows the ritual procedure should then wipe it again with a pure garment. (11)
One should worship Śiva with various substances such as perfumes and the like, and with devotion using sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and so forth. (12)
One should worship properly with bilva leaves, jasmine, mallikā, blue lotuses, and lotuses, or likewise with dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, and sesame seeds.
One should burn guggulu, heavy resinous exudations, and the essence of sāl;
that [incense] combined with ghee, O Indra, as well as a wick combined with clarified butter.
O Nandikeśvara, one should know the ritual for the lamp and the night-vigil according to the prescribed rule:
in the first watch there should be milk-rice (pāyasa), and in the second watch there should be rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara).
On the third day, pure food is offered; on the fourth,
pure rice accompanied by all kinds of side dishes, having presented the great sacrificial oblation.
O Nandikeśvara, one should cause clarified butter, sugar, and items for mouth-freshening mixed with the essence of ghee to be given.
One should cause the *ārātrika* lamp, together with incense, to be offered;
the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed in the Śiva-fire, either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a ritual mound (*sthaṇḍila*). (18)
Having mentally conceived a seat for the Śiva-fire within his heart according to the prescribed rite, the Guru,
having worshipped it there, should offer oblations into the blazing fire for the sake of the Deity.

With fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and so forth, as well as parched grains and sesame seeds, the oblation for other mantras— excluding Śiva’s— should be one-tenth of that [offered] to Śiva, performed with the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, and the Brahma-mantras.
p.
810) Increasing by tens from ten up to fifty oblations, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the sealing of the absence of defects is performed by Śiva alone. || 21 ||
Having mixed that ash together and having paid homage to the Lord of Gods,
one should worship Īśa once again, offering prostrations repeatedly.
Having worshipped the deity as before, one should then proceed with the worship of the guru;
thereafter, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), avoiding any stinginess regarding one's wealth.

A Brāhmaṇa should worship with devotion and according to his capacity those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins) and devotees of Śiva, as well as the lunar days (tithis), after having properly completed the worship.
By recollecting the god Śiva, the supreme cause, who is equal to Viṣṇu and Brahmā, one shall become complete; and likewise by recollecting the goddess Ramā, who is his equal. (25)
Whatever sin may arise even from merely recollecting Sarasvatī and Ramā, all that sin is entirely eradicated by the bestower of the knowledge of Śiva. (26)
Thinking thus of Śiva alone and his Guru alone, that man shall [purify] again all the sin he has committed. || 27 ||
That night brings about auspiciousness; it is nothing but merit, there is no doubt.
A merit equal to Śivarātri has never existed, nor will it ever exist. (28)
This is the fifty-first chapter, the procedure for the worship of Śivarātri, which eternally removes all sins and is the most excellent among all vows, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
In the month of Māgha, under the constellation of Māgha, one should indeed perform the Ghṛtakambala rite,
using nine *prasthas* of Kapila cow’s ghee that is free from insects, worms, and other impurities. (1)
The Guru should kindle a lamp that is new, well-purified, and fragrant; he should sprinkle water while reciting the Astra-mantra and the Varuna-bija.

Then, having formed that clarified butter into the shape of a *piṇḍa*, immediately thereafter, there should be a special ceremonial bath with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), performed by Śiva.
One should worship the imperishable Śiva with water scented with the eight fragrances; having performed this special worship, one should install the imperishable Śiva.
One should properly recite the heart-mantra while offering perfumes, incense, and so forth,
and perform the *saṃpāta* oblation into the clarified butter according to the procedure for the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropa*).
Having prepared it, one should place the pitcher with its lid upon the sacrificial mound; then,
having enveloped it with the *kavaca* mantra, [one should perform this] at both morning and midday.
Having worshipped the deity as before, accompanied by the ritual bathing and other rites, and having honored him especially with all his ornaments; (7)
Having performed the circumambulation of the sacred abode while reciting the Śiva-mantra,
one should smear the Liṅga everywhere, including the pedestal and all its components, up to the edge of the seat.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should wrap [the image] in a woolen blanket;
O Śambhu, one should place the deity outside, accompanied by betel leaf.
At the end of the twilight rite, or on the following day, having discarded the woolen blanket and other items,
one should worship the Deity as before and then honor the Guru.
One should cause a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given to him according to the extent of one's wealth;
it should be performed either as an odd number or as the final [offering], or one may not perform it at all. (11)
By the gift of a ghee-blanket (*ghṛtakambala*), one shall attain all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*).
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the ritual for the ghee-blanket, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall specifically declare the supreme determination of merit—merit that is beneficial to all the worlds and the bestower of all accomplishments. || 1 ||
Having seen the abode of Śiva on Śikharabhūta, one should pay obeisance;
the sin committed in previous births certainly falls away at that very moment. || 2 ||

Even for one who has traveled a long distance on foot to perform a peaceful circumambulation of a temple of Śiva, Śiva himself shall [remove] that fatigue; furthermore, it becomes the destroyer of a multitude of sins. (3)
One obtains twice that fruit from the abode of the Guru’s country;
therefore, a twofold excellence arises from the sight of the Guru.
From salutation, however, it becomes twofold; through hymn of praise, it becomes a hundredfold.
Through attentive service performed with reverence, liberation certainly comes to pass.
Alternatively, if one desires worldly enjoyments, one should perform the rites together with the limbs and sub-limbs;
likewise, one who exerts effort during the time of the festival of the Lord [attains such results].
Just as there is the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step, so it is likewise with the Guru;
for one who performs circumambulation at the time of hoisting the banner.
In this very world, he shall become wealthy, illustrious, and possessed of an increase in sons and grandsons;
for at the time of hoisting the banner, an offering of a bull should be presented.
Having consumed that, a woman who has been barren for three years will undoubtedly obtain a son;
this is simply by performing circumambulation in a temple of the gods.
One is not liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes on that very day,
provided one performs a circumambulation at the time of the daily festival.
One attains the state of Rudra; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Just as one has performed the salutation, so shall one be well-honored in the world.
By means of one limb, two limbs, three limbs, five limbs,
and eight limbs respectively, one shall obtain their corresponding fruits.
Salutation with the head alone is proclaimed as "one-limbed" (ekāṅga);
salutation with both the head and the right hand constitutes this "two-limbed" (dvyaṅga) form. || 13 ||
With both hands and the head, it is proclaimed as the "three-limbed" (trayaṅga);
with the head, hands, and feet, it becomes the "five-limbed" (pañcāṅga) prostration like a staff (daṇḍavat).
With the head, the chin, the two ears, the two knees, and joined by the two hands—this is proclaimed as the eight-limbed [prostration]. || 15 ||
O Nandikeśvara, by means of these five kinds of salutations,
one attains sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, and likewise sārṣṭi.
Through acts such as prostration and worship, they attain the fitness for [their] acquisition; having stood before the temple, one should personally perform three circumambulations. (17)
Having performed [this], he attains proximity at all times; of this there is no doubt—wherein the yogi of knowledge and action [remains] for half a day, or likewise for a full day. (18)
Whether for one day, two days, or even more,
that sacred ford is a penance, a sacrifice, a mantra, and a purifier.
One should dwell there with a concentrated mind for even half a ghaṭikā with full awareness;
whatever sin is committed anywhere will certainly go to destruction. || 20 ||
Whether the water be pure or impure, if it flows near the abode of Śiva, one should know it as the divine Gaṅgā; and whatever man bathes therein, [attains the highest merit].
O Nandikeśvara, the sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed by this very act; one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the water from the feet of the Preceptor.
His sinful deeds and other such actions are certainly destroyed at that very moment,
provided he has heard the remains of the teacher’s meal according to the instruction of his guru. (23)
He attains equanimity, of this there is no doubt;
as for the pacification of great sins, there is no need for further deliberation here. (24)
By the touch of the feet of the true guru, one is liberated from all sins;
it is equivalent to the gift of gold such as Hemādri, or the gift of ten million cows.
The gift of a hundred million maidens is equal to the sight of the Liṅga;
by devoutly touching the Liṅga, one is liberated from all sins.
Just as iron, through contact with fire, is instantly transformed into gold, so too one who is liberated through contact [with the Guru]—of this there is no need for doubt. (27)
He who, out of devotion to Śiva, offers various flowers produced from perfumes, blossoms, and water, is likewise glorified in the world of Śiva. (28)
In that place, a flower is seen intended for the deity;
whatever is done there while recollecting Śiva shall indeed become the gateway to liberation. (29)
He who constructs a garden for the God of gods with devotion shall become wealthy and illustrious in this very world, and at the end, he shall attain the state of Rudra.
If one gives even a mere handful of grass for the sake of cows at the time of dawn,
one attains liberation from poverty and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving ten million gifts to Brahmins learned in the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, that same fruit is attained by giving even a mere morsel of alms to a Shiva-yogi.
(825) He who gives ten thousand cows to a learned Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas obtains the same merit as by bathing [the deity] with milk at the sacred site known as Gosajñā. || 33 ||
He who bathes the Liṅga according to the prescribed rite with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is glorified in the world of Rudra, traveling in a golden celestial chariot.
Then, according to his capacity, he performed the consecration of Śaṅkara with the milk and ghee of a tawny cow mixed with water. || 35 ||
That man who, endowed with devotion, performs the ritual bathing as prescribed by the injunctions, attains the state of Rudra; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (36)
One shall enjoy various pleasures and be honored in the world of Śiva;
[one should offer] cool water situated within a river, mixed with fragrant flowers. || 37 ||
By sprinkling [the offering] for Devadatta, one shall attain that very form of Rudra;
indeed, whatever substance is fit to be eaten, one should offer as the *pūrvapakṣa* to Śiva. (38)
Fruits, flowers, and so forth, as well as the increase of wealth and grain,
[are obtained] whether [the worship is performed] at a liṅga, or in a cloth-image (vṛtamāyā), or in a maṇḍala, or on a wall-painting.
Whether on a pedestal, or on a wooden plank, or in a momentary mental [visualization],
one should worship the Liṅga according to the prescribed rule at the proper times, for it is dear to Him.

The mental mandala is the most excellent; from the [drawn] mandala, the lakṣaṇī is superior for a long time; from the momentary [image], the phalakā is superior; and likewise, the cloth [painting] is superior to the phalakā. (41)
The manifestation as a cloth is superior; from that manifestation, the image (bimba) is supreme.
From that image, the linga is superior; the one made of crystal or born of stone (bāṇaja) is the best.
It shall remove all sins and be meritorious; it shall yield the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha), as well as the fruit of all gifts and the fruit of all sacrifices. || 43 ||

Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of an embryo, a slayer of a kinsman, one who violates the teacher’s bed, a slayer of a relative, a slayer of a hero, or even a slayer of his mother or father; || 44 ||
Whether he be a killer of cows, ungrateful, or even a slayer of his own son or brother;
whether he be a betrayer of friends, possessed of great sins, or an adulterer with another's wife—(45)
The practitioner of the yoga of knowledge, having worshipped Śiva by offering oblations according to the prescribed rule even once at the proper time in the abode of Śiva, is liberated from all sins.
Whether small or great, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor;
even in this very life, such a person becomes rich and glorious, and in the end, he shall attain liberation.
For ascetics, celibates, and householders alike— even for those with sons— charity, arising from the practice of knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and meditation, is the destroyer of poverty. (48)
Sons, grandsons, and others increase, as do wealth and grain; likewise, conchs, chowries, musical instruments, mirrors, umbrellas, and garments [abound]. (49)
By the gift of vessels made of copper, iron, and other metals, poverty is destroyed;
thereafter, one attains the state of Rudra—of this there is no doubt.
One should offer a bell for incense, a great bell, to the deity;
fame, prosperity, renown, and freedom from poverty will surely be attained—of this there is no doubt. (51)
Whoever should give a seat, a bed, a horse, or a palanquin and the like to the God of gods, shall attain proximity to Him. (52)
One who has immediately constructed for the deity a palace, a pavilion, a wall, or a gate tower, shall attain the state of having the same form as the deity. (53)
By giving ornaments and the like to the King, and by offering lamps, incense, and so forth,
one becomes possessed of fame and prosperity in this world, and in the end, shall attain the Divine.
One should offer ground the size of a cow's hide for the sake of auspiciousness;
that indeed yields the fruit of all gifts and is the destroyer of all sins.
A wise person should cause a field joined with water to be given for the sake of crops;
by the gift of trees to Śiva, there is an increase in all enjoyments.
The man who performs the Śiva-sacrifice with ritual worship, having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 57 ||
Having known the Lord of Gods through the yoga of knowledge by means of the mouth of the Guru, one attains the God through devotion; He does not grant rebirth. (58)
One who is rich in abundant wealth, diligently constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like for the sake of the Divine, shall attain Śiva at the end of that life.
He who worships the bed according to the prescribed rite with devotion shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Śiva.
One should completely renounce one's life for the sake of the three tasks beginning with Śiva;
it is impossible even to describe the full attainment of the fruit for such a person. 61.
Devotion is of three kinds: natural, acquired, and artificial. That devotion which is innate bestows happiness both in this world and the next. (62)
If it is indeed artificial and constructed, it bestows happiness in the hereafter.
An area extending one hundred and fifty cubits from the *liṅga* is traditionally known as the sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva. (63)
If death occurs through some calamity in the vicinity of that Śiva-kṣetra, he goes to the proximity of Śiva; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (64)
In other numerous treatises, the fruit may be merely heaven;
but the Śiva-śāstra, in particular, bestows both enjoyment and liberation with ease.
Success is not attained through mere birth; one must contemplate the true path within the Cintāmaṇi jewel.
