Therefore, with every effort, one should practice that which is called the "Contemplated Reality" (cintyasāda).
And by the command of the Guru, all acts such as giving gifts and reciting mantras should always be performed.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter [on the ritual of merit] in the Acintyaviśvasādākhya.
(832) Those monasteries and shrines for deities that have passed away,
as well as the lingas, lotus ponds, and other such things established by someone [in the past], [are likewise subject to decay]. || 1 ||
The merit of his original consecration is multiplied a thousandfold;
in the restoration of a ruined shrine, it becomes a hundredfold, and through the destruction of sin, it becomes equal [to the former]. || 2 ||
And as many lingas as have been worshipped constantly,
and as much splendor as has been established and worshipped with devotion upon the surface of the earth— (3)
One earns merit equal to that number by constructing a temple, a monastery,
or by giving a garment, a bull, a horse, or even a bull named Vṛṣa.
Who that man, having obtained the status of a lunar day (tithi), would abandon the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika) which, by marking his body with its signs, yields the fruit of a human sacrifice?
It is said that when ten million high-souled Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the meaning of the four Vedas have been fed by the Teacher, it is called "Bhojita. (833.6)
When the practitioner is worshipped there, the fruit of merit shall be one hundred thousand;
or for a son, ten thousand merits—this is your entire agreement.
A devotee of Maheśvara shall enjoy for a hundred [years], provided with ghee and side dishes,
as well as moving rice-ear flowers, a lamp, clothing, fruits, and so forth.
One should offer the Śaiva [gift] to the Guru for the sake of Śiva; hear now the specific fruits thereof:
hair, rice-grains, flowers, lamps, threads, and indeed fruits.
For as many thousands of ages as there are counts of those substances and enumerations, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who, filled with devotion, constructs a garden dedicated to Śiva—
then that garden shall exist as long as there are leaves, flowers, and fruits. (11)
The number of Śivalokas attained shall be equal to that count;
the devotee of Śiva should wear matted hair, adding to his matted locks day by day.
One obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) without a doubt,
whether one has a shaven head or a topknot, provided one says "Śivāya."
If one should cause a linga to be given for the worship of a devotee of Śiva, day after day, it is as meritorious as the merit of a human sacrifice.
As many as are the number of sesame seeds in the measurement of the linga and its pedestal,
for that many tens of thousands of divine kalpas shall he be glorified in the world of Śiva.
By removing small insects for the sake of Śiva and likewise for the Guru,
sweeping [the temple] for even a single day shall yield the fruit of a Cāndrāyaṇa fast. (16)
He who performs the sweeping likewise for an entire fortnight without interruption is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred crores of divine yugas.
By offering the *nīrājana* lamp when various auspicious times have arrived,
one becomes equal to ten million suns and shall dwell eternally in the world of Śiva.
Having bathed the Liṅga once with curd, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu for a thousand crores of kalpas, [possessing] a collection of garments.
All that, such as the bathing with ghee and other substances, perishes at that very moment;
by bathing the Liṅga with honey, one removes all sin.
Having been honored with fire, one is glorified in the world of Agni;
likewise, by means of sugarcane juice alone, a hero becomes a lord of the earth. (21)
By means of massages with sesame oil, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
he who bathes the sin-destroying Liṅga with the essence of fruits [attains the same].
At the end of the body, the vehicle of the ancestors goes forth; of this there is no doubt. By means of white ash, one should always bathe the Liṅga like Śiva himself.
He is indeed worthy of worship in worlds such as the realm of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Even a measure of just one *tuṭi* [of time] offered to Śiva and likewise to the Guru [is sufficient]. (24)
One who gives a golden image of Indra, a jewel, or a *brahmavṛkṣa* shall attain the world of Brahmā; likewise, one who gives *devadāru*, *meru*, *sajja*, *śrīvāsa*, or *kundara*. (25)
By offering incense mixed with *śrīphala* (bilva fruit) and other ingredients, one becomes the lord of fortune (*lakṣmīpati*).
One who possesses fragrance should burn incense that is a thousand times superior in quality. (26)
Ten thousand units of guggulu are prescribed, and a thousand of those mixed with clarified butter—twice that amount, resembling the color of buffalo-eyes, bestows fruits equal to those of Śiva. (27)
Incense produced from black agallochum destroys all sins;
having once applied fragrant sandalwood paste to the linga, [one attains the same merit].
One is glorified in the world of Rudra for ten million divine years.
Sandalwood is superior to agallochum, and kamūṣṇaka is superior to that. (29)
The saffron should be more than that, and each subsequent ingredient should be eight times greater than the preceding;
other ingredients should be four times [the base], and the incense mixed with guggulu is the best.
Half of that [should be] for fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*), even those that are juicy;
there should also be betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) combined with oil, camphor, and *viphala*. (31)
A gift given to Śiva and likewise to the Guru is exceedingly supreme;
it brings wealth and glory in this very world, and the highest state in the next.
The drum of immortality, the hairima, the rava, the timila, the paṭaha, and so forth; the conch, the tālaka, the kāṃsya, and so forth, the kāhala, and the flute that brings delight.
By dedicating it to Śiva through this ritual application,
one shall dwell happily for ten thousand kalpas in a celestial chariot in the world of Śiva, endowed with strength equal to that of Śiva himself.
Whoever constructs [a temple] adorned with the triple beauty of pearl necklaces, whether it be a palace or even a monastery, shall rejoice for a long time like Śiva throughout all the worlds. (35)
Endowed with supreme devotion, he offered hymns and songs to the God;
and those who heard them—the trees, as well as the worms, insects, and so forth—[likewise participated]. (36)
One attains the same world as Śiva; how much more so, then, one who possesses the power of praise and song?
Listen now to the fruit obtained by whoever performs a dance for Śiva. (37)
He who worships the Sun, being served by hosts of apsarases and accompanied by dance, song, and other arts, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 38 ||

Whether out of desire or even without desire, sins such as the killing of a fetus—all that [is purified] by the gift of the scripture, which removes uncertainty regarding the nature of Nātha and Māyā. (39)
By means of the Mahāpadma celestial chariot, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
for all forms of knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct have devotion as their primary essence. || 40 ||
Therefore, O Nandikeśvara, listen to that which is centered primarily on devotion:
affection for my devotees and rejoicing in their worship. (41)
Worshiping me personally with devotion for my sake,
and devotion to hearing my stories, which manifests as changes in the voice, eyes, and limbs— 42.
Constant remembrance of me and living by means of me—
this eightfold devotion indeed exists even in a barbarian.
That lord of sages, the illustrious ascetic Vākpati, is a scholar;
yet, even one who knows the four Vedas is not dear to me if he lacks devotion, whereas even a dog-eater who is my devotee is dear to me.
These [qualities] of his should be diligently accepted, and he should be honored just as I am;
indeed, upon seeing a devotee of Śiva approaching, one should offer him a celestial vehicle (vimāna).
O Nandin, that great being is always as dear to me as the sight of you;
he is endowed with faith and serves Śiva [with devotion]. (46)
For twenty thousand years he is honored in the world of the Moon;
there is no doubt that the merit gained by merely seeing [the deity] is equal to the merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (47)
By washing the feet of a devotee of Śiva with water, one rejoices for five yugas by taking refuge in Yaśovatī. 48.
Having anointed and rubbed [the body] with ghee, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
likewise, he who devoutly gives mouth-freshener to a devotee of Śiva [attains the same]. || 49 ||

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) correctly, one should thereafter offer the respectful oblation (arghya); [thus] one shall attain the city of Kubera for thousands of millions of years.
He who gives [a lamp] to a devotee of Śiva is honored in the world of Śiva;
the offering of a lamp to a devotee of Śiva is the supreme knowledge. (51)
Indeed, he who fans a devotee of Śiva with a palm-leaf fan goes to the world of Vāyu, being honored by the wind himself.
One who is capable and gives a woolen cloak to a devotee of Śiva is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of millions of aeons. (53)
Merely by the removal of hair, the fruit of giving gold shall be attained;
likewise, by [giving] the skins of tigers and other animals, one shall obtain the respective fruits [of those gifts]. (54)
Listen to the fruit of that which one gives as food to a devotee of Śiva:
for thousands of crores of kalpas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra. (55)
In worlds such as the realm of Śiva and others, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva himself. || 56 ||
Having gradually ascended through this world, he becomes a righteous king;
or else, having attained the yoga of knowledge and other means, he shall obtain liberation.
He who, intending for his ancestors, feeds those devoted to Śiva, all those ancestors as well are honored in the world of Śiva. || 58 ||
By giving fragrant substances such as the scent of the pāṭalī and utpala flowers, which are cool and pleasing, one attains the world of Varuṇa through the gift of a devotee of Śiva. (59)
He who gives auspicious items such as a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) to a devotee of Śiva shall be honored by Viṣṇu for ten million divine years.
By giving the section on Viśvabheṣaja and others to a devotee of Śiva,
one shall be honored by the Sun for thousands of millions of kalpas. (61)
The man who, having performed the protection of the deposit, bestows it upon a devotee of Śiva, reaches the world of Śiva and does not return to this world again. || 62 ||
He who bestows medicines upon a devotee of Śiva afflicted by disease is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of yugas. || 63 ||
Therefore, he who gives a vessel filled with ashes to a devotee attains the fruit of all sacred fords and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 64 ||
And that man who gives a yogapaṭṭa to a devotee of Śiva shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand pairs of garments. || 65 ||
He who gives a manuscript of the Śiva-knowledge to one devoted to the Śiva-knowledge has given everything; like Śiva himself, he rejoices for a long time. (66)
By the gift of a manuscript for the purpose of studying the Śiva-śāstra, one certainly attains merit multiplied by ten million times ten million; of this there is no doubt. (67)
That man who, for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Śiva, bestows a rosary of rudrākṣa beads upon a devotee of Śiva, shall attain a fruit that is beyond the reach of words. (68)
He attains the state of Rudra and is glorified in the world of Rudra—he who gives an umbrella together with its staff to a devotee of Śiva. || 69 ||
That man who gives a pair of sandals as a gift to a devotee of Śiva enjoys the earth, extending for a hundred yojanas, together with his wife. (70)
Having obtained a vehicle such as a chariot, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
for without instruction, one should not practice the dharma of Śiva. (71)
The instructor, the one who consents, the one who provides the tools for the ritual,
and the one who covers over what has been done— these five are recorded as having equal shares in the fruit.
Among all these as well, the one endowed with passion is the most excellent;
[yet] everything beginning with the *ālaya* is devoid of the syllable *rakṣa*. (73)
Everything indeed comes to destruction; therefore, he is the supreme protector.
For the protector is the creator of the world, and the protector is the teacher of the world. || 74 ||

For the father and mother are protectors, and a well-wisher is always a protector; likewise are the initiate (samayin) and the follower of the path of the servant (dāsamārga), provided they are solely devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 75 ||
p.
847) These are indeed synonyms for one who abides by the *samaya*:
a worshiper of Śiva, one on the path of the sons (*putramārgin*), and one initiated through the consecration of a son (*putrasaṃskāradīkṣita*). || 76 ||
"Sahamārga," "Yogī," "Sādhaka," "Yogadīkṣaka," and "one consecrated by practitioners"—these are his synonymous designations. (77)

Whether he has been initiated into gnosis (jñāna) or higher knowledge (vijñāna), or has been consecrated with various [empowerments], these names—such as "one who follows the true path" (sanmārgī)—belong truly only to the teacher (deśika). || 78 ||

The devotee, the one who has received initiation, and the one bound by the observances (samayin) are distinguished; the best of practitioners, being joined with the observances, quickly attains the purificatory rite (saṃskāra). || 79 ||
If that very same person is joined with yoga, he suddenly attains the highest quality;
indeed, having become the head himself, he is suddenly distinguished.
The teacher Lohita is said to be the first, possessing twenty-five thousand [verses] of the Śivajñāna; he who possesses fifty thousand [verses] is the second. (81)
He who has studied one hundred thousand chapters is called a Madhyamācārya; he is the best among them.
And from the very essence of all the Āgamas, this Tantra known as the Sārāt sāra [was extracted]. (82)
Therefore, for one who excels among those who know all the ancillaries of this study, only the path of devotion and the act of giving are prescribed here in the scripture. (83)
The fruit [of the practice] beginning with the *samaya* and ending with the *deśika* is like that of the *vaiśiṣya* and so forth;
indeed, in the offerings of the gift of Dharma and so on, *vaiśiṣya* is intended. (84)
O devotee of Śiva, a gift given with the hand out of compassion shall be equal [to other forms of merit].
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the determination of merit, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
From hereafter, I shall describe the vow for the benefit of those who have been initiated;
for the vow is indeed twofold: Vedic and Śaiva. (1)
For those of the three twice-born castes, the Vedic rites such as initiation (upanayana) and so forth must be performed;
however, the bestowal of Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) is supremely excellent for Śaivas.
Because Vāgdevī was born from the womb and because she is the daughter of Śiva, the state of being a Yogin arises for the ten castes, beginning with the Brahmins. (3)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—thus there are the four stages of life (āśramas); however, there are five spheres of activity (gocarās).
For the religious life (brahmacarya) is indeed twofold: the lifelong and likewise the temporary;
the lifelong celibacy lasts from birth until the end of death.
Wearing matted hair, or shaven-headed, or with a topknot; clad in a loincloth and a girdle; wearing the sacred thread and carrying a staff; with his body smeared with ashes. (6)
With his body marked by the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and adorned with rudrākṣa beads,
he should be self-controlled and perform his ablutions either three times or once a day.
He was a speaker of truth, one who slept on the ground, endowed with forbearance, and firm in his vows;
he was devoted to the service of his guru and intent upon carrying out his commands.
Subsisting on alms for the sake of maintaining his body, he should eat only once a day at the house of his guru;
likewise, he must avoid betel, collyrium, turmeric, and salt.
One should describe the sandals, the crown, or the perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
one should always dwell in the place of the Guru and should not sleep in another's house.
Having abandoned one's own autonomy and so forth, and being united with the autonomy of the Guru,
[one attains] sacred fields, holy fords, charity, ritual acts, and the like. (11)
All great compassion and repeated acts of seeing [the guru] are, however, fruitless if they are devoid of the guru’s command; likewise, asceticism, charity, and so forth are without result. 12.
Now listen to the rule for lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya) for householders:
having determined the duration according to the procedure as before, one should observe the vow of celibacy.
Having performed a sacrifice before Vrateśvara, one should then proceed with the marriage ceremony;
one should practice the conduct of a householder and the two kinds of celibacy (brahmacarya).
I shall describe the vow for householders; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
Having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rite, one is indeed joined with a wife.
Endowed with devotion, one should constantly perform the worship of the Guru, the gods, and the fire;
and one should also honor guests and visitors according to one's ability. (16)
The entirety of the duties of householders, the construction of palaces and monasteries, the increase of progeny, and especially all matters concerning the Rākṣasas. || 17 ||
Teaching and studying the Vedas, performing sacrifices and officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving and receiving gifts—these six duties are indeed proclaimed in the sacred tradition. (18)
If one is endowed with the consecration of a true teacher, officiating at sacrifices may take place;
however, for a householder this is to be done [only occasionally], whereas for lifelong celibates it is their constant duty.

One who has a topknot, or one whose hair is tied up, or one wearing an external sacred thread, or even one afflicted by illness—especially one who is initiated (dīkṣita)—[should not touch another]. || 20 ||

The sacrificial post (yaṣṭi) should have its body adorned with rudrākṣa, gold, gems, and the like, as well as with crystal, silver, and so forth, and likewise with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. || 21 ||
Association with you is constant, especially at the time of death;
for the sake of progeny, one who possesses wealth should engage in sexual union with those beginning from sixteen years of age.
O Nandikeśvara, such is the conduct for the householder stage of life that ought to be performed;
now hear the rules of conduct for those established in the forest-dweller stage of life.
Whether accompanied by a wife or devoid of a wife, there are two kinds [of practitioners] mentioned by Śiva:
those who dwell constantly in the forest, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits. (24)
For householders, it is indeed the same [observance], but accompanied by a wife;
now listen, O Nandikeśvara, to the vow for those who are separated from their wives. 25.
One's family— sons, grandsons, and so forth— as well as one's wife, maternal uncles, brothers, friends, father, and likewise mother; (26)
The Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, as well as the sacrificial thread, the topknot, and likewise the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, and even the Tretā age itself; || 27 ||
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and dispute; hypocrisy, foul speech, and likewise the three types of fear. (28)
O Nandikeśvara, one should renounce everything— the attainment of the seven netherworlds, likewise refuge in the seven worlds, and the entire group of eight powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
Endowed with the state of being Śiva, possessed of external and internal purity, and engaged in bathing at the three times of day or even at a single time; || 30 ||
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, wearing a washed saffron robe,
equipped with a loincloth and a staff, he was devoted solely to the worship of the Liṅga. (31)
Contented through the yoga of Śiva, devoted to the meditation on Śiva, endowed with the direct experience of Śiva, he was entirely free from all afflictions. || 32 ||
He is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same;
he possesses a state of universal friendliness and is always endowed with contentment. || 33 ||
Beholding a woman as if she were a corpse, endowed with the disposition of Śiva,
he is eternally indivisible from the intoxicated state, and being identified with Śiva, he perceives that which creates division.

Having cast aside his sorrows and miseries, that sorrowful one, filled with compassion for those who do not trust, exerts himself for the sake of the True Principle, pained by the suffering of others. (35)
p.
856) One who is thus endowed with these qualities should constantly recite the root mantra, being solely intent on meditation upon Śiva, even if he is like a child, a madman, or a Piśāca. || 36 ||
One who has concluded the recitation (japa) should practice meditation (dhyāna) alone;
one who has concluded the meditation should always thereafter perform the root-recitation (mūla-japa).
For the sake of pacifying the affliction of hunger, one should seek medicine, food, drink, and so forth;
for the purpose of alms, one should enter a village or reside at the foot of a tree or in a monastery. (38)
He may reside in monasteries and similar places provided they have been prepared by another;
and he should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā) for ascetics through the twilight of knowledge (jñāna-sandhyā).
Ascetics are to be known as threefold: the practitioner of austerity, the man of learning, and likewise the wise man;
thus they are declared to be of three kinds—listen now to their distinctions in order. (40)
(857) For one who is established in austerity and is an ascetic, this is the proper rule:
he must not study, nor form intentions, nor listen in any way whatsoever. 41.
One should not gather disciples nor reveal the knowledge;
one should not speak in the refined (Sanskrit) language, nor carry a staff or a ritual circle.
Having worshipped the Liṅga for even a moment with mere devotion, there is no doubt;
having resolved upon the pleasant and the unpleasant, he regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Alone at the foot of a tree or in a forest devoid of people, filled with fear of men, he should dwell using his own arms as a pillow. || 44 ||
Whatever clothing, as well as food and drink, he may receive from anyone, let him accept it in the hollow of his hand; thus he shall live on what is obtained by begging at his side. (45)
Therefore, O Nandikeśvara, if the conduct of even a learned man or an ascetic is such, he may indeed be a practitioner who is truly an ascetic. (46)
Teaching, studying, listening, and reflecting—this fourfold practice belongs especially to that wise man. (47)
There is a distinction between a learned man (*vidvat*) and one who strives for knowledge (*yatī*); the latter involves exposition and reflection.
One who is endowed with the consecration of a true teacher is designated as a "learned man" (*vidvat*). || 48 ||
"O ascetic, you indeed know the threefold [paths] and the four stages of life (āśramas) of the Śaivas;
now hear the specific vow among those of the four stages of life. (49)
Śiva, Śikhā, likewise Jyotis, Sāvitrī, and Vyomagocarā—these shall be enumerated according to their number; listen now to the sequence of their manifestations.
Regarding the five spheres of activity, there should be reverence for living beings and so forth;
at the proper time, [there should be] private recitation and truthfulness. (51)
Thus, observing celibacy, he should practice this auspicious vow of Prajāpati,
as well as rites for pacification and nourishment, and likewise always for those who are difficult to subdue.
O protector of the earth, that vow [of yours] has fallen from all sides into the cycle of existence,
like drops of water falling to the ground as if they had approached for the purpose of being consumed.
Those whose wealth consists of the livelihood of pigeons are indeed known as the Kāpotikas;
through constant practice, they [study] the great and illustrious texts, such as the Āmama and others.
For the sake of their livelihood from the deities, they indeed lived there, covered by that book;
having built a hut on the riverbank at the water's edge, they made it their dwelling.
For this is proclaimed as the "Kuṭika" vow of the religious student (*brahmacārivrata*).
These five vows have been declared [for the purpose of subduing] the *preta* and *vetāla* spirits. (56)
Accompanied by his wife, whether at a sacred ford, on a mountain peak, or in a forest,
he should be endowed with the zeal for austerity and possessed of a form resembling a Vetāla.
Eating arka leaves for the sake of reaching [the goal], and accompanied by oblations of leaves, he who belongs to the forest-dweller stage of life [should remain] upon the ground... 58.
And those *haṃsakas* are considered to be self-arisen. || 59 ||
Thereafter, joined with celibacy, he observed the vow of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
as a practitioner of yoga, he conquered the organs of action and perception.
Having traveled from one country to another, he should observe the vow of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
thereafter, having attained the knowledge of Śiva, he should remain concealed in his conduct and well-guarded.
Having Śiva as his sole refuge and being free from sin, he should adhere to that single vow;
thereafter, he should dwell in a cow-pen, living among the cattle.
Devoted to recitation and meditation, he should daily drink the five products of the cow;
joined with the Vāyavya-tīrtha, he is liberated from the bondage of the five senses.

One should become a follower of the cowherd’s vow (gopālavratiga) even at the expense of one's threefold wealth; by the constant practice of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, all sin is utterly destroyed. || 64 ||
For this is the vow of the huts: the illumination of the yoga of knowledge. || 65 ||
One who is devoted to the knowledge of Dharma, resides in a monastery, has conquered his senses,
and constantly eats food obtained as alms— this shall be the vow known as Maṭhaka. (66)
Having protected his body by that means, he shall become an ascetic known as a Ghuṭikā-vratī. || 67 ||
One who is endowed with the staff-posture (daṇḍāsana) should undertake that Daṇḍavrata;
joined with meditation on Śiva, one should practice the restraint of the staff and its collection.
First the vow beginning with Brahmā, then the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*),
and subsequently the *kuṭīcāra* vow; thereafter, remaining established in one's own wife,
one is endowed with immediate mental wealth, especially through the *kuṭīcāra* stage.
This indeed is known as the *kundīcāra* [observance], which pertains to householders.
There, whether in that country or in the forest, one should be devoted to recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*).
Those who are devoted to the vows of the swan (haṃsa) are therefore called Paramahaṃsaka.
By staying for only one night in a village, they have traversed the entire earth for the sake of the Paramahaṃsa ascetics.
O Nandin, one who has been initiated should indeed practice the specific (vaiśeṣika) rite as prescribed;
remaining observant of vows for as long as he lives, he should be joined with the formal determination of time.
O Nandikeśvara, listen now to that sacrifice to the Lord of Vows (Vrateśvara), which is excellent for one who strives when the appointed time has concluded and while the vow is still fresh.
Having adorned the sacrificial site, beautifying it with garlands of flowers,
and having applied a coating of cow dung, one should prepare a square mandala. (76)
One should correctly draw the *bhūtapadma*; there should be a white lotus in the center, a lotus in the eastern quarter, and one made of collyrium in the south. (77)
White in the western part, [and so on]... in the north;
in the sequence beginning with Īśāna, [these are placed] in the five lotuses and so forth in the center. (78)

The best of preceptors should worship the Lord of Vows (Vrateśvara) with devotion, identifying him with the nature of the five Brahmans, after having recited their respective mantras one hundred times. (79)
Having informed the Lord of his vow, for the sake of fulfilling that vow,
[he should perform the rite] with five jars consecrated by the Five Brahmans and other mantras.

The preceptor should bathe the disciple with those very [substances] while reciting the mantra "vratam. Having prostrated before Vrateśvara and heard it himself, he should cause the disciple to hear the vow. (81)
In its absence, one should recite [the mantra] over a liṅga; in its absence, specifically a liṅga made of clay or one produced from cow dung.

Having worshipped [the image] made of flour, produced from sand, or originating from a riverbank and so forth, one should do so with devotion for the purpose of fulfilling the vow and its concluding rites.
One should sprinkle with water [consecrated] by Śiva, which pervades the sky;
having thus offered the oblation, everything else shall become equal.
Now I shall describe specifically the supreme vow of the Vanas;
listen, O Nandikeśvara, to that which is being told as a special distinction. (85)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
the conduct of these four stages of life has already been described in due order. (86)
One should become initiated into the renunciant stage (sannyāsāśrama), which grants ultimate liberation;
therefore, liberation through that [other] vow alone is not the cause of absolute isolation (kaivalya). || 87 ||
If one endowed with the practice of celibacy and other virtues should enter the stage of the householder, or even the stage of the forest-dweller, it is superior to that of householders. (88)
Among those established in the stages of life, the renunciant (saṃnyāsī) is distinguished;
even among these, the primary renunciation is ordained as the most suitable. (89)
Liberation is here declared for those established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya).
One should worship Sadyojāta and the others within the five previously mentioned lotuses. (90)
In that regard, the girdle, the loincloth, the staff, the ashes, and the matted hair—these constitute the five limbs of the vow; for each one, however, one should offer a hundred oblations. (91)

The most excellent preceptor, having fasted, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), bringing the limbs of the head and body [of the disciple] into the ritual. 92.
One should cause sandalwood and other substances to be offered with the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*;
having ground them according to the prescribed rite, one should cast them into the water and let them flow away.
The preceptor should give a pair of new garments to the disciple;
likewise, those who intend to marry women of noble family should give [gifts] according to their respective desires.
Having spoken thus, he should establish the initiated disciple in the householder stage—
whether as a forest-dweller, a householder, or even one endowed with the vow of celibacy.

O Nandikeśvara, for the sake of accomplishing the vow of renunciation (*sannyāsa*) and for liberation from the previous stage of life, one should take recourse to the conduct of an ascetic (*yati*); I shall now describe that to you. (96)
Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite in the five previously mentioned lotuses,
one should gaze with divine vision from the feet up to the crown of the head.
For the sake of accomplishing the liberation of the disciple, having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of withdrawal,
he should fashion him as one with matted hair, or a topknot, or shaven-headed.
One should discard the sacred thread on the ground or in water with the recitation of the mantra of renunciation;
[one should likewise renounce] mother, father, son, wife, and the sacred thread itself.
"Having abandoned Śiva and Truth, that has been renounced by me here"—one should recite this mantra five times in the presence of a true guru. (100)
p.
870) With the *sadyojāta* mantra, [he should take] the loincloth and the saffron-colored garment;
with the *astra* mantra, the bamboo staff; and with the *śiva* mantra, the bag for alms-food. || 101 ||
Having consecrated the alms-bowl, the head-ornament,
and the veil with these mantras, the Guru should bestow them upon the disciple.
One should cause a Bāṇaliṅga and a book of Śiva-knowledge to be given;
indeed, for as long as it takes, Śiva-knowledge shall become firmly established therein.
The preceptor, filled with compassion, should say to that disciple: "And for as long as it must be performed, you must especially engage in listening [to the teachings] and so forth. (104)

The liberation of those who have performed their duties among the Śaivas has thus been described in brief and in due order; now, however, those residing in other liṅgas should be understood according to the rules prescribed for each of them. (105)
Listen now in due order to the specific liberations through vows, the attainment of Śaiva-hood,
the emergence of purification, and the non-binding [of karma] among those who stand at the crest of the teachers of the single reality (tattva). (106)
They heard of bliss from the mouth of the Blessed One regarding Vedānta and the reality of the Self;
and regarding the reality of Māyā in the Pāśupata system and the reality of Vidyā, they were those of great vows.

For the followers of other sects, such as the Sugatas and Buddhists, the procedure for liberation consists of observing either a five-night or a three-night fast, being entirely devoted to the practice of fasting.
The preceptor, always endowed with devotion, should perform that rite of atonement outside the pavilion itself, having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, the preceptor should also remove the marks of their vows;
he should then offer into the fire separately each element, beginning with the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) and ending with the tree.
Having offered oblations with the mantra of each respective name, the leader of the true path performs the conjunction of the channels for those situated outside. (111)
Having properly performed the ritual and likewise the specific act of plowing,
and having established [the deity] within one's own self, one should offer oblations with the root mantra accompanied by the word "svāhā."
Indeed, for the sake of that specific fruit of merit, one should offer oblations into the fire with the Astra-mantra eight thousand times for each and every possessor of a linga.
Having extracted the five pentads for the sake of the liberation of those whose reality is rooted in the Root [Prakṛti],
one should apply that narrative to the principles of the intellect (buddhi-tattva).
Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the yoga, the preceptor should again join the prior limit into the Śiva-fire,
having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra.
Having sprinkled water upon the rounded corners with the *pāśupata* [mantra], or else for the sake of the work of passion (*rāgakārya*), there should be only ghee; hear now the sequence. (116)
Having performed the external worship as before, the preceptor, the leader of the true path,
should draw a lotus provided with eight petals.
One should place the syllable *kṣoṃ* in the center of the pericarp, with the mantras of Śiva on the petals of the directions;
the *ka*-group in the northeast, and the *ca*-group on the petal in the northwest direction.
The *tavarga* is in the west, and the *ṭavarga* is in the southwest;
the *cavarga* is in the south, and the *kavarga* is on the petal of the southeast direction.
The best of preceptors should arrange the *avarga* in the eastern quarter,
along with the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the sixteen vowels.
Having worshipped Kṣoṃkāra and Śiva, one should perform oblations (homa) into each respective fire;
furthermore, one should worship again for the sake of satiating the eight groups of phonemes (varṇavarga). || 121 ||
O Nandikeśvara, having made an añjali gesture toward the fire, the leader of the true path should perform the union of the disciple's consciousness as previously described.
Then, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the Guru should offer one hundred oblations with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga),
drawing [the deity] from the fire in the proper sequence.
Having cast all the water-limbs into the flow of water,
and subsequently having offered the weapon-mantra, one should perform the rite of initiation.
And one who is intent on his future spiritual state should engage him in the hermitage of ascetics;
he should especially initiate him according to the specific requirements of those respective initiations.
Having dismissed the mantra and other elements exceeding [the required number] upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should purify it with the Astra-mantra.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*, concerning the rules for the attainment of the ritual procedure (*vṛtti*).
From hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme ritual procedure for the Vāstu-homa.
Having prepared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the rules, it should be provided with sixty-four squares.
One should place a water vessel in the center of the area extending from the east to the cardinal directions;
and in the center, one should worship Brahmā with the four-footed [mantra].
One should perform all the rites beginning with the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya);
one should worship the deities of the site (vāstudeva) with fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), or sacrificial porridge (caru), using their respective mantras.
The mantra-expert should offer oblations separately forty-nine times;
[the deities are] Śaṅkara, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Mahendraka. (4)
Mārtāṇḍa, Satyaka, Bhraṃśa, and likewise Antarikṣa; Vahni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Graha, Kṣata, and Yama. || 5 ||
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Ṛtaga, Nirṛti,
Dauvārika, Sāva, and likewise Puṣpadanta. (6)
Aruṇa, Asura, Rudra, and likewise Rudrajaya; Marīci, Savitṛ, Mitra, and Dharādhara. || 7 ||
And Carikarī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī;
Skanda, Aryaman, Jambhaga, and Phalapiñchaka. || 8 ||
In the center, first, one should perform the Vāstuhoma for the gods with their respective names;
having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) using six bunches of Darbha grass, being composed in mind.
One should sprinkle [water] at all sacred fords (tīrthas) for the pacification of all defects;
and the Vāstuhoma sacrifice must be performed, especially at the beginning of a consecration ceremony.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the fire-oblation of the site (*vāstuhoma*) in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall explain specifically the supreme characteristics of consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
according to the application of Śiva-mantras for the pedestal-power (pīṭhaśakti) as well as for Śiva. (1)
Piṅga is known as Śiva; its yoga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Regarding that yoga, the five varieties beginning with Pratiṣṭhā have been declared by me.
The enemy of the color, conjunction with fire, the foundation, and so forth have been declared;
and on the pedestal, the entry and installation should take place according to the appropriate application.
Indeed, the maintenance of the distinction between the two types of Liṅgas is precisely what constitutes their establishment;
they are intent upon the extraction and removal of the Liṅga known as Uttāpana.
When the liṅga is indeed placed upon her and the consecration is performed, it is called *āsthāpana*; thus, she is established as Śivā in five ways.
By means of the installation of Viṣṇu and the other deities, according to the distinction between those who are already established and those who are to be raised up,
fivefold [installations] are prescribed therein; they should occur in sequence according to the appropriate application.
When performing works such as palaces and other structures, there should then be an examination of the ground;
it is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.

The earth possesses the fragrance of clarified butter, [the fragrance of] * * * * *, and the fragrance of red sandalwood; likewise, it possesses the fragrance of nectar—these are the fragrances corresponding to the number [of castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, within the Earth.
Something slightly more abundant than the lord (īśa), provided it is accompanied by praise, is recommended.
In the absence of clay of the prescribed color, that which does not obstruct the color is declared acceptable.
When the clay measures exactly one cubit (hastamātra), one should take that clay again;
if it should become excessive, one should fill it with more clay until it is level.

Then, having prepared the ground on the earth as a sacrificial site according to the ritual procedure, one should purify it with a thousand recitations of the Aghora weapon mantra and likewise with saffron.
Then, one should perform everything in due order with offerings of clarified butter, unbroken rice, and so forth;
likewise, one should worship Īśāna in the eastern pitcher and Śiva in the center.
Having worshipped with the water of the site (vāstutoya), one should join the earrings and other ornaments;
the Rakṣas and Grahas are to be worshipped outside, and [the materials] should be cast away according to the prescribed rite.
Having withdrawn [the deity] and worshipped it within the pitcher at an auspicious moment in the fire-chamber,
one should lead it forth through the opening of a *khardāla* vessel sprinkled with honey.
Having offered a handful of earth to the Rākṣasa quarter, or water from a jar to a banyan tree,
and having well-bathed that spot of ground, one should thereafter worship the spade and other implements.
Having wrapped [the vessel] with a pair of garments and having performed the *kumbhaka* rite for the twice-born at the junction of the day,
one should likewise perform the five sounds accompanied by the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*).
Especially with the blessings of the Brahmins, he reached the eastern boundary of the city;
having stayed there for a moment with a serene mind, he then entered the city. || 17 ||
Having established the mark of the boundary limit, one should circumambulate all around;
by the circumambulation of the northeast, the thread, and the water-pot.
O Nandikeśvara, this which has been declared regarding the offering of the *arghya* and so forth was spoken by Vāma;
when this is performed, O Earth, the ritual of formal acquisition (*parigraha*) is said to be accomplished. (19)

However, for the sake of removing the remaining fragments of the arrow-head, the king, having dug up the area where the end of the work or the end of the decay is located, should extract it according to the prescribed ritual.
Having specifically ascertained the *śalya* by means of the wheel known as the *mahīcakra*,
one should indeed perform the *homa-śalyaka* rite there, situated according to the strength of the preceptor and the [proper] time.
If Venus and Jupiter are in Pisces, and lead and so forth have been fashioned with silver discs,
then if Saturn is present, one knows the arrowhead to be made of iron.
Having identified the thorn, such as Kaṃsa and others, within the sun, one should extract that thorn;
for indeed, at that time, the syllables of the Praśna [Upaniṣad] manifest.
The letter *a*, the letter *i*, and the letter *u* immediately following that;
likewise the letter *e* and the letter *o*: this shall be the fivefold form (*pañcākāra*). || 24 ||
Indeed, by virtue of their association with these qualities, the five planets alone correspond respectively to earth, water, fire, air, and ether. (25)
O Nandikeśvara, having joined [the vowels] beginning with *a* to the letters [consonants],
[one obtains the results] for the Sun, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury respectively. (26)
For the sequence of syllables should indeed be "Śa-Śī-Śa-Ni";
having arranged it thus, one should likewise recite the "thorn" (śalya) and the other [mantras] with those very same [syllables]. || 27 ||
The banner, smoke, lion, bull, elephant, and crow are likewise situated in the directions starting from the east, in their respective order. (28)
The size of every arrow [embedded] is determined by the movements of the patient's limbs;
the knowledge of arrows situated at his sides is obtained from that wheel of arrows.

Having observed the results of the planets, one should declare the entire piercing (śalya); even when the piercing has been removed from its place, it may recur due to the causes of swiftness or slowness [of planetary motion]. || 30 ||
Having sprinkled [the ground] with blessings, he offered eight-finger-widths of clay along with cakes in his hands;
having filled it up, he ensured it was slightly less than knee-deep by striking it with old mudga-beans.
Then one should have that well-constructed boat floated;
meanwhile, the pavilion to be described later shall be known as the *sāmānyaka*. || 32 ||
Having worshipped the lords of the archways, one should enter by the western door;
one should perform the purification of the stone and so forth, which brings about the purification of the sacrificial pit and the mandala.
One should perform the worship of the world-protectors and Śiva using a water-pot (kumbha) joined with a secondary vessel (vardhanī),
and all rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) for the fire should also be performed as previously described.
Once the performer has been honored, he should go to the pavilion for the bathing of the stone;
[the measurements] for the pedestal of the temple-liṅga are designated as half a foot and so forth.
Stones that are eight finger-breadths high, square, and as long as one cubit are recommended;
one should make the stone slab [of this size], or else half of that, or even a brick.
The temple [should be constructed] with stone slabs and bricks filled with *iṣṭakāmaya* (brick-work),
along with the *aṅgin*, *āsana*, *vajra*, and so forth— either five [elements] or marked by the fivefold set.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Arikta, and Pūrṇā are indeed the five Śilās;
their lords are Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and likewise Makara.
And the ocean is the fifth; these are the treasure-pots in sequence:
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Pūrṇā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā. (39)
And there was a stone named Dharaṇī, known as Vijayā and Maṅgalā;
and Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sundara, and Puṣpanandana.
Jayo, Vijaya, and Kumbhakarṇa as the last— these are declared to be the sequence of the treasures (nidhi) for the nine [planets] respectively. (41)
Having provided a sloping seat and entered [the body] with the Astra-mantra, one should strike it;
this is called the "veiling" (avakuṇṭhana) of all [the goddesses] by means of the Kavaca-mantra. || 42 ||
One should wash with clay, cow dung, and cow urine, and with scented water;
the impurity-bath is performed with the Astra-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ. (43)

One should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rule with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); thereafter, one should bathe with fragrant water marked by one's own name and perfumed with scents.
Furthermore, one should smear the tips of the fruits, gems, and gold with water and sandalwood paste, and then cover the stones with the Astra-mantra.
There, the seat should be released for the circumambulation of the sacrifice;
however, with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should place [the deity] upon the bed on a couch of *kuśa* grass. (46)
Having deposited the principles (tattvas) and worshipped the collection of principles upon the earth,
one should place there that which pervades the three sections, ending with Padma, Vidyā, and Śiva.

O Nandikeśvara, having performed the placement in sequence according to the rite, this is the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the elements beginning with the intellect (buddhi) and ending with the mind (citta), along with their respective mantras, in the prescribed procedure.
The state [of the elements] from the subtle elements (tanmātra) down to the earth exists as the essence of Śiva and Vidyā;
one should worship the principles (tattvas) and the lords of those principles with their respective mantras and with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
And in places adorned with flower garlands and the like,
listen, O Nandikeśvara, to the respective measures according to their sequence.
Oṃ haṃ, the mantra ending with "namas" for the Śiva-tattva;
and also: Oṃ hāṃ, "namaḥ" to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-tattva. || 51 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, ending with "namas" for the Vidyā-tattva; immediately after that, Oṃ hrīṃ, [ending with] "namaḥ" for Viṣṇu, the lord of the Vidyā-tattva. || 52 ||
One should utter "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (ātmatattva)," ending with *namaḥ*; and likewise, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self. || 53 ||
In this manner, the Guru should indeed perform the sequential placement (vinyāsa) there;
namely, Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Ether.
There, one should install the eight forms upon each individual stone:
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, and Maheśvara.
And [to] Mahādeva, Bhīma, and likewise to the Lords of the Forms:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the Lord of the Chariot. || 56 ||
Thus, endowed with their respective names as the lords of speech,
the world-protectors [should be worshipped] with their own mantras in due order.
Having arranged them, one should worship the jars with their respective mantras and with one's own seed-syllables (arṇaka),
as well as the seed-syllables of the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in due order.
Dhṛṃ rūṃ śrūṃ srūṃ kṣūm iti namaḥ; [and] in the installations of Śiva, one should again proceed with that subsequent [mantra]. || 59 ||
One should specifically assign the state of being perceived to the five [elements],
and one should also worship their five subtle forms, beginning with earth (dharā).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these indeed are the portions of the five forms (pañcamūrti) who are to be praised in those [images] as before. (61)
"Oṃ, obeisance to the lord of the earth-manifestation.
Having thus recited this mantra and having worshipped the jars as well, [he should proceed]. 62.
One should worship the five [deities] by their own respective names;
according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the central stones in due order.
Then one should fashion a [mudrā] with a blade of grass, followed by auspicious darbha grass and sesame seeds;
one should worship and satisfy Ādhāraśakti within the pitcher.
One should worship the Lords of the Principles (Tattvādhipas) and the embodied Lords (Mūrtīśas) with clarified butter and other offerings;
then, in the Ajāṃśa-śuddha [fire], one should sequentially shake off the defects of the root-mantra and its limbs.
p.

890) From the worship of Indra and the other deities up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the Guru should subsequently worship the disciple and the stones with the waters of pacification (śāntijala) and with *kuśa* grass, according to each respective principle (*tattva*) in due order.
Having established the connection for presence and performed purification, one should install [the deity] again;
thus, having proceeded through each of the three parts, one should perform the rite repeatedly.
One should also touch the triad beginning with Brahmāṃśa with the roots of kuśa grass and so forth;
furthermore, one should perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) of the principles (tattvas) and others through the application of short and long [vowels]. 68.
Oṃ, salutation to the *ātmatattva* and the *vidyātattva*.
Oṃ kṣṝṃ saṃ ūṃ, salutation to the *śivatattva* and the *vidyātattva*. || 69 ||
One should fill copper jars with clarified butter and honey,
consecrated with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, and dedicated to the deities who preside over the world-protectors (lokapāla).

Having worshipped [the deities] with their respective mantras, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in their presence; one should likewise meditate upon the presiding deities (adhidevatāḥ) of all the stones. (71)
Having performed their ceremonial bath according to the form of the Vidyā, they were golden-hued, with faces like those of hermits,
adorned with all ornaments— the presiding deities of the Śilās.
For the sake of remedying any deficiency, for the final purpose, and for the purification of the site-ground,
there shall be one hundred oblations each, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* performed with the *heti* mantra.
Thereafter, having established a field of sixty-four squares with equal divisions according to the requirements of the site, one should fashion the Vāstu-maṇḍala for you.
One should place bamboo poles in the interior chambers, as well as ropes and woolen blankets;
then one should worship those sixty-two two-footed and two four-footed [images] according to their respective [prescribed] order.
Whether the hair be curled or arranged in the form of a circle of pearls, one should meditate upon the Cave and so forth,
which destroys all residual sounds of impurity during worship. (76)
It is attached to the knees and elbows in the fire-altar shaped like Śiva;
the head is in the northeast (aiśāna) direction, and the two feet are joined in the southwest (rākṣasa) direction.
Having cast his agitation into his heart, even that great asura known as Sattva,
unable himself to endure the lion, discharged his semen which was produced with great intensity through anger.
That Asura presented it many times in the world;
therefore, these auspicious gods remain established and are honored. (79)

The lords of the eight corners are well-established in the eight corners; starting from the south and proceeding in order, they arise in the center and then in the directions beginning with the east (Indra).
In the center, upon the four-footed [pedestal], Brahmā is situated; in the middle, however, the one-footed ones are recorded.
The convergence of all the channels (nāḍīs) is the great lotus of Dharma and the plow. (81)
The trident, the svastika, the vajra, the great svastika and the saṃpuṭa,
the binding of the three joints and actions, and likewise the stage of utter purity.
Thus, one should assign the twelve vital points (marmas) of the site (vāstu) with the words "īśāya" and so forth;
[one should offer] rice to Īśa and ghee mixed with water to Parjanya.
Jayanta receives a banner and a goad. For Satya, one offers ghee and wheat; for Mṛga, beans and cooked rice;
and for Antarikṣa, meat and food—these on eight bunches of grass in the east.
A vessel filled with milk, clarified butter, and honey, as well as a sacrificial ladle (sruva), should belong to Śaśin;
one should present a golden net to Pūrṇa and to Vitatha.
One should give a field to Gṛhakṣata, rice with fruit to Amarejya,
fragrance to Gandharvarāja, and the tongue to Bhraṃśa among the birds.
The ancestral offering consists of blue rice, milk, and a tooth-stick produced from a tree. || 88 ||
And darbha grass for Puṣpadanta, and blood for Pracetas. || 89 ||

One should also offer wine mixed with water-lilies for the Asuras, and liquor for the Suras; for the women, there should be clarified butter and food, while ghee and fried cakes are for the sacrifice.
p.
895) Lāja is said to be the group of eight deities (devāṣṭaka) in the Śvimamājā;
Nāgakesara is for passion (rāga), like one who has not [yet] reached the yellow banner (pītadhvaja). || 91 ||
One should offer various foods to Mukhya, well-prepared mung-bean soup to Bhallāṭa, milk-rice with ghee to Soma, and rice mixed with sesamum to Mudgava.
Having offered the *iṣṭakā* (brick) to Aditi with honey and clarified butter, one should place a fruit along with a *modaka* sweet and an eye toward the front of Brahmā.
Specifically for Marīci, who is situated there among the six-footed [deities],
one should offer a jewel-flower to Savitṛ in the fire-corner cell as well.
In the corner cell below that as well, there is a lotus for Savitṛ;
and in the corner cell below that too, there is Kuśa-water for Sāvitrī.
To the one established in the sixfold state, red sandalwood is offered to Viśva;
and in the south-western corner cell, food mixed with turmeric is offered to Indra.
One should cause mixed food to be given for Indrajaya, and below Indra, however,
one should give gulmodana (rice with jujube) along with the Varuna, Pada, Ahina, Mitra, and Īśa [deities].
And for the Rudras, food prepared with ghee; in the north-west corner, the word "Dharā";
below that, for the servant of Rudra, raw meat; and then in the north, [the same].

When the moon is situated in the sixth lunar mansion (Ṣaṭpada) during the month of Dharāyana, one should offer an oblation of black gram (māṣa); having offered it to Śiva Karṇa, [one should likewise offer] to his lineage on that very day.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the officiant should gradually bestow the authority upon Brahmā, who is situated in the center for the sake of one whose four feet have perished. 100.
In this manner, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) accompanied by cow-products and unbroken grains, along with clarified butter,
beginning from Īśāna and ending with Vāyu, as well as in the intermediate corners, in due order. || 101 ||
And outside the site, one should worship the four [deities] beginning with Rakṣā according to the rule:
ghee, meat, blood, and curd, along with a lotus, in the ritual procedure.
One should offer a lotus and a jewel for the sake of falling [from one's position];
and for the two Rākṣasīs, Asthinī and Aparā, one should offer blood and red fruits.
Then, one should duly offer rice mixed with black gram to Skanda in the east;
and to Īśa, the lord of the south, cakes accompanied by *kṛsara*.
One should cause flesh, food, and blood to be given to Antaka;
and red food and flowers to Bali and Piñcha in the western direction.
One should worship [the deities] here with sesame seeds placed upon kusa grass as prescribed;
one should also perform the rite for the Vāstu deity on walls and other such surfaces using an eighty-one-square grid.

One should make a cord of three parts; as for the six-part [cord], he spoke previously regarding the horse. From the northeast, starting from the one-footed [line], there are the square-cells for the *carcaka* (the ritual attendant).
Marīci and the others, who abide in six squares, and Brahmā, who is in nine squares;
one should worship those beginning with Īśāna, starting with Raktā and the others, outside as before.
For each deity, there shall indeed be three oblations;
having offered the *bhūtakrūra* bali, one should commence the *nyāsa* at an auspicious moment.
One should place the Śakti in the auspicious center after the jar-bath and the triple [rite];
with the root-mantra of the Earth-seed-syllable and "hrīṃ me," one should [place] the stone of the earth.

Having placed eight jars in the directions starting from the east and so forth, beginning with the ocean and proceeding in order, one should assign them by means of the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapāla), upon which their respective powers (śakti) have been assigned. || 111 ||
One should not take up stones, but rather place them in sequence upon those [spots],
according to the directions and the center, with the *śambara* mantras of the Lords of Liberation.
Furthermore, eight deities presiding over the Dharma should be placed according to the division of each corner;
or else, one should place them starting with Ajita in the eastern directions, such as Karyā and the others.
Having placed Brahmā above and Maheśvara as the pervasive one,
one should thereafter contemplate the path, the imperishable temple of Yoga.
Having offered the bali-oblation and the Veda-weapon for the pacification of the defects caused by obstacles,
silence is likewise prescribed even during the five-day period of the stone.

Having placed the eastern stone in the center, one who is skilled in the ocean [of ritual] should place Nandā and the others upon the lotuses and so forth, in the corners starting from the southeast, in due order. (116)
The four [vowels] excluding the middle one (e) are equal in measure to the presence of the *mātrās*.
The *ūrṇā* is the principle (*tattva*), the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), characterized by the collection of all things.
"O daughter of Aṅgiras, perform everything here in its entirety!
Om, O Nandinī, Nandinī! Because of your masculinity, I establish these mantras. (118)
Dwell in the palace with your friend as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure;
it shall bestow longevity and prosperity upon the embodied beings dwelling within the body. 119.
In this palace, protection must always be maintained with diligence;
Oṃ Bhadre, O Kāśyapī, bring about the welfare of the worlds! 120.
May the Goddess, the giver of life and the fulfiller of desires, always remain well-pleased.
O Goddess, you whose seed-syllable is *oṃ*, stay forever here; you have been installed by me. (121)
Be ever a knower of your portion for the victory and prosperity of your master!
Om! O you who are empty in the void, the destroyer of faults, the bestower of success and liberation, the auspicious one! 122.
One should meditate upon the sky as the abode, always present in all places within this [body] which has the form of the Lord, and there one should install the three principles (tattvas). || 123 ||
Then, having performed the expiation, one should conclude the sacrifice according to the prescribed rule;
thus has the procedure for the laying of the stone been briefly declared.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform [the rite] according to the sequence of the path already described;
now I shall speak specifically regarding the ritual for the installation of the Liṅga. 125.
The pavilion and all other equipment for the consecration ceremony should always be prepared for the sake of liberation; O Lord, this should take place on a day [conducive] to liberation. (126)

And [one should perform] at the beginning of the months, excluding Caitra, during the five months of consecration, as well as during the performance of rites such as *karaṇa*, when Jupiter and Venus are rising. || 127 ||
Especially during the bright fortnight, the five days beginning with the first of the dark fortnight are auspicious,
provided one avoids the Riktā tithis, the ninth, the sixth, and the fourteenth.
All the remaining lunar days are auspicious when they are free from the malefic weekdays;
likewise, Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣaj, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras [are auspicious].
Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Hasta, Uttarāṣāḍhā,
and Pūrvāṣāḍhā— these constellations are said to be especially auspicious for a twice-born man.
Furthermore, Citrā, Punarvasu, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śravaṇā—
these are indeed prescribed for the installation of a Kṣatriya. (131)
For a Śūdra as well, Jyeṣṭhā, Svātī, Phalgunī, and also Makhā are specifically prescribed as the sequence of asterisms. 132.
Having left from the palace a ground measuring five times [the width] of the building,
one should construct a maṇḍala twelve cubits in front of the staircase.
The Veda-śāstra has four doors; its location is half [of that], and half of that again.
The mouth of the Veda should be in the northeast, or in the east or north. (134)
And for the first three liṅgas, one should construct three pavilions;
the liṅga should be one cubit [in height], and the pavilion should be eight cubits [in size].
The second [type] of liṅga measurement increases by one cubit for each [unit];
the fourth type of liṅga measurement increases by two cubits [for each unit]. (136)
Thus, for a nine-cubit liṅga, there should be twenty-two cubits;
or, for a ten-cubit or twelve-cubit liṅga, it should be one cubit according to the measurement of the liṅga itself.

The pavilions, inner chambers, and other structures should have an interval of two cubits; for lingas with increased proportions such as the Vṛddhipāda type, one should construct them according to the prescribed measurements.
O Nandikeśvara, one should likewise construct a pavilion with an extent of one cubit for both the Bāṇa Liṅga made of jewels and the iron Liṅga.
The pavilion for these should also be like a palace;
the first is called Ghanamaṃ and the second is known as Ghoṣa.
The third should be the Virāja, and the fourth the Kāñcana;
thereafter, O Nandin, there should be five pavilions (maṇḍapas) for the rites of Rāma.
The sixth is called Kāmarāja, the seventh is Sukhaveśa, and the eighth is named Gharghara; this is the maṇḍapa of Dadakṣa.
There should be four pillars at each corner, two at each door of one cubit's width;
however, in a wide [temple], others may be conceived according to what is beautiful.
In the center, there is an altar four cubits in size, joined with pillars at the corners;
by the sages, the height of these altars is declared to be eight fingers.
If the height is two finger-breadths, the width should be at most one cubit; for these [altars], as many [units] increase in sequence up to the number of the sun (twelve). 145.
In rites for pacification (śāntika), one should increase the size by a quarter both in width and in height;
likewise, among the eighty-one squares, it should be done so within the central nine.

One should perform this especially; even outside [the main area], one should abandon [the central space] and provide a triple [layer] beginning with the foot; the pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be at its side. || 147 ||
One should construct either nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) or five there;
or eight, two, and eight pits, with the ninth being in the northeast.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be established in the four directions, as it is taught;
or else, there may be a single pit either in the north-east or in the east.
To the west or behind the sacrificial post, the pit should be either quadrangular or circular;
when the linga is one cubit in height, the pit should likewise be one cubit.
For the remaining types of liṅgas as well, the pit (kuṇḍa) is twelve finger-breadths [in depth]; however,
for a liṅga of nine cubits, it is two cubits less one-third.
One should fashion tridents, arrows, jewels, and other such items suitable for the pavilion; likewise, they may be placed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one fist or even one cubit.
The number of oblations for a one-cubit vessel is indeed one hundred;
for a two-cubit vessel, it is one thousand; and for a four-cubit vessel, it is ten thousand. || 153 ||
For a four-cubit [temple], the [mantra] count should be one hundred thousand; for two cubits, it is considered to be two hundred thousand;
for eight cubits, it should be three hundred thousand; beyond that, one should not perform it.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have also been described by me previously;
a Plakṣa tree is prescribed for the east, and an Udumbara for the south.
The Audumbara [pad] is in the west, while the Vāruṇa is in the north;
the one named Śānti is in the east, and the one designated as Bhūti is in the south. (156)
In the western direction there shall be the one named Bala, and in the north there shall be Ārogya;
or even if none of these four guardians are obtained, it shall be exactly thus.
Having established them in all directions, hear now their height:
for the smallest [shrines], the arches (toraṇas) are five, six, or seven cubits.
O Nandikeśvara! Beginning from the four [finger-width] linga, one should increase the three middle lingas by an increment of two finger-widths each. 159.
In the case of a liṅga up to nine cubits in height, there is an increase by eight finger-breadths;
however, for a liṅga consisting of as many syllables as its measurement, it shall be four and a half cubits.
The measurement for the smallest gateways is one cubit (*hasta*) for the site;
for the three middle-sized ones, it increases by four finger-breadths (*catur-aṅgula*). || 161 ||
For the three highest [types], however, the supreme [measure] shall be one and a half cubits;
by increasing it by two finger-breadths, the middle [type] begins at one and a half cubits and goes up to six cubits.
Alternatively, the excavation for all [the shrines] may be one-fifth [of the area];
its height, beginning from the base, and its width should be equal to the height. || 163 ||
Those that are worn are equal to that [measurement], but for the majority they are six finger-breadths;
indeed, for all others, it is five cubits, and for the remaining [categories], it is one finger-breadth per [unit].
One should increase it in this manner step by step until the *śalya* measures eight finger-breadths;
likewise, one should fashion the *piṇḍa* in the same proportion over the course of the months.
The height of the śūla is one-fifth [of the total], constructed with a width of one-eighth. || 166 ||
The width of the base of the trident is one-third of its height;
it is two thumb-breadths in the first section, and for the others, it increases by one finger-breadth each.
One should place a lotus, a svastika, or even a *laṅka* in the left hand;
specifically at the door, one should place a plantain pillar with sprouts. (168)
One should beautifully adorn it with aśvattha leaves and darbha grass;
at the eastern gate, there should be Sāmba, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (169)
O Nandikeśvara, one may also arrange the Goddess and the God, as well as others,
according to the desire of the sacrificer, either on the right or likewise on the west.
Resembling a rainbow, red, black, smoke-colored, moon-like,
the color of collyrium, golden, and like crystal— such are the banners. (171)
In the northeast, the station of the red moon-Brahmā should be established;
in the southwest, she who has a blue complexion; and in the center, she who is variegated or white.
One should make those [staffs] five cubits long and as wide as their respective [hands];
the banners, however, should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide.
The entry of the flagstaff [into the base] should indeed be five finger-breadths in length;
this is also known as the *bhāstika* [measure]. || 174 ||
The banners should be ten *hasta*s long, with their bases set at one-fifth of that length;
one should construct the joints (*kapā*) using seven, ten, or twenty [units].
The inferior, the middling, and the superior [measures] are two cubits wide;
the best are eight cubits long, and indeed two cubits in width. (176)
O sinless one, I have observed that, in due order, the pedestal made from a milky tree should be twice the size of the portion belonging to Brahmā. (177)
It has four legs, is marked with a lotus, and is sixteen finger-breadths in height;
furthermore, its stated height is twice as much in width.
The *bhadrapīṭha* for the smallest [type of image] should have a length twice its width;
it should indeed increase by four *aṅgulas* [for each subsequent size]. || 179 ||
Alternatively, for the nine others, one should arrange the seats in sequence;
likewise, the characteristic is that three are seen upon those very pedestals. || 180 ||
From the Unmanifest, from the gateway of a Kṣatriya, from the bank of the Sindhu, from Halā, from Kuśa,
from an anthill, from Karaṇa, from the tip of a tooth, from a cow-horn, and from a cluster of lotuses. (181)
From a boar, from the middle of a cow-pen, and from a place where three roads meet—these twelve types of clay are indeed praiseworthy and should especially be taken. (182)
Or else, there are eight in Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise Pinākī;
[these are formed] from the growths of the Aśvattha, Jambū, Nyagrodha, Cūta, Udumbara, and Koda trees.
O Nandikeśvara, bark is indeed for the purpose of begging; likewise, there are these five [items], especially flowers, [roots,] fruits, and so forth.
Fragrant waters from sacred fords, as well as water containing great medicinal herbs, all types of grain, every kind of flower, fruit, gold, and jewels. (185)
One should distinguish the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using water from the tip of a blade of *gobhī* grass;
likewise, one should grind the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) as well as substances such as the vajra. || 186 ||
And for the sake of auspiciousness, camphor, yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (agaru), and sandalwood; || 187 ||
A hundred roots of medicinal herbs are: vijayā, lakṣaṇā, balā, galūcī, āhibalā, apāmārga, sahadevī, and śatāvarī. || 188 ||

Vṛddhi, suvarcalā, and vṛddhi were each separately prescribed for the bath; likewise, a powder of wheat, barley, śāli rice, and bilva fruits was [prescribed], as well as sandalwood for the purpose of anointment, and a bathing-jar by Indra. 190.
One should also construct a pavilion with two canopies from Bandhūka and Uttara cloth,
and it should be adorned with various moon-rises and faces. || 191 ||
There should be two beds, each provided with pillows, comfortable limbs, and joined by a pair of small baskets, with two washed tail-fans placed at their feet. || 192 ||
Vessels filled with honey and clarified butter, along with sacrificial ladles used for oblations,
[should be given] in amounts starting from three, two, and one māṣa respectively, to the three [sons] beginning with the eldest.
One should prepare a *vardhanī* vessel, a full pitcher, and pitchers for the world-protectors (*lokapāla*),
as well as one pitcher for the purpose of dreams, and as many pitchers as there are sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) for the sake of pacification.

There are also the pitchers of the guardians of the directions, and their specific dharma; furthermore, there are the pitchers beginning with Praśānta, as well as the pitcher of Vāstulakṣmī in the lord of pitchers.
One should also [consecrate] all the water-pots (kalaśa), which are joined with the Vidyā-mantra,
adorned with cloth, gold, and the nine precious gems. (196)

There were vessels of fragrant water and golden-winged birds, accompanied by full bowls and fruits; they were provided with flowing mouths, possessed beautiful faces, and bore auspicious marks. || 197 ||
All the jars, along with the archways of the jars, should be provided with cloths;
the pillars should be covered with garments and sprinkled with white mustard seeds.
The parched grains (lājā), Sahadeva, and the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga) as before;
the covered caru-offering, the pot (kuṃbhī), and the ladle (darvī) fashioned from copper. || 199 ||
A vessel containing clarified butter and honey should likewise be placed at his two feet;
specifically, there should be thirty seats made of darbha grass blades.
Furthermore, they should be made with a length equal to the arms;
likewise, there should be four fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood for each.
The gourd-vessel, the oblation-bowl, the vessels for sesame and clarified butter, all the mantras of honey, and the twenty kinds of fruits. || 202 ||
The bell and the incense burner are primary; the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles extend as far as the *vikaṭa*;
the pure, dried, and [properly prepared] sacrificial fuel is fivefold, ending with the *kālakam*.
For the sake of the ritual embellishment (vyañjana), there is the palm-leaf fan, the lotus flower both detached and attached,
guggulu resin, bilva leaves, incense, and saffron-binder.
O Nandikeśvara, one should prepare lamps filled with clarified butter,
as well as rice, a trident, ghee, perfume, barley, and sesame seeds.

Having received the initiation upon *kuśa* grass and *darbha* blades, one should again prepare the three sweets for the sake of pacification, as well as pure milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), according to the prescribed rule. (206)
O Nandikeśvara, [the rite is performed] with sacrificial materials, with cloth from the feet, and with blazing fuel-sticks;
and [it lasts for] ten nights less [one].
The finger [mudrā] should be known as threefold, distinguished by the middle finger and the others;
it may be inferior, middling, or superior, according to the will of the Guru. (208)
One should make the length of the *sruva* ladle thirty-six finger-breadths; one should determine its girth according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior [proportions]. (209)
One should fashion the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with a measurement of one *aṅgula*;
their characteristics have been described previously, being somewhat like those of the staff (*daṇḍa*).
The characteristic of its neck is that it has eight [parts] and seven [parts] for the altar (*vedi*). The circumference and length of the staff (*daṇḍa*) should be twenty-six [units]. (211)
In the water-pot (kumbha), there should be a knot measuring three finger-breadths (guṇavedāṅgula) and two finger-breadths thick;
it should be four-cornered and four finger-breadths long, and one should dig a circular hole of two finger-breadths.
The goddess should be thirty units from its two fingertips;
the path for the exit of the clarified butter and the width of the water at the little finger should also be [thirty]. 213.
The girdle and so forth are one finger-breadth in circumference;
the length of the *sruva* ladle is two finger-breadths; the handle is twenty-two finger-breadths long, and its width is four finger-breadths.
The *kramuka* is known to be two finger-breadths wide, shaped like a deer's footprint in the mud;
at the tip of the staff it is formidable, and the *daṇḍī* should be like a bracelet.
Vikaṅkata, Śrīparṇī, Śiṃśupā, Dārubīja,
Sūcyagra, Kiṃśuka, and others are declared to be trees suitable for sacrificial purposes. (216)
And for the planets beginning with the Sun, the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are produced from the arka and palāśa trees;
likewise, those for the others are from khadira, kiṇi, pippala, and udumbara.

One should collect in order all the blazing matted locks arising from *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *kuśa* grasses—more than a hundred in number; in the absence of those, one should take barley and sesame seeds.
One should present these items, beginning with the seat, to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
all household utensils, the cooking pot, the ladle, and the ritual vessel.
A mortar and pestle, a sword and a dagger, as well as an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, and a mirror. || 220 ||
A skull-cup, a bowl for receiving alms, a small water-vessel, a pair of sandals, a container for sindūra, and likewise betel nuts. || 221 ||
Likewise, [he should provide] betel-leaves, water for rinsing the mouth, a box,
a vessel for the five kinds of food, a meditation belt, and a broom.
One should bring the silk cloth, ornaments, sandalwood paste and other unguents, as well as everything suitable for bathing, for the purpose of consecration.
Having bathed, he should consecrate the stone altar and the bull,
as well as the crown, earrings, necklace, armlets, and finger-ring.
One should bring various garments, fine linen, and the like for the satisfaction of the Guru; one must not practice stinginess with wealth, especially toward the Ācārya. (225)
The joy of that [Guru] is indeed the joy of the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
