By worshipping the pair of feet of the glorious Guru, all things are worshipped. (226)
Then, for those engaged in praising the weapon and for those who have become its embodied forms,
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall consist of one foot less than that [standard] foot-measure.
The worship performed by an astrologer and a craftsman is equal to that of the four [other classes].
Likewise, there are the Pavira, the Karmin, the Nīla, and the Mattinīla. (228)
Pearl, topaz, ruby, and likewise lapis lazuli—these eight are declared to be especially precious as the "Womb of Jewels" (ratnagarbha). || 229 ||
Candanāgaruraktā, Candana, Uśīra, Mādhavā, Śrīkaṇṭhakaṇṭha, as well as Śārī and Śākhinī; || 230 ||
p.
923) Now hear likewise of the groups of medicinal herbs and of metals: gold, copper, the class of iron, bhaṅga, māra, and sa-kāryaka. || 231 ||
Lead, realgar, yellow orpiment, and the eighth, antimony, vitriol, copper pyrite, and red ochre devoid of mineral oil; 232.
Sulphur is the eighth; thus the eight elements are proclaimed.
Likewise, wheat, sesame, black gram, and mung bean [are mentioned]. (233)
In this manner, eight measures of rice are proclaimed for each day of the week;
alternatively, one may collect five handfuls for each of the eight digits (kalās).
Jīraka, sahadeva, and likewise svarṇakālayava;
pasarpa, yavāhā, mercury, or even gold. (235)
p.
924) One should fashion a tortoise, an earth-bull, and a lotus— each made of gold and other materials— in the Vyāptaka [mandala], using one *māṣaka* for each in successive order.
At the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga, one should collect everything with large black gram (bṛhanmāṣaiḥ) and,
using the materials previously prepared, worship the preceptor and the others.
Now I shall explain specifically how the Guru should perform the ritual bath; having performed his daily rites, he himself should then recite the *prāṇava* (the syllable Om) and the *vyāhṛtis*.
Accompanied by his companions who have become as his very form, the Guru should go to Mahālaya with the twice-born;
he should worship everything, including the archway named Śānta.
In clockwise order, one should worship their foremost gatekeepers:
Nandin and Mahākāla in the east, and Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka in the south.
When Vṛṣabha and Skanda are in the west, and Devanandika and Praśāntaśikhara are at the northern branch-base, situated there [at those points], (241).
The Guru should worship in sequence two [deities] each: Parjanya and Śoka, who are surrounded by Bhūta and Saṃjīvana; and Dhanada and Śrīprada. (242)

With their respective names, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the dative case, and concluding with *namaḥ*, [one should worship] the worlds, the planets, one's own state, and Nandin— two by two.
The three Ravis, the Yugas, the Vedas, Lakṣmī, and Gaṇapati—
these deities stand at the base of the sacrifice, at every archway.
For the very purpose of protecting the sacrifice and for the crushing of obstacles,
one should also worship the weapons in order, starting from the east.
And likewise, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, the mace, the trident,
the discus, the lotus, and the flag, in their respective order. (246)
Saying "Oṃ Hūṃ" to Cāmuṇḍī and likewise to Vajrā, one should worship with these mantras, ending with "Hūṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ," in this manner. || 247 ||
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, homage to Śakti, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ! Oṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ, homage to Daṇḍa, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ! || 248 ||
In this manner, one should worship them in sequence with this very mantra:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Vāmana. (249)
One should visualize Śaṅkhakarṇa, Vetraka, the one named Sumukha, and the one named Supratiṣṭhita as being at the forefront of the elephants. (250)
Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with a sword in his hand, mounted upon a corpse, possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal, with red eyes and drinking blood. || 251 ||
Resembling the autumnal moon, auspicious, holding a serpent-noose, adorned with many jewels, and seated upon a sea-monster (makara). || 252 ||
O Nandikeśvara, one should meditate upon Varuṇa in the western quarter, holding a swaying banner in his hand, with a beautiful body that is yellowish-dark in hue. || 253 ||
Pṛṣadaśva, he who is the vital breath among all beings, the wind;
Śarva mounted upon a horse; and Śarvarīra and Kubera. 254.

One should meditate upon the Lord of the Northern Quarter, who is golden-hued, holds a mace in his hand, is mounted upon a bull, and is the Sovereign (Īśāna) bearing a trident and a serpent. || 255 ||
Resembling the autumnal moon, his body smeared with ashes,
three-eyed, with matted locks reaching his crest and the crescent of the autumnal moon as his head-ornament. (256)
Endowed with a thousand hoods, with eyes resembling white lotuses,
and resembling ten million flashes of lightning, he is immediately mounted upon the Tortoise.
One should worship [the deity] in its lower part, and above that, one should honor Brahmā—the four-faced, golden-hued, incomparable one mounted upon a swan. (258)
Then, one should place the rosary, the staff, and the water-pot at the base of the pillar; likewise, one should install the Vedas, the Dharma, and the other [deities] within the jars themselves.
Alternatively, one should worship Ananta and the other deities in the pitchers placed in the cardinal directions;
then, by the command of Śiva, one should cause that Vardhanī pitcher to circumambulate the main pitcher.
p.
929) One should cause [the mantra] to be heard and then place the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*;
thereafter, one should place the Lord upon a stable seat within the *kumbha*, and the weapon (*śastra*) upon a fixed seat. || 261 ||
Having worshipped the God as before, he should touch him with the mudrā called udbhava, saying:
"O Lord of the World, protect your own sacrifice out of compassion for your devotees. (262)
Having thus caused [the mantra] to be heard, one should offer a sword into the pitcher for the sake of protection;
or else, one should worship Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the pitcher, or in the mandala. || 263 ||
And in the mandala, one should worship the imperishable Śiva as before;
moreover, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the mandala.
In the first part, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made; in the second, the filaments (kesarāṇi);
the third part is for the junction of the petals (dalasandhi); and the fourth is for the [petals themselves]. (265)
There, the pericarp (karṇikā) should indeed be eight finger-breadths in measure;
the tips of the lotus petals, the stalks, and the joints between the petals [are likewise measured]. (266)
One should draw it in sequence according to its beauty with a measurement of four finger-breadths;
having placed the tip of each petal upon the petal, there is a mandala for every quarter.
O Nandikeśvara, it should be performed using exactly one full finger-breadth;
therein, the seat of Śiva, together with the pathways and so forth, should be present.
The door should be made with one-quarter of the street-width, or even with half of that;
the side-entrances (śobhā) should be according to the measurement of the main entrance, and the corner-pieces (kapāla) should be made with half of that.
The site [of the pedestal] should be red or black, while the lid is silver or yellow;
one should fashion this according to the family [tradition], and the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be six finger-breadths in size.
Having worshipped Śiva right there, they should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The image-guardians (mūrtipās), preceded by their respective portions and the center of the pit,
shall perform the consecration of the pit and other rites according to the instructions of the preceptor (deśika).

Those who are practitioners of recitation should perform their chanting; others, however, should recite the *saṃhitā*. Brahmins learned in the four Vedas should recite the hymns for peace (*śāntisūkta*).
The one who knows the Rigveda should recite the Pavamānī hymns, the Sūktas, the Maitra, and the Vṛṣākapi in the east; all of this is then equal [in merit]. || 274 ||
These lead to the state of Puruṣa; however, the Sāmavedin goes to the South. || 275 ||
A Brāhmaṇa of the Yajurveda should specifically recite the Rudra, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Ślokādhyāya while facing the west. (276)
In the north, one who is versed in the Atharvaveda should quickly recite the Sarvaśīrṣa, the Nīlarudra, and likewise the Sruvasūkta.
The preceptor, having generated the fire, should cast it into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) starting from the east of the fire,
proceeding in order with the eastern pit and the others.
When incense, lamps, and forms have been prepared, one should not remove the fire; [one should perform] the satiation with mantras in the fire for the sake of the deity.
For the sake of averting ill omens and for the attainment of prosperity, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the water-pot (kumbha) as previously described.
The most excellent preceptor should cause the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be constructed according to the appropriate requirements;
the patron (*yajamāna*) should also adorn them with the aforementioned ornaments. (281)
Adorned with ornaments, they all proceeded to the bathing pavilion;
they entered the lotus-seat situated in the center of the seat of the Praṇava.
Having invoked Śiva there and struck [the vessel], one should perform the piercing;
likewise, one should bathe it with ochre-colored water and compassion.
Or else, with cow urine and cow dung, alternating with pure water, using scented water accompanied by the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*, and with pure water; || 284 ||
Having bathed [the deity] even with ashes and worshipped according to the prescribed rule,
the Guru should have the purification of the feet and hands performed by the image-keepers.
Having now covered [the image] with a garment that has been spun, consecrated by recitation,
and dyed yellow, and having worshipped it well with pure flowers, one should lead it to the northern altar.
Having properly settled [the deity] upon the bed and seat with threads reddened by saffron,
the Guru himself should wipe it and draw [the lines] there with a golden needle.
The artisan who has performed the preliminary rites should recite [the mantra] thirty times; the teacher, however, should do so thirty times for awakening, or even half of that, or a quarter.
And an auspicious limb (śubhamaṅga) must be fashioned for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims;
it is made by subtracting one part from the three parts into which the length of the liṅga has been divided. || 289 ||

In the seven-spoked [mandala], there should be a pair of lingas at the location of the linga and at the top of the linga; if it is the eight-fold field, there should be a mark on the head, which is said to be two parts.
In the sections concerning the subjugation of portions, one should discard the two lower parts;
however, that which is connected to the back part arises from the drawing and the swirling. || 291 ||
Whether it be made of jewels or of metal, [the image] at the Narmadā is manifest; indeed,
having placed it there, one should perform the opening of the eyes as its characteristic mark,
and now fill the path of the auspicious marks even with ghee.
One should worship the supreme liṅga, even if it has defects in craftsmanship;
[one should also offer] beds, ornaments, vessels, and so forth.
Having satisfied the artisan who removed the śalākā, the patron should honor him with various ornaments and with cows abundant in milk. (295)

Then one should worship the Liṅga with incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings, while women whose sons are living and who have their brothers present sing auspicious songs. (296)
And with the right hand, having touched [the site] with the sky-hand (vyomahasta), or with a thread or kusha grass,
and having applied yellow pigment (rocanā), one should perform the ritual threats against obstacles and other such rites.
The performer should satisfy the recipient with grains, salts, pure sugar, and other such items, as well as with various gifts of gold. (298)

The preceptor, together with the image-makers, [should perform the purification] within the water using earth, cow dung, cow urine, and ashes, either with the *praṇava* or with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (299)
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow, preceded by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and immediately thereafter having cleansed it with water infused with saffron; 300.
One should perform the consecration with water containing all medicinal herbs, auspicious flowers and fruits, as well as water from gems, horns, gold, and so forth. (301)
With water possessing a thousand streams, with divine medicinal waters,
with water from sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, and with water that bestows lotuses.

With jars [filled with substances] such as kākā and arṇava, and with the water from the jar of Śiva, one should apply a smear of fragrant sandalwood and other perfumes, free from impurities. || 303 ||

With auspicious flowers and the limbs of Brahmā, and with the armor-mantra (varma) and red ointments, one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) with the Aghora mantra; then, a tilaka should be made with sacred ash.
With dances, songs, instrumental music, auspicious sounds such as the chanting of the Vedas,
and with substances previously prescribed, such as lotuses, cumin, and emblic myrobalan.

One should honor the contented [deity] there with auspicious acts such as recitation and praise; especially by a man, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then [proceed] on foot. (306)
In this manner, one should address the deity, saying, "May the Blessed One proceed.
Then, having mounted [the deity] upon a chariot, one should lead him to the pavilion or to the city itself.
And at the tip of the hundred-fold [altar], when the vessel has been sprinkled by the preceptor,
he should proceed together with the Ṛṣis and others who follow the path of the chariot.
Speak of garments and the like, gold and jewels and the like, and the seven [substances];
as well as with dances, songs, and the like, and with fragrant garlands.
And according to one's means, there should be a lamp all around; first, at the door of the pavilion, those seated upon auspicious thrones [should be honored]. 310.
Having worshipped Śiva and the level ground, and when the rite for auspiciousness has been performed,
this is the procedure for one facing west; for one facing east, it is the reverse.
There, having obtained sleep from a hundred weapons, he sat firm as a jar.

Having performed the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the northeast corner and having offered the water of honor (*arghya*) with the Heart-mantra, he should thereafter [offer] the fruit along with the head [of the deity]. || 313 ||
And one should bestow the planets and so forth upon the feet with the heart-mantra according to one's own capacity. || 314 ||
For the purpose of anointing, a vessel containing ghee and honey is placed at the feet and other limbs;
the Guru, stationed there, [then recites] the collection of the thirty-six principles.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from Śakti down to the Earth, conjoined with the lords of their respective principles (tattva), one should fashion the triple-tilaka mark (tripuṇḍra) with garlands of flowers. || 316 ||
Now, regarding the message:
[it is derived] from Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, and Moon. (318)
One should place those whose essential nature is the form of space, along with their presiding lords:
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, and Īśvara. (319)
And [he should worship] Mahādeva and Bhīma with mantras whose names correspond to their true meanings; [preceded by] the Tāra (*oṃ*)...
Alternatively, in the fifth [case], one should establish the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍamūrti) and likewise [the other elements] beginning with the earth (kṣmā).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva [are worshipped] in the order of creation for the sake of enjoyment, and in the reverse order for the sake of liberation. || 322 ||
For one desiring liberation, [the mantras] beginning with vanivṛtti and those beginning with ajāta are his lords;
there, having performed the placement (nyāsa), one should place the pair everywhere, for the pair is the cause of all.

In the pure path, the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are to be seen; in the impure [path], the Leaders of the World (lokanāyakas). These guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) are enjoyers (*bhogins*). || 324 ||
Eight, five, and three respectively;
having performed the ritual bath, [they were adorned] with sandalwood and other [unguents]. || 325 ||
[One should place] those joined with the five red [substances], situated to the north of the *liṅga*. (326)
One should worship them duly, having performed the ritual arrangement as for the *liṅga*;
then, having performed the bath and other rites, one should place Śivā at the base of the *liṅga*.

Having performed the purificatory rites such as bathing and so forth, and likewise having been invested with the [initiation] ending in the power (śakti), one should [employ] the syllable preceded by Tāra (Om) and the seed-syllables Mūla, Sū, Hrīṃ, and any one of the others from the middle.
One should offer the *piṇḍa* resembling the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) [to] Śiśalā...
for the sake of protection of the lords of the directions... Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Saḥ Oṃ Hāṃ Bhauri Rudra—thus also [one offers] to the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with "Svāhā. (330)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull (Vṛṣabha).
She is the Sustainer (Dhārikā), radiant, most fierce, the Moonlight (Jyotsnā), and exceedingly intense in her consciousness. 331.
Or, one may install the five deities whose forms are established by the Dhātrī, namely the five channels (nāḍikās);
or else, one should install the three: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Kriyā, which are Jñāna and Ceṣṭā.
Action, knowledge, [and] ... | May there be no liberation, no decay, no sleep, no death, no illusion, and no fear for the wheel-bearer. || 333 ||
One should place [the mantras] within the three forms known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. || 334 ||
Here too, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be established upon the Brahma-stone according to the prescribed rule;
one should worship it thoroughly with the mantras of Gaurī and the others, just as before.
Then, having gone to the side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rule:
the Lord of Gods in the center of the pit, and the Great Sound (mahatsvara) upon the girdles (mekhalā). (336)
One should place [the deity] upon the seat;
in the jar, on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and so forth, one performs the ritual installation. || 337 ||
They proceed by way of the empty path; having emerged, they depart. || 338 ||

They proceed by way of emptiness; one should contemplate their state of self-abiding there. O Nandikeśvara, this is the twilight [meditation] to be performed there by the image-keepers among themselves.

Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and offered libations into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in due order, one should satisfy the principles (tattva), the lords of the principles (tattveśvara), the forms (mūrti), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśa) with clarified butter and other offerings.
Having gratified and worshipped [the deity] with the Saṃhitā mantras,
one should perform a thousand or even a hundred oblations with the final offering (pūrṇāhuti). || 341 ||
Then, with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries, and with substances, time, and the self,
one should sprinkle [the area] from the base of the kuśa grass with the waters from the peace-pitcher.
Having touched the base of the *liṅga*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the prescribed number;
for the sake of invoking its presence, one should perform the *rodha* and *avakuṇṭhana* with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Then, one should perform the rite with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), especially for the image-protectors (*mūrtipā*).
As before, the number of oblations (*homa*) and so forth [should be performed].
The sequential reconnection is now stated here as follows:
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ vaṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ vāṃ, salutation to the Fire-form (Vahnimūrti). || 347 ||

Then, for the sake of union, one should gradually perform the union with the forms of the sacrificer and so forth; likewise, the union with the five forms is performed by means of the heart and the other limbs.
It should be known that [the rite] consists of the three principles (*tattva*) by means of the *svadhā* seeds and the root mantra;
even in the case of a tree, one should go there oneself with men for the sake of its growth.
Having performed one hundred oblations for each part in order to purify the portions, and having offered one hundred oblations,
one should dedicate whatever action has been performed to the ear of Śiva.
p.
947) O Lord! This rite has indeed been declared by me for the sake of the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
Om! Salutations to the Blessed Rudra, who is the creator of the Rudrāmāvīta. || 351 ||
Having first performed the ritual according to one's capacity, and having worshipped with the solar domestic rite, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ hrīṃ, O Śāṅkarī, fulfill [this], svāhā. || 352 ||
One should install [the deity] thus upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and likewise install it upon the primary liṅga.
[The installation] on the support (ādhāra) [should be performed] for seven nights, five nights, or three nights. || 354 ||
Whether it has been consecrated for one night, or even immediately, if it is devoid of consecration, the yoga will attain fruitlessness. || 355 ||
One should offer one hundred oblations for each with their respective mantras; one should perform the ritual offering to the directions according to the rules and worship the Śiva-kumbha. || 356 ||

O Nandikeśvara, when this rite of formal acceptance (adhivāsa) has been performed in this manner, one should perform the worship of the door and carry out the [other] rites; having duly worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), and the Vardhanī vessel. (358)
Having worshipped the Liṅga and the Fire in sequence with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā),
one should proceed there by the command of Śiva and utter the Weapon-mantra (śastra).
One should ward it off with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
One must not stand in the middle of the Liṅga out of fear of disturbing the resonance of the Vedas. (360)
Having abandoned the middle and the ends for the sake of increase, one should therefore rely upon Īśāna and place the stone in the center. (361)
One should install that immovable stone, known as Ananta, with the root mantra;
or else, with this mantra, one should install it as the seat-form of Śiva.
Oṃ, O pervasive Nara, in the stable, the moving, and the eternal, hrīṃ svāhā!
By the command of Śiva, you must remain here perpetually.
Having spoken thus, one should restrain [the breath] with the rodha-mudrā;
then, from the vajra to the end of the cānta, as well as the medicinal herbs beginning with uśīra. (364)
Having likewise arranged heaps of gold and other metals, as well as the previously mentioned piles of grain, in their proper sequence; || 365 ||
p.

950) But having been consecrated by the mantras of the Lords of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), [the practitioner] should [place them] one by one in order upon the eight limbs starting from the east. || 366 ||
One should fashion a tortoise or a bull made of gold or copper facing the door, combined with earth from a riverbank or earth from a mountain peak and so forth. || 367 ||
Combined with Madhuka and unbroken rice grains, and endowed with collyrium. || 368 ||
Whether it be silver or earth, one should deposit it together with all kinds of seeds and gold. || 369 ||
One should move through the golden [path] by means of the jewel-mantra;
in the Veda, the seat for the New [Moon] begins with Śakti and extends up to Śakti.
One should prepare [the offering] with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or otherwise scatter *guggulu* resin;
having covered one's own ground with a cloth, one performs protection with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*). || 371 ||
Having offered the bali-oblation to the lords of the directions, the preceptor always remains composed;
for the sake of pacifying any defects arising from the stone or the cord, he performs [the rite] with the root mantra.
Or else, one should offer oblations one hundred times correctly with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*);
or alternatively, one should offer oblations to each of the Vāstu deities in sequence using blades of grass.
Having raised the deity with the heart-mantra and with those [other mantras],
the performer, together with his own kinsmen, should perform [the rite], whether he be a descendant of the western lineage or even a divine officiant.
Then, one should wander through palaces, villages, and so forth, either sequentially or otherwise;
having established the *liṅga* in the water, [one should perform] the *Bhadrā* rite, which is excellent and half of the *Bhadrāsya*.
Thereafter, one should lead [the image] to the palace, especially the Ratnagarbha;
[this is done] through the door, at the door-joint, or by means of the doorway itself, even without that [specific door]. (376)
When the stone-hero (śilāśūra) has closed the door, and subsequently when its master is above it,
one should release [the breath] by touching the door and lie down through that very door.
This very same rule is to be understood in every respect even regarding one who possesses manifest gender;
entry into the house through that [door] has also been declared by the enemies of the foes (the gods).
But if one enters through a side door, the destruction of the lineage follows immediately;
however, for the destruction of the agent, it is held that one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti). || 379 ||

If it is afflicted by defects such as being worn out, or if it was fashioned through an improper opening, then even if the liṅga is subsequently placed upon the pedestal facing the door, [it remains defective]. (380)
One should worship with auspicious sounds of musical instruments, unbroken grains, and dūrvā grass;
then the preceptor, together with the image-guardians, should depart satisfied.
Having anointed the holder of the yantra with sandalwood or saffron,
the Śiva-yogin, contemplating the oneness of Śakti and Śiva, performs the suspension (lambana).
Having uttered the root-mantra ending with *laya*, one should place it in the sky (*ākāśa*) by means of emission (*sṛṣṭi*);
either in the portion of Brahmā by a third part, or else by two-thirds.
With half [the thickness] or an eighth part, there should be an entry below for everything; furthermore, lead and tin are beneficial when their ends are long and equal to the interior. (384)
And having first [visualized] the stable form with sand on the peaks,
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) after uttering the root-mantra ending with the Śakti, while beholding the partless (niṣkala).
But when the *liṅga* is being installed, whichever direction it may lean toward,
one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) accompanied by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) using the mantra of the presiding deity of that respective direction. (386)

While they are clearly revolving in the mouth and joined with the utterance of sound, one should perform [the rite] a hundred times with the root mantra, or it may be done with half a *vāra*. || 387 ||
In other regions as well, one should perform peace rites in this manner;
specifically, for the pacification of defects, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed for the Liṅga. || 388 ||
And having filled the junction of the ground with sand, one should perform the smearing for the sacrifice. || 389 ||

The preceptor, together with the image-makers, having bathed [the deity] with the water from the peace-pitcher and with the offered jars, likewise with the five nectars and other substances; || 390 ||
Having thoroughly anointed Śiva with sandalwood and other substances and worshipped him,
the preceptor [performs] the touching of the linga with the two mantras of Umā and Maheśa. (391)
And one should fashion the Śakti upon the pedestal. || 392 ||
Having thus performed the ritual placement in sequence, one should worship the Lord of the World,
having anointed him with saffron, agallochum, and camphor, and then adorned him with ornaments.
Having burned guggulu resin with clarified butter, one should install Śiva as the pervasive presence;
likewise, one should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and fruits with the heart mantra.
Then one should present the offering (*nivedya*), [performing] the ritual with equanimity...
956) ...having thus prostrated and gone outside, either with the *praṇava* or with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
One should place the bull behind and perform the oblation in front. || 396 ||
Then, O Lord, for the sake of liberation from defects such as debt, having offered into the fire that which was acquired through death, [one should act] for the sake of peace in Śiva... 397.
For the sake of attaining gold, cattle, prosperity, and so forth,
one should perform a great festival and acts of charity for four days.
The image-keepers (mūrtipās), together with [the officiant], should perform the oblation (homa) at the three junctions of the day for three days;
and on the fourth day, they should perform it with the Pūrṇāhuti and the Bahurūpa mantra.
One should subsequently offer the *caru* oblation, and immediately after that, the *naivedya*;
then, one should take the purified *saṃpāta* oblation from all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
p.
957) In the third [section], ... and above that, the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
Having removed the remains of offerings and bathed [the deity], one should worship thoroughly. || 401 ||
One should perform the dismissal by reciting one's own mantra, while the liṅga is endowed with consciousness;
for extraordinary liṅgas, the dismissal is performed with the words, "Forgive me."
He manifests the invocation immediately through the form of Śakti;
and at the conclusion of the installation, the seven oblations beginning with Sthira should be performed.
Likewise, there is the higher awakening of those who are steadfast, self-sustained, and immeasurable;
and also the eternal, the all-pervading, the desireless, and the truly contented. || 404 ||
Listen now to these [mantras] proclaimed for the purpose of attaining the presence of Śiva:
Oṃ namaḥ śivāya * * * * * * * * * *. (405)
Having thus accomplished and performed [the rite], [he attains] that which is imperishable like the jar of Śiva.
And from among those two jars,
having bathed one jar as it was [prepared], the second one is for the consecration of the patron.
Having offered the *bali* offering and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should go outside;
having gone outside by the command of Śiva, one should proceed to the exterior of the *jagatī* with auspicious [materials]. (408)
And in the northeast, the Guru should also cause Caṇḍadhāman to be prepared according to the prescribed rite,
upon his own seat arranged on a pedestal of the appropriate dimensions.
The ancillary limbs (aṅgas) and the Brahma-mantras have been previously described by you, excluding the [specific] year.
Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Sadyojāta, hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ! Oṃ saṃ, homage to Vāmadeva, hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ! || 411 ||
Oṃ cuṃ, homage to Aghora, huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ ceṃ, homage to Tatpuruṣa, huṃ phaṭ! || 412 ||
Oṃ coṃ, homage to Īśāna, hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ! Having gratified him with this salutation, one should likewise offer the sacrificial food and perform the recitation. (413)
Having made this request with devotion, as long as he remains present there, you, O Lord, must likewise remain present and accept [the offering]. || 414 ||
In the case of a mobile liṅga, a metallic liṅga, a Bāṇa-liṅga, or a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga; || 415 ||
And one should not perform the fierce rite (*caṇḍa*) there, especially in the Ratnagarbhaka [mandala],
nor on a sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) endowed with the meditation on non-duality, for up to three [successive] times. (416)
Having thus established Caṇḍa for the sake of removing the fault of Caṇḍa,
[he should appoint] the agent together with his kinsmen, wife, sons, and possessions.
The preceptor, the best of guides, should establish [the deity] with the eastern pitcher;
the patron, moreover, should perform the worship of the preceptor as if he were Śiva himself.
If the guru lacks satisfaction, even the patron (yajamāna) is fruitless. || 419 ||
He should also give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his capacity, especially to the image-protectors, the twice-born, the astrologer, and likewise the artisans. (420)
The patron himself, as well as others, should especially satisfy the blind, the pot-bellied, the wretched, and those afflicted by leprosy and other diseases. (421)
When the Guru is satisfied with the performer, he shall demonstrate the fruit in this way:
as many atoms as there are in the images, liṅgas, and goddesses, [so many worlds shall be attained]. || 422 ||
For as many thousands of ages as I have here urged [you] toward being present before me, O Lord,
you who are an ocean of compassion, forgive all of that from me today. 424.
Having thus informed the deity, the preceptor, filled with devotion, should perform the consecration and the meritorious rite during a radiant and auspicious constellation.
One should offer it with one's own hand, accompanied by water and flowers;
thereafter, having recited the Pāśupata mantra and bowed to the imperishable Śiva. (426)
You must remain for as long as that [person] remains. 427.
And the deities should be installed there specifically with their respective mantras. || 428 ||

By means of the first syllable, the various divisions— the deities such as those to be accomplished, the sages, the constellations, and likewise men— are permeated by the state of pervading the principles (tattvas).
O Nandikeśvara, because they are real, these are not mere emanations;
specifically, they are the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the river Sarasvatī. (430)
O Nandikeśvara, they indeed abide specifically within the water-tattva;
furthermore, those [elements] bestow mind and intellect, while the three tattvas belong to Brahmā.
The station ending with Manas, Dhī, Śuddhavidyā, and likewise Gaṇapati; ending with Māyā, it is Ravi, and the internal station is indeed Śakti. (433)
This abode of Śiva, ending with Śakti, is a specific attribute of the Liṅga;
it indeed concludes with worship, preceded by the Kūrma and other seats.
One should also deposit the five jewels and other items within the pit;
furthermore, a Śiva-liṅga or another [image of] Brahmā should be fashioned.
Having divided the *garbha* into six parts, one should set aside one part for the back;
then, [one should set aside] five parts for the *saṃ*... [etc. || 436 ||
The seat, the water for bathing and washing the feet, and likewise the placement of jewels and so forth.
And it should be performed with waterless [mantras], as well as with meditative visualization (bhāvanā) and mudrās;
especially in the case of a mobile liṅga, it may be done with three or five [of these].
O Nandikeśvara, listen now to the shadow [measurement] for the pedestal (*pīṭha*); it should be made as three parts or even two parts. (439)
He should perform the same [rite] for the pedestals (pīṭhas) and likewise for the lingas;
furthermore, he should perform the consecration (saṃskāra) of crystals and other materials with the Viṣṭamantra.
Furthermore, one should mentally contemplate the union with Brahmasilā;
there is no need for the ritual consecration of the seats (pīṭha-saṃskāra) for Bāṇa, Svayambhū, and the others. || 441 ||
One should perform the installation, the placement of mantras from the Saṃhitā, and the fire-oblation;
likewise, there may be a momentary liṅga made of flour, clay, or other materials. || 442 ||
Having performed the sprinkling and other rites, he should then worship;
having established the mantras within himself, he should cast them again into that water. (443)
O Nandikeśvara, [this is] within a year...
Thus ends the chapter concerning the characteristics of installation in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*.
O Nandikeśvara, [prepare] the pavilion, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit as before; having bathed the Goddess and placed her upon the bed as previously described, (p. 966) || 1 ||
From the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) to the forehead, from the forehead to the heart, from the heart to the navel, and from the navel to the perineum (mūlādhāra). || 2 ||
One should perform the installation of the forms and so forth from the knees down to the feet;
however, one should perform the installation of Īśāna from the Self (Ātman) through Vidyā up to Śiva.
Having deposited [the mantra] immediately after that which is called Aparā,
and having offered oblations and drunk [the nectar] in due order, one should then perform the Sandhyā-āma.

Having meditated upon the pervasive [power] and likewise upon the one in whom the jewels and other [attributes] have been deposited, one should thereafter establish the Goddess of Gods and unite her with that very [power]. || 5 ||
Having assumed that [form] through the yoga of emanation by means of his own mantra,
he should then project the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which consists of the form of *nyāsa*.
Then, in the case of a conflict, one should project the pervasive power (vyāpinī-śakti) in the form of energy;
having touched the image named "Amukeśī," one should worship it.
Oṃ Āṃ, obeisance to the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti). || 8 ||
Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to the one whose stalk is the *kaṇḍa* [and] whose eyes are the *nāla*.
Oṃ ḷṃ, salutation to dispassion (*vairāgya*). Oṃ ḷṃ, salutation to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). || 9 ||
Oṃ ṛṃ, homage to Adharma. Oṃ ṝṃ, homage to Ignorance. Oṃ ḷṃ, homage to Lack of Dispassion. Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Lack of Sovereignty. || 10 ||
Oṃ, homage to the lower covering. Oṃ aṃ, homage to the upper covering.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lotus. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the filaments. || 11 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the pericarp (karṇikā). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lotus-petals (puṣkara).
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the wise one (prājñā). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the knowing one (jñānī). || 12 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. || 13 ||
Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Having thus assigned these nine powers, one should cause the visualization of the Goddess to be performed. || 14 ||
Golden-hued, adorned with flowers, and anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents;
four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 15 ||
Adorned with many ornaments,
having thus meditated upon the Mother of the World, who possesses the luster of Gaurī... || 16 ||
Oṃ gauṃ, salutation to Gaurī. [Repeated salutations].
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ, salutation to Mahāgaurī, the beloved of Rudra. || 17 ||
"Oṃ namo gaurī rudradayitāyai svāhā"—this is the root mantra. Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to the heart. || 18 ||
Oṃ gīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ gūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ gaiṃ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ gauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. || 19 ||
Oṃ gaḥ astrāya phaṭ | Oṃ sīṃ jñānaśaktaye namaḥ | Oṃ siṃ namaḥ | (p. 970)
Oṃ saiṃ, obeisance to Kāmamālinī. || 21 ||
O Nandikeśvara, these Śaktis should be like Gaurī;
having thus meditated upon them and worshipped them well with fragrant flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
Having offered the oblations for the sensations (*vedanā*) and so forth as previously described, O Nandikeśvara!
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Gaurī," within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Then one should place the three syllables *gaṃ sa tra* at the end of the mantra.

Having placed Īśvara there, one should perform the purification and so forth of the pentad beginning with space (vyoman) and ending with earth (kṣmā), as before; and having formed the *piṇḍa* as before.
Then, having placed five jewels arranged as far as the edge of the footprint in that location,
he established them according to the rules from all sides with his power.
The preceptor should duly install the Sūrya [image] up to the point of the Śakti within the Sthāṇu;
the Sūrya-mantras should be propitiated [therein].
[This should be done] in a grove, in a temple, or in a sacred and delightful place.
And its establishment is prescribed for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
p.
972) Indeed, its movement for the sake of others is proclaimed as its specific quality;
the pavilion, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit are to be prepared as before, O Nandikeśvara! (7)
Now the retinue from the east up to the northeast is described:
I bow to Unmatta, Lalita, Bhīma, and Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra.
One should fashion [the deity] Vi* * * * * * * * * * * * * and place the one named Bhīma, who is formidable, at the side of the gate. || 9 ||
And Kumbhodaka, Nirmālya, and Dhāraṇa among the preceptors;
likewise Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and Durmukha. || 10 ||
He is free from obstacles, the king of obstacles, a consumer of offerings, and five-handed;
for these are the lords of the eight forms, or he is the one with the face of an elephant. (11)
On the Vimāna, the two door-keepers Bhūta and Rūpa are two-armed, holding ploughs and staffs.
With faces terrible with fangs, they have Skanda as their feet.
In the central lotus is Gaṇādhyakṣa, adorned with all ornaments;
he has the face of an elephant, a massive body, and is endowed with a protruding belly. || 13 ||
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and is endowed with two short arms;
he resembles the clouds at twilight or has the luster of a blue lotus.
He may resemble molten gold, or be like pure crystal,
or even possess a dark complexion, according to the attainment of his desired fruit.
He holds a noose, a goad, his own tooth, a sweetmeat ball, and likewise a blue lotus;
he is endowed with a crown and a tiara, and wears a white sacred thread.
Adorned with all ornaments and resplendent with three eyes, one should visualize him as seated upon a throne, or upon a rat, or else upon a lion. (17)
Then, having performed the purification of the village and other areas,
one should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) for the image, which is provided with a hanging beard (lambakūrca).
Thereafter, one should place eight jars representing the eight holy sites beginning with the Narmadā;
or alternatively, one may likewise arrange five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Having performed the removal of the artisan's work, one should have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) formula;
then, having brought Vighneśa from the water, one should install him upon the bathing altar.
On the northern side of the pavilion, one should perform the ritual bathing as before;
having tied the protective thread, the wise practitioner should recite the root mantra.
One should place eight jars all around the region of the head;
having placed the nine gems and other items therein, one should wrap them with two cloths in the prescribed order.
Then, one should satisfy [the deity] with offerings such as flowers from the vessel-oblation (pātrahoma) and so forth, and subsequently perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
One should likewise offer sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru), performing the oblation with these eight substances.
One thousand, or half of that, or fifty, or one hundred and eight;
this is the modification for the ten ancillary parts derived from the root mantra.
For the image-worshippers (mūrtipas), that [number] shall be halved; there is an oblation for each principle (tattva) and its presiding deity.
For the sake of pacification, the Guru should cause the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) to be performed with the respective mantra of each.
Or he may perform the touching with *darbha* grass at each division;
thus the Guru himself should sit during the morning session.
Having performed the two daily rites (*nityakarman*), one should enter the mandala and so forth;
having raised Vighnarāja, one should worship the water-jar (*kumbha*), the fire, and the other [deities]. (27)
One should perform the expiation with the Aghora mantra, or offer a hundred oblations;
one should also offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and then the venerable Guru should enter.

Having placed upon it a stone slab composed of the essence of Brahman, joined with jewels, medicinal herbs, and other substances, and filled [with water], he should thereafter install the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa).
One should worship with the root mantra and the principal mantra,
especially at an auspicious moment, and perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) and other rites.
If the image is mobile, then the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and so forth should take place upon the bathing altar;
one should then perform the consecration in those respective locations using the waters from each of the ritual jars.
The Guru should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the *tattva-mūrti* and so forth as before;
and having thus performed the ceremonial bath (*snapana*), he should present the food offering (*naivedya*). (32)
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor and especially the guardians of the images;
one should praise the guru and the image-guardians with garments, gold, rings, and other such gifts.
Indeed, through the installation of Vighneśa, all accomplishments (siddhis) come to pass.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the installation of Vighneśa in the Acintyaviśvasādākhya [Tantra].
O Nandīśa! Your installation bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
[you are] three-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, and standing with palms joined in reverence. || 1 ||
I bow to the one who holds a deer and an axe, who grasps a staff in his hand,
who is adorned with a crown of matted hair, and whose radiance is like that of the sun.
On the left, however, he is joined by Queen Suyaśā, endowed with auspicious marks;
he has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament and is resplendent with a dark-blue throat.
[He saw] one resembling the rising sun, endowed with the characteristics of Rudrākṣas, and the Goddess, possessing a dark complexion and adorned with all ornaments. || 4 ||
O Nandikeśvara, the planting of the sprout, the arrangement of jewels, the consecration and so forth, as well as the placing upon the bed, should be performed just as before.

In front of the deity, one should place the water-pot (kumbha) facing the altar (vedi), and the prosperity-pot (vardhanī); one should also place the eight pots (vasukumbha) in the cardinal directions and worship them as well.

One should install the three principles (tritatva), the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) like Śiva; the deity should be joined with the limbs of the Vāma-bīja, and the Goddess as the possessor of power (śaktimat).
The fire-offering ritual (homakarma) should be performed as before, within the Ratnagarbha [mandala];
at dawn, the Guru, together with the image-protectors (mūrtipās), should perform the ceremonial bath according to the prescribed rite.
Having likewise offered everything from perfumes and flowers up to the food offering (naivedya),
one should then worship Nandīśa with devotion from that time forward.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Nandikeśvara," within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*.
Listen now to the procedure for the perpetual festival for the sake of others and for the sacred site itself:
it should be performed either to the south or to the left on pure ground.
In a palace or even in a pavilion, there should be a smearing with cow-dung;
having performed a sprinkling with the Astra-mantra, one should prepare a vessel endowed with the proper characteristics.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or combined with clay;
beginning with a hole of one finger-breadth, it increases by one finger-breadth up to five finger-breadths.
The measurement of the vessels should be thirty-two finger-breadths;
they should be perfectly circular, provided with a pedestal, and adorned with a pericarp and petals.

Beside that, in vessels representing seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four,

twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four, thirty-five, thirty-six, thirty-seven, thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty, forty-one, forty-two, forty-three, forty-four, forty-five, forty-six, forty-seven, forty-eight, forty-nine, fifty, fifty-one, fifty-two, fifty-three, fifty-four, fifty-five, fifty-six, fifty-seven, fifty-eight, fifty-nine, sixty, sixty-one, sixty-two, sixty-three, sixty-four, sixty-five, sixty-six, sixty-seven, sixty-eight, sixty-nine, seventy, seventy-one, seventy-two, seventy-three, seventy-four, seventy-five, seventy-six, seventy-seven, seventy-eight, seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, eighty-two, eighty-three, eighty-four, eighty-five, eighty-six, eighty-seven, eighty-eight, eighty-nine, ninety, ninety-one, ninety-two, ninety-three, ninety-four, ninety-five, ninety-six, ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine, and one hundred, there may be [the respective results] one, two, three, four, five, six, and so forth.
With the remainder, the measurement for the description of the eight-petaled lotus of transformation is considered;
the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one and a half measures, or two measures.
p.
981) For those possessing [the requisite qualities], the vessel should be provided with all its accompaniments or alone; the rule begins with two families and extends up to many families.
One should prepare rice for the sake of the food-liṅga as prescribed;
the food-liṅga should be offered at all three times: morning, midday, and evening.
One should fashion a flower-liṅga in the forenoon or at midday;
at dusk, there should be a liṅga made of parched grain, wherein the Pāśupata [rite] is performed.

The Pāśupata is to be known as threefold—namely, that which is conjoined with Candraśekhara, that which is devoid of him, and the mixed—according to the divisions of peaceful (śānta) and fierce (ugra). || 10 ||
Two-armed and four-armed, gentle and endowed with gentle eyes,
resembling a garland of lightning, he is adorned with matted locks and a crown.
Or he may have hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, endowed with all the auspicious marks. || 12 ||
Having indeed set aside the noose and rosary, one should sequentially employ the lotus and bell;
thus he shall possess a gentle form, especially one containing jewels within.
I shall describe the Raudra-Pāśupata; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
[The deity] holds a trident-base and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and is endowed with the tip of a trident and the gesture of granting boons.

One should worship Raudrī, meditating upon her as having a fierce gaze, flaming hair, and hands crossed over a trident, holding a trident-weapon in her hand; [one should do so] with "vauṣaṭ," recollecting her threefold form.
This [form] is mixed, and thus he would be of mixed nature; carrying an axe and a trident in the right hands, and a noose and a deer in the left, though it is described otherwise as well.
Holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in the right hand, and a noose with the radiance of the boon-granting gesture;
this is declared to be twofold, while the Pāśupata is threefold as a mixture.
One should worship with flowers, unbroken rice, and food upon the lingas according to the prescribed mantras;
or else, an image should be fashioned according to its proper proportions.
One should worship [the deity] fashioned upon a pedestal that has the shape of a seat and a sphere,
or [one] the size of an *annaliṅga*, with a base equal in extent to the root-fire (*mūlāgni*).
Or one should worship [the image] up to the limit of the hands, characterized by all the marks, together with the staff of the wish-fulfilling pillar (sthalī-kāmānanda-daṇḍa). || 20 ||
The image of Induśekhara (Śiva) should be fashioned according to the characteristics of an icon;
from a three-finger-high sandal, it should increase by one finger at a time in thickness.
The two goddesses [of the door] should end at the measure of the lunar day (tithi);
according to the length, one should make the width half of that, and the height half of the width. (22)
The middle [portion] should be bent down by one-eighth; this is the *anupānaka* [style].
Between those two, the bull is to be worshipped, or it is proclaimed that [the worship] ends with the ritual bath.
The world-protectors (Lokapālas) are to be worshipped on all sides, beginning from the east and ending with the northeast;
then, having joined the nine-limbed liṅga, one should perform the daily festival.
Endowed with all of these, one should then perform the perpetual festival;
[this may be done] with two, three, or four [of them], both in the forenoon and at the time of dusk.
At midday, he alone is to be worshipped, or else the one called Pāśupata;
whether on the stage, in a palanquin, or upon the heads of the attendants.
Having placed the well-fashioned image of the God upon it, provided with a canopy,
equipped with an umbrella and chowries, and adorned with various banners; (27)
Then one should perform a circumambulation accompanied by dance and song;
for the first circumambulation, Bhṛṅgiṇī should perform it in time with rhythmic beats.
For Vṛṣa, there should be vṛṣalamba; for Bhṛṅgin, tālavahni and tālaka; for the Mothers, candratāla; and for Vighneśa, it should be dharakī. || 29 ||
In the Jyeṣṭhā [nakṣatra] during a planetary seizure, it is said that there is a "puṇnitālaka" [affliction];
in Durgā, a "taṭaprabhāra"; and in Caṇḍikā, a "viṣamacintā."
Whether in a village or even in a city, or indeed outside the ramparts—this second circumambulation is the circumambulation of the Great Seat (mahāpīṭha). || 31 ||
Either one, two, or three [images] accompanied by Śambarī,
or else on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), they should be provided with Brahmā and Tāla. || 32 ||
One should perform two circumambulations accompanied by the *gajatāla* rhythm;
in the *paiśāca* [mode], it should be thus with the *jvala* [rhythm], and in the *śābarī* [mode], it is joined with the *tāla* rhythm.
At the gate, there should be music devoid of instruments, accompanied by the sound of conchs;
on the right, Bhṛṅginī with rhythmic beats, accompanied by Kauśika.
Combined with the *cālophāṇi* [mantra], it is considered the *ḍhakkarī* in the temple of Śaṅkara;
having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter the third abode. || 35 ||
Having washed their feet, everyone should enter the temple of Śiva; or else, they should proceed in order to the location of the pedestal in the pavilion or similar place.
Having worshipped with offerings such as musical instruments and the like, one should cause [the disciple] to enter.
Thus, having caused him to emerge from the *liṅga*, one should seat him to the right of the *liṅga*. (37)
The feet of Śiva, or his sandals on the right and left, are to be worshipped;
for other goddesses and gods as well, it is according to their primary image (mūlabimba).
Having personally established another form [of the deity], one should then perform the perpetual festival;
having accomplished that, one should indeed always perform the perpetual festival. (39)
Then, the weapon should be worshipped in the food-liṅga and other such forms, as well as one's own vehicle;
the pair of sandals should be worshipped according to the sequence of the rules for the daily festival.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, the procedure for the eternal festival, in the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is inconceivable.
(988) O Nandikeśvara, listen! I shall now describe the installation of Viṣṇu.
The pavilion, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be prepared according to the previously prescribed rules.
Having likewise performed all the rites such as the ritual bathing and so forth,
one should arrange an auspicious throne for the elephant, endowed with the proper characteristics, just as before.
Or else, one may perform obeisance to Tāra, Pāśa, Mahāmāyā, Aghorīśa, and Bhavasthā;
furthermore, all [mantras] beginning with Praṇava should indeed include obeisance to them. (3)
The fourth [syllable] ends with *kanyā*; the fifth consists of the heart, head, crest, and armor, with the weapon-mantras situated in the middle.
The mantras begin with "Padma" and so forth; such is their sequence as told by you.
They are joined with the Heart-mantra (Namaḥ) and likewise with "Bhagavate. (5)
"Vāsudevāya"— this twelve-syllabled great mantra is declared to be the form to be meditated upon in its intermediate aspect. (6)
By this very mantra, Viṣṇu himself is directly present;
one should perform the consecration of the pavilion and other structures, as well as the invocation of the lords of the directions.
Having performed [the rites] with the heart-mantra, the heart-weapon mantra, the Gāyatrī, and by means of speech,
one should then restore Lakṣmī and the deity to their respective places in due order.
Having had [the image] clothed in garments and having provided a seat as before,
one should then place the form of the deity upon the bed.

Immediately after performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the twelve-syllable mantra, the practitioner of mantras should perform the placement of the sword and other implements as follows: || 10 ||
One should meditate on the head, the nose, the forehead, the mouth, the two ears, and the heart;
then on the right and left feet respectively, and finally on the toes of the right and left feet in sequence. (11)
My [weapon], possessing a radiance equal to the sun of the [thousand-]spoked wheel, shall envelop him in flames—yellow, white, red, and blue; lightning-yellow, white, and reddish-brown.
One should sequentially assign the twelve syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *ya*;
the placement of the sword (*khaḍga*) is on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and likewise the *jagava* on the forehead (*lalāṭa*).
With one's own name in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ," preceded by the syllable Om,
[one should worship] the plough and the pestle outside, immediately after the single oblation.

Mounted with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), they are positioned in the center of the heart-wheel; with the mantra ending in salutation (*namaḥ*), they are placed on the navel, the abdomen, and the back.
Then, having worshipped with the syllable *praṇava*, one should likewise offer salutations with "Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkha.
[One should worship] the Guru and Śaṅkha... [and so forth]. (16)
Preceded by *tāra* (om), [one should worship] with the mantra *śvaṃ ḍhaṃ pāṣaṃ gadāyai ca namaḥ*. || 17 ||

One should place [the deity] whose self is the knowledge of mantras upon the shanks and knees; Mādhava on the neck, Govinda on the ear, Viṣṇu on the heart, and likewise Madhusūdana on the spinal column.
One should meditate on Trivikrama in the belly, Vāmana in the pair of thighs,
Śrīdhara in the shanks, and immediately thereafter Hṛṣīkeśa.
One should place all [the syllables] at the feet and so forth in the eastern part;
now, the second [part], beginning with the heart, is being described as follows.
Following that, one should offer with the heart-mantra and others, as well as those beginning with "Oṃ Hrīṃ" and so forth. || 22 ||
O Nandikeśvara, the mantra "Oṃ namo viṣṇave namaḥ" is known as the *hṛdaya*; the mantra designated as the *śiras* is well-known among the learned. (23)

Beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, [one should worship] with the *dhruva* mantra "brahmaṇe" for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and for the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) in sequence, they recite "oṃ cakrī. (24)
Oṃ kābhradvinamaḥ and antaḥ are these two for Śambhu and Vijayā;
likewise, one should recite Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, beginning with Oṃ and ending with namaḥ. || 25 ||
Beginning with *Tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, with *kṣī* situated in the middle,
this seven-syllable mantra known as the *piṇḍa* bestows all accomplishments. || 26 ||
One should place this mantra ending in the dative case, as well as the mantras for the planets and others ending in the dative,
and also the Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī mantras, upon the left and right eyes respectively.
Having assigned [the deity] to its proper place, one should worship it endowed with devotion:
"Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to the one in the form of Piṅgalākṣa. || 28 ||
The wheels [should be] twelve-spoked, and the supreme Sun-god [should be] with light;
and in the center of that, O Lord, there should again be an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place the Heart-mantra in the pericarp, the Head-mantra likewise in the eastern face, the Crest-mantra on the southern petal, and the Armor-mantra in the western [petal]. (30)
Having placed the Astra-mantra in the north, one should place Gāyatrī on the petal of the fire (southeast),
Sāvitrī on the petal of Īśāna (northeast), and the Rakṣas-eye mantra on the [western] petal. (31)
The Piṅgalā weapon is on the wind-petal, and it should be reddish-brown in the intermediate space;
now, the second enclosure is indeed at the location of the gates in the wheel.

One should perform obeisance with the names beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara, joined with the syllable *namaḥ* and one's own name, in the mantras according to the sequence starting from the east.
Having placed those [seeds] first, one should subsequently place on the outside the sword, the Kaumodakī mace,
the mallet, the discus, the conch, the lotus, and the plow.
O Nandikeśvara, one should likewise place the mace and the Śārṅga bow, and worship them with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, garments, ornaments, and so forth. || 35 ||
One should worship Vāsudeva well with all the limbs and coverings;
however, in the ritual of placement (nyāsa), at the conclusion of the five forms, the root mantra should be as follows. (36)
"Namaste vāsudevāya," "Oṃ haṃ," and so forth;
likewise, "Oṃ hāṃ rīṃ raṃ aṃ"; and "Oṃ aṃ oṃ," preceded by the pair. (37)
Those known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—these names of Nārāyaṇa, in their respective order, are joined with the fourth case ending and followed by "namaḥ. (38)
Thereafter, one should worship the five forms of Mūrtīśa, beginning with Earth (kṣiti),
and likewise perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the limbs and their worship as previously described.

In the case of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti) and other such systems, however, the preceptor should recite the previously mentioned mantras for those respective lords, as well as the root mantra one thousand times or half of that.
One should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation; having offered it, one should present it to the ears.
To eliminate any defects in the sacrifice, one should also cause the offering of a *bali* oblation to be made. (41)
Having likewise offered it into the heart, one should then fashion the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
It should be perceived through its form like the word "namaḥ," and not with "oṃ bhaṃ phaṃ dhruvānirā."
Having meditated with this mantra and having become Lakṣmī as before,
he is established in the midst of those [deities] by means of the mantras ending in the number five.

Or, in some cases, one may use the collective [mantra] consisting of the words for armor (*varman*) and eyes (*netra*) applied to the heart and head of the weapon-mantra, ending with *huṃ phaṭ* at the conclusion of the weapon-mantra.
Then, recollecting its former state, one should cause it to enter into the vessel of clarity;
[one should establish] the pervasive primordial nature (prakṛti) and the pedestal with the Lakṣmī-mantra.
Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the form of Lakṣmī. Oṃ yaṃ ṭaṃ raṃ bhaṃ phaṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī.
And there, one should place the previously assigned gems and the twelve-syllable mantra. (46)

Having pronounced the word "Puruṣānta," [one should meditate on Him] wearing yellow garments, four-armed, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a sword, smeared with ashes, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
One should place the entire wheel, and the lotus seat should be at the center of the wheel; ending with "namas" and followed by "vyāpaka," it should likewise be joined with the two forms.

The self-principle (ātmatattva) exists within the subtle elements (tanmātras), while the knowledge-principle (vidyātattva) has primordial matter (pradhāna) as its primary constituent; having meditated upon the Lord (Īśa) as extending up to the individual soul (puruṣa), one should thereafter contemplate what follows.
Having invoked the God, who encompasses the high and the low and is endowed with three enclosures,
and having worshipped Him according to the rules with devotion, one should perform for them the rites as previously described.
One should bear the name of the god Viṣṇu, ending in the word *svāmin* or *mādhava*, joined with the name of the performer; this is the most excellent consecration (*sthāpana*). (51)
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of Viṣṇu," within the *Viśvasādākhyam*, the Inconceivable [Tantra].
Now I shall specifically describe the consecration of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
Knowledge is said to be of two kinds: that which consists of ritual refinement (saṃskṛti) and that which is of the nature of the Self (anyātmikā). || 1 ||
Whether in a palace, a monastery, a pure region, or even a house; whether in a place recommended by a devotee, or in the vicinity of any sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). || 2 ||
Either read the aforementioned book, or else listen to the characteristics. || 3 ||
Starting from three finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth up to the void (zero),
the length of the manuscript shall range up to twenty-five mātrās.
Or, by increasing the space-parts by one-quarter at each step, it should conclude with half a measure;
its extent should be broad, or else joined with the wings and the fire.
Or on birch bark where the sound has been removed, or on a collection of palm leaves;
or on a palm leaf, or a birch leaf, or on a golden plate at the beginning of the verse.
On a stone, on wood, or other such surfaces, one should write [the mantra] with auspicious liquid substances, or with ink, or even with mineral pigments, using either a stylus or a brush.
The preceptor or even the disciple may perform [the rite] with a nārāca arrow on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation, at a propitious moment, with a serene mind.
One should never cause the knowledge of Śiva to be written down by Brahmins or others who have not received initiation.
Furthermore, one must especially not study it in the presence of those who are uninitiated. (9)
One should cause it to be written with clear letters produced from various regions and refined by grammatical rules; then one should perform the auspicious recitation (japa) for a long duration.
Having worshipped with auspicious fragrances the Mātṛkā, who is the very form of Śiva—untainted by any others and mutually unmixed—one should [proceed]. (11)
The preceptor should also worship a written leaf among these with garments and other offerings,
on a patch of ground smeared with cow dung and beautifully adorned with heaps of flowers.
Provided with perfumes, incense, and the like, and accompanied by a burning lamp,
one who is united with the pure Śaiva [tradition] should either write it down or maintain its recitation.
Because the manuscript of the Śivajñāna has been worn out over a long period of time,
it may contain omissions or additions due to the negligence of those [who copied it]. (14)
[This concerns] the recitation studied through negligence and corrupted by those of small intellect, who possess only meager knowledge and have not been refined by their teachers. (15)
Even for one who has attained wealth that is useless, repetition without cause,
being utterly lost to the meters, and being devoid of heard meaning—
for one possessed of such faults here and there— (the following applies). 17.
Furthermore, that wise teacher who correctly performs the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is none other than the Supreme Lord Śiva himself; he is Vidyā, the Supreme Sovereign.
One should not instruct devotees who are not devotees of Śiva, but one should instruct those who are devotees of Śiva;
that which is given according to the Śiva-vidyā is called the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna). || 19 ||
By means of words in Sanskrit or Prakrit, those arising from regional dialects,
and by pure words derived from Sanskrit as well.
The supreme teacher should awaken [the disciple] by means of local dialects and other such methods, as well as through traditional scriptures and statements applicable to specific contexts. (21)
Just as there is no end to the greatness of Śiva, who is perfectly complete, so too [the one who destroys the knowledge of Śiva] may attain great fame, prosperity, happiness, and liberation;
yet the destroyer of the knowledge of Śiva goes to a terrible hell. (23)
Thereafter, one should worship like Śiva that which illuminates the knowledge of Śiva;
the wise person should cause the Vidyās to be written every day according to his capacity. (24)
For as many thousands of ages as there are syllables in the book of the Śiva-jñāna, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having rescued ten ancestors and ten descendants of his lineage,
and having attained heaven for the sake of his own merit through his mother’s dharma, he reaches the celestial realm.
Having established all others in heaven, he himself shall dwell in the state of Śiva,
even if it be but a single verse, half a verse, or a single statement of the knowledge of Śiva.
One should recite it, or contemplate it, or write it, or cause it to be written;
or, with a single-pointed mind, one should listen to it and retain its meaning.
For one who causes others to hear this, the fruit of merit is great;
likewise, providing food and clothing for one devoted to the knowledge of Śiva is a great act. (29)
The fruit of the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna) shall be obtained by protecting [the recipient] until completion;
furthermore, he who masters the syllable "Na" (*nakāra*) enjoys that very same fruit.
In whose kingdom the exposition of the knowledge of Śiva occurs constantly, that king abides in his realm; that monarch shall also be unconquered. || 31 ||

The king, the kingdom, the preceptor, and the leader— these should be appointed to the office of commander-in-chief, to other duties, to the position of domestic priest, and to all matters concerning royal affairs and the administration of justice.
All those who have been initiated, as well as others who are practitioners of Yoga, [are included];
therefore, because of the splitting apart of the pure Śaivas by the Siddhānta-Śaiva, [the latter are considered distinct].
(1005) The rites of pacification (śāntika) and enrichment (pauṣṭika) are not to be performed by a king, especially so;
for such is the power of this vidyā. Now listen indeed to how it is purifying. || 34 ||
The three threads should extend all around by thirty-three finger-breadths;
the hall of learning (vidyāśālā) should be spacious, whether it be in a palace or a pavilion.
The expansion of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), characterized by features such as the single-hall (ekaśāla) and other varieties,
is seven finger-breadths in width.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, supreme, and possessed of the correct proportions of measurement, it should be square, or its length may be greater [than its width]. (37)
On another seat prescribed by the ritual rules, the Guru should worship the Śivajñāna;
he should then sprinkle the one known as the Śivajñānavidyā with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the pavilion, one should place them upon cloth; and the seat and other requisites should be provided for the forms together with their presiding deities (mūrtīśas). || 39 ||
In the Śiva division, Śiva is to be worshipped; indeed, in the Rudra division, he alone is so.
In the center, however, there is the Śiva-pitcher, and on both sides, two crocodiles.
Having worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) there as before, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), the Guru [should worship] the Supreme Śiva in the center.
One should place the supremely beautiful Goddess there upon the tablet.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the Vidyā, in the Acintyaviśvasādākhya.
1007) Now I shall explain specifically the installation of devotees for Śiva:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, those of intermediate castes, or even women. || 1 ||
Whether they are living or dead, those who have attained devotion to Śiva—
one should fashion an image of them, install it, and perform the rites.
Those who are Śaivas, Pāśupatas, and those who observe the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), and by whichever path they have been initiated through the Kaumāra, Raurava, and other [tantras]; || 3 ||
For them, the primary rite of installation is performed by that very same path.
For all Śaivas as well, the installation is considered to be of two kinds. (4)
It may be independent as a primary rite or subordinate as an auxiliary, especially the Ratnagarbha;
it may be performed in a gift-village, at the beginning of a city, on a riverbank, or even in a forest.
In a garden, by a lotus pond or similar feature, or in any other delightful place,
one should construct a temple for one's chosen deity.
In a temple, at Yetāra or elsewhere, in a consecrated shrine,
one should have the principal deity installed together with his retinue.
In temples and all other places, such as in flower-garden pavilions and the like,
that which is conceived without a retinue is considered to be a single-limbed [deity].
Starting from three cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
the width of the vimāna is prescribed to extend up to twenty-one cubits.
One should examine the length, height, interior space, and so forth of the pavilion and other structures, as well as the enclosure wall, the gate-towers, the courtyards, the garlands, and the rest.
The performance of the first sacrifice, as well as the establishment of the embryo (garbha),
and the laying of the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā), have been declared as before. || 11 ||
At that time, it may be a Śiva-liṅga, or an image of Śiva,
or indeed an image-form of Vighneśa, Guha, Nandin, and so forth.
A wise person should have everything constructed from gold, silver, copper, and so forth; or with metals such as gold, or with woods, or even with earthen materials.
O Nandikeśvara, one should fashion [the deity] on a wall, in a painting, or even on a cloth;
or else, one should have a linga or an image made according to the prescribed method.
The preceptor should cause the palaces and other structures to be built according to the path described by the measuring finger (mānāṅgula),
endowed with all auspicious characteristics and adorned with every measurement.
One should construct palaces provided with gates and gate-towers;
therein, one should fashion an image in accordance with the specific form of Rudra.
And that linga should be fashioned according to the ritual procedure in the Ratnagarbhaka [mandala];
it is prescribed as being eight tālas in measurement for the image.
Seated upon the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), or else standing upon a vehicle and so forth,
he is seated on a throne the width of a man, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Whether he be shaven-headed, or have matted locks, or have his hair tied up, or wear a topknot, or be adorned with a crown— if he is a Kṣatriya, he should be fashioned adorned with all ornaments.
One should further adorn [the deity] with whatever weapons are desired, or accompanied by salutations; likewise, one should adorn the women with white silk garments and ornaments.
The characteristics have thus been explained; now the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites are being described.
According to the method prescribed for the image, one should perform the rites with beeswax and other materials. (21)
The Guru should likewise cause the placement of jewels and other items upon the various limbs,
as well as the ritual opening of the eyes, according to the prescribed rules.
O Nandikeśvara, the pavilion, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit should be prepared as before;
then the Guru should fashion a pedestal upon the sacrificial mound and inscribe the Praṇava thereon.
Having established the jar upon that [altar], one should perform the nyāsa of the image;
with gold and a load of wealth, one should draw a black maṇḍala.
Having drawn a circle of fire with an eye the size of a louse,
and having recited the mantra of the eye, one should perform this rite.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with eyes made from gold and dūrvā grass leaves;
having filled both [eyes] with either ghee or honey, one should show them. (26)
Indeed, the fivefold bedding consists of either cloths or skins;
furthermore, there is the preparation of seats such as the Ananta-ādhāra, Dharma, and so forth.
O Nandikeśvara, one should fashion a human pedestal with the syllable *tāreṇa*;
then, one should place the image, which has been consecrated in water, upon the bathing altar.
The Guru should perform the excellent ceremonial bath upon the pedestal according to the prescribed rite;
he should then adorn the image again with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
Having tied the protective amulet (kautuka), one should place it upon the bed;
one should position the image with its head toward the east and cause a water-pot (kumbha) to be placed to its north.
One should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) conjoined with the ajapā mantra,
together with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) joined with the syllables of space (vyomākṣara). || 31 ||
Upon the installation of the female deities (Aṅganās), one should also employ the seed-syllable of Śakti;
the five Brahmans and the six-limbed ritual (Ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed with their respective seed-syllables.
There, accompanied by Jaya and the others, one should place each syllable individually;
this is proclaimed as the installation of a female deity when her own mantras are used in the Vardhanī vessel.
The pentad beginning with earth, as well as mind, ego, and intellect—these are considered the eight Vasus for worship in the attendant jar (parivāra-ghaṭa). || 34 ||
The eastern directions for women were proclaimed by them [the Daityas] to belong to the Daityas;
or else, the world-protectors are placed in the eight jars starting from the east, or in the male figure.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install the Lords of the Principles (tattva).
The triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva has thus been declared. (36)
