O Nandikeśvara, one should worship the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self in succession as the presiding deities.

For women as well, it should be exactly the same; the earth and the others are considered the offerings (āhuti), while Nivṛtti and the rest are specifically the guardians of the forms within the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti). || 38 ||
There, one should likewise assign the forms of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their attendants (mūrtipās),
and then perform the assignment of the Mātṛkās from the letter 'A' to the letter 'Kṣa'.

The placement [of mantras] with one's own mantra is declared to be the "placement of the life-force" (jīvanyāsa). Having performed the placement of the limbs with that same [mantra], one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having covered [the fire] with a cloth and armor, one should perform the rite of homa;
[this includes] the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*) and the satiation of the vital breaths (*jīva-tarpaṇa*). (41)
Having performed the remainder of the rites, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*), according to the previously stated procedure,
[one should place] the *brahmavṛkṣa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees in the directions starting from the east, in due order.
In the case of the fire-altars and so forth, the *śamī* tree, as well as the *khara*, *māyūra*, and *cillaka* trees, are primary;
the *brahma* tree may be used, or one hundred, half of that, or half of the latter [fifty].
Having performed the concluding oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should install the Lords of the respective Tattvas;
O Nandikeśvara, one should offer three oblations for each one.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra for the sake of expiation,
the preceptor should then sprinkle [the disciple] from the head down to the feet with the water of peace (śāntitoya).
Having offered the inner and outer oblations (balis), perform the washing of the feet.
At dawn, the preceptor, having bathed with the image-keepers (mūrtipās), shall remain engaged in his daily rites.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing a turban and an upper garment, he was accompanied by students, astrologers, and artisans. || 47 ||
Having worshipped the guardians of the doors and performed the worship of the ritual pitcher (kumbha), the Guru,
having completed the fire-oblation up to the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti), then raises the image.
One should gradually bring that image from the temple to its bed there;
provided with the placement of jewels and other rites, one should install it in the bathing pit.
Having made the syllable *TĀR* the seat, fashioned according to the form-mantras,
and having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the placement of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*).
The preceptor should bathe [the image] with the water from the jars that have been set out, using perfumes and flowers; then, having adorned it with garments and ornaments, he should proceed. (51)
Then one should offer the food offering (nivedya) preceded by the ritual services (upacāra),
and having honored the devotees of Śiva according to the extent of one's wealth.
From that time forward, having worshipped [the deity] constantly just like Śiva,
one should always follow the path of the virtuous, employing the six limbs of the self-mantra.
Or, having worshipped [the deity] with devotion up to the offering of the bali-oblation, he becomes a leader on the true path.
The mantra ending with "namaskāra" and known by the name Taruñjapā,
as well as the one ending with "svāhā," are proclaimed as the root mantras for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
p.
1018) Or on the birthday of the devotee, or even on the birthday of the performer [of the rite], one should perform a monthly festival according to one's means. || 56 ||
One who desires to perform [the rite] should first raise the banner;
on that banner one should depict a bull, and the festival should be celebrated like that of Śiva.
O Nandikeśvara, having completed the full festival endowed with perpetual celebration, the preceptor must perform the preliminary festival for those who have attained self-mastery.
That best of men who performs the installation of a Śiva devotee shall attain prosperity and victory for a long time, and ultimately achieve liberation through union with the Divine (sāyujya).
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Devotees," within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
(1019) O Nandīśa, listen as I describe the consecration of the door in its proper sequence.
Having consecrated the components of the door with the Jayā and other mantras, one should install the sanctuary.

Having sequentially deposited the three principles— the Self (ātman), Knowledge (vidyā), and Śiva— at the base, middle, and top parts [of the body], one should then restrain [the breath] and perform the fire oblation (homa).
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the victory rite in a fitting manner according to the prescribed rule;
having worshipped the deities of the site, the doors, and so forth, right there with the Ananta mantra.
Having placed the five jewels and other offerings, one should perform the rite of pacification.
There shall be beauty, the accomplishment of goals, and prosperity, along with the increase of barley, accompanied by a younger brother.
Endowed with the characteristics of Gomanda, Daroga, Indra, and Mohinī,
these are Nāra, Agvadha, Dūrvā, and the leaf known as Sāndaghna.
Having fashioned [the bolt] from udumbara wood and bound it with the syllable *ra* using the *praṇava*,
one should install it slightly leaning toward the north at the door.
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is situated below, while the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is in the two branches;
Śiva, however, pervades all individual souls in the region of space.
Then, one should install Maheśāna and the others with the root mantra,
and Nandin and the others stationed at the doors with their own names joined with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should offer one hundred oblations, or twice that number, or according to one's capacity;
for the sake of releasing from defects, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra.
Having performed the offering to the directions as before, one should bestow the sacrificial fees and so forth.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the door, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Resembling a shimmering star, it becomes equal to the *dvādaśānta*;
one should deposit it within the womb of the *kumbha*, having established the resident [deity] according to the tantra. (6)
One should place there the *vigraha*, the indicators of its qualities (*tadguṇa*), the *kalā* and so forth ending with *kṣmī*, the *śekhara*, and the final *tattva*.
One should [worship] the ten channels, the ten vital breaths, and the thirteen sense organs,
as well as their respective presiding deities, by means of their own names preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ).

By virtue of their own causal agency, they impel the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), who themselves govern Māyā and Kāla; and Śambhu, in turn, impels those Lords of Knowledge by means of his supreme boons.
Having cast off the limbs and restrained [the breath] with the rodha-mudrā,
one should [visualize] the Puruṣa arising from gold and so forth, [and then] another Puruṣa.
The connection of the *caitanya* (consciousness) with the temple will now be explained.
At the completion of the *śūla-nāsā*, from the center of the eastern altar (*pūrva-vedī*), [the following is to be done]. (1)
One should place Ānanda in the Śakti-padmam with the Praṇava;
[the vessel] should be one of the full [vessels], purified, and combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A jar filled with honey and milk, in which the five substances beginning with gems have been placed, smeared with fragrance, covered with cloth, and perfumed with incense and flowers; || 3 ||

One whose body has been consecrated through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa should take up with inhalation (pūraka) the heart-lotus, which is enriched by a face like a mango sprout, and place it within the heart.
Then the Guru, possessing self-knowledge, [taught] the Self as non-different from the Universal Self, the wind of one's own nature, the single banner of Śambhu, and the Sthāṇu. || 5 ||
Then, having purified it as before with the five products of the cow, decoctions, and so forth,
one should place it upon the bed and meditate upon Rudra at the conclusion.
And with the Śiva-mantra, one should perform the placement [of the deity] upon that [liṅga] as its pervasive presence;
furthermore, for the purpose of bringing about the presence [of the deity], one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), touching (sparśana), and recitation (japa).
Having performed the complete ascent and descent through the three divisions in their respective parts,
up to the limit of Prakṛti, one should place them within the Kumbha.
The Cūlikā, the Dhvajadaṇḍa, and likewise the Dhvajadevakṛta;
thereafter the Pratiṣṭhā has been indicated, and it is now described here.
Alternatively, [the installation] occurs after half of Brahmā’s body has entered [the image], or after the entire half has entered;
in the case of an image made of flour-paste (paiṣṭika), a wooden pin (śūla) is used, while in a temple made of stone, a stone pin is used.
It should be fashioned according to the measurement of the *liṅga*, or according to the prescribed measurement for the *kumbha*.
And that [image] should be joined with a trident; by means of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one pacifies the afflictions caused by the planets. (16)
The Lord is declared to be the trident (śūla), while that which encircles the trident is the handle (veṣṭaka).
A staff (daṇḍa) is considered to be [measured] by five, nine, or even eight cubits. || 17 ||
Joined with a citron fruit according to the sequence stated by the path, the variegated and radiant mass that arises from half the height of the two shanks [is the pedestal]. || 18 ||
Or if the staff is being measured, the door may be [determined] by chance;
the encasement of the pedestal is with white [pigments]. || 19 ||

That [sound] should be understood by the wise according to the sequence beginning with the best (uttama) and so forth—whether it be born from the letter *ra*, born from the *vaṃśa* (the *vaṃśī* flute), or else beloved by Sundarī. (20)
Therefore, the rite should be auspicious, for it shall grant all desires.
Yet, if this [image], while being installed, should cry out or move, (21)
Or, if there should be fear arising from a conflict with one who is being born, or from one who knows the door [of the enemy],
then a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed as before, or it may be done with the Bahurūpa mantra.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers and other deities, as well as the libation for their mantras,
one should establish the ritual image and the staff with the Astra-mantra.
Having thus consecrated the banner with that [mantra] and especially with [other rites],
one should perform the installation of the temple using water mixed with clay, astringents, and so forth.
Having smeared and covered it, the Guru should place it upon the bed as before;
likewise, he should perform the installation of the crest-jewel (cūlikā) like that of the Liṅga, as well as the rites of wisdom-worship (vijñānārcā).
Due to the distinction [of the levels], it extends up to the fourth, yet there is no conceptualization of a "staff" (daṇḍa).
Thus, one should know the staff, the reality of the self (ātmatattva), and beyond that, the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva). || 26 ||
The mantra-practitioner should also worship Laṃcā in her presence with the Saṃhitā mantras;
and whatever appears upon the banner, that pedestal [should be worshipped] with those respective mantras.
Whatever modification of substances has been performed, all of that has been demonstrated through the ritual procedure for the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga). || 28 ||
In the palace, which is adorned with pillars and so forth, above the *jaṅghā* (the plinth) is the triple principle (*tritatva*). || 29 ||
Having meditated upon Śiva as consisting of all reality and as all-pervading, one should place him;
then one should meditate upon Ananta and Kālarudra with their lotus feet.
Accompanied by the Kūṣmāṇḍas and Jaṭakas, together with the inhabitants of Pātāla and the Tārakas, and surrounded by the worlds, the world-protectors, the hundred Rudras, and others. (31)
Having meditated on it as being of the nature of Brahman, one should contemplate it in the shank, endowed with the five elements: water, fire, air, and ether.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) up to the limit of the eight wombs (yoni), which is associated with the notion of all obscurations, endowed with the eight wombs, and possesses the three qualities (guṇas).
One should sequentially place the Puruṣa-mantra in the pitcher (kumbha),
the Lion-mantra (siṃha) in the lion-seat, and the four additional Vidyās upon the Mañjarī-altar.
In the *kuṇḍa* is Māyā together with Rudra; in the *vāmalasāraka* is Vidyā;
in its *kalaśeśvara* image is Vidyeśvara immediately following.
One should place the crescent moon shining upon his matted locks, the wielder of the trident, as well as Will, Knowledge, and Action, and the primordial Sound (nāda) within the staff. (36)
On the banner, one should contemplate the radiant abode as possessing earrings;
having joined it to the lower part of the abode, just as [one joins] the pedestal with the linga.
As before, having completed and prepared all the mantras according to the prescribed rite,
[one should proceed] with the chanting of the Vedas, the sounding of musical instruments, and auspicious Vedic songs.
Having raised the entire Śiva-trident and the banner by means of their respective mantras, one who assumes the form of the Guru should install them upon the lotus of Śakti.
Upon the base, one should place a jeweled pedestal and fix the banner there;
when the banner is fixed, the patron, together with friends and kinsmen, [should perform the rite]. (40)
Having performed the circumambulation of the village, he attains his desired fruit;
meditating on Guru Paśupati, who is steadfast and joined by the lords of the weapons. (41)
One should restrain the presiding deities and those joined with weapons for the sake of protection;
and for the sake of pacifying defects such as deficiency or excess, one should perform oblations and give the fruit thereof. (42)
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor for the removal of defects in the sacrifice;
[the fee should be equal in value] to as many atoms as there are in the images, the liṅgas, and the altars.
The fruit enjoyed by the maker for thousands of yugas is multiplied ten million times by the merit gained from hoisting the banner upon a temple.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for hoisting the banner in the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is inconceivable.
Otherwise, the master of the mantra will certainly not attain truth; this is the certainty.
On the fourteenth day of Āṣāḍha and so forth, or then on the fourteenth days of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada. || 1 ||
It should be performed on the white and black fortnights, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days;
during these three months, [the results are] excellent, middling, and inferior respectively.
A single purifier must be made; otherwise, it causes harm.
For the sake of Hari’s own three-month sleep in the Ocean of Milk, [this is ordained]. (3)
One should indeed perform the Pavitraka rite in sequence starting from the month of Āṣāḍha;
one should know that it is of three kinds, and this [present] is the supreme occasional (naimittika) rite.
Because it must be performed every day, and especially because it serves as a cause [for purification],
this rite is clearly known by the name "the occasional purifier" (naimittika-pavitraka).

But for the daily worship of the eternal [deity], one should prepare the *pavitra* with leaves, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth, every single day, even at times other than [the specific ritual occasions].
In Vahni, Brahmā, Gaurī, Vighna, Nāga, and Guha;
likewise in Arka, Śūlinī, Tārā, Caṇḍikā, and Yama.
Beginning on the first lunar day (pratipad) and continuing in sequence for five hundred [days] among Indra, Viṣṇu, Kāma, Mahādeva, and the Pitṛs; || 8 ||
In the Kṛta and subsequent ages, the sacred thread (pavitraka) is made respectively of gold, silver, and copper; and in the Kali age, it is made from cotton thread.
One who has performed the rites for a twice-born girl or others should make it threefold;
one should prepare an auspicious thread that has been washed, dried, and spun from fibers.
Silk, lotus-fiber, bark, linen, darbha-grass, hemp, and that which is produced from muñja grass— these types of thread are suitable for use in that purificatory rite (pavitraka). (11)

One should have the sacred thread (pavitraka) made from threads equal in number to the sun (twelve), the moon (one), fire (three), the unborn (four), the serpent (eight), Skanda (six), Sādākhya (five), and Viśvatman (ten).
One purificatory thread (pavitraka) should consist of one hundred and eight strands;
likewise, there may be three, half of that [number], twenty, or seven.
It should be made with eighty-one, thirty-eight, or five hundred knots, each having an equal interval between them. || 14 ||
They should indeed measure twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths [in height];
or else, they should be measured according to the width of the liṅga, [starting] with four finger-breadths.
Having worshipped that [liṅga], one should perform the fourth rite, the touching of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā-sparśa*), which pertains to all the principles (*sarvatātvika*);
one should also perform the descent of the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgāvatāraka*), provided with small bells (*kiṃkiṇī*).
The purification of the thread is performed with the Ajāta [mantra], and it is well-colored by the Guhyaka; one should worship the purification with the Aghora mantra and the Vaktra mantra. 17.
One should color the sacred thread with yellow sandalwood, camphor, musk, saffron, as well as turmeric, red ochre, and royal indigo.
One should likewise place ten knots, or according to the number of threads,
with an interval between them of one, two, or four finger-breadths, as it appears most beautiful.
Pauruṣaprakṛti is Vīrā, and Rājatā is the fourth;
Jāyā is another, Vijayā is the sixth, and Ajitā is Sadāśivā.
p.
1034) Thereafter, the tenth [knot], Manonmanī, which faces all directions, is proclaimed;
or, according to what is beautiful, additional auspicious knots should be made. || 21 ||

The preceptor should cause the purificatory rite (pavitra) to be performed according to the appropriate method for [liṅgas made of] stone, metal, a sacrificial mound on the ground, or those born of gems.
The thread of Ravicaṇḍeśa and of the fires shall be like that of Śiva;
the Guru should cause the purificatory rite (pavitra) for these deities to be performed.
One should install [the deities] in the book, in one's own image, in the Guru, in Īśa, and in Gaṇeśvara; and in each of the doors, the guardians of the directions, the water-jars, and so forth.
The purifier (pavitra) should measure up to nine cubits, starting from one cubit and so on in sequence;
it should have twenty-eight knots, with ten knots for each [cubit].
The intermediate spaces, beginning with two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*) and increasing by one finger-breadth in succession,
as well as their respective names, are joined with the width of the knots. (26)
On the thirteenth day of the seventh lunar fortnight, having performed the daily rites and being pure,
he should adorn the sacrificial hall with red silken cloths and flowers.
One should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) and especially the libation (tarpaṇa);
there, on a consecrated plot of ground, one should worship [the deity].

The Lord, having offered the *arghya* with the *praṇava* and having consecrated his body through the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite, should sprinkle the doors with the *astra-mantra* and worship them in order, starting from the east.
Oṃ, obeisance to the door of the Śāntikalā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Nivṛttikalā.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Pratiṣṭhākalā. || 30 ||
One should worship the *kalās* in the directions in order, from the east to the north;
likewise, one should worship two on each of the door-frames in their proper sequence. (31)
And Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, and Vināyaka;
the protective thread, the loincloth, the alms-bowl, and the staff;
the comb, saffron, oil, collyrium, and likewise a mirror. (33)
One should also place betel, yellow pigment (rocanā), a seat, sandals, a vessel, an elephant-hide rug, and a parasol in the northern direction.

One should offer [the oblation] in the northeast with the Īśa mantra for the satisfaction of Īśāna; and in the east, one should offer caru mixed with clarified butter, along with perfumes and other items ending with "sāntam," O Nara.
When all [the materials] have been prepared, one should mentally visualize them; then, having taken up the purifying substances, they should be sprinkled with the water of the *arghya* offering. (36)
Having covered it with a black antelope skin and other materials, he should meditate upon the year as his own self.
And [he meditated upon] Śiva, the immutable protector and witness of all actions,
by means of the application of "svā" and "heti," and again by means of the collection of mantras.
Indeed, there are twenty-one purifiers for those [who have fallen];
they take refuge in the sacrifice, dharma, the station of the bull, the temple, and fire. (39)
One should encircle the multitude of instruments with the thread and the armor;
then, having offered scented purifiers to the worshipped Sun, [one should proceed].
Having sipped water for purification and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
one should offer the prepared water for honor (*arghya*) and the sacred fragrance and purifier (*pavitra*) to the gatekeepers, beginning with Nandin.
Having entered, one should then offer the purifiers to Ka, Tvaṣṭṛ, Āditya, and Brahmā,
as well as to the Śāstras and the World-Protectors, each by their own names.
One should offer the Śiva-pitcher and other vessels into the Vardhanī for Lambodara;
having worshipped according to the rules, [one should worship] the lotus-feet of the Lord of the Śikhā.
One should worship it with perfumes and flowers after placing it upon a sacred thread (*pavitraka*),
which is smeared with fifty medicinal herbs and free from human hair.
When joined with flowers, dūrvā grass, and the like, and especially when perfumed with incense,
it is endowed with one-pointedness and results in the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life.

Having consecrated the thread with the *mātrā* mantra and placed it within his joined palms, the preceptor should perform the sacrifice according to the rules, even if he is not himself a reciter of mantras. Thus it is said: "For even one who does not recite [mantras] shall attain success. (46)

Oṃ! For the sake of filling every deficiency according to the prescribed rule regarding this sacrifice, may you, having measured the triad of powers as your own essence, act as the agent of the pervasion of your will.
O Lord of the ignorant, even for one who is truly wise, these [faults] surely exist;
O Śambhu, may there be salutation to You in every way and at all times—be gracious to me. 48.
O Lord of Gods, you have been invited together with the Goddess, the lords of the Gaṇas, the guardians of the three worlds, and your retinue, accompanied by mantras. (49)
"I announce to you that at dawn I shall offer the sacred thread (pavitraka),
and by your command, O Supreme Lord, I shall observe the religious vow."
Having thus addressed the disciple who has been initiated by means of the exhalation (*recaka*),
one should utter the root mantra up to the end of Śiva and offer that to Śiva. (51)
One should satisfy the Supreme Lord with recitations and hymns according to the prescribed measures;
then, having offered the third portion of the sacrificial porridge (caru) into the fire, one offers it to the Śiva-fire.
Then, [one offers] with "svāhā" to the lords of the directions, the groups of Mothers, the Rudras, and the Kṣetrapālas residing in the eastern and other directions. || 53 ||
Then, according to the distinction of their names and so forth, the Guru should offer an outer bali in all directions; thereafter, he should offer the bali to Vāyu and the bali to the Kṣetrapāla.
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the oblation that fills the gaps;
having offered the final oblation and the Vyāhṛtis, one should extinguish the fire.
Therein: Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Soma!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! || 56 ||
O Nandikeśvara, having first worshipped the Goddess upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should subsequently perform the oblations in the fire with these four offerings.
O Nandikeśvara, one should join [the breath] by means of the procedure for the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*),
having purified it with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and [then] with the Śiva-mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nandin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākāla. || 59 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Goddess. || 60 ||
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa. Having thus worshipped them in sequence, one should install the door-keepers and the others. || 61 ||
Having entered here at the eastern gate, one should worship Nandikeśvara;
[one should perform] the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the special arghya offering, the use of uśīra root, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and so forth.
As before, one should perform the withdrawal of the limbs with the *aham-mantra* according to the rule,
using flowers, unbroken grains, *dūrvā* grass, sandalwood paste, and the like, as well as clay and other materials.
Having indeed performed the Śivahasta rite, one should place it upon one's own head, while first understanding the knowledge that "I am Śiva" in all respects. (64)
The supreme Guru should first establish the knowledge and then perform the visualization;
having reached the southern quarter (rākṣasī kāṣṭhā), he should cast [the oblation] during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).

One should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) below, and the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇṭapa) all around; then, one should thoroughly purify the four [directions] with the final consecrations, such as the marking of characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and so forth. || 66 ||
The king and others should scatter materials; there should be a bundle of kuśa grass and kusa roots. One should also prepare a vardhanī vessel for the purpose of a seat right here.
One should worship the deity of the site (Vāstudeva) in the southwest and Lakṣmī at the door;
the water-pot, placed upon all kinds of grain, should face eastward or another direction.
Then, having worshipped Śiva mounted upon a bull with the Praṇava and Pārvatī seated upon a lion with the Śiva-mantras, one should worship the Vardhanī vessel with the mantra.
One should worship Indra and the others, beginning with Aja, as well as the ten guardians of the directions;
and likewise, one should properly worship the water-pot (kumbha), the cow, and the vardhanī vessel.
The Guru, having proclaimed the command of Śiva, from the eastern direction up to the northeast,
should recite the root mantra while pouring an unbroken stream of water. (71)
One should wave this *vardhanī* vessel, which has the form of gold, for the sake of protection;
having first placed the water-pot (*ghaṭa*), one places the *vardhanī* at its side.
One should collect [the substances] in the jar and worship the deity on a firm seat;
then, the Tārā vessel is placed upon the Vardhanī, and the seat is likewise for both.
One should perform the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* by means of the *liṅgamudrā*;
having placed the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) into the vessel, one should then recite the root mantra (*mūlāṇu*).
One should request protection with a tenth part of that [offering] in the Vardhanī vessel;
furthermore, one should worship the four-armed Lambodara in the southwest (nairṛtya). || 75 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should place the Guru, who is equipped with weapons, radiant like a ruby, and the supreme destroyer of obstacles, in the northeastern quarter.
Having worshipped the preceptor, who bestows all knowledge, as if he were Śiva himself,
one should subsequently install him according to the rules with scented water and likewise with pure water.
Thereafter, one should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite along with the gatekeepers;
then, preceded by the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should fully worship the Śiva-fire.
One should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) as prescribed by the rules, purified by the oblation of the residual drops (saṃpātāhuti).
One should divide it threefold with the ladle according to the distinction between the deity, the fire, and the self.
Having offered two portions into the fire of Śiva, he should set aside one for his own sake,
and he should offer the previously mentioned tooth-stick made from a milky tree.
With the Kavaca mantra and the Nara mantra, the tooth-stick (dantadhāvana) should be offered in the east;
with the Rūpin mantra, the ashes (bhasma) should be given in the south, or else with the Śikhā mantra.
One should place clay, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and fragrant substances [in the center];
one should place flowers in the northeast (*īśāna*) and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) in the southeastern direction (*āgneyī*).
For a Rākṣasa [birth], agarwood; for a Māruta [birth], the four spices (cāturjāta);
and for a Sadyojāta [birth], all the materials for the oblation together with kuśa grass.
A rosary, a loincloth, an alms-bowl, a staff, a comb, saffron, oil, collyrium, and likewise a mirror. (84)
One should also place betel-leaf and yellow pigment in the northern direction;
as well as a seat, sandals, a vessel, an elephant-hide rug, and a parasol. (85)

One should offer [oblations] in the northeast with the Īśa mantra for the satisfaction of Īśāna; and one should first present the sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with clarified butter, along with food, fragrance, and other offerings, O man, in the east.
When all [the vessels] have been prepared, one should mentally visualize that [deity];
then, taking up the purificatory materials which have been sprinkled with the water of the *arghya* offering, [one should proceed].
Having brought forth from the fire the mantras purified by the Saṃhitā,
and having covered [the vessel] with a black antelope skin and other materials, he should remember that which consists of the year.
Furthermore, one should worship Śiva, the imperishable witness and protector of all actions,
by means of the application of "svāhā" and "vaṣaṭ," and again with the collection of mantras.
Having indeed purified and cleansed the sacrificial ground, the site for the bull, and the temple situated near the fire, twenty-one times over.
One should encircle the multitude of ritual implements with the thread and the armor; then, having offered perfume and the sacred thread to the worshiped Sun, [one should proceed]. (91)

Having sipped water for purification and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should prostrate to Kṛtārthaka and offer fragrant purifiers (gandhapavitra) to the gatekeepers, beginning with Nandin.

Then, having entered, he should offer the purificatory oblations (pavitrāṇi) to Ka, Stunā, and the others, as well as to Brahmā, the various scriptures, and the world-protectors (lokapālas), using their respective names.
One should place the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha) and other vessels in the vardhanī vessel for Lambodara;
and having worshipped Vighnarāja and the lotus-feet of the Preceptor (deśika).
One should worship with perfumes and flowers, and having offered food upon the sacred thread (*pavitraka*),
which is smeared with fifty medicinal herbs and free from measures of weight or volume.
(1049) When combined with flowers, dūrvā grass, and the like, and especially when fumigated,
[the thread] adorned with a single knot and a short cord brings about the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. (96)
Having prepared a thread consecrated with mantras and placed it between his cupped palms, the preceptor should likewise perform the sacrifice while reciting this very mantra.
Oṃ! Regarding this sacrifice for the purpose of filling all deficiencies according to the prescribed rules, I invoke you;
your will brings about pervasion. 98.
O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious, grant success to that [work] which has been born;
O Śambhu, salutations to you in every way and at all times—be gracious! 99.
O Lord of Gods! You have been invited by Sahadevī and the lords of the Gaṇas, together with the protectors of the three worlds and their retinues, through these mantras. || 100 ||
(1050) "I announce to you, O Supreme Lord, that at dawn I shall perform the purification rite; by your command, I shall observe the fivefold restraint. (101)
Having thus consecrated it with the *recaka* breath while reciting "Amantra evam," one should utter the root mantra up to the end of Śiva and offer it to Śiva. (102)
One should satisfy the Supreme Lord with recitations, hymns of praise, and prostrations;
having offered a third portion of the sacrificial porridge (caru) into the fire, one should thereafter lead the remainder to Śiva.
"To those dwelling in the directions beginning with the East—to the lords of the directions, the host of Mothers, Rudra, and the Kṣetrapālas—svāhā! || 104 ||

Then, one should offer an external oblation to these [deities] in all directions according to the distinctions of the Sāman and other [Vedic branches]; furthermore, perform the oblation for Vāyu and the oblation for the Kṣetrapāla.
Having sipped water according to the rules, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) that fills the gaps;
having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the vyāhṛtis, one should extinguish the fire with arundhatī.
Therein: Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Soma;
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 107 ||
"Kṛte svāhā.
O Nandikeśvara, one should likewise perform [this] with four oblations.

O Nandikeśvara, having worshipped the deity upon that sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should thereafter unite [the soul] with the fire according to the rite of joining the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna).
One should perform the purification with the Astra-mantra; place the bracelet on a pure vessel, and one should fasten the sacred threads (pavitra) with the mantra known as Hṛdaya.
p.

1052) With a concentrated mind, one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the rules, using the six-limbed kalā-mantras or the Brahmā-aṅgas, and especially with the limb-mantras (aṅga-mantras). || 111 ||
Endowed with devotion, one should bow to Śiva and worship him for the sake of protection;
having then worshipped him according to the prescribed rite with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
O Nandikeśvara! Having worshipped the Siddhānta scripture according to the prescribed rite, one should go with devotion to the presence of the Guru and offer him the pavitraka.

Having gone outside and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-stick upon three circles made of cow dung.
Having sipped water according to the prescribed rite, the Guru, having established the presence [of the deity] through music,
should, desiring liberation, remember the Lord with His own mantra while seated upon a bed of darbha grass.
One who desires liberation should likewise enter [the fire] in this very manner;
however, he should do so while lying on a bed of ashes, fasting, and with a concentrated mind. (116)

This is the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the purifier; herein the procedure is fully set forth: having risen in the morning and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one who has completed the morning rites with a concentrated mind [should proceed].

Having performed the twilight rituals (saṃdhyā), the mantra-practitioner, having taken up the purificatory items (pavitra) and before the deities have been dismissed, should enter the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
Having placed [the deity] in a pure vessel within a mandala constructed in the northeast,
one should dismiss the deity and remove the floral remains (nirmālya) outside of it.
Having performed the daily rites as before upon the auspicious ground,
[one should worship] in the Śiva-pitcher, the Vardhanī vessel, and in the deities of the door, the guardians of the directions, and the fire.
O Ānandikeśvara! Having first worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the extensive worship endowed with the occasional (naimittika) ritual procedure. (121)
One should perform the libation for the Manus with the *śiroṇu* mantra as an expiation;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should then again offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having offered the *pavitra* of Arka and sipped water according to the rule,
[he should offer it] to the gatekeepers and so forth, and to the pitchers and *vardhanikā* vessels of the guardians of the directions.
Then, having sat down within the teaching of Śambhu's presence,
one should offer the *pavitra* for oneself to the Gaṇa in the lotus of the Guru.
Then, taking a purifying blade of grass (pavitraka) and facing the jar, while recollecting the Lord who consists of the [sixteen] digits (kalās), one should address Śaṅkara as follows: || 125 ||
O Lord, whatever was desired by you in your aspect as *kalā* within my ritual procedure—
whatever was performed with difficulty, what was prescribed, what was maintained, what was concealed, and whatever else was done; || 126 ||
Let it be afflicted or unafflicted, well-nourished or disregarded;
O Śambhu, let the all-pervading Self be bound by Your thread through the wind, by Your will. (127)
Oṃ, fulfill, fulfill the sacrifice for Niyameśvara, svāhā!
[This is] within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), ending with Prakṛti, protected by the Lotus-born One. || 128 ||
Having recited the root mantra from beginning to end, one should worship Śiva with the purifying thread;
likewise at the conclusion of the Vidyā-tattva, when the Viṣṇu-cause is protected.
Having recited up to the end of Īśvara, one should place the sacred thread;
then, at the end of Śiva, in the Śivatattva protected by Rudra as the cause.
Having recited the root mantra up to the end of Śiva, one should place the sacred thread upon the child, who is firm in his vows, amidst all causes and all principles. (131)
One should bestow the descent of the Gaṅgā from the root [mantra] and the *layā*;
it is the purifier for those seeking liberation, pertaining respectively to the knowledge of the Self and Śiva. (132)
And for those seeking worldly enjoyment, one should sequentially utter these mantras—consisting of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman—as proclaimed by them, ending either with "svāhā" or with "namaḥ. || 133 ||
The preceptor of all the gods should again perform the purification with:
"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva). || 134 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva). || 135 ||
In this manner, the wise one should gradually have a purifying thread (*pavitra*) prepared for the deity:
*oṃ hāṃ, to Śiva, the lord of all principles, svāhā*. (136)
With this very mantra, one should perform the descent of the Gaṅgā;
with devotion, one should present both hands full of flowers to the Guru.
You are the stability of all the gods, and you abide as both the moving and the unmoving; having seen the end of all beings through your power, you are therefore the Supreme Lord.
In deed, thought, or speech, there is no other refuge for me but you.
Whatever has been done by me that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in conduct—[may it be forgiven]. (139)
O Maheśvara! Previously, my daily ritual service to you was deficient in recitation, fire-offerings, and worship; it was performed poorly and lacked proper execution. (140)
O Lord of the Gods, that well-purified one is holy and the destroyer of sins;
by you, the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, has been purified. (141)
O Goddess! Whatever portion has been broken by me through the occurrence of negligence—may all of that become unified, strung together by the thread for the sake of those who know reality. (142)
Having recited [the mantra] and offered [oblations] to the God with devotion, and having presented the hymn of praise,
one should bow down with a wholehearted mind and contemplate Śiva as being well-pleased.
Four, three, two, or even one; or for half a month, or for seven days, five nights, three days, or even a single day. || 144 ||
Having received the instruction from the teachers and likewise undertaken the observance,
he bowed to and asked forgiveness of the Lord, then went toward the edge of the sacrificial pit.

1059) Thus, having worshipped the four sets of purifiers (pavitra) with flowers, incense, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, he remained standing even while [the thread] was fixed upon Śiva. || 146 ||
One should offer the inner oblation (antarbali) and the purifier (pavitra) to Rudra and the other deities;
having praised Śiva and entered within, one should bow to him and ask for his forgiveness. || 147 ||
Having performed the expiatory fire-sacrifice (prāyaścitta-homa) and having offered milk-rice (pāyasa),
he should slowly offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and worship Śiva, who is established as the father within his own self.
Or one may perform the oblation with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, drawing forth the vital breath from the center with the *niṣṭhurā* mantra;
then, indeed, having offered four oblations to the *suditi*s.
Then, having offered the external bali-oblation and the purifier (pavitra) to the guardians of the directions,
he should then properly place the purifier upon the book of the Siddhānta.
Oṃ hāṃ bhūḥ svāhā; oṃ hāṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā;
oṃ hāṃ suvaḥ svāhā; oṃ hāṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā. || 151 ||
The best of preceptors should offer oblations with the four *vyāhṛtis*:
"Oṃ hāṃ to Agni, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ to Soma, svāhā! (152)
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma; Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations in this sequence. || 153 ||
Having worshipped the teacher like Śiva with mudrās, ornaments, and garments,
Śaṅkara is immediately pleased when the teacher returns to them.
The Guru alone is the supreme deity; the Guru alone is the supreme goal.
O Nandikeśvara! There exists nothing other than the propitiation of the Guru. 155.
Then one should place the purifying thread upon the guru, who is to be held at the heart;
immediately thereafter, one should feed all those beginning with the half-vessel and the chest-offering.
One should devoutly honor them with garments, ornaments, beds, and so forth, saying:
"May Sadāśiva, who is worthy of gifts from the Lord of Gods, be pleased with me. (157)
Having performed acts such as giving charity, one should bring the purifying substances for the Lord;
one should worship him with eight flowers and, with devotion, bid him farewell.
One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites extensively according to the prescribed rule;
having placed the sacred threads upon [the deity] and having prostrated, one should worship Śiva in the fire.
Then, having offered the expiatory oblation with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One who desires liberation for Śiva should perform the dedication of the rite.
By your grace, may this rite of mine be effective in bringing about its fruit;
O Lord, may this rite be for me a bond that leads to worldly enjoyment. (161)
Through the yoga of the station of fire and other stations, may Śiva unite me with Śiva;
having placed [the fire] purified by mantra within the heart, one should then release the fire once more.

Having entered within and fully absorbed [the deity], one should join the mantras residing in the *kumbha* with Śiva while maintaining a sense of dependence, and then dismiss them, saying, "Forgive me."
Then, having dismissed the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), one should cause that purifier (pavitraka) to be given;
and if one performs the worship of Caṇḍa, one should do so after offering the purifier.
One should offer the floral remains (nirmālya) and other such items, along with the purifier (pavitra), to him;
or one should worship Caṇḍeśa on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or on a pedestal (pīṭha), as previously described.
Whatever ritual act pertaining to the *vāpī* has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive,
may it become complete for me through the command of the fourfold Śiva. (166)
Having informed Caṇḍeśa thus, one should dismiss Nandin with salutations;
or else, one should cast that offering (nirmālya) into a well or into water.
Having thus worshipped Caṇḍeśa, one should smear the ground with cow dung;
having purified oneself and become clean of body, one should bathe Śiva and proceed there.
Within five yojanas from the presence of the Guru lies the sacred ground;
by performing [the rite] according to this procedure, one obtains the desired fruit. || 169 ||
"O Nandikeśvara, the pavitra must be performed in this manner according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, the Pavitravidhi, within the Acintyaviśvasādākhya [Tantra].
In ancient times, from the wrath of Īśa, Bhairava known as Damana was born;
by him all the Asuras and the exceedingly powerful Dānavas were produced. (1)
Then, having been brought down to the surface of the earth by the gracious Śiva,
she will surely attain me for the sake of enjoyment.
Those men who shall worship [the deity] with sprouts and other offerings will go to the supreme abode through the grace of Damana.
Furthermore, for those young men who will not cause [the festival] to be performed,
I have bestowed the fruit of that merit upon them during the month of Caitra.
Having gone to the presence of the *damanaka* plant on the seventh and thirteenth lunar days,
and having purified it with the *astra-mantra*, one should worship it with the *saṃhitā-mantras*.
The knower of mantras should satisfy that gift with the [following] words: "O Blessed One, you have been recognized through the grace of Īśa; be present for my sake. (6)
"You must be led away for the sake of Śiva’s work by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed Damana and protected him, he should depart from that place.
Having specially brought the clay situated in front along with fine earth,
one should then place it in a vessel filled with that fine earth and worship it.
One should again perform the invitation (āmantraṇa) according to the previously mentioned rule;
indeed, at the time of evening, one should perform the adhi-vāsana.
Having brought the sacrificial garments and performed their ablutions and other rites, the women worshipped the Sun, Śaṅkara, and Agni according to the prescribed rule.
To the western side of the deity, its root [mantra] is declared;
O Lord, having then taken that [root] from the heart with the Sadyojāta mantra, || 11 ||
With the left head, or likewise with the stalk, the nurse [should place] the vessel of ashes on the north;
and with the right [head], or with the crest, the vessel of ashes [is placed] on the south.
With the hide of an eastern animal, he should perform the cleansing of teeth with flowers;
using the root of a Bilva tree with sandalwood paste, he should do so in the northeast while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with joined palms (añjali) containing flowers, a garland, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
one should address the Lord of Gods regarding the ascent of the *damanaka* plant.
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, you were invited by me this morning;
whatever is to be done according to our capacity shall all be performed at your command. (15)
Having thus informed [the deity], one should offer a handful of flowers (kusumāñjali) upon the head of the Lord;
then, having joined [the hands in prayer], one should perform the recitation (japa), especially with the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 16 ||
Having placed the special substance into the vessel, one should perform the rite with the second [mantra] and envelop it with the Kavaca [mantra] according to the procedure for the Pavitraka.
Having thus made it well-protected, he should offer it to Śiva;
or else, the preceptor, remaining without food, should consume the sacrificial oblation (havis). 18.
Having awakened before the Lord with prayers and songs,
and having bathed in the morning, one should offer the eight flowers to the Lord of the World.
One should perform the regular and occasional worship, especially with particular devotion;
one should worship the God even with *damanaka* flowers, even if they are broken, using the five limbs [of the ritual].
Having taken the remainder in his joined palms, together with *dūrvā* grass, perfumes, and unbroken rice grains,
[he should offer it] to Sadāśiva, who resembles pure crystal and has five faces. (21)
Having meditated thus with [the deity] facing him, one should perform worship, O Nandikeśvara!
[One should worship] with the principles (tattvas) of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva, beginning from the root and ending with Īśvara.
One should properly worship the Lord of Devas according to the path described for purification:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātma-tattva. (23)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva). || 24 ||
Having thus offered a handful of flowers according to the rite, the knower of mantras then [recites]:
"Oṃ hauṃ! To Māheśvara, the wielder of the trident, who fulfills the sacrifice, obeisance! (25)
Having prostrated and worshipped Śiva and the Fire according to the prescribed rules,
one who possesses such knowledge should with devotion address the Lord, the bestower of the fruits of desired objects. (26)
O Blessed One, whatever I have done that is either excessive or deficient, may all of it become complete; may everything be conducive to the rite of subduing.
Having thus performed the rite for the sacred abode, one should perform the worship of the Guru;
then, for the sake of satisfaction, one should especially honor the Brāhmaṇas and others.
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one observes a restrictive vow according to the rule, then worship performed in the month of Caitra shall become fruitless. (29)
The Lord became exceedingly pleased because of Damana's propitiation.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, concerning the ritual procedure for *damanaka* flowers, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
1070) Now I shall explain specifically the extraction of a worn-out *liṅga*;
for a *liṅga* that has become the abode of worldly existence would continue to exist [as such] unless it is extracted from its decayed state. (1)
And to the north was a dilapidated linga, distinguished by its great power of merit;
it had a worn-out shaft, was not firmly rooted, and was devoid of auspicious marks.

One that is devoid of its pedestal, or is marred by flaws such as cracks and the like, or is enclosed within a casing, or has a defective linga, or is situated between the banks of two rivers; || 3 ||
Having abandoned such a linga as is defiled by these and other defects, as well as one that is afflicted, a bull, a ram, or likewise one that is moving, the wise man [should proceed].
Whether it be low, high, uneven, or if one is confused about the directions, having thus understood this procedure, if one attains Nirvāṇa... || 5 ||
If [the image] is carried away by the current of a river or the like,
it should especially be reinstalled there by means of the ritual acts prescribed in the injunctions. (6)
One should not move a Śiva-liṅga, whether it be well-established or poorly established;
however, one should protect with a thousandfold effort a liṅga that was installed by a peaceful person.
That which is joined with Pūrṇa and others, yet [suffers] from decay and so forth,
or that which is devoid of worship— its very foundation is unstable.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "by a hundred [coins] for installation" and so forth is as follows: if, through delusion, the installed *liṅga* should sink into a depression or the like, [the following applies]. || 9 ||
Then, by performing a fire sacrifice of a thousand oblations and more, he protected his intended goal; he abandoned the application of the stone and attained Nirvāṇa characterized by those marks.
The practitioner of mantras should thus fix the mantra firmly upon the northern [direction] for the purpose of its installation;
by means of this ritual, whatever has been moved shall result in the attainment of the previously mentioned fruits.
One should construct a pavilion endowed with the proper characteristics at both the Īśa and Yama points;
the worship of the door-arches and the worship of the doors and so forth should be performed as previously described.
Having worshipped the Lord of the sacrificial ground (Sthāṇḍileśa) with mantras preceded by libations,
and having worshipped the deity of the site (Vāstudeva), one should offer the oblation to the guardians of the directions.
The preceptor, having sipped water for purification, should feed the brahmins who are like the liṅgas;
afterwards, he should re-install the deity, [saying], "O Lord, this liṅga was defective."
O Maheśvara! With the desire that there might be peace through its extraction, it was empowered by means of the ritual for the weapon (astra-vidhāna). || 15 ||
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should perform the pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*):
honey, clarified butter, milk, and *dūrvā* grass, [offered] one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. (16)
Then, having worshipped the Liṅga, one should likewise worship the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila);
the worship of Śiva concludes with the mantra "Oṃ Vyāpakeśvarāya. (17)
Oṃ, obeisance to the heart of Vyāpakeśvara. Oṃ, obeisance to the head of Vyāpakeśvara. || 18 ||
Oṃ, to Vyāpakeśvara, for the crest-lock, Vaṣaṭ! Oṃ, to Vyāpakeśvara, for the armor, Huṃ! || 19 ||
Oṃ, to Vyāpakeśvara, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ, to Vyāpakeśvara, to the weapon, phaṭ! || 20 ||
Having thus properly worshipped Śaṅkara with the five-limbed mantra,
the Guru should cause the being residing within the *tantra* to hear the *astra-mantra*.
The Satvaka remains by resorting to a *liṅga*;
having abandoned the *liṅga*, he goes wherever he desires by the commands of Śiva. || 22 ||
Where Śambhu will be present together with the Vidyās and the lords of the Vidyās (Vidyeśvaras),
one should offer a thousand oblations with the Pāśupata-weapon mantra.
One should release each part specifically with pure water;
afterwards, one should wipe it with *kāśa* grass and especially give a gift.
Then, immediately thereafter, one should worship this fruit, as well as the presiding deity of that reality (tattva), and especially the forms, the lords of the forms, the lingas, and the pedestals.
Having released [the beast] with a golden noose, you, whose shoulders are like those of a bull,
then took up the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) while uttering "May there be auspiciousness for Śiva" along with the people.
The practitioner of mantras should cast that [mixture] into water; for the sake of nourishment, he should perform a hundred oblations.
He should perform the libation to the guardians of the directions one hundred times each, for the purification of the site (vāstu).
Having performed protection for that abode by means of the Mahāpāśupata weapon,
the Guru should duly install the Liṅga there, consisting of those [subtle] elements alone.
Established by Brahmins, sages, and gods who know the truth, one should not move it even if it is decayed or broken. (29)
In this manner, the ritual procedure must be performed for the restoration of a dilapidated temple;
one should cause another temple to be built using the collection of sword-mantras (*khaḍgamantra*).
When there is contraction, death is proclaimed; when there is expansion, however, there is loss of wealth.
That object, or that excellent object, or that task shall be of that same measure. (31)
The extraction of those [impurities] filled with undigested matter is prescribed according to the rule;
otherwise, that would be useless, so one should perform it according to the rule.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, concerning the procedure for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple], in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
I shall describe the consecration of a monastery; listen, O Nandikeśvara!
The preceptor should cause a pavilion, a mandala, and a sacrificial pit to be prepared as previously described.
Established as a manifest form for the sake of favoring the worlds, one should construct monasteries and other such structures in either the northern quarter or one of the others. || 2 ||
A *maṭha* is considered to be a dwelling place for all visiting and resident ascetics,
provided with food and drink, or even consisting of a single building alone. (3)
The pedestal (pīṭha) is desired to be joined with two ear-threads alone;
those which are the feet of the previously mentioned Vāstu are thus proclaimed.
This is the rule for monasteries and the like, as well as for villages and similar places;
whether by night or by day, it applies to houses, temples, and so forth.
In a temple or in a village and such places, the Śiva-brahmin is distinguished;
however, in one's own home, the Anuśaiva, Mahā, Antara, and Śailaka [are preferred].

There, the twice-born one, who is Śiva himself, should have a sacrificial mound prepared with eight petals and a pericarp; upon his shoulder, he should carry the Śiva-pitcher covered with a pair of cloths.
One should place the *tattva* in the temple; having placed the *dhārikā-śakti*,
one should place the *ātma-tattva* in the lower portion, extending as far as Brahmā.
One should place the *sadya*-tattva in the center, following the position of the *buddhi*-tattva;
above that shall be the *śiva*-tattva, ending with *śuddhavidyā*.
Having performed the placement of the three instruments, one should perform the placement of Śiva along with his limbs (the mantras).
Then, one should perform the invocation of the principles (tattvas), purification, sprinkling, touching, and recitation.
Proximity, obstruction, worship, union, and the realization of reality—
thus, in every case, the ritual procedure performed according to rule shall attain its prior state.
Having secured an auspicious moment, one should respectfully install the flagstaff;
thereafter, one should establish the temple with fruits and other auspicious items.
p.

1079) When [the site] is covered with wood, grass, and so forth, the placement of mantras (nyāsa) is described here. Having established the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), one should smear it with cow dung. || 13 ||
Both externally and internally, it should be beautifully adorned with flowers and perfumes; one should especially provide banners, archways, and the like there.
Together with many friends, the performer of the rite, who honors his guru,
shall act as the patron (yajamāna) at an auspicious moment, having bathed and performed the auspicious ceremonies.
The wise one should place the fourfold desire on the altar facing north;
furthermore, there should be gifts for the Brahmins and especially for the astrologer.
Then one should give to the artisan according to the extent of one's wealth;
one should worship the pitchers previously placed in the two-cubit pavilion for the site (vāstu).

*Ja* is for movement and the footstool; *jaṅghā* (the shank) and *kapotaka* (the ankle) likewise; and according to their respective divisions, one should assign the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti. (18)

Having worshipped them with the heart-mantra, one should also worship the Śaktis and the guardians of the directions, preceded by meditation, using their respective names while performing the ritual expansion (vyāpaka).
Having reached the fire-chamber, one should satisfy the deities of the site (vāstudevatās),
as well as the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti and the guardians of the gates, with their respective mantras.
Having offered the oblation to the quarters (digbali) and sipped water for purification (ācamana), his body consecrated by the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
[he should worship] with sweet mangoes, wood-apples, and citron fruits.
Having established [the deity] with jujube, *āmalaka*, eggplant, cucumber, *likuca*, and other fruits,
one should bathe it with water from the pitcher and move the pavilion above.

For the sake of manifesting power, for the sake of a stable cause, for the increase of the continuum and so forth, and for the sake of fame, one should proclaim the name, preceded by the names of the author and the person [being honored]. (23)
The best of teachers should indeed construct one well-known monastery;
O Nandikeśvara, the consecration of the monastery should be performed in this manner.
I shall now describe the consecration of a lotus pond; listen briefly.
Having worshipped the deity of the site (vāstudeva), especially within a square [enclosure], || 25 ||
The female-footed goddesses, conquered by Rudra, are to be worshipped in the corners in sequence,
beginning from the directions of Īśāna, Pitṛ, and Vāyu, respectively.
Parjanya and the others are established one by one in each step in their respective order;
the waters are situated within the cavity of the *karaka* vessel, followed by the twelve Marīcis.
In the central region of a grid consisting of twenty-five squares, one should worship Brahmā;
during the consecration, one should worship Vāstu in an auspicious pavilion in the western direction.
Having taken possession of the center of the site, one should begin according to the prescribed rule;
one should worship it with its name, joined with the Tāraka-mantra and the limbs of the Mūrti.
On an eight-petaled white lotus, one should indeed worship Kālāgni in the center;
one should approach Hāṭakeśa, Bali, and Śāntibalinātha.
One should worship Mahābdhi, Kalaśāmbhodhi, and Virūpākṣa;
then, following the sequence of the eastern petals, one should worship Bhrūkuṭī in the northeast; this concludes the final pavilion.

Then, with minute particles [of colored powder], one should worship those beginning with Ananta and ending with Kārkoṭaka in the pit; outside the sacrificial pavilion, however, one should worship those headed by Carakī.
One should take the lords of the worlds and others, as well as eight silver serpents; therein [are] Ananta, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, and likewise Gulika. (33)
One should place the eight [serpents]— Śaṅkha, Vāsuki, Padma, and Kārkoṭa—
and having performed worship, one should then place them in order starting from the east.
Having likewise scattered six medicinal herbs and serpents all around,
he also placed the Matsyākṣī, the Sabhā, and the one called Sṛṣṭi there.
One should cast a tortoise, the five jewels, the fivefold water of mercury and fragrances, the water for the arghya offering, and the five products of the cow into the lotus pond.
Twice the length of the mouth, with the middle part reduced by one-quarter or increased by one-quarter:
*Huṃ Āṃ, homage to Ananta Nāga, the lord of serpents.* || 37 ||
Having established [the object] with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra, one should also perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) with the *astra* mantra.
Then, having removed it from the razor-sharp blade, one should cast it into the water held in the left hand.
Taking up a silver noose and mounting the back of a tawny cow, the preceptor should recite the Pāśupata mantra while crossing over the sacrificers in that [river]. || 39 ||
There, by means of the [mantra] ending with *saṃtaraṇa*, he crossed the Vaitaraṇī river;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, especially to Rūpiṇī. (40)
O Nandikeśvara, having gratified Pracetas according to the prescribed rite, one should offer the oblation to the Lord of Gods known as Vāmadeva. || 41 ||
There, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the caru using the Śiva-mantra.
This cow should be given by the Guru along with garments, ornaments, and other such items.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, concerning the ritual for the lotus pond in the monastery of the Inconceivable Viśvasāda.
O Nandikeśvara! Regarding the subject of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), it will be explained therein:
having worshipped the deity of the site (vāstudeva) together with the mandalas. || 1 ||
Īśa, Agnitṛka, Putra, Roga, Marut, and Dvibha—
these are the leaders of two and a half squares each, located in the corners starting from Īśa and ending at Īśāna.
O Nandikeśvara! The [names] beginning with Parjanya and ending with Sapaḍika are as before;
or rather, specifically, those beginning with Āpāda consist of two words. || 3 ||
The portions of light, such as Marīci and others, and Brahmā from his thirty-six parts,
as well as Carakī and others, and Skanda and others, are to be worshipped outside like the principal deities.

Or, immediately after that, one should worship the deities beginning with Pūrvaka and Rudra in sequence within the lotus of one's own nature, using mantras prescribed for independent rites as traditionally remembered.
In the western quarter of the well, one should worship [the deity] within a pavilion,
surrounded by eight silver serpents, according to the procedure previously described.
Having eaten and offered the bali-oblation, the Guru should then cast jewels and other items into the well; thereafter, for the sake of pacification, he should sprinkle the patron with water.
The performer should satisfy the preceptor with cows, gold, garments, and other such gifts;
thereafter, he should provide food and other necessities to those in need according to his capacity.
For all excavations as well, expiation should be performed just as for a well;
the throwing [of earth] and the filling [of the pit] are approved to be done with both the left and the right hand.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of Wells and Other Structures," in the *Viśvasādākhya* [Tantra], which is inconceivable.
Now, I shall explain specifically the consecration of trees.
Being fully concentrated, one should offer oblations with ghee and sesame seeds in the proper manner. || 1 ||
In the case of a grove or a garden, one should perform the bathing, worship, and ritual placement (nyāsa) of the grapevines in a pavilion constructed in the eastern direction,
using their respective seed-mantras.
The Guru should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the pleasure of the presiding deity of the tree.
(Thus, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*, the seventy-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for the consecration of a tree.
Now, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), and the spiritual son (*putraka*).
The ritual for these [deceased persons] ending with death is called the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi). || 1 ||
The funeral rite performed by those devoid of the purification of reality is called the *antyeṣṭi* (last rites).
Here, even a mind adorned with fresh bamboo and other materials is made beautiful. (2)
One should place the corpse upon a heap of sand for Śaṅkara, which is adorned with flower garlands and provided with steps leading to heaven. Then, one should cause it to be ascended.

One should maintain the weapon-mantra with those who have undergone initiation (dīkṣita), who are of the same caste, who wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), who possess firm shoulders, and who are engaged in the recitation (japa).
When the fire has been purified with parched grain, one should specifically cause [the body] to descend before the spirits,
having positioned the head of the deceased toward the south.
One should construct that peaked temple (kūṭa) measuring four cubits,
provided with a porch (prapā), endowed with all ornaments, and beautifully adorned with all kinds of garlands.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule as a single square mandala;
in the northwest, there should be an altar (sthaṇḍila) made of that same clay, six finger-breadths in height.
The fire-pit known as Citā, which has four corners, should be situated to the south;
it is endowed with an expansive shape and is eight finger-breadths less [in height].
Having smeared the triad of sacrificial pits and other areas with cow-dung and water,
the Guru, having bathed and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), holds weapons and other implements in his hands.
Having performed a circumambulation of that sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) facing north,
he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), protected by the weapon-mantra (hetimantra).
Remaining silent and having performed the internal sacrifice, he [poured] that water— which increases the power of the mantras, the ancestors, and the weapons—
into a field consisting of twenty-five squares.
Adorned with five colors— white, yellow, red, black, and bright white— respectively, the elements beginning with earth are decorated according to their true forms. (12)
When afflictions such as lineage-fever (vaṃśajvara) have arisen, one should install the deity of the site (vāstudeva);
and one should install Brahmā in the central square among the five squares.
In the southwest, one should place Niśrāddha; in the four squares of Viṣṇu’s enclosure, and likewise in the four squares of the southeast corner, one should place Rudra together with Jvalana.
In the wind-corner of the four-square grid, one should worship Anīśvara together with Vāyu;
likewise, in the fourth square of that same grid, in the northeast, one should worship Sadāśiva together with Gaganā.
One should worship the four [deities] beginning with Makara in the individual squares of the eastern and other directions;
one should offer the bali-oblation with their respective names, ending with "namaḥ" and "svāhā."
"Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site.
Having thus placed [the mantra] upon the ground, one should worship Brahmā according to the prescribed rite. || 17 ||
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. O Nandikeśvara, having thus worshipped Govinda within the water, [one should proceed]. 18.
One should worship the Fire with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra," and one should likewise worship Īśa in the northwest wind with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. || 19 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to Sadāśiva. With the mantras beginning with "Sadāśiva" and so forth, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel in the northeast corner within the space.
One should indeed worship the mantra known as Pāśupata correctly in this manner;
the Guru should then contemplate eight jars and place them all around.

One should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, along with their armies in the eight directions; and having offered the pedestal of sovereignty and so forth, one should place [the deity] in the center of the lotus upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should worship the wheel of powers (śakticakra) beginning with Manonmanī and ending with Vāmā;
then, having scattered sesame seeds, ashes, and so forth, one should worship the Lord (Īśa) together with his limbs (sāṅga).
Having cast [the materials] into the southern fire-pit (kuṇḍa), he should generate the fire as before;
having worshipped Īśa and offered oblations into the fire, he should perform the final oblation of the preceding [rite].
Then, having consecrated another [vessel] with the Astra-mantra, one should bury it in the corners in a clockwise direction, starting from the southeast,
and encircle it with a red thread.
Having filled the funeral pyre with fuel—consisting of dry wood, twigs, and branches, with roots turned upward and tips downward—along with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and sesame seeds; || 26 ||
One should worship [the vessel] with the King of Weapons mantra while it is covered by an inverted jar;
having bathed the deceased with clay, cow dung, and water, and having dusted him, one should bring him [there]. (27)
One should give garments and the sacred thread as before, without regard for those [previous offerings].
Then, here, once it has been purified by concentration (dhāraṇā) and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth— || 28 ||
Having seized the life-force by means of the Mahājāla-prayoga, one should deposit it [therein]:
Oṃ huṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ huṃ, obeisance to the self of so-and-so. || 29 ||
One should place the Vidyā-deha upon the head of that body, and the Kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā on the face, the heart, the navel, and the lower part of the body respectively.
Having deposited the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), the wheel of power (śakticakra), and likewise Śiva,
one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the presence of consciousness.
Having undertaken the rites of withdrawal and so forth, either simultaneously or in sequence,
one should worship in the fire, perform the union, and carry out the invocation of Śiva and the other deities. (32)
Having performed the separation of the seat and the extraction of the individual soul (jīva),
one should perform everything there— including the [realization of] the self as Śiva— just as in the case of initiation.
The enjoyment of authority over the tantras, dissolution, the purified stream, liberation, concealment, and the release of the fettered soul from his bonds. || 34 ||
The kneading [of the clay] is circular in shape; likewise, there is the rite of offering oblations with the feet, the invocation of the causal deity, and the surrender of authority. || 35 ||

Having performed the rites for the dissolution of the self in that which is devoid of qualities, one should unite it with the imperishable consciousness in Śiva, who is brought forth through meditation.
Having placed the corpse on the sacrificial ground with its head toward the south in the fire,
and having raised it onto the funeral pyre, one should provide it with excellent fuel.
Thereafter, one should ignite the funeral pyre with the fire located within the sacrificial pit;
when the region of the head has blazed up, one should again offer oblations while facing north.
And you, O Nandikeśvara, should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire;
at that time, you shall be the Dakṣiṇāgni of the fire, and thus a hundred oblations will have been offered by you in due course.
Take this Śāvyā creeper, consecrated with mantras by the great-souled ones;
having offered it with this very mantra, bring about the fulfillment [of the rite].
One should then cast the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, with their openings facing downwards, into the blazing fire;
one should then place the *vardhanī* vessel, consecrated with the weapon-mantra, upon the left shoulder.
Having established [the deity] there, one should then proceed clockwise toward the western door;
releasing [the thread], one should cast it back into that very place from which it was originally lifted.
Having gone to the bank of a river, one should look back [at the village];
then, having bathed, spread out the ritual offerings, and performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), [one should proceed]. || 43 ||
Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become Īśa; svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become Sadāśiva; svāhā! || 44 ||
"Oṃ hāṃ, O pure-souled one, be peaceful, svāhā!
With these mantras, one should perform the libation for the ancestors with a concentrated mind. (45)
Having bathed, the preceptor should perform one hundred recitations with the Aghora mantra;
the donors of the shoulder-bearer [the palanquin] should perform double that number, after which they shall go to the refuge of Yama.
Having worshipped the deity there, specifically with that [deceased] in mind,
one should perform the collection of the funeral pyre on either the first or the third day. (47)
Taking a water-pot filled with milk or else filled with water,
and having placed it there, one should offer three pieces of wood upon the funeral pyre.
O Nandikeśvara, one should gradually, starting from the feet and ending at the head, render it motionless and place it silently according to the prescribed rite.
Therefore, O Nandikeśvara, having taken a portion from that place and having dug it out according to the prescribed rite, one should deposit it in a watery region of rivers and install it there.
Now, in this case, an untimely death (durmaraṇa) and cremation are prescribed for one who dies without initiation and for one who dies even while possessed of Śiva-initiation. || 51 ||
Even while living, if one is bound by the curse of desire, the initiation of death (mṛtadīkṣā) is prescribed—
whether by means of weapons, wild animals, elephants, water, or the consumption of poison. (52)
By the falling of walls, trees, and the like; by being struck or pierced with the hands;
by snake bites; and by being bound with ropes and killed. || 53 ||
For these others who have died in such a manner—as well as for those whose bodies are no longer present and for those with mangled bodies—the funeral rites are performed as previously described. (54)

O Nandikeśvara! [This applies] upon death from consumption, leprosy, piśācas, and the like, as well as from the sight or even the death of those afflicted by epilepsy, planetary spirits, and so forth.
Then, one should fashion an image endowed with the proper characteristics, using either kuśa grass, wood, or sprouts from the palāśa tree, measuring thirty-six [aṅgulas].
One should prepare [the image] with flour, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and cow dung;
the ritual for it should be performed in due order according to the desired dimensions.
With the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, as well as with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *śiva* [mantra],
one should likewise sprinkle her with streams of clarified butter, honey, and milk.
Having established the image upon a seat of flowers on the southern side of one's own self, one should perform the ritual with buds from the *karavīra* plant.
One should arrange all the principles (tattvas) according to their respective positions;
or else, one may do so with cow dung or ashes placed upon the sky [the space].
Having cleansed it with the five products of the cow, the wise one should have an image fashioned;
having written the name made upon birch bark, he should place it in the heart.
Having visualized a well within the heart on its left and right sides, one should likewise contemplate the *śuddhā*, the *piṅgalā*, and the *suṣumnā* there. (62)
One should install Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī as the triad of Śaktis;
