one should also install both dharma and adharma, as well as all karmas.
Wherever it may be situated, by means of the Mahājālaka mantra—namely, *oṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ*—this [deity] is drawn forth with the left [hand]. || 64 ||
The triad of lotuses known as karma;
for the purpose of this propitiation and binding, one should perform oblations with their respective names. 65.
Having performed five oblations for each of the five [limbs], one should perform the ritual placement up to the head:
Paraśiva at the region of the head, Śakti and Bindu at the face.
One should know Maheśa, whose sound is below that [forehead], on the forehead;
Sadāśiva above the uvula; and one should place [the remaining deities] at the joints of the arms. (67)
The mandala of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) is on the left side;
one should place Māyā on the right side and the principle of Time (Kālatattva).
In the region above that is Kalā, and in the heart is Nīlalohita;
in that very place is Śuddhavidyā, and thus it is called Puṣpa.
One should place the principle of Prakṛti at the navel in due order,
and the subtle elements together with the three qualities (guṇas) in the region of the back.
The wise one should place the three Puruṣas in the navel and the private organ;
the Trika should be at the joints, the intellect (buddhi) should be there, and one should place the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) in the private organ.
One should likewise place Vyomavāgīśvarī and Vāyu within the space of the womb;
one should place Agni in the mind and Varuṇa there in the lower part.

In reality, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five groups of eight Rudras, who consist of the wind in the sky of the intellect and have the form of fire; therefore, [one should place them] below that.
Outside of that, one should indeed worship the hundred Rudras and the world-protectors (Lokapālas);
and at the ankles and at the beginning of the worlds, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
One should sequentially place the seven netherworlds (pātālas) below the ankle;
having placed all the hells within the Kula, one should place them upon the top of the big toe.

In this manner, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of Kālāgni in the respective locations from the crown of the head down to the tips of the thumbs, as well as the principles (tattvas) beginning with Paraśiva and ending with Kālāgni.
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the *kalā-dīkṣā*, one should,
by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [unify] the Self— which is the essence of Śiva— with the Supreme Śiva. (77)
Having offered a full oblation of everything complete, soaked in honey, milk, and ghee, he,
with a fulfilled mind, should offer into the fire.
Afterwards, one should burn that image as well according to the previously mentioned method,
O auspicious lady, under the Tripada asterisms and during the periods of Venus, Mars, and Jupiter.
In the event of a fire or death, there shall be the destruction of that family;
therefore, to eliminate the fault in that case, one should perform the cremation once again.
And for the ascetics who have renounced all ties, who are supreme sages (paramahaṃsas),
[the rites are performed] after first transferring the fires of the world into the fire of their own bellies.
And because of the absence of external fire-rituals, one should have [the image] laid down along with the characteristic marks;
even in the case of excavation, there should be no depression, and the length should be equal to the altar (veda). || 82 ||
The excavation below should be two cubits in width and four cubits deep;
one should perform all rites as before, except for the fire-ritual (agnikārya). || 83 ||
Because he was engaged in the rites of the Śiva-fire, he should burn [the body] along with the ascetics;
likewise, during the digging and burning, [he should do so] together with the staff and the loincloth.
In that place, one should also cause the installation of a *liṅga* or other [emblem], or else a statue of that [deity], or a pedestal, or even a mural painting on a wall. (85)
Or one should have a gabled temple built in that place;
the ritual, from the invocation up to the offering of bali, or ending with the lamps, should be performed as before.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, concerning the ritual for the final rites, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Now I shall describe the Śiva-śrāddha, which is indeed called the Ekoddiṣṭa. When the day at the end of the period of impurity has arrived, the Ekoddiṣṭa is prescribed. (1)
Immediately after the piling of the funeral fire, or on the tenth or eleventh day,
the supreme śrāddha must likewise be performed for those who died by weapons.
Worldly duties should be performed according to the requirements of one's own respective caste;
for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, purification occurs after ten days and twelve days respectively.
For Vaiśyas, purification occurs on the fifteenth day, while for Śūdras it is indeed after one month;
for all castes who have been initiated, the purification is like that of their fathers.

This Ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed every month until the anniversary of death; moreover, in the specific case of an Ekoddiṣṭa, there should be only one offering of water (arghya) and one sacred thread (pavitraka).
p. 1106) The ritual for the fire-offering (agnikārya) should be performed there during the rite of the śrāddha;
one should accomplish the śrāddha on all the lunar days (tithis) within the fortnights dedicated to the śrāddha.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śiveśa, and the one known as Susaṃjñaka,
along with Ekanetra and Ekarudra— these are the [deities] among the Trimūrtis in the elemental [creation].
By reversing the order starting from Trimūrti and the others, the triad beginning with Mātrā arises;
and by reversing the order starting from Śivottama up to Ananteśa, the triad beginning with Pitṛ arises respectively.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are declared to be the two Viśvedevas;
for householders there are six deities, but for those bearing the sectarian marks (liṅgins), there are three deities.
Those who bear the marks [of a religious order], such as Brāhmaṇas and others, who have been initiated into Śiva with faith—
if they are devoid of the Śiva-śrāddha— they attain the state of a Piśāca.
At the gate, in the heap of ashes, and likewise in the intermediate space,
he remains as a ghost for four constellations (one year). || 11 ||
Especially for those who are lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), they indeed become lifelong celibates;
for in the Śiva-śrāddha, the ascetics are Lord Sadāśiva himself, who is eternally peaceful and auspicious.
Rudra is named Anātata, and the two Viśvedevas are situated in the two [remaining] positions;
however, for those initiated into Nirvāṇa who possess portions of Rudra, it is otherwise than this.
In those [two], Nandi and Mahākāla are the Viśvedevas; in the two [others], they are the Gaṇas.
In the three [remaining], Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Gaṇādhīśa are the Gaṇas, respectively.
Thus, Vidhi, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, along with the Viśvedevas, Yama, and Aruṇa—although there is a fivefold state everywhere, it is said that there are two persons. || 15 ||
One should conceive of those three as one through the division of that head.
On the remaining festival days and on the eighth day, the ritual for the group of Mothers is prescribed.
On the previous day, one should invite [the guest] with sincere care and respect;
thereafter, on the following day, one should summon them, even in the evening.

In the bright fortnight, however, it should be performed in the forenoon; in the dark fortnight, in the afternoon. Having completed the daily rites and being pure in disposition, [one should proceed]. || 18 ||
On the wrist, one should first draw two square mandalas with four corners each,
situated from south to north, measuring exactly one handspan in length.
Likewise, one should worship Viśvedevas in a circular [area] in the west;
and the Pitṛdeva is situated to the south, facing the west.

One should offer barley with kuśa grass for the two classes of deities, and sesame seeds for the two classes of ancestors; there, one should arrange white flowers in sequence upon a square altar in the proper order. (21)
One should offer the arghya for two or three [deities] with barley together with sesame seeds;
for the sake of the specific occasion, one should cause it to be given with sesame seeds and water.
With mantras ending in *svāhā* or *svadhā*, accompanied by his own name and the syllable *oṃ*,
he should wash his feet with clay on the right side while reciting the *vāmadeva* mantra.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) with the word "saumya," and at the end of the word "svāhā," one should cause them to enter;
one should not seat them thus on seats purified by the left hand.
Having first sprinkled the two [deities] facing east with water for the guest-offering (arghya), and then the three facing north, he, being composed, should pray to them.
p.
1110) "Just as [one says], 'I shall perform the śrāddha here; do so,' in brief, with two [verses] ending in the syllable *jā*, one places kuśa grass on the two seats with the left hand. (26)
For all three, the procedure is always performed in this manner by circling counter-clockwise;
immediately thereafter, one should invoke all five according to their names.
Protection should be performed with sesame seeds in sequence using the two [mantras] beginning with *dvāme*.

For the purpose of invoking the presence (*sānnidhya*), the *arghya* offering should be made with water containing flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting the *aghora* mantra.

With two or three [offerings], one should offer them to the Lord while kneeling upon the ground; one should worship [the deity] from the feet to the head with barley grains, using the Bahurūpa mantra.
One should worship [the deity] starting from the head with sesame seeds and restraint;
and with the left hand, one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
Having given [the gift], one should say "May it be complete" regarding the purificatory rite (pavitra) and so forth;
any other limb of the śrāddha not explicitly mentioned should be consecrated with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). || 31 ||
Then, having made them the recipients [of the offerings], one who knows the ritual procedure should cause them to hear [the announcement];
without vacating the place of the ancestors, he should set down the vessel face-down below.
One who is endowed with devotion and firm in his vows should partake of refined food;
however, he must avoid kodrava, all types of salt, and likewise the fruits of the jambu tree.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, lābu, vārtāka, buffalo milk, the decoctions of bījapūraka, as well as marīca and pippalī—these [should be avoided]. (34)
Salt has been prepared, and all the finest of bamboo species have been avoided;
all red substances are to be shunned, with the sole exception of saffron.
Those resinous exudates that are reddish, visible salts, kulattha beans touched by the feet, anything dried, and anything that has been kept overnight— [these are forbidden]. (36)
Likewise, oil-cakes that have been soaked, as well as salt, and condiments with salt given by hand out of affection—[these are forbidden]. (37)

The donors do not receive the merit, and the consumer eats only the sin; likewise for a śrāddha performed without the thumb, or an oblation offered with the knees outside [the sacrificial ground]. (38)
Whatever is eaten with the knees extended outward is entirely demonic;
likewise, sipping water (ācamana) should specifically be done with the knees drawn inward. || 39 ||
O Nandikeśvara! Worship of Śiva should be performed in the north, the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the south, and the service of the fire must indeed be carried out in the middle.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), especially for rites intended for the ancestors, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, to Soma accompanied by the ancestors... || 41 ||
Having taken the best portion of all the cooked food and offered it into the fire during the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), [one recites]:
"Āṃ, svadhā and obeisance to Kavyavāhana... || 42 ||
With this [mantra], one should immediately offer three rice-balls (piṇḍas) into the fire;
at the [three] junctions [of the day], one should take up the food remaining from the oblation while reciting the Nara-mantra.
Likewise, for the sake of purification, a man should offer sweet food soaked in ghee into the fire while reciting the Aghora mantra, and he should also touch it.
Placing the left thumb upon the right one, not touching the ground,
one should rotate the left hand, which is the conqueror of death, all around while reciting the mantra.
One should place food upon the sprout-like hands using the *apāmārga* mantra;
those who eat while maintaining silence are designated as the *dhvaja*. (46)

The practitioner should remain reciting the mantra while facing the Lord; having worshipped those with similar countenances and those who have come as supplicants with devotion, he may move [the image] even at that very moment.
Having taken food and being satisfied, you should eat that food slowly from this [plate];
then one should cast that food upon the ground and offer water once for each [guest].
One should prepare a mandala with fresh cow dung near the leavings;
then, with the left hand, one should scatter sesame seeds over the arrangement.
Facing south, one should offer three balls of all the food mixed with sesame seeds,
circumambulating them with *darbha* grass while reciting the mantras beginning with Īśa in their proper sequence.
O Nandikeśvara! One should pour a stream of water with the Vāmadeva mantra, worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and prostrate oneself. || 51 ||
Having asked for forgiveness and withdrawn [the offerings], and having sipped water according to the rules,
one who knows the ritual procedure should first give the ācamana to the three [deities] and then give it to the two [others].
One should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and, with a joyful countenance, treat them as worthy recipients;
having circumambulated all of them and prostrated, one should dismiss them once more.
One should offer the middle piṇḍa from the rows for the sake of attaining the sons of Rudra;
or else, one may offer it to a Brāhmaṇa, or into water, or into fire, or likewise to a bull.
O Nandikeśvara, one should indeed offer three balls of rice and cast them [into the water], provided that the Śrāddha has been performed for those human ancestors, the Pitṛs, and the Daityas. (55)
The mantras following Śiva increase both lineages;
when the Śiva-śrāddha is performed, the gods and especially the ancestors [are gratified]. (56)
They cause both families to prosper; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Afterwards, one may perform the installation of a liṅga or the ancestral rite of installation.
Or one may create a mural painting; the consecration should be performed as before. One should have the temple, gate-towers, and so forth constructed there according to the previous [rules]. || 58 ||
In this way, it shall indeed be established by means of the five obstructions;
as for the specific rites of worship and so forth, they are as before, O Nandikeśvara! (59)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the Śiva-śrāddha within the Acintyaviśvasādākhya [Tantra].
Now I shall specifically describe the form of the determination of the castes (jāti):
the liṅga is indeed called the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), and the pedestal (pīṭhikā) is the power of illusion (māyāśakti).
And the two supreme among the Ātmans, bearing the forms known as Viṣṇu and Vedhas, [should be placed],
with Puruṣottama on the left and Brahmā on the right.
The state of the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva-pada) is indeed the cause of maintenance, and it is specifically for Viṣṇu that it serves as the cause of maintenance. || 3 ||
Indeed, through the sovereignty of the principle of the Self, the act of creation was performed for the sake of the unborn;
yet, by perceiving that Brahman as a mere sign, the moving and unmoving world resides within the belly.
Having first recollected the four [faces], he indeed brought forth the universe through the sequence of the mantras of Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, Īśa, and Sadyojāta.
The divine scriptures and the Vedas were born from the crown of the Liṅga.
At the first creation, however, there arose gods, humans, cattle, and birds. (6)
Reptiles, trees, creepers, shrubs, and so forth,
as well as many sages, are declared to be known by the name Brāhmaṇa.
The second were born as Kṣatriyas, the third as the Vaiśya castes, and the fourth were the Śūdras; thus the fourfold classes were produced.
In reality, there is no such thing as "birth"; it is merely a conceptual construction.
Those who were born first from the portion of the head, and secondly from the arms, [are the Brahmins]. (9)
Just as the third foot is seen as the thigh and the fourth as the foot, so too the form of creation is the form of Brahman; therefore, these castes are born from the limbs of Brahman.
One born from the mouth would be a Brāhmaṇa, likewise a Kṣatriya born from the arms;
one born from the thighs would be a Vaiśya, and from the feet, a Śūdra indeed. (11)
Out of respect for the protection of knowledge,
the Brahmin is joined with the Kṣatriya for the sake of protection and for the preservation of prosperity.
That which is proclaimed as the designation "Kṣatra" is for the increase of the sense of ownership (mamatva),
while the caste-designation "Vaiśya" arises from the pride of protecting wealth.
The sense of ownership regarding the production of grain is declared to belong to the Śūdra;
this applies specifically to Bhārata-varṣa among the nine divisions of the continent.
This distinction of genus is merely a conceptual construction; it does not exist in other places.
Therefore, the notion of a distinction of genus is nothing more than a mental fabrication. (15)
p.
1120) Here, the distinction of castes (*jāti*) is imagined through the sequence of high and low;
likewise, [the duties of] studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, and officiating at sacrifices [are imagined]. (16)
Giving and receiving—these are said to be their six duties;
moreover, they should always protect living beings from weapons and missiles.
The protection of the world, the suppression of the wicked, and the honoring of the virtuous—this is declared to be the duty of kings; yet, when envy arises in them, [it leads to ruin]. (18)

The livelihood of the Vaiśya caste consists of the sale of wealth, grain, and so forth; by means of that, he should increase his capital for the purpose of giving gifts from his accumulated riches. (19)
A Śūdra, however, should make his livelihood by producing grain and practicing agriculture;
in this way, through such distinctions, the livelihood of the world indeed comes to be.
The activity of those four does not proceed mutually; therefore, there is no differentiator for the increase and decrease [of the aeons]. (21)
O Nandikeśvara, listen to these favorable words concerning Dharma:
one born to a twice-born man from a maiden is called a *kānīna*. || 22 ||
A twice-born man should indeed perform his daily rites as brought forth by a Brahmin;
furthermore, rites for pacification and nourishment should be performed according to the path proclaimed in the Atharvaveda. (23)
By the king's command, he learned of the chariot, the elephant, and the horse as vehicles,
and having mastered Ayurveda and Atharvaveda from the mouth of his preceptor.

Having diagnosed the diseases of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, one should treat them; and one should appoint a commander of armies who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities. (25)
p. 1122) These five, born from the [five] families, would be the most excellent for initiation.
One born to a twice-born man from a Vaiśya maiden is known as an Ambaṣṭha. || 26 ||
Brought by a twice-born man, he was intent upon his ritual duties;
he would touch the bodies of the four classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, with his hand when they were afflicted by disease. || 27 ||
Thereafter, one should perform medical treatment through the application of substances of similar color;
furthermore, surgical procedures (śalyakriyā) should be carried out, as well as the extraction of pus (pītaka) and the removal of loose tissue (calana). || 28 ||
One born from a Brahmin father and a Śūdra mother is known as a Pāraśava;
he should worship Bhadrakālī according to the path prescribed in his family’s scriptures. || 29 ||
Painting, the arts, dancing, singing, and instrumental music; likewise, the profession of a masseur, and fortune-telling by hand-marks as well. (30)
Taking up the trident and the musical instruments of Rudra, accompanied by various types of stringed and percussion instruments, he should go from house to house and beg, saying, "Give! Give! (31).
One should always practice in this manner until the end of life.
A son born to a king from a Vaiśya maiden is called a Māhiṣa.
The office of royal treasurer, the occupation of a Vaiśya, guarding the king's inner apartments, and living by [the performance of] sacrifices; || 33 ||
Born from the king’s Śūdra wife, he was known as Ugra;
at that time, he caused the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras to perform service.
By the king's command, he should punish those deserving of punishment without hesitation.
One born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is known as a Kāravika. || 35 ||
p.
1124) His livelihood shall depend upon [the drafting of] royal edicts and letters;
he should worship Brahmā daily, especially within his own home. || 36 ||
Furthermore, one who makes a living by selling betel leaves, areca nuts, and the like;
these five are born from women of lower caste than the father and are known as *anuloma* (born in the natural order). || 37 ||
These [persons] are especially unfit for the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*) because they are born of a lineage connection; likewise, such individuals are mere fettered souls (*paśu*).

Because desire is characterized by misconduct and because conceptualization is fragmented, many types of beings— such as those born in reverse order (pratiloma) and others— arise from the various divisions of evil.
For a Brāhmaṇa born of a Brāhmaṇa woman, even if he is secretly [born], his status as a Vipra is established by authoritative proof; his [duty] consists merely in wearing the sacred thread.
Honey, *hiṅgu*, as well as cakes, water, oil, and rock salt; all types of seed-substances, *sarjarasa*, and *guggulu*. (41)
All fragrant substances [are forbidden], as well as black [grains] and other medicinal herbs and the like; [these constitute] living by means of buying and selling.

That very same [impurity], when united with the husband, is called a *kuṇḍa*; through separation from him, it becomes what is called a *golaka*. Thus, the mode of operation is indeed just as before. (43)
For kings and for the Brāhmaṇa alone, this [work] was born from the thief;
it is Jyotiṣa, Bhūtatantra, and Arthaniścaya. || 44 ||
O Nandikeśvara! Having mastered the eightfold Ayurveda as well as the characteristics of women from the ocean, he lived his entire life by that very knowledge.
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother through theft is known as a Vaikambhuka;
his occupations are working with earthenware, making images, painting, and whitewashing. (46)
One should perform the worship of Mohinī according to the injunctions of the Kula scriptures;
likewise, one should worship Śānta, Tāra, Daṇḍapāla, and Hemakeśī.
Whether during birth-impurity (sūtaka), death-impurity (pretaka), or likewise when initiated (upanīta),
the smearing [of ash] above the navel for them is declared to be devotion (bhakti).
Born from a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa through theft, he is called a Śūdraka;
his livelihood consists of capturing wild beasts, deer, and other animals in the forest. (49)
From a Vaiśya through theft, one begotten upon a Vaiśya woman becomes a Maṇikāraka;
he should engage in the sale of conch shells and the purchase of bracelets made of conch shells.
The Vaiśyakuṇḍa is the Maṇikāra (bead-maker), and the Golaka is the Śaṅkhakāraka (conch-shell worker). From the theft of a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman, the Kaṭakara is born. (51)
He should perform the worship of Viṣṇu, while his livelihood consists of working with mats;
he is known as a Mālavaka, born from a Śūdra through a Śūdra woman by means of theft. || 52 ||
One should cause the grass-bundle of those known as Syāla, Gaja, and others to be burned;
this indeed is the Śūdra-kuṇḍa, and the Golaka is said to be their livelihood.
He should perform service for the king and thereby sustain his livelihood day by day;
at that time, fourteen [castes] are declared according to the order of natural sequence (anuloma).
The potter Kulabandhi was equal to others in his initiation;
listen now, O Nandikeśvara, to how he subsequently acted in a contrary manner.
If a son is born according to the rule from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother among those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), he is honored and is known by the name Sūta. (56)
His livelihood consists of expounding the Purāṇas and other texts, as well as the Pāñcarātra;
and he should worship Janārdana according to the path prescribed in the Viṣṇu-tantras.
By the king's command, he should drive both the chariot and Bhava,
and he should cause the cooking to be done for the sake of the king's meal.
One born to a Vaiśya from a Brāhmaṇa maiden is called a Mātaṅga;
he must perform the recitation of all [the names] and especially offer salutations. (59)
One born to a Vaiśya from a Kṣatriya maiden is known as an Āyogava;
his livelihood shall consist of weaving cloth and the buying and selling of goods.
One born to a Śūdra from a king’s daughter is called a Puṣkala;
he deals in the purchase and sale of both Soma and liquor. (61)
One should play great instruments such as the mṛdaṅga accompanied by song.
A son born to a Śūdra from a Vaiśya maiden is called a Sthapati.
Likewise, the abode of the gods, the house of Brahmins and others, all objects made of jewels, and ornaments for the sick and so forth; || 63 ||
And there were models of all kinds of weapons and treatises from every quarter,
various vessels and the like, and the splendor of white-washed buildings.
The layout of the sites for the sacred ground, as well as the extraction of hidden defects—all that which constitutes their livelihood was performed according to the prescribed characteristics. (65)
(1130) These are declared to be in the inverse order; their intermixture is now described.
From a Brāhmaṇa and a Brāhmaṇī woman, [a son] is born in the same lineage (gotra). || 66 ||
He too is called a Caṇḍāla; now hear his conduct as well: furthermore, his residence shall be at a distance of one krośa from the village. (67)
One should take the characteristics of cranes, donkeys, and dogs;
having taken a cloth from a cremation ground, it shall serve as his covering.
One should eat from an earthen vessel and likewise wear ornaments of iron;
one's bed should consist of pieces of cow-hide or even the skin of a buffalo. (69)
In the forenoon he should enter the village, but in the afternoon he should not enter;
Gadādhara should perform the purification of the village during the foremost procession for the deceased.
During the festival of Bhadrakālī, as well as during village affairs, one may take up the musical instruments of the Caṇḍālas and thereafter partake of their food. (71)
A certain person born among worthy recipients (pātras) who has renounced worldly life after becoming a deceased Brahmin is called a Caṇḍāla; his conduct is as previously described.
One born to a Śūdra from a Brāhmaṇa woman is known as a Caṇḍāla;
his livelihood and mode of life shall be exactly like those of the aforementioned Caṇḍālas. || 73 ||
But from a Śūdra father and a Nṛpā mother was born one named Bailava; he is known as Spṛss, who, along with those of his own caste, is the player of musical instruments.
The livelihood of all these is said to be by looking after [cattle];
one born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is known as a Śvaki. || 75 ||

Producing oil and other substances by means of a press, and the sale of oil and oil-cakes; likewise, making a living through the sale of alkaline substances and salt—this is considered permissible. (76)
The confusion of those born in the inverse order has been described; indeed, they enter among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, causing further confusion.
Among them, O Brāhmaṇa,
when the word "sātyakarṇaka" is uttered, a son is born from a Brahmin woman by one who knows the rules of transgression.
That very [mantra], through its association with the Kṣatriya [tattva], is proclaimed as "Ādānta" at the beginning;
it effects the subjugation of enemies by means of mantras, tantras, ritual actions, and so forth. (79)
His livelihood has been declared; he is remembered as one who subsists on flowers.
Taking up medicinal herbs and mantras, he should practice the domestic rites (*gṛhya*). 80.
The son born of a Vaiśya woman by a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is known as a Vaikhānasa;
he should worship Viṣṇu constantly, and his livelihood consists of living by gleaning ears of grain. 81.
But one born from a Śūdra woman in this manner is known as a Takṣaka;
his livelihood is said to consist of the duties of a Kṣatriya alone. || 82 ||
Having insulted both the Kṣatriya and the Brāhmaṇa, he was called by the name Khalla;
O Keśava, he appeared in the form of a thief.
The livelihood of kings, however, consists of inciting others to action;
it was through that very [means] that a Kṣatriya born from Yoga became known as a Malla. (84)
Having learned of the conduct of another king, he should report it to his own king;
by this means, it is said, he shall obtain his livelihood, entering [the service] day after day. 85.
One should cause a maternity chamber to be constructed as well as protective charms;
then, one born of a Vaiśya woman is called Maitraka. (86)
Having entered into the Sogatas, one should worship the creator-deities;
likewise, one born from union with a Vṛṣalī is remembered as a Bhāgavata. (87)

Therefore, one whose livelihood consists of the worship of Viṣṇu is called *sāttvika*; he is declared to belong to the *prātyavarga* (the group of those who have returned). Now hear about the *saṃkara* (mixed) class resulting from intermixture.
It is recorded that Sumatika was born from a daughter of a Vipra, a thief, and a Ugra;
the livelihood of a king, however, is said to be the protection of elephants. 89.
One born to a twice-born man from an Ambaṣṭha maiden is known as a Svābhrika;
his livelihood shall consist of tending goats and buffaloes. (90)
Because he is born from the union of a twice-born man and a woman of low caste (ayogavī), he is indeed called a Yava;
he is said to be a performer of their work, and his livelihood is that of a boatman. (91)
A Brahmin born from union with a Bailava woman is called a Kukkuṭa;
he should perform the work of a weaver, and by that his livelihood is said to be sustained. (92)
Born from the union of a one-eyed woman and a horse, he was a maker of wooden images;
at festivals and sacrifices of the gods, he fashioned paintings and other works according to the prescribed rules. (93)
One should provide firm protection; by that, his livelihood is declared.
Born from the union of a Sthapati and an Ambaṣṭha, he is called a Vaiṇava.
One should practice the bamboo-like conduct; by that, one's livelihood is said to be [proper].
Because of its connection with the master-builder (sthapati), it is called "made of bamboo" (vaiṇava) and "up to the pinnacle" (āpiṇḍika). || 95 ||
He should especially inflict harm upon those men who are traitors to the king;
however, he must provide external protection for him, for that alone is his livelihood. (96)
Born from the union and separation of the Magadha and Yoga [elements], he was named Śauruṇḍa;
having performed the moistening according to the ritual procedure, he engaged in my buying and selling.
One may capture a tiger, deer, rabbit, or black antelope using nets and other such means;
by selling their meat, one's livelihood is said to be sustained. (98)
One born from the union of Puṣkara and Yogavī is called a Nāvika;
his livelihood shall be that of a boatman for as long as he lives. (99)
Born from the union of Sthapati and Yogā, he is known as Maitra;
he should strike the bell with a great sound early in the morning.
But for the sake of the awakening of Kṣatriyas, that life-force is said to be supreme. Furthermore, one born from an Ambaṣṭha father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is called a Nāvika. (101)
In the Vindhya region, the livelihood of the Turaṇḍaka and others shall be [the making of] boats;
one born from an Ambaṣṭha father and a Nṛpa mother is called a Nāvika (boatman). 102.
For those born in the natural order from the four castes, the shaving [of the head] should not take place below the navel.
One born to a Brahmin woman from a Mahiṣa is indeed called a Vaiṇava.
His livelihood shall indeed consist of bamboo-work, provided it is not associated with the sale of food;
furthermore, the dwelling, bedding, and other requirements for Brahmins and the rest, as well as for kings, [shall be provided]. 104.
By establishing a connection with the [proper] caste, one is released from that livelihood;
born of a Nṛpā woman by a Cūcuka, he is a Vaivatsya-bandhaka. || 105 ||
One born to a Vaidehaka woman from a Rajaka father is known as a Jāla; he catches fish with nets and fishing lines and sells them. (106)
The cleaning of clothes is declared as his livelihood;
born from an Āyogava father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, he is called a Tāmraka.
Having performed all transactions involving copper, including its purchase and sale, one who is born from a Nṛpā woman by a Yogaka is known as a Bandhaka. || 108 ||
Having been freed from the fault of clothing and having attained purity of livelihood, those who were formerly Vṛṣalīs are said to have become Kukkuṭas through me alone. 109.
Having performed the purification of the gate-towers (gopuras), he made his livelihood by means of them;
born to an Ambaṣṭha woman from a Videha man, he is called Baila.
Having purified the *paṭabha* and other such items by means of a fist-closure (*muṣṭi*),
one may perform the illusions of Indra’s net and so forth, and subsist by means of that. (111)
From the very application of that [practice], one is said to have attained the state of "tvagata" (beyond the skin);
in the forest, [one perceives] predatory beasts and the like, as well as various tubers and roots. (112)
One may live by selling all kinds of medicinal herbs. However, one born from a Caṇḍāla father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is called a Svapāka. || 113 ||
Having wrapped his ears with a piece of hide and dwelling in the cremation ground,
he enters the village in the forenoon and returns to his dwelling in the afternoon.
Then, having removed all impurities, the practitioner [should consume] the flesh of dogs;
having made footwear and the like from their hides, he should engage in their purchase and sale. (115)
From a Vaideha man and a Nṛpa woman is born the Sūtika;
he should sew clothes with a needle, making his living in that manner. (116)
From Puṣkara and a Brāhmaṇa woman was born one who subsists on water;
he then diligently collects all lost articles. || 117 ||
The Gurulka, the Aśvapa, the Aśva, the Mleccha, the Panaka, and so forth—O Nandikeśvara, this is declared to be the classification of castes in their respective order. (118)
The sons of the Vrātyas are ten; then the Mādhavas are for the initiation (dīkṣā).
Of the excellent ones, the middling are five each according to the Adhimāna. 119.
Furthermore, ten types of the lowest of the low have been specifically mentioned,
as well as those thirty-four mortals who are related to the Kula.
The Guru should exclude from initiation those who are characterized by base conduct, those engaged in cruel deeds, and those whose livelihood is lowly. (121)
Even those of birth unfit for initiation and the like, whose bodies are marked with the triple-tilaka by means of ash according to the ritual manual, and who wear rudrākṣa beads; || 122 ||

Those who are without mantras should themselves, afterwards, always perform prostrations and other such acts from afar with devotion toward others endowed with devotion to Śiva and toward the wearer of the liṅga.

Having first established a temple for Śiva and so forth according to the requirements of one's own respective caste, one should perform [the rites] as is appropriate; by that, one shall attain heaven.
But having been born on the earth hereafter, they shall attain liberation through initiation;
especially so for one who has been initiated according to the rules, who bears the *liṅga*, and who is a lifelong celibate ascetic (*naiṣṭhika*).
"O Nandikeśvara! For that [individual], there is no such connection to birth;
especially for one who is material, this is due to conformity with worldly custom. (126)
"However, one must speak according to one's previous birth; such is the definitive conclusion of the Śāstra.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, the Rule for Determining Birth, within the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
"O Nandikeśvara, listen! I shall now declare the rule for the origin of the elements (*bhūta*)."
The manifestation of the mother is that which distinguishes the species within its various divisions. || 1 ||
The egg-born, the sweat-born, the womb-born, and the sprout-born—thus the fourfold division of birth has been declared; now hear from me the classification of castes. || 2 ||

(1143) Those that have arisen by breaking through the earth are called *udbhidaḥ*, such as stationary beings (*sthāvara*) and the like; grasses, shrubs, creepers, and so forth are also proclaimed to be *udbhidaḥ*. || 3 ||
Those born from moisture arise from things that are being moistened; such as bugs, bedbugs, and the like, as well as ants and other similar creatures—these are proclaimed to be moisture-born. (4)
Birds, serpents, monitor lizards, fish, tortoises, crocodiles, and grāhas—all these are proclaimed to be egg-born (aṇḍaja). || 5 ||
The viviparous and the domestic originate from the gross in succession;
and the viviparous indeed become the root from which medicinal herbs are produced in abundance.
But when the time was ripe, the earth, moistened and endowed with warmth,
being stirred by the wind, attained the state of living beings in the sky.
Just as seasonal seeds, having been sown, again reach the stage of swelling, becoming moist and tender, and gradually attain the state of a root portion. (8)
From that root comes the production of the sprout;
from the sprout, the sheath; from that, the leaf-stalk; from the leaf-stalk, the stem; and from the stem, the flowering again.
From the flower comes the perfection of milk; from the milk comes the preparation of rice;
and from the cooking of the rice, various kinds of medicinal herbs emerge.

Then, the annual plants (ayavādya) are proclaimed to end with the seventeen types of hemp (śaṇa), as well as the various species of medicinal herbs (oṣadhijāti) which terminate with those that perish upon the ripening of their fruit. || 11 ||
The essence of herbs is proclaimed to be sixfold:
that which is to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, drunk, and smeared.
In sweet mangoes, there is saltiness, bitterness, pungency, and astringency. || 13 ||
Thus, through the combination of the six flavors, people consume food;
having reached the stomach (āmāśaya), it is sequentially established as the vital breath (prāṇa) and the other [vital airs]. || 14 ||
Furthermore, the food becomes burnt, especially by the wind;
the portion of the food and the portion of water are consumed by the powerful fire. (15)
Then, by means of the water of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), the fire is gradually [kindled];
by that fire the water is heated, and by it the food is also digested. (16)
The separate portion and the separate insect shall again become twofold;
the dross proceeds through the twelvefold path from the limb of fire.
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, penis, anus, nails,
the receptacles of impurities, phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine are known as the twelve [openings]. (18)
All the channels connected to the heart-lotus on every side,
along with the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu), should deposit subtle essence at the openings of the channels.
By that very tongue, the channel is filled from the front;
in the midst of the channels is the essence of phlegm, whose body is the vital breath (prāṇa). || 20 ||
As they are being cooked, there occurs again a twofold ripening;
from the essence (rasa) arise the skin and blood, and from the blood arises the flesh.
Flesh, fat, sinews, bone, and finally marrow are produced in succession;
thereafter, semen also arises, which becomes threefold. (22)
The semen of food is white, and from that white [semen] arises the body;
this is especially so for the offspring of Prajāpati during the period of the menses. (23)

The semen, free from defects, originating from the womb and mixed with the woman's blood, together with the soul residing within the sour food and joined with the instruments of perception [the senses], [enters the womb]. || 24 ||
It enters the womb out of its own volition, through its own past actions;
on the first day, it becomes mixed with that [blood] and reaches the stage called *kalā*. || 25 ||
From the *kalala*, after five nights, it attains the state of a *budbuda* (bubble); having become a *vimardaka* after seven nights, from the *budbuda* it proceeds to the stage of the *peśī*.
On the fourteenth day, the *peśī* becomes firm as blood and flesh;
thereafter, on the twenty-fifth day, the emergence of the sprout from the seed occurs.
Furthermore, at that time, from mere flesh alone, five things arise:
the head, the neck, the shoulder, the backbone, and likewise the lower part. (28)
Likewise, the hands, feet, sides, hips, and limbs are gradually formed; thus, the development of the body's parts occurs over the course of two months. (29)
Within one month alone, all the limbs, sprouts, and joints are produced;
and after four months, the fingers and the cavity of the abdomen are formed.
In the fifth month, the face, as well as the nose and ears, the private parts, and the rows of teeth are formed; however, the nails and hair do not yet appear.
Within just six months, the openings of the ears and other [senses] are formed,
as well as the anus, the penis, the generative organ, the navel, and the bones of the spinal column.
In the seventh month, the joints within the limbs are produced;
[the embryo] becomes complete with all its major and minor parts, endowed with a fully formed head. (33)
In the eighth month, he is born with clearly defined limbs;
when the ninth month has arrived, Vāruṇa is endowed with complete knowledge.
Furthermore, through the sixfold taste derived from the mother's food, it is constantly nourished and pervaded throughout the intermediate period. || 35 ||
One experiences pleasure and pain, sleeps while dreaming of past deeds, appears as if aged, and appears as if dead, undergoing birth after birth again and again. (36)

Whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, was performed for the sake of this life or another life, by that alone shall I burn here alone; those [deceased] have departed as enjoyers of the fruits. (37)
When I am fit, I shall take refuge in that Maheśvara,
the performer of the destruction of inauspiciousness, the supreme bestower of liberation. || 38 ||
While staying in the womb, being tormented again and again by webs of insects,
he thinks of whatever means by which dwelling in the womb might not occur.
In whatever manner it may be, there shall be the worship of Śiva, whether one is constantly contemplating while still in the womb or once one has emerged from it. (40)
Thus, distressed by such thoughts and oppressed by the suffering of the womb, the living being, following the bonds of karma, reflects upon liberation. (41)
Just as one pressed down by massive rocks remains there in agony at times,
so too does the living being remain enveloped by the great membrane of the womb.
Sunk in the ocean of saṃsāra, the person remains distressed and agitated; his limbs are obscured by the state of being in the womb and other such conditions. (43)
Just as someone might enter an iron vessel by means of fire,
so too the embryo within the womb is heated by the digestive fire.
Whatever suffering arises for one who is incessantly pierced by types of heated iron, may that [suffering] become a virtue within the wombs. (45)
There is no dwelling more painful than dwelling in the womb;
for embodied beings, this [womb] is a terrible fire, a great and abundant suffering. (46)
For the embryos of both mobile and immobile beings, according to their respective types,
there is suffering ten million times greater than that in the womb due to the crushing pressure of the vaginal canal.
With all his limbs thoroughly crushed, though afflicted by pain and filled with fear, he is squeezed on every side by the machine as if it were sesame seeds being pressed. (48)
For that very being as he emerges from the womb, great suffering indeed occurs due to the powerful winds of labor.
Just as sesame seeds and sugarcane, when crushed in a press,
are deprived of their essence, so too does he, having become essence-less, fall helplessly downward.
With bones for its rafters and beams, bound together by the machinery of tendons, plastered with the mud of blood and flesh, it is a vessel for the substances of feces and urine. (51)
Covered with hair, body-hair, and grass, it is the abode of diseases;
it has the mouth as its single great door and is adorned with eight windows. (52)
With its lower lip as its door-panel, closed by the tongue-bar,
with the flow of veins and sweat, and flooded with the lotus of phlegm. (53)
It is completely bound by afflictions, possessed by the fire of time, overcome by the fuel of desire and anger, and crushed by calamities. (54)
Afflicted by thirst for enjoyments, following the sway of hypocrisy, passion, and hatred,
he emerged through the birth canal, which is narrow and impure.
With its limbs drenched in feces, urine, and blood, it emerges from the womb;
indeed, the primary bones are three hundred and eight.
It measures one and a half crores and five hundred million yojanas, and is surrounded on all sides by seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs). || 57 ||
O Nandikeśvara, it is said that embodied beings possess two *prasthas* of fat. (58)
One should declare the enumeration of the urines and the excretions;
thus indeed, the body [is maintained] as the constant abode of the self. (59)
Even for one who is pure, [the body] appears defiled, being produced from the bondage of karma;
for the body arises from the union of semen and blood. (60)
Where can purity be found in a jar filled with excrement?
Even while being cleansed, this body remains certainly impure; this is the certainty. (61)
Upon quickly obtaining that which is heart-pleasing and fragrant, one becomes pure;
yet in an instant it returns to a state of impurity—what else could be more impure than this? (62)
For one whose streams constantly flow through the subtle openings of the channels with a foul odor, what else could be impure? (63)
Even toward such a body as this, smeared with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other unguents, no one feels revulsion. (64)
It does not abandon its own odor, like a dog's tail that cannot be bent;
even though it is constantly being cleansed, it never attains purity. (65)
Even while smelling a foul odor or seeing one's own excrement,
there exists nothing else in this world more effective than the body itself as a cause for detachment.
The entire world is indeed pure; it is only the body that is supremely impure.
Purity of disposition is true purity; this has been declared by me for the sake of purification.

If purification is performed while devoid of right intention (bhāva), that purity of intention alone bestows complete purification. One might be cleansed by the waters of the Gaṅgā and by mountain-like loads of clay from sacred fords (tīrtha). (68)

One who is devoid of purity of intention remains impure for a long time; even one who has bathed in thousands of pure holy places remains devoid of purity of intention if lacking such internal purity. (69)
Even by that, he would not become pure, just as a dog's skin is not purified even when washed;
a person of wicked soul would never become pure, even through union with fire.
There is no heaven nor liberation; there is only the destruction of the body.
Purity is the supreme standard for the purification of one's state of being in all actions.
Just as a wife or a daughter is embraced with different feelings according to their respective natures,
so too does the human intellect differ even regarding objects that are fundamentally identical.

O Nandin, just as a son everywhere, while meditating upon the breast [of his mother], becomes moist with desire in his heart by meditating on that very same thing, so too does a husband become moist with desire in his heart. (73)
Even when embraced, a wife who is devoid of feeling does not desire [her husband];
therefore, supreme existence arises from non-existence, for feeling is the cause of everything.
Purity of mind is indeed supreme purity; what is the use of other purifications?
Through purification by fire, one obtains everything—of this there is no doubt. (75)

Furthermore, for persons who have become stainless through the water of knowledge, there occurs the cleansing of the stains and odors of the excrement and urine of passion by means of the clay of true detachment. (76)
By its very nature, this body is at best a vessel for impurities;
it is utterly devoid of essence, consisting of nothing more than skin, and is like the trunk of a plantain tree. (77)
In this way, when the wise one who is awakened becomes relaxed regarding the body, he indeed crosses the terrible ocean of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. (78)
Thus has this great misery of the womb been proclaimed;
yet for men, due to the power of various karmas, it remains unknown in its entirety. (79)
The mindfulness that existed while dwelling in the womb is lost;
passing through the narrow passage of birth, one becomes helpless. (80)
Touched by the Marut while uttering the syllable Om, he then falls under the sway of delusion, and a loss of memory arises due to the power of his past karma. (81)
The fire of his own afflictions quickly consumes him; his delight lies in that very birth, for being deluded and stained by greed, he does not recognize his own self.
Even though endowed with eyes, one never perceives the real entity. (83)
Thus proceeding on the pure and even path, he remains steady;
yet, following the sway of greed, delusion, and anger, he suffers in saṃsāra.
In childhood, there is great suffering and fear because the sense faculties are not yet manifest;
even if one desires to perform virtuous deeds, one is unable to speak or act upon them. (85)
At the time of the eruption of his teeth, he shall suffer from diseases;
in childhood, moreover, he will especially be afflicted by many ailments particular to children. (86)
With his body overwhelmed by hunger and ravenous appetite, he stands somewhere crying out;
out of delusion and childishness, he might even consume urine, excrement, and the like. (87)
From the piercing of the ears, from the cutting of the scalp, from being beaten by one's mother and father,
from the study of letters and the like, and from the instruction of a teacher, suffering arises. (88)
With his limbs weakened by the fever of desire and afflicted by delusion in youth, great suffering arises for him due to envy and out of that very delusion. (89)
For that person, suffering indeed arises in the eyes; of this there is no doubt.
Tormented by the fire of desire, he finds no sleep at night. (90)
Even during the day, there is no happiness at all for a man whose body is attached to women, due to the anxiety over his wealth and mind; such is the case with those white drops [of semen].
For one afflicted by leprosy being tormented by worms,
and for one suffering from fever, that which arises from scratching or from the heat of fire is the same in all three cases.
Whatever pleasure one considers to arise from the cessation of itching, such pleasure alone one experiences; it does not exist in other women. (93)
Know that it is the same with women; there is no happiness in them from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Just as there is pleasure from the single discharge of feces and urine, so should it be understood regarding [the union with] one's beloved and son; others have conceived of it otherwise.
There is no happiness in women who are unreal and the refuge of evils; there is only anxiety, especially if one reflects upon it. (96)
In dishonor there is honor; in separation, the meeting with what is lost;
through old age, youth is destroyed. Alas, where is there happiness that is free from affliction?
With their bodies made frail by wrinkles, gray hair, and the loss of vitality,
men and women, who once mutually increased each other’s youth, [now face one another]. (98)
That body, seized by old age, becomes unpleasant in an instant;
one should behold one's own self as it has become frail through old age. (99)
Therefore, one should not become dispassionate [toward worldly life], for it is known that there is no sovereign power;
one is overcome by old age along with sons, friends, wives, and kinsmen. (100)
Furthermore, one is humiliated by servants who delight in misconduct;
moreover, the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa will not ripen.
O Nandikeśvara! One should practice the protection of Dharma during youth;
for the body, composed of wind, bile, and phlegm, is a mine of diseases. (102)
Because this very body of one's own is the nature of disease,
within this body there are a hundred deaths, each joined with another hundred. (103)

Among those, one is called "time" (kālaja), which is considered incurable even at the end; whereas the adventitious ones (āgantuja) reach pacification through medicines and other such means, but not the others.
The death brought about by Time cannot be pacified by any means such as recitation of mantras or burnt offerings;
nor can the various forms of death caused by weapons, serpents, or venomous beasts. (105)
Through sorcery and malevolent incantations, one may go to the house of Yama;
no one at all can protect a living being who has fallen under the power of timely death. (106)

Neither through austerity, nor recitation, nor worship, nor medicinal herbs, nor even through charity, nor by means of the best elixirs and yogic practices, can one attain divinity within this [limited] time.
Nevertheless, even over a long period of time, that Death does not spare anyone from its time. There is no suffering equal to death; there is no fear equal to death. (108)
For all embodied beings, there is no disease equal to death;
it seizes even one's virtuous sons, friends, wife, kingdom, sovereignty, and the like. (109)
The Rākṣasa Death seizes both those who are without kinsmen and their enemies,
just as a thunderbolt strikes down sixty [trees] after having struck one.
From the commencement of the first year until falling under the power of death in the middle of life—death at midnight is equal for all living beings; such is the nature of this [life]. (111)
Even in childhood, one is deluded; in youth, one is tormented by desire;
in old age, one is seized by decay; and in between, one is afflicted by hundreds of diseases.
A man is constantly afflicted by all the enemies born of the body: by lust, anger, delusion, as well as pride and envy. (113)
Furthermore, even while living, one experiences the affliction of urine and feces;
indeed, for a living being, not the slightest happiness exists at any time during the night.
Tormented by diseases and other such miseries, he eventually undergoes death. (115)
Driven by karma, one is born again and again for tens of millions of lifetimes, addressed by various terms such as "mother," "father," "son," or "kinsman. (116)
Due to the distinctions of classes such as wife, servant, and cattle, and through the association of actions, there arises the occurrence of debts, measures, and so forth. (117)
Therefore, in terms of ultimate reality, there is neither "is" nor "is not" regarding being a mother, father, and so forth;
one may likewise attain union with the Dharma and so on, as well as with the body. (118)
Thus has the womb been described as the ultimate source of suffering;
and the misery of death that occurs is a hundred times greater than that. (119)
And Yama, afflicted by that curse and tormented, cried out again and again like a frog that has entered the mouth of a serpent. || 120 ||
Though attended by kinsmen, wives, mothers, and fathers,
he would become parched with thirst even as he breathed heavily.
Placing his head at the end of his feet, and likewise his feet at the end of his head—
seeking the ground from the bed, he shall then go from the ground back to the bed.
For whom will there be death from the insult of water at a withered trunk? || 123 ||
Thus muttering [the mantra], devoid of shame upon the surface of the earth,
with his body smeared with urine and excrement, he dies again by death.
One should gradually proceed toward the cremation ground, burning the body along the path, even through terrible thieves and wild elephants;
for the prayer of a wise person is superior even to death. (125)
The suffering at death is momentary, yet it is encompassed by endless yearnings;
whereas the disease of hunger is a constant malady—this is the very nature of this world.
It is pacified by the great medicine of food and drink, and not otherwise; the procedure for treating a wound is the cause of the ultimate destruction of strength. (127)
In the absence of that, however, one dies; this is the supreme medicine for disease.
This should be known by the wise as the medicine for disease according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha). || 128 ||
And he who lies down having abandoned all attachment, appearing as if dead to all worldly affairs—for him whose self is shrouded by darkness, no happiness exists there. (129)
How can there be happiness even upon awakening for one whose self is burdened by activities such as the service of elephants and horses, trade, and the toil of cattle-rearing? (130)
One becomes miserable for the sake of acquiring wealth, and [miserable] for its protection once acquired;
cows are lost, agriculture is ruined, and wealth and grain are destroyed; the house is broken by neck-cords and the like, and by hundreds of royal edicts from kings and others. (132)
"My wife has young children; who indeed will provide for them once I am cut down?
And what will become of my daughters?"—thus was he overcome by anxiety for others. (133)
Oppressed by a continuous stream of anxieties regarding the protection of his family, his knowledge, learning, conduct, virtues, and humility likewise vanished. (134)
Like water in an unbaked clay vessel, this [body] goes to destruction along with its milkings;
since it is of the nature of earth, whence can there be happiness? What kind of happiness could that possibly be? (135)
When fear arises equally for all living beings, the state of desiring the same object is proclaimed as "enmity. (136)
Because they desired [the throne] for only one month, they lived together in mutual concealment; yet, O King, there was no enmity among them, nor was there any discord in their singing.
There was also an obscuration by clouds, and here and there a thundering roar;
the clouds were driven by the wind, and the power of the wind was checked by the mountains. (138)
Mountains are consumed by fire, and fire is overcome by water;
the waters constantly go to their drying up by the rays of the sun. (139)
Indeed, the entire single day of the Unborn (Aja) certainly comes to an end;
even Viriñca, along with others, perishes after a period of two *parārdhas*.
And when two parārdhas of time have passed, even Śiva goes to destruction;
moreover, there is no power superior to all others within the circle of saṃsāra.
Having thus abandoned the Lord of the World— who is immutable, all-pervading, and sovereign—
and having understood this, one should indeed relinquish all ignorance.
Therefore, in the three worlds, there is no one who is a hero, nor anyone who is a scholar;
there is truly no one at all who is omniscient, and even one who is liberated does not exist anywhere. (143)
Whoever understands a given thing and remains established in that reality is both healthy and wise;
yet, there is no power equal to this at all times and in all places. (144)
No one possesses absolute power, because all things exist in a state of relative superiority;
the gods were defeated by the asuras, and the asuras were defeated by the immortals.
Victory and defeat exist through mutual dependence;
[one who is] satisfied with a mere *prastha* of food and endowed with two garments [is truly successful]. (146)
By which even a single bed and seat become a source of particular suffering for one dwelling in a house consisting of seven stories, upon a couch occupying but a single spot. (147)
Since it is known that at a festival there is great abundance for the sake of hair,
the king’s excessive pride indeed becomes an ornament for his hair. (148)
Perfumes, ointments, and the like turn into filth;
song is but idle chatter, and dance is the behavior of a madman. (149)
For one who understands the certainty [of things], how can there be happiness from the enjoyments of sovereignty, given that all kings are driven by the desire to conquer one another? (150)
Happiness through sovereignty, power, and the like never truly exists;
for even in heaven, one beholds women of extraordinary beauty who bring happiness from every quarter. (151)
Higher and higher among the gods exists a state of mutual excellence;
however, through the exhaustion of the fruits of merit, the fall of men occurs. (152)
No action whatsoever is performed there; a great fault would arise.
One whose root is severed acts in such a way that he inevitably falls to the earth. (153)
In heaven there would be no happiness whatsoever, because of the exhaustion of the fruits of meritorious deeds within one's own experience. (154)
Then, by virtue of his actions—whether through various terrible deeds of speech, mind, or body—he surely falls into the horrific hells such as Raurava and others. (155)
Through intense urges, postures, and by means of axes and other weapons, as well as through moistening and striking, one attains the state of being stationary.
Furthermore, there was the falling of the branches and fruits of the *phaṇī* trees due to fierce winds, as well as their breaking and crushing by elephants and other living beings. (157)
In the state of being a stationary being (a plant), there is great fear from the heat and withering caused by forest fires;
for serpents, there is much suffering from the heat of the sun and the terrible agony of lameness. (158)
There is binding with nooses, especially for the wicked, and the sudden death of insects and other creatures day after day. (159)
Thus suffering arises for all reptiles, and for all predatory beasts there is fear of rain, cold, and heat. (160)
The suffering of carrying burdens, the torment of training and combat, separation from one's own herd, and the binding upon being led away for the first time. (161)
And for all beings, such as cattle and others, suffering arises in this very way;
since the entire world of moving and non-moving things is pervaded by such sufferings as these. (162)
From hell and other realms, the wise man should proceed toward the state of humans;
just as one who travels shifts his burden from one shoulder to the other to rest. (163)
Therefore, this entire world is stilled from suffering by means of suffering;
yet, through the power of meritorious karma, one may be born among thousands of various wombs.
Even in heaven there are various diseases; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, the head of Vajra, which had been severed, was indeed reattached. || 165 ||
In the same way, the head of a disciple is undoubtedly the sacrifice itself;
likewise, the leprosy of Mārtaṇḍabhaṅgu and the water-disease of Pracetas [are explained]. (166)
The Sun suffered from a deficiency of teeth; Indra’s arm was paralyzed;
Bhaga became afflicted with a wasting disease, and he indeed remained in a state of emaciation.
In the case of constant fever, Dakṣa indeed [commits] the very impurity of Viṣṇu, as well as the decapitation of Brahmā; all these [sins] are present. || 168 ||
In every kalpa, following each dissolution, [this] certainly occurs;
at the end of two parārdhas, it shall happen for Brahmā.
Because Brahmā lusted after Dakṣa’s granddaughter, the maiden, the Lord Ajaya, the Goddess established in Yoga, cursed him in anger. 170.
Listen, it is indeed there that one is born through the Creator and the defects such as passion;
all sufferings are certainly present there, without a doubt. (171)
Overcome by suffering, one might fall from it in an instant, being agitated by pain;
yet, through world-weariness, having reached a state of exhaustion, one may attain detachment. || 172 ||

One who is effortless, untouchable, and immediately free from desire shall attain liberation; for men, [this leads] from the suffering of rebirth to liberation itself through even a fraction of that. (173)
By whatever means possible, that guru shall attain the world of Śiva;
he shall have fourteen births, endowed with eightfold divinity.
The Piśācas and others have been fully described; furthermore, humans and animals, as well as the stationary beings—among these fourteen [classes], indeed, [the following occurs]. 175.
By means of austerities, righteous deeds, gifts, and even various forms of joy,
having abandoned the Piśāca and Rākṣasa births, one is born among the divine species.
One attains the human state with merit and demerit in equal measure, or through slight merits and demerits, or by the predominance of one's own [karmic] nature. (177)
One attains the state of a domestic animal, and then hear about birth as a wild beast: through passion and hatred, O Nandikeśvara, the state of a wild beast is born. (178)
Due to the diversity of births, one attains the state of various bird species;
indeed, [beings] are born as vultures, serpents, worms, and insects. (179)
From malice they become the grass and other plant species; from delusion and grief, they become trees.
For all these species, dharma, adharma, and so forth exist above [the body]. (180)
In accordance with his merit and demerit, a man is born into all types of wombs;
having attained birth as animals and the like, he likewise undergoes death. (181)
Having subsequently reached the realm of the plowman (the preta world), his command bestows birth and experience;
yet the subtle element of the earth's fragrance does not descend to that level. (182)
Form, conjoined with taste and smell, enters into fire;
taste, smell, and the nature of sound go to touch, which belongs to the wind. (183)
Through these four spaces, one proceeds to the subtle element of sound;
and the five subtle elements quickly attain the principle of the mind (manas). || 184 ||
All six sense organs reach the principle of intellect (buddhi);
these seven, moreover, pervade the ego (ahaṃkāra), thus indeed forming eight groups.
O Nandikeśvara, the body is conceived as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka);
and within this body resides the Puruṣa, endowed with the principle of sound (śabdatattva).
And by the command of Śiva, within the proximity of this mind, there arise two kinds of bodies: those resulting from meritorious deeds and likewise those resulting from evil deeds. (187)
"By means of good deeds, grant him happiness; by means of evil deeds, [make him] afflicted by torment.
Thus is death described, and immediately following that, rebirth. (188)
Having attained the state of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), he does not fall back into that [very same body];
having passed from ether into air, he creates fire from air.
Having reached the waters and fire, he creates the earth;
likewise for all plants that sprout from the soil and those born of moisture. 190.
Having attained their respective fitness, and having attained the state of being sons [of the Lord], let the viviparous and the oviparous also know and obtain the *vauṣaṭ*. || 191 ||
Furthermore, the food consumed by the parents became equal [to their own] within that [embryo];
from the essence (rasa) blood was produced, and from blood the formation of flesh occurred. (192)
From the flesh, fat is produced; from fat, the sinews are produced;
within the sinews, marrow is produced; and from that marrow, semen arises. (193)
From the food and so forth up to the semen, this self gradually becomes other;
together with that semen, it falls into the mother’s womb as blood.
Through such deaths, one undergoes death again;
and having attained birth once more, one returns to the state of the five elements once again. (195)
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Method of the Origination of Beings," within the *Viśvasādākhya*, which is inconceivable.
Listen briefly, O Nandikeśvara, to the arising of Time;
by knowing Time through its three divisions, one conquers death in every respect.
All yogins with tranquil minds, for the arising of knowledge regarding time,
should first examine the lifespan and thereafter attain discernment. (2)
In a mortal devoid of longevity, consciousness becomes fruitless;
therefore, having understood this, the knower of yoga should indeed exert every effort regarding time.
Thereafter, one should perform the Kālottara [rite] born of meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and yoga.
Time is declared to be Vāyu; Time is called the Omniscient One.
Time is Yama and Time is Sūrya; Time is the deity Soma.
Knowing that Time consists of all the gods, one should practice [the yoga of] Time.
Aries, Cancer, Libra, and likewise Capricorn are called the movable signs (cararāśis); they move in the left nostril.
The Bull, the Lion, the Scorpion, and the Water-pot likewise— these,
known as the "Stable" signs, move correctly through the southern nostril. (7)
Likewise, Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces—
because they possess both non-natural and natural characteristics, one should indeed practice in both ways.
Thus, through the yoga of practice and by the instruction of the teacher,
the wise man conquers death by practicing day after day.
One who is free from disease and endowed with youth shall attain strength and childhood again.
Ida is to be known as a digit of the moon, and Pingala as originating from the sun.
The portion of the fire is Suṣumnā; from night, it consists of five ghaṭikās for the day and five for the night, on the left and the right respectively.
Poison flows through the right-moving [nāḍī], and nectar indeed through the left;
the Suṣumnā carries a mixture [of both], each within its own respective channel. (12)
In the system of sixty [breaths], the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs; six prāṇas are recorded as one ghaṭikā.
Sixty ghaṭikās constitute a day and night; he who performs this calculation of the life-force (jīva) [attains mastery]. || 13 ||
Two ayutas, six thousand, and six hundred more;
by means of this movement during a day and night, there is indeed the movement of the breaths. (14)
Just as a leech moves from one blade of grass to another until it reaches its destination,
so too does the tongue [move] toward the supportless tip of the nose at a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
Uttering "haṃsa, haṃsa," he performs inhalation and exhalation;
when there is a reduction of four finger-breadths, that is called the loss of lifespan.
One should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma), with each exhalation lasting eight finger-breadths;
for if one is devoid of breath control, death occurs due to the disorder of the vital energies.
In the center of the navel is the peak-shaped [center] at its root within nine sections;
one should examine it during the two solstices at the time of dawn.
First, one should walk on the right foot for the duration of a quarter-day;
thereafter, alternating between left and right, one should continue until the sun has set.
The six elements, the seven Vasus, and the series of planets likewise constitute the fortnight of the nāḍīs;
hear now that sequence of their setting.
And there are twenty-six [divisions] according to the number of the root schisms;
furthermore, there are thirty, forty-four, fifty-two, and sixty. (21)
Indeed, the number one hundred and eighty years is stated in reverse order:
half a day, a full day, two days, and likewise three days. (22)
O Lord, the period of the armor (varman) shall be four days; the period of the twenty-fifth [digit] is proclaimed to be eight years, with the number of the sun (twelve) constituting ten years.
Thus it should be for four years; hear now the sequence for what follows:
if [the child] has been carried for ten days, there should be illumination and a great song.
Likewise, there is one night for fifteen days;
there is the omission of twenty-six days, and then again on the twenty-seventh day.
The vehicles and the lifespan for twenty-eight days are likewise thirty, thirty-one, and thirty days respectively. (26)
One should practice the state [of breath] for ten days, seven days,
four days, three days, two days, and for a single day. (27)
Thus, the examination of the wind is said to be concurrent with that of time; thereafter, the fire is on the path, and then it becomes the staff-touching earth. (28)
The wind [should be directed] to the sides, while in the middle, the movement reaches the wind;
there should be four *kumbhakas*, and the hands should be joined in the *añjali* gesture at the forehead. || 29 ||
That lotus has the form of a stone; by its mere sight, it is a great source of life.
Having joined with the first lunar day (pratipad) and so forth, it stands above the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa).
Wherever the entire line [of the shadow] falls on that day, death shall occur;
where there is no shadow at all, death certainly happens right there. (31)
O Nandikeśvara, even upon seeing smoke or likewise the form of fire, one will certainly meet death within three months; this is certain.
At the time of a desired transit, by observing the solar disc, [one should know] four, three, two, and likewise one month. || 33 ||

The object of focus is perceived by means of a mind distinguished from reality, through a pure disposition, skillfully in the southern, western, northern, or eastern city, within one, two, three, or six palaces;
one sees the aperture in the center for ten days, and likewise the fifth [sign] filled with smoke.
The lord of yogis should observe the time with an undisturbed mind. || 34 ||
If Kṛṣṇa [is absent] for exactly one month, or half a month, or even half of that;
if he has fallen away for seven days, then for seven days it shall be empty.
The halo around the sun and moon, the observation of the solar disc,
the various types of lunar months, and the falling of stars and so forth— [these are described]. (36)
In one month from being smokeless, it becomes treeless and half-treeless;
in another month, it becomes smoky; and in yet another month, it becomes a mandala of fire.
And in the fifth [section], there are those with golden forms, with eight auspicious signs on their feet like fire,
possessing the radiance of the sun individually, and likewise two suns for each.
A single circle of light, cast upon the black sky;
the burning of the earth from its smoke, and likewise the three [sounds] through the roars of the earth. (39)
Having seen this in the mortal world, the sight of the Sun arises from the state of being male;
it is deficient by one year from the head, and all else is less than half of that.
The shadow-ground consists of thirty-three [units]; twenty-five less two;
in the case of a hunchback, the man is twenty-four [units], while the head and nose are half of that. (41)
Within four days, one should mutter the supreme mantra in the form of the sun;
with lamps and incense on the fifth day, and together with lamps for half a fortnight.
The group of seven from non-existence, Kālarātri as the fifth,
half [of the cycle] as the ninth, and likewise that which is the resort of death.
In the thirteenth year, death occurs for those with one head and many bodies;
likewise, in the fourteenth year, death shall come to those who reside in that place. || 44 ||
If a black dot is seen [on the forehead], one will meet death within a month;
if it is located on the throat, death shall occur within these very days.
If there is a black spot in the middle of the ear, one will die within half a month;
if it is on the side of the ear, death occurs after fifty days. (46)
If the area around the ear becomes black, death will occur within twenty days;
if blackness is seen on the teeth, one shall meet death within a month. (47)
If there is a black dot there, death occurs after twenty-five days;
if its base is black in color, death occurs after twenty-eight days.
The tip of the tongue indeed becomes black for forty days,
sometimes due to itching, [the appearance of] blisters, or from biting.
And he shall live for thirty days, joined with your words, O Kṛṣṇa;
however, death after thirty days has been declared, O Nandikeśvara.
If there is a black line on the nails and the soles of the feet, death occurs within fourteen days;
and if there is exhaustion in the middle of the footprints, one shall meet with death.
If there is blackness on their sides, death occurs after twenty-seven days;
if there is poison and itching on the feet, death shall come after six days.
In that case, if there is a black line, one shall meet death within ten days;
if the face is devoid of luster, one meets death [within seven days].
If the knees, the shanks, and the skin are black, death occurs after thirty-three days;
for this [period] beginning from the lines is indeed one year, while for the eyes and ears it is twenty-two [days].
If there is black discoloration at the crown of the head, death will occur in three days.
Having heard this great knowledge regarding the time [of death], who would not [act accordingly]? 55.
p.
1193) Your pupils are flashing with sudden anger, and your eye-corner is twitching;
there is a terrible sound in the ocean, like the roar of an expiring breath. (56)

One should know that the taking of life occurs at the end of a year, at half of its [sixteenth] part, likewise at the end of a month, at half of that, at five days, on a single day, and during the day itself. *vidyāt is used here in the sense of "one should know."
One should thus contemplate time, from a lava up to the dissolution of the universe, as being like the piercing of a cluster of lotus fibers with a fine needle. (58)
The time that passes in each *dala* is called a *lava*;
thirty *lavas* constitute a *truṭi*, and they know thirty *truṭis* to be a *kala*. (59)
A *kāṣṭhā* is to be known as [the duration of] thirty *kalās*; thirty *kalās* constitute a *nimeṣa*, and thirty *nimeṣas* constitute a *muhūrta*—thus is the fifth [unit].
Having thus understood the time, one should practice the fivefold division of time.
