Thus ends the eightieth chapter, the Procedure for the Arising of Time, within the Inconceivable Viśvasādākhya.
Now I shall explain in detail the procedure for atonement; listen. "Prāya" is said to mean destruction, while "citta" is that which is restored. (1)
It is recorded in the Smṛti that without that [knowledge], there is no attainment of composure, and thus it is called expiation (prāyaścitta).
At the time of morning, one should likewise perform purification and sipping of water (ācamana). || 2 ||
Having become composed in mind and endowed with faith and devotion, one should perform the bath, the smearing with ashes, and the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth. || 3 ||
One who is free from passion, hatred, and the like, patient, devoted to meditation,
and possessing perfectly clear insight into the inner self, should perform the rite of expiation.
I shall now describe the purification of vessels and so forth individually;
likewise, the purification of cloths stained with feces, urine, and the like is performed even with earth and water.
Having washed it again with alkaline substances, one should also purify it with cow urine;
one should then cleanse it with water until neither the coating nor the odor remains.
One should perform the same procedure for other suitable collections of materials;
woolen cloth, linen, and silk should be purified with white mustard seeds.

The purification of silk cloths and fine fabrics should be performed with bilva fruits; likewise, the purification of leather is like that of cotton cloth, using arishta decoctions ending with the kuntapa plant.
Likewise, at the time of the Rajyu and Prashana rites, as well as for the chowries,
there shall then be the purification of your ancestors, beginning with Kalā.
For the purification of garments, leather bags, vessels, and split-bamboo items,
rubbing with cow-hair is specifically prescribed.
O Nandikeśvara! For vessels made of copper, bell-metal, and the like, as well as for those made of tin and lead, purification shall be achieved by means of water alone placed within a water-pot.
Gold and silver, when free from stains, are pure after being washed with water from the vessel;
likewise, the ruby, pearl, conch, coral, and pearl [are pure].
As before, purification by water has thus been described by me for a vessel used during childbirth when it is touched by a crow or defiled by feces, urine, and the like.
In the case of fire, by means of contact with it one may cleanse [an object] so that it becomes fit for purification;
this applies to grass, stones, wood, as well as to *valā*, *landa*, *lava*, and creepers.
O Nandikeśvara! Purification by sprinkling with water is prescribed for the mortar, the pestle, the sacrificial ladles, the offering spoons, and so forth.
p.
1197) Purification by means of hot water shall apply to a winnowing basket, a vessel for curd-liquor, and a bowl;
likewise, even for a vessel for Vedic study, purification occurs at that very moment. || 16 ||
However, for substances that have been contaminated by one another, purification is achieved with cow urine;
but for grains that have been mixed together, they become pure through sprinkling.
O Nandikeśvara, there should be a cleansing of grains, vegetables, roots, and fruits due to contact with worms, insects, and moths.
Purification from contact with dogs, boars, donkeys, or camels is always achieved by sprinkling with water while reciting the Astra-mantra. (19)
Even in the case of an ointment, one should discard it from the spot where it was touched and rinse with water;
likewise when it is mixed with flies or hair, or combined with husks and charcoal.
Even if this [place] is especially defiled by the dust from feet and the like,
one should dig up the ground touched by that [impurity] and dry it in water as previously described. (21)
One should also purify it by sprinkling clarified butter and by means of ashes,
as well as with cow dung, urine, anthill earth, clay, ashes, and water.
Purification of houses containing weapons occurs by these means;
or at times such as teaching and the like, one is pure through a mind focused on the forest as prescribed. (23)

Everywhere the ground is pure; it is the birthplace of gold, gems, and other such things. Even when in contact with despicable substances, purification is said to occur right here [on that very spot].
One becomes pure by going to a city or a village and washing one's feet;
likewise when the temple has cracked, broken, or even when the pedestal has shifted. (25)
Furthermore, when the temple has collapsed, or when the *liṅga*, the images, the wall,
or the painting have been destroyed, or when the cloth [scroll] is torn, broken, or covered by bamboo and grass; (26)
And likewise when it is devoid of the eight bonds, or similarly burnt by fire,
or broken by the current of a river, or otherwise shattered.

When [the water] has been touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla), dog-cookers (śvapaca), and the like, or by one who lacks initiation (dīkṣā); or when it has been touched by cocks and the like, and especially by brown-colored creatures (babhru). || 28 ||
Especially upon contact with crows and owls, as well as by touching a donkey, a camel, a boar, a cat, a goat, or a bull. (29)

By midwives, by thieves, by those of inverse or low castes, by those who have fallen from their caste (vrātyas), by those associated with the dead, and even by those afflicted with a multitude of diseases; || 30 ||
Nor [should one touch it] when touched by fools, nor likewise upon touching a *liṅga* or similar objects;
nor when the daily worship has been omitted, nor when the image is devoid of its ritual covering. (31)
Indeed, when it is devoid of bathing and consecration, lacking the offering of oblations and the like, and bereft of flowers, perfumes, incense, and water for the feet; || 32 ||
If the twilight lamps are lacking, or likewise if the sacrificial oblation is missing;
if the time has passed, or if there is a transposition or a violation of the mantras—(33)

When the head [of the deity] is devoid of flowers, when the rites of bathing are omitted, when the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is neglected, and likewise when the offering of the *damanaka* flower is not performed; || 34 ||
But for one who lacks the woolen blanket, who has neglected Śivarātri, who performs sacrifice for his own sake, and who is devoid of the [proper] distinction; || 35 ||
In cases of leaping over [the fire], using it for impure offerings or as a sun-bath, in acts of schism, when joined with the great sins (mahāpātaka), or when the five sins have arisen; || 36 ||

Or [if one is] deprived of the sacred thread (upavīta), or devoid of the observance of restrictive rules (niyamācāra), or in the case of a confusion of mantras, or if one has abandoned the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and so forth; || 37 ||
If the rite of *śrāddha* is omitted, an expiation for all [the faults] is prescribed;
however, if the temple is cracked or broken, the destruction of the builder shall occur. (38)

Having fashioned a male effigy, the Guru should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); then, having performed all the rites such as the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) as before, he should worship it.
If the pedestal (piṇḍikā) becomes loose, it will suffer displacement from its position;
one should stabilize it as before and join it with the eight types of bonds.
The most excellent preceptor should perform a ceremonial bath with the five products of the cow and other substances;
however, if the pedestal is broken or cracked, he should have it fashioned anew from unbroken grain.
O Nandikeśvara, one should perform the bathing according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual ablution;
if the liṅga is broken or cracked, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the kingdom.
Having discarded that [image] made of jewels or even one made of clay as before,
and having fashioned a linga from earth, one should duly perform the consecration ceremony.
One should not perform the removal of that [defilement] from a self-manifested liṅga;
rather, the preceptor should perform the ritual bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as previously described.
Or, if there is a deficiency in the limbs, one should complete each respective part;
O Nandikeśvara, all rites such as the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) and so forth should be performed as before.
If the *liṅga*, the cloth, or even the *vācā* and so forth are carried away by an enemy, there will be the destruction of the patron (*yajamāna*) and famine shall follow thereafter. (46)
Having conceived of it as the abode of the Child (Bāla), one should place the pericarp in its center;
one should carefully encompass the interior of the Linga-worship up to its end.
All rites such as the sprinkling of water and so forth should be performed as before; the bathing should likewise take place.
However, if the eight-fold binding is omitted, there will undoubtedly be no rain.
As before, one should perform the binding and recite the root mantra one hundred times over the temple, the liṅga, the image, the sacrificial oblation (caru), the vessel, and so forth. (49)
Food that has been burnt by fire is destroyed by timely rain;
one should perform the ritual bathing as before, especially for the liṅga and other such objects. (50)
If the cloth has been prepared otherwise, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should take place as before;
if the painting is devoid of form, one should paint the image again.
All rites such as the sprinkling of water and so forth should be performed as before; the bathing should likewise take place.
It is said that if [the image] is touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and the like, or by enemies, fear arises.
O Nandikeśvara! The bathing, sprinkling, and other rites are as before;
the Guru should quickly repeat the Pāśupata mantra one hundred times. (53)
If the daily worship is omitted, the people shall suffer;
if even one joint [of the ritual] is missing, one should perform the worship twice again.
But in the case of an inferior [image], one should first perform a thousand oblations;
and for one lacking the three joints, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 55 ||
If the three-day period is deficient in worship, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed there as before;
having performed the bathing on the fifth day, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Brahmāṅga mantras.
If the rite lacks the fortnightly [observance], one should perform sprinkling and bathing with the products of the cow (gavya);
likewise, if there is a lack of worship for one month, there must be sprinkling with the products of the cow.
O Nandikeśvara, one should again perform the ceremonial bathing as before with fragrant water and other substances; one should then offer oblations with the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
If the worship is deficient for more than a month, one should perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa);
if the worship is deficient for a full cycle (āvṛt), there will be the destruction of the group of servants.
Recalling each respective mantra, one should offer eight thousand oblations;
for if the offering of the bali is omitted, all the deities remain displeased.
Having recollected the *bali* mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
If this is omitted during the ritual bath, a drought will occur instantly. (61)
Having recited the root mantra one hundred times, the water should become twice that amount;
however, if it is devoid of fragrant substances, it will bring about the destruction of children.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times within the heart;
however, if the materials such as water for the feet are lacking, a great plague will break out.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
however, if the twilight lamp is omitted, eye disease arises.
Having recited the Netra-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the lamp offering twice that amount;
however, if the sacrificial oblation (havir) is deficient, there will be famine, so one should cause that [oblation] to be given twice over.
One should perform eight thousand oblations with the heart-mantra itself;
if one has failed to observe the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), fear will enter from enemies. (66)
The preceptor should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
however, if the rite of bathing is omitted, a great wind arises.
Having recited the Astra-mantra one hundred times,
one should thereafter accept a substitute for the contact with those who are uninitiated, whether it be a linga or an image.
One should know that the destruction of the country occurs [if this is neglected]; one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is omitted, there will be fear from a foreign army.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) as before for the sake of the complete attainment of all siddhis;
provided that the festival was not performed during the prescribed month and its corresponding lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
One should perform the festival once again and offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra. When it is thus applied for the sake of others, that is called purification for one's own sake. (71)
Listen now in due order to [the practice] for one's own sake, for the sake of others, and for both mixed together;
as well as when there is fear of kings or thieves, or when the body is afflicted by disease and the like.
In matters concerning the gods, the sacred fire, and one's teachers, there is no fault in the constant omission [of duties] for a dispassionate householder; his expiation shall be twofold. (73)
It is declared that [the merit] for one who has taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika) is double that of a householder, especially so.
One is a child until the end of the sixteenth year; from eighty until the end of a hundred years [one is considered an elder]. (74)
If one should be an elder (sthavira), there is no penance for those two; likewise, women afflicted by disease are entitled to half the penance. (75)
Even in that case, having understood the difficulties involved, one should have it made at half or even a quarter of the size;
if one is unable to do it oneself, it may be done by another, in which case the fee shall be double. (76)

Through the conditions of place, time, and so forth, as well as through knowledge, devotion, ritual action, and the like, there shall be the region of the field of merit; these are the teacher, initiation, the syllables, the place, and the time. (77)
Or at the time of the equinoxes, solstices, and so forth;
there is indeed fear of calamities for the kingdom, as well as emptiness, disease, and the like. (78)
These and other such states are proclaimed as "unattainable";
however, the preceptor, having deliberated, should cause [the rite] to be performed immediately thereafter.
Whatever has been seen or heard in accordance with the Śaiva way of life, and whatever has been formulated by the gurus—adherence to that is not a cause for fault here. (80)
Even for a householder, one should avoid giving gifts and performing worship at night,
as well as during lunar eclipses, the equinoxes, and other auspicious times of transit. (81)
At night and during sacrifices and other such rites, worship should be performed as it bestows many accomplishments;
however, for a householder at any other time, worship at night would bring about fault.
One should perform the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, or even more; this applies always to the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), both at night and on the day of worship.
But if even one [recitation] is omitted, one should mutter the *sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times;
for one who omits two of the two daily junctures (*saṃdhyā*), three hundred recitations are prescribed.
If everything should occur through desire, one should observe the fast in due order;
if the worship at a single time is deficient, one should recite the Ghorasahasra mantra a thousand times.
If one observes the fast out of desire, [performing it] for two or three periods of time, having thus recited [the mantra] for one day, on the second day as well— (86)
O Nandin, one should increase it by one thousand on the third day, adding three hundred more;
thus the wise man should increase it day by day.
If the fortnightly worship is omitted,
however, one should increase the number by twenty thousand two hundred for each month, starting from the initial amount of twenty thousand.
When the planet has been lost due to thieves, rats, *kāśa* grass, and the like; or by dogs, monkeys, and so forth; or even by snakes, fish, and the like; and likewise when it has been destroyed. (89)
If a linga intended for one's own use is seen to be burnt or stuck in its pedestal and so forth,
one should observe a fast for one day and thereafter subsist on food eaten only at night.
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, with two * * * [syllables] in between;
likewise, the *liṅga* bestowed by the Guru and by the Elder [Preceptor] should also be treated in that same manner. (91)
Having taken up another linga, one should worship it according to the previously mentioned procedure;
and in this manner, having consecrated the pedestals, one should then perform the worship.
When this mixture is rolled two thousand times, it is called *lākṣā*; its purification is achieved by rolling it three or four times with *bandhūka* flowers.

The two [periods] consisting of the striking of the *gaṇḍūka*, the *kalaśa*, and so forth, as well as the *tāḍana* and *āyuṣmat* measures, amount to ten thousand (*ayuta*). Immediately after that, there is the measure of the "fall of intoxication" (*madapāta*), which has slipped away. 94.
Likewise, when performed on a soft spot that has a support, it is joined with *tā*;
when it is unbroken and without support, it is twice as many forms. || 95 ||
If the *liṅga* falls from a height of eight *tālas* or becomes shattered,
or if it is pierced out of desire for gain, there is no expiation for that. (96)
The entire palace should be thus; furthermore, there exists an expiation (prāyaścitta), and for the destruction of great sins, a multiform rite is praised.
That which is rolled about out of lust and that which is a fall resulting in being shattered—there is indeed no atonement for such a person who is a great sinner. 98.
But if the *liṅga* has been touched by a foot, or touched, or even defiled by phlegm,
one should then recite the Aghora mantra twenty thousand times, or indeed thirty thousand times.
Upon touching one who has not been initiated by a twice-born person, one hundred and four repetitions [of the mantra] should be performed at the linga;
upon touching an outsider, however, one thousand; but in the case of a pratiloma (one of inverse caste), one hundred thousand.
Even when touched by the class of crows and other such beings, twenty thousand [repetitions] are prescribed;
likewise when filled with skulls that are endowed with the supreme path. (101)
If the Liṅga is touched by those endowed with the Great Vows (Mahāvrata), one should recite four hundred [times];
likewise, if it is touched by Pāśupatas, one should then recite four hundred [times].
If one installs the liṅga and the pedestal after having divided them,
one should perform a recitation (japa) of one hundred thousand times in many forms for the sake of purification.
If the *liṅga* is indeed properly joined for the sake of oneself and for the sake of others,
it is protected from kings and the like, from quadrupeds, and even from terrible primordial winds.
O Nandikeśvara, having abandoned that very limb of the deity and having recited the Aghora mantra ten thousand times, one should install another liṅga and worship it.
Having established [the fire] in the sacrificial pit for one who is intent on the sacrificial fees,
he shall attain Nirvāṇa after fasting for one night. || 106 ||
One should indeed recite the *sahasrabahurūpa* mantra one thousand times for its pacification;
by reciting it ten thousand times for three nights, purification arises.

If one has not performed worship at the three junctions of the day nor likewise on the three Ekādaśī days, one does not attain purity; therefore, one should perform the recitation (japa) while observing the rule of abstaining from bathing.
If one has previously worshipped the deity, the preceptor, and the fire with devotion,
then even if the offering of a bali-oblation is omitted, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
In the event of the violation of a restrictive rule, a vow, or a ritual act,
one should especially recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
On the fourteenth lunar day, or on a festival day when the daily worship has been omitted, the [transgression] becomes fourfold; however, one is purified through penance. || 111 ||
If worship has not been performed during an eclipse or at the equinox,
one should recite the Aghora mantra twenty thousand times for the sake of purification.
If one is deprived of Śivarātri, then one must perform a hundred thousand recitations of the root mantra;
furthermore, if the junction of that day is missed, there should be eight recitations.
The purificatory rite (pavitra) should be performed first, and one should not perform it in the middle;
having recited the Aghora mantra and the pair of light mantras, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa recitation.
Censuring Śiva, censuring one's guru, and likewise censuring the wise; being intent on seizing the property of the gods, and destroying the belongings of the guru. (115)
One who steals its property, a drinker of liquor, one who likewise consumes the food of the *gaṇa*, an ungrateful person, or one who oppresses his elder— these ten are the most extreme sinners. (116)
Their purification is observed to extend even until the limit of death;
however, one who delights in reviling Śiva must perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
One should recite the Śiva-mantra ten million times for the sake of purification; even one who is intent on reviling the guru may [attain it] through the grace of the guru as a prerequisite. (118)
One should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances with many mantras as before;
likewise, O Nandikeśvara, for the disparagement of the knowledge of Śiva, as previously stated. (119)
One who steals the property of a deity shall be made to give back that object doubled;
furthermore, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, recitations, and so forth, in sequence as previously prescribed.
But in the case of destroying the property of a guru, one should give double that amount to him;
one should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, and it is said that the recitation (*japa*) is as before. (121)
That which is given by a teacher out of affection to a disciple brings happiness;
however, for one who drinks liquor, purification does not occur even after a long period of time.
Having heated the liquor until it has the appearance of fire, one should make [the offender] drink it; death is certain.
By that, purification is ordained, and a higher quality of merit exists [therein]. 123.

If, however, through negligence he should [violate] it, he should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the Śiva-mantra and eight Cāndrāyaṇa penances, by which his purification shall be attained.

An ungrateful person and one who is arrogant toward his elder brother would be equal to those who revile their gurus; likewise, one who approaches the bed of his guru and one who takes pleasure in his teacher's wife [are equal]. (125)
Even in the presence of such a person, or likewise in the case of stealing gold—even Antaka (the God of Death) would [be overcome];
these five indeed are endowed with great sin. (126)
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall cut off his own penis with a weapon;
then, carrying a palm leaf, he shall go toward the southern direction.
And at the end of life there will be departure; by that, purification will come about.
Likewise, even before the guide, one who speaks unpleasantly [will suffer]. 128.
One should perform the cutting off of the tongue, by which death itself would occur;
or else, through the grace of that Guru, purification is ordained for him. (129)
One should constantly mutter the name of the Guru, remaining silent and intent upon the knowledge of Him;
one should do this until death, for by that means, even he becomes partaker of purification.
Similarly, one who is devoted to the eldest [brother] should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
thereafter, remaining silent, he should cast off his body, and by that means purification is attained. (131)

If there is a statement regarding the recollection of one's birth as a Brahmin or other caste directed at a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), it should be known as equal to reviling Śiva; one should mutter the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.

The body is not endowed with purity due to contact with feces, urine, and semen; likewise, because it arises from the *māyā* of the atoms (*vāṇava*), it is subject to such qualities as impurity. (133)
If an ignorant person incurs impurity from its loss, the wise one attains purity through the bliss arising from the study and reception of that which has been experienced by Śiva. || 134 ||

One should perform penance in a place endowed with groves of ascetics and the like; for very great sins such as pātaka, it should be performed at the end [of life], while for upapātaka and similar offenses, it may be performed along with the fire.

Having observed the performance of vows, hardships, and the like, as well as residence in sacred fords and holy fields, and even further, the attainment of even small degrees of supernatural power through fierce asceticism; (136)
Austerities such as the Kṛcchra and others have been described, as well as the Taptakṛcchra; the Atikṛcchra would be the third, and Parāka is of a distinct nature.
After a hundred *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, listen now to the sequence beginning with the *kṛcchra* penance:
eating only once a day for three nights, or fasting for three days. (138)
The Kṛcchra penance is thus fully described and is known as the Prājāpatya;
having drunk warm water for three days, one should eat only milk while keeping the senses under control. (139)
For three days one should consume warm clarified butter, or for three days only water; this is known as *taptakṛcchra*. Now, the *atikṛcchra* is described.
Twenty-one lunar mansions, three fortnights, and subsisting on a diet of milk—this is declared to be the *atikṛcchra*; now the *parāka* is described here. (141)
The twelve-day fast without food is known as the *parāka*.
In the bright fortnight, one should increase the morsels of food by one each day, and in the dark fortnight, one should decrease them accordingly. 142.
The Cāndrāyaṇa penance consists of half a barley grain; beyond that is the one called Pipīlaka.
For half a month, one should consume a mouthful per day, decreasing it during the dark fortnight and increasing it during the bright fortnight.
This is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, which consists of water alone; it is performed with water at the beginning and end of the day, as well as in the evening, morning, and midday.
One who wanders about should observe the fast and consume the fourfold water; one of middling capacity may observe three of these, or half of that, or even just the sound [of the recitation]. (145)
Fasting is declared to be the holy ford (*tīrtha*) of the Gaṅgā and other rivers;
indeed, the vow consists of celibacy and so forth, and therein the [proper] eating is described. (146)
Food fit for oblation, measured portions, alms-food, a diet of milk, vegetables, barley-gruel, oil-cakes, and the consumption of bulbs, roots, and leaves. (147)
One should practice such things as inhaling air and fasting;
that is, one should perform those actions for which there is neither injunction nor prohibition when they have been undertaken. (148)
In that case, neither merit nor sin accrues; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
One should immediately perform propitiatory rites, including oblations and other ceremonies, for the sake of atonement. 149.
One should examine the day, the lunar fortnight, the asterism, the ascendant, and so forth;
a penance performed immediately [without such examination], even if it consists of the "Jewel-womb" (ratnagarbha) rite, is not praised.
The middling [period] occurs after seven days or after a fortnight;
that which concludes at the end of a month is the inferior, as is the case with Īśvara. (151)
And at that time, in the rule for expiation, a specific quality was declared for one's own sake. || 152 ||
At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), [the mantra] ends with "svāhā," and at the time of recitation (japa), it ends with "namaḥ.
At the end of "svāhā," the words "bhagavan kṣobhaya vaṃśa" are added again.
Thereafter, immediately following, the sinner [should recite] either a hundred mantras or another [number]. || 154 ||
O Nandikeśvara, having performed the recitation at the time of chanting, and especially at the time of the fire-oblation, one should offer the final oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Within one, three, five, seven, or nine weeks;
or within a fortnight, three weeks, or seven lunar mansions—from whichever [time] it may be, [the result] remains uninterrupted. (156)
When one hundred thousand recitations have been performed, one should perform them again; if more are required, one should increase the number further.
Whether it be a liṅga for one's own sake, one worshipped by another, or one worshipped by oneself again—[the same rule applies]. (157)
However, an expiation must be performed through recitation and other means as prescribed in the scriptures, even for a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) if he uses turmeric or betel leaf. 158.
One should recite the *dakṣiṇa* mantra a thousand times every day in succession;
after seven days have passed in this manner, the wise man should perform one *kṛcchra* penance.
For one who is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), mounting a palanquin, a swing, a horse,
or similar conveyances results in the recitation of the Aghora mantra a thousand times for every single day.
Ascending [the cremation pyre] due to disease and the like never leads to any fault for the heart;
however, it is forbidden in cases of treachery toward Śiva, treachery toward one's guru, reviling the wise, and so forth, as well as during a vow. (161)
And likewise in the Raurava and other hells, as well as in their various subdivisions,
and even in the most dreadful hell of twenty-eight crores.
One who has [the mark] up to the pupils from birth will certainly be constantly afflicted by disease;
for the sake of a very great sin, he is tormented for half that duration of time. (163)
The duration of time for that [sin] shall be one-tenth; in the case of the five [sins], it shall be as previously stated. For those equal to that, the residence in hell shall always be half of that.
Even when the killing of deer, birds, and so forth results in the commission of a minor offense (upapātaka),
if it is equal to that [major offense], there will indeed be half of that suffering in hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon sins and other such evils. || 166 ||
Rebirth does not exist for one who has been initiated, especially so; from sin comes the attainment of hell, therefore one should not commit sin. (167)
In rites for pacification or nourishment, as well as in recitations for expiation and the like, one should face east; for subjugation, one faces south, and for malevolent rites, likewise south.
One should know that the western [direction] bestows wealth, while the northern would grant peace.
The Uṣṇīṣa [deity] is the destroyer of the Kañcukīs; he is covered by flowing water and has disheveled hair.
One who has not purified his hands and is impure should never recite [the mantra].
Likewise, one should avoid yawning, spitting, sneezing, rubbing [the body], and [playing] stringed instruments. (170)
One should avoid looking at those of low or outcaste status during the act of recitation;
they must perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and one should remember Vāmā accompanied by Umā.

One should not look at the stars, nor should one perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) on a public road, in an inauspicious place, or especially in darkness; nor should one recite [mantras] with feet outstretched, for the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana) is new [and improper]. 173.

Whether mounted on a vehicle, in bed, or the like, or when mental agitation arises—if one is fully capable, one should perform the entire recitation with all the powers according to one's capacity. (174)
At the beginning there is the *yoga*, and at the end there are two *pallava-sampuṭas*; this is called *grathana*. When it is interspersed with two [elements], it is declared to be *vidarbha*. (175)
If the letter 'ya' occurs at the middle, beginning, and end [of the mantra], it is for the purpose of the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
One should know that *tambhana* (paralysis) is used in *rodhana* (obstruction), while *dvidarbhaṇa* (the doubling of syllables) is used in *ākṛṣṭi* (attraction).
In rites of eradication and killing, the sprout (pallava) should be employed especially;
whatever is performed that is unspecified or lacks a designation shall be in vain.
The ritual act performed for a specific purpose is said to grant success for that purpose;
however, in the case of liberation, penances, and the seven types of impurities, it shall be recitation (japa). 178.

One should perform the rite of driving away (*udveṣaṇa*) in summer; in the rainy season, there shall be the rite of expulsion (*uccāṭana*); one should perform the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) in the cold season, and likewise other rites during spring. (179)
Peaceful rites are prescribed for the forenoon; those for the sake of victory are for midday;
eradication occurs in the afternoon, or alternatively, the cold-season rite is for midday.
In the winter season, ritual action is praised during the forenoon and also at midday;
in the period after half a watch has passed, ritual action in winter is commended. (181)
In the latter watch after half a watch has passed, it is the *makara* [sign] during the afternoon;
at midnight it would be the *cāra-da* [sign], and the *vāsanta* [sign] occurs when half a watch remains.
Peace everywhere. [The section on] "To be Contemplated" is completed.
p.
1231) The Great Festival Arising from Yoga: Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of rites for the festival of Śiva.
For the sake of the cessation of all faults, it brings happiness to the entire world. || 1 ||
It shall be for the sake of pleasing all the gods, bringing happiness to all living beings,
yielding crops and fruits for the kingdom, and bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It is for the sake of the victory of kings and for the accomplishment of all forms of protection;
it provides for festivals with their various divisions, in abundance and accompanied by victory.
That which is expressed by speech is called the "articulated sound" (*śabdabhāṣita*);
because it brings about the manifest creation, it is sequentially described as the "festival" (*utsava*). || 4 ||
The ritual for the festival of consecration, as well as the sequence of rituals for the monthly festival;
likewise, the monthly festival beginning from the new moon day (amāvāsyā). || 5 ||
(1232) Likewise, the ritual for the Spring Festival (Vasantotsava) is performed during the months of Puṣya;
and on the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra, as well as the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of that month.
In the month of Vaiśākha, the spring festival ending with the Viśākhā constellation must be performed;
indeed, the entire sequence of the great festival rites should be carried out in every month.
Having determined the auspicious lunar mansion for the seat, the festival was thus proclaimed:
the sixteenth [day] for the sake of all protection, and likewise the twelfth day of Caitra.
It is said that [the lunar day] brings happiness for nine days, and it becomes auspicious for seven days;
likewise, the earthly [day] lasts five days, and similarly, it brings increase for two days.
A wise person should cause a festival of Śiva alone to be celebrated for one day,
preceded by the hoisting of the banner on the twenty-seventh lunar mansion.
p.
1233) Beginning first with the beating of the drum, it shall last for eighteen days.
Having first performed the rite of sowing the sprouts, one should subsequently worship the banner. || 11 ||
One should cause the drum to be beaten, and there shall be the worship of the deities of the weapons;
one should perform a festival for all, and first of all, one should worship the bull.
On the night preceding that day, one should perform the sacrifice of the bull;
one should prepare the pavilion according to the sequence beginning with the consecration.
The characteristic of the banner is that it should be made of white cotton;
it should be twelve cubits long, or ten, or even nine.
The pinnacle (śikhara) of the banner should be one-fifth of its length and exactly one cubit;
the tail (puccha) is said to be half a cubit, while there may be three tails or two tails.
Having divided that cloth into five parts, one should draw a bull in the central section;
Lakṣmī above it, and water-jars in the lower section. (16)
Above that should be the deity of the weapon (astra), and above that, the parasol and the fly-whisk;
on the sides, however, only a lamp is prescribed, or alternatively, a skull-bowl (kūrma).
It is declared that [the deity] is adorned with incense bells and full water-jars, as well as white and red flowers and every kind of ornament. (18)
One should cause a white-colored bull to bring about all accomplishments;
for desired ends, one should use the color of Hara (Śiva), while for malevolent rites (*ābhicāra*), one should use [the appropriate color]. 19.
The wise one should likewise draw the bull as the bed of Śambhu,
adorned with the hair of a child and yellow in color, according to the prescribed hues.
The eye, however, is black in color; it may also be red, blue, or a mixture of these.
It is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with all kinds of flowers. || 21 ||
In front of Śiva, he should prepare a pavilion that has been washed and smeared with cow dung,
encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with hanging strings of pearls.
In the center of that, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice;
half of that amount with rice grains, and half of that again with sesame seeds.
Having drawn a lotus in the center of that [diagram] with the bull-bannered god (Śiva) in its middle,
one should prepare an altar in front of it and place the Netrabhaṅga [mantra] there.
Having placed eight jars around [the central one], he should worship them in the prescribed order as before;
in the center, having invoked the Bull (Vṛṣabha), he should honor him with perfumes and flowers.
Having placed eight jars all around, one should install them with their respective seed-syllables:
Ikṣu, Gopati, and likewise Śaṅkukarṇa. (26)
One should worship Tīkṣṇaśṛṅga, Anandin, Vṛṣabha, Laja, and Mahodarauṣṭha by their respective names. (27)
One should place the bull-pitcher (vṛṣakumbha) in sequence with the mantra of Vṛṣagāyatrī;
in front of that, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of white sand.
The preceptor should fashion a square seat measuring one cubit;
there should be three lines for the east and likewise three lines for the north.
With the mantra "brahmajajñānaṃ," one should draw the central line;
with the mantra "nāke suparṇaṃ," the wise one should draw [the lines] on the south.
With the mantra "āpyāyasva," one should draw [the lines] on the north;
likewise, with the mantra "yo rudraḥ," one should draw the thread toward the north.
One should draw the eastern line with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," and one should draw the western line with the mantra "indraṃ viśvā."
Having sprinkled the *kūrca* with auspicious water, one should worship it for a span of twelve fingers;
one should then worship Vāgīśvara, Vāgīśī, and the seat.
Having established the fire before that [image] and performed the fire-oblation (homa),
the wise preceptor should perform the consecration of the fire as before and worship the bull.
Having worshipped Brahmā in the south and Viṣṇu in the north,
one should offer darbha grass and other materials upon the sacrificial strewn grass (paristaraṇa) and spread them out.
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel above and the *praṇītā* vessel below,
and having likewise placed the *ājyasthālī*, one should then place the *carusthālī*. (36)
Having placed the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels facing the *sruk* and *sruva*, one should then set down the *ājyasthālī* with its opening turned downwards. || 37 ||
With a fuel-stick (*samidh*) measuring a span (*prādeśa*), as well as the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*);
preceded by two fuel-sticks, [he should perform]... || 38 ||
There, one should prepare the fuel and kindle the fire in due order;
one should offer three oblations and perform the homa with the Vyāhṛtis in sequence. (39)
The wise practitioner should perform oblations in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
therein, he should offer three oblations with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
One should offer the fuel sticks with the Sadyojāta mantra and the clarified butter with the Vāmadeva mantra;
the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the parched grain (lāja) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra. (41)
One should offer sesame seeds with the *Īśāna* mantra and mustard seeds with the *Kavaca* mantra;
likewise, one should offer an *āḍhaka* measure of mung beans and black gram (*māṣa*) in the same sequence.
One should offer ten oblations for each [deity] with the Śiva-mantra;
at the conclusion of the homa, there should be a bull-vessel (vṛṣakumbha), and that bull-vessel shall be embodied.
At its front, there should be the deity Bherī; one should arrange it with a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as the presiding deities (adhidevas). || 44 ||
One should worship Lord Bhairava with perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings; the preceptor should then strike [the drum] in due order.
Having summoned the musicians afterwards, [he should perform] the Śuddhapāraśiva [rite],
likewise joined with the limbs (aṅga), complete, and accompanied by Śakti. (46)
A wise person should perform [the rite] without one who lacks power;
however, having invoked Nandikeśvara, he should avoid musical instruments that do not bring success to the heart. 47.
The sacrifice shall consist of incense and lamps; one should place a flower in the hand [of the deity], and that flower should be cast into the drum while the musicians play in rhythmic unison.
This is declared to be the "Seven-Palm" [mandala] by the teacher or even the disciple;
having worshipped the deity of the weapon (Astra), one should worship Rudra upon the central petal.
One should place Brahmā on the right petal and Janārdana on the left petal;
likewise, one should place Gaurī at the middle node and Sarasvatī on the right.
One should place Lakṣmī on the left petal and Gaṅgā in the center;
likewise, one should place Gaṇeśa in the middle of the *pālikā* and Skanda at the tip of the staff.
One should place Khaṇḍya in the infinite direction (the center) upon the *pālikā*;
likewise, Kṣetrapāla in the northeast, and the Teacher (Śāstṛ) in the middle of the staff.
One should worship the moon, sun, and other lunar mansions within the staff (daṇḍa),
and Caṇḍeśa at the base of the staff, along with all the gods in their collective assembly.
Having invoked all the deities, one should perform the rite with the Astra-mantra alone,
offering incense, lamps, and the food offerings for all the deities.
The Astra-deva Liṅga, the Bali-vessel, likewise the Praticandradhara, and also the Vṛṣadhvaja. || 55 ||
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and worship the deities of the offerings (bali-devas).
Having invoked the deity of the day, one should place him either before the pedestal or at the tip of the banner. (56)
The first is the Night of Vighna; the second is that of the Piśācas;
the third is the Night of Brahmā; and the fourth is that of the Gandharvas. || 57 ||
The fifth should be the Bhūtarātra, the sixth indeed the Guharātra;
the seventh should be the Ṛṣirātra, and the eighth the Nāgarātra. || 58 ||
The ninth is Indrarātra, the tenth is Viṣṇurātraka;
the eleventh is Rudrarātra, and the twelfth is Śivarātrika. || 59 ||
The thirteenth is the Gaṇarātra, the fourteenth is likewise the Rākṣasa,
the fifteenth is the night of the Teacher (Śāstr), and the sixteenth is the Śaktirātra.
From Vighna up to Śiva, there is indeed the ancestral festival (paitṛka-utsava);
and from Vighna up to Indra, there is indeed the festival of happiness (saukhya-utsava). || 61 ||
The festival shall last for seven days, beginning with Vighna and ending with the night of the Sages (Ṛṣirātra).
Furthermore, the festival of the earthen image (pārthiva) likewise begins with Vighna and concludes with Bhūta.
The festival shall last for seven days, beginning with Vighna and ending with the night of the Sages (Ṛṣirātra).
Furthermore, the festival of the earthen image (pārthiva) begins with Vighna and concludes with Bhūta. (63)
From Vighna up to Brahmā, as well as the Sāttvika festival,
the first night of the festival for Gaṇapati may thus take place.
First, having offered a cake, sesame powder, and pure food to Vighnarāja, one should cast the bali offering during the Vighnarātri rite.
On the second day, while reciting the Paiśāca mantra, one should offer pure rice and *kṛsarā* rice mixed with black gram and immersed in curd. (66)
Pure food, *bṛhatī*, clarified butter, curd, and milk—
these should be given on the third day as a mixed offering, while recollecting the Brahma-mantra.
On the fourth day, one should offer kṛsarānna, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), clarified butter, and plantains along with sugar-cane juice, while reciting the Gāndharva mantra.
On the fifth day, one should offer food made of mung beans mixed with molasses, along with honey, milk, and ghee, while recollecting the mantra of Bhūta.
On the sixth day, one should offer milk-rice and ghee combined with plantains and sugar-cane, while recollecting the mantra of Skanda.
On the seventh day, one should offer pure food mixed with ghee and the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant, while recollecting the mantra of the *ṛṣi*.
It is recorded that [the offering] should consist of rice, black gram, honey, ghee, and sugarcane;
it should be given on the eighth day while recollecting the mantra of the Nāgas.
On the ninth day, one should offer pure food, ghee, milk, and likewise jackfruit and mango, while recollecting the mantra of Manu.
Pure rice mixed with curd and combined with jaggery and sugar-candy, along with plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and coconut fruits. (74)
On the tenth day, while recollecting the mantra of Viṣṇu,
one should give food made with black gram mixed with ghee, as well as milk, jaggery, and sugar-candy.
One should perform eleven offerings while recollecting the Rudra-mantra,
[offering] pure food mixed with curd and combined with the root of the *bṛhatī* plant. (76)
On the twelfth day, while recollecting the Śiva-mantra,
one should give kṛsarā-rice, ghee, clarified butter, honey, milk, and fruit.
On the thirteenth day, while reciting the mantra of the Gaṇas,
one should offer food consisting of mung beans mixed with black gram, along with molasses, milk, and ghee.
On the fourteenth day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the Rākṣasa mantra:
milk-rice mixed with ghee and combined with jaggery and sugar-candy.
On the fifteenth day, while recollecting the mantra of the Teacher,
one should give pure food, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), clarified butter, plantains, and kāravallikā.
On the sixteenth day, one should administer the root of the *vallī* creeper, as well as the tuber (*kanda*), cow's milk, and ghee, while recollecting the Śakti mantra. (81)
Having invoked the deity of the day, one should always perform the sequence of offerings (bali) in this manner;
one should cast the offering for the world-protectors (lokapāla), beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
Pure food mixed with ghee, along with curd and milk as the "mixed" offering,
should be presented in due order as the bali for the Vāstu-bhūtas at the western gatehouse.
From Brahmā to Nirṛti, and from Varuṇa onwards in a clockwise direction—
one should perform the sequence of offerings in this manner and cast the bali daily.
Having offered an oblation at that gate,
one should then offer an oblation there to the bull and to the deities beginning with Jyeṣṭhā and ending with Vighna, each by their own name.
Having invoked the deity of the day, one should offer the *bali* in front of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
One should offer the entire *bali*, from the flagstaff (*dhvaja*) down to the *balipīṭha*. || 86 ||
One should offer a bali-oblation at the front of all temples and at the village gate; one should offer a bali-oblation to the goddess Mahāmoṭī-Durgā at the well;
and one should offer a bali-oblation to Sundarī in the cremation ground and at the temple storehouse. || 88 ||
Listen now to the procedure for casting the *bali* offering with the respective mantras of their individual names:
one should perform a circumambulation of the village and cast the *bali* at the great sacred seat (*mahāpīṭha*). (89)
One should discard the food-liṅga upon the great pedestal of the Liṅga;
however, one should cast it into water as an offering to the spirits (bhūtakam) and release the food-liṅga.
One should perform the offering for invocation (*āvāhana-bali*) as well as the offering for dismissal (*udvāsana-bali*),
following the sequence of thirty offerings on the sixteenth day itself. (91)
On the twelfth day itself, one should perform twenty-four offerings;
on the Saumya day, one should likewise perform eighteen offerings—thus it is prescribed.
One should cause the Kauśika rite to be performed on a single day by Manu; this is declared to be the number of offerings (bali). Now hear the procedure for the festival.
The wise man should cause a festival to be held under an auspicious lunar mansion;
however, if the festival for the installation and so forth is deficient, he may observe the month as desired.
On a lunar mansion auspicious for the birth of a king, and one that brings happiness and joy, the door-sill (*dvārapīṭha*) was indeed raised up by the gracious [deity]. 95.
One should perform the festival after repairing those [temples] whose structural members have been pervaded by defects;
however, one should avoid the festival if the pinnacle (śikhara) is deficient for the consecration.
The primary limbs, secondary limbs, and minor limbs, together with their retinue,
as well as the temple doors and so forth— this is what is described here.
But when the festival is deficient, the wise man should avoid it;
if the festival is commenced despite being deficient, he may observe it as desired month by month.
Having performed [the rite] hastily, one should later perform the festival;
due to defects such as the lapse of time, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). || 99 ||
During a disturbance of the king, one should not perform festivals or even minor celebrations;
once the kingdom and the king have attained peace, one may perform a festival again.
And in a month devoid of the previous festival, one should celebrate as desired;
one should perform the rite of atonement and carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
The month, the lunar mansion, the sacred ford, the end of [the rite], the end of Ārdrā, and the supreme festival.
The wise [preceptor] should determine the village, the asterism, the limit of the sacred ford,
and the asterism for the installation itself according to the asterism of the king's birth or according to the will of the patron.
The lunar [measure] refers to the previously mentioned nakṣatras, while the solar measure is that of the *tīrthaka*.
At that time, the wise man should begin the *tīrtha* and continue until the *saṃkrānti*. 104.
Even when Jupiter or Venus are in their state of setting (astama), one should perform the festival during that month;
thereafter, the wise man should have the image fashioned from the prescribed materials.
One should cause the festival to be performed in all months in due order.
The festival is of three kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). (106)
One should perform the perpetual festival constantly, and especially the occasional festival;
the optional festival is said to be according to one's desire—thus the festival is of three kinds. (107)
Thereafter, one should perform the perpetual festival and the occasional great festival;
the wise man should cause the festival for specific desires to be held during the months favorable for those wishes.
Except during the perpetual festival, one should not perform the great festival; moreover, a wise person should avoid the hoisting of the banner.
One should act according to the desire of the patron, measuring [the temple] as desired month by month;
one should not place a banner atop a banner, but rather a bull-banner atop a banner.
p.
1253) One should perform the Śiva-sacrifice, which is declared to bestow auspiciousness upon Viṣṇu;
one should also perform the sacrifice to the deities, but one should avoid the Viṣṇu-sacrifice. || 111 ||
One should not cause even the gods, nor kings and others, to perform auspicious rites in a village, a city, a town, or a capital. 112.
One should perform the festival for all the gods upon a single object;
there may be Hari [therein], and the back of Hari is indeed beautiful. (113)
One should perform the festival for all the deities according to the sequence of offerings within a single sacred site;
the wise man should first conduct the festival during an auspicious month.

In the month of Māgha, [the rite lasts] until the end of Māgha; in Phālguna, until the end of Uttarā; in the month of Caitra, until the end of Citrā; and in Vaiśākha, it is indeed until Viśākhā. (115)

In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the festival lasts until the end of the root [nakṣatra], ending on the eighth day of the dark fortnight; in Āṣāḍha, it ends under the Pūrva-nakṣatras, and in Śrāvaṇa, it ends with Vaiṣṇava. (116)
One should arrange for the Rohiṇī constellation during the third days of the bright fortnight;
when the month and the lunar mansion are both complete, a bath in the ocean is most excellent.
In the month of Bhādrapada, the festival ends with Pūrvāṣāḍhā; in the month of Aśvina, it ends with Aśvinī; and in Kārttika, the supreme festival ends either with Kṛttikā or Ārdrā.
In the lunar month, however, it is extensive; in the solar month, it is highly praised;
in the asterism, it is a universal festival; and in the solar [reckoning], it indeed marks the end of happiness.
Their undertaking is of three kinds: preceded by the tying of auspicious knots, preceded by the beating of drums, and preceded by the offering of ritual sprouts. || 120 ||
The sprout of the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) is established at the end of the bull;
the second is the festival-sprout (*utsavāṅkura*), and the third is the sacred ford-sprout (*tīrthāṅkura*). (121)
One should perform the festival for all [the deities]; the sprouting [of the seeds] is of two kinds:
the opening of the eyes and the releasing, excluding the ritual immersion in water.
The preceptor, with the hand of the artisan, should perform the opening of the eyes;
in the midst of that [ritual], there should be rice grains and likewise up to the bull and the water-pot.
One should place the bull and the other [deities] into the jar using the jar of the eight directions;
there, one should cause the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) and perform a fire sacrifice (homa), especially.
At an auspicious moment, the wise one should prepare a golden needle,
as well as honey and clarified butter, and likewise perform the touching of the eyes.
One should likewise offer incense and lamps, and the vision of grain will arise;
one should perform the consecration with a mirror and present an offering of mung-bean rice. (126)
One should dismiss the artisans and likewise smear the pavilion with cow-dung;
having thoroughly decorated it, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center.
And one should draw a lotus there, with a bull and a water-pot in the center;
around it, one should place eight jars, beginning with the bull, in their proper order.

One should cause a golden nail and a blade of dūrvā grass to be placed upon the sacrificial mound there; at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should perform the opening of the eyes with honey and clarified butter as the collyrium.
The wise one should display the mirror joined with the ritual substances for the consecration; he should likewise cause the mirror, the water-impregnation, and the installation to be performed.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and likewise smear it with cow dung;
within the pavilion, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) using eight *droṇas* of rice.
Having fashioned a lotus in the center of that, the wise one should install the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) and bind the marriage-thread (kautuka) with a cord of gold or silver.
Alternatively, there may be a cotton thread; one should tie it to the horn of a bull.
There, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited and bind the protective amulet (kautuka) in the prescribed order.
One should bind a protective thread with the Tṛyambaka mantra;
one should prepare a bed and a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of that, within the bull-vessel (vṛṣakumbhaka).
One should place eight jars around [the central one], beginning with that of the bull, in their proper order;
then, having established the fire in front of them, the Guru should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as previously described.
In front of that, there should be the deity Bherī; one should cause an altar (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared there.
To the west, however, one should gradually prepare an altar with rice for the deity Astra. || 136 ||
Having adorned it with parched grain and flowers and provided it with a garland of darbha grass,
the wise one should perform the fire-oblation according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-rite.

One should place the vessel for sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), the vessel for the consecrated water (praṇītā), and the pot for clarified butter (ājyasthālī). Having prepared a seat in the north, one should arrange it facing downwards.

Taking the vessel for sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), provided with water, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and likewise containing a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca) one span long, he should touch the water three times.
One should sprinkle the ghee-pot, the praṇītā vessel, and everything up to the upward-facing [vessel],
as well as the prokṣaṇī vessel and the water contained within that prokṣaṇī vessel.
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water and joined it with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
one should invoke Janārdana and place it in the north.
To the south, in the water, [he should place] the Brahmakūrca accompanied by flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata);
likewise, he should perform the consecration of fire and the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya). 142.
Having filled the vessel for clarified butter with ghee and placed a grass-bundle (kūrca) measuring one span (prādeśa),
one should perform the touching at the span-measure and then dismiss the fire itself.

One should circumambulate the darbha-grass and the fire, as well as perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya); thus indeed, the consecration is to be performed exactly as previously described.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, black gram, śāli rice, barley, sesame, mustard, mung beans, molasses, and sugar-candy—these ten are prescribed [as offerings]. || 145 ||
Having disposed of the darbha grass used for strewing and the three enclosing sticks, and having placed the fuel-sticks upright, one should immediately perform the sprinkling around [the fire]. (146)
Thus, the consecration of the fire as well as the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) is performed;
the clarified butter is offered with the *sadyojāta* mantra using the left hand. || 147 ||
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, the parched grain (lāja) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
the sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra, and the mustard seeds with the Kavaca mantra.
Mudga beans, māṣa beans, and barley are offered with the Śiva-mantra, as is the root of the vṛṣa plant; and the Gāyatrī is recited one hundred and eight times.

Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of the substances with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should perform the *jayādi* offerings, the re-establishment of the fires (*āgnīndhana*), and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations in their proper sequence.
Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) while recollecting the seed-syllable of fire with his head bowed,
he should cause betel to be offered and perform the visualization of the form within the *vṛṣabha-kumbhaka* breath-retention. (151)
Then the knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root-mantra of Vṛṣabha;
thereafter, he should make the sound of a drum, and then the invocation (āvāhana) is described.
After summoning the musicians, those who are pure Śiva-devotees (pāraśivas) are prescribed [to play];
however, the preceptor (ācārya) shall strike them in sequence for all those who have been initiated.
He should also provide a new upper garment and a sacred thread,
endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of flower.
Accompanied by a handful of flowers and joined with the sound of kettledrums, the preceptor and the disciple alike should strike the nine rhythmic beats (navatāla). 155.
Having fully worshipped the deity of the weapon, the invocation of the deities should take place;
perform the rite of invocation for all [deities] from Śiva down to Caṇḍa. (156)
The wise one should present the oblation; he should present it to all the gods, together with the vessel for the bali offering, as well as the food, the liṅga, and the weapon.
Having taken up the banner, Caṇḍeśvara, the circumambulation of the village,
and the bull-mechanism, one should fasten the banner-peg in due order.
Having invoked the deity of the junction (sandhidevatā) together with the deities of the day,
one should offer the oblation (bali) at the end of the preliminary sacrifice according to the sequence of the internal offering.
Having invoked the deity of the day, the wise one should offer the bali-oblation either in front of the pedestal;
he should worship everything first, and afterwards offer the bali-oblation to Vāstu.
Having taken up a mechanical pedestal made of jewels or likewise of metal,
or else a wooden pedestal, according to the measurement of one palm (tāla). || 161 ||
Alternatively, one should cast the offering for the exterior of the site upon a plantain leaf;
having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should cast the offering for the great seat (mahāpīṭha).
One should offer an oblation (bali) in the water to the forms of the unmanifest Liṅga;
likewise, the flag-cloth and the vessel should be placed at the base of the staff.
The characteristics of the staff have already been described; one may have it made of wood, or likewise, the seat should be made of Khadira, Bilva, or Campaka wood. (164)
It was joined with *devadāru* trees, accompanied by *vyāghra* trees, as well as *madhūka*, *arjuna*, and *kṛṣṇa* trees. || 165 ||
The *kramuka* and the bamboo staff (*veṇudaṇḍaka*) produced from the tree of the Sage should be free from being crooked, split, hollow, or infested with worm-holes. (166)

Thus, a man [should construct] the inner essence (antassāra), while the outer essence (bahissāra) is of the śaktika type; it may extend to the top of the spire (sthūpī), or to the end of the vāgalā, or be equal in measure to the vṛṣasthala.
And that [area] outside should be equal, or equal to the gopura,
measuring thirty-three cubits or twenty-five cubits.
It is also declared that the staff should have a banner at its top;
having taken a branch from a milk-exuding tree, the wise man should fashion it into a pole. (169)
It is said to be four *tālas* in height, provided with three *tālas* [in width],
one *aṅgula* thick at the base, and adorned with four shapes.
Provided with two hollows and endowed with a half-moon [at its tip],
the bamboo staff is prescribed according to the measurement of the *upadaṇḍa*. || 171 ||
One should construct that [upper pillar] at nine tālas; the middle one at seven tālas;
and the lower pillar (upadaṇḍaka) at six or five tālas.
One should also fasten an iron ring to the secondary staff;
the cotton thread or rope should be twice the size of the ring.
The base of the staff, measuring the length of the little finger, should be fixed into the ground;
one should perform the sprinkling of the site while it is joined with the binding of the staff.
One should establish the staff (daṇḍa) upon a cushion made of śāli rice;
the tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana), however, should be made of gems, silver, or metal. || 175 ||
One should attach a staff made of five metals to the base;
it should be three cubits in measure, or one may proceed by making it two cubits in sequence.
There, at an auspicious moment, the wise one should cause the proclamation of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha);
the characteristics of the altar (vedikā) have been declared, as well as its various divisions.
Alternatively, having taken clay, one should fashion [the altar] provided with three tiers,
two cubits in width and one cubit in height.
Its height should be one *ratni* or even just a fist;
its width, however, should be equal to its height, or at best, one cubit (*hasta*). || 179 ||

A wise person should construct the hand (hasta) at the base of the staff (daṇḍa) with a measure of twenty-four finger-breadths according to the *mātrā-aṅgula*; this is declared to be the characteristic of the pedestal (*vedikā*).
The wise one should dismiss the artisan; thereafter, he should smear [the area] with cow dung.
The wise one should then bind the protective amulet (kautuka) firmly upon the middle of the staff.
One should worship Vināyaka there and then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
[one should place] an iron ring upon the root, doubled by a cord.
The wise man should fasten a banner adorned with garlands of flowers, joined with a wreath of *darbha* grass, and beautified with small bells and flowers.
The bull and the water-jar shall constitute the form, accompanied by incense and lamps; and at an auspicious moment, one should perform the hoisting of the banner.
A wise person should join it firmly with cotton;
however, if the healing is done incorrectly, an expiation is prescribed.
Then one should perform the *śānti*-oblation and carry out the re-consecration (*punassandhāna*).
Having invoked all the deities, one should join them at the base of the staff. (186)
Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should bind the deities of the directions in due order,
accompanied by dance and song and endowed with all sounds.
One should offer food made with mung beans, and one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa);
thereafter, one should indeed prepare sacrificial food (balyanna) in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should bestow that which is endowed with the production of a fetus and possesses auspiciousness;
for the wise man knows that an inauspicious girl indeed brings about epilepsy firmly.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
one should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and smear it with cow dung.
Thus, up to Umā and Skanda, one should bind the *kautuka* in due order;
it may be made of gold, silver, or even cotton. (191)
In the rite of binding the protective thread with the *triyambaka* mantra,
one should prepare a small altar (*sthalika*) and a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and place the protector of the thread in their midst.
The attendant, with his hand, circumambulates [the image] clockwise;
it is adorned with new garments and accompanied by the sound of musical instruments. || 193 ||
One should cause him to stand before it and then have him recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
with the *tryambaka* mantra, one should firmly bind the protection-thread (*rakṣāsūtra*).
One should depict [the deity] together with Umā, or indeed as Candraśekhara alone;
thereafter, one should construct a flower garland, or a peaked roof (kūṭa), or a pavilion (maṇṭapa).
Whether in the direction of Indra, or Agni, or Yama, or even Rākṣasa;
or in Vāyu, Soma, or likewise in the north-east (Īśānī)—there, one should construct the sacrificial pavilion. || 196 ||
Having thoroughly decorated the pavilion, construct an altar within it,
one cubit in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
It should have a width of two cubits and be joined with a small altar (upavedī);
nine fire-pits constitute the best [type], while five fire-pits would be the middling. || 198 ||
The lowest [type] has a single fire and its shape is either circular or square;
one may construct it with a single fire, or indeed with the eastern and western fires.
The door facing which the liṅga is situated—that door is for the worship of the water-pot (kumbha).
In front of that, the wise practitioner should either prepare a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) or perform the fire-oblation (homa). || 200 ||
It should be provided with sixteen pillars, or even twelve pillars,
or joined with four pillars, and endowed with four gates. (201)
It was joined with twin gate-arches, provided with garlands of *darbha* grass,
equipped with body-wrappings, and adorned with banners and flags.
Above the altar, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice;
half of that [measure] is prescribed for rice grains, and half of that again for sesame seeds.
In the center of that, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp,
one should place Sadāśiva in the middle, and likewise the *kumbha* and *vardhanī* vessels in the north.
These eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras), taking the door-pitcher with their respective mantras, should worship it starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Prākumbha, Agnikumbha, and Nirṛti—these three;
likewise Vāruṇī and Bhūta; similarly Vāyu and Soma; and the triad of Kumbhas at the end of the Yuga in Īśa. || 206 ||
One should worship the door-pitcher with the respective mantra of its own name;
having invoked all the deities, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) accompanied by incense and lamps, the wise one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there and should bind the protective amulet (kautuka) in due order.
Regarding the rite of curiosity (kautuka), it is specifically prescribed for each individual fire-pit;
indeed, the purification of the pit is taught, as well as the kindling of the fire itself. (209)
The procedure for the fire-ritual has been declared; one should perform the oblation at each individual fire-pit.
The wise preceptor, accompanied by his disciples, should perform the oblation. (210)
For the king, [the wood] should be of *pālāśa*, *audumbara*, *apāmārga*,
*bilva*, *khadira*, *nyagrodha*, and likewise *vahlīka*. (211)
Fuel-sticks made of *vaikaṅkata* and *kāśmīra* wood are prescribed, as well as the *darbha* grass for the surrounding strewing and the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
To the east and above, he should offer two pieces of fuel-wood and the *viṣṭhara* grass;
having honored Brahmā on the south and Janārdana on the north.
Having taken the vessels for sprinkling, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel,
and the *praṇītā* vessel, one should worship Janārdana.
The consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) has been described, along with the utterance of "svāhā";
at the conclusion of the oblation, one should offer that bali and place it upon the girdle.

One should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors with their respective mantras bearing their own names. One should perform the external bali-rite and then carry out the internal bali-rite. (216)
Then, one should cast the internal oblation (antarbali) into the fire at the side of the sacrificial pit;
first, eight [offerings] for the Nāgas, and second, twelve and so forth.
Having offered oblations to the various directions, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
recollecting the mantra of Agni, one should join it with the word "svāhā."
Having invoked the form of Agni, one should properly unite it within the center of the pitcher;
there, one should present the sacrificial oblation and all that is to be offered to the deity.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, there should be the sounding of kettledrums, and the ritual of the seven cymbals (tāla) should take place;
thereafter, the teacher and the disciple shall summon the musicians.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, there should be the sounding of drums; one should offer the bali-oblation to the Vāstu-deities.
First, one should perform the internal bali, and second, the bali for the deities of the day.
Listen to the sequence for the consumption of the offerings, beginning from the flagpole and ending at the sacrificial pedestal;
likewise, [the procedure for] the god Umāskandeśvara and the circumambulation of the village.
In that same manner, one should place the deity in a palanquin,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and endowed with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and by those reciting hymns of praise and auspicious verses;
there were also the parasol, the fly-whisk, the fan, and the banner.
Immediately following this, the Yantradīpa, joined with all the deities, belongs to all the devotees, as well as to kings and Brahmins. 225.
The Teacher on the right side, the King on the left side,
Rudra joined with Kanyā, and Gāndharva in front of Śiva. (226)
One should perform a circumambulation of the village, as well as the assembly hall and the pavilion;
[one should offer] water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya), accompanied by incense and lamps.
The wise and learned man should worship throughout the night and cause the sacred ash to fall;
likewise, he should offer a mirror, a chowrie, a fan, and a parasol.
Thereafter, accompanied by the king and his devoted subjects, he should cause the sacred ash to be distributed,
together with coconuts and plantain fruits.
One should offer consecrated betel-leaves;
the sacrifice shall commence from that day and last for seven days.
On the seventh day from that date, for the rite of anointing with oil,
one should prepare an auspicious assembly pavilion smeared with cow dung. (231)
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there using eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
in its center, one should place clarified butter together with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). || 232 ||

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, the wise man should indeed offer clarified butter upon his head, together with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). || 233 ||
Having had him bathed with fifty or twenty-five [measures] of oil-anointing mixed with the sounds of celestial drums and other instruments, || 234 ||
Clad in pure garments, adorned with white garlands, endowed with pearl ornaments, and anointed with white sandalwood paste. || 235 ||
Accompanied by abundant offerings of food and provided with side dishes,
betel-leaf should be presented along with incense and lamps. (236)
One should worship throughout the night and the wise man should cause ashes to be distributed;
he should perform the circumambulation of the village and offer lamps upon entering.
From time to time, especially, one should perform the external fire-oblation (bahirhoma);
thereafter, one should perform the oblation-offering (balihoma) accompanied by the King of Mantras, the Astra-mantra. || 238 ||
One should then offer the *anna-liṅga-bali* and the *candraśekhara-bali*;
at night, one should perform the *bali* for all [deities].
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and enter one's own residence;
then, on the eighth or ninth day, the ritual procedure for the fragrance festival (gandhotsava) should be carried out.
On the third or the second day of that [lunar] day, the planting of the sprouts should take place;
however, on the night preceding that day, perform the auspicious *kautuka* ceremony. (241)
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there accompanied by song, graceful dance, the *bhujaṅga-trāsa* movement, and a single rhythmic dance.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, as well as an assembly hall;
on a pure ground smeared with cow dung, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila).
With eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, half of that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*),
and half of that again combined with sesame seeds, one should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity.

Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, and adorned it with parched grain and blossoms, one should place three pedestals in its center while reciting the mantra "brahmajajñānam. (245)
With the mantra *nāke suparṇam*, he should likewise draw the thread on the south;
with the mantra *āpyāyasva*, he should gradually draw [the lines] on the north.
With the mantra "yo rudra," he should likewise [draw] the north-south thread;
then, with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," he should mark the lines toward the west in due order.
With the mantra "idaṃ viśvam," one should draw the first line;
one should place [the object] in its center and then perform a circumambulation from left to right.
One should worship Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśī with their respective mantras in due order;
having first prepared their seat, one should likewise prepare the Praṇītā and Prokṣaṇī vessels.
One should especially prepare the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) along with the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva),
as well as three fuel-sticks (samidh) and the three enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should fill it with water in due order;
then, one should prepare the *prokṣaṇī* by adding *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). || 251 ||
Having taken the *praṇītā* vessel, which is joined with water, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
and having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) toward the north, one should worship Janārdana.
Having released the knot of the *kūrca* grass, they [placed] the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the ghee, and the thirty-fold *kūrca* for touching within the midst of the fire.
