Likewise, having circumambulated the fire clockwise with the *darbha* grass used for consecration, one should subsequently offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and the mantras beginning with "brahmajajñānam. (254)
Having first consecrated the sacrificial grass for the strewing and the three enclosing sticks, as well as the seat (viṣṭhara),
one should perform the oblation of fuel-sticks.
One should offer clarified butter with the *samidh* mantra and the *sadyojāta* mantra using the left hand;
having offered the *caru* with the *aghora* mantra, one should then offer parched grain (*lāja*) with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra. || 256 ||
Sesame seeds are offered with the *Iśāna* mantra, mustard seeds with the *Kavaca* mantra, and green gram, black gram, and rice with the *Netra* mantra. (257)
Milk-rice and jaggery-sugar are offered with the Śiva-mantra;
one should perform this for each [ingredient], offering ten oblations for each individual item. (258)
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
At the end of each substance, having offered the Vyāhṛtis and performed ten additional oblations, one should conclude the rite.
Offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while recollecting the fire-seed syllable with his head bowed,
he should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) at the end of the homa and again perform the rite for the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
With the *triyambaka* mantra, the wise one should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*) upon Naṭeśvara; he should then fasten the protective thread on the left hand of Śakti.
The protective cord (kautuka) belongs to the weapon-deities, while the mudrā and water for the feet (pādya) are for the protective cord itself;
the wise man should worship throughout the night, accompanied by incense and lamps.
At the specific moment of Sumuhūrta, one should especially bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
there, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are conversant with the four Vedas.
The wise one should offer dance, song, instrumental music, and the recitation of Purāṇas in succession, presenting cakes along with an abundance of food offerings.
Then the mantra-practitioner should offer betel;
he should then perform the *ārātrika* ceremony accompanied by incense and lamps. || 265 ||
The wise king should successively show the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the mirror; he should also cause the devotees to receive the remnants of the sacred ash. (266)
Having adorned him with new garments and performed the *kautuka* rite according to the previous sequence,
he should be provided with all ornaments and decorated with pearl jewelry.
Having adorned it with white flowers and smeared it with white sandalwood paste, the flower will not remain like a blue lotus; it shall become so. (268)
Having prepared rice endowed with power, one should perform a circumambulation of the palace, remaining in the assembly hall or pavilion.
Provided with incense and lamps, and especially with the ritual sprinkling (nīrājana) and collyrium,
one should subsequently cause the ashes to be given, as well as the presentation of the parasol and the fly-whisk.
One should cause the king and the people to receive the remaining ashes;
beginning at the time of dawn, one should follow the ritual sequence for the festival of perfumes (gandhotsava). (271)
The preceptor, having thus performed his own ritual bath, should likewise perform the bathing of the image, having adorned it with variegated cloths and decorated it with all ornaments. (272)
Musk, camphor, and black aloe-wood mixed together [should be offered], accompanied by the sounds of conchs and dundubhi drums, and by hymns and auspicious recitations. || 273 ||
Having entered the pavilion of the assembly hall, one should perform a circumambulation of the village;
and when one has arrived in the presence of the deity, one should especially perform a fire sacrifice (homa).

Having established the fire as before, the wise and discerning one should perform the rites prescribed for the fire-sacrifice; having performed the oblation, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
(1286) Endowed with all fragrances and preeminent with black fragrance,
one should smear Naṭeśvara with black fragrance at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa). || 276 ||
Having obtained fragrant substances when possible, the wise man should feed the Brāhmaṇas there at an auspicious moment, accompanied by the Svasti-sūkta.
The weapon-deity (astradeva) and the great drum (subherī) are for the clay instrument,
while the root-image (mūlabera) shall be fragrant and accompanied by its retinue.
One should cause black fragrant substances to be offered to the Lord of Sacrifice and the gods;
one should feed the twice-born who are expounders of the four Vedas in due order.
Pure dance, especially when accompanied by song and instrumental music, as well as the sight of a cow and the auspicious occasion arising from the sight of a maiden—[these bring great merit]. (280)
Having struck the drum and likewise the hand of the preceptor,
the wise one should strike it with the mantra "gandhadvārā". (281)
Having summoned the musicians, he should then place a flower in his hand;
having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) with a prostration, he should strike the musical instruments in sequence.
The procedure for the seven palm-claps has been declared, as well as the preceptor and the disciple;
having uttered the Nandi-mantra, one should strike the clay drum. || 283 ||
Afterwards, the teacher should strike [the drums], and immediately thereafter the musicians [should play] the jhallarī,
the mukha, the paṭaha, and likewise the mardala.
One should then perform the great dance, endowed with great melody and accompanied by the seven rhythmic measures (tāla). || 285 ||
Having paid homage to the God of gods, and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping,
one should especially perform the waving of lights (nīrājana) accompanied by incense and lamps. || 286 ||
Afterwards, the wise one should cause the sacred ash to be given, and then sequentially show the mirror,
the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the fan.
Combined with the remaining ashes, it especially [attracts] kings and indeed the fragrance of all devotees without exception. (288)
A great oblation should be offered, and one should present betel-leaf;
accompanied by incense and lamps, one should worship the Night Goddess (Ārātri) in due order.
Having adorned it with all kinds of flowers, accompanied by every sound,
joined with the blast of conchs and provided with drums and mṛdaṅgas.
(1289) Endowed with the radiance of flowers and possessed of variegated light,
[the image] should be placed in either a chariot or a palanquin, accompanied by various lamps. || 291 ||
Then, having entered the assembly pavilion, one should perform the sevenfold worship (saptāgraha),
accompanied by water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), incense (dhūpa), and a lamp (dīpa).
Then one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and cause the ashes to be offered in due order,
together with coconut, as well as plantain and jackfruit.
Having caused betel-leaf to be offered, one should then show the mirror in due order;
one should likewise provide the parasol and the fly-whisk, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Having performed the ceremonial bath with fifty or twenty-five [substances],
one should arrange the ritual as before after performing the bath.
The wise one should take parched grain flour, powdered dung, and clay;
he should perform the consecration and carry out the ritual bathing in the proper sequence. (296)
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day accompanied by the sound of the Vedas;
[the officiant] should be dressed in white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents. (297)
It is joined with white sandalwood and mixed with camphor;
there is also a white sacred thread and a white upper garment. || 298 ||
The wise man should present the sacrificial offering and provide betel there;
then he should perform the circumambulation of the palanquin and the enclosure wall. || 299 ||
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, as well as an assembly hall,
provided with incense and lamps, and equipped for the *ārātrika* ceremony.
Accompanied by the dance of the Piśācas, there is also the Great Drama (Mahānāṭaka);
beginning at the time of dawn, [the performer] wears a variegated cloth as an upper garment. (301)
Adorned with all ornaments and embellished with every auspicious thing, there were all kinds of auspicious musical instruments, as well as conchs and trumpets. || 302 ||
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and enter one's own abode;
having stayed in the assembly pavilion provided with incense and lamps. (303)
Having worshipped throughout the night, and having especially offered sacred ash,
one should then present the mirror, the fly-whisk, and the fan in due order.
Then the king, especially, should prepare the remaining ashes;
having given the ashes to all his devotees, he should cause them to be distributed.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the prescribed rule, one should then offer as an oblation a jackfruit together with a coconut and a plantain fruit. (306)
Having commenced the hunting expedition, one should perform the preliminary consecration during the first part of the night;
likewise, one should fashion an image of the Destroyer of Tripura that is auspicious and beautiful.
Horse-drawn chariots stood at the edge, while elephant-mounted royal chariots were positioned there; some were moved by artisans at will, or at certain times during the festival of Śiva.
Some were bearing swords, some were wielding axes,
and likewise all of them went forth having donned their bows.
Likewise, at the commencement of battle, all these—deer, birds, boars, peacocks, and cocks—will quickly become agitated. (310)
Adorned with pearl ornaments and accompanied by a forest procession,
he should proceed together with his devotees, speaking with playful grace and charm. (311)
One should perform the circumambulation of Gaurī, Caṇḍeśvara, Mahākāla, and likewise the Bull, and then enter the temple together with them.
At the time of dusk, the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha) should take place;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva using eight droṇas of śāli rice.
In the center of that, one should fashion a lotus and place a tripod there;
having filled it with rice grains and *śāli* rice, one should place a water-pot in its center while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having likewise worshipped Umāskandeśvara together with the deity of the weapon (Astradeva),
as well as Bherīdeva and the image of Caṇḍeśa.
The wise one should tie the *kautuka* (protective thread), as well as [the image of] Umāskandeśvara;
he should perform the *puṇyāha* rite as before and tie the *kautuka* with the heart-mantra.
One should firmly bind the protection-thread with the *triyambaka* mantra;
one should perform the *kautuka* rite with the *astra* mantra, and the binding of the *kautuka* upon the drum.
At the riverbank, provided with water and sacred bathing-places (tīrtha),
one should invoke all the gods and complete the seven-threaded sacrifice (saptatantu).
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there and place the water-pot in due order;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there, accompanied by perfumes and flowers.
The preceptor, together with his disciples and all the devotees, being a knower of the reality of the weapon-mantra, should perform the rite of the seven palm trees after having bathed.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and enter toward the temple.
Having performed the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha), listen now to the great sacred site (mahātīrtha). || 321 ||
Beginning at the time of dawn, one should perform the supreme bath of nectar;
or else, at the time of the morning conjunction or at the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should perform the sequence of offerings.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village as well as of Umāskandeśvara,
remaining in the assembly pavilion provided with incense and lamps.
Then one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), especially in front of the pavilion,
on a pure ground smeared with cow-dung and decorated with white colors.
In the middle of that, one should fashion a small bowl; the mortar, however, is with the pestle.
The mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the pestle has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
There, one should spread out a cloth together with *dūrvā* grass and flowers;
likewise, a mortar filled with *rajanī* and *droṇa* [grain] should be placed there. (326)
Having performed a special bath accompanied by a Rudrākṣa maiden, he should be adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of sacred ash and decorated with white garments. || 327 ||
One should place a flower accompanied by incense and a lamp upon the *kūrca*;
then, having paid homage to the mortar and the powder of turmeric.
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and provided with all kinds of musical instruments,
having filled the mortar on the night [of the ritual] and being joined in the presence of the deity.
At that very spot, the wise one, having surrounded the auspicious sprouts, should place flowers and a tuft of grass made from unbroken grains of *kuśa* at an auspicious moment.

There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; then, the pouring of oil upon the head, and the ritual of anointing with oil all around the primary image (*mūlabera*). || 331 ||
Having especially worshipped Umāskandeśvara, Astra, Bherī, and Tailaka upon the head with sprouts of dūrvā grass and unbroken grains of rice (akṣata). || 332 ||
One should provide incense and lamps, accompanied by the *ārātrika* ceremony, and there one should offer betel-leaf along with various kinds of solid and soft foods.
There, one should show a mirror, as well as a fly-whisk and a fan;
and there, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with knowledge of the four Vedas.
Every month, at the beginning of the oil-pressing, the wise man should suddenly place a powder upon the heads of the weapon-deities.
Oil and the vessel for the powder, accompanied by the weapon-deity (astradeva),
together with the sounding of a conch— this is the sequence of the offering to the Vāstu deity. || 336 ||
One should see a king surrounded by a wall, filled with jars, and crowded;
he is accompanied by a great army and smeared with oil. (337)
Accompanied by singers, instrumentalists, dancers, or courtesans,
he [established] that sacred site dedicated to Maheśvara on the bank of that river or by a pond.
One should specially prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there according to the prescribed rules;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there, accompanied by perfumes and flowers. || 339 ||
Likewise, one should worship the water-pot with a layering of *darbha* grass,
having invoked all the gods together with all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*).

The procedure for the seven palm-tree measures has been declared for both the teacher and the disciple; by means of the weapon-mantra (astra), a thousandfold ablution is prescribed for all devotees. (341)
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and enter one's own abode;
likewise, there should be the ceremonial bathing of the root deity and the bathing of the image.
There, one should worship the Lord of Sacrifice (Yāgeśa) and perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, the preceptor, together with his attendants, should lift up the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha).
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and likewise of the pavilion in front of Śiva;
there, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day and have the consecration performed.
One should perform the auspicious ceremonial bathing of Yāgeśvara, adorned with a cloth, there at the outer seat (pīṭha) of the gods, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
And one should likewise perform the ceremonial bathing of Umāskandeśvara there;
one hundred and eight [offerings] is best, as are fifty or twenty-five. (346)

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the gods with eight droṇas of śāli rice, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) there and perform the ritual bathing (snapana). || 347 ||
One should cause him to wear clean garments, to be beautifully adorned with white garlands, and to offer sacrificial oblations along with betel-leaf. || 348 ||
Having offered incense and lamps, especially performing the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
and observing a vow of silence, everyone likewise performed the circumambulation of the village.
Having taken parched grain and flowers, and having had the Brahmins recite auspicious blessings,
the preceptor should then enter the temple and perform worship.
There,
with the materials for the sacrificial assistance, garments, gold, and finger-rings,
one should feed the Brahmins along with the attendants of the devotees. (351)
Having worshipped the deity Dhvajadeva, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice;
then, one should perform the ritual descent accompanied by conchs, kāhala trumpets, and mṛdaṅga drums.
Accompanied by the sound of drums and adorned with all ornaments,
one should circumambulate the enclosure wall and perform the Caṇḍa-sacrifice.
Having bathed Caṇḍeśa and endowed him with garments and ornaments,
one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) accompanied by oblations (homa) in front of Caṇḍa.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should offer a bali-oblation and present betel-leaf,
having especially honored [the deity] with incense and lamps.

Having taken up the weapon-deity (astradeva), which is joined with its own insignia (liṅga) and accompanied by the vessel for the offering (balipātra), one should perform the bali-offering while maintaining silence. || 356 ||
All those observing the vow of silence should bid farewell to the offering deities;
likewise, one should ensure the lamp is not extinguished and proclaim the name of the Lord of Light.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should offer the bali-oblation at the great seats (mahāpīṭha);
then, having washed one's feet, one should likewise enter the temple.
I shall describe the Gaurīyāga; one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the first part of the night.
Then, at sunset, beginning the festival, [one should worship] Umā, Skanda, and Īśvara.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and then carry out a festival of devotion;
it brings happiness to all people, is meritorious, and increases the prosperity of the entire kingdom. (360)
The festival is declared, in due order, to be the pacifier of all poverty for kings, the increaser of victory, and the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (361)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the festival of the Yoga-born [Śiva].
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva.
With one lotus root, and with the stalk, leaf, and flower,
as well as with one linga, the festival arises in due order.

The *liṅga* is indeed the root of the lotus, while the stalk of the lotus is known as the banner (*dhvaja*). Maheśa and the others are the petals, and the *kumbha* and so forth are known as the flower. || 2 ||
The three channels (nāḍīs) are indeed merged within the Liṅga during the festival of Śiva,
especially in the jars of Maheśa and others, and in the banners.

Clarified butter and other offerings should be poured into the fire; having attained satisfaction therein, Śiva is worshipped with mantras and water-pots in the jar, and Sadāśiva, who is satisfied in the liṅga, is worshipped. || 4 ||
Initiation (dīkṣā) is of two kinds: that which is preceded by consciousness and that which is without consciousness;
the former consists of four varieties of initiation based on prior impressions (saṃskāra). || 5 ||
The fourfold expiation consists of: from the plowing up [of the site] to the consecration; from the consecration to the worship; and from the worship to the festival. (6)
The period beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration is proclaimed as the *samaya*.
The wise know that worship is of four kinds: special (*viśeṣa*), optional (*kāmya*), regular (*nitya*), and occasional (*naimittika*).

The purification of the festival banner and the ritual bathing at the conclusion of the pilgrimage site constitute the expiation; it is recorded in the tradition that this applies even when the subsidiary rites have been omitted.
From the ritual bath at the conclusion of the pledge (samaya-snāna) up to the purification by the fulfillment of knowledge (jñānapūrti-pavitraka),
and from the hoisting of the banner (dhvajāroha) up to the pilgrimage to the sacred sites (tīrtha), this constitutes the tenfold duty (daśakārya). || 9 ||
These ten varieties are applicable to the three categories [of ritual objects]:
the sowing of seeds and sprouts, and the hoisting of the banner.
All this is the very nature of reality; within it is seen the arrangement [of the mandala].
Through it, there occurs the purification of the path via sacrifice and initiation—the form of the Self mounted upon the bull.
The vision of the self as the rider of the chariot, the purification of the self through the black ointment,
and the observation of the lamp are remembered as the form of Śiva.
One should know that the sight [of the deity] is the *tīrtha*, while the ritual bath with the water-pot is *yoga*.
The procession (*yātrā*) of Maheśa is Śakti, and it is traditionally remembered as the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of Śiva. (13)
Thus, the ten rites are said to constitute the festival of initiation (dīkṣācotsava).
The flagstaff is to be known as the Lord (pati), and the bull situated upon the flag is the bound soul (paśu). || 14 ||
The triad of powers—will, knowledge, and action—constitutes this triple staff.
The staff is indeed the sound, while the ring is the bindu;
the agency of the festival is said to be the hoisting of the banner. (16)
Oṃ, let us know that Great Lord; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is purified;
may that Śiva inspire us. || 17 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one with seven tongues; may we meditate upon the bearer of oblations;
may that Agni inspire us. || 18 ||
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva;
may that Rudra inspire us. [Gāyatrī of Rudra] 19.
Oṃ, let us know Nārāyaṇa; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May that Viṣṇu inspire us. || 20 ||
Oṃ, let us know Him who is mounted upon a swan; let us meditate upon Him whose hand holds the *kūrca*;
may that Brahmā inspire us. (21)
Oṃ, let us know Gaṇāmbikā; let us meditate upon Umāśakti;
may that Goddess inspire us. || 22 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one with the curved trunk; may we meditate upon the one with the winnowing-basket ears; may that elephant-faced one inspire us.
Oṃ, let us know the Wielder of the Bow; may we meditate upon all accomplishments;
may that Dharā inspire us. (24)
Oṃ, may we know the Great Goddess; may we meditate upon the Consort of Rudra;
may Gaurī inspire us. || 25 ||
Oṃ, let us know Him who has sharp horns; let us meditate upon Him whose feet are the Vedas;
may that Bull inspire us. || 26 ||
Oṃ, may we know all powers; may we meditate upon the one of seven forms; may those Mothers inspire us. || 27 ||
Oṃ, may we know that Viśākha; may we meditate upon him who holds a bow in his hand;
may Skanda inspire us. [Gāyatrī Mantra] 28.
Oṃ, may we know her who bestows fruits, and may we meditate upon her who destroys sin;
may that Jyeṣṭhā inspire us. || 29 ||
Oṃ. We know Kātyāyanī; we meditate upon Kanyākumārī. May that Durgā inspire us. (30)
Oṃ, may we know the one with the horse-banner; may we meditate upon the one with the lotus in his hand;
may that Sūrya inspire us. || 31 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one whose banner is the fish; may we meditate upon the one who holds a lotus in his hand.
May that Hero inspire us. || 32 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one whose banner is the swan; may we meditate upon the short one.
May that Brāhmī inspire us. || 33 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one whose banner is the bull; may we meditate upon the hand;
may Śaṅkara impel that for us. 34.
Oṃ, let us know the one whose banner is the peacock; let us meditate upon the one who wields the spear;
may that Kaumārī inspire us. || 35 ||
Oṃ, let us know the one whose banner is the discus; let us meditate upon the one who holds the conch in his hand.
May that Vaiṣṇavī inspire us. || 36 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one whose banner is the buffalo; may we meditate upon the one who holds a staff in his hand.
May Vārāhī impel us toward that [goal]. || 37 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one whose banner is the elephant; may we meditate upon the one who holds the thunderbolt in his hand;
may Indrāṇī inspire us thereto. || 38 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one who holds a noose in his hand; may we meditate upon the one who holds a trident in his hand;
may that Cāmuṇḍī inspire us. || 39 ||
Oṃ, let us know the one who holds a trident in his hand; let us meditate upon the one whose vehicle is a dog;
may that Bhairava inspire us. [Gāyatrī Mantra] 40.
Oṃ, let us know the King of Birds; let us meditate upon the one with white-cornered eyes;
may that Peacock inspire us. || 41 ||
We know Mahāsena; we meditate upon the six-faced one;
may that Skanda inspire us. || 42 ||
Oṃ, may we know the one of white complexion; may we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk;
may that Lord of Elephants inspire us. 43.
Oṃ, may we know him who holds a staff in his hand; may we meditate upon him who holds a ṭaṅka-axe in his hand;
may that Nandin inspire us. || 44 ||
Oṃ, let us know him who holds the ṭaṅka-weapon in his hand; let us meditate upon him whose mark is Śiva; may that Caṇḍa inspire us. || 45 ||
Oṃ, let us know him who holds a lotus in his hand; let us meditate upon him whose emblem is Gaurī;
may that Caṇḍī inspire us. 46.
Oṃ, may we know the one with variegated hands; may we meditate upon the swan of the wings;
may that Swan inspire us. || 47 ||
Oṃ, may we know the King of Serpents; may we meditate upon the King of Nagas;
may Ananta inspire us. || 48 ||
Oṃ, let us know the one who is the sky and beyond the sky; let us meditate upon the one who is subtle and beyond the subtle; may that Rudra inspire us. || 49 ||
Oṃ, may we know that Great Lord; may we meditate upon Him whose speech is pure;
may that Śiva inspire us. || 50 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon. Oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon. This is the Śiva-weapon.
Oṃ prasphura prasphura, you whose form is most terrible and more terrible than the terrible, caṭacaṭa! || 58 ||
*Pracaṭa pracaṭa kuha kuha vama vama bandhaya bandhaya ghātaya ghātaya!* Thus is the Aghora-weapon mantra. 59.
Oṃ śrīṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ. Homage to the Pāśupata weapon.
Thus ends the Pāśupata weapon. || 60 ||
Oṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ! O Śṛṅkhalā residing in Rudra, O Sarvatobhadra! O you who uphold the command of Kaṭirudra, protect us; may Pratyaṅgirā bestow prosperity upon us. 61.
Dhāma jyotiḥ, jyotiḥ suvaḥ, suvaḥ bhūpate namo 'stu svāhā! Thus [ends] the Pratyaṅgirā-weapon. || 62 ||
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Maheśvara. Oṃ hlīṃ haṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. || 63 ||
Oṃ hyāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Śiva together with Sūrya.
Oṃ gaṃ gāṃ gauṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ sauṃ, salutation to Ṣaṇmukha, born from the Śaraṇa reed-thicket. || 64 ||
Oṃ tumburu tumburu, obeisance to Ānanda Tāṇḍaveśvara! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra! Oṃ juṃsaḥ oṃ! || 65 ||
Hrīṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka for the removal of calamities;
Oṃ haṃsaḥ, obeisance to Śiva—this is the five-syllable mantra of the self.
The three-syllabled *onnamaḥ* is *oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ*; "salutation to Mahī, who pervades the sky.
Thus is the *Śāmbara*. *Iṃ kṣmraṃ* is for the principal [deity];
*phaṭ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ* is the triple refuge. || 67 ||
Vra śirase svāhā; O, the seed-syllable of the razor for initiation; Oṃ ṣaṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ vyomavyāpine huṃ phaṭ. This is the twelve-syllable mantra. (68)
O tranquil one, praised by the Puruṣa of the Praṇava! Oṃ juṃ saṃ | Hrīṃ, salutations to the Vidyā for protection from weapons. || 69 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ vaṃ, obeisance to her who consists of the Supreme Power (parāśakti). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhuvaneśvarī. || 70 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Mahāgaurī. || 71 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Umādevī.
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. || 72 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Kamalavāsinī. Oṃ raṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ traṃ haṃ, obeisance to Amṛteśvara. || 73 ||
"Hauṃ" he spoke the Siddhaprāsāda; "Hauṃ" he spoke the Kalāprāsāda; "Hrīṃ" he spoke the Kamalākṛtaprāsāda; "Hāṃ" he spoke the Kṣamaṇaprāsāda. || 74 ||
I declare the Haṃ-annastha-prāsāda:
*hṛṃ sṛṃ kṣmṛṃ ḷṃ vṛṃ śraṃ traṃ ūṃ*. I declare the Kaṇṭherṇya-prāsāda. || 75 ||
He speaks of the palace of the reality of the Self: * * * * * * *.
He speaks of the palace of Āditya: * * * * * * *. || 76 ||
Āṃ Saḥ—this he calls the Ātmaprāsāda mantra. Oṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ Śivāya Namaḥ. This is the five-syllabled Prāsāda mantra. || 77 ||
"Namaḥ śivāya"—this [mantra] is both gross and subtle... [omitted].
The gross form is "namaḥ śivāya," while the subtle form is established as "namo 'ntaṃ śivāya. (78)
This [work] has thus been completed.
